summary: What's changed Added permissions.blockWritesOutsideWorkingDirectories : Write, Edit and NotebookEdit refuse paths outside the working directories in every permission mode Added an optional groups list to Claude apps gateway upstreams: only developers in the listed IdP groups are sent to that upstream, on failover too Added guardrail_trace to Claude apps gateway Bedrock upstreams, to log which Amazon Bedrock guardrail filter fired on a request, without the matched text Added idle compaction...
content: What's changed Added permissions.blockWritesOutsideWorkingDirectories : Write, Edit and NotebookEdit refuse paths outside the working directories in every permission mode Added an optional groups list to Claude apps gateway upstreams: only developers in the listed IdP groups are sent to that upstream, on failover too Added guardrail_trace to Claude apps gateway Bedrock upstreams, to log which Amazon Bedrock guardrail filter fired on a request, without the matched text Added idle compaction to VS Code and Claude Desktop's Code tab: a 200K+ token conversation left idle is summarized, and the summary is used on your next message if the prompt cache has expired Fixed sessions failing turn after turn with "Invalid effort level" when an organization's admin caps a model's effort: Claude Code now lowers the effort, retries, and says which level it uses Fixed claude -p exiting with code 0 and no output when startup failed; it now prints the error and exits 1 Fixed Bedrock sessions with many images failing every turn and /compact with "400 Input is too long." instead of removing older images and compacting Fixed Microsoft Foundry sessions failing when the resource has no deployment for the default Sonnet, Opus or Haiku model: Claude Code now falls back to an older model of that family Fixed repeated refused requests behind a gateway that doesn't accept tool search's tool_reference blocks: the request is sent again once without tool search, and the session remembers Fixed TLS connections failing with UNABLE_TO_GET_ISSUER_CERT when the system certificate store holds a renewed root certificate that is cross-signed with its predecessor Fixed MCP servers that also work without sign-in showing "needs authentication" after their stored sign-in stopped working; they are now used signed out Fixed claude mcp logout reporting success when the MCP sign-in was not removed, for example while the macOS keychain is locked over SSH Fixed extra sign-in renewals when several sessions share an Anthropic profile login and the credentials lock is busy Fixed claude ultrareview and claude remote-control asking the workspace trust question in a CI job that has a terminal; with CI set they now refuse an untrusted folder at once Fixed an administrator's TLS trust settings in managed settings not being applied in Claude Desktop sessions Fixed model switching being refused on machines with managed plugin settings when one of your own --plugin-dir or --plugin-url plugins had a broken manifest or failed to download Fixed the Bedrock and Vertex model upgrade offer coming back at every start when managed settings pin the model Fixed forceRemoteSettingsRefresh set only in remote managed settings no longer applying once the stored copy had expired, which let sessions start without policy when the server could not be reached Fixed "Continue automatically at usage limit" continuing more than three times without a prompt from you when a task restarted itself between waits (a /goal check-in, a background or scheduled task) Fixed background and cloud sessions started with Ultracode turning it back on at their next start after it had been switched off Fixed the last broken reply and its retry prompts staying in the conversation after Claude gave up on a tool call that could not be parsed Fixed a PreCompact hook with very large output making compaction fail or repeat; each hook's output is now cut at 10,000 characters Fixed background diff refreshes briefly taking the repository's index lock, which could make a git command run at the same moment fail with "Unable to create '.git/index.lock': File exists" Fixed markdown tables jumping between grid and stacked layouts on half-typed rows while streaming, and long tables falling back to raw pipes Fixed the /resume picker showing the text of CLAUDE.md or CLAUDE.local.md as a session's title when the session only ran slash commands Fixed /btw answering from the main conversation when asked from a subagent's open transcript Fixed pasting an image over SSH to a Linux machine doing nothing silently; the prompt now says to copy the file over and paste its path Fixed claude remote-control sessions that failed to start when the session service was slow for a moment: the worker's registration is now retried with growing waits Fixed model switches over Remote Control that take over 8 seconds getting a "still pending" error instead of the final result Fixed the sandbox.excludedCommands setting description saying listed commands always run outside the sandbox; it now says every command in a call must match an entry Fixed shell and MCP calls that auto mode, a deny rule or a PreToolUse hook blocked, or that otherwise did not run, reading as if they ran in a collapsed tool group Fixed sandbox protections not applying to a worktree entered by claude -p --resume or --continue Fixed hooks matching Bash not running on shell commands started by the Monitor tool; such hooks can block or ask, but not approve or rewrite those commands Fixed a settings file excluded with --setting-sources still supplying some settings, such as auto mode rules and saved permission consents Fixed auto mode reporting a call as blocked, and listing it in /permissions , when its safety check gave no verdict Fixed a Claude apps gateway Vertex upstream hanging for minutes when a Google token endpoint accepts the connection and never answers Fixed the Claude apps gateway's start-up warning for a deprecated Claude Desktop key that it still serves as written saying "stops being accepted" after the key's end date Fixed /upgrade opening the browser and starting a new login for plans billed through the App Store or Google Play; it now says where to change the plan Fixed --resume , and rewinding past a switch to another model after a refusal, moving a session on a model name Claude Code doesn't recognize to a different model Fixed requests failing when a gateway or cloud provider refuses one of Claude Code's beta headers by name: the request is sent again without it Fixed model IDs spelled with a dot behind an LLM gateway, such as claude-opus-4.8 , being treated as an older model with the wrong context window, output limit, effort, thinking mode and cost Fixed Remote Control clients showing a stray "Compacted (ctrl+o to see full summary)" row after /compact Fixed the cloud sessions tip and the Remote Control idle notice showing when an organization's policy turns those features off Fixed a resumed claude.ai cloud session making a model call nobody asked for when the previous worker stopped just after receiving a new chat's files Fixed WebFetch in Cowork cloud sessions silently dropping a PDF's text past 100,000 characters; it now says how much was unread and where to read on Fixed Claude being told only that a command was declined after you stopped it with Esc or Stop in a cloud session or the IDE; it now also hears that the command may have run Fixed blank lines at the top of a code block disappearing when the code block opens a quote Fixed a blank line appearing above some ⎿ rows in the transcript view (Ctrl+O) Fixed vim mode dw , dW , yw and yW carrying on past the end of the line, and made w and W stop on empty lines Fixed x and Enter in the agent panel sometimes acting on the wrong agent when another agent started or finished Fixed pasted text and dragged-in files being lost in Claude's question dialog unless the "Other" row had focus Fixed pasted text being lost when a row in the prompt footer was selected Fixed vim mode p over a character selection ignoring whether the yanked text was whole lines Fixed vim mode aw and iw taking the line break at the end of a line Fixed ↓ selecting footer items hidden by the ? help menu, the command list or a paste hint Fixed Esc on a command's panel, such as /btw , also interrupting the subagent whose transcript is open Fixed the welcome header in fullscreen mode showing the session's model while viewing a subagent or teammate that runs on a different model Fixed the fullscreen transcript being left mid-conversation after "Restore conversation" in the rewind menu while scrolled up Fixed a rare case where a deleted session could reappear in the resume list as an almost empty entry Fixed prompts containing tags such as or not being acknowledged to a local stream-json host Fixed sessions staying untitled when the first prompt failed (for example on a usage limit) and the conversation continued afterward Fixed the skill file watcher checking every removed skill kept in ~/.claude/skills/.trash , which added file system load that grew with each removal Fixed the session name from /rename disappearing while Claude asks for permission or a plan decision, so side-by-side sessions stay identifiable Fixed background sessions that fail to start being reported as a deleted daemon binary when the binary is still on disk Fixed the tip and idle reminder about push notifications appearing when the push settings in /config are hidden or your organization has turned off Remote Control Fixed ~/.claude/skills/.trash and ~/.claude/plugins/.trash growing without limit: each now holds about 1024 entries, whatever cleanupPeriodDays says Fixed the Bash edit diff listing a whole file as changed when a CRLF file under git's line-ending conversion was re-saved unchanged or had one line edited Self-hosted runner: Fixed an idle session moving to another runner instead of pausing when the runner's request to pause it lost its connection before Anthropic answered Improved memory use in long headless and SDK turns that run many subagents: the parent session no longer keeps each subagent's tool results until the turn ends Improved prompt history: Ctrl+R now matches text inside collapsed [Pasted text] pills Improved the /design-sync upload prompt to show the folder, the project and the files it will upload or delete Improved /permissions review tab, now called Recently blocked: the footer says what Esc will do with marked rows Improved auto mode's blocked calls: messages name the command, say Claude may retry and auto mode checks again, and point to /permissions to review Improved permission prompts: a long reason takes fewer rows, so it pushes the command being approved off the screen on fewer terminals Improved the cloud session error shown while a request refused for your claude.ai login is still being retried: it now also suggests claude auth login Improved the behavior of stored claude.ai, Team, and Enterprise logins when MDM and remote settings differ on base URL or apiKeyHelper Improved /config in agent view to say how to stop agent view opening by default Improved session auto-titles: a session that starts with a skill or a prompt-based command such as /security-review now gets a title from it instead of staying untitled Improved --resume speed and memory use on damaged transcripts Improved /context speed in sessions with ten thousand or more MCP tools Self-hosted runner: Improved the error shown when a session's branch isn't on the git remote: it now covers a never-pushed branch, says how to fix each case, and no longer suggests retrying Updated the /claude-api skill: its Datadog setup for API tracing now sends the dd-llmobs-enabled: true header, as the Console does, and its ant install instructions drop the outdated macOS xattr step Updated the bundled dataviz skill to advise printing y-axis tick labels in full under 10,000, and horizontal ones in full under a million where they fit Updated the bundled dataviz skill to answer donut and pie chart requests with ranked bars or a segmented bar that prints its values Changed Claude's file tools to ask before editing the local copy of your organization's server-managed settings, as they do for your settings files Changed /ultrareview to check workspace trust before it runs git, as claude ultrareview does Changed the Bash tool's shell to clear any inherited which alias or function and to stop passing exported which / unsetenv functions to commands, so which is the system command or zsh builtin Changed /permissions Recently blocked to refuse approving a call you can't read in full, including one the terminal is too short to show Changed auto mode in Cowork cloud sessions: a hook's allow of an MCP tool call now counts as no answer, so the classifier or a permission prompt decides Changed hook if conditions such as Monitor(tail *) to match the Monitor tool's shell commands as Bash(tail *) matches Bash's Changed the claude-api skill to ask to read a Managed Agents workflow run's workflow before changing the agent to improve that run Changed flagged requests to retry on another model, not end in a refusal, when ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL , availableModels or deniedModels leaves only an older Opus model, or none Changed idle compaction to also run for subscribers with telemetry turned off, and on Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry and LLM gateways once the one-hour prompt cache is on Changed FORCE_HYPERLINK=false (also no and off ) to turn hyperlinks off instead of on macOS: Changed git grep in most commands that Claude runs to use the C locale, to avoid a reported memory leak in macOS's regex library on files that aren't valid UTF-8 [VSCode] Fixed "Clear authentication" for MCP servers reporting success when the saved sign-in could not be removed [VSCode] Fixed missing spinner and Stop button while a queued message's hooks run [VSCode] Fixed session group changes that cannot be saved, such as a delete, failing silently; an error notification now appears [VSCode] Fixed Cmd+F / Ctrl+F not opening the find widget in the plan preview tab [VSCode] Fixed the voice dictation shortcut (Ctrl+D) doing nothing under non-Latin keyboard layouts such as Russian, Greek or Hebrew [VSCode] Fixed missed one-time saved scheduled tasks being deleted without asking when the extension opened without a chat [VSCode] Changed CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_CFC_PROMPT to also stop the extension adding the Claude in Chrome instructions to a session's messages; the browser tools stay available [Cloud sessions] Added an Include completed button to the Scheduled tasks page when finished one-off tasks are the only ones hidden, so you can show them without opening the Sort menu [Cloud sessions] Fixed recently used self-hosted environments never appearing among the recent environments on the new session card [Cloud sessions] Fixed cloud sessions reporting uncommitted changes every turn after Claude moved a branch to a commit it had pushed from another worktree [Cloud sessions] Fixed the self-hosted environment details dialog in admin settings squeezing its content out of view in very short windows or at high zoom; the dialog now scrolls [Cloud sessions] Fixed the permission mode picker staying on Auto after a running cloud or Remote Control session refused the switch; it now shows the mode in use and tells you [Cloud sessions] Improved scheduled tasks: runs in Anthropic's cloud now load the plugins enabled on your claude.ai account [Cloud sessions] Improved Test connection for GitHub Enterprise in admin settings to also connect the way cloud sessions do, and to warn you when that second test fails [Cloud sessions] Improved cloud session transcripts: a rename row now names the new title, and repository and environment lists show as a table instead of one line of JSON [Cloud sessions] Changed cloud sessions from the web, desktop and mobile apps to start even when a setup script exits with an error, instead of failing to start [Remote Control] Fixed the permission mode button in Remote Control sessions showing the wrong mode until you typed; while your computer is online it now shows the real mode on open [Claude Tag] Added a dismissible link to the Claude Tag API docs on the Bundles and Channels tabs in admin settings, for Enterprise organizations with Slack connected [Claude Tag] Fixed @Claude !restart giving up after one failed workspace check in channels shared across Enterprise Grid workspaces; it now retries, then asks you to run it again [Claude Tag] Fixed a second confirmation DM and channel note when you connect your Claude account from Slack twice from the same link within a few minutes [Claude Tag] Fixed follow-up messages in Slack showing no sign of progress while Claude's session waits for a self-hosted runner; Claude now posts a wait notice in the thread [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude sometimes not answering a tag in its own thread in Slack Connect channels where both organizations have installed Claude [Claude Tag] Fixed Retry on plugin and skill pages in Claude Tag admin settings discarding unsaved access changes after a failed load; your edits now stay in place [Claude Tag] Fixed the repositories control in Claude Tag admin settings showing the same action twice; its menu now lists only what the button doesn't already do

content: This is a gateway-only extended-stable release, which is our current equivalent to LTS. This release is OpenClaw from the end of September 2026, plus critical security updates, reliability and performance fixes, and features like new model support. The latest version of OpenClaw at the time of this release is 2026.10.9 2026.9.36 Highlights Failed updates stay recoverable: a failed npm rollback no longer leaves the installed package missing, and update checks keep Doctor recovery guidance, stop recopying private rehearsal databases, and no longer reopen candidate-migrated state. Fixes #184889 . ( #185160 , #186177 ) Thanks @syxscott , @LiuwqGit , and @RomneyDa . Workspace restrictions reach Gateway-built tools: with tools.fs.workspaceOnly , openclaw delegates built through Gateway loopback and skill dispatch now require approval as intended, and media tools stay inside the workspace. ( #185094 ) Thanks @eleqtrizit and @RomneyDa . Microsoft Teams allowlists stay restrictive: name-keyed teams or groupAllowFrom entries that do not resolve now grant nothing instead of opening the bot to every team or group. ( #184989 ) Thanks @eleqtrizit , @RomneyDa , and @shakkernerd . Untrusted input is bounded: malformed media metadata, inbound mail addresses, TOML, URIs, oversized collections in custom A2UI schemas and Discord's embedded SDK, and response-controlled Microsoft authentication routing can no longer cause unbounded work or alter identity. ( #187288 , #187282 , #187283 , #187305 , #187289 , #187287 ) Thanks @RomneyDa and @cyyynthia . Replies keep their text: comparison prose after emoji and other astral characters is no longer stripped from outbound replies. ( #187415 ) Thanks @RomneyDa . Changes Certificate trust and Docker images: the eMudhra trust remediation is applied, and Docker release images carry source/version-bound evidence with more reliable architecture builds. ( #186639 ) Thanks @RomneyDa . Fixes Credential and content boundaries: derive the filesystem policy for Gateway-built OpenClaw tools, keep unresolved Microsoft Teams allowlists closed, and scope the patched MSAL to the affected Teams and Azure Identity consumers. ( #185094 , #184989 , #187287 ) Thanks @eleqtrizit , @RomneyDa , and @shakkernerd . Untrusted parsing: bound Matrix media metadata and IMAP mail parsing, the TOML key parser, URI parsing, and oversized Zod collections in custom A2UI schemas and Discord's embedded SDK. title: How the UK Amazon Quick User Group grew in 2026
summary: The UK Amazon Quick User Group's 2026 roundup: three quarterly meetups, 150+ attendees, and customer stories from Arriva, Carsa, and Propulse Lab on using agentic AI and Amazon Quick to turn data into faster decisions, higher satisfaction, and scalable growth.
content: The Amazon Quick User Group – United Kingdom is a community of Amazon Quick users in the United Kingdom who meet quarterly to exchange knowledge, share best practices, learn through hands-on sessions, and discuss their experiences using the service. These user groups function as collaborative forums where members learn, connect, and innovate together. Whether you’re already using Amazon Quick or just getting started, we’d love for you to join the UK Amazon Quick User Group and become part of a growing community that’s redefining how organizations make decisions with data. In this post, we’re thrilled to share our 2026 yearly roundup, highlighting all three quarterly meetups that have taken place since the group’s launch and the momentum that has followed. The events drew more than 150 attendees, and the energy in the room, fueled by agentic AI and the potential of Amazon Quick, was clear. Across industries, customers are using Amazon Quick to turn data chaos into faster decisions, higher satisfaction, and scalable growth. Their work spans real-time incident management, eliminating dashboard sprawl with governed data layers, and automating most support workflows with AI. Why Amazon Quick user groups matter The UK Amazon Quick User Group is a local community of Amazon Quick users who come together quarterly to share knowledge, best practices, and experiences with the service. Amazon Quick user groups serve as collaborative forums where members can: Learn and share – Exchange real-world insights about the capabilities of Amazon Quick, from interactive dashboards and data storytelling to agentic AI-powered automations and custom agents. Members share what works, what doesn’t, and new approaches that drive results. Network – Connect with regional professionals who are solving similar use cases with Amazon Quick for enterprise AI applications, data analytics, and workplace productivity. Problem-solve – Tackle challenges collaboratively by discussing solutions and use cases across different industries and business contexts. Stay updated – Get firsthand knowledge about new features, updates, and emerging best practices directly from peers and experts. Build community – Foster a local support network that complements the broader Amazon Quick community, with trusted contacts who understand UK market and business context. Event overview Over three quarterly meetups this year, the UK community spent real time with Amazon Quick. Not slide decks about it, actual time building with it. People created Amazon Quick custom chat agents for their teams without writing code. They tried Amazon Quick Desktop running on their own laptops, connected to local files and using a connector to access Outlook. They also used Amazon Quick Apps to turn a plain-language description into a working web application. The workshops had attendees automating processes with Amazon Quick Flows and Amazon Quick Automate , while Amazon Quick Research showed how it significantly cuts down the time spent on research. The Amazon Quick chat agent tied it together, an assistant that connects to tools, data and takes actions on your behalf. Every quarter, the sessions got more practical and the questions from the room got sharper. What a typical event looks like All three events were held at the Amazon UK Corporate Office in Shoreditch, London. By 9:45 AM, the room is already buzzing. People reconnect over coffee, swap updates from the last quarter, and newcomers get pulled into conversations before the day even officially begins. From there, the energy carries through the full agenda: customers share real stories about what they’ve built with Amazon Quick, product leads walk through the latest updates, and panels spark the kind of back-and-forth you don’t get from a webinar. The 75-minute hands-on workshop is where it really comes alive, with attendees rolling up their sleeves in provisioned sandbox accounts and experimenting together. By the time we close with a feedback session, the room feels more like a working group than an audience. The format has shifted each quarter. Q1 leaned more on introductions and demos because the group was meeting for the first time. By Q2, we added an icebreaker quiz, and ran a focused workshop on Quick Flows and automation. For Q3 we brought in a specialist panel, a group quiz, and a networking slot at the end. That last one came about because people were already staying behind to talk after the close, so we stopped packing up around them and put it in the schedule. Figure 1: Attendees at a UK Amazon Quick User Group meetup What customers shared Customer stories have been part of the community from the start. Each speaker brought a different problem into the room, showing how teams are applying Quick in very different environments. At the first event, the conversation centered on getting insight into the hands of the people who need it. At Arriva UK Trains, critical data wasn’t reaching the people who needed it most. Train and station managers were constantly on the move, relying solely on their work mobiles. Sofia Bourika’s team built dynamic, role-based dashboards with mobile-friendly views and introduced pixel perfect reports automatically delivered through scheduled email, giving managers immediate visibility of incidents and performance. The result: faster decisions, better incident management, and a stronger data-driven culture across the organization. By Q2, the discussion had moved toward a different challenge: getting the foundations right before introducing more AI and automation. At Carsa , a used-car retailer, analytics functioned like a service desk. Question in, dashboard out. The same question gave different answers. It wasn’t a data problem. It was a definitions problem. Tobi Daramola’s team at Carsa fixed this by building a single governed data layer, with metrics defined once and consumed by Amazon Quick and AI assistants alike. As a result, they removed 50 percent of dashboards while surfacing more data. Customer satisfaction (CSAT) scores moved 10 percent in 30 days, complaints same-day close rate jumped 20 percent, and AI on the layer cut recurring tasks from 45 minutes to 5. Q3 brought the conversation further into automation and agentic workflows. Propulse Lab , a Swiss operating system for B2C subscription businesses, was handling 1 million support tickets a year. Their teams were stuck firefighting instead of driving growth. After deploying a multi-agent AI pipeline in Amazon Quick Automate, built from their best past customer service interactions, they cut request handling from 7 minutes to 70 seconds. The pipeline also automated 80 percent of routine workflows. “What was once a cost centre became a growth engine – their product managers now own the entire system without writing a single line of code, and their support teams focus on proactive, revenue-driving conversations instead.” — Guirec Lecointre, Growth Operations Specialist, Propulse Lab The use cases vary widely, and that’s exactly the point. Rather than presenting a single vision for Amazon Quick, practitioners show what they’ve tried against real business problems, from governed analytics and frontline reporting to automation and AI. That shifts the conversation in the room. Attendees ask direct questions about implementation, adoption, and what didn’t work. Speakers share the practical lessons behind the finished solution. People leave with ideas they can apply to their own organizations, not just another customer story. From presentations to participation Attendees changed across the three events. A listen-and-learn turned into building meaningful relationships by Q3. People were new to the group and new to each other. By Q2, the icebreaker quiz loosened things up early. The feedback sessions got more specific too: instead of “this was great,” people were requesting topics and offering to contribute. Q3 pushes this further. Sofia Bourika, who joined the leadership team early on and presented the Arriva customer story at the first event, came up with an icebreaker called “What Are You Proud Of?”, attendees share something they’ve built with Amazon Quick. We’ve already got someone who was previously sitting in the audience volunteering to present their work. That kind of shift, from attending to contributing, took three events to happen, but it happened. Q3 also introduced a new segment, the Amazon Quick specialist panel. Questions were pre-collected from the audience and posed to an invited specialist, who brought real depth to the answers and shared first-hand experience of working with attendees’ customers. It sparked a different kind of thinking in the room, with the audience connecting the dots between the specialist’s insights and their own day-to-day challenges. Our community stayed connected all year. Our LinkedIn group had weekly contributions and our email lists encouraged involvement. Collective impact in action A huge thank you to our dedicated AWS Partner, Data Reply , whose consistent contributions and thought leadership have been instrumental in making every UK user group meetup a success. Our UK leadership team led us to reach every milestone: Liam Yusuph , AI and Data Delivery Lead, Data Reply Priyanka Bettaswamygowda , Solutions Architect, AWS Sahar Shahbaz, Data Analyst, Data Reply Sofia Bourika, Lead BI Developer, Arriva Tobi Daramola, Senior Data and Analytics Lead, Carsa Ali Hayat , AV Support Associate, Amazon Lam Phan , BI Developer, AWS Rikhi Singh , ADC Engineer, AWS Figure 2: The UK Amazon Quick User Group leadership team Amazon Quick Community resources The Amazon Quick Community website has tens of thousands of members and thousands of searchable questions. It also offers over 600 learning resources on accelerating your productivity with agentic AI and Amazon Quick. “The Quick Community is about learning together and building connections. It’s where users at any skill level can find help, learn something new, and meet others. What I love most about the Quick Community is how genuinely helpful everyone is. It’s a place that reveals possibilities you wouldn’t have thought to explore on your own, where you stumble into people working on projects and use cases, you’d never even think to ask about, and suddenly your world gets a whole lot bigger.” — Kristin Mandia, Sr. Community Manager, AWS Learning opportunities include approximately two free live online sessions per week, monthly feature update detailed and advanced automation sessions, and 4-hour Immersion Day workshops. AWS Solutions Architects, Product Managers, and subject matter experts are active on the platform and available for direct messaging. Kristin continues, “People jump in to help solve tricky problems, share their clever workarounds, and experiment with new ways to use Quick together.” Key takeaways A few themes came up consistently across the three events. The format keeps changing because we listen The Amazon Quick User Group UK runs on a set structure: an introduction, a product update, customer stories, a hands-on workshop, and a feedback session. But we’ve been adjusting it every quarter. Early on, we had the “What’s New with Quick” segment right after customer stories, and it broke the flow. People were engaged with how a real company was using the product, then we’d switch to feature announcements. We moved “What’s New” so the customer stories lead straight into the workshop, and the difference was noticeable. For Q3, we added an interactive quiz to get more back-and-forth going in the room. Attendees also called out the overall format and pacing, and the chance to meet new people. As one first-time attendee put it, “the networking opportunities were excellent… I thoroughly enjoyed the day!”. Customers present, not us At least one customer shares how they use Amazon Quick at each event. Across three events, we’ve had Carsa, Arriva, Propulse Lab, and a few other customers on stage. After the very first event, one of the clearest pieces of feedback was that people wanted more customer speakers. That told us we were on the right track. The sessions work because the audience is hearing from peers who face similar problems, not from someone trying to sell them something. The impact goes beyond the event itself. Attendees said the customer stories showed them new ways to use the tools and started useful discussions about return on investment (ROI). One attendee told us a customer session “has already prompted a lot of conversation internally” at their organization. The workshop is where it clicks Every event has a hands-on workshop, and people consistently tell us it’s the part they get the most out of. There’s a gap between watching someone demo a product and sitting down with it yourself. That gap is where most attendees say Amazon Quick starts to make sense for what they’re trying to do. We know it lands because the most common question afterwards is whether they can keep access to the workshop environment so they can carry on experimenting on their own. Conclusion The success of this year’s meetups is a testament to every single member who showed up, shared their knowledge, and contributed to making this community what it is today. As we look ahead, we’re more energized than ever to keep this momentum going and continue pushing the boundaries of what’s possible with Amazon Quick. Get involved To learn more about Amazon Quick and connect with the community: Join the UK Amazon Quick User Group on LinkedIn . Join the Amazon Quick Community to learn agentic AI together and access over 600 learning resources. Explore Amazon Bedrock for additional generative AI capabilities. Register for the next UK Amazon Quick User Group meetup: January 28, 2027 . Not in the UK? Attend a meetup in Austin, Phoenix, Chicago, Boston, Los Angeles, New York City, or Munich/DACH . Complete the leadership interest form to start an Amazon Quick User Group in your city. For questions about the event or the Amazon Quick Community, Kristin Mandia, Sr. Community Manager, Amazon Quick Community and User Group program, at kmandia@amazon.com .   About the authors Priyanka Bettaswamygowda Priyanka is a Solutions Architect at AWS and has a great passion for Amazon Quick. Priyanka works with customers across the UK regional public sector to help adopt cloud technologies and accelerate innovation. Liam Yusuph Liam is an AI & Data Delivery Lead at Data Reply with a passion for AI-powered analytics and Amazon Quick. Liam leads the delivery of AI and data solutions, helping organizations turn emerging technologies into practical business value.

title: Building intent-driven UI testing with Amazon Nova Act
summary: Epsilon's Agentic Platform team delivers UI testing as a managed, multi-tenant service built on Amazon Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool. Tests are written in plain English and run on browsers managed by AWS, giving every product team resilient, intent-driven testing with zero per-team infrastructure overhead.
content: To scale intent-driven UI testing across its product teams, Epsilon , a data, technology, and marketing-services company and part of Publicis Groupe , turned to Amazon Nova Act . With hundreds of millions of consumer profiles and thousands of brand relationships, Epsilon needed UI testing that could keep pace with rapid application changes. The solution could not create maintenance overhead for every product team. Within Epsilon, the Agentic Platform team (50 engineers) builds shared infrastructure so other product teams can build, deploy, govern, and run AI agents safely. With this shared platform, teams get a skills-based agent builder. They also get federated identity and pre-flight authorization, Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration, and cross-account provisioning. When a product team wants to adopt AI tooling, they get capabilities without additional configuration and without re-solving identity, security, browser infrastructure, or model integration on their own. One of those managed capabilities is UI testing . With Amazon Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser (a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore), Epsilon’s platform team could deliver resilient, intent-driven testing as a service to teams on the platform. In this post, we walk through Epsilon’s architecture for delivering UI testing as a managed platform service, show the core Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool integration code, highlight a concrete 18-step test workflow, and share best practices and measured results. The challenge: Enhancing coverage, not replacing what works Epsilon’s existing UI testing practice was not broken. The team maintained a Playwright-based regression suite that validated functionality across their web applications, and it worked well. Playwright remains their regression backbone today. The opportunity Epsilon identified was additive, not corrective: Scripted Playwright tests are effective for deterministic regression checks. However, they are tightly coupled to selectors and page structure. Cosmetic UI changes can break them even when the underlying functionality is sound. Multiple product teams needed full testing coverage against their own applications. Standing up browser infrastructure, managing dependencies, and integrating with identity systems per team created duplicative effort. The platform team wanted UI testing to be a managed capability that fit their existing agent model, not a custom CLI that every onboarded team had to operate. The goal: layer intent-based testing on top of the existing Playwright regression suite. Deliver it as a multi-tenant platform service so that each Epsilon product team could consume through the same API surface they used for every other agent capability. Why Epsilon chose Amazon Nova Act and the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool Epsilon evaluated options against two requirements: natural-language test authoring (to complement selector-based Playwright tests) and managed browser infrastructure (to fit their multi-tenant platform model). With Amazon Nova Act combined with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool, Epsilon could address both. Natural-language steps. Test steps are plain-English instructions executed by Nova Act. They are resilient to cosmetic UI changes and readable by non-engineers. A step like “Confirm the rewards balance is visible” ages far better than a brittle CSS selector. AWS managed, ephemeral browser sessions. With Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool, teams get isolated browser instances with no binaries to ship and no display server to maintain. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool also offers live view for human observation or takeover (useful for CAPTCHAs or multi-factor authentication), session recording to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), and AWS CloudTrail audit, all without additional configuration. AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM)-based authentication. With Nova Act, you can authenticate through the standard AWS credential chain (the task role). This fits Epsilon’s existing security model without distributing separate API keys. Cross-account friendly. With Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool, you can slot into your existing AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) AssumeRole provisioning. Each onboarded team can run tests inside their own AWS account under a scoped role. This maintains isolation and auditability. Epsilon chose Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool specifically because it eliminates the operational burden of managing browser binaries, display servers, and session lifecycle. The Agentic Platform team had no interest in owning that infrastructure. The solution: Architecture and implementation Epsilon’s solution has three main components: a platform API for creating workflows, a background task runner for executing them, and the Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool integration that drives the browser. Platform architecture Epsilon’s UI testing capability follows a clear pipeline: A user creates a workflow through the platform API, specifying a target_url and a list of natural-language steps. On create, the platform registers a Nova Act workflow definition on AWS. On execute, a background task runner ( Celery , a Python framework for asynchronous job processing) opens an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool browser session. It runs each step through Nova Act over a Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) WebSocket (the standard interface for programmatically controlling Chromium browsers), including conditional logic (for example, “if a tour box appears, skip it” ). The system captures a screenshot per step, tracks pass/fail per step, computes an overall pass rate, and stores everything (results JSON, screenshots in Amazon S3, session ID). A completion hook fires so the result is recorded back into the platform. Figure 1: Epsilon’s UI Testing Service architecture Figure 1 shows the layered architecture of Epsilon’s UI Testing Service. User requests flow from the Agent Cloud Frontend through an API Gateway with authentication and permission checks. The API layer (Django REST) exposes endpoints for workflows, executions, automation suites, and stats. The business logic layer includes a Workflow Manager, Execution Orchestrator, and Suite Coordinator. Test jobs are queued in Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) and picked up by the Runner Service running on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), which contains the Nova Act engine and a headless Chromium browser. Results, screenshots, trajectories, and HTML reports are stored in Amazon S3. The capability is exposed as a standard agent ( ui-test-agent ) with two skills: ui-test-recorder : Explore a scenario interactively and record natural-language steps. ui-test-executor : Run recorded steps and return structured results. Onboarded teams consume UI testing the same way they consume any other platform agent. No additional infrastructure to manage. The onboarding process is straightforward. The platform team provisions a cross-account IAM role for the new team, registers their target application URLs, and grants access to the ui-test-agent through the existing platform API. From that point, teams create workflows, trigger executions, and retrieve results through the same interface they already use for other platform capabilities. The core integration The Nova Act + Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool integration is concise: import boto3 from bedrock_agentcore.tools.browser_client import browser_session from nova_act import NovaAct boto_session = boto3.Session(region_name=region) with browser_session(region) as client: ws_url, headers = client.generate_ws_headers() with NovaAct( cdp_endpoint_url=ws_url, cdp_headers=headers, boto_session=boto_session, starting_page=url ) as nova_act: result = nova_act.act(instruction) This pattern (open a managed browser session, connect through the CDP WebSocket, and drive actions with natural language) is the foundation. Epsilon wraps it with their platform’s multi-tenant orchestration, result capture, and observability layers. Example: Automating the ‘Create an agent’ flow To illustrate intent-based testing, here is a representative workflow from Epsilon’s platform. It exercises login, form entry, conditional handling, scrolling, and verification. The following steps highlight the differentiating patterns of Nova Act: Step Instruction 1 Type the username and choose Next 2 Enter the password and choose Verify 3 Navigate to Create Agent and select the Design a new specification card 4 If an onboarding tour box appears, choose Skip Tour , then verify the correct page loaded 5 Fill in the agent name and description fields 6 Scroll down until the Goal Statement field is visible, then fill it in 7 If the skills search box is not visible, scroll until it appears. Then search for and add a skill 8 Choose Save , confirm the success prompt, navigate back, and verify the new agent appears in the list Steps 4 and 7 demonstrate conditional logic : “if an element appears, handle it” and “if a target isn’t visible, scroll until it is.” These patterns would require explicit branching in a traditional framework. Nova Act handles them naturally through language understanding. Runtime isolation Epsilon runs UI tests in a dedicated runner service (a FastAPI sidecar) that pins nova-act 3.x with Workflow and IAM authentication support, plus the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool client. This keeps dependencies separate from the main backend so they don’t collide with the Strands agent stack. The worker falls back to in-process execution if the runner is disabled, providing resilience during deployments. Best practices Based on their experience building UI testing as a platform capability, the Epsilon team recommends: 1. Write steps as intent, not mechanics GOOD: "Confirm the rewards balance is visible" BAD: await page.locator('#rewards-balance-container > span.amount').toBeVisible() Intent-based steps survive UI redesigns. Product managers and quality assurance (QA) leads who might not write code can review them directly. 2. Isolate the Nova Act runtime Pin Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool dependencies in a dedicated service or container. Epsilon learned that the signing endpoint for Nova Act targets us-east-1 regardless of the browser session’s region. Running it in a separate service with its own dependency lockfile prevents hard-to-debug conflicts. 3. Reuse recorded trajectories to cut cost Epsilon uses trajectory retries in draft state , saves the successful trajectory, and replays it in active state . Repeat runs skip redundant large language model (LLM) “thinking,” reducing both latency and cost for regression-style repeated executions. 4. Design for multi-tenancy from day one Use cross-account AssumeRole with scoped IAM policies. Each tenant’s tests run under their own role in their own account. This provides isolation, auditability, and failure scope containment without custom infrastructure per team. 5. Lean on managed observability With Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool, teams get live view, session recording, and AWS CloudTrail integration. Epsilon uses these built-in capabilities instead of building custom observability, reducing maintenance and giving compliance teams familiar audit surfaces. 6. Account for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool viewport behavior When prompting Nova Act steps, account for the browser viewport defaults of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool. Steps that reference scrolling (for example, “scroll down until the Goal Statement textbox is visible”) verify that Nova Act handles content in the lower portion of the page correctly. Results and impact Epsilon’s UI testing capability is operational across multiple teams, with the multi-tenant architecture proven in production. Dimension Amazon Nova Act Playwright (equivalent) Lines authored 18 natural-language steps ~80-150 lines of code Selector/DOM inspection None Required per interactive step Authoring time (per workflow) ~5-10 minutes ~30-90 minutes Effort ratio Baseline 4-6x more effort Here are the measured outcomes: 4-6x faster test authoring (based on Epsilon’s internal benchmarks). A representative 18-step workflow took 5–10 minutes to author with Nova Act, compared to 30–90 minutes for the equivalent Playwright script (80–150 lines of code). Each interactive step in the Playwright script requires inspecting the DOM, choosing a stable selector, and coding explicit waits, assertions, and branching for conditional cases. Nova Act replaces that per-step overhead with 18 natural-language instructions and zero selector or DOM inspection, with conditional logic (such as the tour-box and scroll-until-visible steps) expressed in plain English. 100 percent pass rate on trajectory replay (based on Epsilon’s internal benchmarks). After a workflow passes the initial explore phase (typically 4–5 prompt iterations), Epsilon saves the successful trajectory and replays it deterministically. Saved trajectories achieve a 100 percent pass rate across repeated runs. Lower barrier to test authoring. Steps read like plain English. Team members beyond core test engineers can read, review, and propose tests, broadening ownership of quality. Built-in audit trail. AWS CloudTrail integration and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool session recording made debugging and compliance conversations easier. This was a benefit the team did not initially set out to achieve. Zero per-team infrastructure overhead. Onboarded teams get UI testing through the same API surface as every other platform agent. No browser binaries, no Selenium grid, no display servers to manage. Pass/fail visibility per step. Screenshot capture at each step provides granular debugging context, reducing mean time to diagnose failures. “Nova Act let us turn UI testing from a brittle, selector-chasing chore into a managed platform capability. Our tests now describe intent in plain English, run on AWS managed browsers, and every product team we onboard gets reliable testing without additional configuration.” — Epsilon Agentic Platform Team Learn more Epsilon’s Agentic Platform team demonstrated how to deliver resilient, intent-driven UI testing as a managed service using Amazon Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool. You can apply the same pattern to your own multi-tenant platform to eliminate browser infrastructure overhead and make test authoring accessible to non-engineers. If you want to build similar intent-driven UI testing capabilities with Amazon Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool, here are resources to get started: Amazon Nova Act Documentation Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool User Guide Nova Act Python SDK on PyPI Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Documentation Nova Act + Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool sample code (GitHub) Related post: Accelerating software delivery with agentic QA automation using Amazon Nova Act To learn more about how your organization can use intent-based browser automation for testing, visit the Amazon Nova Act product page . Epsilon is a Publicis Groupe company. Learn more at epsilon.com .   About the authors Sakthivel Chellapparimanam Sakthivel is a Solutions Architect at Amazon Web Services based in Chennai, India. He works with enterprise customers on AI/ML adoption, agentic architectures, and cloud-native modernization. Sidhartha Kotha Sidhartha is a Technical Account Manager at AWS. He works with enterprise customers on AI-driven solutions and focuses on adopting generative AI for operational efficiency. Outside of work, he enjoys exploring open-source automation frameworks and mentoring aspiring cloud engineers. Manik Sahu Manik is a Senior Software Engineering Manager at Epsilon, specializing in Data Engineering, Agentic AI, and Cloud Architecture. Based in Bengaluru, he brings extensive expertise in designing advanced technical systems using frameworks like FastAPI, Amazon Bedrock, and LangGraph. Swastika Sinha Swastika is a Software Engineer at Epsilon, working on the Agentic Platform team in Bangalore, India. Her work focuses on architecting and building Generative AI platforms and services that enable the building and hosting of AI agents, knowledge graphs, MCP servers, agentic workflows, and other next-generation GenAI technologies. Sekh Mohammad Warish Sekh is a Dallas-based Senior Technical Account Manager at AWS with 22 years of IT experience across GenAI, SAP, and cloud modernization. title: Build a repeatable PHP-to-Java migration engine with Kiro
summary: Turn a PHP-to-Java migration from a one-time leap of faith into a measurable, repeatable process with Kiro. This post walks through a reusable engine: a mechanical discovery scanner and an eight-phase, parity-first workflow that treats the original PHP application as the specification and verifies the Java port with a parity harness.
content: When your team moves a mature PHP application to Java, you gain stronger type safety, broader library support, and more predictable scaling. A PHP codebase built over the years with Laravel, Symfony, or Doctrine carries business rules in places that are not obvious, from Eloquent traits to XML mapping files, so a structurally similar Java port can compile cleanly and still behave differently. This post shows how to turn PHP-to-Java migration from a one-time leap of faith into a measurable, repeatable process using Kiro . Kiro is an AI integrated development environment (IDE) that pairs an AI agent with your codebase to run multi-step engineering tasks with you in the loop. The approach centers on a reusable engine: a shared methodology, a mechanical discovery scanner, and an eight-phase workflow. This engine treats the original PHP application as the specification and refuses to declare the Java port correct until a parity harness verifies it. Prerequisites Before getting started, you need: Familiarity with PHP (Laravel/Eloquent or Symfony/Doctrine). Java knowledge (Spring Boot, JPA) helps you review the generated output, but the engine produces idiomatic Java for you, so you don’t need to rewrite the application in Java yourself. A Kiro workspace with access to Skills and Steering files. PHP 8.0 or newer on the machine running the discovery scanner, and Java 21 with Maven for the generated Spring Boot projects. A basic understanding of migration planning (discovery, translation, and validation). What you will learn in this post You start with an open repository, so you can run the engine yourself rather than read about it. Everything the engine knows lives in a small set of skill files, and with those files, you can run the same methodology in more than one way. Two ways to run the engine: Kiro and AWS Transform Everything here is packaged as skill files: versioned Markdown capability packages that encode the migration methodology (php-to-java-migration) and the discovery scanner workflow (php-model-discovery). Because that knowledge lives in files rather than any one tool, you can run the same methodology in two ways. Method 1: Kiro, interactive and developer-in-the-loop Kiro brings an AI agent into your editor to drive a migration step by step. Open the repository root as a Kiro workspace and the skills activate automatically when you ask Kiro to migrate a PHP application. Kiro then walks the eight-phase workflow with explicit approval gates, so you review the discovery manifest, approve the rulebook, and sign off on each phase before the next begins. It’s the mode used for every example in this post. Method 2: AWS Transform, agentic and at portfolio scale AWS Transform is the AWS agentic AI service for large-scale migration and modernization, and it now integrates natively with Kiro. Through that integration, you can hand AWS Transform the same skill files that govern an interactive Kiro session, so discovery before translation, the parity harness as referee, and ‘ fix the loop, not the code ’ apply to an autonomous run. When each path fits Control and autonomy: Use Kiro to work through the code first: run the skill on one application, read the generated Java, and run the tests. When you want to migrate more, AWS Transform runs the same methodology agentically with review at the checkpoints the skill defines. Scale and novelty: Kiro handles one application at a time and suits first-of-a-kind frameworks. AWS Transform runs many applications as parallel jobs. A shared feedback loop: Both paths read the same skill files, so every rulebook fix made in Kiro improves the next AWS Transform run, and vice versa. Solution overview: One shared brain, many projects The engine is organized around a single principle: one shared brain, many projects. To open it, clone the repository locally, then in Kiro open a folder and select the repository root (the folder containing .kiro/). Kiro loads the skills and steering automatically, with fuller steps in “Getting started.” The workspace separates a shared methodology layer from the individual projects that use it, as shown in the following diagram. At the top is a global .kiro/ layer that every project draws on. Beneath it sit the per-project folders, each with its own PHP source, Java output, and specification sub-folder. Figure 1: The workspace is split into a shared, global methodology layer and per-project code and spec folders Those same shared skill files can be run in two different ways, shown in the following diagram. The identical eight-phase, parity-first pipeline can be driven either by Kiro (interactive, one application at a time) or by AWS Transform (agentic, at portfolio scale), and both convert PHP source into parity-verified Spring Boot Java. Figure 2: The same shared skill files drive two execution paths: Kiro (interactive, one app at a time) and AWS Transform (agentic, portfolio scale). Both run the identical eight-phase parity-first pipeline, converting PHP source into parity-verified Spring Boot Java A shared, global layer under .kiro/ holds two Skills, php-model-discovery (the scanner) and php-to-java-migration (the eight-phase playbook), plus the core-workflow.md Steering file. Each per-project folder holds its own PHP source, Java output, and spec sub-folder under .kiro/specs/, so improving the methodology once lets every project inherit the gain. Discovery before translation The single most important rule fires before anything else: Don’t read, guess at, or hand-translate a model or entity file until the scanner has run. The scanner works in a single pass with no dependencies, as shown in the following diagram. It applies three discovery strategies to the source tokens and emits one JSON manifest, with anything ambiguous routed to a review-flag queue for a human to resolve. Figure 3: The scanner runs three discovery strategies over source tokens and emits a single JSON manifest with a review-flag queue The scanner is discover-models.php, a single-file, dependency-free PHP command-line tool that doesn’t execute the target code. It only reads source text as tokens, so it runs against apps of your choice whether its dependencies are installed. It runs three strategies on every scan: Eloquent model discovery (walking the class inheritance chain to Illuminate\Database\Eloquent\Model), Doctrine attribute detection (the #[ORM\Entity] attribute), and ORM XML mapping (external *.orm.xml files). The output is a single JSON manifest. A models[] array carries every field, cast, relationship, and visibility rule, and a flags[] array appears on every entry. The scanner flags ambiguity rather than guessing. For example, a $fillable list built from a runtime expression becomes a plain-English flag, and that flag list is the human review queue. The parity-first pipeline Phase 0 is preparatory: it runs the scanner and assembles the inventory. The first three phases then concentrate human expertise. Phase 1 builds the parity harness before Java is written, replaying request/response pairs against both the PHP original and the Java port. The harness must pass against working PHP and fail when you break it deliberately, because a harness that misses injected breakage is not trusted. Phase 2 seeds the rulebook and gap inventory (RULEBOOK.md, GAP_INVENTORY.md), and Phase 3 stress-tests it against representative files before committing it across the application. Figure 4: Human judgment is front-loaded into a preparatory Phase 0 and Phases 1–3. Phases 4–8 are mostly self-driving loops, refereed by a parity harness The first four phases concentrate human expertise. Phase 0 runs the scanner and assembles the inventory. Phase 1 builds the parity harness before Java is written, replaying request/response pairs against both the PHP original and the Java port. The harness must pass against working PHP and fail when you break it deliberately, because a harness that misses injected breakage is not trusted. Phase 2 seeds the rulebook and gap inventory (RULEBOOK.md, GAP_INVENTORY.md), and Phase 3 stress-tests it against representative files before committing it across the application. Phase Name Deliverable 0 Assess and discover Model manifest + inventory + cutover choice 1 Build the judge Parity harness runnable against PHP and Java 2 Rulebook + gap inventory RULEBOOK.md, GAP_INVENTORY.md 3 Stress-test the rulebook Hardened rulebook, validated against representative files 4 Scaffold Compiling Spring Boot project 5 Translate the data model JPA entities + schema baseline 6 Translate the I/O layer Controllers, security, templates respond 7 Convert business logic Logic converted, tests green 8 Prove parity and cut over Parity report + cutover checklist Phases 4–8 are mostly self-driving loops: Phase 4 scaffolds the project, Phase 5 translates the data model from the manifest, Phase 6 translates the I/O layer (routes become controllers, middleware becomes filters, validation becomes annotated data transfer objects), Phase 7 converts business logic in batches, and Phase 8 proves parity against the harness and cuts over. Two principles govern the loop. First, the PHP code is the specification: the port is done when the referee agrees, or each mismatch is logged as an approved change. Second, you fix the loop, not the code, amending the rulebook and regenerating rather than hand-patching. Walkthrough: From Eloquent to Spring Boot The laravel-eloquent-sample project is a working, bounded example: a read-only slice of an open source Laravel application, with the Book, Chapter, Page, and User models migrated to Spring Boot 3.4.1 on Java 21 with Maven and an in-memory H2 database. The mapping from PHP to Spring Boot is mechanical and traceable, as shown in the following diagram. Each manifest entry on the left maps to a Java construct on the right, producing the layered runtime architecture of the generated application slice. Figure 5: Manifest-driven mappings on the left. The layered runtime architecture of the generated application slice on the right The mappings are mechanical and traceable back to the manifest: a PHP namespace becomes a Java package, an Eloquent model becomes a JPA @Entity , has Many and belongs to relationships become @OneToMany and @ManyToOne , and Eloquent query scopes become Spring Data repository methods. The discipline shows in serialization: html, markdown, and text carry @JsonIgnore because the manifest recorded them in Page’s $hidden list, while Book’s description deliberately doesn’t. The spec is candid that only 4 of 37 models were ported and, most important, that the parity harness was never built for this slice, which it calls “the single biggest gap.” Documenting where it falls short is itself part of the design. Getting started The complete migration engine is available in the sample PHP-to-Java migration repository . To use it: Clone the repository and open its root as your Kiro workspace (open a folder and select the folder containing .kiro/). Nothing to install beyond PHP 8.0+ for the scanner and Java 21 with Maven. Fetch the PHP source into the project’s source-php/ folder. The README pins the exact upstream commits used for parity so anyone can reproduce the baseline. Ask Kiro to migrate the application. The php-to-java-migration skill activates automatically, runs the scanner first, generates a fresh spec under .kiro/specs/, and walks you through the approval gates. For an agentic run, point AWS Transform at the same skill files, so its agents execute the identical methodology across your portfolio. The methodology auto-detects Laravel, Symfony, CodeIgniter, and plain PHP, and extension is additive: add a detection row and a references/ -to-spring.md guide for a new framework. Because Kiro and AWS Transform read the same files, refining them once upgrades both engines.   Clean up If you deployed the sample Spring Boot application during this walkthrough: Stop the running Spring Boot application (the in-memory H2 database is ephemeral and requires no separate cleanup). Remove the generated Java project folder from your workspace if no longer needed. The discovery scanner produces only a JSON manifest file. Delete the discovery scanner’s JSON manifest from your working directory if you don’t plan to reference it. No AWS resources are provisioned by the migration engine itself, so there are no cloud resources to deprovision.   Conclusion We showed how to build a repeatable PHP-to-Java migration engine with Kiro that turns large-scale rewrites into a measurable, compounding process. The key principles are: Discovery before translation: A mechanical scanner inventories every model, field, and relationship, so you don’t guess at structure. Build the judge before the code: A parity harness defines done before the first line of Java is written. Fix the loop, not the code: When the same mistake appears across files, amend the rulebook and regenerate rather than hand-patching. One shared brain: The methodology is written once, shared across projects, and improves with each migration. None of this is specific to PHP or Java. The same shape applies to other migrations where the old system is the only complete specification. Clone the sample PHP-to-Java migration repository , open it as a Kiro workspace, and explore the Skills and Steering capabilities that power it, or bring the same skill files to AWS Transform. For more about language migration patterns on AWS, see the AWS Prescriptive Guidance documentation.     About the authors Sarat Guttikonda Sarat is a Principal Solutions Architect at Amazon Web Services (AWS), where he partners with Strategic Accounts to design and deliver cloud solutions at scale. Passionate about artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML), he helps customers drive innovation and transformation while preserving business agility. Outside of work, Sarat enjoys playing co-op games on the PS5 with his son, traveling, and playing badminton. Phani Parcha Phani is a Senior Technical Account Manager (Strat) at Amazon Web Services with 22+ years of experience in building and scaling enterprise platforms. He drives architecture excellence, system reliability, and operational performance for large-scale enterprise workloads. Phani specializes in distributed systems, microservices architecture, and cloud-native platforms, with a focus on enabling enterprise transformation and Generative AI solutions. Pallavi Jha Pallavi is a Technical Consultant at Amazon Web Services, helping customers boost developer productivity through Kiro and the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AIDLC). She works with enterprises modernizing their engineering practices, focusing on delivering higher-quality software faster with AI-assisted, spec-driven development. Outside work, she enjoys creating music and hiking.
