title: Lend and borrow resources across teams with AWS Batch’s quota management for SageMaker Training jobs
summary: AWS Batch quota management is a new scheduling capability you can use to divide GPU capacity into quota shares per team or project, automatically lend idle capacity across shares, and use preemption to run your highest-priority SageMaker Training jobs first, all without manual coordination.
content: With the launch of AWS Batch support for Amazon SageMaker Training jobs, customers gained a new fully managed way to queue, schedule, and retry machine learning (ML) training workloads without building their own infrastructure. Instead, they use the queuing and scheduling features of AWS Batch. As organizations scale their artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) operations and onboard more teams, coordinating access to shared graphics processing unit (GPU) capacity can introduce additional communication, coordination, and configuration overhead for administrators. This overhead includes setting up separate queues, adjusting capacity limits, and carefully orchestrating the right workloads to get the right resources at the right time. A core value proposition of AWS Batch is helping customers increase utilization of their compute, and as training environments grow, so does the opportunity to do more with existing capacity. Working backward from customers managing multi-team training environments, we heard a consistent request: give us a way to define allocations per team or project, share idle capacity automatically, and run our highest-priority workloads first. This request led us to build quota management , a new scheduling capability for AWS Batch. Administrators can use it to divide compute capacity into quota shares, organized by team, project, or workload. Each quota share uses configurable resource-sharing strategies that maximize GPU utilization while honoring each team’s allocation when it matters most. This post shows how quota management works, including how to configure quota shares with lending and borrowing strategies, set up in-share preemption for priority workloads, and get started using the SageMaker Python SDK. Quota shares and preemption Administrators can allocate and share constrained GPU resources by defining a quota share for separate entities, such as individual teams or projects. Each quota share includes compute quotas (capacity limits) and resource-sharing strategies for idle compute. These strategies determine whether idle compute is reserved until jobs arrive ( RESERVE ), lent to other quota shares that have work available ( LEND ), or both lent when idle and borrowed when the share has work that might benefit ( LEND_AND_BORROW ). A quota share operates as a virtual queue nested hierarchically within an associated job queue. When scheduling jobs for a job queue, AWS Batch prioritizes quota shares that are under their capacity limits as it iterates through the associated quota shares. If jobs arrive in a quota share that has lent out its capacity, AWS Batch performs cross-share preemption. This reclaims resources for the lending quota share, so administrators don’t need to track down the jobs borrowing capacity and terminate them on their own. If jobs arrive in a quota share that is at or above its capacity limit, AWS Batch checks whether there’s available capacity to borrow from another quota share. If so, workloads can run using otherwise-idle capacity. You can turn on priority-based in-share preemption when you configure a quota share. Where cross-share preemption reclaims lent capacity as jobs arrive in a lending quota share, in-share preemption preempts lower priority jobs that are in the SCHEDULED, STARTING, or RUNNING state. This allows higher priority jobs at the front of the queue to start running sooner. Prerequisites Before you proceed with this example, you must have an AWS account with permissions to create and manage AWS Batch resources. For this example, see the sample IAM permissions needed to invoke AWS Batch and SageMaker APIs. The example uses the SageMaker Python SDK v3. Complete the setup required to install a compatible version of the SageMaker Python SDK: !pip install sagemaker Configuring quota management resources Using the new quota management capabilities requires creating a Scheduling Policy that contains a quotaSharePolicy , a Service Environment that specifies its capacity limits in terms of specific instances, and a SageMaker Training job queue that is connected to both. After that, you can associate quota shares to a job queue. The user guide has AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) and console examples for configuring quota management resources and quota shares . An end-to-end example of quota management integrated with the aws_batch module in the SageMaker Python SDK v3 is contained in a sample notebook . In this example, we step through code snippets that summarize the key components, and use the helper functions from the notebook to create a Scheduling Policy, Service Environment, Job Queue, and three Quota Shares. The three quota shares configured here represent three different projects. Each has the same capacity limit set: a single ml.g5.xlarge instance. The QS1 quota share represents background jobs. For this project, you want to run the most important background job first and borrow as much spare capacity as is available. Within this quota share, no jobs are urgent, and preemptions are acceptable because all jobs use checkpointing. This quota share uses the LEND_AND_BORROW resource-sharing strategy and has in-share preemption turned on. Higher priority jobs within the same quota share can then preempt running jobs that are lower priority. from sagemaker.train.aws_batch.boto_client import get_batch_boto_client from utils.aws_batch_resource_management import AwsBatchResourceManager, QuotaShareConfig, create_quota_management_resources INSTANCE_TYPE = "ml.g5.xlarge" # Create SchedulingPolicy, ServiceEnvironment, JobQueue, and QuotaShares resource_manager = AwsBatchResourceManager(get_batch_boto_client()) qs1 = QuotaShareConfig( name="QS1", capacity_unit=INSTANCE_TYPE, max_capacity=1, in_share_preemption=True, sharing_strategy="LEND_AND_BORROW", borrow_limit=200 ) QS2 represents medium priority workloads. Teams choosing this configuration would prefer to wait for capacity to become available rather than endure additional preemptions. Those preemptions come from borrowed capacity being reclaimed or from in-share preemptions because of higher priority job submission. This is appropriate for shorter jobs, or when most submitted jobs have similar priorities. The quota share still benefits from job priority being taken into consideration at job dispatch. Submitted jobs trigger AWS Batch to reclaim any lent capacity needed to run the jobs. qs2 = QuotaShareConfig( name="QS2", capacity_unit=INSTANCE_TYPE, max_capacity=1, in_share_preemption=False, sharing_strategy="LEND" ) QS3 represents workloads that need to start as quickly as possible with minimal interruptions. It’s configured to reserve capacity and neither lends nor borrows to other quota shares. It doesn’t experience cross-share preemptions, because its workloads don’t exceed their capacity limits. By also turning off in-share preemption, workloads submitted to this quota share are not preempted by AWS Batch as long as the capacity limit is unchanged. qs3 = QuotaShareConfig( name="QS3", capacity_unit=INSTANCE_TYPE, max_capacity=1, in_share_preemption=False, sharing_strategy="RESERVE" ) These quota share configurations are inputs to the create_quota_management_resources function in the sample notebook, which also configures the corresponding Scheduling Policy, Service Environment, and Job Queue with the constant names chosen. SCHEDULING_POLICY_NAME = "my-qm-scheduling-policy" JOB_QUEUE_NAME = "my-sm-training-qm-jq" SERVICE_ENVIRONMENT_NAME = "my-sm-training-qm-se" resources = create_quota_management_resources( resource_manager=resource_manager, scheduling_policy_name=SCHEDULING_POLICY_NAME, job_queue_name=JOB_QUEUE_NAME, service_environment_name=SERVICE_ENVIRONMENT_NAME, capacity_unit=INSTANCE_TYPE, max_capacity=3, quota_share_configs=[qs1, qs2, qs3] ) Submit SageMaker Training jobs to QS1 The aws_batch module within the SageMaker Python SDK has been extended to allow programmatic submission of SageMaker Training jobs to a quota-management-enabled AWS Batch job queue. To demonstrate these new capabilities, we use a Hello World ModelTrainer that’s submitted to the job queue. The following code snippet identifies an image URI to use based on the Region and instance type selected. import logging logging.basicConfig( level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s - %(name)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s" ) logging.getLogger("botocore.client").setLevel(level=logging.WARN) logger = logging.getLogger(__name__) from sagemaker.core.helper.session_helper import Session from sagemaker.core import image_uris session = Session() image_uri = image_uris.retrieve( framework="pytorch", region=session.boto_session.region_name, version="2.5", instance_type=INSTANCE_TYPE, image_scope="training", ) We use this image URI within a basic hello world model trainer example: from sagemaker.train.model_trainer import ModelTrainer from sagemaker.train.configs import SourceCode, Compute, StoppingCondition TRAINING_JOB_NAME = "hello-world-simple-job" MAX_RUN_TIME = 300 source_code = SourceCode(command="echo 'Hello World'") model_trainer = ModelTrainer( training_image=image_uri, source_code=source_code, base_job_name=TRAINING_JOB_NAME, compute=Compute(instance_type=INSTANCE_TYPE, instance_count=INSTANCE_COUNT), stopping_condition=StoppingCondition(max_runtime_in_seconds=MAX_RUN_TIME), ) To use the job queue within the SageMaker Python SDK, provide the queue name to the TrainingQueue constructor within the aws_batch module. from sagemaker.train.aws_batch.training_queue import TrainingQueue, TrainingQueuedJob # Construct the queue object using the SageMaker Python SDK queue = TrainingQueue(JOB_QUEUE_NAME) logger.info(f"Using queue: {queue.queue_name}") We can then submit three jobs to QS1, our background jobs quota share. The first job submitted has the highest priority, followed by the medium priority job, and then the lowest priority job. As nothing is currently running in QS1 or QS2, two instances’ worth of jobs should start, corresponding to the first and second jobs submitted (as they had the highest relative priority). Note that because this is only a hello world training job, it doesn’t require data, but typically a ModelTrainer requires data to perform training. from utils.aws_batch_resource_management import JobStatus, await_jobs, list_jobs_by_quota_share # Submit three jobs to QS1, all with different priorities to guarantee dispatch ordering. qs1_job_high: TrainingQueuedJob = queue.submit(job_name="qs1_job_high", training_job=model_trainer, quota_share_name=qs1.name, priority=3, inputs=None) qs1_job_med: TrainingQueuedJob = queue.submit(job_name="qs1_job_med", training_job=model_trainer, quota_share_name=qs1.name, priority=2, inputs=None) qs1_job_low: TrainingQueuedJob = queue.submit(job_name="qs1_job_low", training_job=model_trainer, quota_share_name=qs1.name, priority=1, inputs=None) logger.info(f"Submitted jobs: {qs1_job_high.job_name}, {qs1_job_med.job_name}, {qs1_job_low.job_name}") logger.info(f"Waiting for jobs to transition...") # qs1_job_high is dispatched first using capacity from QS1, and qs1_job_med is dispatched second borrowing idle capacity from QS2 await_jobs([([qs1_job_high, qs1_job_med], JobStatus.dispatched() | JobStatus.terminal())]) list_jobs_by_quota_share(queue, [qs1.name, qs2.name, qs3.name], JobStatus.active()) Submitting jobs to QS2 triggers cross-share preemption to reclaim lent capacity The team that owns QS2 might discover they have work to perform and submit a job to QS2. Doing so triggers a preemption of capacity back from QS1, which is currently borrowing that capacity (QS3’s capacity isn’t configured to be borrowed). This is a cross-share preemption. # When a job is submitted to QS2, it will preempt its capacity back from QS1 qs2_job_1: TrainingQueuedJob = queue.submit(job_name="qs2_job_1", training_job=model_trainer, quota_share_name=qs2.name, priority=1, inputs=None) logger.info(f"Submitted job {qs2_job_1.job_name}") logger.info(f"Waiting for jobs to transition...") await_jobs([ ([qs2_job_1], JobStatus.dispatched() | JobStatus.terminal()), ([qs1_job_med], {JobStatus.RUNNABLE}) # Lowest priority QS1 job will be preempted ]) list_jobs_by_quota_share(queue, [qs1.name, qs2.name, qs3.name], JobStatus.active()) Updating job priorities in QS1 triggers in-share preemption to run highest priority jobs If a scientist realizes that the qs1_job_low job in QS1, which is still RUNNABLE, needs to begin running now because of changing priorities, they can use the new UpdateServiceJob API to increase the priority of an already submitted job in QS1. Because there’s no available capacity to borrow, this kicks off an in-share preemption, so that the job currently running is preempted and qs1_job_low can begin. # Updating qs1_job_low to be the highest priority job in QS1 qs1_job_low.update(scheduling_priority=4) logger.info(f"Updated job {qs1_job_low.job_name} to increase its priority") logger.info(f"Waiting for jobs to transition...") await_jobs([ ([qs1_job_low], JobStatus.dispatched() | JobStatus.terminal()), ([qs1_job_high], {JobStatus.RUNNABLE}) # High priority job will preempt lower priority jobs within the same quota share ]) list_jobs_by_quota_share(queue, [qs1.name, qs2.name, qs3.name], JobStatus.active()) (Optional) Clean up created resources To clean up the resources created in this post, run the following code: from utils.aws_batch_resource_management import delete_resources delete_resources(resource_manager, resources) Conclusion In this post, we covered quota management, a new scheduling capability in AWS Batch, and how to use it with SageMaker Training jobs and get started setting up quota shares for your own projects. For more details, see the AWS Batch quota management user guide . AWS Batch with quota management can help your organization increase compute utilization and more effectively prioritize your teams and workloads, freeing up time for your infrastructure admins and ML scientists. By implementing quota management, your teams can focus on their workloads and reduce time spent managing and coordinating infrastructure. This capability is especially powerful with Amazon SageMaker AI training plans, so that your organization can reserve capacity in the quantity you need, during the time you need it. By using AWS Batch with SageMaker AI, you can make full use of the training plan. We encourage you to try out this new capability so it can make a meaningful impact in your operations.   About the authors Michelle Goodstein Michelle is a Principal Engineer on Amazon Athena. While working on AWS Batch, she led scheduling improvements for AI/ML, including quota management for SageMaker Training jobs, to drive utilization, efficiency, and cost optimization, as well as improved observability into the job execution lifecycle. She enjoys building innovative solutions to distributed systems problems spanning data, compute, and AI/ML. David Lindskog David is a Senior Software Engineer at AWS Batch. He was project lead for AWS Batch support for SageMaker Training jobs and most recently led the launch of AWS Batch’s first free CloudWatch metrics.  Across his time at Amazon, David has enjoyed designing and building highly scalable and operationally robust backend systems for compute-heavy workloads, robotics telemetry, and AI/ML training. Tom Burggraf Tom is the Head of Software Strategy for US Federal Supercomputing at AWS, where he shapes strategy across AWS services for federal research and scientific computing customers. While leading product for AWS Batch, he drove features that help research platform builders scale efficiently, including AWS Batch support for SageMaker Training jobs and quota management. Prior to AWS, he was a product leader in FinTech and a consultant for product organizations across multiple industries.

title: How MoEngage turned over 400 APIs into agent tools with AgentCore Gateway
summary: MoEngage turned roughly 400 private REST APIs across 7 AWS Regions into permission-scoped agent tools with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway. No per-service MCP servers, no public endpoints, and no 400-tool context bloat. See how OpenAPI specs, Cedar policies, and managed Amazon VPC Lattice egress made it work.
content: This post was co-written with Nikhil Kumar and Shakir Khan from MoEngage. When engineering teams start building AI agents, the capabilities those agents need usually already exist as internal APIs. Campaign creation, segment queries, delivery stats. The challenge isn’t building new functionality. The challenge is making hundreds of private APIs safely reachable by agents without exposing them to the public internet, without giving models control over identity, and without flooding context windows with hundreds of tool definitions. MoEngage, the agentic customer engagement platform that more than 1,350 consumer brands use to deliver personalized experiences across push, email, in-app, SMS, WhatsApp, and RCS, faced exactly this problem. Behind the product sit roughly 400 internal REST APIs, built by 25 engineering teams, running in private virtual private clouds (VPCs) across seven AWS Regions. MoEngage isolates these APIs regionally to meet data residency commitments and doesn’t expose them to the public internet. The capability the agents needed was already running in production. Making it reachable, safely, was the hard part. In this post, we walk through how MoEngage used AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to turn those private APIs into permission-scoped agent tools. The approach saved MoEngage an estimated six months of platform engineering effort, and onboarding a new API now takes hours instead of days. No product team wrote Model Context Protocol (MCP) server code, no networking was provisioned per integration, and no public endpoint exists anywhere in the path. Why 20 MCP servers was the wrong answer The Model Context Protocol (MCP) gives agents a standard way to discover and call tools. The straightforward path to adopting it is for each team to expose its own MCP server. MoEngage costed that out and rejected it. Over 20 MCP servers means over 20 deployments to monitor, patch, and keep protocol-compatible as MCP evolves. Cross-domain agents, the useful ones that read a campaign, check its segment, and inspect delivery stats, would need to connect to several servers and reconcile them. And every team would need MCP expertise unrelated to its actual product work. So MoEngage established the principle that shaped everything that followed: Individual engineering teams do not implement MCP. Teams build REST APIs and declare which operations should be tools. The AI Platform team owns the MCP layer end to end. A team’s responsibility ends at a well-described OpenAPI spec. That principle immediately created three requirements: a central tool surface that agents connect to once rather than per-service, per-agent authorization enforced server-side rather than by convention, and private connectivity that does not need to be rebuilt for every new API. Building all of this from scratch was an option. A custom central MCP server would solve the 20-servers problem but leave MoEngage building a tool-generation pipeline, a policy file format, a tool-alias registry for renames, and circuit breakers. All custom code, all owned by one team, all of it undifferentiated work that does not make MoEngage’s agents smarter or its customers’ campaigns better. Four constraints that shaped the architecture Before evaluating any solution, MoEngage defined four constraints. All four had to be met simultaneously. A solution that addressed two but broke the third and fourth was not viable. Nothing gets a public endpoint. MoEngage’s internal APIs are VPC-private by policy. Any solution that required exposing them, even behind additional authentication, was a non-starter. The conventional workaround is per-integration networking: a NAT gateway here, a reverse proxy there, a VPN tunnel for the third one. Multiply that by seven Regions and the operational surface grows faster than the set of agents does. Every new API would mean another networking change request, another set of security reviews, another piece of infrastructure to maintain. Identity can’t be an agent’s decision. Every internal API call carries tenant, user, role, and database context. If that context is a large language model (LLM)-visible tool parameter, a model can get it wrong or be talked into changing it. MoEngage needed identity to be structurally out of the model’s reach, injected by the calling service and not surfaced as something the model can set or override. A 400-tool catalog doesn’t fit in a context window. At roughly 50 tokens of JSON schema per tool, a full tools/list across the estate is over 20,000 tokens transmitted on every connection. That token budget is spent before the agent does anything useful, and it crowds out the context the agent actually needs to reason about the task. Client-side filtering ( tool_filter in ADK or the MCP SDK) doesn’t fix this. The full catalog has already crossed the wire, and filtering by client convention isn’t an authorization boundary. An agent that is not supposed to see write operations shouldn’t receive them in the first place. That last constraint is the one that avoided the obvious alternatives. A custom central MCP server solves the 20-servers problem but still leaves MoEngage building a tool-generation pipeline, a policy file format, a tool-alias registry for renames, and circuit breakers. All custom code, all owned by one team, none of it making MoEngage’s product better. How AgentCore Gateway maps to those constraints Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway is a fully managed MCP server. You register OpenAPI specs as targets and the gateway generates MCP tools from them, then routes calls to the backing services. Four properties mapped directly onto MoEngage’s constraints. OpenAPI in, MCP tools out. There’s no MCP server to build or operate, and no separate artifact to keep in sync with the API. The spec teams already maintain is the tool definition. Each operation becomes a tool named Target___operationId , for example CampaignsAPI___searchCampaigns . When the spec changes, the tool changes. When a team adds an endpoint, the tool appears. When a team removes one, the tool disappears. No deployment, no protocol expertise, no coordination with the AI Platform team. Cedar policies, evaluated before the catalog is serialized. The AgentCore policy engine uses partial evaluation to filter tools/list per principal. Each agent authenticates as its own IAM role, and its Cedar policy determines which tools it can see and call. This is what makes 400 tools tractable. It isn’t client-side filtering after the fact, but server-side scoping before the response is built. A campaign QA bot, for example, gets read access to campaign and segment tools but can’t call a write operation: permit( principal == Agent::"campaign-qa-bot-v1", action == Action::"tools/call", resource in ToolGroup::"campaigns-read" ); forbid( principal == Agent::"campaign-qa-bot-v1", action == Action::"tools/call", resource in ToolGroup::"write-actions" ); The bot doesn’t see write tools in its tools/list response. There’s nothing to filter on the client side because the tools weren’t sent. Managed egress over Amazon VPC Lattice. The gateway reaches MoEngage’s internal services through AgentCore managed egress rather than through networking MoEngage builds and operates. Inbound, the gateway is reachable only through a VPC interface endpoint with private DNS. There’s no public path to it. Onboarding a new API adds a target, not a network topology change. This is the property that broke the multiply by seven Regions problem. The networking exists once and every API uses it. Semantic search as a gateway capability. With the x_amz_bedrock_agentcore_search capability, an agent can find tools by describing the task instead of naming the tool. It removed the need for a custom discovery layer. It also removed rename fragility as a side effect: if get_segment_user_count becomes get_segment_size , an agent searching for segment user count still finds it, because matching happens on description rather than identifier. The architecture in practice The request flow from agent to internal API is short, and every layer has a specific job. Agent services connect through a VPC interface endpoint to AgentCore Gateway, which evaluates Cedar policies and routes tool calls through managed egress over Amazon VPC Lattice to internal APIs. The following diagram shows how the components connect. Figure 1: MoEngage AgentCore Gateway architecture An agent service running on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) or in a container calls the MCP client. The client can be the official MCP SDK, LangChain, Google ADK, or MoEngage’s own agent runner. The client signs the request with SigV4 using the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role the service already has. The request travels over HTTPS to a VPC interface endpoint with private DNS. There’s no public hop. AgentCore Gateway receives the request and evaluates Cedar policies to determine what this principal can see or call. It then routes tool invocations through managed egress over Amazon VPC Lattice to the internal API. MoEngage made two authentication decisions worth calling out. First, they chose SigV4 over JWT for the internal gateway. Agents here are services that already have IAM roles. With SigV4, they can sign with credentials they already have. Nothing new to issue, rotate, or store. MoEngage’s separate public MCP server, which serves human-authenticated sessions from Claude and other clients, uses OIDC JWTs on AgentCore runtime. That is a different surface with different requirements. Second, identity travels as headers, not as tool arguments. Tenant, user, role, and database context are converted by the client library from a small Identity object into X-MOE-* headers. The model doesn’t see them and can’t set them. One detail matters for anyone building something similar: Because SigV4 signing occupies the Authorization header, caller-forwarded bearer tokens must move elsewhere. MoEngage propagates it as a dedicated MoEngage-prefixed header. Header propagation is also capped, so the set of headers is deliberate rather than accumulated. Discovery and execution have different identity requirements. Listing and searching tools carries no tenant identity. Only tools/call does. That separation keeps discovery cheap and makes the audit trail unambiguous. Every identity-bearing request is an actual data access. Even with Cedar scoping an agent to a subset of the catalog, the subset can be large. MoEngage’s client library exposes a single meta-tool, search_tools , to the model. The model describes what it needs, the gateway’s semantic search returns candidates, and only those candidates become callable for the rest of the turn. The full catalog doesn’t enter context. The agent’s context contains one tool definition at the start and a handful of relevant ones after a search, instead of several hundred definitions it will never use. Onboarding a new API A team exposing an API as an agent tool adds a block to its existing OpenAPI spec: paths: /campaigns: get: operationId: listCampaigns description: | Returns a paginated list of campaigns. Supports filtering by status, channel, date range, and tags. x-moe-mcp: expose: external: false internal: true tool_description: | Find campaigns by status or channel. Returns campaign ID, name, status, and channel. Use the returned campaign_id with get_campaign for full details, or send_campaign to launch it. param_overrides: status: description: | Filter by campaign status. Use 'active' for running campaigns, 'scheduled' for upcoming. Omit for all. Four design choices in that block are worth explaining. Exposure is explicit opt-in . An endpoint with no x-moe-mcp block is not a tool. Continuous integration (CI) does not warn about its absence, because for most endpoints absence is the correct state. Cache-warmup routes and migration triggers are not agent tools, and nothing should nudge a team toward making them one. With the internal and external flags, a team can expose an operation to internal agents, to the public MCP server, or to both, independently. Tool descriptions aren’t API descriptions . An API description tells a developer reading docs what an endpoint returns. A tool description tells a model when to reach for this tool and what to pass. MoEngage found that reusing API descriptions verbatim led to poor tool selection. Models picked tools based on implementation detail (“Returns a paginated list”) rather than intent (“Find campaigns by status or channel”). The tool_description and param_overrides fields exist specifically to give teams a place to write model-facing text without changing their developer-facing docs. The CI pipeline handles everything from spec to running tool . When a team pushes a spec change, the pipeline validates the x-moe-mcp block, registers the target with AgentCore Gateway, and applies the Cedar policy. No manual steps, no tickets to the AI Platform team. A team that has never thought about MCP can have an operation available as an agent tool in the time it takes the pipeline to run. The client library comes in two modes . A plug-in mode wraps the AgentCore Gateway MCP server inside LangChain, Google ADK, or an MCP-compatible framework as a tool provider. An agent runner mode runs a complete agent loop for teams that want a standalone agent without adopting a framework. What MoEngage runs today MoEngage’s AgentCore Gateway deployment runs in seven AWS Regions today. The gateway serves roughly 400 registered API operations to 10 internal agents. No product team has written MCP server code. No product team has provisioned networking for an agent integration. No product team has implemented Cedar policies. The AI Platform team owns all of that, and the cost of onboarding a new API is a spec annotation and a CI run. AgentCore feature availability varies by Region. For supported Regions, see the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation . The system has been running in production for three months. The agents span the workflow a marketing team member touches daily. A campaign QA agent validates targeting rules and content before launch. A delivery health agent monitors send rates and bounce patterns across channels. A segment builder agent translates natural-language audience descriptions into segment queries. Each agent authenticates with its own IAM role, sees only the tools its Cedar policy permits, and discovers tools by describing the task rather than memorizing tool names. By removing the need to build and operate 20 separate MCP servers and provision per-API networking across seven Regions, MoEngage estimates the approach saved approximately six months of engineering effort. Onboarding a new API now takes hours of spec annotation instead of days of networking provisioning and security review. The search-first pattern changed how MoEngage thinks about agent design. New agents start with zero hardcoded tool references. They describe intent, receive candidates, and call what they find. When a team renames an operation or ships a new one, existing agents pick it up without a code change. Conclusion The key insight behind MoEngage’s approach is a separation of concerns that maps to how engineering organizations actually work. Product teams own APIs and describe them well. A platform team owns the protocol layer, the policy layer, and the connectivity layer. AgentCore Gateway made that split practical by removing the undifferentiated work in between: no MCP server code, no per-API networking, no client-side filtering pretending to be authorization. The result is an agent system where adding a new tool is a spec change, restricting access is a policy change, and neither requires the other team to be involved. To get started with AgentCore Gateway, see the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation . For Cedar policy authoring, see the Cedar policy language reference . For private connectivity patterns, see the Amazon VPC Lattice documentation . To discuss a similar architecture for your organization, contact your AWS account team or reach out to AWS .   About the authors Nikhil Kumar Nikhil is a Lead Software Engineer in the CTO’s office at MoEngage, where he leads the AI Labs team building agentic AI capabilities. His work spans MCP server and tool-catalog architecture, LLM gateway and routing infrastructure, and evaluating agent frameworks for both internal tooling and public agent experiences. He has over 4 years of experience building software and cloud infrastructure at scale. Shakir Khan Shakir is an Architect at MoEngage, where he leads API governance and builds core streaming infrastructure powering the company’s customer engagement platform. His work spans gateway architecture, real-time streaming with Flink and Kafka, and large-scale data migrations. He has over 11 years of experience designing systems that serve billions of customer interactions, including 5 years at MoEngage. Bhupesh Chadha Bhupesh is a Principal Account Manager at Amazon Web Services, where he partners with independent software vendors (ISVs) to align their platform strategy with their business goals. He works with C-suite and senior leadership to accelerate growth, bring new capabilities to market, and turn technical investments into customer reach and differentiation. Anant Murarka Anant is a Solutions Architect at Amazon Web Services, where he works with ISV customers to design multi-tenant architectures and productionize AI-driven solutions. His areas of expertise include agentic AI, agent orchestration patterns, responsible AI, and helping product companies adopt generative AI on AWS. Outside of work, Anant is passionate about exploring how emerging AI paradigms reshape the way software products are built and delivered.

title: Speeding up language models for travel applications
summary: Two optimization techniques, when combined, can significantly improve a model’s speed and cost effectiveness without sacrificing quality.
content: Travel platforms serve millions of daily users by answering questions about destinations, offering hotel recommendations, and helping users plan their trips. In recent years, many platforms have turned to large language models (LLMs) to improve these services. The LLMs give accurate, contextually relevant travel advice thanks to their size: they typically have tens of billions of parameters. Unfortunately, such large models are also computationally expensive, and that expense scales with the number of customer queries. What’s more, such large models can be too slow for web and mobile applications, where a delay of even 100 milliseconds can cost a company customers and revenue. To address these scaling and latency challenges, we explored two complementary optimization techniques. One is a compression technique known as knowledge distillation (KD), in which a slow but powerful model produces training targets for a faster, lightweight model. The other, called Medusa, is a framework that transforms sequential next-token predictions — a common bottleneck in LLMs — into parallel computations. Working with leading online travel agency Booking.com, we applied KD and Medusa techniques to the LLMs that power various aspects of its user experience, looking to improve either latency or cost effectiveness. We focused on three features in particular: The AI Trip Planner: A conversational assistant that must extract travel preferences from dialogue in less than a second (latency); Smart Filters: A feature that converts natural-language search queries into structured information filters in real time (latency); Accommodation Description Generation: A feature that produces property descriptions on the scale of millions of listings (cost effectiveness). We demonstrated that combining both KD and Medusa maintains the quality of the best open-source LLMs at less than one-third the cost while running up to 20 times as fast. Our framework ensures that travel platforms or other applications that rely on LLMs can deliver fast, cost-effective, accurate responses in real-world scenarios. We presented these techniques at last year’s meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL), where it received the Industry Track best-paper award. Our approach: Medusa plus knowledge distillation Medusa is a framework designed to reduce LLM latency in real-time applications such as chat and code generation. It improves computational efficiency at run time — inference time — rather than during training. Ordinarily, an LLM generates text one token — word or word part — at a time. Medusa accelerates this process by predicting multiple tokens in parallel. Medusa does this by adding prediction modules, called Medusa heads, to the base LLM, one head for each token decoded in parallel. GPU hardware that LLMs run on is optimized for parallelism, so it can handle parallel token decoding with little additional overhead. Medusa offers significant speedups, typically two- to fourfold without compromising generation quality. Knowledge distillation addresses the deployment challenges of large, parameter-heavy models by transferring knowledge from larger “teacher” models to smaller “student” models. Typically, a teacher model is first trained or fine-tuned on high-quality labeled data, then used to generate predictions on additional unlabeled data. The manually labeled and machine-labeled data are then combined to train a smaller student model, which learns to mimic the teacher’s behavior. The student model retains much of the teacher’s performance but is significantly more efficient, making it better suited for real-world scenarios such as high-volume consumer-facing websites. In our work, we integrate KD and Medusa in a unified pipeline starting with pretrained base models. As in standard KD, we fine-tune the teacher on the labeled dataset and use it to generate predictions on unlabeled, domain-relevant text. During the student-training stage, however, we attach Medusa heads to the student model and train it on the combined corpus of teacher predictions and labeled data. This produces a single compact model that inherits the teacher's knowledge while also gaining multitoken-prediction capabilities. The experiment We chose TinyLlama — a compact model with 1.1 billion parameters — as our student and Llama-3.1 with 70 billion parameters as the teacher. We ran four progressive experiments, each building on the last. We first fine-tuned TinyLlama on task-specific data for each of our three use cases — AI trip planning, smart filtering, and accommodation description generation. Even without further optimization, the fine-tuned models were significantly more accurate than few-shot GPT-4o, confirming that domain-specific fine tuning compensates for their compact size. However, their performance still fell short of the much larger teacher model’s. Applying knowledge distillation — training the student on a blend of human-annotated and teacher-annotated data — closed that gap by more than 90%, bringing the small model to near parity with the teacher. The smaller model size also made inference roughly six times as fast, but that’s still not fast enough for real-time use. Adding Medusa heads, however, sped up inference an additional 2 to 3.6 times. We tested two Medusa variants: with Medusa-1, we first fine-tuned the base LLM, then froze its weights and fine-tuned the Medusa heads separately; with Medusa-2, we trained everything in a single stage. Both achieved comparable speedups with no meaningful quality loss, but Medusa-2's simpler pipeline made it more practical for production teams managing multiple models. Outcomes Combining KD with Medusa-2 delivered both gains simultaneously: our final model matched the quality of the 70-billion-parameter teacher while running 10 to 20 times as fast, depending on the use case. For each of the three use cases, we used the pipeline described above to fine-tune a dedicated model with domain-specific data. For AI Trip Planner, we showed a 2.9% increase in user engagement versus GPT-3.5. For Smart Filters, we achieved responses that were 15 times as fast for 99 percent of queries. For AI-generated accommodation descriptions, we showed 1.4% more “helpful” ratings from users, at less than one-third the cost of GPT-4. With acknowledgements to our AWS colleague Aleksandra Dokic and to the Booking.com team: Emmanouil Stergiadis, Eran Fainman, Ilya Gusev, and Moran Beladev.

title: Accelerate agentic AI with NVIDIA Nemotron models on Amazon EKS and SageMaker HyperPod EKS
summary: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is a 120B-parameter mixture-of-experts model that pairs reasoning and tool use with multimodal understanding. This post explores its architecture and use cases, then shows how to deploy it on Amazon EKS, EKS Auto Mode, and Amazon SageMaker HyperPod EKS with NVIDIA Dynamo and vLLM.
content: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL joins the NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano , Nano Omni , Super , Ultra , and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning models already available on AWS. It’s a 120B-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model that activates 12B parameters per token. It combines reasoning and tool use with text, image, document, and video understanding, so one model serves both text and visual tasks. This post explores its architecture and use cases, then shows how to deploy it on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) , Amazon EKS Auto Mode , and Amazon SageMaker HyperPod EKS . About Nemotron 3.5 Super VL NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is an open multimodal model distilled from Nemotron 3 Ultra. NVIDIA publishes the weights, training datasets, and post-training recipes, so you can customize the model for domain-specific workloads and run it on infrastructure you control. Model details: 120B total parameters, 12B active per token. Hybrid Mamba-2, MoE , and attention layers with a RADIO vision encoder. Context length up to 1M tokens. Input: text, image, document, and video. Output: text. BF16 and NVFP4 checkpoints. NVIDIA reports 63.44 percent on Hermes Bench and 87.05 percent on LangChain agent evaluations, and 80.8 percent on the CharXiv chart-reasoning benchmark. ( technical report ) Model architecture Nemotron 3.5 Super VL uses a hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE architecture, interleaving Mamba-2, attention, and expert layers. Sparse routing activates 12B of the 120B parameters per token, so compute per token matches a much smaller model while GPU memory still holds the full weights. Mamba-2 layers carry a constant-size state during generation, so their memory does not grow with sequence length the way KV cache does, which keeps long contexts affordable. A recursively shared Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) head supports native speculative decoding. Use cases Nemotron 3.5 Super VL supports agent workflows that combine reasoning with visual understanding: Coding: test and validate code, analyze errors, recommend fixes. Web research: cross-reference and verify sources returned by search tools. Document intelligence: read tables, charts, and page layouts to produce summaries. Cyber security: identify vulnerabilities and triage threats. Video understanding: search, content, review, and incident analysis. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL integrates with major open agent frameworks and orchestration systems through NVIDIA reference implementations, cookbooks, and the NVIDIA Agent Toolkit . For the full list of supported frameworks, see the NVIDIA developer blog . Minimum GPU configurations vLLM (GPU Model / min count) BF16 NVFP4 B200/GB200 8 2 B300/GB300 4 1 H200 8 4 H100 16 8 Deployment on AWS This section gives an overview of architecture, validation, and performance evaluation approaches. A detailed walkthrough of deploying Nemotron 3.5 Super VL and Nemotron 3 Ultra on AWS is available in the aws-do-eks project, including prerequisites, cluster creation, model weights download, deployment, testing, benchmarking, and cleanup. The same pattern can also be applied to other models in the NVIDIA Nemotron family. Deployment architecture The reference implementation runs on standard Amazon EKS, EKS Auto Mode, and SageMaker HyperPod EKS. With EKS Auto Mode, AWS manages scaling, GPU, and EFA support in the cluster on your behalf. The Kubernetes manifests for model deployment are the same for each of the orchestrator options. Each cluster has a control plane hosting the Kubernetes API and a data plane of CPU and GPU nodes. CPU nodes run system and test pods, while the GPU nodes run the model. Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) stores the container images, a shared Amazon FSx for Lustre volume holds the model weights, and Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) connects the GPU nodes. The following figure shows a standard Amazon EKS cluster. Figure 1: Standard Amazon EKS cluster architecture for serving NVIDIA Nemotron models NVIDIA Dynamo serves the model aggregated on a single node or disaggregated with prefill and decode on different nodes. For vision-language models, the image/video encoding stage can in addition run disaggregated on its own node. Validation and performance This architecture has been validated on both p6-b200.48xlarge (8 x NVIDIA B200 GPUs) and p5en.48xlarge (8 x NVIDIA H200 GPUs) instances. You can validate the cluster and its network with an NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) all-reduce micro-benchmark. Figure 2: GPU and EFA utilization during an NCCL all-reduce validation test Seeing utilization on all GPUs and traffic on all EFA adapters while the NCCL test is running, verifies that the cluster is working as expected. You can measure the performance of a deployed model on the cluster with the NVIDIA aiperf tool. Figure 3: aiperf performance metrics for the deployed model The aiperf output in the upper left pane shows key performance indicators (KPIs) like time to first token (TTFT), inter-token latency (ITL), and throughput in tokens per second (TPS). By taking these measurements at various levels of concurrency, we can study how latency and throughput depend on the number of concurrent requests. This information is essential to thoughtfully plan capacity and model deployment topology. The aws-do-eks container provides automation for visualizing GPU and EFA utilization as well as running aiperf and concurrency sweeps with single commands. Figure 4: Concurrency sweep comparing aggregated and disaggregated deployments The preceding concurrency sweep diagram reveals that the inference of Nemotron 3.5 Super VL has lower TTFT and about the same ITL between aggregated and disaggregated deployments on two nodes. A chart like this is useful when making deployment decisions. Draw your latency budget as horizontal lines, for example TTFT under 600 ms (about 1 second) and ITL under 100 ms per token. The rightmost point under both lines is the throughput one replica of this topology can serve within the service level objective (SLO), here c32, or about 320 tokens per second. To plan capacity, divide your target tokens per second by this per-replica throughput and find the number of prefill-decode pairs to deploy. Re-running the same sweep after a change (precision, TP/PP shape, aggregated versus disaggregated, a new Dynamo or vLLM release) makes the trade-off visible immediately. A curve that moves right and down is a win. Because TTFT and ITL are plotted separately, it also tells you which side to scale: rising ITL says add decode capacity, and rising TTFT says add prefill capacity. Conclusion This post covers the architecture and performance evaluation patterns for serving NVIDIA Nemotron models on Amazon EKS, EKS Auto Mode, and SageMaker HyperPod EKS with NVIDIA Dynamo and vLLM. To get started, deploy Nemotron 3.5 Super VL in your own account, using the reference implementation . More inference blueprints are also available in the AI on EKS project. To get further hands-on experience with inference on EKS, register for our upcoming workshops . Over the past 10 years, Alex has worked on helping customers do more on AWS, democratizing AI and ML, combating climate change, and making travel safer, healthcare better, and energy smarter. As a veteran CUDA programmer and Kubernetes expert, he helps enterprises integrate NVIDIA technologies for distributed training, specializing in EKS and Slurm implementations. Anton works closely with MENA Region and government sector clients to optimize generative AI solutions. He holds a patent pending for machine learning edge computing systems. She specializes in inference engineering, model benchmarking, production architecture design, and optimizing performance from cold start to sustained throughput. Her recent work includes open-source TTS inference stacks on EKS and GPU benchmarking tools across the G and P instance families. A teacher at heart enjoys making the complexities of AI feel approachable. He collaborates with cloud providers to enhance AI workload performance and drive adoption of NVIDIA-powered AI and generative AI solutions. Slice Into GFN Thursday: ‘Phantom Blade Zero’ Launches on GeForce NOW
summary: This Halloween week, GFN Thursday is delivering a fresh batch of gaming treats. Something wicked this blade comes. S-GAME’s Phantom Blade Zero launches on GeForce NOW today, bringing a scarily good blend of martial arts and punk fantasy to the cloud. content: This Halloween week, GFN Thursday is delivering a fresh batch of gaming treats. Something wicked this blade comes. S-GAME’s Phantom Blade Zero launches on GeForce NOW today, bringing a scarily good blend of martial arts and punk fantasy to the cloud. There’s also something on the horizon for adventurers: World of Warcraft: Forever arrives Wednesday, Nov. 4 at 3 p.m. PST, with a launch-week access reward coming for GeForce NOW members. This week’s lineup also includes nine games streaming from the GeForce NOW library , alongside new mod support for Cyberpunk 2077 and The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered . That means more options to play, with no downloads or installs to haunt gamers’ devices . There’s another sweet update for gamers in India: The option to sign up for four-month Performance and Ultimate memberships is launching tomorrow. Visit the GeForce NOW website for more information. Cold Steel Meets Cloud Power Framed for his master’s murder and gravely wounded, a warrior named Soul has 66 days to uncover a conspiracy threatening the martial world in S-GAME’s Phantom Blade Zero . Powered by Unreal Engine 5, the game combines wuxia storytelling with cinematic action. Master more than 30 primary weapons and over 20 Phantom Edges, chaining evasions, deflections and counterattacks into fluid combat. Traditional Chinese martial arts meet mechanical prosthetics, industrial ruins and rock music in a distinctive kungfupunk world. Ultimate members can wield GeForce RTX 5080-class performance in the cloud across PCs, Macs, handhelds, mobile devices, browsers, compatible TVs and more. GeForce NOW handles the game’s downloads and storage, leaving more time for the next clash. Soul’s clock is ticking, but the download bar doesn’t have to. Cut to the chase and hop into the game today. Azeroth Awaits Get ready for Blizzard Entertainment’s World of Warcraft: Forever , arriving Wednesday, Nov. 4, at 3 p.m. PT, on GeForce NOW. Explore an iconic world reimagined with new and expanded zones, new gameplay enhancements, upgraded graphics and more. A new reward will give eligible GeForce NOW members access to join beginning at launch and ending Wednesday, Nov. 11, at 11:59 p.m. PT. The reward is available across all GeForce NOW membership tiers for new WoW users who don’t already have a subscription, while supplies last, on a first-come, first-served basis. Once available, members can sign in to their GeForce NOW account and head to the Account Portal to redeem. Mark the calendar and gather the party — launch week is approaching. New Tricks and Treats It’s a mod world. Familiar favorites have a few new tricks, too: Mod.io support is now available directly in game for Cyberpunk 2077 and The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Remastered , bringing more ways to make Night City and the Continent feel different. And the treats keep coming with the following games joining the GeForce NOW library this week: Phantom Blade Zero (New release on Steam , Oct. 28) ATMOSFAR (New release on Steam , Oct. 29) Hunting Simulator 3 (New release on Steam , Oct. 29) Queen’s Domain (New release on Steam , Oct. 30) Dimraeth ( Steam ) Dressmaker ( Steam ) Halloween ( Epic Games Store ) Hell Let Loose: Vietnam ( Epic Games Store ) The Seance of Blake Manor ( Steam ) Dates listed above reflect when games are released on their respective stores. GeForce NOW availability may vary, as games are onboarded after they’re released and added throughout the week. Keep an eye on GeForce NOW channels and GFN Thursdays for availability updates to announced titles. Settle in for a scary-good gaming session: Grab a day pass to experience Performance or Ultimate cloud gaming. Gamers can then apply the cost applicable toward a first monthly membership upgrade. What’s haunting the gaming playlist this weekend? Let us know on X or in the comments below.
