title: Building an Agentic AI Platform on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
summary: Stand up a governed, multi-account Agentic AI Platform on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. This post walks through the architecture and an open-source reference blueprint: the operating model, control plane, per-Workstream cells, separate inference and tool gateways, and a CI/CD evaluation pipeline that gates each agent before production.
content: If you’ve tried to get an agent into production, the model and tool use are not the blocker. The main bottleneck is everything around them: how many teams can build within a secure environment, which team owns each model and tool, how AgentOps and error handling stay inside a pre-defined boundary, and how platform, Workstream, and finance teams see cost and health across accounts. For a Platform team that wants to support many agentic use cases, that’s a platform product to design and operate. In this post, we refer to the team that manages the platform as the Platform team, and to the teams that build on it as Workstream teams. Workstream teams are the domain or product teams that build and own agents on the platform. Each Workstream team needs a paved road with approved models and tools, short-lived workload identity, isolated runtime and memory, automated evaluation, rollback, telemetry, and cost attribution. These controls need to remain consistent as Workstream teams customize prompts, tools, data access, and application behavior. When every team assembles them, controls drift, shared services become a bottleneck, and ownership is difficult to audit. In this post, we walk through the architecture and reference implementation of an enterprise Agentic AI Platform on Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. We cover the multi-account operating model, the Platform control plane, a repeatable per-Workstream deployment pattern, separate inference and tool gateways, and an evaluation pipeline that gates each agent before promotion to production. By the end, you should be able to deploy a governed Workstream from the companion blueprint, validate its security and lifecycle contracts, and use it as the foundation for your own agentic AI platform in the organization. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides modular services for building, deploying, and operating agents at scale, including runtime, gateway, identity, memory, policy, registry, and evaluations. The Enterprise Agentic AI Platform Blueprint , built on AgentCore, adds the surrounding enterprise contracts as deployable infrastructure as code: ownership, account boundaries, software delivery, observability, cost governance, and retirement. Architectural principles Before diving into the solution details, it helps to understand the organizational needs that drive the platform architecture. The common challenges we have heard from customers who establish an agent platform fall into these five categories: Governed model access: Every untrusted inference request must pass through an approved inference gateway. The gateway applies the organization’s guardrails (for example, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails or a third-party provider), restricts which models and inference AWS Regions each Workstream can use, and enforces per-Workstream rate limits, token quotas, and budgets so that no single team can exhaust shared capacity. It also carries workload identity and emits attribution data. Governed tool access: Agents must discover and invoke only approved tools through an authenticated Model Context Protocol (MCP) gateway, with exact targets, least-privilege execution roles, policy decisions, and an auditable owner. Delegated delivery: Workstream teams (for example, product teams) need to ship and roll back independently inside pre-approved boundaries, without waiting for the platform team to deploy each application or granting developers a direct infrastructure write path. Fleet operations and cost: Several personas need visibility across accounts without gaining write access to team workloads. Agent operations engineers need logs, metrics, traces, and quotas. Workstream owners need cost per agent against their budgets. FinOps and finance teams need chargeback by team or business unit through AWS Cost Explorer and the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR) . Security and governance leads need evidence of which workload called which model and tool. Bounded evidence and lifecycle: Every agent release needs proof at each boundary it touches: Model access: An approved model call succeeds, and a call to an unapproved model or Region is denied. Tool access: A subscribed tool call succeeds, and a call to a tool outside the agent’s subscription is denied with the expected error. Identity: A request from another workstream’s account or identity is rejected. Release: The previous agent runtime version can be restored. Retirement: Teardown removes the agent’s runtime, memory, tool gateway, and tool grants in dependency order, and confirms nothing is left behind. The blueprint addresses these needs through four connected planes: developer experience, platform control, Workstream execution, and assurance and operations. The unit of scale is the Workstream cell, not a manually configured agent or one shared workload account. The blueprint README documents the responsibilities of each plane in detail. And you will read the main planes: Agentic AI Platform control plane and Repeatable Workstream cell in the later paragraphs. Operating models and platform components Enterprises usually adopt one of three operating models for agentic AI: Centralized: A single artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) team builds and runs every agent. Governance is consistent, but that team quickly becomes a bottleneck as the number of use cases grows. Decentralized: Each business unit builds and operates its own agents. Teams can move quickly, but without shared standards, controls tend to drift, effort gets duplicated, and cost visibility suffers. Federated: A central Platform team provides shared, governed services while domain teams retain ownership of their agents, tools, and data. This model balances team autonomy with consistent guardrails and is where most enterprises land. For assistance choosing, see the AWS Prescriptive Guidance page on Governance Models . Following patterns we have observed in customer engagements, the blueprint implements the federated model. The Platform team is the hub, typically a Platform product manager, architect, platform engineers, agent operations engineers, and a security and governance lead. Workstream teams are the spokes, made up of agent developers, a domain tech lead, and AI/ML engineers. An executive sponsor and the CISO sit above both. In this blueprint, the Platform team owns the definition of each component: templates, versions, policies, and admission. Each Workstream account runs its own instance of the per-team components (Runtime, Memory, Tool Gateway), so a failure or rollback stays inside one team’s boundary. Solution overview This solution delivers a governed, multi-account Agentic AI Platform that platform teams operate, and workstream teams such as internal product and engineering teams consume through versioned, self-service interfaces. At enterprise scale, the developer experience plane is a catalog of organization-approved, versioned agent templates. The blueprint ships reference templates for Strands , LangGraph , and CrewAI , but you can use your choice of framework when the template preserves the same inference gateway, tool gateway, identity, policy, evaluation, and delivery contracts. Application teams own prompts, agent logic, tools, and evaluation cases. The Platform team owns the common controls and release requirements. Out of the four planes, two carry most of the architecture: Agentic AI Platform control plane: The Platform account publishes versioned templates and interfaces, operates AWS Agent Registry governance records and shared Inference Gateways, admits models and Guardrails, orchestrates reviewed releases, and aggregates fleet signals. Teams consume these capabilities through code, descriptors, and pipelines rather than administrator sessions or deployment tickets. Repeatable Workstream cell: Each product or domain receives an isolated boundary with a team-owned source repository, a Workload pipeline, and three Amazon Bedrock AgentCore capabilities: AgentCore Runtime, actor-scoped AgentCore Memory, and an AgentCore Gateway that uses AWS_IAM authorization and exposes only the approved tool targets. The cell also holds local customer managed AWS KMS keys, tags, alarms, budgets, and a CloudWatch Observability Access Manager (OAM) source link. One cell can deploy, fail, roll back, or retire without coordinating with another team’s release. Key components The following diagram illustrates the operating model and governed flow of the solution. Figure 1: Enterprise Agentic AI Platform operating model, showing the governance foundation, the Platform control plane, repeatable team-owned Workstream cells, and the software delivery, inference, tool, telemetry, and ownership flows between them. The architecture consists of the following account layers: Management and governance foundation. AWS Organizations, AWS IAM Identity Center, preventive policy, audit, retention, and cost policy establish the enterprise boundary. These are logical responsibilities that can map to an existing AWS Control Tower landing zone rather than requiring a duplicate account structure. Security, audit, and observability layer. AWS CloudTrail, AWS Config, AWS Security Hub, Amazon GuardDuty, log archive, and an Amazon CloudWatch OAM sink provide independent control-plane evidence and fleet visibility. Central operators can query shared signals without gaining write access to Workstream resources. Platform layer of Agentic AI Platform . Separate Platform environments own golden paths, the governance catalog, Guardrails, shared Inference Gateways, exact tool aliases, pipelines, compatibility, quotas, and common operational interfaces. Platform changes are tested against representative cells before wider rollout. Workstream fleet layer. Each product, domain, or regulated boundary receives one or more nonproduction and production cells. Teams own Runtime, Memory, Tool Gateway, tools, data, prompts, evaluation cases, application incidents, and service-level objectives (SLOs). The same baseline can be repeated across many cells while preserving account-level isolation. Solution walkthrough The following sections trace the key design decisions: account topology, preventive and detective controls, the AgentCore execution path, and the delivery pipeline. Account topology and organizational units The blueprint defines logical account roles that separate enterprise governance, shared Platform services, and team-owned execution: Role Landing-zone placement Purpose Management foundation Root / Security and Management Organizations, Identity Center, preventive policy, audit, retention, and cost policy Security and log archive Security CloudTrail, AWS Config, Security Hub, GuardDuty, and retained audit data Observability Security or Operations CloudWatch OAM sink and fleet logs, metrics, traces, and cost views Agentic AI Platform Agent Platform Golden paths, AWS Agent Registry, Guardrails, Inference Gateways, pipelines, and fleet controls Workstream cell Agent Workstreams Team-owned Runtime, Memory, Tool Gateway, tools, data, evaluation, and application SLOs Additional Workstream cells Agent Workstreams Repeat the same baseline per product, domain, environment, or regulated boundary This topology integrates into an existing landing zone, a pre-configured, secure, and scalable multi-account AWS environment, where the Management, Platform, and Workstream labels describe responsibilities rather than a fixed three-account estate. An organization can operate multiple validated Platform environments and many Workstream account pairs. Start with one representative cell and prove onboarding, production promotion, rollback, centralized observability, and zero-residual retirement before repeating the baseline. Service control policies Service control policies constrain the maximum permissions available to Platform and Workstream accounts. They complement, rather than replace, IAM, gateway authorization, Guardrails, resource policies, network controls, and pipeline evidence. The blueprint renders and reviews the effective policies for the exact account and Region instead of relying on source-code intent alone. Model and Region admission: Organization policy and Gateway execution roles restrict inference to approved models and the supported Region. Adding a model or Region requires service availability, residency, IAM, quality, cost, rollback, observability, and denial validation. Guardrail and inference enforcement: Agents do not call model providers directly. Inference crosses the governed gateway, where the stage Guardrail and model allow-list are applied. Pipeline-only Workstream mutation: Workstream teams open pull requests and use the Workload pipeline. Direct developer deployment into Workstream accounts is outside the supported operating model, which keeps the reviewed release and evidence path non-bypassable. Registry and Gateway governance: Workstream Gateway synthesis fails when a subscribed Registry record is missing, changed, or not approved. Scoped deployment roles: Bootstrap policies are generated per account and Region, validated with AWS Identity and Access Management Access (IAM) Analyzer, and checked through effective-policy simulation. Administrator access is reserved for initial setup rather than routine pipeline execution. Separation of duties and adversarial proof: Platform controls model, Guardrail, Registry, and shared-service admission. Workstream teams control application behavior. Every denied path is paired with an authorized positive call and a mutation that proves the intended control caused the denial. An administrator inside a Workstream account can’t create a supported fast path around these controls. New or changed organization policies need a sandbox or representative-cell soak, exact allow and deny tests, and a rollback plan before broad attachment. CI/CD pipeline with evaluation gates The blueprint uses reviewed Platform and Workload pipelines to enforce the following promotion sequence: Source and review: A pull request establishes the immutable source revision. The pipeline pins the intended branch so an unmerged change can’t silently build the repository default branch. Build and synth: The pipeline compiles code, runs tests and linting, creates the agent manifest, scans the digest-bound image, validates policies, resolves approved Registry descriptors, and inspects synthesized AWS CloudFormation and cdk-nag output. Stable roles and permission handoff: The Workload pipeline creates stable Workstream roles and pauses. The Platform pipeline grants exact tool aliases to the exact Gateway role, live policies are verified, and only then does the Workload pipeline continue. Deploy to nonproduction: The pipeline deploys Runtime, Memory, Tool Gateway, observability, alarms, budgets, tags, and application resources into the cell’s nonproduction boundary. Evaluate the deployed agent: The gate invokes the real Runtime and measures regression, quality, tool success, refusal behavior, first-token latency, and cost. Every authorized call is paired with an adversarial twin: the gate calls an approved model and confirms success, then calls an unapproved model and confirms the denial. The same pattern applies to tools, cross-account identity, and throttling. If an expected denial is missing, the gate fails the build. Human approval: A reviewer examines the deployed evidence, known limitations, and residual risk. A generic green build is not enough when a required probe, resource, or expected denial is missing. Promote, observe, and roll back: Production promotion uses the reviewed revision and continuity checks. Runtime sessions are sampled through update, cancellation, rollback, restore, and re-run so the pipeline proves both the forward path and recovery path. No Workstream deployment step has a manual fast track. The Platform team owns the release contract, but Workstream teams operate their own pipeline instances and deployment cadence. Retirement follows a strict dependency order: Platform alias grants are revoked first, then Workstream Gateway and tool roles, then Runtime, Memory, and application resources. Each step is verified before proceeding, and a final inventory confirms zero residual resources remain. Security and governance The blueprint implements defense in depth through reinforcing identity, policy, delivery, data, and evidence controls: Identity and trust boundaries: AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Amazon Cognito provide short-lived inference credentials. AWS_IAM and SigV4 authenticate tool traffic. Exact Runtime and Gateway roles, issuer and audience checks, account and Region context, and scoped bootstrap trust limit each principal to its intended path. Model safety and admission: Inference flows through the governed gateway described in the Solution overview, applying Guardrails and model allow-lists before every call. Tool authorization: The Tool Gateway invokes only Registry-approved aliases, as detailed in the Solution overview. Cedar policies provide authorization, with a retained AWS Lambda wrapper for defense in depth. Tenant data protection: Workstream accounts isolate application state. AgentCore memory uses actor-scoped namespaces and customer-managed KMS keys. Tools and application data remain team-owned, and retention, deletion, and access policies are explicit rather than inherited from a shared mutable workload account. Software supply chain and release: Reviewed source, manifest hashing, reproducible builds, digest-bound image scanning, policy validation, cdk-nag checks, deployed-runtime evaluation, human approval, rollback, and dependency-ordered teardown form one release contract. A missing check fails closed. Audit, observability, and cost governance: CloudTrail and retained control-plane data corroborate pipeline evidence. OAM shares logs, metrics, and traces with central operators. Standard allocation tags, budgets, quotas, and AWS Cost and Usage Report reconciliation assign ownership without giving the agent permission to rewrite its own attribution. The repository is a reference implementation. Developers can adjust it to address their needs. The deployment and available features are based on the eu-west-1 (Ireland) Region. A substituted component, another Region, or a wider organizational rollout requires its own availability, security, load, rollback, observability, and teardown evidence. Conclusion In this post, we walked through an enterprise Agentic AI Platform built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The architecture separates a centrally governed Platform control plane from repeatable, team-owned Workstream cells, with distinct inference and tool gateways, and production promotion gated by deployed-runtime evaluation. The companion repository includes a blueprint that validates these controls end to end, from pipeline gates and adversarial boundary tests through zero-residual teardown. The support claim stops at that tested boundary. To get started, deploy one representative Workstream cell from the companion repository, prove its full lifecycle, and then automate additional cells from the same versioned baseline. Related resources: Enterprise Agentic AI Platform Blueprint on GitHub Enterprise multi-account architecture for running agentic AI in production on AWS (Prescriptive Guidance) Building an Enterprise Agentic AI Platform on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Workshop Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation   About the authors Omar Elkharbotly Omar is a Senior GenAI/ML Specialist Solutions Architect at AWS. He works with enterprise customers across the UK and Ireland to design and deploy generative AI and machine learning solutions using Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to build scalable, production-ready applications. Mia Chang Mia is a Specialist Solutions Architect for Agentic AI, based in Berlin, Germany. She helps enterprise customers across EMEA design, operationalize, and scale agentic AI workloads, from first agents to production on managed platforms; and hybrid architectures with self-managed infrastructure. Her expertise spans agentic application architecture, agent security and governance, Responsible AI, and platform engineering. Siva Shanmugam Siva is a Senior Solutions Architect at Amazon Web Services, specializing in AI/ML, Data, and cloud-native architecture. His expertise spans Generative and Agentic AI applications, Developer Experience Transformation — including Agentic Coding and AI-powered engineering practices — and end-to-end enterprise cloud solutions.

title: Distributed training with Ray Train DLCs and EFA on EKS
summary: The Ray Train Deep Learning Container ships the full CUDA-through-EFA stack, so you build no image. This post walks through a reproducible sample that fine-tunes Qwen2.5-1.5B with PyTorch FSDP across eight GPUs on two EFA-enabled g6.12xlarge instances on Amazon EKS, using the container exactly as published.
content: What usually stops PyTorch training from scaling out to a cluster is the container, not the model code. Every container needs the same CUDA runtime , a PyTorch build compiled against it, NCCL (NVIDIA Collective Communications Library), the Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) userspace libraries, the AWS OFI NCCL plugin that connects NCCL to EFA, and a Ray version the cluster operator agrees with. Building that image and rebuilding it each time one of those pieces moves is a project of its own, and it has nothing to do with the model you set out to train. The Ray Train Deep Learning Container (DLC) is that image, built by AWS. AWS assembles the stack, tests it as one unit, publishes it in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) Public and keeps it patched. Figure 1: One EKS cluster with a control plane managed by AWS, a CPU system node (m7i.xlarge) running the KubeRay operator and Ray head, and two EFA-enabled g6.12xlarge nodes in one Availability Zone. KubeRay builds it from one RayCluster manifest, Ray Train places eight workers, one per GPU, and inter-node collectives cross over EFA. Ray runs a job across machines as a single cluster with two roles. The Ray head coordinates and runs the global control store that tracks cluster state, the dashboard and job server you submit jobs to. Ray worker nodes supply the GPUs and run the training processes. Each worker joins the cluster by connecting to the head’s address when it starts. On Kubernetes, each of these is a pod. Kubernetes has no built-in idea of a Ray cluster, so something must create the head and worker pods, start Ray in the right role in each, point the workers at the head, and replace pods that fail. KubeRay does this. It’s an open source Kubernetes operator that adds a RayCluster resource: you describe a head group and a worker group in one manifest, and KubeRay builds and maintains the cluster from it. A single tagged image runs as both the Ray head and the Ray workers, whether KubeRay starts it on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) or you start it yourself on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2). What you add is configuration: which instances, how many GPUs each pod gets, which network transport NCCL uses, and which extra Python packages a job needs. All of it is set from outside the image. This post walks through a sample that uses the DLC exactly as published to fine-tune Qwen2.5-1.5B with PyTorch Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) across eight NVIDIA L4 GPUs on two g6.12xlarge instances. The training code is one function, the cluster is one RayCluster manifest plus a file of variables, and no image is built at any point. Because the DLC already carries the EFA stack, collectives between the two instances run over the EFA as soon as the pods request it. The entire solution is in this sample repository , and it uses the same KubeRay-on-EKS foundation as our multi-node Ray Serve walkthrough . What you get without building anything The Ray Train DLC is the PyTorch training image with Ray’s training libraries on top. The tag this sample pulls, public.ecr.aws/deep-learning-containers/ray:train-ml-cuda-v1.1 , replaces a build that would otherwise look like this: Layer What you would otherwise build and keep aligned In the Ray Train DLC Distributed runtime Ray with the dashboard and job server, at a version KubeRay supports Ray 2.58.0 with Train, Tune and Data Framework PyTorch compiled for your CUDA version PyTorch 2.13.0, torchvision 0.28.0 GPU runtime CUDA, cuDNN and NCCL releases that agree with each other CUDA 13.0.2, cuDNN, NCCL 2.29.7 Networking EFA installer, libfabric and aws-ofi-nccl , built against that NCCL EFA latest, AWS OFI NCCL plugin, GDRCopy Training libraries DeepSpeed, flash-attn and Transformer Engine compiled for your CUDA DeepSpeed, flash-attn, Transformer Engine, PyTorch Lightning, Hugging Face libraries Diagnostics NCCL tests built from source all_reduce_perf already on the path The networking row is the one most teams would least like to own. A mismatch there doesn’t produce an error. NCCL drops to TCP sockets, and the job runs to completion at a fraction of the speed. In the DLC, those libraries are built and tested together, and AWS gates each release on multi-node EFA and multi-node KubeRay training tests, which are exactly the paths this sample uses. A few more properties remove work that you would otherwise do per cluster: No registry setup –  The image is public, so nodes pull it without credentials and nothing is built or pushed on the way. No driver matching –  On startup the entrypoint checks the host’s NVIDIA driver and, if it is older than the image’s CUDA, turns on the bundled CUDA forward-compatibility libraries automatically. No head-versus-worker images –  The image has no fixed role. Whatever starts the container supplies the ray start command, so one tag serves every pod. No separate inference image family –  Ray Train shares the ray ECR repository with the Ray Serve DLC and Ray LLM DLCs , under the train-ml tag prefix. Configure it, don’t rebuild it Everything that differs between one training job and the next is set around the image. The sample uses each of these mechanisms: What you control How you set it In this sample Head or worker role KubeRay rayStartParams per pod group Same DLC_IMAGE for both. Head runs with num-gpus: "0" GPUs and EFA per pod Kubernetes resource requests nvidia.com/gpu: 4 , vpc.amazonaws.com/efa: 1 Network transport Environment variables on the pod or the job FI_PROVIDER , NCCL_NET_PLUGIN , NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME , NCCL_DEBUG Extra Python packages Ray runtime_env at submit time Any package a job needs, installed at submit time Image version Versioned or digest-pinned tag in DLC_IMAGE train-ml-cuda-v1.1 Cluster shape Variables in scripts/ env.sh Instance type, node count, GPUs per node, Region, AZ Training job Arguments to train.py Model, steps, sequence length, batch size Packages per job. The image ships the HuggingFace training stack, so this sample’s job needs nothing added. When an experiment does need a library the image does not carry, Ray installs it for that job at submit time through runtime_env and the image is unchanged. No new image, no new tag. Transport per job. The image defaults to FI_PROVIDER=efa , and its NCCL configuration excludes the loopback and Docker bridge interfaces. On EKS you point NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME at the pod’s eth0 . The sample sets all four networking variables in the manifest anyway, so the behavior is visible in one file and doesn’t depend on image defaults. Because these are plain environment variables, a single job can override them through its runtime_env . Versions you choose. The sample pins train-ml-cuda-v1.1 , the current minor release, so a cluster is reproducible from one run to the next. The vX.Y tags move with security rebuilds. The fully qualified vX.Y.Z tags stay frozen at the original release build, so pin a digest when you need a byte-identical run. The same image is also available from private ECR URIs. How the cluster is laid out Figure 2: The sample’s cluster. Every pod runs the same Ray Train DLC from Amazon ECR Public. The CPU system node runs the KubeRay operator and a Ray head with no GPUs. Each EFA-enabled g6.12xlarge, both in one Availability Zone, runs a single four-GPU Ray worker pod. All nodes sit in private subnets of one virtual private cloud (VPC) and reach the internet only through a NAT Gateway, which is how every node pulls the DLC from Amazon ECR Public and how workers download model weights from Hugging Face. One m7i.xlarge forms the system node group, hosting kube-system add-ons, the KubeRay operator and the Ray head. The head runs the job server on port 8265 and Ray’s control store on 6379, and it advertises no GPUs, so no training work lands on it. Jobs are submitted from inside the head pod with kubectl exec , through the EKS API, so port 8265 is never exposed outside the cluster. Training runs on two g6.12xlarge instances, each with four NVIDIA L4 GPUs, 48 vCPUs, 192 GiB of memory, 40 Gbps of networking and one EFA interface. Each runs one Ray worker pod that claims all four GPUs and the EFA interface, and Ray Train places four workers in each pod: ranks 0–3 on one instance, 4–7 on the other. Because EFA traffic doesn’t cross Availability Zones, the scripts place both instances in a single zone that has been checked to offer g6.12xlarge. What Ray Train does inside the container The DLC provides the stack. Ray Train provides the part that would otherwise be launcher code. Multi-node PyTorch normally means starting a process per GPU on every host and giving each one its rank, the world size and a rendezvous address. With Ray Train you write the training loop as a function and pass it to TorchTrainer with a ScalingConfig . Ray starts one worker per GPU wherever the cluster has GPUs, forms the torch.distributed process group, and runs your function on each worker. This sample asks Ray Train for FSDP , which splits the model’s weights, gradients and optimizer state across all eight GPUs rather than copying them to each one. Qwen2.5-1.5B in bfloat16 needs about 12 GB for those four tensors. Sharded eight ways, each L4 GPU holds roughly 1.5 GB. The price is communication: FSDP gathers each layer’s weights before using it and reduce-scatters gradients afterwards, so the whole model crosses between ranks on every step. Between the two instances, that traffic is what the DLC’s EFA stack carries. Prerequisites You must have the following in place before you start: Tools: AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) v2 signed in to the target account, eksctl, kubectl, Helm, and envsubst from GNU gettext. Quota: 96 vCPUs of G-family On-Demand capacity for the two g6.12xlarge instances, in an AWS Region where at least one zone offers them. If you already hold an On-Demand Capacity Reservation for the instances, set CAPACITY_RESERVATION_ID instead. The scripts launch the node group into it and skip the capacity search. Budget: about $9.50 an hour while the GPU instances are up, covering both instances, the EKS control plane and the NAT Gateway. A quick way to confirm that the CLI is pointed at the account that you expect: aws sts get-caller-identity The training code: One function and a trainer code/train.py is the whole job, and it contains nothing specific to the container, the cluster or the network. Ray runs train_func once per GPU. It asks Ray for its rank, loads the model, hands it to prepare_model for FSDP, and runs an ordinary PyTorch loop: code/train.py — the per-GPU function (abridged) def train_func(config): ctx = ray.train.get_context() world_size, rank = ctx.get_world_size(), ctx.get_world_rank() device = ray.train.torch.get_device() model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(config["model_id"], torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16) # Any submodule above 10M parameters becomes its own FSDP unit. Wrapping by # size, not by a model-specific layer class, keeps the script model-agnostic. auto_wrap_policy = partial(size_based_auto_wrap_policy, min_num_params=int(1e7)) model = ray.train.torch.prepare_model( model, parallel_strategy="fsdp", parallel_strategy_kwargs={"auto_wrap_policy": auto_wrap_policy}, ) optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=config["learning_rate"]) for step in range(config["steps"]): input_ids = torch.randint(0, model.config.vocab_size, (config["batch_size"], config["seq_len"]), device=device) optimizer.zero_grad() loss = model(input_ids=input_ids, labels=input_ids).loss loss.backward() # parameters gathered again, gradients reduce-scattered optimizer.step() # local: each rank updates only its own slice ray.train.report({"step": step, "loss": loss.item()}) The driver joins the running cluster, counts its GPUs and starts the trainer. Because the worker count comes from the cluster, the same script runs unchanged on one node or many: code/train.py — the driver (abridged) ray.init(address="auto") # join the RayCluster num_workers = int(ray.cluster_resources().get("GPU", 0)) # 8 here trainer = TorchTrainer( train_func, train_loop_config={...}, scaling_config=ScalingConfig(num_workers=num_workers, use_gpu=True), run_config=RunConfig(name="ray-train-fsdp-llm"), ) result = trainer.fit() The batches are random token IDs so that the run depends on nothing but the cluster. The sample is judged on whether real FSDP collectives crossed both nodes and the job completed. For a real fine-tune, replace the random tensor with a Ray Data or DataLoader pipeline. Nothing else in the function changes. The manifest: The only place the DLC is configured manifest/raycluster.yaml is where the image meets the cluster, and it is short because the image needs so little. The head’s only special setting is NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=void , which stops the container runtime’s NVIDIA hook from failing on a node that has no GPU. The worker group holds everything else: manifest/raycluster.yaml — worker group (abridged) workerGroupSpecs: - groupName: gpu-workers replicas: 2 rayStartParams: num-gpus: "${GPUS_PER_NODE}" # keeps Ray's GPU count equal to the pod's template: spec: nodeSelector: { role: gpu-worker } containers: - name: ray-worker image: "${DLC_IMAGE}" # the DLC as published; same tag as the head env: - { name: NCCL_DEBUG, value: "INFO" } # print the chosen transport - { name: NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME, value: "eth0" } # pod network on EKS - { name: FI_PROVIDER, value: "efa" } # libfabric: EFA, nothing else - { name: NCCL_NET_PLUGIN, value: "ofi" } # load the AWS OFI plugin resources: limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: "${GPUS_PER_NODE}", vpc.amazonaws.com/efa: "1", cpu: "40", memory: 160Gi } requests: { nvidia.com/gpu: "${GPUS_PER_NODE}", vpc.amazonaws.com/efa: "1", cpu: "40", memory: 160Gi } Read it as three decisions. Which image: ${DLC_IMAGE} , unmodified, for both head and workers. Which hardware: four GPUs and the node’s single EFA interface per pod. Requesting vpc.amazonaws.com/efa is what makes the EFA device plugin mount the interface into the container. Without it, NCCL can’t see EFA and falls back to sockets. Which transport: four environment variables, so nothing is left to auto-detection. Two smaller details keep a multi-node job stable. First, requests should equal limits, which places the workers in Kubernetes’ Guaranteed Quality of Service (QoS) class. This matters because a single throttled or evicted rank stalls the other seven. Second, num-gpus is derived from the same variable as the GPU request, so Ray’s view of capacity always matches Kubernetes’. Bringing it up: One command for the infrastructure, then the job Configuration lives in one place, scripts/env.sh : cluster name, Region, Kubernetes version, node types and counts, the image, pinned versions of KubeRay and both device plugins, and the training parameters. Export any of them to change it for a run. All five scripts are idempotent and safe to re-run. deploy_cluster.sh , deploy_node_group.sh , and deploy_ray_train_job.sh each prompt before creating or touching cluster resources. install_gpu_plugins.sh and install_kuberay.sh are reconcilers and run straight through. cd training/ray-train/scripts source ./env.sh ./deploy_all.sh – Finds where the capacity actually is, then builds the infrastructure there. g6.12xlarge capacity shifts between Regions and Availability Zones day to day, so this is the starting point rather than a Region guessed up front in env.sh . It first runs find_gpu_capacity.sh , which checks, per candidate Region: whether g6.12xlarge is offered in each Availability Zone, whether the account’s On-Demand G/VT-family vCPU quota has room for the requested node count, and the EC2 Spot placement score as a capacity signal. With --probe , which deploy_all.sh passes by default, it gets a definitive answer by creating and immediately canceling a real Capacity Reservation in each candidate zone. It then shows the plan and asks once: Proceed with the whole chain without further prompts? (y/N): Answering y runs, in order, deploy_cluster.sh , deploy_node_group.sh , install_gpu_plugins.sh , and install_kuberay.sh in the recommended Region, each skipping its own repeat confirmation because this one already asked ( -y skips this prompt too, and --plan shows the plan without creating anything). If the GPU node group can’t launch in the best zone, the script removes it and tries the next zone the probe confirmed. GPU_AZ is also cross-checked against the cluster’s actual private subnets, not only where g6.12xlarge happens to be offered, so the GPU node group can’t end up pinned to an Availability Zone the cluster has no subnet in. The chosen Region and zone are saved to scripts/.placement.env , which every other script reads, so later commands target the same place without re-exporting anything. Together the four steps take 20 to 30 minutes on a fresh Region. An existing cluster or node group is detected and reused. deploy_cluster.sh creates the EKS control plane, VPC, OpenID Connect (OIDC) provider, core add-ons, and the m7i.xlarge system node group, choosing subnets in zones that actually offer g6.12xlarge. deploy_node_group.sh adds the two g6.12xlarge instances with EFA turned on, labeled role=gpu-worker and nvidia.com/gpu.present=true . The second label is one that teams often overlook. Without it, the NVIDIA device plugin chart’s DaemonSet runs on zero nodes, with no error pointing at the cause. install_gpu_plugins.sh makes sure both device plugins are present. Recent eksctl bundles them into an EFA-enabled node group, so on a fresh cluster it finds them and skips. Otherwise it installs them at pinned chart versions. Either way it verifies nvidia.com/gpu and vpc.amazonaws.com/efa are allocatable on every GPU node rather than trusting a successful Helm release. install_kuberay.sh installs the KubeRay operator onto the system node, keeping it off the GPU instances. What deploy_all.sh does not do by default is run the training job. That stays a separate step you can re-run as often as you like, because it is a real job run rather than infrastructure, and a failed job then never sends you back through cluster setup. Pass --train to chain it: ./deploy_ray_train_job.sh — the RayCluster, the job, and the checks. Renders the manifest with envsubst and applies it. It then re-reads each GPU node’s allocatable resources before waiting on any pod: if a device plugin didn’t come up, you get a clear error here rather than a pod that sits in Pending until a timeout. Once the head is Ready and both workers are Ready, it copies code/ onto the head and, through kubectl exec , submits from inside it: ray job submit --address http://localhost:8265 --working-dir /tmp/ray-train-code \ python3 train.py --model_id Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B The submit call streams logs from all eight ranks and returns when the job does. The script then inspects which transport NCCL used and exits with an error if the job failed or EFA wasn’t in the path, which also makes it usable as a continuous integration (CI) gate. ./deploy_ray_train_job.sh status prints the RayCluster state, which instance hosts each pod, and GPU capacity. A correctly provisioned cluster looks like this: $ kubectl get nodes -l role=gpu-worker \ -o custom-columns='NAME:.metadata.name,GPU:.status.allocatable.nvidia\.com/gpu,EFA:.status.allocatable.vpc\.amazonaws\.com/efa' NAME GPU EFA ip-192-168-70-51 4 1 ip-192-168-92-26 4 1 Figure 3: One FSDP step on this cluster. Weights are gathered in the forward and backward passes and gradients are reduce-scattered. Traffic between the instances takes the path the DLC ships, NCCL → AWS OFI NCCL plugin → libfabric → EFA, or falls back to TCP sockets when that path is missing. Adapting it to your workload Because the image is used as published and the job learns its scale from the cluster, most changes touch exactly one file: You want to change Where No changes needed to The model MODEL_ID Code, manifest, image Steps, sequence length, batch size STEPS , SEQ_LEN , BATCH_SIZE Code, manifest, image The training loop itself Body of train_func Trainer, manifest, image, scripts An additional Python package --runtime-env-json pip list Image A pinned DLC release DLC_IMAGE to a versioned tag Everything else The GPU instance family GPU_NODE_TYPE , GPUS_PER_NODE Code, image How many GPU instances GPU_NODE_COUNT , plus replicas , minReplicas and maxReplicas in the manifest Code (it counts the GPUs) Region or zone REGION , optionally GPU_AZ Everything else Variables in the table live in env.sh unless stated otherwise. When switching instance families, GPUS_PER_NODE has to match the hardware, and the family needs EFA support plus a place on the EFA device plugin’s list of allowed instance types. The plugin version pinned here is known to include g6.12xlarge. Moving to p5 or another GPUDirect-capable family needs no change to the image or the training code. Tearing it down The GPU instances are the expensive part, at around $9.50 an hour together with the control plane and NAT Gateway. Remove things in the opposite order to how they were created: ./delete_ray_train_job.sh # RayCluster ./install_kuberay.sh cleanup # KubeRay operator ./install_gpu_plugins.sh cleanup # NVIDIA and EFA device plugins ./delete_node_group.sh # GPU instances ./delete_cluster.sh # EKS cluster, VPC and system node Where to go next Two instances and eight GPUs ran a sharded fine-tune on EKS with a container nobody built. The Ray Train DLC supplied a tested stack from CUDA through EFA. KubeRay started it as head and workers from one tag. Ray Train placed the workers and formed the process group. Everything that varied, from hardware to transport to Python packages, was set from outside the image. The EFA path the image ships engaged with four environment variables and doubled throughput over TCP on unchanged code. Natural next moves: Replace the random batches with a real dataset, and checkpoint to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) or Amazon FSx for Lustre. Pin DLC_IMAGE to a versioned tag for reproducible runs. Turn on FailureConfig so long runs survive a lost instance. Move to a larger model on a GPUDirect RDMA family such as p5. The image and code stay the same.   About the authors Sunita Koppar Sunita is a Senior Specialist Solutions Architect in Generative AI and Machine Learning at AWS, where she partners with customers across diverse industries to design solutions, build proof-of-concepts, and drive measurable business outcomes. Beyond her professional role, she is deeply passionate about learning and teaching Sanskrit, actively engaging with student communities to help them upskill and grow. Kevin Wang Kevin is a Software Development Engineer on the AWS Deep Learning Containers/AMIs team, where he builds and maintains deep learning images that customers run on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2), Amazon SageMaker AI, and Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). His team manages the images and their build systems as open source on GitHub. He holds a bachelor’s degree from Peking University and a master’s degree from the University of Southern California, both in computer science. Sukhmeet Singh Sukhmeet is a Senior Specialist Solutions Architect in Generative AI and Machine Learning at AWS. He partners with independent software vendor (ISV) customers to design AI solutions, build proof of concept, and take them into production with measurable business results. His interests cover generative AI, Computer Vision, IoT, ML Infrastructure, and Natural Language Processing. He especially enjoys connecting these areas to solve real-world problems at scale.

title: Accelerating software delivery with agentic QA automation using Amazon Nova Act – Part 3
summary: As QA test automation spreads across an organization, organizing tests and controlling who owns them becomes the real work. Part 3 of the QA Studio series on Amazon Nova Act adds applications that organize tests and report health metrics, plus team-based user management that controls who can see and change what.
content: As quality assurance (QA) automation adoption grows inside an organization, a new problem appears that has nothing to do with writing tests. A platform team stands up test automation, then a second team wants to join, then a dozen more. Soon hundreds of test cases belong to different products and squads, and everyone can see everyone else’s tests. No one can answer a basic question at a glance: is this application’s test coverage healthy right now? Test authoring stops being the bottleneck. Organizing tests and controlling who can touch them becomes the work. A second, related question follows close behind: who owns this application and its tests, and who is accountable when coverage slips? Without a clear owner, health problems have no one to land on. In the first post , we introduced QA Studio, a reference solution built with Amazon Nova Act . Teams use it to define tests in natural language and run them through AI-powered visual navigation. In the second post , we added test suites and a CLI for batch regression testing in continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines. In this post, we cover two capabilities that help QA Studio scale across an organization. The first, applications , organizes tests and reports health metrics. The second, team-based user management , controls who can see and change what. Organizing tests with applications An application in QA Studio represents the system under test: a website, a web app, a service front end. It’s the container that gives a collection of tests, a home, and an owner. Use cases (the individual tests from Part 1) and test suites (the regression collections from Part 2) belong to an application, and they inherit its ownership. Instead of one flat list of every test in the deployment, each team works inside the applications they own. Creating an application takes a name, a base URL, and an optional set of environments such as development, staging, and production. From the application page, teams create new use cases directly in context, add existing ones, and group them into test suites. This is also where QA Studio reports on the health of the tests it runs. Figure 1: The application detail page, showing pass rate, executions, and failures with the use cases and test suites tabs Understanding application health with metrics Tests produce results. Understanding those results over time is what tells a team whether the development lifecycle for an application is healthy, not only whether a single build is ready for release. QA Studio records the outcome of every execution as Amazon CloudWatch custom metrics, dimensioned by application and by environment. It turns these metrics into a health view on the application page. The top of the page answers the immediate question with three figures: the pass rate over the selected window, the total number of executions, and the current failure count. Alongside them, QA Studio computes a health score of 0–100. The score starts from the pass rate and subtracts a penalty for flaky tests. That way, an application whose tests pass but flip between pass and fail doesn’t present a falsely perfect picture. A team scanning a portfolio of applications can tell the stable ones from the ones that need attention without opening each result. The metrics tab moves from the current snapshot to trends. Teams choose a 7-day window with hourly granularity or a 30-day window with daily granularity, and QA Studio charts executions, successes, failures, and average duration across that period. Because the underlying metrics carry an environment dimension, teams filter the view to a single environment. For example, they can compare how staging behaves against production for the same set of tests. Two views target the tests that cost teams the most time. The flaky tests view ranks use cases by how often they flipped between passing and failing over the last seven days. This surfaces the intermittent failures that erode trust in a suite before they turn into a production miss. The recent failures view lists the latest failed executions for quick triage. Each one links back to the Amazon Nova Act trajectory logs and session recordings described in Part 1. That way, moving from “this test is failing” to “here is exactly what the agent saw” takes one click. Figure 2: The metrics tab: pass rate, executions, and average duration over the selected window, with the daily success-and-failure chart, failure hotspots, and the flaky use case ranking Controlling access with teams and roles Metrics tell a team how their applications are doing. Team-based user management decides which applications are theirs in the first place. QA Studio organizes access around teams, and an application belongs to exactly one team. Members of that team work with its applications. Everyone else doesn’t see them. Every team member holds one of five roles, and each role includes the permissions of the ones below it: Admin : Studio-wide access to every team, application, and user, including creating teams and assigning applications. Admin is a studio-wide role rather than a per-team assignment. Team Lead : Manages their own team members and creates applications for the team. Editor : Creates and edits use cases and test suites within the team’s applications. Executor : Runs use cases and suites but doesn’t modify them. Viewer : Read-only access to the team’s applications and results. Because roles are cumulative, a Team Lead has everything an Editor has, and so on down to Viewer. Access to a use case or a test suite follows the application that contains it. If a member can work with the application, they can work with its tests, bounded by their role. This keeps permission management at the application level instead of on thousands of individual tests. An administrator sees the whole studio. The Users page lists every account with its team and role in one place. An admin can tell who holds Team Lead on which team and who carries Studio-wide Administrator rights. In the reference deployment shown here, four users span two teams: two Team Leads, one Viewer, and one Studio-wide Administrator. The Teams page rolls the same data up by team, showing each team’s member count and application count side by side. An admin can see which teams are expanding before opening any one of them. Figure 3: The studio-wide Users page: every account with its team and role, filterable by team and by role The same membership data, rolled up by team, appears on the Teams page. Figure 4: The Teams page: each team with its member and application counts Switching from teams to applications, the studio-wide Applications list shows every application across all teams. Figure 5: The studio-wide Applications list: every application with its base URL, owning team, use-case count, and last execution status Sharing applications between teams Teams rarely work in complete isolation. A platform team might own an application that a feature team needs to run against, without handing over the ability to change it. QA Studio supports this with shared access: the owning team grants another team access to an application at a view, execute, or full level. Shared access follows a ceiling rule. A user’s effective permission on a shared application is the lower of their own role and the level of the grant. A Viewer who is given full access to a shared application remains view-only, because their role is the ceiling. This way, an owning team can share widely without granting more than a recipient’s role allows. What a team lead sees A team lead works inside a single team rather than the whole studio. Opening My Team presents four tabs that cover everything the lead controls: Members, Applications, Use Cases, and Shared Access. The Members tab lists the people on the team. The lead can change any member’s role inline or add a new one, so day-to-day access management stays with the person closest to the work. In the AWS Team shown here, the lead manages two members, one Team Lead and one Viewer. Figure 6: The team lead’s Members tab, with inline role assignment for each member The Applications tab shows only the applications the team owns, each with its test-case count and last-run time. This keeps the lead focused on their own surface rather than the full studio inventory. The Shared Access tab is where cross-team sharing becomes concrete. Here the AWS Team has granted the AMZN Team view access to an application, and the lead can grant, revoke, or change the level of that access. Because the grant was view level, an AMZN Team Editor still sees the shared application read-only: the ceiling rule from the previous section, applied in practice. Figure 7: The team lead’s Applications tab, scoped to the team’s own applications The same Team Lead’s Shared Access tab records which other teams can reach the team’s applications, and at what level. Figure 8: The team lead’s Shared Access tab, showing a view-level grant to another team How it works QA Studio builds team-based access control and metrics on the same serverless foundation described in the earlier posts, adding a few AWS services to the mix: Amazon Cognito : Each team maps to a set of Cognito groups, one per role. An AWS Lambda authorizer resolves a caller’s groups into API scopes and team context on every request. Amazon DynamoDB : Teams, memberships, application ownership, and cross-team share grants are stored in the existing single-table design. Amazon CloudWatch : Every execution emits custom metrics in the QAStudio/Executions namespace, dimensioned by application and environment. The metrics API reads them back to build the health view and trend charts. AWS Lambda and Amazon API Gateway : The backend enforces access at two layers: the scope a caller’s role grants, and a resource check that confirms the caller’s team owns or has been shared with the application. Because access is derived from Cognito group membership, the OAuth client credentials flow from Part 2 fits the same model. A CI pipeline authenticates as a machine identity with the scopes it needs and no more. Getting started Applications, metrics, and team-based access control are part of the QA Studio reference solution, which you deploy in your own AWS account with the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) . All test data, results, and metrics stay within your account boundaries. After deploying, an administrator creates teams, assigns members and roles, and assigns applications to teams. Each team’s health metrics begin populating as their tests run. For deployment instructions and configuration details, see the QA Studio GitHub repository and its documentation. Conclusion In this post, we showed how QA Studio scales agentic QA automation from individual tests to an organization. Applications give every team a home for their use cases and test suites. They report health through pass rate, trend charts, a flaky-adjusted health score, and failure triage built on Amazon CloudWatch metrics. Team-based user management, backed by Amazon Cognito, keeps each team working within the applications they own, with cross-team sharing bounded by a clear ceiling rule. These capabilities build on the natural language test authoring from Part 1 and the suites and CI/CD integration from Part 2. Together, they help QA automation grow across many teams without losing visibility or control. To try it in your own environment, deploy the reference solution from the QA Studio GitHub repository, create your first team and application, and run a few use cases to watch the metrics take shape. To learn more about the agent behind it, see the Amazon Nova Act product page .   About the authors Vinicius Pedroni Vinicius is a Senior Solutions Architect at AWS for the Travel and Hospitality Industry, with focus on Edge Services and Generative AI. Vinicius is also passionate about assisting customers on their Cloud Journey, allowing them to adopt the right strategies at the right moment. Jan Wiemers Jan is a Senior Solutions Architect at AWS, working with customers in the Travel, Transportation & Logistics industry. With over 20 years of experience in the software industry, he focuses on the AI Product Development Lifecycle and Test Automation, helping customers accelerate how they build, test, and deploy AI-driven solutions.

Thin, Light and Built for Everything: NVIDIA RTX Spark Windows Laptops Gain New Models, Agent Tools and Games
summary: NVIDIA RTX Spark powers thin and light laptops built for everything that developers, creators and gamers do. RTX Spark laptops are now available from ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft and MSI. These powerful systems combine an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU and an NVIDIA Grace CPU in a single superchip with up to 128GB of unified […]
content: NVIDIA RTX Spark powers thin and light laptops built for everything that developers, creators and gamers do. RTX Spark laptops are now available from ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft and MSI. These powerful systems combine an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU and an NVIDIA Grace CPU in a single superchip with up to 128GB of unified memory and up to 1 petaflop of FP4 AI performance. That puts the NVIDIA CUDA platform, RTX graphics and the capabilities of a personal AI supercomputer inside premium Windows laptops built to go anywhere. New and expected RTX Spark updates, coming soon, include: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe, an open weight speech model for transcription, speaker attribution and translation is available on RTX Spark. The LFM3 family of open models with day-zero support. Resource management controls in NVIDIA App to allocate GPU resources between foreground apps and background agents. Phantom Blade Zero , S-GAME’s highly-anticipated action role-playing game, launches with ray tracing and NVIDIA DLSS 4.5. Experience Minecraft with path tracing and DLSS with RTX Remix1.6, available now for RTX Spark. Turn Recorded Audio Into Useful Information With NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe Introduced today, NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe is a new, open weight speech model that turns recorded conversations into useful information. Instead of needing multiple models for transcription, speaker labels and translation, developers can use one promptable model that handles all three, plus questions about the audio. It transcribes 40 languages, including seven Indic languages. Developers guide the model with plain-language prompts. For example, for a single recorded meeting, users can ask it to: “Transcribe this recording and label each speaker.” “Translate this audio into English.” “List what decisions were made in this meeting.” Prompts can also include product terms and formatting conventions, which helps the model handle specialized vocabulary in fields like healthcare, financial services and customer service. Because the weights are open, developers can choose where audio is processed, from a desktop to the cloud. Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe ranks No. 1 on the Hugging Face Open ASR and No. 2 among open weight models on Artificial Analysis — delivering leading accuracy with approximately 4.3 billion active parameters, 80% fewer than the No. 1 open weight model, making high-quality, intelligent transcription more practical on local hardware. It’s available today on Hugging Face . Quantized versions are coming soon, so developers can run Transcribe locally onNVIDIA RTX Spark and DGX Spark systems, Jetson AGX Thor devices or scale up on NVIDIA Blackwell data center GPUs. NVFP4 versions will be deployable through NeMo-Speech.cpp or vLLM. Learn more in the NVIDIA technical blog . Control How Agents and PC Apps Share GPU Resources On RTX Spark, users can have long-running agents working alongside their favorite applications. Both share the system’s GPU compute, and the right balance of resources depends on what matters to users at that moment. With the new resource management feature in NVIDIA App , users can now choose how GPU resources are shared. They can prioritize their foreground app for the best performance, or give their background-running agent more resources to get work done faster. Access control resource sharing from System > Advanced in the NVIDIA App. This feature requires hardware-accelerated GPU scheduling to be enabled in Windows Settings. Liquid AI : One Model Family, Many Ways to Work Liquid AI’s LFM3 provides a new generation of Liquid Foundation Models designed for specialized tasks. The family spans text, vision, audio, omni and decision models built on one shared backbone, with base and post-trained models available as open weights. The models are compact and fast: Liquid AI’s new 1.7-billion-parameter base model outperforms its previous 2.6-billion-parameter base model. These models support local workflows such as agents running in Hermes Agent, Pi and OpenClaw to triage inboxes and manage calendars, read documents and app screens, transcribe and translate speech, answer spoken questions about handwritten math, and route support tickets or voice requests. Developers can run LFM3 models on RTX Spark with native support through llama.cpp and vLLM, and fine-tune the models locally. ‘Phantom Blade Zero’ Launches With DLSS 4.5 S-GAME’s Phantom Blade Zero launches tonight, Oct. 28, at 7 p.m. PT on Steam and the Epic Games Store . Players can take on the role of Soul, a swordsman framed for his master’s murder, as he travels the martial world to uncover a conspiracy. NVIDIA worked with S-GAME Studio and S-GAME Publishing to add ray-traced effects to the title. On RTX Spark laptops and GeForce RTX GPU-powered PCs, ray tracing adds more accurate bounced lighting, detailed reflections and realistic shadows on foliage and terrain. The NVIDIA DLSS Dynamic Multi Frame Generation feature boosts frame rates with up to 6x frame generation, or adjusts the multiplier on the fly to hit a player’s target frame rate. Read more on GeForce.com . RTX Remix Breathes New Life Into Classics NVIDIA RTX Remix , the modding platform for remastering classic games with path tracing and DLSS, released version 1.6 last week. This update brought RTX Remix to the world’s largest gaming community: Minecraft . Both creators and players can render Minecraft Java Edition 1.21.1 through RTX Remix with DLSS-accelerated path tracing and take full advantage of realistic lighting and materials in their future creations. The update also adds DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering, up to 6x Multi Frame Generation, native RTX Spark support and agent-assisted workflows. Starting today, those upgrades come to Portal with RTX and the Half-Life 2 RTX demo. Both now support RTX Spark, with DLSS 3D-Guided Neural Rendering for more lifelike lighting and materials, a new Performance Mode for DLSS Frame Generation and new options that speed up path tracing. RTX Remix 1.6 also makes AI-powered modding simpler. A redesigned ComfyUI workflow lets modders generate physically based materials directly inside RTX Remix, with no application programming interface setup, batch processing for full projects and presets for less technical creators. Plus, with NVIDIA agent skills, compatible AI agents can work directly with RTX Remix to help speed up remastering projects. Learn more in the RTX Remix blog . RTX Spark Laptops: Beautifully Designed, Built for Everything RTX Spark laptops come in a range of designs, so users can choose one that fits how they work and play. Options include different screen sizes, colors, touchscreens, pen support and two-in-one convertibles. RTX Spark laptops are as thin as 14mm and as light as three pounds, with all-day battery life. Such slim designs are possible because RTX Spark places the GPU, CPU and up to 128GB of unified memory on one power-efficient superchip. Creative projects and AI models draw from the same memory pool, so a laptop can take on work that used to call for a desktop workstation, even when unplugged. Here’s what this means for: AI developers: Run models and agents locally on NVIDIA CUDA — the same platform that powers AI in the cloud — with a path to deploy across more than 150 million NVIDIA RTX AI PCs and NVIDIA GPUs in the cloud. Creators: RTX Spark can edit camera native 4:2:2 video and render 3D scenes of up to 90GB. Adobe Photoshop and Premiere offer native RTX Spark support through beta releases. Gamers: Hundreds of games run on RTX Spark, with NVIDIA DLSS, ray tracing, Reflex and G-SYNC delivering sharper visuals and smoother, more responsive gameplay. RTX Spark laptops are available now from ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft and MSI, starting at $2,599, with 128GB configurations on shelves. Find a laptop on the RTX Spark product page . #ICYMI: More Updates From NVIDIA Local AI Microducks learn to walk with help from RTX Spark: During the GTC Berlin keynote, NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang showed how AI agents running on RTX Spark can help train Hugging Face’s Microduck robot . A new NVIDIA technical blog walks through the workflow: Hermes Agent and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt plan an obstacle course on RTX Spark, Astra builds the 3D assets, NVIDIA Isaac Lab trains the navigation policy and RTX Spark validates it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. Watch the demo and try the playbook . NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB is now available , enabling natural conversations and multistep agent tasks with as little as 4GB of memory. The model powers local voice assistants, game characters and embedded interfaces on RTX Spark, DGX Spark, GeForce RTX GPUs and NVIDIA Jetson devices. It supports llama.cpp, vLLM, Ollama, Unsloth and LM Studio, and works with Hermes and OpenClaw. For more demanding agent workloads, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is designed to run local agents on RTX Spark. Black Forest Labs’ FLUX 3 Image Klein is a 5.6-billion-parameter open weights model that lets users generate and edit images locally. NVIDIA-optimized versions run on RTX GPUs with as little as 8GB of VRAM. Developers can also fine-tune the model on RTX Spark using an NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel recipe to customize it for specific creative workflows. NVIDIA DGX Spark 64GB is now available to purchase from manufacturer partners, giving developers and researchers another way to build and run AI locally. Powered by the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip, it combines 64GB of unified memory with DGX OS and the NVIDIA AI software stack for agent development, inference and fine-tuning. Learn more and explore purchase options . Follow NVIDIA RTX Spark on X , Instagram , TikTok and Facebook — and stay informed by subscribing to the NVIDIA Local AI newsletter . Follow NVIDIA Workstation on LinkedIn and X . See notice regarding software product information.

Run either one and choose a time range. #4284 366fafb Thanks @7Sageer ! - Sessions in web and desktop now unload from memory after 30 minutes idle and resume transparently on next access. #4247 0325b75 Thanks @RealKai42 ! - Plan mode now starts only when you turn it on, and every plan waits for your review: the agent can no longer enter Plan mode by itself, Never Ask no longer approves plans automatically, and kimi -p skips default_plan_mode and cannot approve the plan of a session that is already in Plan mode. #4316 874d9ab Thanks @huangzheng2016 ! - Add /provider refresh [providerId] to re-fetch provider model lists at runtime; unknown /provider subcommands now show a usage hint instead of opening the manager. #4347 b3c6e0a Thanks @Grapedge ! - Report main-session and subagent status to compatible terminals with OSC 7501, including pending interactions and retained results. #4312 01ef64e Thanks @tpoisonooo ! - Raise Tower's default agent concurrency limit from 16 to 256, support the existing max_running_tasks limit and per-spawn model selection, and reduce lock contention during inbox, review, and status processing. Patch Changes #4428 461c6e9 Thanks @wbxl2000 ! - Fix cancelled questions showing as answered in session history. #4410 a9dc3a9 Thanks @RealKai42 ! - Fix compaction missing the prompt cache when dynamically loaded MCP tools are enabled. #4364 7ccac2b Thanks @pvzheroes125 ! - Fix missing dynamically loaded MCP tools in the first conversation turn. #4431 98c1cfb Thanks @pvzheroes125 ! - Fix MCP authorization completion being delayed by idle browser connections. #4460 78b72fe Thanks @kimi-agent-bot ! - Fix Swarm mode being ignored when submitting a prompt. #4434 f47400a Thanks @kimi-agent-bot ! - Fix copying and saving data and blob images on non-loopback Web connections. #4435 70a661c Thanks @kimi-agent-bot ! - Fix Shiki code highlighting on non-loopback Web connections. #4310 8df234a Thanks @Grapedge ! - Keep fullscreen approval options visible while long requests scroll. #4310 8df234a Thanks @Grapedge ! - Stop clicks used to refocus the fullscreen terminal from activating controls, opening links, or moving the editor caret. #4310 8df234a Thanks @Grapedge ! - Add mouse selection to fullscreen approval, Settings, permission, and workspace trust dialogs, and fade the editor and waiting panels when they lose focus. #4331 759958a Thanks @RealKai42 ! - Update cross-tool imports for custom homes, instruction duplicate checks, project skills, and MCP settings; stop importing standalone .claude/AGENTS.md , project .codex/AGENTS.md , .codex/CLAUDE.md , and loose skill files, which can still be copied manually. #4428 461c6e9 Thanks @wbxl2000 ! - Replace the server's WebSocket event.approval.* and event.question.* events with a single flat interaction frame, and replace POST /sessions/{id}/approvals/{id} , POST /sessions/{id}/questions/{id} and POST /sessions/{id}/questions/{id}:dismiss with POST /sessions/{id}/interactions/{id} ; the old events and endpoints, along with GET /sessions/{id}/approvals and GET /sessions/{id}/questions , are removed. #4413 8dabf4a Thanks @7Sageer ! - Stop resending full-size images on every turn after the provider rejects them as too large or unsupported; later turns and compaction keep the reduced images until you switch models or the conversation history is rewritten. #4283 4be3f0b Thanks @sailist ! - Reconnect workspace MCP servers automatically with backoff when the initial connection fails or the connection drops, so their tools come back on their own; tune the interval with [mcp] reconnect_initial_delay_ms and reconnect_max_delay_ms . #4310 8df234a Thanks @Grapedge ! - Show NotifyUser updates in cards with an Update badge, streaming titles, and expandable messages. #4310 8df234a Thanks @Grapedge ! - Show each option's description in the plan approval panel. #4313 256ce61 Thanks @huangzheng2016 ! - Speed up session resume for long conversations. #4422 2e539f2 Thanks @sailist ! - Fix workspace resource leaks by releasing resources when no live sessions remain. #4346 f70c365 Thanks @Grapedge ! - Show a Compacting spinner with working tips in the activity pane instead of the in-progress transcript card. #4430 93137ca Thanks @RealKai42 ! - Pass the text a subagent wrote before it was stopped, timed out, or failed back to the parent agent, marked as incomplete. #4310 8df234a Thanks @Grapedge ! - Move todo lists into expandable transcript cards and remove the old input-area panel and Ctrl-T shortcut. #4365 eb1205c Thanks @kimi-agent-bot ! - Fix corrupted characters appearing in truncated tool results that contain emoji or other non-BMP characters. #4347 b3c6e0a Thanks @Grapedge ! - Fix CJK autocomplete and Markdown rendering, keyboard handling, and fullscreen image rendering. #4310 8df234a Thanks @Grapedge ! - Add keyboard and mouse navigation to the experimental Updates panel, with clearer focus styling and a reading position that stays put; enable it with KIMI_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_NOTIFY_USER=1 . #4495 e851723 Thanks @kimi-agent-bot ! - web: Improved interactions and fixed known bugs. #4280 67325c1 Thanks @sailist ! - Fix the conversation view freezing at an old point after restarting the app when a turn had been interrupted; interrupted turns are now marked instead of shown as completed.

summary: What's changed Added oidc.user_id_claim to the Claude apps gateway, to identify people by an id_token claim other than sub , such as Microsoft Entra ID's oid Added click to send: in fullscreen, clicking the "to send now" hint under a queued message sends it right away, as its key does Fixed managed settings and organization policy not being fetched for the rest of the session after signing in from the VS Code extension Fixed Claude overwriting a very large CLAUDE.md, rules file or @-included...
content: What's changed Added oidc.user_id_claim to the Claude apps gateway, to identify people by an id_token claim other than sub , such as Microsoft Entra ID's oid Added click to send: in fullscreen, clicking the "to send now" hint under a queued message sends it right away, as its key does Fixed managed settings and organization policy not being fetched for the rest of the session after signing in from the VS Code extension Fixed Claude overwriting a very large CLAUDE.md, rules file or @-included file in a subdirectory after seeing only its start; Write now asks Claude to read it all or edit in place Fixed per-directory and paths: skills not being found after a Bash cd deeper into a git repository Fixed a rare case where the first reply after resuming a session in the terminal could be missing the next time the session was resumed Fixed a command with an invalid name stopping all commands from loading, which could leave claude -p with no output Fixed the Read tool sometimes failing on PDF pages with "pdftoppm failed: Could not write image" when the clean-up of old session files ran at the same time Fixed the spinner, OpenTelemetry effort values and transcripts naming a newly picked effort level during a task before the model applied it; they now show the level in force Fixed the /model and /effort cache warning saying the re-read waits for your next message; a change made while Claude is working can trigger it sooner Fixed some sessions showing as waiting on you when the last message only mentioned items waiting on you mid-sentence Fixed agent view restoring input text on the next launch after it was cleared with Ctrl+C just before exiting Fixed agent view reopening in shell mode after exiting with Ctrl+D from an empty ! input Fixed vim mode d , c and y with a gj or gk count larger than the lines left deleting or copying text; like Vim, they now only move the cursor Fixed /verify showing a long description meant for Claude in /help and the / command menu instead of a short one Improved the prompt's effort indicator: a change made mid-task now says it may wait for your next message, and the note clears when it no longer applies Improved WebFetch errors in cloud sessions: a host that does not resolve is now explained as possibly outside the allowed network domains, so Claude names the host to allow Changed Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry and Mantle to use the shorter system prompt for model names Claude Code doesn't recognize, such as custom deployment names and inference profile ARNs, even when they front Sonnet or Haiku; set CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE_SYSTEM_PROMPT=0 to keep the full prompt Changed automatic model switches after a flagged message to also cover model names Claude Code doesn't recognize, such as custom deployment names; set CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_REFUSAL_FALLBACK=1 to turn them off Changed usage limit messages to call the 5-hour window the "5-hour limit" instead of the "session limit" Changed cloud sessions started from the CLI to get their names and branch names from the server Changed prompt and agent hooks to run at most 24 at a time per session, sub-agents included, plus at most 12 that have waited longer than their event's timeout; a timeout under 1 second now counts as 1 second Changed a subagent's autoCompactWindow to lower the window set by CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW , where it had no effect before; it still never raises that window Changed OpenTelemetry mcp_server.name to report the real name of fixed-URL remote MCP servers declared by plugins from the official Anthropic marketplace, instead of custom Changed Claude Code to stop sending the claude_code.safety_event OpenTelemetry event [VSCode] Fixed sessions ending on a bare exit code when your organization's settings couldn't be loaded or were refused at startup; the tab now says why and offers Retry or Sign in again [VSCode] Changed usage limit resets to show a clock time ("Resets at 3:10 PM") and to say "5-hour limit" [Cloud sessions] Added an effort level to the model picker when you create or edit a routine that runs in the cloud [Cloud sessions] Added a Bash editor with colors, line numbers and a Copy button to the setup script box in cloud environment settings [Cloud sessions] Improved the step shown when Claude adds a repository to a cloud session: opening it now shows a short table of what happened instead of raw JSON [Cloud sessions] Fixed resending an unchanged message after a failed send in a cloud session sometimes running it twice [Cloud sessions] Fixed a failed cloud environment creation showing its error only as a toast outside the open dialog; it now appears inside the dialog [Cloud sessions] Fixed Edit in a routine's menu on the Routines page going to the routine's page without opening its edit dialog [Remote Control] Fixed an unarchived Remote Control session showing as working until a computer reconnected; it now shows as idle [Claude Tag] Improved Claude Tag's retry notice in Slack to name the model in use, or say rate limits were hit, instead of a generic API error [Claude Tag] Fixed a Claude Tag channel's on/off switch and agent settings falling back to workspace defaults when an older private Slack channel goes public and gets a new ID [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude in Slack not replying in channels whose environment has network access set to None [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude in Slack sometimes posting a file in the wrong thread when it was answering in another thread of the same channel [Code Review] Fixed Code Review reviewing an outdated commit, or none at all, when GitHub delivered a push event late; it now reviews the pull request's current commit
