title: AWS named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for Contact Center as a Service
summary: AWS has been named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for Contact Center as a Service (CCaaS) for AWS Connect Customer. This recognition marks an important milestone for our team, and it reflects years of work pushing on what's possible in customer experience.
content: I’m proud to share that Amazon Web Services (AWS) has been named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for Contact Center as a Service (CCaaS) for Amazon Connect for the fourth consecutive year. We believe this recognition reflects years of work pushing on what’s possible in customer experience. When we launched Amazon Connect Customer, we set out to evolve how businesses serve their customers: to make personalized, intelligent experiences possible without giving up efficiency, flexibility, or control. That belief still drives how we build today. Customer expectations have shifted. People expect you to recognize them, understand what they need, and stay consistent across every channel. They don’t want to repeat themselves. They don’t want to navigate disconnected systems to solve a simple problem. They want interactions that feel natural, relevant, and genuinely helpful. Meeting that takes more than traditional contact center technology, it takes a comprehensive solution that brings together customer context, AI, and the flexibility to adapt. That’s what we’re building with Amazon Connect Customer. Customer experience without compromise What matters most to your customers hasn’t changed: they want to be known, they want their problems fully resolved, and they want to trust you in the moments that matter. Read the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant to know why we are recognized. Experiences that start with knowing the customer.  Connect Customer builds a living picture of every customer: who they are, what they’ve been through, what they need next. Every touchpoint draws on that intelligence. Your customer feels known before a single word is exchanged. That’s what personal actually looks like. Resolution that carries all the way through. Most of the industry is still optimizing for deflection: getting customers away from humans as fast as possible. We took a different path. Connect Customer is built for the hard things: the disputed claim, the renegotiated mortgage, the disrupted itinerary that needs real action and can’t go wrong. We carry those interactions all the way through to resolution, and we make them feel natural and personal. Generative and agentic AI push this further: understanding what a customer needs and acting on it. Every action is auditable. Humans step in when the moment calls for it. You get enterprise scale and the confidence that nothing slips through the cracks. Building for what’s next The companies that win the next decade of customer experience won’t be the ones with the most channels or the fastest bot. They’ll be the ones whose customers feel known, whose problems actually get resolved, and whose trust is earned in the moments that matter most. Connect Customer exists to make that real for businesses of every size. I’m proud of the Connect Customer team for receiving this recognition for the fourth year in a row. Our engineers, product teams, partners, and customers shaped what we’ve built. This is a moment to celebrate how far we’ve come, and a signal of what’s ahead. Every customer is unique. Every interaction should reflect that. Founded in 2015, AWS Connect Customer is a purpose-built agentic AI solution for customer experience powering the full lifecycle of customer interactions, from proactive outreach to self-service resolution to agent assistance, on any channel and at enterprise scale. Under Pasquale’s leadership, AWS Connect Customer has become one of the fastest-growing services in AWS history. He has 20+ years of experience in delivering world-class B2B and B2C products. His specialties include operating SaaS at world-leading scale, delivering exceptional customer experiences, and driving UX and technology innovation. Announcing SOCI-indexed images for faster SageMaker AI jobs
summary: Seekable OCI (SOCI) indexing for Amazon SageMaker AI training and processing jobs takes full container image download off the critical path. SageMaker AI lazy-loads your image to start containers in seconds instead of minutes, with no changes to your job definition. See the benchmarks and how to adopt it.
content: Every minute your deep learning container image spends downloading is a minute you pay for and a minute your team waits. Container image download is pure overhead: billable job time that produces no model progress. For modern deep learning images, that overhead is several minutes on every single job. Today, we’re excited to announce Seekable OCI (SOCI) indexing for Amazon SageMaker AI Training and Amazon SageMaker AI processing jobs , which takes full container image download off the critical path of every job. With SOCI indexing, SageMaker AI lazy-loads your container image. It fetches only the files needed to start the container and streams the rest in the background as your code runs, so your job begins in seconds instead of minutes. You adopt it by pointing to a pre-indexed AWS Deep Learning Container (DLC) or adding an index to your own image. Neither approach requires changes to your job definition, entry point, or data channels. The result is faster job starts, lower job cost, and more time spent building models rather than waiting on infrastructure. SOCI-indexed images start Amazon SageMaker AI training containers in seconds, with no impact on training performance. As we show in the What we measured section, this reduced GPU idle time during image pulls by up to 90 percent in our benchmarks. This post shows how to adopt SOCI indexing: what it is, the results we measured, and how to turn it on for your own jobs. The challenge SageMaker AI training and processing jobs run inside container images stored in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR). Before a job can execute your code, the service downloads the entire image to the instance. It decompresses and writes every layer to disk. For small images this takes seconds. But deep learning images routinely exceed 10 GB or more. That download adds minutes to every job, and you pay for it as job time. The impact is largest exactly where iteration speed matters most: hyperparameter tuning sweeps for hundreds of jobs, quick experiments, and short processing jobs, where image download can dominate total runtime. How SOCI indexing works Seekable OCI (SOCI) is an open source technology that lazy loads container images. Instead of downloading the whole image before starting, the runtime uses a SOCI index to fetch only the files needed to launch the container immediately. It then streams the rest in the background as your code accesses it. A SOCI index is metadata that maps every file inside your image. You store it in Amazon ECR as an OCI-compliant artifact linked to your original image. Because the index is a separate artifact, your image digest and any existing signatures remain valid. SageMaker AI checks for an index automatically When you create a training or processing job, SageMaker AI checks whether the image you specified has a SOCI index and behaves accordingly: Scenario What happens The image includes a SOCI index SageMaker AI lazy-loads the image and starts your container before the full download completes The image has no SOCI index Standard download, no change in behavior The index can’t be read, or lazy loading doesn’t succeed The job falls back to a standard download and continues running Because jobs always fall back to a standard download when needed, adding a SOCI index never prevents your job from running. You only gain faster startup. You never risk breaking an existing workflow. What we measured We pulled the same container images two ways on real SageMaker AI training jobs: standard download and SOCI-indexed lazy loading. We then ran full training jobs from both to measure the effect on training speed. Setup Eight images , 1.8–35.4 GB compressed. GPU and CPU instances ml.g4dn, ml.g5, ml.g6, ml.g6e, ml.g7, ml.g7e, ml.p4d, ml.p5, and ml.m7i, from xlarge to 48xlarge, in the US West (Oregon) Region (us-west-2) and the US East (N. Virginia) Region (us-east-1). Download time measured from the start of the image pull until the container is ready to run. All figures are medians of repeated runs. Result 1: Download time drops from minutes to seconds at every image size Image size (compressed) Standard download Lazy loading Improvement 1.8 GB 48 s 3-11 s ~8x 13.2 GB 3 min 42 s ~6 s ~34x 35.4 GB 7 min 17 s 3-11 s ~38x The following chart compares container image download time for a standard Docker pull against SOCI lazy loading across eight image sizes, from 1.8 GB to 35.4 GB. Each image size shows two bars. The Docker download time bar (blue) grows steadily with image size, from 48 seconds at 1.8 GB to 7 minutes 17 seconds at 35.4 GB. A speedup label above each pair shows the ratio of Docker time to SOCI time. Speedups range from approximately 10x for the smallest image to over 35x for the largest. Figure 1: Container image download time, standard Docker pull compared to SOCI lazy loading, across eight image sizes Standard download time grows with image size because every file is decompressed and written. Lazy loading stayed at 3–11 seconds regardless of size, an 8x–46x improvement. The bigger the image, the more minutes you save. Result 2: The saving holds on every instance type and size Running the 13.2 GB image across 13 instance type/size combinations, standard download ranged from 3 min 16 s to 4 min 20 s, while lazy loading held at 6-8 s. That is about 34x faster on every configuration. You don’t need to change instance type or size to benefit. Figure 2: Download time for a 13.2 GB image across 13 instance type and size combinations Result 3: Training performance is unaffected beyond a first-epoch penalty We ran two kinds of full training jobs from the Docker-pulled and from the SOCI-indexed image and compared every epoch: Image classification on ResNet-50 on Imagenette (9,469 images) Container images: PyTorch (13.2 GB DLC) and TensorFlow (9.9 GB DLC) Instances: ml.p5.48xlarge, ml.p4d.24xlarge, ml.g7e.48xlarge, ml.g7.48xlarge, ml.g6e.12xlarge, ml.g6e.24xlarge, and ml.g6e.48xlarge. Large language model (LLM) fine-tuning: full-parameter supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of Qwen2.5-0.5B on alpaca-cleaned (51,760 examples) with the Hugging Face Trainer. Container image: 9.4 GB Hugging Face PyTorch DLC. Instances: ml.p5.48xlarge, ml.p4d.24xlarge, ml.g6.48xlarge. The following chart breaks job startup into image download time and first training epoch time, comparing a standard Docker pull with a SOCI-indexed image across GPU and CPU configurations for both workloads. Figure 3: Job startup split into image download time and first training epoch time, standard Docker pull compared to a SOCI-indexed image From the second epoch on, time per epoch is the same (within run-to-run variation) on every instance, for both workloads. The first epoch takes 3–16 s longer from the lazy-loaded image, while files the framework touches for the first time are fetched. This first-epoch cost is the same on every instance size. Net: each job finished 1-6 min sooner. That is the download saving minus the one-time first-epoch cost, a fixed saving per job. Test this on your own workload These numbers are from the two workloads described earlier. The first-epoch cost depends on your image and what your code touches at startup: Lazy loading wins when the first training step needs only a fraction of the image, the rest streams in while you train. If your entry point reads most of the image before training starts (for example, scanning, checksumming, or preloading its contents), the first epoch waits for roughly the same bytes a full pull would have fetched. The net improvement would be small. Front-loaded starts still came out ahead in our tests: torch.compile and a just-in-time (JIT) built CUDA extension added 7-15 s to the first epoch (net saving still 3 min 25 s–3 min 56 s) A 6 GB model baked into the image streamed its weights at load time, adding 2-3.5 min, but the overall job still finished 2-2.5 mins sooner on the indexed image. Getting started You can adopt SOCI indexing two ways: use a pre-indexed AWS Deep Learning Container or create an index for your own custom image. Option 1: Use a pre-indexed AWS Deep Learning Container AWS publishes SOCI-indexed variants of several popular Deep Learning Containers, identified by the -soci suffix on the image tag: 763104351884.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/pytorch-training:2.9-gpu-py312-cu130-ubuntu22.04-sagemaker-v1-soci Pre-indexed variants are available for PyTorch Training, TensorFlow Training, vLLM, and SGLang, including arm64 variants for some frameworks. To adopt lazy loading, update the image tag in your job definition to the -soci variant. Browse the full list in the AWS Deep Learning Containers Gallery . Note: If you build your own image FROM a DLC base image, you must create a SOCI index for your final image. The index from the base image does not carry forward to derived images. Option 2: Create a SOCI index for your own image To index a custom image, you need a Linux host (such as an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance running Amazon Linux 2023) with containerd , the SOCI snapshotter , and either Finch or nerdctl installed. Set your environment variables . ACCOUNT_ID="111122223333" REGION="us-east-1" REPOSITORY_NAME="my-training-image" ORIGINAL_IMAGE_TAG="v1.0" SOCI_IMAGE_TAG="v1.0-soci" REGISTRY="$ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.$REGION.amazonaws.com" Install the required tools . sudo dnf install -y containerd fuse soci-snapshotter runfinch-finch sudo systemctl start soci-snapshotter sudo systemctl restart containerd Authenticate to Amazon ECR . aws ecr get-login-password --region "$REGION" \ | sudo nerdctl login -u AWS --password-stdin "$REGISTRY" Pull your original image . sudo nerdctl pull "$REGISTRY/$REPOSITORY_NAME:$ORIGINAL_IMAGE_TAG" Create the SOCI-indexed image . sudo nerdctl image convert --soci \ "$REGISTRY/$REPOSITORY_NAME:$ORIGINAL_IMAGE_TAG" \ "$REGISTRY/$REPOSITORY_NAME:$SOCI_IMAGE_TAG" Push the indexed image . sudo nerdctl push --platform linux/amd64 \ "$REGISTRY/$REPOSITORY_NAME:$SOCI_IMAGE_TAG" This creates two artifacts in your repository: the SOCI index and an OCI-compliant image index manifest linking your image to the index. Your original image and its digest remain unchanged. Automate index creation in CI/CD To generate indexes automatically on every push, deploy the CFN ECR SOCI Index Builder . It uses an Amazon EventBridge rule to detect Amazon ECR image push events and build the index. No changes to your build pipeline are required. Use the indexed image in your SageMaker AI job Reference your SOCI-indexed image exactly as you would any other image. No API changes are needed. Only the tag differs. Training example (SageMaker Python SDK) from sagemaker.train import ModelTrainer from sagemaker.train.configs import Compute trainer = ModelTrainer( training_image="111122223333.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/my-training-image:v1.0-soci", role="arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/SageMakerExecutionRole", compute=Compute( instance_type="ml.g5.12xlarge", instance_count=2, ), ) trainer.train() Verify that your image includes a SOCI index Before launching, confirm your tag resolves to an indexed image: aws ecr batch-get-image \ --repository-name "$REPOSITORY_NAME" \ --image-ids imageTag="$SOCI_IMAGE_TAG" \ --accepted-media-types \ "application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json" \ --query 'images[0].imageManifest' --output text \ | jq '.manifests[] | {mediaType, artifactType}' Look for a child manifest whose artifactType begins with application/vnd.amazon.soci.index. alongside your platform manifest. If it isn’t there, the tag does not point to an indexed image. Things to keep in mind Amazon ECR private repositories only. Images in other registries, or pulled through a private Docker registry (TrainingRepositoryAccessMode set to Vpc), are not eligible for lazy loading. Improvement scales with image size. Images smaller than roughly 4 GB see relatively small improvements. Check for Docker-specific assumptions. SOCI-indexed images run on a containerd-based runtime. Review entry points and setup scripts for code that calls the Docker CLI, reads /var/run/docker.sock, or derives identifiers from cgroup paths. SageMaker AI mounts a /.dockerenv marker for backward compatibility, but avoid adding new dependencies on it. SOCI indexing for SageMaker AI jobs is available across all AWS Regions. Conclusion With SOCI indexing, you can minimize container image download time from your SageMaker AI training and processing jobs. Add a SOCI index to your images, or switch to a pre-indexed AWS Deep Learning Container. Either way, you cut startup time from minutes to seconds, reduce total job cost, and accelerate your machine learning (ML) iteration cycle. And your existing job definitions, API calls, and data pipelines stay exactly the same. To learn more about Amazon SageMaker AI and start using SOCI indexing, explore the following resources: Pick a SOCI-indexed Deep Learning Container. Browse the Deep Learning Containers Gallery and append -soci to your image tag. For framework-specific guidance, see SOCI index for AWS Deep Learning Containers . Index your own custom image. Follow the step-by-step walkthrough in the SageMaker AI Developer Guide , or refer to the SOCI snapshotter getting-started guide for advanced options. Automate indexing in your CI/CD pipeline. Deploy the CFN ECR SOCI Index Builder to generate indexes automatically on every image push. No pipeline changes are required. Test locally with Finch. Use the Finch lazy-loading walkthrough to validate your image on a containerd-based runtime before you submit a job. Dive deeper into the technology. Read Reducing container cold start times using SOCI index on DLAMI and DLC on the AWS Machine Learning Blog for benchmarks, or explore Under the hood: Lazy loading container images with Seekable OCI and AWS Fargate on the AWS Containers Blog to understand the lazy-loading mechanism in detail. Faster container startup is only one image tag away. Try it on your next SageMaker AI job and see the difference. About the authors Kanwaljit Khurmi Kanwaljit is a Senior Manager of Solutions Architecture and Data Scientists at Amazon Web Services, specializing in AI and ML. He collaborates with AWS product teams, engineering, and customers to provide guidance and technical assistance for maximizing the value of their hybrid GenAI solutions on AWS. Kanwaljit specializes in helping customers with containerized, data science, and machine learning applications. Mona Mona Mona currently works as Sr AI/ML specialist Solutions Architect at Amazon. She is a published author of three books and her latest book is AI Agents on AWS. She has authored 20+ blogs on AI/ML and cloud technology and a co-author on a research paper on CORD19 Neural Search which won an award for Best Research Paper at the prestigious AAAI (Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence) conference. Michael Oguike Michael is a Product Manager for Amazon SageMaker AI. He is driven by the application of technology and AI to solve real-world problems. At AWS, he helps customers across industries build, train, and deploy AI/ML models at scale. Before AWS, Michael designed and operated offshore oil and gas wells and facilities. Outside of work he enjoys exploring behavioral science and psychology through books and podcast. Deep Shah Deep is a Software Development Engineer on the Amazon SageMaker team, where he works on the infrastructure that powers model training on AWS. When he’s not scaling training systems, he enjoys sim racing, reading, and traveling.

title: Fix evaluation bias to unlock better models on Amazon Bedrock
summary: Property Finder found that 96.8% of their vision-AI evaluation labels were inherited from the incumbent model, hiding its true accuracy. See how they built unbiased ground truth, applied evolutionary prompt optimization, and selected a more accurate, cost-effective model on Amazon Bedrock, cutting cost by 86% across 11 image-quality attributes.
content: This post was co-authored with Khaled Thabit, Meriem Boughrara, and Mohamed Desouky from Property Finder. The engineering team at Property Finder , a digital real estate application, discovered that 96.8 percent of their evaluation labels had been inherited directly from a single model’s predictions rather than verified by human experts. Their ground truth was systematically skewed toward the incumbent model, making every alternative appear to underperform. The labels also had errors, but the bias was what blocked objective model comparison. They uncovered this when migrating their vision AI workload to a more cost-effective option on Amazon Bedrock . Property Finder processes tens of thousands of property images every day across the Middle East and North Africa (MENA). Their system evaluates 11 quality attributes per image. These cover watermark detection, room classification, furnishing status, photo quality, and construction indicators. That’s thousands of new property listings with an average of 15 images each. All need quality assessment before going live. Property Finder needed a more cost-effective option. But measured against those labels, any alternative was at a disadvantage. The hardest part was not finding a better model. It was discovering that their evaluation methodology itself was the blocker. In this post, we share how Property Finder identified evaluation bias, built unbiased ground truth, and applied evolutionary prompt optimization to select the right model on Amazon Bedrock, achieving higher accuracy at 86 percent lower cost. We walk through the methodology and iteration examples, with lessons you can apply to your own workloads. The following figure illustrates the prompt optimization loop that Property Finder and the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center team used to iteratively improve classification accuracy on Amazon Bedrock. Figure 1: Prompt optimization loop architecture The diagram shows the iterative prompt optimization cycle. A property image is processed by Amazon Bedrock, which outputs the predicted attributes in JSON format. During optimization, these predictions are scored with Micro F1 against the 256-image expert-annotated development set. Error analysis then inspects failed images and identifies visual patterns, which inform the next prompt version. The loop ran from v0 to v27. AI assistants helped refine the prompts, and later versions used automated optimization. Your evaluation might be lying Many teams encounter this scenario. You want to compare vision models, so you build an evaluation dataset. The most common way to get labels is to run your current model and treat its outputs as ground truth. The model has been running in production and nobody complained, so the labels must be good enough. But this creates a circular evaluation where any alternative gets judged by how closely it matches the incumbent’s behavior, not by actual correctness. Property Finder’s evaluation dataset had exactly this problem. Of their labeled samples, 96.8 percent came directly from the predictions of the existing vision language model (VLM) rather than independent human verification. Any alternative model was structurally disadvantaged before a single image was even processed. Hidden errors confirmed the severity. Watermark text extraction had character-level mistakes marked as correct, including hallucinated brand names and missing characters. Photo classification forced single labels onto images containing multiple room types. In the remaining 3.2 percent of human-labeled samples, annotators had introduced categories outside the original specification, like Office appearing where no such label existed in the prompt. A model comparison loses validity when the answer key was written by the model you are trying to replace. Building ground truth you can trust To break the cycle, you need human experts with real domain knowledge doing fresh annotations independently. No reference to previous model outputs. No access to what the incumbent predicted. Dataset scope Property Finder’s team hand-annotated 356 UAE images and a separate set of Egypt images. The team selected these from unlabeled production listings across representative industry segments. This post reports results on the UAE images. The Egypt images served as a cross-regional check on 230 images and are not reported here. The first 256 UAE images to be annotated formed the development set for tuning. The evaluation set for the final model comparison uses all 356, adding 100 images annotated after the development runs. A set of 356 images is roughly sufficient to detect moderate differences between models. Rare classes within individual attributes have fewer examples, so smaller differences on those attributes might not be detectable. Expert annotation A strategy and analytics expert annotated all images. They brought specialized knowledge of real estate listing quality standards. The AWS Generative AI Innovation Center team conducted systematic quality reviews through dedicated clarification sessions. Those reviews settled ambiguous cases and kept the labeling consistent across the dataset. Multi-label transition Real estate images frequently show multiple rooms through doorways or display overlapping quality characteristics. The switch from single-label to multi-label classification alleviated a major source of artificial ambiguity. A hallway photo showing a bedroom through a doorway is genuinely both. After you allow multiple labels, you measure what the model gets right rather than penalizing it for reasonable secondary predictions. A hybrid approach could complement this methodology: models from different families surface candidate labels and disagreements, and human experts adjudicate every case, so no model output is used directly as a label. This would reduce the annotation burden for future dataset expansion. Metrics selection Micro F1 served as the primary metric because it weights each prediction equally, which matches the business goal of overall label correctness. Macro F1 was reported alongside it because Micro F1 is dominated by frequent classes and can hide weak performance on rare attributes. Per-label precision and recall helped identify specific failure modes. Per-sample intersection over union (IoU) measured how closely each image’s predicted labels overlapped the expert’s labels. The nine single-label attributes, such as rotation or watermark detection, have one right answer per image. The AWS team also scored them with exact-match accuracy, the share of images where the answer matches the expert label. Prompt optimization as reinforcement learning With unbiased evaluation in place, you can start improving. You cannot improve what you cannot measure correctly. The optimization follows a loop analogous to reinforcement learning. Think of each prompt version as an agent, the Micro F1 score as the reward signal, and error analysis as the gradient for improvement. The idea resembles GEPA (Genetic-Pareto reflective prompt evolution) , where you mutate prompt components, evaluate fitness, select survivors, and iterate. In this engagement, the AWS team refined most versions from error analysis, with AI assistants reviewing failed images and proposing changes. MIPROv2 , an automated prompt optimization framework from the DSPy library, complemented this manual process for the photo classification task in v27. Where it started The first prompt (v0) used generic classification instructions, simplified here for illustration: “Classify this image into one of the following categories: Living Room, Kitchen, Bedroom, Bathroom…” Proprietary model A, Property Finder’s production baseline, scored a Micro F1 of 0.55 on the 256-image development set. It used v22, a prompt tuned for its model family. Scores before v21 used the earlier single-label setup and aren’t directly comparable. Iteration by iteration The AWS team tested early versions on several candidate models and added structured output formatting and attribute-specific definitions. The most instructive fix came from image-level error analysis. In the early single-label versions, the model consistently classified rooms visible through doorways as the secondary room type. The AWS Generative AI Innovation Center team added explicit instructions to classify based on the room occupying the majority of the frame. The later switch to multi-label output kept the main room as a label and allowed rooms visible through doorways as additional labels. Regional customization produced the next gain. In some regions, listing photos carry decorative Arabic text overlays that are not watermarks. Rules for that text removed a whole category of false positives. The v21 prompt switched photo classification and room category to multi-label output and became the shared starting prompt for every model. With it, Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct from Meta scored a Micro F1 of 0.75 on the development set. From there, the AWS team tuned each model’s prompt separately. For this model, v24 targeted room size overestimation, multi-label handling, and output format. Then v25, an automatically optimized version, moved the critical tasks first. In v27, MIPROv2 restructured the photo classification task, and the model’s Micro F1 on that task reached 0.76. Where it ended The final prompt, v27_PF, is v27 plus rules that Property Finder added for renders, images with borders or frames, and corridors. Like v27, it keeps the Arabic text rules and output format instructions. A normalization step after each model call handles remaining format differences. With v27_PF, Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct scored a Micro F1 of 0.80 on the 356-image evaluation set, where proprietary model A scored 0.56 with v22. The evaluation set includes the 256 development images, and both models’ prompts were tuned on those images. These scores are therefore optimistic. The switch from proprietary model A to Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct, each on its own tuned prompt, lifted Micro F1 from 0.55 to 0.81 on the development set. That is a 47 percent relative gain. Prompt tuning alone, on Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct, raised it from 0.75 with the shared v21 prompt to 0.81 with v27. Lessons from failed approaches Not everything succeeded. The 2-bucket approach put the watermark attributes and the other attributes in two separate API calls. It brought no meaningful accuracy gain. Boxed-image detection also dropped sharply. Without the watermark attributes in the same prompt, the models mistook watermark overlays for image borders. Generic prompts also failed regardless of which model you ran them on. Real estate imagery has too much domain specificity for a one-size-fits-all instruction. Results: Cost, accuracy, and speed The AWS Generative AI Innovation Center team evaluated multiple models on Amazon Bedrock with the unbiased evaluation framework. All models started from the shared v21 prompt and were then tuned for their model family on the development set. Proprietary model A got one tuning round, v22. Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct got several, v24 to v27, plus Property Finder’s edge-case rules, so it had more tuning effort behind it. The final comparison against proprietary model A used the 356-image evaluation set. Property Finder selected Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct for their production workload based on accuracy across all 11 attributes and cost efficiency. For model availability by Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock . The following table shows the exact-match accuracy that Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct (v27_PF) reached on each single-label attribute, scored on the 356-image evaluation set. It scored 90 percent or higher on six of the nine, and matched or exceeded proprietary model A on all 11 attributes. On photo classification, which can have several labels per image, the two scored the same. Attribute Exact-match accuracy Rotation detection 100% People detection 97% Boxed-image detection 97% Watermark detection 94% Render detection 93% Furnished status 91% Room under construction 81% Room size 65% Watermark text extraction 55% Cost per 1,000 images Property Finder scores tens of thousands of images a day, so per-image cost matters. Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct is a cost-effective open-weight model, and the pipeline gets all attributes for an image in a single call. Result Value Estimated cost per 1,000 images $2.35 Cost reduction compared with Property Finder’s previous setup 86% These figures are estimates as of December 2025 in the US East (Ohio) Region. The Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct figure assumes 9,000 input tokens and 200 output tokens per image, from the original two-call cost analysis. A single call with the production prompt carries about 7,500–8,000 input tokens, so this is an upper estimate. The 86 percent compares it with the cost analysis estimate for Property Finder’s previous setup, which used the v21 prompt. The accuracy comparison used v22, which was tuned from v21, so its cost might differ. For current pricing, refer to Amazon Bedrock pricing . Inference speed Property Finder runs this optimized pipeline in production, processing tens of thousands of images daily with Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct on Amazon Bedrock. In their own monitoring, Property Finder observed a 40–60 percent reduction in inference latency compared with their previous setup. Apply this to your workloads Start by auditing your evaluation labels. If they came from model predictions rather than human experts, you have the same bias problem Property Finder found. Build domain-expert ground truth for a few hundred representative samples, and keep a separate test split that you never use for tuning. Adopt multi-label metrics where your classification task involves overlapping attributes. Then iterate on prompts using image error analysis, treating each iteration as a generation in an evolutionary optimization loop. When you deploy a pipeline like this, add responsible AI controls. For example, you can use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to enforce content policies and filter inappropriate model outputs. The attribute predictions in this pipeline don’t come with a calibrated confidence score, so use a practical signal to choose images for human review. Model disagreement is one such signal. When two models give different answers for an attribute, the image is often ambiguous. A second model on every image adds cost, so you can start with a sample. Check how often the signal catches real errors on your development set before you rely on it. Conclusion In this post, we walked through how Property Finder identified evaluation bias, built unbiased ground truth, and applied evolutionary prompt optimization to achieve better accuracy at lower cost through model selection on Amazon Bedrock. Three elements needed to come together for this result: unbiased evaluation to measure honestly, the flexibility to evaluate and switch between model families without re-platforming, and carefully evolved prompts tailored to the domain. Amazon Bedrock provided the foundation. It gave Property Finder access to multiple model families through a single API, inherited AWS governance and security controls, and the ability to adopt new models as they become available without changing their infrastructure. To get started with model evaluation and selection on Amazon Bedrock, visit the Amazon Bedrock documentation . If you process vision workloads at scale and want help building an unbiased evaluation framework, reach out to the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center . Share your experiences with model evaluation and prompt optimization in the comments. Acknowledgments Additional contributors from AWS include Yousuf Albannai, Amine Sehili, Thomas Ounnas, Aris Tsakpinis, Rafik Soliman, Nikhil Ulhas Pandit, and Sneh Sharma.   About the authors Khaled Thabit Khaled Thabit is the Director of Data Engineering at Property Finder, where he leads the company’s data and AI strategy. He is passionate about using AI and data to shape the future of the property marketplace in MENA. Meriem Boughrara Meriem Boughrara is a Senior Data Engineer at Property Finder, where she leads AI and data engineering initiatives across the platform. She oversees project delivery for AI-driven solutions and works closely with cross-functional teams to bring them to production. Mohamed Desouky Mohamed Desouky is a Data Engineer at Property Finder, where he builds and maintains data pipelines powering AI-driven listing quality systems across MENA markets. He enjoys building scalable data solutions that drive measurable business impact. Mina Metias Mina Metias manages the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center team in the MENA region, overseeing customer engagements from discovery through production deployment and supporting delivery of measurable business outcomes. Vadim Selyutin Vadim Selyutin is a Senior Data Scientist at the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center. He provides technical leadership on customer engagements, partnering with organizations to design, build, and deliver generative AI solutions from ideation through production deployment. Mohamed Noordeen Alaudeen Mohamed Noordeen Alaudeen is a Data Scientist at the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, where he builds and deploys generative AI solutions that solve real-world business problems for enterprise customers across industries. He enjoys tackling complex technical challenges and turning them into production-ready solutions.

title: Exowatt beats frontier models on accuracy with SageMaker serverless model customization
summary: In this post, we show how Exowatt used Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization to build a repeatable AI pipeline that produces task-specific fine-tuned models for two deployment targets, edge and cloud, achieving higher accuracy than frontier models at up to 49x lower cost.
content: Exowatt builds modular, dispatchable solar systems that deliver reliable power for energy-intensive applications such as AI data centers. Its flagship product, the Exowatt P3, captures solar energy through optical lenses, stores it as heat in a long-duration thermal battery, and dispatches electricity on demand through a heat engine. Unlike grid-tied photovoltaic solar systems, P3 powers data centers directly behind the meter, helping data centers come online without waiting in multi-year grid interconnection queues. Exowatt builds a fleet of AI agents that monitor and triage live alarms and support operational decisions for solar systems, often at the edge, with limited or no connectivity. As its fleet scales from test benches toward manufacturing and thousands of deployed field units, the intelligence layer that operates these systems must scale with it. In this post, we show how Exowatt used Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization to build a repeatable AI pipeline. The pipeline produces task-specific fine-tuned models for two deployment targets, edge and cloud, achieving higher accuracy than frontier models at up to 49× lower cost. The two models described here are the first outputs of that pipeline rather than the end goal. The more durable result of the engagement was the pipeline itself: a repeatable path from raw operational data to a certified training set, a fine-tuned model, and an evaluated deployment artifact. Exowatt can now run this path in days rather than months. Alarm triage and energy-market analysis are two of many narrow, high-value tasks where the same approach applies. The challenge: AI on physical energy infrastructure Exowatt’s energy management system (EMS) runs across a growing fleet of operational sites. Each site continuously produces alarms: a hardware component operating out of spec, a dropped connection, an out-of-range voltage reading, and similar events. As the fleet scales toward thousands of field units, a human operator can’t monitor every site in real time. Exowatt needed an AI agent that could read the alarm state on each site and take or recommend the correct next action autonomously and reliably. A frontier model couldn’t solve this problem for three reasons: The task is narrow and proprietary. Alarm triage on Exowatt’s EMS depends on their specific hardware, data, and operating logic. A general-purpose frontier model isn’t specialized for it. It must run at the edge, with no GPU and often no internet. Many sites have limited or intermittent connectivity, so an agent that depends on a cloud call to a frontier model leaves the operator without coverage when the connection drops. Cost doesn’t scale at fleet level. Routing every operational decision to a frontier model across thousands of sites is not economical for a decision that repeats continuously. This is where Exowatt turned to model customization. Exowatt’s initial fine-tuning workflow relied on selecting an open-weight model, building a container, and creating a custom training recipe before any experiment could run. This was a major blocker for model experimentation. Additionally, they had to decide GPU hardware requirements of model fine-tuning. As the team increased the pace of experimentation, each run first required choosing a specific GPU instance type and then waiting for that self-selected capacity to become available. When a chosen instance type was unavailable, this could delay the start of a run or block it entirely. They needed a model small enough to run on a no-GPU edge controller, yet accurate enough compared to the frontier model on the specific task to act autonomously. Fine-tuning closed that gap: a compact, task-specialized model that is both deployable in the cloud and at the edge. Solution overview Exowatt addressed these challenges by adopting a cloud-native, serverless model customization approach on Amazon SageMaker AI. The same training pipeline produces fine-tuned models for two deployment targets: the edge and the cloud. Exowatt implemented this approach on the Qwen3-1.7B model for the first use case, edge alarm triage, then applied the same approach to the Qwen3-14B model for the second use case, cloud energy-market analysis. The company plans to reuse this solution to build smaller, task-specific models across the fleet. Figure 1: Exowatt fine-tuning and deployment pipeline, spanning the build, cloud-serving, and edge-serving stages The following seven AWS services power the AI pipeline, with no instances, clusters, or endpoints to manage: AWS Service Purpose Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) Data, manifests, model artifacts, and test sets Amazon SageMaker AI serverless fine-tuning Every fine-tune run, launched from Public Hub recipes Amazon SageMaker AI serverless evaluation 2,000 answers per candidate scored as a managed job SageMaker Model Registry Every completed fine-tune with its evidence and metrics Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import Hosts the fine-tuned Qwen3-14B for Cloud EMS, invoked privately from the Cloud EMS service. No idle cost Amazon Bedrock (Claude, Qwen3) Paraphrase (three rewrites per answer in the training data) and frontier model benchmarking Alarm-triage paraphrases use Qwen3-VL-235B on Amazon Bedrock. Energy-market paraphrases use Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock. AWS Lambda + Amazon EventBridge Serverless-evaluation scorer and a scheduled keep-warm invocation of the custom model The workflow is organized into three stages: Model customization (cloud): Exowatt fine-tunes open-weight base models using serverless model customization, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on SageMaker AI. Because serverless training allocates capacity on demand, the team runs multiple experiments per day rather than waiting for self-selected GPU. After evaluation, the best model is registered in the SageMaker AI Model Registry. Edge deployment: For latency-sensitive, connectivity-constrained work such as alarm triage, the fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B model is frozen, quantized to the GGUF format, and run with llama.cpp inside Kubernetes pods at the edge using on-site controllers. This path requires no GPU and operates without internet connectivity. Cloud deployment (elastic): For internet-connected, fleet-level analysis, the fine-tuned Qwen3-14B energy-market model is served through Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import, which runs with no idle cost and bills only while the model is active. Why Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization service provides a wide selection of open-weight models with ready-made fine-tuning recipes from the SageMaker Public Hub, so the team avoided building and optimizing a custom training container, work that can otherwise take weeks. For Exowatt, this turned fine-tuning from a scarce, scheduled event into a routine, on-demand one. This makes a rapid experimentation-and-test loop practical while keeping experimentation cost low. Fine-tuning on provisioned GPUs requires choosing a specific instance type, requesting that capacity, waiting for it to become available, running the job, and paying for the instance for as long as it is held. The held time typically includes the idle time between experiments when a dedicated instance is kept running. For a small team running many experiments, this slows down innovation and increases cost. Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization automatically manages and orchestrates the infrastructure required to run the fine-tuning job, removing the pain of capacity management, and charges only for the time the fine-tuning job runs. Use case 1: Edge alarm triage with Qwen3-1.7B Exowatt sites raise alarms around the clock. A compact on-site model reads each alarm together with the site’s own status and telemetry and returns one of a small fixed set of classifications with cited evidence (such as an offline system, derated component, or sensor mismatch) or an explicit abstention when the evidence is insufficient. Model selection and training data The team first tried Qwen3-8B with prompting and guardrails, which plateaued below the target (0.735 macro-F1). A fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B changed that: it outperformed the Qwen3-8B plus prompting setup on this narrow, single-turn task at roughly one-fifth the parameters, while staying small enough for GPU-free edge inference. Thirteen fine-tuned Qwen3-8B candidates across 12 dataset versions never beat the prompted 8B baseline. The smaller model with more varied data did. The training set was small and curated: 2,522 examples built from 684 verified decisions on generated site scenarios plus 1,838 certified paraphrases that kept each decision fixed while rewriting the prose. The paraphrases were generated by Qwen3-235B on Amazon Bedrock for about $3.72. Each paraphrase was kept only if deterministic checks confirmed that the decision, labels, evidence citations, and every number were unchanged (1,838 of 2,218 candidates passed). One fault family was held out of training entirely, and 320 cases were reserved for testing. Training and deployment Training completed in about 32 minutes on SageMaker serverless fine-tuning for roughly $20–$25. Quantized to 8 bits (about 1.71 GiB), the model runs offline in a 6 GiB llama.cpp pod on the site’s existing CPU server. It also runs on a t3.2xlarge instance type. Use case 2: Cloud energy-market analysis with Qwen3-14B Dispatchable storage turns timing into an operational decision: each site must continually decide how much stored energy to hold for its load and when to release it, and for grid-connected sites market conditions feed into that choice. The fine-tuned model reads a six-hour packet of live market data (about 90 rows of real-time prices, day-ahead forecasts, and grid notices) and returns one of five market events (such as a price spike or scarcity adder) in about four seconds. Every claim is tied to a specific data row to inform the dispatch strategy. Why Qwen3-14B Qwen3-14B was chosen because it is supported by Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import, it ships as a SageMaker Public Hub model with a ready LoRA recipe (no custom container or instance type to manage), and at about 28 GiB it is small enough to serve cost-effectively. Training data and process Exowatt fine-tuned the model on public Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) market data drawn from five years of history (about 163 million rows across 12 tables). The team rule-labeled this data into 25,000 examples (22,000 for training, 1,000 for validation, and 2,000 held out for testing). They then expanded the training set to 86,281 rows by having Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock rewrite the prose of each example while its labels and numeric fields stayed fixed. Training was a single LoRA epoch (rank 16, alpha 32), completed in about 8.5 hours of managed serverless fine-tuning with up to four jobs running at once. The team ran 23 jobs and about 155 hours of managed training in the six days from initial plan to a champion model serving in Cloud EMS. The decisive improvement came from paraphrase diversity: adding three rewrites per answer lifted macro-F1 from 0.950 to 0.975. The base model scored only 0.415 macro-F1. It produced valid JSON but did not yet know the market. Fine-tuning fixed that. Deployment The merged checkpoint was imported to Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import in about 14 minutes. The model runs with no idle cost and bills at $6.86 per hour only while active. Benchmark results On the edge alarm-triage task the fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B went from a model that couldn’t produce a valid answer to 0.911 macro-F1 with 320 test cases, ahead of every frontier baseline. Applying the identical fine-tune-and-evaluate loop to the energy-market task with 2,000 test cases, the Qwen3-14B reached 0.975 macro-F1, again ahead of the frontier baseline and at a fraction of the cost. In both cases a small, fine-tuned model beat far larger general-purpose models on the specific task. Both models return strict JSON in which every claim cites a specific input data row. Any unsupported claim is dropped before it reaches an operator, which is what lets the team trust small models in autonomous, physical settings.   Model Macro-F1 $ / 1,000 decisions Offline? Claude Haiku 4.5 0.519 ~$4.70 No Claude Opus 4.7 0.680 ~$22 No Claude Sonnet 4.6 0.698 ~$15 No Fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B 0.911 $0 * Yes Base Qwen3-1.7B No score (failed the validity gate) Table 1: Edge alarm triage results, fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B compared to frontier models $0 per 1,000 decisions means no metered API or GPU inference cost. The quantized model runs on the site’s existing CPU. Model Macro-F1 Event Acc. Valid JSON $ / 1,000 answers Base Qwen3-14B 0.415 0.54 0.834 $0.64 Claude Sonnet 4.6 0.538 0.584 0.991 $17.79 Claude Opus 4.7 0.625 0.718 0.9995 $29.26 Fine-tuned Qwen3-14B 0.975 0.983 1.000 $0.60 Table 2: Cloud energy-market analysis results, fine-tuned Qwen3-14B compared to frontier models Costs are Amazon Bedrock list prices times measured tokens per answer. Fine-tuning lifted an open model from last place to first: +0.35 macro-F1 over Claude Opus 4.7 (95 percent confidence interval 0.324 to 0.371) at about 49× lower cost per 1,000 answers ($0.60 compared to $29.26). The model held 0.968 macro-F1 on a second, later test set. Business benefits Faster iteration and faster time to market: Exowatt moved its customized model from experimentation to production in only nine days. This process could have taken months if the team had to build and optimize custom containers and training recipes, provision GPUs, and manage infrastructure. With SageMaker AI serverless model customization, the team trained Qwen3-1.7B in about 32 minutes and Qwen3-14B in about 8.5 hours, with no capacity requests and up to four training jobs running concurrently. For the energy-market use case, Exowatt ran 23 jobs totaling about 155 hours of managed training and moved from the base model to a fine-tuned model serving in Cloud EMS in six days. The merged checkpoint was imported into Amazon Bedrock in about 14 minutes. The end-to-end pipeline used seven AWS serverless services, with no instances, clusters, or endpoints for Exowatt to manage. Higher accuracy compared to frontier models: Both fine-tuned models beat the larger frontier models on their own task: Qwen3-1.7B at 0.911 macro-F1 (compared to 0.698 for Claude Sonnet 4.6) and Qwen3-14B at 0.975 (compared to 0.625 for Claude Opus 4.7). Lower cost across both deployments: In the cloud, the Qwen3-14B serves at $0.60 per 1,000 answers versus $29.26 for Claude Opus 4.7 (about 49× lower), with no idle cost and $6.86 per hour only while active on Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import. At the edge, the quantized Qwen3-1.7B runs on the site’s existing CPU with no per-inference cost and no dependency on connectivity. Grounded, low-risk outputs: Across both models, the evidence fence removed every uncited claim (any evidence citation whose source, field, or value does not literally match the input), and the edge model abstains rather than guesses when unsure. This is what let the team run it autonomously in shadow mode on a cloud-hosted replica of a site. Lessons learned For specific tasks, smaller fine-tuned large language models can outperform large frontier models: Fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-14B models each outperformed frontier models on the target task, delivering higher accuracy at a fraction of the cost with significantly smaller models. Data quality and variety outweigh raw volume and extra epochs: For tightly scoped tasks, data quality mattered more than model size or data volume. On the alarm-triage model, more verified training variety moved macro-F1 from 0.584 (trained on the 684 verified decisions alone) to 0.911 (with the paraphrase-expanded 2,522-row set). Simply running more epochs over the same rows did worse: a control run that trained on the 684 original rows for 11 epochs (the same number of steps) reached only 0.879. Curated data mattered more than dataset size throughout. Removing the provisioning step changes how a team works: When a training run no longer requires waiting for GPU capacity, fine-tuning shifts from a rare event to a routine, iterative one. One training pipeline serves two deployment targets: Separating model training from deployment lets Exowatt use the same pipeline for both offline edge deployment and connected fleet-level analysis, simplifying operations and accelerating model deployment in the cloud. Conclusion Exowatt now has one reusable AI pipeline that took a task from model specific data preparation to model deployment. Rather than tuning one model for different tasks, Exowatt plans to apply the same fine-tuning principles to different tasks, each with its own data, specific models, and evaluations, across the fleet as new device types and market tasks come online. The pattern generalizes beyond energy industry segments. AI engineers, data scientists, and customers across industry segments can adopt the same principles. Use Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization as a low-overhead AI pipeline to fine-tune small, task-specific models, then deploy them where the work happens: at the edge when connectivity or latency requires it, and through a managed cloud endpoint such as Amazon SageMaker AI for elastic workloads. To learn more, see Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization and Amazon Bedrock . About the authors Purna Sanyal Purna is a GenAI Specialist Architect at AWS, helping customers to building Agentic AI applications with custom model and inferencing at scale with successful adoption of cloud native architecture. He has specialization in data strategy, GenAI Infra and Applied AI. He is passionate about architecting scalable AI systems that drive innovation and user impact. Tim Child Tim is Chief Engineer of Software and AI at Exowatt, where he leads the software, AI and digital systems behind the company’s clean, dispatchable energy for AI datacenters. He leads Exowatt’s energy management system that runs Exowatt’s sites, the company’s AI strategy, and the AI tools and agents the whole company depends on. Before Exowatt, he earned a PhD in Physics (quantum computing) at the University of British Columbia. Felipe Arce Felipe is a Lead Software Engineer at Exowatt, working where AI meets energy infrastructure. He built the fine-tuned model factory and helps build the energy management system that runs Exowatt’s sites and the digital twins that bring them to life in simulation. Before Exowatt, he spent four years on Microsoft Azure’s incident platform. He loves infrastructure, especially the platforms other engineers build on. Jingchao Yang Jingchao is a Senior Solutions Architect for Startups at AWS, where he specializes in building lakehouse architectures for agentic systems. Jingchao brings 8+ years of data engineering experience with a PhD in Geoinformation Science.

title: How AI Is Changing the Pace of Discovery for Millions Living With Dementia
summary: There are 57 million people worldwide living with dementia today. For the researchers working to help them, the obstacle isn’t a lack of effort — it’s too much data, too few experts to synthesize it and a pace of discovery that can’t keep up with the disease. The Consortium for Biomedical Research and AI in […]
content: There are 57 million people worldwide living with dementia today. For the researchers working to help them, the obstacle isn’t a lack of effort — it’s too much data, too few experts to synthesize it and a pace of discovery that can’t keep up with the disease. The Consortium for Biomedical Research and AI in Neurodegeneration (C-BRAIN), working with NVIDIA, is using AI to change that. Alzheimer’s disease is one of today’s leading global health challenges, with over 10 million new dementia cases diagnosed each year. Despite a 7x increase in National Institutes of Health funding in the last 15 years — reaching $3.9 billion annually — no treatment has been found to stop, prevent or reverse the disease yet. The bottlenecks are not enough high impact scientific findings, too much data living in institutional silos and too slow a pace of synthesis to keep up with the research that is published. C-BRAIN, led by Dr. Randall Bateman and a consortium of 18 member institutions across academic, philanthropic, pharma and research organizations, launched in November 2025 to help scientists make better, faster discoveries by accelerating the research that makes new treatments possible. “We have a window of opportunity with artificial intelligence to do research fundamentally different than we’ve ever done before, in a way that accelerates discoveries to help patients,” said Bateman, founder and director of C-BRAIN and the Charles F. and Joanne Knight Distinguished Professor of Neurology at the Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis. He described their work as “AI tools built by scientists, for scientists.” The consortium is building a system that harnesses previously untapped Alzheimer’s research data to support scientists’ work. Speeding Research From Weeks to Hours Essential assets in Alzheimer’s research are datasets that have never been publicly accessible to AI tools or human researchers. This includes unpublished findings, negative results and governed proprietary data from member institutions. “A lot of life sciences data doesn’t make its way into the frontier models,” said Dr. Ade Ojewole, chief technology officer of C-BRAIN. “The consequence of that is we’re leaving a lot of intelligence on the table.” C-BRAIN refers to this as “dark data,” which slows down Alzheimer’s research. Some dark data is directly deposited into secure computer systems for AI tools to access. To use this data without compromising patient privacy or institutional governance, C-BRAIN uses a hybrid centralized and federated approach — where AI models learn from data at each institution without that data ever having to leave its walls. This kind of infrastructure is technically demanding to build and scale, which is part of what NVIDIA brings to the collaboration. C-BRAIN currently runs 64 NVIDIA data center GPUs on premises alongside cloud-based nodes on Microsoft Azure, with additional NVIDIA GPU capacity, including NVIDIA Blackwell systems , on the horizon as the consortium’s ambitions scale. To explore how AI and accelerated computing can advance Alzheimer’s research while navigating its technical demands, C-BRAIN is working with NVIDIA to incorporate technologies including the NVIDIA BioNeMo open developer platform and the MONAI framework for C-BRAIN’s research pipelines. “The C-BRAIN collaboration with NVIDIA aims to unlock those models in a way that they can deliver something quite impactful and important,” said Bateman. “A great deal of optimization is going to be needed as we push the boundaries of what today’s spatial omics machine learning architectures can model,” Ojewole said. “NVIDIA software is definitely going to come into play there.” Researchers at C-BRAIN have already built two tools: OpenScientist — built with Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in an effort led by research scientist Justin Reese — and InsightEngine , built with 387 Labs. OpenScientist is an open source agentic AI co-scientist that takes a scientist’s research question and dataset, then semi-autonomously generates hypotheses, runs analyses and produces verifiable, auditable insights. InsightEngine is an open source research platform that uses agentic AI to test hypotheses against the scientific literature, analyzing user-supplied datasets, exploring a biomedical knowledge graph and checking every claim against evidence to catch hallucinations before researchers commit to costly experiments. In published case studies, OpenScientist completed analyses in minutes that domain scientists estimated would take weeks to months, at a cost of under $10 per run. At C-BRAIN’s current reach of over 200 research groups, this capability could release substantial research capacity, potentially exceeding one million hours annually at scale. From Correlation to Cause Looking ahead, C-BRAIN aims to build a multimodal biological foundation model trained on the full breadth of its data — neuroimaging, multi-omics, fluid biomarkers and longitudinal clinical measures. By year three, it aims to discover new causal mechanisms of brain aging and Alzheimer’s disease, moving to testable scientific principles using the full scope of available research and data. Bateman said, “ AI that can think and reason has the potential to accelerate discoveries that will lead to powerful and implementable preventions and treatments for the entire population.”

content: 2026.10.10-beta.4 Highlights Changes Fixes Automations: preserve authenticated operator authority for explicit same-conversation scheduled follow-ups, including one-shot next_check rearming, while retaining role, session, cancellation, target, and tool-policy revocation boundaries. ( #176422 ) Thanks @RomneyDa . Gateway security: keep an environment-referenced hooks.token out of agent host-exec and CLI child environments at startup and across config reloads, while preserving explicit per-command overrides. ( #179199 ) Thanks @VACInc and @RomneyDa . Memory Wiki: preserve human-authored Notes when OKF concept pages are re-imported or removed from the producer bundle, including changed producer content and legacy pages without a marked Notes slot. ( #175707 , #179657 ; related #175700 ) Thanks @YangManBOBO and @RomneyDa . Claude CLI: keep the native Claude session and its context when subagent completions or channel turns run in a Control UI-started session, instead of reseeding from saved history each time. ( #178955 ; fixes #178953 ) Thanks @Marvinthebored and @RomneyDa . Model catalogs: honor a configured primary account pin when deciding model readiness, so native Claude CLI models no longer appear as missing auth when the selected token profile is ready. ( #178522 ; related #178502 ) Thanks @ericcaiwx-star , @RomneyDa , and @eduardonunesfreire-rgb . Backup and restore: preserve supported legacy exec-approval allowlists when sanitizing snapshots instead of replacing them with deny-all; malformed policies remain fail-closed. ( #164297 ) Thanks @wangmiao0668000666 , @RomneyDa , @shanselman , @dor-sr , @cristianoc , and @brucemccurdy . Linux companion: persist each saved Gateway dashboard's private browser identity across restarts, while removing storage for deleted Gateways so re-added endpoints pair as fresh devices. ( #158908 ) Thanks @dor-sr , @RomneyDa , @shanselman , @wangmiao0668000666 , and @brucemccurdy . Agent database lifecycle: keep peer readers and borrowers alive when maintenance or PostgreSQL opening is refused, preserve the original refusal and clean-restart seal, and retain pre-dispatch recovery behavior when a worker generation disappears. ( #175987 , #163258 , #179320 ) Thanks @RomneyDa , @shanselman , @dor-sr , @wangmiao0668000666 , @brucemccurdy , @goutamadwant , and @hawkit . macOS bundled Gateway: show the actual installed Gateway version, keep failed or incomplete recovery actionable, and prevent stale or pending update receipts from blocking a valid repair. ( #181389 ) Thanks @shanselman , @RomneyDa , @dor-sr , @wangmiao0668000666 , and @brucemccurdy . Model refresh: let explicit catalog refreshes use their existing extended discovery budget through HTTP acquisition while ordinary preparation remains bounded. ( #177313 ) Thanks @jlapenna and @RomneyDa . Webhooks and scheduled scripts: classify trusted immediate producers as events, retain each webhook's own automation scope, and refresh disposed script hooks before execution without replaying completed effects. ( #172775 , #177825 , #178904 ) Thanks @RomneyDa , @jlapenna , and @jalehman . Runtime security: backport patched embedded runtimes to the 2026.10.10 line. ( #181074 ) Thanks @RomneyDa and @joshavant . Update finalization: keep a verified healthy target successful when a recognized late restart-health or legacy-wrapper maintenance step fails, while authority, data-at-risk, deferred-admission, and unknown failures remain fatal. ( #181166 ; fixes #181020 ) Thanks @najef1979-code . Package update recovery: automatically settle verified interrupted publications or retire untouched preparations, preserve the installed candidate and original Gateway recovery evidence, and keep live update ownership and restart authority fenced. ( #181307 ; fixes #181235 ) Thanks @agroman1993 . CLI config writes and setup with a running Gateway: openclaw config set , config unset , and openclaw setup now send their change through the running Gateway as one config.patch instead of refusing, with the same result as an offline write, no restart while reload is off, and a success acknowledgement when the Gateway accepts a restart, so Windows companion setup completes again. ( #182951 , #184194 , #184392 , #184532 , #185109 ) Thanks @RomneyDa . Codex native subagents: unblock parent replies after native children finish, are interrupted, or complete follow-ups; stop resurrecting undeliverable child completions; replay completed grandchildren correctly after Gateway restarts; keep native tool declarations across completion turns; and let Stop succeed after parent thread reuse. ( #173018 , #175246 , #177577 , #179050 , #179099 , #183286 , #181475 ; fixes #178395 ) Thanks @quqi1599 , @Stronggenetics , @linancn , @mmartoccia , @wtfichigo , @Marvinthebored , and @RomneyDa . Claude CLI: stop prompt-cache prefix churn after a child completion. ( #172026 ) Thanks @Marvinthebored and @VACInc . Scheduled runs: wait for tool results before answering, so cron run summaries report the real result instead of a premature "no results" reply. ( #179690 ) Thanks @obviyus . Agent restart recovery: release restart-recovery fences for killed runs so their conversations no longer stay blocked. ( #181992 ; fixes #181952 ) Thanks @najef1979-code . Windows exec: restore command execution for Gateways running as an S4U scheduled task when Store PowerShell is installed. ( #182898 ; fixes #182652 ) Thanks @RomneyDa and @tre1d . Kimi: give Kimi K3.1 Pro the K3 thinking and video controls. ( #181923 ) Thanks @obviyus . content: This is a gateway-only extended-stable release, which is our current equivalent to LTS. This release is OpenClaw from the end of September 2026, plus critical security updates, reliability and performance fixes, and features like new model support. The latest version of OpenClaw at the time of this release is 2026.10.7 2026.9.35 Highlights Steadier memory under service managers: worker heap caps now apply even when the Gateway service passes a process-wide --max-old-space-size , idle Codex app-server clients retire after 30 seconds, and archive workers are reused between session deletes, so long-running Gateways stop accumulating memory. Fixes #179515 , #169797 , #165663 . ( #166581 , #171490 , #168387 , #171156 , #175091 ) Thanks @valkyriweb and @RomneyDa . Updates finish more often: update-time Doctor now removes leftover unknown config keys after migrations, accepts a missing legacy OAuth directory, keeps a valid config that lacks meta , settles a completed package publication that already serves the candidate, and no longer overflows on very large session histories. Fixes #174618 , #183479 . ( #175404 , #180174 , #183703 , #180414 ) Gateway stays responsive: crafted Microsoft Teams HTML, replies shaped like tool calls, and long streamed HTML or JSX answers no longer stall the Gateway event loop for seconds at a time. ( #183438 , #183252 , #174833 , #175472 , #180765 ) Thanks @LeizhenZhang and @JasonBuildAI . Replies reach the user: the message tool stays directly visible under Tool Search, model fallback works after an unexecuted tool call and for compaction, timed-out MCP sessions no longer break the next turn, and Claude CLI turns that hit the output limit fail fast instead of stalling for 15 minutes. Fixes #176045 . ( #179450 , #183282 , #182189 , #159931 ) Thanks @hehuang139 , @pstarkgit , @aniketkrs , and @Terwox . Codex native subagents settle correctly: parents are no longer blocked after native children finish, are interrupted, or complete a follow-up; undeliverable completions are not resurrected; and completed grandchildren no longer replay after a Gateway restart. ( #173018 , #175246 , #179050 , #179099 , #177577 , #181839 ) Thanks @quqi1599 , @wtfichigo , @linancn , and @sunlit-deng . Safer by default: test -v exec operands now require approval in allowlist mode, browser proxy commands are refused through generic node invoke, generated-video downloads use the SSRF guard, and openclaw mcp list / show plus logs redact credentials. ( #180880 , #179880 , #182425 , #180321 , #183193 ) Thanks @eleqtrizit , @brandon-julio-t , and @LeizhenZhang . SQLite 3.54 data safety: Doctor and update snapshots now repair stale full-text indexes left by the SQLite tokenizer change instead of quarantining agent databases. Fixes #176220 . ( #176234 , #181206 ) Changes Kimi K3.1 Pro: moonshot/kimi-k3.1-pro , kimi/k3.1-pro , and their Highspeed variants get the K3 thinking, effort, and video controls; K3.1 rejects off locally instead of returning a provider 400. ( #181923 ) Thanks @obviyus . Known-issue documentation: documented the --preserve-symlinks plugin capture workaround, the 2026.8.35 updater's schema warning, and recovery after a publication-journal device-number change. Related #175591 , #170031 . ( #184143 ) Thanks @RomneyDa . Fixes Credential and content boundaries: require approval for test / [ -v operands, refuse browser proxy commands on generic node invoke, guard generated-video downloads, redact MCP inspection output and Google OAuth client secrets, keep commentary out of turns whose replies are disabled, and keep private media out of silent turns. ( #180880 , #179880 , #182425 , #180321 , #183193 , #178518 , #129244 ) Thanks @eleqtrizit , @brandon-julio-t , @LeizhenZhang , and @obviyus . Reply delivery and fallback: keep the message tool visible under Tool Search, allow model fallback after unexecuted tool calls and for compaction, fall back immediately on exhausted Anthropic usage caps, recover unfinished tool work after empty length stops, and keep rejected Claude CLI drafts out of final replies. Fixes #176045 , #176179 . ( #169091 , #179450 , #183282 , #176186 , #153728 , #168764 ) Thanks @hehuang139 , @pstarkgit , @sunlit-deng , @zhangguiping-xydt , and @ruel225 . Gateway responsiveness: bound regex and tag scans for Microsoft Teams HTML, tool-call-shaped replies, and long streamed markup. ( #183438 , #183252 , #174833 , #175472 , #180765 ) Thanks @LeizhenZhang and @JasonBuildAI . Claude CLI sessions: ignore request echoes when checking for orphaned tool calls, classify rejected resume checkpoints as an expired session, end output-limit stalls promptly, and stop announce wakes from resetting CLI chats. ( #172026 , #159931 , #181308 , #176218 ) Thanks @Terwox , @mushuiyu886 , and @eliavb43 . Agent runtime: release completed attempt callbacks, finish parent handoff after cancelling child tasks, cap large subagent completion batches, preserve memory captures during concurrent session resets, load skills when macOS workspace casing differs, and stop thinking-only replies from utility models, including custom GLM title models. ( #183884 , #178893 , #172068 , #181081 , #181236 , #169920 , #172580 ) Thanks @brianmcguire and @jason-allen-oneal . Codex: retire idle unowned app-server clients, keep native tool declarations stable on completion turns, keep native liveness during host work, and settle native subagent completions, interruptions, follow-ups, and restart replay. Fixes #165663 . ( #168387 , #183286 , #181839 , #173018 , #175246 , #179050 , #179099 , #177577 ) Thanks @sunlit-deng , @quqi1599 , @wtfichigo , and @linancn . Channels: recover Slack socket mode from an isolated invalid_auth and Slack relay connections from silent network drops, tag only Matrix control commands with a command source, keep Telegram offset checkpoints working on Bun, keep the realtime voice transport runtime for callbacks, and keep channel accounts restarting after an exited run is cancelled. Fixes #179398 . ( #181056 , #182368 , #179506 , #178909 , #179462 , #182433 ) Thanks @mushuiyu886 , @xiaopan-xydt , @brianmcguire , and @shoaibulhaque . MCP and GitHub tools: let concurrent agents read a fresh shared MCP OAuth credential without the exclusive lease, and accept GitHub PR publishing from operators whose profile attaches after connect. ( #179997 , #169400 ) Thanks @maliv2 and @Gigaxel . Gateway, state, and readiness: answer trusted-proxy readiness probes without forwarded headers, bound channel-identity admission waits so stalled admission cannot pin WAL checkpoints, keep queued startup work off temporary SQLite reader scopes, avoid writer stalls during initial host admission, preserve live state-lock owners while recovering stale Linux locks, and finish worker shutdown after inventory retirement. Related #143524 . ( #182823 , #172244 , #182615 , #171549 , #175118 , #168862 ) Thanks @ericcaiwx-star , @xialonglee , and @xiaopan-xydt . Update, install, and Doctor: remove unowned config keys during updates, accept a missing legacy OAuth directory, keep a valid config that lacks meta , route debug logs off JSON stdout during admission, bound the post-activation Doctor step and update baseline checks, recover the Node runtime when started from / , accept unchanged dist files with extra execute bits, tolerate absent optional packages in Windows swaps, launch SQLite helpers hidden on Windows, create the state directory 0700 regardless of umask, admit group-writable plugin secret resolvers, allow SQLite readers during stopped backups, import transcripts whose filename differs from the header, read cron history identities before payloads, avoid stack overflow on very large session histories, settle a completed package publication that already serves the candidate, and refuse a registry update before staging when the Gateway's Node does not satisfy the target's engines.node instead of crash-looping after the switch. Fixes #174618 , #183479 , #183149 . ( #180769 , #175404 , #180174 , #183703 , #182850 , #173862 , #181906 , #178112 , #181141 , #181596 , #174969 , #179538 , #181127 , #180827 , #178146 , #174530 , #180414 ) Thanks @jalehman and @wangmiao0668000666 . Plugins: replace dangling dependency junctions instead of refusing plugin migration, copy native captures across filesystems, and tolerate ctime-only stat drift in native companion admission. ( #179549 , #179445 , #179949 ) Thanks @coaiMax . SQLite full-text indexes: repair stale FTS indexes after the SQLite 3.54 tokenizer change in Doctor and update snapshots instead of quarantining agent data. Fixes #176220 . ( #176234 , #181206 ) Release validation compatibility: carry the release-retrospective batch 5 tooling (admission pins, compact reuse plans, Plugin SDK revision rendering) needed by current full-release validation. ( #181920 ) Thanks @RomneyDa . Complete contribution record The 2026.9.35 maintenance audit covers all 3,595 main commits from beaee570a5d4 (2026-10-21) through f227543e4815 , plus open P0/P1 issues and operator-requested PRs. 78 fixes from 77 numbered PRs and 3 branch-specific repairs were applied or adapted; the rest were classified as not affected, already covered, or excluded with a reason. The complete PR inventory, adaptations, exclusions, and corrections to the 2026.9.34 audit are preserved in the 2026.9.35 extended-stable backport audit . The grouped notes above remain the user-impact summary.
