content: What's changed Added --hold-idle-file and --max-hold-min to self-hosted-runner , to keep an idle session while your host reports processes it left running Added a tip for the Explanatory output style, shown when you ask Claude for explanations Fixed long freezes at startup and after reading or editing files when a CLAUDE.md file holds a very long list item Fixed interrupting Claude not taking effect until a timeout while an MCP server had not answered a resource read or a skill was still downloading Fixed standard-context sessions stopping with "Usage credits required for 1M context" when a request ran over 200K tokens; Claude Code now compacts the conversation and continues Fixed Write and Edit stalling for up to 5 seconds after they ran, and reporting 0 lines changed, when changing thousands of lines in a file Fixed subagents being unable to use MCP tools from servers that finish connecting after the subagent starts Fixed Claude seeing stale MEMORY.md and CLAUDE.md content right after automatic compaction when those files were edited earlier in the session Fixed claude -p and SDK sessions saving transcript messages out of order or keeping messages that were taken back Fixed SubagentStop hooks running about twice a minute for each running subagent instead of once when it finishes Fixed the @ file picker ignoring .ignore / .rgignore negation rules that re-include git-ignored files Fixed a subagent's isolated worktree being removed while a background subagent it started was still working in it Fixed background agents in auto mode that wait on their own shells starting a new main conversation turn on every wake Fixed the Bash tool description claiming the working directory always persists between calls Fixed the environment block naming a shell commands don't run in, such as fish when the Bash tool uses zsh Fixed claude mcp add , claude mcp remove and /mcp naming the current folder instead of the project entry in ~/.claude.json that holds a local-scope server when run below a repository root Fixed claude mcp list and claude mcp get showing the error code twice on failed-connection lines (for example ENOENT: ENOENT: … ) Fixed Remote Control sessions staying on "Connecting" for about two minutes when a network proxy blocks a startup request Fixed messages that Claude sends to a cloud or Remote Control session appearing as your own message in the Claude mobile apps Fixed Claude not being told the cause when a file attached to a message sent over Remote Control or to a cloud session could not be saved because the disk was full, or that a message's attachments past the first 20 were left out Fixed WebFetch and WebSearch hanging on a stalled response in Cowork cloud sessions; an unfinished request now fails after 300 seconds Fixed a background session that crashed between turns not being restarted while it was attached, pinned, or had a scheduled task or wake-up set Fixed the "background service did not respond" error suggesting the disabled claude daemon restart ; it now suggests claude daemon stop --any and says it ends background sessions Fixed claude respawn starting the background service before reporting that no background session matches the id Fixed /effort not warning about a prompt cache miss in plan mode when the plan model differs from the session model Fixed /ide saying the VS Code extension was installed before the install finished or when it failed Fixed the Write tool's file preview skipping rows and miscounting hidden lines when a line is wider than the terminal Fixed ↑ in an agent's chat tab recalling a message that was still waiting to be delivered, so resending it sent a second copy Fixed Cowork cloud sessions losing their connectors and most tools after a restart when a plugin or your settings named an agent ; Cowork cloud sessions now ignore that setting Fixed agent teams sessions showing an empty task list when coming back with --resume , --continue , /resume or --session-id , including after /clear or a crash, and /branch writing to the original session's list Fixed pasting text that mentions an image file, such as ! open /tmp/shot.png or /review look at /tmp/shot.png , attaching the image and dropping its path from the prompt Fixed the feedback draft card showing its 1/2/0 and Esc shortcuts while the prompt has text, when those keys act on the prompt instead of the card Fixed a lone backslash in quotes or brackets, like "\" or (\) , disappearing from Claude's responses Fixed agent teammates compacting their history when DISABLE_COMPACT is set Fixed the rewind menu offering "Summarize from here" and "Summarize up to here" when DISABLE_COMPACT is set Fixed a finished /code-review , or another skill that runs in a sub-agent, running a second time when a cloud or background session restarts Fixed long hidden thinking being cut off as idle on Google Vertex AI, Microsoft Foundry and Claude Platform on AWS, where the endpoint sends thinking progress updates Fixed /ide saying it had installed the JetBrains plugin when nothing was installed Fixed Claude Pro and Max subscribers being told to ask their admin when their subscription can't be used; the message now points to billing settings Fixed the diff pane opening by itself after an edit in wide fullscreen terminals when it had nothing to show Fixed /mcp showing a remote server as failed after "Clear authentication" when the server works without sign-in Fixed /mcp showing "authenticated" for a remote server that Claude Code sends no credentials to Fixed a --plugin-dir folder of plugins loading as one plugin when an empty .mcp.json was at its top Fixed /usage never showing large prompt-cache misses under "What's contributing to your limits usage?" Fixed status line links staying plain text in background sessions after you open them from a terminal that supports links Fixed the /rewind confirmation saying the conversation "will be forked" when the later messages are removed from the conversation Fixed the /rewind warning that wrongly said manual and Bash edits are never affected by a code restore Fixed plan approval in screen reader mode sending feedback you had dismissed with Escape Fixed Claude Code retrying requests the API marked not to retry, which could hold a turn for minutes or, in unattended retry mode ( CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG ), indefinitely Linux: Fixed sandboxed Bash commands failing with bwrap: Can't create file when a --plugin-dir folder was also an added directory and permissions.blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories was on Self-hosted runner: Fixed a session failing to start when a rate limit (HTTP 429, or a git wrapper that exits 75) blocks an added read-only repository; it now starts without that repository Improved startup time for Pro and Max accounts by skipping two network requests on launches within an hour of the last check Improved /teleport and claude --teleport to warn when a compacted cloud session loads from its last compaction, so the messages it summarized aren't in the local copy Improved the messages shown when a background session's process exits: they no longer promise a restart that isn't coming, and they say how to resume the session Improved artifacts with several views: Claude now routes each view on the link's #name and no longer says the address bar stays the same as you switch views Improved shell commands that reach their timeout: the result now shows the output so far and says the command is still running in the background Improved compaction: when the model's reply has no summary in it, Claude Code now usually asks for the summary once more before it replaces the conversation Improved the Artifact tool's choice between a page and a document: explainers and visual or interactive work become artifact pages; documents are for writing people keep editing or pass around Improved startup time for launches whose only arguments are options and their values, such as claude --model opus Improved the "Connection dropped" API error: it now says where to look first (the proxy or gateway in use, else VPN or firewall; Anthropic API only, Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry are unchanged) Improved screen reader mode: deleting a rule in /permissions says "Deleted allow rule …" right away Improved the message shown when a pasted sign-in code is refused: it now says the code may have expired or been used, and to sign in again Improved Slack connector sends: Claude now checks a channel's topic for posting rules before messaging a channel you didn't name Improved screen reader mode: Claude's questions are listed as "Questions: Color (answered), Pages", without arrows or symbols Changed ultrathink in the interactive terminal to run its turn at xhigh effort on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 and Fable 5.1 through Anthropic's API; typed while Claude is working, it raises the rest of that turn Changed the ultrathink rainbow to appear only where the keyword can raise effort, and not when the word is quoted or part of a file path Changed Ctrl+D in agent view to match the prompt: on an empty input, pressing it twice exits Changed --output-format json and stream-json output to write DEL, C1 control and Unicode format characters inside strings as \uXXXX escapes; parsed values are unchanged Changed model names and IDs to drop the [1m] suffix and its label on models where the suffix has no effect; the suffix is still accepted Changed startup warnings about permission rules in settings files to show once per user until the rule changes Changed /code-review to tell Claude to put the effort level first and use max only when asked Changed DISABLE_COMPACT in settings files and in a mod's $.env.set so they can only turn compaction off, not back on Changed Claude Code on Bedrock, Mantle, Vertex, and Foundry to load model settings from a signed file on downloads.claude.ai; set CLAUDE_CODE_MODEL_CATALOG=off to turn this off Changed sessions that set CLAUDE_CODE_SYNC_SKILLS with feature-flag fetching off to reuse a claude.ai skills list up to 10 minutes old that another session on the machine fetched Changed clicks on scrollbar arrows and bars in fullscreen lists to act when the mouse button is released, so moving off the scrollbar before letting go cancels the click Changed claude purge to say it deletes data only on this computer, not anything stored by Anthropic [VSCode] Added syntax coloring to code blocks in Claude's replies, in light, dark and high contrast dark themes [VSCode] Added a "Running UserPromptSubmit hooks" spinner status and screen reader announcement for slow UserPromptSubmit hooks [VSCode] Fixed custom skills and custom slash commands sent from the VS Code or JetBrains panel leaving out the open file or selected lines that ordinary messages include ( #102799 ) [VSCode] Fixed the extension host freezing while the login shell ran its start-up files to read PATH on macOS and Linux [VSCode] Fixed clicking an image in a tool result, or closing its preview, also opening the result's text in an editor tab [VSCode] Fixed voice dictation continuing to record after a message was sent with the Send button; sending now stops dictation first, as pressing Enter already did [VSCode] Changed the extension to start Claude Code sessions with DISABLE_TELEMETRY set while VS Code's telemetry setting is off, so they send no usage metrics or error reports and fetch no feature flags [VSCode] Changed the session list side bar to load Web sessions when the Web tab is first opened, not at startup [Cloud sessions] Fixed routines in Anthropic-hosted environments staying locked after their owner left the organization and rejoined; the owner can now turn them back on [Cloud sessions] Fixed a failed routine API token delete or regenerate showing nothing if the edit dialog had already closed; it now shows an error toast [Cloud sessions] Fixed cloud environment dialogs, including the admin dialog, accepting duplicate names; they now refuse a name another listed environment already has [Claude Tag] Added a Skills view to Claude Tag analytics showing how often Claude runs each attached skill in Slack channels and which go unused, with Usage links in admin settings [Claude Tag] Improved Claude Tag routines that run in a new session: a run with nothing to report can now end without posting a throwaway message to the channel [Claude Tag] Changed Claude Tag admin settings to show a lock instead of # for private Slack channels that your own Slack account can see [Code Review] Improved Code Review's check run to say no further automatic review will start when the model still can't analyze a change on the automatic retry [Code Review] Improved Code Review reliability: a review whose session fails to start because of a transient server fault is now retried once automatically, and its check run says so

title: Fleet-wide computer vision lifecycle at the edge with SageMaker SDK v3
summary: Fleet-wide computer vision needs a model per camera, not one model for the whole fleet. This post presents a working Amazon SageMaker SDK v3 reference architecture that trains, quality-gates, compiles per-camera models with SageMaker Neo, and versions thousands of them, with an AWS Step Functions layer pacing fleet-scale retraining within account quotas.
content: Fleet-wide computer vision model lifecycle management is a problem that shows up the moment a quality inspection proof of concept succeeds. One camera and one model work fine. Then the plant asks for the same result on 40 lines, each with several cameras, and every camera sees the world differently. Each has a different angle, different glare off the same stainless surface, and different ambient light depending on which bay door is open. In production deployments we have worked on, a single model trained on pooled footage underperforms enough individual cameras that each camera ends up with its own fine-tuned model. Now the real problem is no longer training one model well. It’s training, evaluating, versioning, and shipping thousands of them without a human in the loop for each one. This post updates the pattern introduced in the 2023 series Build an end-to-end MLOps pipeline for visual quality inspection at the edge for the current Amazon SageMaker Python SDK v3. It replaces the since-deprecated Amazon SageMaker Edge Manager with Amazon SageMaker Neo for edge optimization. I walk through a dual-branch Amazon SageMaker Pipeline that trains an anomaly detector and a defect classifier per camera, with quality gates that block underperforming models. An in-pipeline SageMaker Neo compilation step ensures every registered model ships with a device-optimized artifact, and an AWS Step Functions orchestration layer paces fleet training. You deploy everything with the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK), and a full pipeline run on synthetic data costs about $0.07 in compute. The complete sample is available in the aws-samples GitHub repository . Solution overview The following diagram shows the sample’s fleet-wide model lifecycle. An orchestration layer queues re-training requests and limits concurrent work. A per-camera training pipeline prepares data, trains and evaluates an anomaly detector and a classifier, and produces versioned model artifacts for edge devices. Figure 1: Solution architecture The training half is a single SageMaker Pipeline, parameterized by camera, that runs 13 steps per execution. Three entry steps run in parallel: Preprocess, Fetch Latest Anomaly, and Fetch Latest Classifier. The pipeline preprocesses that camera’s images and fetches the camera’s most recent approved model for each branch, then trains two models. The first is a small convolutional autoencoder that learns what normal product looks like and flags anomalies by reconstruction error. The second is a ResNet18 classifier fine-tuned to confirm the defect. Each branch exports its model to ONNX, evaluates the exported artifact against held-out data, and passes through a quality gate. Past the gate, the model is compiled with SageMaker Neo for the configured edge target, and only then registered in the SageMaker Model Registry. As a result, every approved package has a device-ready compiled artifact. Packages carry the camera ID as metadata, and each branch’s warm-start fetch filters on it, so re-training always resumes from that camera’s own history. The orchestration half paces the fleet. Re-training requests land on an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue, and an AWS Lambda function starts a Step Functions execution per request. Each execution acquires a slot through a DynamoDB semaphore before starting its pipeline, so a burst of requests drains at a steady rate instead of all launching at once. Completions publish to Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS), and operational failures reach the same topic through an Amazon EventBridge rule with the original error preserved. The output of the system is versioned, quality-gated, per-camera model artifacts. The Model Registry holds the portable ONNX, and S3 holds the Neo-compiled build of that model, which is a device-optimized shared library loaded by the DLR runtime rather than ONNX. Both are ready for whatever delivery mechanism your plant uses. Prerequisites To deploy the sample you need the following: An AWS account with permissions to create AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles. An Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket. An Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repository. The SageMaker AI, AWS Step Functions, AWS Lambda, Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS), Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS), Amazon EventBridge, and Amazon DynamoDB resources in the stacks. Python 3.10, 3.11, or 3.12, Docker. The AWS CDK CLI version 2.1131.0 or later. Previous CLI versions fail with a cloud assembly schema mismatch against recent versions of aws-cdk-lib . No service quota increase is needed. The orchestration layer admits at most five pipeline executions at a time by default, which keeps concurrent SageMaker training jobs inside the standard account quota. If you deploy to an AWS Region other than your CLI default, set all three of AWS_REGION , AWS_DEFAULT_REGION , and CDK_DEFAULT_REGION on the deploy command itself rather than in your shell profile, for example, AWS_REGION=us-east-2 AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-2 CDK_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-2 cdk deploy --all . The CDK CLI, Boto3, and the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) resolve the Region from overlapping but not identical variable sets, and a mismatch produces confusing partial deployments. Prefixing the command sets all three for that invocation only, so your own default Region is left unchanged. Defining the training pipeline with SDK v3 The code in this section is excerpted from the CDK application in the repository rather than a standalone script, and it runs during cdk deploy, when the stack synthesizes the pipeline definition. Environment setup and the deploy commands come later, under Deploying and running the sample. SDK v3 reorganized the SageMaker Python SDK into modular packages, and the imports show the new shape of the library: from sagemaker.train import ModelTrainer from sagemaker.train.configs import InputData, Compute, OutputDataConfig from sagemaker.core.training.configs import MetricDefinition from sagemaker.serve.model_builder import ModelBuilder from sagemaker.mlops.workflow.pipeline import Pipeline from sagemaker.mlops.workflow.steps import ProcessingStep, TrainingStep from sagemaker.mlops.workflow.model_step import ModelStep from sagemaker.mlops.workflow.condition_step import ConditionStep from sagemaker.core.workflow.conditions import ConditionGreaterThanOrEqualTo from sagemaker.core.workflow.functions import JsonGet Installing sagemaker>=3.0.0, pulls in sagemaker-core , sagemaker-train , sagemaker-serve , and sagemaker-mlops as separate packages. Training configuration that v2 spread across Estimator constructor arguments now lives in typed config objects passed to ModelTrainer . This is the anomaly branch’s trainer, verbatim from the sample: anomalib_trainer = ModelTrainer( training_image=custom_training_image_uri, compute=Compute( instance_type=training_instance_type.to_string(), instance_count=1, ), base_job_name="cv-pipeline-anomalib-train", sagemaker_session=pipeline_session, role=role_arn, hyperparameters={ "program": "train_anomalib.py", "model_name": "autoencoder", "image_size": "256", "num_epochs": "3", "batch_size": "16", "learning_rate": "0.001", }, input_data_config=anomalib_input_data, output_data_config=OutputDataConfig( s3_output_path=run_prefix("anomalib-training") ), ).with_metric_definitions( [ MetricDefinition( name="image_auroc", regex=r"validation:image_auroc=([0-9]*\.?[0-9]+)", ), ] ) anomalib_input_data wires four channels ( train , validation , test , pretrained_model ) from upstream step properties, and run_prefix scopes every S3 path to the pipeline execution ID so concurrent fleet runs never collide. Both are in the repository. Two v3 behaviors matter when the pipeline lives inside a CDK application, and neither appears in the changelog as a breaking change. First, SDK v3 validates the pipeline’s execution role against live IAM while building the pipeline definition. This validation happens at synthesis time rather than execution time. A CDK app can’t create the role and the pipeline in one deployment, because the role doesn’t exist yet when the SDK validates it. This is separate from cdk bootstrap, which provisions the CDK toolkit resources once per account and Region and might already be done in your account. The sample’s own two-phase deploy is driven by a context flag that happens to share that name. An initial pass with -c bootstrap=true creates the role, bucket, and ECR repository, and the second pass synthesizes the pipeline against the now-existing role. The role Amazon Resource Name (ARN) embedded in the pipeline definition must also be a concrete string, not an unresolved CDK token. Second, the v3 role validator simulates ECR pull permissions without a resource ARN, so an execution role scoped to a single ECR repository fails validation even though it would work at runtime. The sample’s role carries a broader ECR grant for this reason. Lastly, one v3 habit the sample uses: constructing the pipeline with PipelineSession(default_bucket=your_bucket) routes SDK-managed uploads, such as step code, into the pipeline’s own bucket, so every artifact lives in one place and the execution role’s permissions cover a single bucket. (Granting the role access to the SDK’s default bucket works too. This approach is tidier.) Quality gates that match how defect data behaves Every trained model is evaluated before registration, and the evaluation runs against the exported ONNX artifact rather than the in-memory PyTorch model. That distinction matters: the artifact you gate is the artifact you ship, so an export problem can never slip a broken model past a healthy-looking training run. The anomaly branch gates on AUROC of at least 0.8. The classifier branch gates on two metrics at once, and the choice of metrics is shaped by the defining property of defect data: heavy class imbalance. In this sample roughly 90 percent of images are good, which is realistic for a production line. Against that distribution, plain accuracy is meaningless, because a model that predicts “good” for every image scores about 0.9 while catching zero defects. Balanced accuracy, the mean of per-class recall, corrects for that, but it has its own blind spot. A model with perfect recall on good parts and only 20 percent recall on defects still scores (1.0 + 0.2) / 2 = 0.6. So the gate requires balanced accuracy of at least 0.6 and defect recall of at least 0.5, together: step_check_classifier = ConditionStep( name="CheckClassifierQuality", conditions=[ ConditionGreaterThanOrEqualTo( left=JsonGet( step_name=step_eval_classifier.name, property_file="evaluation", json_path="balanced_accuracy", ), right=min_accuracy, ), ConditionGreaterThanOrEqualTo( left=JsonGet( step_name=step_eval_classifier.name, property_file="evaluation", json_path="defect_recall", ), right=min_defect_recall, ), ], if_steps=[step_compile_classifier, step_register_classifier], else_steps=[step_fail_classifier], depends_on=[step_eval_classifier], ) A ConditionStep ANDs its conditions, so both must pass. The thresholds are pipeline parameters, adjustable per execution without redeploying. If a gate fails, a FailStep marks the execution failed and that branch’s model never reaches the registry (the two branches gate independently, so the other branch’s model may still register). The fleet keeps serving the previous approved model for that camera. The training code addresses the same imbalance from the other side. The classifier is a fine-tuned resnet18 with ImageNet weights and a two-class head. At per-camera dataset sizes, fine-tuning pretrained weights is what keeps the model from collapsing onto the majority class. The training code balances training batches with a WeightedRandomSampler using inverse class frequencies, while the loss stays unweighted. Combining a weighted loss with weighted sampling over-corrects toward the minority class. Compiling for the edge with SageMaker Neo, inside the pipeline Notice the gate’s if_steps in the preceding code: past the gate, compilation runs first and registration depends on it. Both training scripts export ONNX with dynamic batch axes. The quality gates score those exported artifacts under ONNX Runtime, and then a CompileAnomalibNeo or CompileClassifierNeo step hands the gated artifact to SageMaker Neo . The invariant is gate, then compile, then register. A model only becomes an Approved package if it also compiled for the fleet’s edge target, so the registry never advertises a model the devices cannot run. The compile step encapsulates three error-prone details. Neo requires the input tarball to contain only the model file, but training jobs emit model.tar.gz with the checkpoint and metrics alongside the ONNX model. The step repackages an ONNX-only tarball first. Neo also requires concrete input shapes while the exports declare a dynamic batch axis, so batch size 1 is pinned in the compilation request. And because pipeline steps can retry, the compilation job name derives deterministically from the execution ID, so a retry resumes polling the job it already started instead of orphaning it. The target is a pipeline parameter: NeoTargetDevice selects a named device such as jetson_xavier or rasp4b , and its default compiles for the NeoTargetOs / NeoTargetArch platform, LINUX/X86_64 by default. The compiled package contains the optimized compiled.so plus the DLR runtime for loading it. The default output runs on any x86_64 Linux host, so you can validate it before committing to device-specific targets. Compilation itself incurs no charge. You pay for the processing instance that drives it and the S3 storage of the outputs. For compiling an already-registered model for additional device types later, without re-training, the repository includes an ad-hoc script that runs the same flow against the Model Registry. Per-camera models in the Model Registry Each branch registers into its own model package group, and every package carries the camera ID and its evaluation metrics. From the sample, with the metrics wiring elided: classifier_model_builder = ModelBuilder( s3_model_data_url=classifier_model_data, image_uri=custom_training_image_uri, sagemaker_session=pipeline_session, role_arn=role_arn, ) step_register_classifier = ModelStep( name="RegisterClassifierModel", depends_on=[step_compile_classifier], step_args=classifier_model_builder.register( model_package_group_name="sm1k-classifier-model-group", approval_status="Approved", model_metrics=classifier_metrics, customer_metadata_properties={"CameraId": camera_id}, ), ) Camera identity in customer_metadata_properties is what turns two shared package groups into a fleet catalog. Packages from all cameras live in the same groups, and per-camera history is recovered by filtering on the metadata. Each branch has a fetch step that pages through approved packages newest-first until it finds the requesting camera’s latest model, because ListModelPackages cannot filter on customer metadata server-side. On a camera’s first run the fetch finds nothing and training falls back to its cold-start initialization (ImageNet weights for the classifier, random initialization for the autoencoder). Every later run resumes from that camera’s own prior model, which is what makes frequent, cheap, incremental re-training viable across a fleet. Note what these registry entries are and are not: they catalog versioned, quality-gated artifacts, but their container reference is the training image, which serves no inference endpoints. They exist for a fleet workflow where a downstream system pulls artifacts and ships them to devices, not for CreateEndpoint . Orchestrating fleet training requests Every AWS account has service quotas on concurrent SageMaker training jobs, and each pipeline execution here launches several jobs, so fleet re-training needs pacing. Something has to keep a burst of 500 requests from becoming 500 simultaneous pipeline launches. The sample uses a semaphore, a counter of available slots that works like a parking lot with five spaces. Before the Step Functions state machine starts a pipeline, it takes a slot by atomically incrementing a counter in DynamoDB, with a condition that refuses the increment once the cap is reached: acquire_semaphore = tasks.DynamoUpdateItem( self, "AcquireSemaphore", table=semaphore_table, key={"LockName": tasks.DynamoAttributeValue.from_string("pipeline-concurrency")}, update_expression="SET ActiveCount = if_not_exists(ActiveCount, :zero) + :one", condition_expression="attribute_not_exists(ActiveCount) OR ActiveCount If all slots are taken, the execution waits and retries. When its pipeline finishes, it decrements the counter to release the slot. One detail is worth carrying into your own designs. The DynamoDB condition expression enforces the cap in a single atomic operation, rather than the state machine reading the counter and deciding, which would leave a race window between the read and the write. The repository implements the rest of the operational hardening, including releasing slots on every failure path and forwarding failed executions to Amazon SNS through Amazon EventBridge. Its README covers sizing the wait bounds. The cap of five is a stack parameter, set low so the sample deploys and runs in any standard account without requesting quota increases. Adjust it to whatever your account’s training-job quotas support. Past a single account’s quotas, scaling fleet training is its own topic. The standard levers are raising the service quotas, spreading training across instance types or Regions, and distributing the fleet across multiple accounts. You can also hold the backlog in SQS and admit work only as capacity frees up. Those choices depend on your fleet’s size and shape. The sample gives you the working skeleton to extend. Deploying and running the sample The walkthrough in the repository README is the authoritative version. The following short form starts from a clean checkout and sets up the environment before the first deploy: git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/sample-sagemaker-fleet-cv-pipeline cd sample-sagemaker-fleet-cv-pipeline && python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate pip install -r requirements.txt cdk bootstrap # once per account/region cdk deploy SageMakerCVPipelineStack -c bootstrap=true # roles, bucket, ECR cdk deploy --all # pipeline + orchestration ./scripts/push_ecr_image.sh # build and push training image By default the pipeline generates synthetic production line images, so you can validate the whole system end to end with no dataset and no data approvals. A full run executes all 13 steps, including both Neo compilations, in about 15 minutes and costs roughly $0.07 in billed ml.m5.xlarge time (US East (Ohio) Region (us-east-2), July 2026, on-demand). The orchestration resources together cost well under $0.10 per month at sample scale. To exercise the pipeline on real images, the repository includes a downloader for the BCCD dataset . The dataset is a collection of 364 annotated blood smear microscopy images originally open sourced on GitHub and reorganized into Pascal VOC format under an MIT license. The same dataset is also distributed by Roboflow as public domain. The script maps platelet presence to the defect class, optionally splits the images per camera to simulate a fleet, and uploads training tarballs to the pipeline bucket. The accompanying notebook runs the full pipeline on the real data and does side-by-side ONNX inference on a normal and an anomalous sample. Treating platelets as defects is an illustrative stand-in for a manufacturing defect distribution, not a clinical claim. Cleaning up Model packages are created at pipeline runtime, so AWS CloudFormation cannot delete them. Remove them with the AWS CLI first, then destroy the stacks with cdk destroy --all -c bootstrap=true --force . The README lists the exact commands. Conclusion In this post, I showed a working SageMaker SDK v3 reference architecture for the fleet-scale computer vision lifecycle. The architecture includes a dual-branch training pipeline where every model is quality-gated on its exported ONNX artifact, compiled with SageMaker Neo, and only then registered. A Model Registry layout uses camera metadata to turn shared package groups into per-camera warm-startable history, and a Step Functions orchestration layer paces fleet training within account quotas. For teams whose needs are met by managed options such as Amazon Lookout for Vision, that is the simpler path. This pattern targets the per-camera, fleet-scale constraint that managed options do not cover. The design rules transfer beyond computer vision: gate on balanced accuracy plus minority-class recall rather than accuracy, evaluate and compile the artifact you ship, and make operational failures notify rather than terminate silently. The sample deploys in minutes and a full validation run costs about seven cents of compute, so a low-cost next step is to clone the repository and run it. From there, point the BCCD downloader at a real bucket, set NeoTargetDevice for your hardware, or size the orchestration bounds to your fleet. For the SDK v3 migration itself, the SageMaker Python SDK documentation and the two-part series announcing the new SDK are the references I kept open throughout. If you want help adapting this pattern to your production environment, reach out to your AWS account team.   About the author Kiowa Jackson Kiowa is a Senior Machine Learning Engineer at AWS ProServe. He specializes in visual intelligence systems that combine computer vision with agentic AI, and he brings these to production in the enterprise industrial sector.

title: Groundhog Day for AI agents: Prompt caching patterns for using OpenAI models on Amazon Bedrock
summary: Every time an agent takes a step, it re-reads its entire context before acting. Here is how prompt caching for OpenAI models on Amazon Bedrock lets your agent remember, cutting input cost and latency without resending the same tools, instructions, and history every turn.
content: Every time you spin off your agent, it has to re-read its whole life story before performing an action. Here’s how to make it remember without having to feed it the same context again. In the movie Groundhog Day , Bill Murray’s character re-lives the same February 2 every day. He wakes up to the same song playing on the radio, in the same inn, and the same small town, again and again for what some movie fans estimate to be 34 years. Nothing he accomplished the day before carries over unless he works it out again from scratch. AI agents live in a version of Groundhog Day. Every time an agent takes a step (calls a tool, reads the result, decides what to do next), it has to send the model its entire story so far to maintain continuity: the tool definitions, the instructions, every previous tool call, and every result. The model only predicts the next token based on the input you provide. It has no internal memory between requests, so it must read all of it again. By turn 20 of a coding session, the model re-reads turns 1–19, and it’s you who pays for every one of those tokens, again and again. Prompt caching breaks the cycle. The service stores your input prompt (instructions, tools, and content) and reuses it on the next request, at a fraction of the input price. In this post, I walk you through an agent’s life, from its first turn to when it gets new tools and spawns helpers. Along the way, I show you how prompt caching keeps costs down and keeps agents responsive and consistent. What an agent sends to its LLM Before talking about caching, it helps to look at what a typical agent’s first invocation to the large language model (LLM) contains: Tool list – The definitions of every function the agent can call. Changes when you ship a new release. Instructions – The developer prompt: rules, persona, policies, examples. Also changes per release. History – Everything that happened in this session so far: the task, the model’s tool calls, and the tool results (which grows every turn). New turn – The latest tool result or user message (which might be different every time). What an agent sends to the model, turn after turn if you don’t set up caching: Figure 1: What an agent sends to the model on every turn How prompt caching works under the hood When a model reads a prompt, it first does a write called prefill . During prefill, it processes every input token and builds its key and value vectors (also known as key-value, or KV), which form the model’s working state. This happens before the model writes its first token. Prompt caching saves that state, which contains the system prompt, tools, content, history, and so on. When a later request starts with the same input tokens (that is, the same text), the prompt caching service loads the saved state instead of computing it again. It then processes only what is new in the next payload to the model. Prompt caching can be implicit, where Amazon Bedrock selects where the reusable prefix ends, or explicit, where your code marks that endpoint using prompt_cache_breakpoint . You can use both approaches together, and we recommend doing so. Turn 1 compared to turn 2 Figure 2: Turn 1 saves the prompt prefix up to the breakpoint, and turn 2 reuses it and pays full price only for the new question Implicit or explicit, and why do we need both? For agentic workloads, implicit caching lets Bedrock choose what to cache as the conversation grows. With explicit caching, you can mark shared content, such as tools and instructions, for reuse across sessions and when spinning up helper agents. You don’t always need both forms of caching, but combining them gives you a reusable starting point while Bedrock manages the growing conversation automatically. New sessions can also reuse that shared starting point while each conversation builds on its own cached history. In this post, we start with the first turn, then show how to carry cached content through later turns, new tools, and across subagents. Hello cached world The first win is to cache the static part of the prompt: the tools and instructions that stay the same across requests. These examples use your existing Amazon Bedrock client, TOOLS , and task . Replace the shortened INSTRUCTIONS string with your real policies and examples. The reusable prefix must reach 1,024 tokens to qualify. When caching static content, use explicit mode: choose where the saved prefix ends. KEY = "support-agent:v7:gpt-6-astra" INSTRUCTIONS = "Your full support policies and examples..." # Rendered context: [provider context][TOOLS][INSTRUCTIONS] | [task] # Cache starts at the beginning; the marker below chooses its end. resp = client.responses.create( model="us.openai.gpt-6-astra", store=False, # Response storage; prompt caching still works. include=["reasoning.encrypted_content"], prompt_cache_key=KEY, prompt_cache_options={"mode": "explicit", "ttl": "30m"}, tools=TOOLS, # Rendered before instructions; keep order stable. input=[ { "role": "developer", "content": [{ "type": "input_text", "text": INSTRUCTIONS, # Save through this whole block, including TOOLS. "prompt_cache_breakpoint": {"mode": "explicit"}, }], }, # User message is processed but not cached. {"role": "user", "content": task}, ], ) The prompt_cache_key tells the service which requests are meant to share a cache. We come back to how to use it when we get to reading the cache in new sessions. In one of our tests using explicit caching, the roughly 4,000-token tools-and-instructions prefix wrote 4,120 tokens on the first request and read those 4,120 tokens on later requests. The task (or user request) comes after the cache boundary, so this doesn’t trigger a write to the cache. Keep in mind that prompt caching works only when you pass exactly the same text. Make sure that the agent’s instructions and tool lists are serialized the same way every time. Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and other forms of tool delivery need to be indexed to make sure they stay consistent. Keep anything that varies, such as the date, the user’s name, or a request ID, after the cached instructions. As the content grows and varies (different tools and content), use implicit mode to let the service follow the conversation. Here, the first request has no explicit marker. Its latest eligible message is the user’s task, so the automatic breakpoint comes after that task and covers the tools, instructions, and task together. The mode is shown explicitly in the following example for clarity, even though implicit is the default. Setting store=False leaves conversation history in your application. It doesn’t disable caching. def ask_with_implicit_cache(history): return client.responses.create( model="us.openai.gpt-6-astra", store=False, include=["reasoning.encrypted_content"], prompt_cache_key=KEY, prompt_cache_options={"mode": "implicit", "ttl": "30m"}, tools=TOOLS, input=history, # Everything gets cached ) history = [ {"role": "developer", "content": INSTRUCTIONS}, {"role": "user", "content": task}, ] # Automatic endpoint: the end of the user message. resp = ask_with_implicit_cache(history) This is useful when the next turn continues the same task. A different task doesn’t match the prefix through the old task, and the implicit write doesn’t necessarily create a separate entry for only the tools and instructions. Use an explicit marker there when you need that shorter shared prefix to be reusable across tasks. Use both when the agent needs a shared starting point and a growing history. Start with the marked developer block in the following code example and call the function ask_with_implicit_cache . The request-level mode stays implicit. The block-level marker adds an explicit save point after the instructions. The service can also save through the latest eligible message. This keeps the shared prefix available while the conversation grows. history = [ { "role": "developer", "content": [{ "type": "input_text", "text": INSTRUCTIONS, "prompt_cache_breakpoint": {"mode": "explicit"}, }], }, {"role": "user", "content": task}, ] # Still implicit mode, now with an explicit startup save point in the history. resp = ask_with_implicit_cache(history) Caching conversation history and tool results The model requests tools by name and supplies their arguments. Your application must execute them. execute_function is a helper you build to route those requests to the matching Python functions and return their results. The following loop uses this helper to run each requested tool. It appends the model’s output and all tool results to the history list, then sends that list again until the model returns a final answer. In implicit mode, Amazon Bedrock can reuse the unchanged prefix and cache the added content through the last tool result. Keep earlier messages and the initial TOOLS unchanged. import json # Map tool names to their Python implementations. TOOL_HANDLERS = { "get_owner": get_owner, # Register your other initial tools here. } def execute_function(name, arguments): """Run the requested tool and return its result.""" handler = TOOL_HANDLERS.get(name) if handler is None: return {"error": f"Unknown tool: {name}"} return handler(**arguments) while True: # Preserve all output items, including encrypted reasoning. history.extend(resp.output) calls = [x for x in resp.output if x.type == "function_call"] if not calls: break for call in calls: result = execute_function(call.name, json.loads(call.arguments)) history.append({ "type": "function_call_output", "call_id": call.call_id, "output": json.dumps(result), }) # The last result in this group supplies the automatic endpoint. resp = ask_with_implicit_cache(history) For follow-ups, append a new user message and call the helper again. Keep earlier messages unchanged so their cached endpoints remain available. Rolling breakpoints: Each turn reads everything before it Figure 3: Rolling breakpoints, where each turn reads everything before it and writes only its own tool result For a separate explicit-only run, recreate the two-message history from the combined Hello cached world example. This loop wraps tool results in input_text blocks and marks the final result in each batch. Earlier markers stay in history . See the current lookup rules for long conversations. import json while True: resp = client.responses.create( model="us.openai.gpt-6-astra", store=False, include=["reasoning.encrypted_content"], tools=TOOLS, prompt_cache_key=KEY, input=history, prompt_cache_options={"mode": "explicit", "ttl": "30m"}, ) d = resp.usage.input_tokens_details print("read", d.cached_tokens, "write", d.cache_write_tokens) history.extend(resp.output) # Includes encrypted reasoning. calls = [x for x in resp.output if x.type == "function_call"] if not calls: break batch = [] for call in calls: result = execute_function(call.name, json.loads(call.arguments)) batch.append({ "type": "function_call_output", "call_id": call.call_id, "output": [{"type": "input_text", "text": json.dumps(result)}], }) # Add the newest boundary; retain every earlier marker. batch[-1]["output"][-1]["prompt_cache_breakpoint"] = {"mode": "explicit"} history.extend(batch) GPT-6 Astra tied for the best implicit result in this six-turn workload: about 62 percent lower input cost than running without caching. Explicit rolling breakpoints saved about 61 percent on the same model. Both reused more history as the conversation grew. These are workload results. Measure your own agent’s savings. Figure 4: Input cost of every caching setup on GPT-6 Astra, relative to no caching Watch out for: Only a static breakpoint in explicit-only mode – The tools and instructions are cached, but the growing history is processed again on every turn (0.61). This limitation doesn’t apply to the combined example, which also saves through eligible conversation endings. Moving a single breakpoint can prevent cache reuse and cause repeated writes in explicit-only mode. Keep the previous turn’s breakpoint too. Only an implicit write through a changing task – A new task might share the tools and instructions but not the previously saved endpoint. Add an explicit marker after the shared instructions if different tasks need to reuse that shorter prefix. When tools change Sometimes an agent’s tool list changes, or new tools get added. Keep the initial list stable: adding, removing, or reordering definitions can invalidate the cached prefix. Choose the approach that fits how the tool becomes available. When known tools are invoked in different steps of the agent’s flow: Send the same sorted TOOLS and use allowed_tools to limit what the model can call. With allowed_tools , "mode": "auto" lets the model decide whether to call an allowed tool, and "mode": "required" requires at least one allowed tool call. Pass this as tool_choice . The restriction doesn’t change the cached catalog: tool_choice={"type": "allowed_tools", "mode": "auto", "tools": [{"type": "function", "name": "get_owner"}]} New tools during a session.  Both Amazon Bedrock Runtime and Amazon Bedrock Mantle endpoints accept an input item type called additional_tools for GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, and GPT-5.6 Luna. For model availability by AWS Region, see Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock . Register the new tool get_due_date in the helper function execute_function , then append its schema to the completed history from the agent loop. Keep the initial TOOLS unchanged: TOOL_HANDLERS["get_due_date"] = get_due_date NEW_TOOL = { "type": "function", "name": "get_due_date", "description": "Return the due date for a support case.", "strict": True, "parameters": { "type": "object", "properties": {"case_id": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["case_id"], "additionalProperties": False, }, } history.append({ "type": "additional_tools", "role": "developer", "tools": [NEW_TOOL], }) history.append({ "role": "user", "content": "Find the due date for case C-123.", }) # Implicit mode saves through this new user message, including NEW_TOOL. resp = ask_with_implicit_cache(history) d = resp.usage.input_tokens_details print("old prefix read", d.cached_tokens, "new write", d.cache_write_tokens) # Example output: # old prefix read 2048 new write 256 A new tool arrives mid-session Figure 5: Appending a tool keeps the earlier prefix reusable, with example counts from GPT-6 Astra on Amazon Bedrock Runtime Continue the tool-execution loop with the new response. The loop adds the model’s output to history , runs any requested tools, and appends their results. Keep the additional_tools item in later requests so the new tool remains available. In implicit mode, Amazon Bedrock can cache through the new user message, including the tool definitions that precede it. In explicit-only mode, retain earlier breakpoints and add one to an input_text block in that user message. The additional_tools item itself can’t hold a breakpoint. Different roles, different catalogs. When different agent roles need different tools, choose a stable tool profile, such as support or billing, at the start of each session. Each profile gets its own cached prefix. Mark the shared instructions so later tasks with that profile can reuse them, then use either mode as the conversation grows. Cached tool profiles Figure 6: Each tool profile has its own cached prefix, reusable by matching sessions Subagents and side calls Delegating shouldn’t make every helper reread the same background. Share the prefix, then add each helper’s task at the end. Be aware that when you use caching with AI agents, tools and system prompts can be leaked or exploited. Establish responsible AI practices that include your prompt caching implementation as part of that governance. Warm once, then fan out. Send an ordinary request first and wait for it to finish before launching helpers. Mark the shared context explicitly in every request, even when the mode is implicit: shared = {"role": "developer", "content": [{ "type": "input_text", "text": INSTRUCTIONS, "prompt_cache_breakpoint": {"mode": "explicit"}, }]} warm = client.responses.create( model="us.openai.gpt-6-astra", store=False, tools=TOOLS, prompt_cache_key=KEY, prompt_cache_options={"mode": "implicit", "ttl": "30m"}, max_output_tokens=16, input=[shared, {"role": "user", "content": "Reply READY."}], ) d = warm.usage.input_tokens_details if not (d.cache_write_tokens or d.cached_tokens): raise RuntimeError("Shared prefix was not cached.") from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor # helper_tasks contains the task text for each helper. helper_inputs = [ [shared, {"role": "user", "content": task}] for task in helper_tasks ] with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as pool: helpers = list(pool.map(ask_with_implicit_cache, helper_inputs)) The helpers use the same TOOLS , model, and KEY as the warm-up. A warm-up that ends at the output cap can still populate the cache. The usage check confirms cache activity before the helpers start. Subagents: Warm the shared prefix once, then fan out Figure 7: Warm the shared prefix before launching helpers, and each helper then adds its own task Give side calls the same beginning. The agent loop builds history by appending every resp.output and its matching tool results, including encrypted reasoning. After the parent finishes, copy that complete list for a summarizer or judge. The same helper keeps the tools, model, and key unchanged: from copy import deepcopy # history is the completed history built by the agent loop above. # Copy it so the helper can add instructions without changing the parent. helper_history = deepcopy(history) helper_history.append({ "role": "developer", "content": "Summarize this conversation in one sentence. Do not call tools.", }) summary = ask_with_implicit_cache(helper_history) d = summary.usage.input_tokens_details print("history read", d.cached_tokens, "write", d.cache_write_tokens) print(summary.output_text) # Example output (assumed values and conversation): # history read 4096 write 32 # Case C-123 is due on October 31, 2026. The helper can reuse the cached portion of history , but the appended developer message doesn’t automatically extend the cache to include the summary instruction. If later requests reuse the same history and instruction, place the instruction in an input_text block with prompt_cache_breakpoint . For a one-time summary, no additional marker is needed. Pauses, restarts, and the cache key Pauses. Cached prefixes have a minimum 30-minute time to live (TTL), refreshed by successful reuse, and might remain longer. If a session resumes soon, an ordinary warm-up can refresh the prefix before it expires. Compare that request’s cost with letting the cache expire. For the TTL rules, see the Amazon Bedrock documentation. New sessions. Keep prompt_cache_key stable for requests that are meant to share a prefix. A session-specific key isolates sessions even when their prompts match. In the following example, switching to a shared key let sessions reuse the prefix. New sessions reuse the cache only if they share the key Figure 8: A session-specific key separates cache entries, and a shared key lets matching sessions reuse them Reuse of existing cache content requires the same model, AWS account, and Region, and an available matching prefix. The following example combines an explicit startup marker with implicit mode. Each session starts with the same instructions and its own task. Both use the same computed key: import hashlib def cache_key(app, model, prompt_version, instructions): digest = hashlib.sha256(instructions.encode()).hexdigest()[:12] return f"{app}:{prompt_version}:{model}:{digest}" KEY = cache_key("support-agent", "us.openai.gpt-6-astra", "v7", INSTRUCTIONS) prefix = {"role": "developer", "content": [{ "type": "input_text", "text": INSTRUCTIONS, "prompt_cache_breakpoint": {"mode": "explicit"}, }]} for label, question in [ ("session A", "Explain the refund policy without calling tools."), ("session B", "Explain the escalation policy without calling tools."), ]: # A fresh conversation for each session; the startup prefix matches. session_history = [prefix, {"role": "user", "content": question}] result = ask_with_implicit_cache(session_history) d = result.usage.input_tokens_details print(label, "read", d.cached_tokens, "write", d.cache_write_tokens) On a cold start, session 1 writes the shared prefix. Session 2 can read it even though its task can be different. Each task can also be cached implicitly. Check the usage counters: matching keys and markers make reuse possible, but a cache entry still has to be available. What prompt caching delivers Cost. For a GPT-6 Astra powered agent with an 8,000-token startup prefix and six turns adding 2,000 tokens each, one-time static caching reduced cost to $0.50, and rolling breakpoints reduced modeled input cost by 64 percent: from $0.87 to $0.32 per session. Figure 9: Cumulative input cost per session for the support-agent example, using Amazon Bedrock on-demand prices for GPT-6 Astra How to tell caching is working Start with response usage. cached_tokens reports input read from the cache, and cache_write_tokens reports input written to it. As the conversation grows, check that later turns reuse earlier history and that new writes reflect the content being added. For production monitoring on the Amazon Bedrock Runtime endpoint, use the CacheReadInputTokenCount and CacheWriteInputTokenCount metrics in Amazon CloudWatch. Enable model invocation logging when you need individual request records, then query them with Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights. For the Amazon Bedrock Mantle endpoint, record the response usage fields in your application logs. Its Amazon CloudWatch namespace currently has no separate cache counters. To check costs, filter AWS Cost Explorer to Amazon Bedrock and group by Usage type . Cache reads, cache writes, and uncached input appear as separate entries per model. Exclude output-token entries when calculating their shares of input cost. A short checklist Keep the reusable prefix stable. Put shared tools and instructions first, then append conversation history and new turns. Changing a timestamp, message, or tool definition prevents reuse beyond that change. A shorter prefix can still be reused if it has its own saved endpoint. Choose boundaries around content you want to reuse. Use implicit caching for growing history, explicit markers for shared prefixes, or both. Explicit-only mode avoids writing disposable suffixes. When extending an explicit-only conversation, retain earlier markers so later requests can find the saved prefixes. Keep the initial tool catalog unchanged. Use allowed_tools to restrict which tools are callable. Append known definitions with additional_tools , or discover them through namespaced client-side tool_search . Choose a stable tool profile when different agent roles need different catalogs. Check prefix size and lifetime. A cacheable prefix must contain at least 1,024 tokens. Cached prefixes remain eligible for reuse for at least 30 minutes after their latest write or successful reuse. Warm shared content before launching helpers. Mark the shared prefix in both the warm-up and helper requests, including when using implicit mode. Finish the warm-up request before starting parallel calls. Keep cache keys stable within each sharing group. Requests intended to reuse a prefix must use the same key. Separate keys can keep cache accounting distinct between customers or users. Measure savings across the workflow. Cache writes cost 1.25 times the normal input rate. Read prices depend on the model. Track write costs alongside read savings, using response usage during development and monitoring and billing data in production. Waking up on February 3rd Bill Murray only escapes Groundhog Day once he stops repeating the same mistakes and starts carrying what he learned from one day to the next. Agents get there in a similar, if less romantic, way: by keeping the start of their prompt byte-for-byte stable and using automatic or explicit cache boundaries as the history grows. In this post, we covered how to cache shared tools and instructions, grow the cache across agent turns, and preserve reuse when adding tools, launching helpers, or starting new sessions. Keep the shared prefix stable and append new information as the workflow progresses. Use implicit caching for growing conversations and explicit breakpoints for shared content. Combine them when you need both, or choose explicit-only mode when a changing suffix is unlikely to be reused. Compare cache reads, writes, total input cost, and latency to find what works best for your agent. To apply these patterns, follow the Amazon Bedrock prompt caching documentation for OpenAI models and check model availability by AWS Region and endpoint . Start with one workflow and measure the savings as your conversations grow.   About the author Claudio Mazzoni Claudio is a Sr Specialist Solutions Architect on the Amazon Bedrock GTM team. Claudio excels at guiding customers through their Gen AI journey. Outside of work, Claudio enjoys spending time with family and working in his home garden.

title: Build agentic retrieval on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with CDK
summary: Build enterprise agentic retrieval on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with the AWS CDK: an agent that routes across two knowledge bases, retrieves through the AgentCore Gateway, and returns grounded, cited answers, with seven layers of observability and both on-demand and continuous evaluation, all deployed as a single CDK application.
content: This post builds enterprise agentic retrieval on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK). To see why that’s worth building, it helps to start with where ordinary Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) breaks down. Most RAG systems start the same way: they embed the question, fetch the nearest chunks from one index, hand them to a model, and return the answer. One retrieval, one generation. For a large class of questions that’s the right design, and there’s no reason to build anything more complicated. It fails in a recognizable way. Ask a question whose answer spans two corpora, and a single retrieval returns half of what the model needs, which is worse than returning nothing, because the answer comes back fluent and incomplete. Ask a question where the right source depends on the question , and a single index has no mechanism to choose. Ask a question that needs a second look at the corpus after seeing the first result, and there is nowhere for that second look to happen. Enterprise agentic retrieval answers all three by putting a reasoning agent in the loop. The agent decides whether to retrieve, which knowledge base to consult, and whether to go back for more before it composes an answer. This is the direction Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases have evolved. With the launch of the Managed Knowledge Base, retrieval is no longer a single embed-and-fetch call. It has become an agentic capability: multi-turn planning, tool-driven retrieval, and grounded, cited answers. The AgenticRetrieveStream API offers this as a first-class service feature rather than something you assemble yourself. That works, and it also introduces a genuinely harder operational problem. A single-shot pipeline is a function you can reason about by reading it. An agent that reasons and retrieves in a loop takes a different path on every question. By default you can see neither the path it took nor whether the answer it produced was any good. Observability stops being a nice-to-have and becomes the only way to know the system works. In August 2024, Build an end-to-end RAG solution using Knowledge Bases for Amazon Bedrock and the AWS CDK deployed the single-shot design as a CDK application: an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) corpus, an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless collection and index, a knowledge base, and a data source, provisioned as CDK stacks whose order you sequenced by hand. Three things have changed since it was published. Amazon Bedrock now offers a managed knowledge base (Type: MANAGED), which owns the ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval itself. The OpenSearch Serverless collection and index that post provisions are no longer something you need to create, scale, or pay for with OpenSearch Compute Units (OCUs). Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides the agentic half , a Gateway that exposes each knowledge base as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool, a Runtime that hosts the reasoning agent, and AgenticRetrieveStream, which reranks internally and returns a synthesized, cited answer. Agentic retrieval is available only on the Managed Knowledge Base. The observability and evaluation story is now something you can provision , not something you bolt on. This solution ships two Amazon CloudWatch dashboards spanning seven layers of telemetry, plus two forms of evaluation, on-demand and continuous, from the same deployment. This post builds that system: an agent that routes across two knowledge bases, retrieves through the Gateway, and returns a grounded, cited answer, with every layer of its behavior instrumented, as a single AWS CDK application in Python. One command deploys all of it, and CDK derives the order. If you read the 2024 post , the path from an Amazon S3 bucket to the knowledge base will look familiar, and everything after it is new: the vector store is gone, the retrieval is agentic, and roughly half of what the app provisions exists to tell you what the agent did. If you didn’t, this post stands on its own. The services at play and the path one question takes through them: the agent decides whether to retrieve and which knowledge base to consult, the Gateway exposes each knowledge base as a tool it can call, the Managed Knowledge Bases search and cite, and the loop repeats as many times as the question needs. Everything the agent does along the way lands in Amazon CloudWatch. Figure 1: The services involved and the path a single question takes through them Background Before the walkthrough, it helps to establish three things: what makes retrieval agentic, why the Managed Knowledge Base is the right foundation for it, and why observability and evaluation belong in the design rather than bolted on later. From RAG to enterprise agentic retrieval Classic Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) does one retrieval and one generation. Enterprise agentic retrieval puts a reasoning agent in the loop: it decides whether and what to retrieve, can retrieve several times to refine, chooses which knowledge base is relevant (semantic routing), and only then composes a grounded answer with citations. With the Managed Knowledge Base, this is a first-class service capability, the AgenticRetrieveStream API performs the multi-turn planning, executes the retrieval, and returns a cited answer, rather than an orchestration layer you build and maintain over a raw vector search. That produces better answers on complex questions, but it also produces a more complex system to operate, which is exactly why observability and evaluation are built in from the start. Managed compared to do-it-yourself Knowledge Bases Amazon Bedrock now offers a Managed Knowledge Base (Type: MANAGED): Amazon Bedrock manages the ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval for you, including embedding and reranking with service-managed models by default, so there is no vector database to provision, scale, or patch . This differs from a Customer-managed (DIY) Knowledge Base, where you choose and operate the vector store (for example, Amazon OpenSearch Serverless) yourself. Two differences matter most for this solution: Capability Amazon Bedrock managed Customer-managed (DIY) Agentic retrieval (AgenticRetrieveStream) Supported Not supported AgentCore Gateway integration Supported Not supported Data store Auto scaling, fully managed by Amazon Bedrock You provision, scale, and maintain it Embedding + reranking Built-in managed models, no extra cost You configure them Infrastructure to manage None Vector DB + more Because agentic retrieval and the AgentCore Gateway connector are available only on the managed knowledge base, it is the natural foundation for enterprise agentic retrieval. It also means Amazon Bedrock manages the storage and indexing for you, so there is no OpenSearch Serverless collection or OCU capacity to provision in this design. The customer-managed option remains the right choice when you want to select and operate your own vector store, for example to reuse an existing OpenSearch Serverless collection or to meet specific data-residency, tuning, or compliance requirements. For enterprise agentic retrieval, the managed knowledge base is what makes the capability possible. Why observability and evaluation An agentic system that returns an answer isn’t enough for production. You need to see how it behaves (latency, call volume, token usage), how good the retrieval and answers are, and you need those signals continuously. This solution ships two CloudWatch dashboards spanning seven layers of telemetry, plus two forms of evaluation (on-demand and continuous), all provisioned by the same CDK application. The grounding, citations, and evaluation layers also support responsible use. Cited answers trace back to their source passages so responses stay auditable, and the faithfulness and correctness scores let you catch answers drifting from their sources rather than finding out in production. Why CDK for this particular solution Any infrastructure-as-code tool can create these resources. CDK earns its place here for a reason specific to this architecture: the four stacks are densely cross-referenced . The Gateway needs both knowledge base ids. The agent needs the URL and ARN for the Gateway. The dashboards need the KB ids, the Gateway ARN, and the agent runtime id, seven values crossing stack boundaries, each one a dimension on a metric or a target on a connector. Written as raw templates, that is a set of stack exports and cross-stack lookups kept in agreement by hand, plus a script that deploys in the right order and threads outputs forward, and both drift the moment anything is renamed. In CDK you pass the construct, and the export and the dependency edge are derived from that one act of passing it. The 2024 solution had three stacks and a mostly linear dependency chain. At four stacks with seven values crossing between them, the difference stops being stylistic. Solution overview Here is the path a single question takes through the system, end to end. It’s worth a slow look, because the rest of the post walks through it left to right. The following diagram traces the end-to-end agentic retrieval workflow. A user’s question enters the agent on the AgentCore Runtime, which routes it through the AgentCore Gateway to one of two AgenticRetrieveStream tools, one per managed knowledge base, financial and weather, each ingested from Amazon S3. The selected tool returns a grounded, cited answer, and every step streams to Amazon CloudWatch and AWS X-Ray. The numbered badges map to the following walkthrough. Figure 2: End-to-end agentic retrieval workflow for a single question The numbered steps in the diagram map to the workflow, which is as follows. Step 0 — one-time, at deploy. Before any question is asked, each corpus in Amazon S3 is ingested into its own Managed Knowledge Base: Amazon Bedrock parses, chunks, embeds, and indexes it automatically. This happens once when the stacks deploy, it isn’t part of the per-question path, so it is drawn as a dashed arrow and marked step 0. Every question then follows steps 1–6: A user sends a question to the agent hosted on the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. The Runtime auto-instruments the whole reason-and-act loop with OpenTelemetry (OTEL) spans, so the system is observable from the very first call. The agent’s reasoning model plans and routes across knowledge bases. Because each knowledge base is exposed as its own retrieval tool, the agent selects the tool whose topic matches the question, financial or weather, rather than searching one blended index. The selected tool call is brokered by the AgentCore Gateway over MCP , authorized by the agent’s IAM task role and signed with SigV4, which invokes that knowledge base’s AgenticRetrieveStream API on the Managed Knowledge Base. AgenticRetrieveStream does the within-knowledge-base work: it decomposes the question into sub-queries, retrieves iteratively from the data store that Amazon Bedrock manages (ingested from the corpora in Amazon S3), and synthesizes a grounded, cited answer that streams back through the Gateway. The agent checks whether the returned context is sufficient. If not, it loops, routing and retrieving again, before composing its final answer. If so, it returns the cited answer to the user. Throughout, the Runtime emits spans, token counts, and metrics to Amazon CloudWatch and AWS X-Ray, populating the seven observability layers and feeding both the on-demand and continuous evaluation scores. Internally, that workflow is one CDK app, app.py , that declares four stacks. You don’t choose the order, CDK derives it from the construct references you pass: kb_stack = KnowledgeBasesStack(app, f"{project}-kb", env=env) gateway_stack = AgenticGatewayStack( app, f"{project}-gateway", env=env, financial_kb=kb_stack.financial_kb, # ← the reference creates the dependency weather_kb=kb_stack.weather_kb, ) agent_stack = AgentRuntimeStack( app, f"{project}-agent", env=env, gateway=gateway_stack.gateway, ) DashboardsStack( app, f"{project}-dashboards", env=env, financial_kb=kb_stack.financial_kb, weather_kb=kb_stack.weather_kb, gateway=gateway_stack.gateway, agent_runtime=agent_stack.agent_runtime, ) That is the whole wiring. Those four constructor calls are what replace the export/import bookkeeping and the deploy script. # Stack What it creates Note 1 -kb S3 bucket, corpora upload, two Type: MANAGED KBs, data sources, IAM, ingestion KBs reach ACTIVE, corpora ingested 2 -gateway Gateway (AWS_IAM / MCP), per-KB AgenticRetrieveStream targets no Cognito needed 3 -agent ECR, CodeBuild, instrumented Strands agent on Runtime, vended logs/traces, online eval ~8–10 min (image build) 4 -dashboards agentic-observability + kb-observability dashboards empty until you drive traffic The agent runs a reason-and-act loop: it thinks (a large language model (LLM) call), decides which KB tool to call, reads what came back through the Gateway, and often retrieves again before composing its final, cited answer. Every step is auto-instrumented by the Runtime, so the seven observability layers fill from real traffic. The seven layers. L1 KB-native metrics, L2 ingestion, L3 agentic retrieval quality, L4 Gateway/MCP metrics, L5 OTEL span tree , L6 token usage, and L7 evaluation scores. Layers 1, 4, and 5 are emitted automatically. Layers 3, 6, and 7 are published as custom metrics by the driver notebook. Everything tunable lives in one file, config.py : Setting Meaning Default EnvSettings.PROJECT_NAME Name prefix for every stack and resource bmkb-obs-cdk EnvSettings.ACCOUNT_REGION AWS Region to deploy into us-west-2 (or your profile’s) KbConfig.EMBEDDING_MODEL_TYPE MANAGED (bundled) or CUSTOM (bring your own ARN) MANAGED AgentConfig.MODEL_ID The agent’s reasoning model, the Layer 6 spend Claude Haiku 4.5 EvalConfig.SAMPLING_PERCENTAGE Online-evaluation sampling rate, see the disclaimer 100 Changing PROJECT_NAME gives you an independently-named copy of the whole solution, so two deployments can coexist in one account. The driver notebook reads the same constant, so it follows the rename automatically, there are no stack names to keep in sync by hand. Describe the dataset The solution ships with two small corpora, bundled in the repository under data/: Financial — A synthetic Octank Financial 10-K (octank_financial_10K.pdf, ~198 KB). Weather — A real, publicly available U.S. Congressional Research Service report on tornadoes ( IF12695 , tornadoes_report.pdf, ~560 KB). About the data:  The financial corpus is synthetic . Octank is a fictional company and the 10-K is model-generated sample data (CC0-licensed). It is n’t  real financial data. The weather corpus is a real, public-domain U.S. Government work and is a Congressional Research Service report, publicly available at sgp.fas.org/crs/misc/IF12695.pdf (works of the U.S. Government aren’t subject to copyright). To use your own data, drop files under data/ and adjust the prefixes in config.py , no other change is required. The two corpora are intentionally distinct, so the agent must route each question to the right knowledge base, the semantic-routing story. Because these are Managed Knowledge Bases, we don’t configure chunking, embedding, or an index: on ingestion, Amazon Bedrock parses each PDF, chunks it, embeds it with its managed model, and indexes it automatically. We use two separate knowledge bases, each exposed through the Gateway as its own retrieval tool, rather than one knowledge base holding both corpora and that choice is deliberate. Giving the agent two named tools makes routing an explicit act of reasoning it can be observed making: the span tree shows which tool it chose for a given question, and the retrieval-quality metrics in Layer 3 stay separable per knowledge base, so financial and weather precision never blur into a single number. A single tool spanning both corpora would collapse that distinction, the routing decision would move inside one index’s ranking, out of view, and every quality signal would be an average across two unrelated domains. Keeping the corpora and their tools separate is what makes the agent’s behavior legible, which is the whole point of the exercise. In CDK, getting the corpora into S3 is a BucketDeployment: s3deploy.BucketDeployment( self, "FinancialCorpus", sources=[s3deploy.Source.asset(str(ROOT / "data" / "financial"))], destination_bucket=self.source_bucket, destination_key_prefix=KbConfig.FINANCIAL_PREFIX, ) BucketDeployment is worth knowing about precisely because the alternative is so tempting: without it, the custom resource that triggers ingestion tends to grow an upload step, and now one resource owns two unrelated jobs. Here it only has to ingest . Managed ingestion scans, chunks, embeds, and indexes each document automatically: one document indexed per knowledge base, zero failures. Figure 3: Managed ingestion results, one document indexed per knowledge base with zero failures Deploy the solution This section walks through deploying the whole solution with one command. After the prerequisites are met, cdk deploy --all provisions all four stacks in CDK’s derived dependency order and threads every cross-stack value through automatically. Prerequisites An AWS account with permissions for Amazon Bedrock, AgentCore (Runtime + Gateway), AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) , CloudWatch, AWS X-Ray , Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) , AWS CodeBuild , Amazon S3, AWS Lambda , and AWS CloudFormation . The agent’s model available in the account (default us.anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5-20251001-v1:0 ). CloudWatch Transaction Search enabled, so OTEL spans land in aws/spans for Layers 5–7. Node.js 18+ and the CDK CLI ( npm install -g aws-cdk ), plus Python 3.13+. The account and region bootstrapped for CDK (cdk bootstrap), once per account/region. No local Docker, the agent image is built by CodeBuild (ARM64). One command To deploy the solution, clone the repository, create a virtual environment, install the dependencies, and run cdk deploy --all . Run the following commands from your terminal: git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/amazon-bedrock-samples.git cd rag/managed-knowledge-bases/07-IaaC/managed-kb-observability-cdk/ python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate pip install -r requirements.txt cdk bootstrap # once per account/region cdk deploy --all The first two commands clone the sample and move into the project directory. The next two create and activate a Python virtual environment and install the CDK app’s dependencies. cdk bootstrap prepares the account and region for CDK (you only need it once per account/region), and cdk deploy --all provisions all four stacks. Account and region come from your AWS profile (CDK_DEFAULT_ACCOUNT / CDK_DEFAULT_REGION), so the app deploys with no edits. Region availability: The managed knowledge base, agentic retrieval (AgenticRetrieveStream), and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (Runtime and Gateway) aren’t available in every AWS Region.
