Before you deploy, confirm that all of these are offered in your target Region, and set ACCOUNT_REGION in config.py accordingly. The default is us-west-2. For current availability, see the Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation and the AWS Regional Services List . There is no deploy script in this version, and that is the point: cdk deploy --all walks the dependency graph it derived from app.py , deploys the four stacks in order, and passes every cross-stack value automatically. The terminal reports each stack as it completes, bmkb-obs-cdk-kb [1/4] (the default PROJECT_NAME), then gateway [2/4], then agent [3/4], then dashboards [4/4] and that order is derived, not declared: it falls out of the construct references between the stacks, so adding a fifth stack that consumes an existing output reorders the deploy on its own. Stack -agent builds the agent container with CodeBuild, so allow roughly 8–10 minutes for that stage. The other three are quick. Each stack prints its outputs on completion, which is where you pick up the knowledge base ids, the Gateway URL, the runtime ARN, and both dashboard URLs. When the deploy finishes, all four stacks are complete. The following screenshot shows the AWS CloudFormation console after a successful cdk deploy --all . Figure 4: AWS CloudFormation console after a successful deploy, with all four stacks CREATE_COMPLETE On the console, all four stacks, kb, gateway, agent, and dashboards, report CREATE_COMPLETE, each with its [n/4] position in the derived dependency order shown in its description. A note on long-running resources Two things in this solution take far longer than the 15-minute ceiling of an AWS Lambda function allows for naive polling: the KB ingestion sync and the CodeBuild image build. The AWS CDK Provider framework handles this with an on_event / is_complete split, where one handler starts the work and a second is polled until it reports done. cr.Provider( self, "IngestSyncProvider", on_event_handler=on_event, # StartIngestionJob, return the job id is_complete_handler=is_complete, # GetIngestionJob, report IsComplete query_interval=Duration.seconds(30), total_timeout=Duration.minutes(30), ) Nothing blocks, the response protocol back to CloudFormation is owned by the framework rather than hand-written into each handler, and the 30-minute budget is a property rather than something to engineer around. Launch and test Open notebooks/01-drive-and-observe.ipynb and run it top to bottom ( pip install -r requirements-notebook.txt first). It reads the stack outputs, then sends topic-specific prompts to the deployed agent, one session per KB , so you can see both the answers and the semantic routing in one place: financial questions are answered from the Octank 10-K and weather questions from the tornadoes report, each routed to the matching AgenticRetrieveStream tool automatically. The notebook discovers everything from the stack outputs, so there is nothing to paste in by hand: # Stack names are derived from the same PROJECT_NAME the CDK app uses, so renaming the # project in config.py cannot leave this notebook pointing at stale stacks. from config import EnvSettings PROJECT = EnvSettings.PROJECT_NAME STACKS = {suffix: f'{PROJECT}-{suffix}' for suffix in ('kb', 'gateway', 'agent', 'dashboards')} def outputs(stack_name): s = cfn.describe_stacks(StackName=stack_name)['Stacks'][0] return {o['OutputKey']: o['OutputValue'] for o in s.get('Outputs', [])} The notebook imports the same config.py the app does, so the two can never disagree about what the stacks are called. The driver sends per-KB prompts through the deployed agent. Financial questions route to the financial KB and weather questions to the weather KB, each with a grounded, cited answer. Figure 5: Per-KB prompts routed to the matching knowledge base, each returning a grounded, cited answer The notebook also computes the reference-free Layer 3 retrieval-quality signals from what the agent actually retrieved and cited, no ground truth, no extra judge, and publishes them to CloudWatch. Figure 6: Reference-free Layer 3 retrieval-quality signals per knowledge base Observe: The seven-layer dashboards The two dashboards are where the seven layers become visible. The stack creates both dashboards, and driving traffic populates them. The following screenshot shows the two dashboards as they appear in the CloudWatch console. Figure 7: The two dashboards in the CloudWatch console, end-to-end agentic observability and per-KB observability Both dashboards appear in the CloudWatch console: one for end-to-end agentic observability and one for per-KB observability (BMKB, Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base). The rest of this section walks through what each layer shows. In this version the dashboards are built from typed objects rather than a JSON string. A metric is a Metric, a widget is a GraphWidget, and the layout is a list of Rows: cw.GraphWidget( title="L4 — Gateway metrics (MCP)", width=12, height=6, period=PERIOD, statistic="Sum", left=[ self._gateway_metric("Invocations", gateway_arn, "tools/call Invocations"), self._gateway_metric("SystemErrors", gateway_arn, "SystemErrors"), self._gateway_metric("UserErrors", gateway_arn, "UserErrors"), self._gateway_metric("Throttles", gateway_arn, "Throttles"), ], ) The practical benefit isn’t fewer lines, dashboards_stack.py runs to 400 lines, more than the equivalent DashboardBody JSON would. It is that a misspelled property or an invalid widget combination fails at cdk synth , on your laptop, in about a second. The same mistake inside a DashboardBody string deploys successfully and renders as a broken widget on the AWS Management Console, where you find it by looking at it. Because a Row accepts any widget, the documentation is part of the layout rather than a wiki page that drifts. Each dashboard interleaves TextWidgets with the graphs: [cw.TextWidget(width=24, height=7, markdown=self._l3_explainer())], [ self._quality_widget("L3 · Financial KB — agentic quality (reference-free, 0–1)", fin_id), self._quality_widget("L3 · Weather KB — agentic quality (reference-free, 0–1)", wx_id), ], _l3_explainer() returns a markdown table defining each ratio and how to read it, so the widget that explains grounded_coverage ships in the same commit as the widget that plots it, and a reader who opens the dashboard cold doesn’t need to guess what a reference-free metric is. Dashboard A — agentic observability (end to end). The board opens with an explainer of how each layer counts a different thing (for N queries you’ll see ~ N agent invocations, ~2 N retrievals, ~3 N LLM calls, and ~5 N Gateway MCP operations, the agentic loop made visible), then shows KB metrics (L1), Gateway metrics and latency (L4), token usage (L6), and because the agent uses AgenticRetrieveStream, which returns a synthesized, cited answer rather than per-chunk scores, the reference-free Layer 3 quality signals, defined inline and plotted per KB. On Dashboard A, the Layer 3 reference-free quality signals are plotted per knowledge base. First, the financial KB. The following chart plots its retrieval_utilization, grounded_coverage, and duplicate_rate. Figure 8: Financial KB Layer 3 quality, plotting retrieval utilization, grounded coverage, and duplicate rate The weather KB shows the same three signals, tracked separately so the two domains never blur into one number. Figure 9: Weather KB Layer 3 quality, tracked separately from the financial KB The two charts plot retrieval_utilization, grounded_coverage, and duplicate_rate for the financial KB (left) and the weather KB (right), so each knowledge base’s retrieval quality stays separable rather than averaged into one number. Dashboard B — per-KB (BMKB) observability. The operational signals that also determine spend, per KB: index size (from S3 source bytes), retrieve volume, agentic tool-calls, session token usage, and generation token usage by model, each with an inline explanation. The following screenshots show Dashboard B’s four metric widgets, populated after a run. The first widget reports index size, derived from S3 source bytes, per knowledge base. Figure 10: Dashboard B index size per knowledge base, derived from Amazon S3 source bytes The second widget counts retrieve calls per knowledge base. Figure 11: Dashboard B retrieve-call count per knowledge base The third widget counts agentic tool-calls through the Gateway. This one is shared across both KBs rather than split. Figure 12: Dashboard B agentic tool-call count through the AgentCore Gateway, shared across both knowledge bases The fourth widget reports session token usage per knowledge base. Figure 13: Dashboard B session token usage per knowledge base The four widgets show index size (from S3 source bytes), retrieve-call volume, agentic tool-calls through the Gateway, and session token usage. Each is broken out per knowledge base except the Gateway tool-call count, which is shared across both. One dimension detail is worth calling out, because the typed API won’t catch it for you: the AWS/Bedrock/KnowledgeBases namespace expects a prefixed id, knowledge-base/ , while the solution’s own BMKB/* namespaces use the bare id. Both are only strings as far as CDK is concerned. # L1 — AWS/Bedrock/KnowledgeBases wants the prefixed form. dimensions_map={"Operation": "Retrieve", "KnowledgeBaseId": f"knowledge-base/{kb_id}"} # BMKB/* — our own namespaces use the bare id. dimensions_map={"KnowledgeBaseId": kb_id} Layer 5: The span tree Layer 5 is the raw OTEL span tree in aws/spans, and it is the layer that shows you the agentic loop directly. It is worth reading carefully, because the nesting isn’t obvious: one LLM call produces three spans. The Strands invoke_agent span wraps the turn, an internal chat span wraps the model call, and a chat span of kind CLIENT is the actual call, and all three repeat the same gen_ai.usage.* token attributes. The following screenshot shows the span tree in aws/spans, with the three-span nesting visible in the top rows. Figure 14: Layer 5 span tree in aws/spans, showing the three-span nesting of a single LLM call Reading the top three rows: an invoke_agent Strands Agents aggregate, then an internal chat span, then a CLIENT chat span, all reporting an identical 7,299 input and 268 output tokens. That is the same LLM call appearing at three levels of the tree, which is why aggregation needs care. That structure matters the moment you aggregate. To count each LLM call once, filter to the CLIENT leaf: fields attributes.gen_ai.request.model as model, attributes.gen_ai.usage.input_tokens as in_tok, attributes.gen_ai.usage.output_tokens as out_tok | filter ispresent(in_tok) and kind = 'CLIENT' and name like /^chat / | stats sum(in_tok) as input_tokens, sum(out_tok) as output_tokens, count(*) as llm_calls by model Without that filter the same query reports three times the tokens and three times the calls. Applying that CLIENT-leaf filter, the following screenshot shows generation token usage by model with each LLM call counted once. Figure 15: Generation token usage by model, with each LLM call counted once With the filter in place, the run shows 14 LLM calls totaling 60,472 input and 2,709 output tokens. Without it, the same query would report three times the calls and three times the tokens. Evaluate: On-demand and continuous Quality is measured two ways, and both are provisioned by the app. On-demand: The driver notebook calls AgentCore There is no deploy script in this version, and that is the point: (LLM-as-judge) over each session’s spans for built-in evaluators, Correctness, Faithfulness, Tool-Selection Accuracy and publishes the scores to CloudWatch, where they appear as Layer 7 on Dashboard A. The following screenshot shows Layer 7 on Dashboard A: on-demand evaluation scores per knowledge base, with the Layer 5 OTEL span table on the same dashboard. Figure 16: Layer 7 on-demand evaluation scores per knowledge base, beside the Layer 5 span table Layer 7 shows the on-demand evaluation scores per knowledge base, with the Layer 5 OTEL span table alongside, so the scores and the spans that produced them read together on one board. Continuous (online):  The agent stack also provisions an AWS::BedrockAgentCore::OnlineEvaluationConfig that samples live sessions and scores them automatically, no notebook run required. The configuration itself is visible in the Bedrock AgentCore console under Assess → Evaluations → Evaluation configurations . Results land in the log group /aws/bedrock-agentcore/evaluations/results/ , and every score is also published as a CloudWatch metric in the Bedrock-AgentCore/Evaluations namespace, keyed by evaluator name and configuration id, so you can graph the scores or alarm on them without parsing logs. The following screenshot shows the online evaluation configuration in the AgentCore console, under Assess, then Evaluations, then Evaluation configurations. Figure 17: The online evaluation configuration in the AgentCore console, with four built-in evaluators at 100 percent sampling The configuration lists four built-in evaluators, Tool-Selection Accuracy, Faithfulness, Correctness, and Response Relevance, set to 100 percent sampling and shown as ACTIVE and enabled. Because the scores are ordinary CloudWatch metrics, they graph like anything else, no log parsing, and the same widget could carry an alarm. The following screenshot shows those four evaluator scores graphed as ordinary CloudWatch metrics. Figure 18: The four continuous evaluator scores graphed as ordinary CloudWatch metrics The four evaluator scores appear as metrics in the Bedrock-AgentCore/Evaluations namespace, each keyed to the evaluation configuration id and the agent’s service name, so you can graph them or alarm on them without parsing logs. Online results only arrive after a session closes . Scoring runs on the completed session, so the results log group stays empty for roughly the session idle timeout (~30 minutes) after you drive traffic. An empty group right after a run is expected, not a misconfiguration. Each result event carries session.id , so it joins to every other layer. The on-demand path in the notebook has no such wait, which is why both are here. Across the four built-in evaluators on this run, the continuous path scored 1.00 on Correctness, Faithfulness, Response Relevance, and Tool-Selection Accuracy, five scored traces per evaluator, each result carrying a written explanation. Sampling and cost. This app sets SAMPLING_PERCENTAGE = 100 purely for the blog experiment , so every session is scored and the results are immediately visible. This isn’t a production recommendation. Online evaluation invokes an LLM-as-judge per sampled session, so cost scales with the sampling rate and traffic volume. For a real deployment, choose a sampling percentage that fits your quality-monitoring needs and budget, and align the configuration with your organization’s own policies and cost-governance requirements before enabling it. The rate is a single constant, EvalConfig.SAMPLING_PERCENTAGE , in config.py . Clean up When you’re finished, remove the solution so it stops incurring charges, since stored KB data, the agent image in ECR, and the still-active online evaluation all cost money while the stacks sit idle. One command tears everything down: cdk destroy --all CDK deletes the stacks in reverse dependency order on its own, dashboards, then agent, then gateway, then kb: the same graph it derived for the deploy, walked backward. There is no teardown script to keep in agreement with the deploy script, which is one of the more quietly valuable properties of modelling the dependencies once. Two removal behaviors are worth knowing, because both replace hand-written cleanup code: self.source_bucket = s3.Bucket( self, "SourceBucket", removal_policy=RemovalPolicy.DESTROY, auto_delete_objects=True, # replaces a list_object_versions delete loop ) self.repository = ecr.Repository( self, "AgentImageRepo", removal_policy=RemovalPolicy.DESTROY, empty_on_delete=True, # replaces an image-delete loop ) Both are set for sample hygiene, for anything you care about, switch the bucket to RemovalPolicy.RETAIN . The CDK bootstrap stack ( CDKToolkit ) and its staging bucket aren’t removed. They are shared account-wide infrastructure that other CDK apps may depend on. What changed since the single-shot solution Both this post and the 2024 solution are CDK applications in Python, deployed with cdk deploy . The authoring tool is the constant here, what changed is the architecture underneath it, and most of the change is subtraction: Concern 2024: Single-shot RAG This solution Vector store An OpenSearch Serverless collection and index you provision, scale, and pay OCU for None. Type: MANAGED, Amazon Bedrock owns storage and indexing Index lifecycle A custom resource creates the index and waits for it to become searchable Nothing to create Embedding model You select it and grant model access Service-managed by default Stacks 3: KB role → OpenSearch infra → KB + data source 4: kb → gateway → agent → dashboards Retrieval One Retrieve, top-k chunks by vector similarity AgenticRetrieveStream, reranked internally, returns a synthesized cited answer Choosing a knowledge base Not applicable, there is one index The agent routes semantically across two Second look at the corpus Not possible in one shot The agent retrieves again before answering Telemetry None provisioned Seven layers, two dashboards Evaluation Manual: sync, pick a model, ask questions On-demand and continuous, both provisioned Cost floor when idle OCU charges accrue whether or not you query Storage only The trade is real in both directions. A single index answering single-shot questions is cheaper per query, simpler to reason about, and entirely sufficient when one corpus holds the answer. Reach for this design when it doesn’t. The CDK constructs doing the work Four constructs carry most of the weight in this app, and they are worth naming because each replaces something people otherwise hand-write: Provider – For custom resources that outlive the 15-minute ceiling of an AWS Lambda function. The on_event / is_complete split means nothing sleeps in a poll loop, and the response protocol back to CloudFormation is the framework’s job rather than a vendored urllib callback in every handler. BucketDeployment – Uploads the corpora, so the ingestion custom resource only ingests. auto_delete_objects=True and empty_on_delete=True , replace the hand-written list_object_versions and image-delete loops that a stack otherwise needs to be destroyable at all. repository.grant_pull_push(project) – One line for the eight ecr:* actions CodeBuild needs, spelled correctly by construction. And typed dashboards, from the Observe section: Metric / GraphWidget / Row objects instead of a DashboardBody JSON string, which moves an invalid widget combination from “renders broken on the console” to “fails at cdk synth .” Two things CDK doesn’t change, and both are worth knowing before you start: Free-form JSON stays camelCase . connector_parameters and parameter_values are passed through verbatim, so the AWS CDK snake_case to PascalCase conversion does not apply inside them. Keys like bucketName and inclusionPrefixes must be spelled exactly as the API expects, and nothing will tell you otherwise until the resource fails. String-typed values are still strings. The knowledge-base/ versus bare dimension difference from the Observe section is invisible to the type system. Typed constructs check structure , not semantics . Neither is a reason to prefer one tool over the other. They are the boundary of what “typed” buys you, and knowing where that boundary sits is most of what makes CDK pleasant instead of surprising. Conclusion We built a complete enterprise agentic retrieval solution on a Managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base and AgentCore: multi-KB semantic routing, a reasoning agent, seven layers of observability, and both on-demand and continuous evaluation, and deployed all of it as a single AWS CDK application. Two things are worth taking away. The managed knowledge base removed infrastructure rather than adding it: no vector store to provision, no index to create and wait on, no OCU line item accruing while the system sits idle. It is also the knowledge base type that supports agentic retrieval and the AgentCore Gateway connector, as described in the Amazon Bedrock documentation . And once retrieval became agentic, observability stopped being optional. Roughly half of what this app provisions exists to answer what the agent actually did and whether the answer was any good, which isn’t overhead on an agentic system. It’s the part that makes one operable. The CDK authoring model earned its place on the seams. Seven values cross stack boundaries in this architecture, and every one of them is a construct reference rather than an export/import pair, which is also why there’s no deploy script, no teardown script, and no fixed order to remember. From here you can point the data sources at your own corpora, place the agent in a virtual private cloud (VPC), tune the online-evaluation sampling rate to your budget and policies, or add more knowledge bases to the router. To learn more, see the Amazon Bedrock detail page and the Amazon Bedrock documentation . The app, the driver notebook, and the self-contained utilities are all in the accompanying GitHub repository , so you can clone it and deploy your own copy with one command.   About the authors Prabhakar Chandrasekaran Prabhakar is a Senior Technical Account Manager with AWS Enterprise Support. Prabhakar enjoys helping customers build AI and ML solutions on the cloud. He also works with enterprise customers providing proactive guidance and operational assistance, helping them improve the value of their solutions when using AWS. Prabhakar holds eight AWS and seven other professional certifications. With over 23 years of professional experience, Prabhakar was a data engineer and a program leader in the financial services space prior to joining AWS. Siddhant Sahu Siddhant is a Senior Product Manager at AWS, where he leads product development for Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base. He focuses on building and rolling out infrastructure software services that handle multi-modal, multi-lingual enterprise data through fully managed ingestion, parsing and agentic search pipelines, in a cost-efficient, accurate and secure way, leveraging state-of-the-art capabilities such as hybrid search, multi-shot retrieval, tool use and embedding techniques. His work enables thousands of enterprise customers and ISVs to build agents at scale.

content: Added Cloud tasks: Settings > API Configuration has a Local | Cloud toggle when cloud sessions are on. Cloud picks the Cline model new cloud tasks run on, saved separately from your local models. Clicking the model label in a cloud session's composer opens it there. Starting or resuming a cloud sandbox shows a progress card with the repo, branch and steps (start sandbox, clone repository, start agent). It collapses once the agent starts. Changed Cloud sessions hide the Plan/Act toggle and the auto-approve bar instead of showing them disabled. With no model chosen, the Cline provider uses Claude Sonnet 5.5 again, which is back at the top of Cline's recommended list. Model requests retry at most 3 times instead of 5. Kimi K3 now gets max reasoning for Extra High and Max, instead of an xhigh setting it rejects. Refreshed the model catalog. Adds the CommandCode, Reflection, Liquid Inference and Munito AI providers and drops CrofAI, iFlow and Llama. The Cline free list adds Reflection Beam, Nemotron 3.5 Lightning and Laguna S 2.1 and drops Mimo V2.6 Flash and Muse Spark 1.3 Contributor. ClinePass now defaults to Kimi K3.1 Pro and adds MiniMax M3.1 Flash and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017. Default models change for most other providers, mostly to Kimi K3.1 Pro, MiniMax M3.1 Flash or DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017. If you use a provider without pinning a model, expect a different default. Fixed GPT-6 models (such as gpt-6-sol and gpt-6.1-sol ) work on OpenAI and Azure OpenAI-compatible endpoints, and SAP AI Core no longer rejects requests with "Unsupported parameter: 'max_tokens'". Both now get max_completion_tokens . Gemini API keys (the gemini provider) no longer send native Google Search. Free-tier keys failed every turn with a 429 quota error on Gemini 3+, and on Gemini 2.x every Cline tool was dropped. Toggling Plan/Act while a task is starting no longer drops your first prompt, and the session no longer keeps running with the other mode's tools. Disabled rules stay disabled. Starting a command no longer moves keyboard focus into the terminal, so text you're typing in the chat no longer lands in the shell. Cancelling a task or opening another one while Cline is asking a question no longer lets your next message get taken as the answer to the old question. A turn whose connection drops after the model has streamed only reasoning is now retried instead of ending the task. Auto-compaction no longer runs for models with an unknown context limit, and it no longer runs again every few tool calls after the first compaction. ask_question : the model keeps going after you pick an option, and empty answers are rejected. run_commands with an empty command list now returns an error instead of a silent success. On PowerShell, the tool tells the model how quote escaping works and to confirm recursive deletes first. Task header badges wrap instead of hiding the close button, the GitHub connection check no longer flashes a loading indicator, and the Local/Cloud toggle's padding is fixed. Full Changelog : v4.1.25...v4.1.26

content: Starting a session that already has a run in progress now reattaches to the live session instead of replacing its runtime. Before, the original run kept going but couldn't be reached, and its transcript writes landed on a stale snapshot. A start that includes a prompt while a run is in progress is rejected The hub records every client that registered a capability for a session, including clients that join a task that's already running, and sends each request to the first one still connected. If none is left, the request fails quickly with a message the user can act on, instead of waiting forever A turn whose connection drops after the model has streamed only reasoning is now retried, and the partial reasoning is discarded. Turns with text, media or tool calls are still never retried Model requests retry at most 3 times after the first attempt (down from 5). Failed attempts are recorded in Langfuse traces, and cancelled requests are no longer reported as Langfuse errors AI SDK updated to ai 7.0.136 / @ai-sdk/provider-utils 5.0.58. max reasoning now reaches the provider: the gateway no longer turns it into xhigh , and Kimi K3 gets max for Extra High and Max. Empty Anthropic turns are still retried despite the new anthropic.* custom stream parts The gemini provider no longer sends native Google Search. On Gemini 3+, free-tier keys failed every turn with a 429 quota error, and on Gemini 2.x it dropped every Cline tool. Vertex keeps native search Auto-compaction no longer runs when the model's input limit is unknown. Manual and overflow-recovery compaction still work After the first compaction, the size estimate now uses the messages as they are actually sent, with tool results truncated. Before, it overestimated about 7x and compaction ran again every few tool calls Checkpoint diffs read file contents with a single git cat-file --batch process instead of up to two git show processes per file. Workspaces with many untracked files used to spawn thousands of git processes SSH remotes work behind a ProxyJump alias. The connect budget goes from 10s to 30s, the per-command limit to 60s, and tunnel readiness to 40s. When ssh exits mid-upload, its real error is reported instead of EPIPE , and a LocalForward on the alias no longer collides with the tunnel ask_question answers are framed so the model keeps going after a bare choice. Empty answers are rejected, and an answer with only an attachment counts as answered run_commands rejects an empty commands list with a tool error, and its schema now advertises minItems: 1 On PowerShell, the run_commands description explains backtick escaping, single-quoting literal paths, preferring cmdlets over cmd /c , and confirming recursive deletes first Plugin commands run in the active session runtime and the hub. Plugin watches start working again when discovery directories appear Compiled binaries load embedded plugin and dashboard resources straight from the binary, and every declared SDK runtime export is packaged A configured CLINE_PLUGIN_RUNTIME_DIR is resolved to an absolute path When OpenRouter has no match for a Cline recommended model, its capabilities are filled in from the Vercel catalog Desktop cloud session orchestration moved into the hub. session.list reports activeCloudCommands , and the hub isn't replaced while cloud commands are still running Core adds conversation summaries and cloud continuation support Run stall telemetry: agent.run-finished and agent.run-failed carry stall signals from a new RunHealthObserver @cline/ui now ships with the SDK packages on the shared version. It adds a Kbd component and token chips for slash commands and file mentions in AgentComposer Refreshed the model catalog (7,041 → 6,457 models). Adds the Liquid Inference, Munito AI and Munito AI (EU) providers and drops CrofAI, iFlow and Llama. The Cline free list adds Reflection Beam, Nemotron 3.5 Lightning and Laguna S 2.1 and drops Mimo V2.6 Flash and Muse Spark 1.3 Contributor. ClinePass adds Kimi K3.1 Pro (now its default), MiniMax M3.1 Flash and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, and drops Mimo V2.5 and V2.5 Pro. Default models change for 56 other providers, mostly to Kimi K3.1 Pro, MiniMax M3.1 Flash or DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 Full Changelog : sdk/sdk/v0.0.95...sdk/sdk/v0.2.0

The latest version of OpenClaw at the time of this release is 2026.10.6 2026.9.34 Highlights Safer agent file edits: apply_patch now validates an ordered envelope before mutating the workspace, so a later invalid hunk cannot delete files changed by an earlier operation. ( #160409 ) Thanks @masatohoshino , @obviyus , and @RomneyDa . Memory Wiki note preservation: retain human-authored notes when OKF concepts are imported again. Fixes #175700 . title: Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning on Amazon SageMaker AI: A hands-on guide
summary: Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning (MTRL) on Amazon SageMaker AI trains models on the outcome of a whole multi-step task rather than labeled steps. This hands-on guide walks the full pipeline using Wordle: deploying the agent and reward on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, preparing the dataset, training, and evaluating at serving settings.
content: Most fine-tuning teaches a model to produce a better answer to a single prompt. Agentic tasks are different. An agent that files an expense report or triages a support ticket takes a sequence of actions, and each step depends on what came before. There’s rarely one correct sequence to imitate, and the only reliable feedback is whether the whole sequence succeeded. Supervised fine-tuning has no labels for that, and single-turn reinforcement learning cannot credit a decision made three steps before the outcome. Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning (MTRL) on Amazon SageMaker AI trains models on exactly that signal. SageMaker AI sends prompts to an agent you host on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, or on your own infrastructure, such as Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2), or AWS Fargate, through an AWS Lambda forwarder . The example here uses AgentCore. The agent calls the policy model being trained, acts in your environment over as many turns as the task needs, and reports one reward when the episode ends. You don’t specify the right trajectory, only how to score the result. This post uses Wordle , a game in which a player has six tries to guess a hidden five-letter word, as the example. After each guess, every letter turns green if it is in the right position, yellow if it’s in the word but in a different position, and gray if it isn’t in the word. The game suits MTRL because the rules are few, each guess depends on the feedback from the last, and the outcome is scored objectively. Wordle is a teaching example, and frontier models already play it well. In practice, you would use MTRL to make a small, low-cost model good at a multi-step task specific to your business, such as an internal workflow that public models were never trained on. The same pipeline applies to that setting. In our run, MTRL took gpt-oss-20b from a 61 to an 84 percent solve rate on held-out words at its default reasoning effort, and from 15 to 69 percent at the low effort it trained at, for about $339 in training tokens. In this post, we walk through the pipeline end-to-end: deploying the agent and reward to AgentCore, preparing the dataset, training, monitoring in MLflow, and evaluating at serving settings. We also share the reward-design mistakes and training failures we hit. Your datasets, agent, and trained model stay in your AWS account and are not used to train the base models . All code is in the accompanying aws-samples repository . Solution overview The system has two halves. SageMaker AI owns the training job and the policy model. AgentCore hosts the agent, the Wordle environment, and the reward function. The following diagram shows how they connect. Figure 1: MTRL on SageMaker AI, where the training job invokes the AgentCore-hosted agent once per rollout to sample the policy model, play the game, and report a reward For every rollout, the MTRL service invokes the AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with one training row, which holds one secret word. A Strands agent in the runtime calls the policy model through the SageMaker Job Runtime’s OpenAI-compatible endpoint. The model plays up to six guesses through one tool, guess_word , and after each guess the environment returns per-letter feedback and a summary of what is known. When the game ends, the agent returns one reward. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) uses the spread of rewards across several rollouts of the same word to update a Low-Rank Adaptation ( LoRA ) adapter on the policy model. Three design points matter for what follows: The agent and reward live in one place. A single Python file deployed to AgentCore holds the environment, the tool, and the scoring function. The dataset carries only the secret word. The word lists bundled with the agent are built from the open-source SCOWL word lists and are used only for scoring. The reward is outcome-dominant. A solve pays 1.05–1.55 depending on speed, a loss pays -0.5, and never making a valid guess pays -1.5. A small shaping term rewards good strategy within each tier. Supported models and AWS Regions MTRL is serverless: you pick a base model and the service provisions the training and sampling infrastructure. At the time of writing, it supports the following base models, each trained with a LoRA adapter: Base model AWS Regions Amazon Nova 2 Lite US East (N. Virginia) (us-east-1), US West (Oregon) (us-west-2) GPT-OSS-20B US East (N. Virginia) (us-east-1), US West (Oregon) (us-west-2) Gemma 4 31B (instruction-tuned) US West (Oregon) (us-west-2) Qwen 3.6 27B US West (Oregon) (us-west-2) We chose GPT-OSS-20B because it has the lowest per-token price of the four and its reasoning effort is controllable per request. See the MTRL documentation for the current list. Pricing You don’t choose instances or size a cluster. You pay per million tokens in three dimensions, priced by base model: Prefill: input tokens the policy model processes. These accumulate in a multi-turn task, because every turn re-reads the history. Sample: tokens the policy model generates, including reasoning tokens. Train: tokens processed in the backward pass that updates the LoRA adapter. The 100-step run consumed 491.6 million prefill, 159.7 million sample, and 643.3 million train tokens across 105,486 rollouts in 12 hours 40 minutes. At GPT-OSS-20B list prices in the US East (N. Virginia) Region (us-east-1) at the time of writing, that is about $339: Dimension Tokens Price per 1M Cost Prefill 491,616,806 $0.12 $58.99 Sample 159,737,098 $0.30 $47.92 Train 643,308,554 $0.36 $231.59 Total 1,294,662,458 $338.50 The train dimension dominates and scales with trajectory length, so shorter games and less verbose reasoning cut the bill. The AgentCore runtime bills separately for the vCPU and memory the agent uses. For this run, that was about $79, from the runtime’s Amazon CloudWatch usage metrics at us-east-1 list prices. DescribeJob reports the token counts under BillableTokenUsage . See Amazon SageMaker AI pricing for current rates. Prerequisites To follow this walkthrough, you need the following. See also the MTRL prerequisites . Python 3.10 or later, uv, Node 20 or later, and the AgentCore CLI ( npm install -g @aws/agentcore ). See Get started with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for installation and the IAM permissions the CLI needs. botocore 1.43.37 or later, on the machine that launches the job. This is the first version that includes the AgentRFT CreateJob operation. Two AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles, described in Step 1. An Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket in the same Region as the agent. The training job must also run in that Region, because CreateJob rejects a cross-Region runtime ARN. Step 1: Create the IAM roles MTRL uses two roles, and one of them has a trust policy that the general SageMaker AI documentation doesn’t mention. Agent runtime role. agentcore deploy creates this role for you. It trusts bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com and needs the AmazonSageMakerJobRuntimeAccess managed policy, which lets the agent call the policy model and report rewards. The CDK stack in the sample repository attaches this policy automatically. Training job role. You create this one. It must trust job.sagemaker.amazonaws.com with both sts:AssumeRole and sts:TagSession , and it needs the AmazonSageMakerJobFullAccess managed policy. { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [{ "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": {"Service": "job.sagemaker.amazonaws.com"}, "Action": ["sts:AssumeRole", "sts:TagSession"] }] } Note: The trust principal is job.sagemaker.amazonaws.com , not sagemaker.amazonaws.com . With the generic principal, CreateJob fails with “Could not assume role,” and the message names the correct principal only after retries. Step 2: Deploy the agent to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Clone the sample repository , set your account and Region in Wordle/agentcore/ aws-targets.json , and deploy: git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/sample-multi-turn-rl-wordle cd sample-multi-turn-rl-wordle/Wordle agentcore validate agentcore deploy The CLI builds the agent’s dependencies for the runtime’s Linux ARM64 platform, creates the execution role with AmazonSageMakerJobRuntimeAccess attached, and deploys through AWS CloudFormation. We recommend it over uploading a code package on the console, where it’s common to get the roughly 700 MB of compiled dependencies or the policy attachment wrong. Note the runtime ARN in the output for the training job. Figure 2: The Wordle agent runtime in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore console with status Ready The runtime reads two environment variables from agentcore.json . REASONING_EFFORT=low sets reasoning_effort on every request to the policy model. In our evaluation jobs, low effort used 63 to 83 percent fewer sample tokens per game than medium. REASONING_PROMPT_HINT=true also adds “Reasoning: low” to the system prompt, which is how gpt-oss reads the setting in its Harmony chat format. Neither variable gives the model any hint about the secret word. Figure 3: Runtime environment variables showing REASONING_EFFORT set to low The agent is one file, main.py . Simplified, its entrypoint looks like the following. For your own task, you change the task parsing, the tools, and the reward: app = BedrockAgentCoreApp() @app.entrypoint # outermost: starts the HTTP server AgentCore invokes @sagemaker_rft_handler # reports the returned reward to SageMaker AI def handle_rollout(payload): prompt, answer = parse_task(payload["prompt"]) game = WordleGame(answer) @tool def guess_word(guess: str) -> str: """Submit a 5-letter Wordle guess and get feedback.""" return game.guess(guess) agent = Agent(model=build_model(), system_prompt=SYSTEM_PROMPT, tools=[guess_word]) agent(prompt) return {"reward": game.final_reward()} Important: The sagemaker_rft_handler decorator does not start an HTTP server by itself. Wrap it with BedrockAgentCoreApp and @app.entrypoint , with the entrypoint decorator outermost. Without this, every invocation times out after 30 seconds. Step 3: Verify the runtime Before spending GPU time, confirm the whole chain works with a payload shaped like the one the training service sends. The repository includes one as Wordle/ payload.json : { "prompt": "{\"prompt\": \"Guess the 5-letter word\", \"answer\": \"beach\", \"id\": \"smoke-test\"}", "metadata": { "jobArn": "arn:aws:sagemaker:us-east-1:111122223333:job/AgentRFT/smoke-test", "rolloutId": "r1" } } The fake job ARN is expected to fail, and the way it fails is the proof. Put your own account ID into it first: for a job ARN in another account, the service returns a 403 before it checks whether the job exists, which looks like a broken IAM setup. From the Wordle directory, run: ACCOUNT=$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text) sed "s/111122223333/$ACCOUNT/" payload.json > /tmp/payload.json aws bedrock-agentcore invoke-agent-runtime \ --agent-runtime-arn \ --runtime-session-id smoke-test-$(date +%s)000000000000000 \ --payload fileb:///tmp/payload.json /dev/stdout In the runtime’s Amazon CloudWatch logs, you see the agent parse the prompt, authenticate to the Job Runtime endpoint, and receive a 400 error reading “Could not find job.” That failure confirms that parsing, authentication, and error reporting work. The command itself prints {“reward”: -1.5}, because the agent never reached the policy model. A 403 reading “not authorized to access this resource” means the job ARN still names another account. A 30-second timeout instead means the HTTP server is not starting (see the Important note in Step 2). Step 4: Prepare the dataset The MTRL dataset has no target responses, transcripts, or labels. Each row is one task for the agent to attempt. Here are the first three rows of the training file: {"prompt": "{\"prompt\": \"Guess the 5-letter word\", \"answer\": \"riser\", \"id\": \"wordle_train_0000\"}"} {"prompt": "{\"prompt\": \"Guess the 5-letter word\", \"answer\": \"swoon\", \"id\": \"wordle_train_0001\"}"} {"prompt": "{\"prompt\": \"Guess the 5-letter word\", \"answer\": \"dirty\", \"id\": \"wordle_train_0002\"}"} The service reads the prompt column (or the first column) and passes the string to your agent verbatim, without parsing it. We made the string a small JSON object with three fields: prompt: the instruction the agent shows the policy model, identical on every row. answer: the secret word. Only the environment and the reward function use it. The policy model never sees it. id: a row ID for tracing a rollout in the logs back to its source row. The sample repository’s make_dataset.py draws 640 training words (five full batches of 128) and 128 validation words from the answer list with no overlap, so the validation solve rate measures generalization. The service also accepts Apache Parquet, JSON arrays, and CSV. Upload both files to Amazon S3: uv run python make_dataset.py aws s3 cp training-data.jsonl s3:// /wordle-mtrl/train/ aws s3 cp validation-data.jsonl s3:// /wordle-mtrl/validation/ Because the service never inspects the prompt string, a production task can pack a full message list, tool configuration, or reward specification into it. See the MTRL documentation for examples, including how to protect sensitive content in the string. Step 5: Launch the training job The launcher uses the MultiTurnRLTrainer class from the sagemaker-train SDK. Point it at the runtime ARN from Step 2, the role from Step 1, the datasets from Step 4, and an MLflow app for metrics. The MLflow app is required, so if you don’t have one, create it first with aws sagemaker create-mlflow-app : uv run python run_mtrl_training.py \ --model openai-reasoning-gpt-oss-20b \ --agent-runtime-arn \ --role-arn arn:aws:iam:: :role/ \ --train-dataset s3:// /wordle-mtrl/train/training-data.jsonl \ --val-dataset s3:// /wordle-mtrl/validation/validation-data.jsonl \ --s3-output-path s3:// /wordle-mtrl/output/ \ --mlflow-app-arn arn:aws:sagemaker: : :mlflow-app/ The launcher overrides three hyperparameters and leaves every other one at the gpt-oss-20b default. It sets sampling_max_tokens to 8192, the service maximum, because at the default of 4096 gpt-oss often ran out of tokens while reasoning, before its first tool call. It sets max_epochs to 20 and max_steps to 100: 640 rows at the default global_batch_size of 128 is 5 steps per epoch, and with the default group_size of 8, each step plays 1,024 games. The job moves through Starting, Downloading, and Pending before reaching Training. After it’s training, your AgentCore runtime begins receiving rollout invocations. Important: Don’t redeploy the agent while a job is running. Redeploying restarts the runtime, in-flight rollouts see no sampling requests, and the service fails the entire job. Step 6: Monitor training in MLflow The service logs reward, token, and turn statistics at every step and runs validation every val_every steps. The metric to watch is val/reward/pass_at_1 , the fraction of held-out words solved. Every solve scores at least 1.01, so it clears the service’s success_threshold of 1.0 and pass@1 counts it. The following chart is built from this run’s MLflow history: Figure 4: Training curves for the 100-step run, with mean reward per game on the left and validation solve rate on the right Training reward climbs to about +0.57 within 15 steps and holds there. Validation reward stays lower, mostly because of temperature 1.0 versus 0 rather than overfitting (see Step 7). The validation solve rate jumps from 2 to 31 percent in the first 10 steps, then moves between 35 and 48 percent. With 128 words, those swings are mostly noise. We did not test whether more steps help at serving settings. The runtime’s OpenTelemetry traces in CloudWatch record every model turn and tool call. Here is one game the trained model played during an evaluation job (medium effort, temperature 1.0), with the reasoning trimmed. The secret word was PASTE: [model] Reasoning: [...] "CRANE" has 5 distinct letters: C,R,A,N,E. [...] We'll guess "CRANE". Tool call: guess_word(guess="CRANE") [tool] Guess 1/6: CRANE -> C=gray, R=gray, A=yellow, N=gray, E=green Current Knowledge: - Correct Position (Green): _ _ _ _ E - In Word, Wrong Position (Yellow): 'A' (at least 1) - Not in Word (Gray): C, N, R - Guesses Remaining: 5 [model] Reasoning: [...] "ALIVE": ends with E, includes A. Letters not C,N,R. Tool call: guess_word(guess="ALIVE") [tool] Guess 2/6: ALIVE -> A=yellow, L=gray, I=gray, V=gray, E=green [model] Reasoning: [...] So positions not 1 or 3 for A. Positions left: 2,4 for A. [...] We might guess "HASTE"? [...] Tool call: guess_word(guess="HASTE") [tool] Guess 3/6: HASTE -> H=gray, A=green, S=green, T=green, E=green [model] Reasoning: We have the word: _ASTE. [...] "PASTE" is a word. PASTE fits. Also "WASTE" also fits [...] Choose "PASTE" maybe. Tool call: guess_word(guess="PASTE") [tool] Guess 4/6: PASTE --- all green. Correct, you solved it! A trained-model rollout from the AgentCore runtime traces. The model keeps green letters in place, never reuses a gray letter, and uses each yellow letter to rule out positions, though nothing in the training data showed it how. Step 7: Evaluate the trained model at serving settings When the job completes, its page in SageMaker AI Studio shows the status and the model package group that holds the trained model. DescribeJob , with JobCategory set to AgentRFT , returns the output model package ARN and the billable token counts. Figure 5: The completed training job in SageMaker AI Studio on the Jobs, Training, Multi-turn RL tab An evaluation job ( JobCategory set to AgentRFTEvaluation ) plays your evaluation prompts through the same AgentCore runtime and reward, on the base model or the trained package, and logs eval/reward/pass_at_1 to MLflow. Unlike training validation, you can set the temperature. The repository’s launcher runs evaluations back to back, because the default quota allows one evaluation job at a time ( you can request an increase ): uv run python run_mtrl_eval.py --runs base:1.0 trained:1.0 \ --model-package-arn \ --agent-runtime-arn \ --role-arn arn:aws:iam:: :role/ \ --dataset s3:// /wordle-mtrl/validation/validation-data.jsonl \ --s3-output-path s3:// /wordle-mtrl/eval/ \ --mlflow-app-arn arn:aws:sagemaker: : :mlflow-app/ Figure 6: Reasoning effort and sampling temperature at each stage, where the training job fixes validation at temperature 0 and the deployed effort while evaluation jobs let you choose Each 128-word evaluation took four to seven minutes. Reasoning effort comes from the agent’s environment variables, so to change it you edit REASONING_EFFORT , redeploy, and evaluate. We evaluated both models at low and medium effort and at temperature 0 and 1.0: Figure 7: Base model versus trained model under four decoding settings, with solve rate on the left and mean reward per game on the right The gray segment of each bar is the base model and the blue segment is the gain from training. The low-effort, temperature-0 pair is the training job’s validation at steps 0 and 100. The medium-effort, temperature-1.0 trained result is the mean of two runs (80 and 88 percent). At temperature 0, both models often end the game without a solve, at either effort. With sampling on, medium effort adds 15 points for the trained model and 46 for the base model. The adapter adds 14–54 points in every setting, so what training taught transfers across settings. The training job’s own validation curve in MLflow told a different story: it peaked at 48 percent at step 90 and ended at 37 percent, scored at temperature 0. The hyperparameters reference recommends temperature 0 for evaluation because greedy decoding makes curves deterministic and comparable across runs. We report temperature 1.0 because that’s how we serve the model. At medium effort and temperature 1.0, the trained model solves 84 percent of held-out words, up from 61 percent for the base model. Tip: Evaluate at the settings you will serve at. The training curve says this adapter ends at 37 percent. At serving settings it solves 84 percent. The evaluation jobs that show this cost about $1.20 in tokens and took about an hour. Step 8: Clean up Training and evaluation jobs stop billing when they complete, but the AgentCore runtime, its IAM role, the MLflow app, and the S3 objects persist. From the project directory: # 1. Agent runtime and its execution role. remove all resets the project config; # the next deploy sees the empty state and tears down the deployed resources. cd sample-multi-turn-rl-wordle/Wordle agentcore remove all agentcore deploy # 2. MLflow app aws sagemaker delete-mlflow-app --arn arn:aws:sagemaker: : :mlflow-app/ # 3. Datasets, job output, and evaluation output aws s3 rm s3:// /wordle-mtrl/ --recursive Because agentcore remove all rewrites the files under agentcore/ , run git checkout -- agentcore/ if you want to redeploy later. Deleting the AgentCore-Wordle-default CloudFormation stack removes the same resources and leaves the files alone. The training job role and the model packages are not billed. Deep dive: Designing the reward Our reward needed one revision, and the mistake is a common one. The first design summed the per-guess scoring from the wordle-lora-rl project over the whole game. That scoring works there because each guess is an independent training sample. Summed into one reward per game, it produced two inversions we found only by reading traces: A lost game paid positive reward. Six turns of bonuses added up to about +0.49. Solving on turn 1 scored below solving on turn 3. A first-guess solve earned +0.99 and a third-guess solve earned +1.61, because the extra turns collected more bonuses. The fix separates a dominant outcome term from a small, bounded shaping term: reward = outcome + w * clip(shaping, -1, 1), w = 0.04 if solved, else 0.15 The outcome term is set entirely by how the game ended: Outcome Value Solved on guess n 1.05 + 0.5 * (6 – n) / 5, so 1.55 on guess 1 down to 1.05 on guess 6 Played all six guesses, unsolved -0.5 Never made a valid guess -1.5 The shaping term is that per-guess scoring, summed over the game: Penalties for contradicting a known green, yellow, or gray letter, for repeating a guess, and for words outside the dictionary. An entropy bonus for a strong opening word. Bonuses for trying new letters and for shrinking the set of remaining possibilities. The sum is clipped to [-1, 1] and scaled by 0.04 for a solve and 0.15 for a loss, so it separates games with the same outcome but never moves a game into another tier. With typical shaping values: Scenario Reward Solve on guess 1 +1.550 Solve on guess 3 +1.375 Solve on guess 6 +1.069 Lost after six guesses -0.427 Never made a valid guess -1.500 A faster solve now always beats a slower one, every solve beats every loss, and never playing is the worst outcome. Our first fix used a single weight of 0.15, which let a guess-3 solve with full shaping (+1.45) outscore a guess-2 solve with the minimum (+1.25). Adjacent guess counts are 0.1 apart, so a smaller solve weight of 0.04 removes the overlap, and the worst solve (+1.01) still clears the 1.0 success threshold. Shaping still matters because GRPO learns from reward variance within a group, so two lost games that differ in clue consistency still teach the model something. As the SageMaker AI documentation advises, start with an outcome-based reward, add shaping sparingly, and check the reward on real trajectories. Deep dive: What went wrong, in the order you will hit it Each of these cost at least one training run. Bearer tokens under concurrency. Minting a token with a fresh botocore session per call starved the credential provider at 32 concurrent rollouts, and caching tokens for an hour returned 403 errors as credentials rotated. The fix is one self-refreshing session, a short cache, and a re-sign on 403. A rollout that never reaches the policy model fails the whole job. When every model call in a rollout failed authentication, the service ended the job with “No sampling requests were received.” Returning an error status fails it too, so always return a reward. A game where the model is sampled but never makes a valid guess is fine: it scores -1.5, and the 100-step run had 51 of them in about 105,000 rollouts. Tool calls drift into plain text. At too high a learning rate, the model wrote tool calls as text, every rollout got the same floor reward, and the gradient vanished. The agent now recovers guesses from raw text with a small formatting penalty. The plateau. Training reward stopped rising after about step 15 and validation stopped improving after about step 30, though at temperature 0 validation understates the model (Step 7). A curriculum that seeds games with prior guesses, or more rollouts per word than the default group_size of 8, is what we would try next. Conclusion MTRL on SageMaker AI trains a model on the outcome of a whole episode. That fits agentic tasks, where the right trajectory is unknown and only the result can be scored. We used a single episode-level reward. When intermediate steps can be scored too, MTRL also accepts one reward per turn through the UpdateReward API . In this post, an open-weight 20B model reached an 84 percent solve rate at serving settings, up from 61 percent, for about $339 in training tokens and about $79 in AgentCore runtime usage. The 37 percent the training curve reports is an artifact of how the training job scores validation, so evaluate at the settings you will serve at. The same pipeline applies to internal procedures, tools, and workflows that public models were never trained on. To get started, clone the sample repository , follow the preceding steps, and run the smoke test in Step 3 before committing GPU time. For the underlying APIs, see the SageMaker AI MTRL documentation .   About the authors Daniel Quang Daniel is a Solutions Architect on the Frontier AI Startups team at AWS, where he helps the world’s largest and most strategic generative AI startups scale their infrastructure on the cloud. He holds a PhD in Computer Science from the University of California, Irvine, with a research focus on machine learning and bioinformatics. Hadrien Almela Hadrien is a Senior Frontier AI Account Manager in the AWS Startup team, helping top AI startups build technical integrations and global go-to-market (GTM) partnerships. He has eight years of experience in the startup landscape. Vinay Bhat Vinay is the Head of Solutions Architecture for Frontier AI at AWS, where he leads a team of technologists helping foundation model labs and AI-native startups build, train, and scale their models and applications on AWS. He brings more than 20 years of experience building technical teams across AWS, Google Cloud, and high-growth startups.
