title: Orchestrating SageMaker AI endpoint auto scaling with AWS CDK
summary: Updating a SageMaker AI endpoint that has Application Auto Scaling registered makes AWS CloudFormation and AWS CDK deployments fail. This post shows how to build a reusable AWS CDK construct with CloudFormation custom resources that deregisters and re-registers auto scaling automatically, so you can update the endpoint and its scaling in a single deployment.
content: Updating the Amazon Sagemaker AI real-time endpoint configuration (changing the instance type, instance count, or environment variables) causes deployments through AWS CloudFormation or the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) to fail. SageMaker AI requires you to deregister the scalable target before updating the endpoint, but when you deregister it, CloudFormation can’t track the AWS Application Auto Scaling resources. In this post, we show you how to use a reusable CDK construct with AWS CloudFormation custom resources to orchestrate deregister and register auto scaling automatically during endpoint updates. You can update your endpoint configuration and auto scaling parameters in a single deployment without manual intervention. Why this problem occurs When you deploy a SageMaker AI endpoint with native CloudFormation auto scaling resources, then change the endpoint configuration and redeploy, several failure modes emerge. The specific failure depends on what you change and how you work around the issue. Changing the endpoint configuration with auto scaling registered CloudFormation tries to update the endpoint while the scalable target is still registered. SageMaker AI rejects the update with the following error: The variant(s) "[AllTraffic]" must be deregistered as scalable targets with Application Auto Scaling before they can be removed or have their instance type updated. SageMaker AI blocks the endpoint update before CloudFormation reaches the auto scaling resources. Manually deregistering auto scaling, then changing only the endpoint configuration If you deregister the scalable target through the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) and redeploy with only an endpoint configuration change, the deployment succeeds. However, CloudFormation doesn’t register auto scaling even though it is in the CloudFormation template. Because the auto scaling parameters in the CloudFormation template haven’t changed, CloudFormation doesn’t register the scalable target or re-apply the scaling policy. The endpoint is now running without auto scaling, and there is no error to indicate anything went wrong. Manually deregistering auto scaling, then changing auto scaling parameters If you deregister the scalable target through the AWS CLI and redeploy with auto scaling parameter changes, CloudFormation tries to update the ScalableTarget resource that no longer exists: Resource of type 'AWS::ApplicationAutoScaling::ScalableTarget' with identifier 'endpoint/ /variant/AllTraffic|sagemaker:variant:DesiredInstanceCount|sagemaker' was not found. This failure is notable because the rollback also fails (UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED), leaving the stack in a broken state that requires manual intervention in the CloudFormation console to recover. Solution overview You can use this CDK construct to replace the native AWS::ApplicationAutoScaling::ScalableTarget and AWS::ApplicationAutoScaling::ScalingPolicy CloudFormation resources with three custom resources. These custom resources deregister and register auto scaling around the endpoint update with explicit dependency ordering, enforced by node.add_dependency calls in CDK. The full sequence is: Deregister (custom resource): Removes the scalable target before the endpoint update begins. On first deploy, no scalable target exists yet, so the handler handles the error gracefully and continues. Endpoint update (CDK-managed): CDK updates the endpoint resource normally, swapping to the new endpoint configuration. Register Scalable Target (custom resource): Waits for the endpoint to reach InService status, then registers the scalable target. Attach Scaling Policy (custom resource): Waits for the scalable target to be queryable, then applies the target tracking policy. Figure 1: Custom resource orchestration of SageMaker AI endpoint auto scaling around a CDK-managed endpoint update. Register Scalable Target and Attach Scaling Policy use the CDK provider’s asynchronous completion pattern. Each custom resource has an on_event handler that returns immediately and an is_complete handler. The provider’s waiter re-invokes the is_complete handler on an interval (every 30 seconds) until its readiness check passes. The provider’s total_timeout (1 hour for Register Scalable Target, 15 minutes for Attach Scaling Policy) bounds the wait, so it isn’t limited by the timeout of any single Lambda invocation. A ConfigHash property on each custom resource forces CloudFormation to re-invoke the Lambda functions whenever a configuration value changes. The endpoint configuration and auto scaling parameters are defined together because a single ConfigHash drives the auto scaling orchestration. While the construct defines three custom resources, the deployed stack contains more than three Lambda functions. Each custom resource is backed by a CDK cr.Provider , and the provider framework generates its own helper Lambda functions. A synchronous provider (Deregister) adds one framework function. An asynchronous provider (Register Scalable Target and Attach Scaling Policy) adds three ( onEvent , isComplete , and onTimeout ) plus an AWS Step Functions state machine that drives the waiter. As a result, the deployed stack contains three custom resources, two Step Functions state machines, and twelve Lambda functions. Five of the resources hold the construct’s own handler code (one for Deregister, and an on_event and is_complete pair for each asynchronous resource), with the remaining seven generated by the provider framework. You don’t write or maintain the framework-generated functions, but they are present in the stack and worth accounting for when you review the deployed resources. Walkthrough In this walkthrough, you deploy a SageMaker AI endpoint with auto scaling using the provided example stack, then verify that configuration updates work correctly. The walkthrough includes the following steps: Clone the repository and install dependencies. Configure your endpoint and auto scaling settings. Deploy and verify. Test an update. The source code is available in the linked GitHub repository . Prerequisites For this walkthrough, you need the following: An AWS account with permissions for Amazon SageMaker AI, AWS Lambda, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), Application Auto Scaling, and Amazon CloudWatch. AWS CDK v2 installed. Python 3.12 or later. uv for Python dependency management. A SageMaker AI model artifact in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and a container image in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR), or a SageMaker AI built-in algorithm container. Clone the repository and install dependencies Clone the repository: git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/sample-sagemaker-endpoint-autoscaling.git cd sample-sagemaker-endpoint-autoscaling Install dependencies: uv sync Configure your endpoint and auto scaling settings The endpoint and auto scaling settings are defined together in config/ config.yaml because a single config_hash drives the auto scaling orchestration. A change to either section triggers the full sequence. Edit config/ config.yaml with your values: endpoint: endpoint_name: "my-model-endpoint" image: "123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/my-model:latest" model_data_url: "s3://my-bucket/models/model.tar.gz" instance_type: "ml.m5.large" initial_instance_count: 1 environment: {} autoscaling: min_capacity: 1 max_capacity: 10 target_value: 100 scale_in_cooldown: 600 scale_out_cooldown: 120 The endpoint parameters map to the SageMaker AI CreateModel and CreateEndpointConfig APIs. The auto scaling parameters map to the Application Auto Scaling RegisterScalableTarget and PutScalingPolicy APIs. Deploy and verify Bootstrap your AWS environment if you haven’t already: uv run cdk bootstrap Deploy the stack: uv run cdk deploy InferenceStack CloudFormation creates the SageMaker AI model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint, then runs the three custom resources in sequence to register auto scaling. Verify that the deployment registered the scalable target: aws application-autoscaling describe-scalable-targets --service-namespace sagemaker --resource-ids endpoint/my-model-endpoint/variant/AllTraffic Verify that the deployment applied the scaling policy: aws application-autoscaling describe-scaling-policies --service-namespace sagemaker --resource-id endpoint/my-model-endpoint/variant/AllTraffic Test an update Change a value in config/ config.yaml , for example, update the instance type from ml.m5.large to ml.m5.xlarge , and redeploy: uv run cdk deploy InferenceStack After the deployment completes, verify that auto scaling is still registered and has the updated values: aws application-autoscaling describe-scalable-targets --service-namespace sagemaker --resource-ids endpoint/my-model-endpoint/variant/AllTraffic Integrating with an existing stack Use the example stack if you’re starting fresh or want a reference implementation. Use the construct directly if you already have a CDK stack with SageMaker AI resources. To integrate with an existing stack, copy the sagemaker_autoscaling/constructs/ directory into your project and add the construct alongside your endpoint resources: import json from sagemaker_autoscaling.constructs.sagemaker_autoscaling_construct import ( AutoscalingConfig, SagemakerAutoscalingConstruct, SagemakerAutoscalingProps, ) # Both endpoint and auto scaling values must be in config_hash so that # a change to either triggers the auto scaling orchestration. config_hash = json.dumps({ "endpoint": { "image": "123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/my-model:latest", "modelDataUrl": "s3://my-bucket/models/model.tar.gz", "instanceType": "ml.m5.large", "initialInstanceCount": 1, }, "autoscaling": { "minCapacity": 1, "maxCapacity": 10, "targetValue": 100, "scaleInCooldown": 600, "scaleOutCooldown": 120, }, }) SagemakerAutoscalingConstruct( self, "Autoscaling", props=SagemakerAutoscalingProps( endpoint=your_endpoint, # your CfnEndpoint autoscaling=AutoscalingConfig( min_capacity=1, max_capacity=10, target_value=100, scale_in_cooldown=600, scale_out_cooldown=120, ), config_hash=config_hash, ), ) How the construct works This section walks through the key implementation details of SagemakerAutoscalingConstruct . Deregister The Deregister custom resource calls deregister_scalable_target before the endpoint update. It handles ObjectNotFoundException for first deployments where no scalable target exists: def handler(event, context): resource_id = event["ResourceProperties"]["ResourceId"] if event["RequestType"] in ("Create", "Update"): try: client.deregister_scalable_target( ServiceNamespace="sagemaker", ResourceId=resource_id, ScalableDimension="sagemaker:variant:DesiredInstanceCount", ) except client.exceptions.ObjectNotFoundException: pass # No scalable target on first deploy return {"PhysicalResourceId": f"deregister-{resource_id}"} The dependency is established in CDK: props.endpoint.node.add_dependency(deregister) Register Scalable Target Even though CloudFormation treats the endpoint resource as complete once the update is accepted, the scalable target can only be registered after the endpoint reaches InService . Rather than block a single Lambda invocation on that wait, Register Scalable Target uses the provider’s asynchronous completion pattern. The on_event handler returns immediately, and the provider’s waiter re-invokes the is_complete handler on query_interval until the endpoint is InService . The provider’s total_timeout (1 hour) bounds the wait, not the timeout of any single Lambda invocation: def handler(event, context): props = event["ResourceProperties"] resource_id = props["ResourceId"] endpoint_name = resource_id.split("/")[1] if event["RequestType"] == "Delete": return {"IsComplete": True} status = sm_client.describe_endpoint(EndpointName=endpoint_name)["EndpointStatus"] if status == "Failed": raise Exception("Endpoint in Failed state") if status != "InService": return {"IsComplete": False} as_client.register_scalable_target( ServiceNamespace="sagemaker", ResourceId=resource_id, ScalableDimension="sagemaker:variant:DesiredInstanceCount", MinCapacity=int(props["MinCapacity"]), MaxCapacity=int(props["MaxCapacity"]), ) return {"IsComplete": True} On stack deletion, the on_event handler deregisters the scalable target to clean up. Attach Scaling Policy There is a brief window after RegisterScalableTarget returns where the target isn’t yet queryable. Attach Scaling Policy uses the same asynchronous completion pattern: the on_event handler returns immediately, and the is_complete handler reports completion only once the scalable target is queryable, at which point it applies the policy. The provider’s total_timeout (15 minutes) bounds the wait: def handler(event, context): props = event["ResourceProperties"] resource_id = props["ResourceId"] if event["RequestType"] == "Delete": return {"IsComplete": True} resp = client.describe_scalable_targets( ServiceNamespace="sagemaker", ResourceIds=[resource_id], ScalableDimension="sagemaker:variant:DesiredInstanceCount", ) if not resp.get("ScalableTargets"): return {"IsComplete": False} client.put_scaling_policy( PolicyName=props["PolicyName"], ServiceNamespace="sagemaker", ResourceId=resource_id, ScalableDimension="sagemaker:variant:DesiredInstanceCount", PolicyType="TargetTrackingScaling", TargetTrackingScalingPolicyConfiguration=json.loads(props["ScalingPolicyConfig"]), ) return {"IsComplete": True} On stack deletion, the on_event handler deletes the scaling policy to clean up. Cleaning up To avoid incurring future charges, delete the resources: uv run cdk destroy InferenceStack This removes the SageMaker AI endpoint, endpoint configuration, model, Lambda functions, IAM roles, Amazon CloudWatch alarms created by the target tracking scaling policy, and deregisters the scalable target. Conclusion In this post, we showed you how to use a reusable CDK construct to deregister and register auto scaling automatically to orchestrate SageMaker AI endpoint updates. The construct uses three CloudFormation custom resources with explicit dependency ordering and a ConfigHash property to keep auto scaling intact across deployments. To get started, clone the sample-sagemaker-endpoint-autoscaling repository and follow the setup instructions. The repository includes an example stack you can deploy directly, or you can integrate the construct into your existing CDK stack. For more information about Application Auto Scaling for SageMaker AI, see Automatically scale Amazon SageMaker AI models . For more information about CloudFormation custom resources, see Custom resources in the AWS CloudFormation User Guide . About the author Lauren Eterno Lauren is an Associate Delivery Consultant with Amazon Web Services specializing in AI/ML. She works with customer teams to design, build, deploy, and scale machine learning and generative AI solutions. She holds a B.S. in Data Science & Analytics and an M.S. in Computer Science from Case Western Reserve University.

title: Visualize points and routes with GeoJSON in Amazon Quick Sight layer maps
summary: Amazon Quick Sight layer maps now support Point and LineString geometry from the same GeoJSON workflow, so you can plot store locations and the routes between them. This post covers the dataset and GeoJSON structure layer maps require, when to choose points or lines, and techniques for viewport control, layering geometries, and dynamic GeoJSON updates.
content: With Amazon Quick Sight layer maps, you can now plot points and routes, like store locations across a city or flights leaving an airport. Geospatial maps help businesses spot patterns that are tied to location, like how a region is performing or where customers are concentrated. Amazon Quick Sight supports this with multiple map types, including point maps, filled maps, and layer maps. When layer maps first launched , you could upload a GeoJSON file to draw custom shape layers, such as sales territories or districts, and join those shapes to a dataset. That handled regions and boundaries well, but it didn’t cover the individual locations inside them or the routes running between them. Layer maps now support two more geometry types from the same GeoJSON workflow: Point and LineString . Points mark specific locations, such as individual store or facility sites. A LineString traces the route between locations, like a delivery path or a flight between airports. Amazon Quick Sight , the business intelligence (BI) capability of Amazon Quick , is a unified BI service. It delivers modern interactive dashboards, natural language querying, pixel-perfect reports, machine learning (ML) insights, and embedded analytics at scale. Amazon Quick brings together AI agents for business insights, research, and automation in one integrated experience, helping you work smarter and faster while maintaining security and access policies. In this post, we walk through the dataset and GeoJSON structure that layer maps require. We also explain how points and lines work in a layer map visual and when to choose each. Finally, we cover advanced techniques for controlling the viewport, layering geometries, and updating GeoJSON files programmatically. Dataset structure considerations A layer map gets its shapes from a GeoJSON file and its metrics from a Quick Sight dataset, and a shared key joins the two. How you structure each one determines what the map can show. This section covers what you need before you start and how a GeoJSON file is organized. Prerequisites The following are the prerequisites that you need before creating a layer map in Quick Sight: A GeoJSON file describing your geometry. A Quick Sight dataset holding the metrics and dimensions. A join key shared between the Quick Sight dataset and the GeoJSON file. The GeoJSON file must be saved in .geojson format, with a maximum supported file size of 100 MB. Structure of the GeoJSON file GeoJSON is a JSON-based format for describing geographic features such as points and lines. { "type": "FeatureCollection", "features": [{ "type": "Feature", "geometry": { "type": "Point", "coordinates": [88.4, 22.6] }, "properties": { "prop0": "value0" } }, { "type": "Feature", "geometry": { "type": "LineString", "coordinates": [ [88.2, 22.4], [88.9, 23.1], [89.5, 22.8], [90.1, 23.6] ] }, "properties": { "prop0": "value0" } }] } The structure of the file is as follows: FeatureCollection is the whole file. It has a type of FeatureCollection and a features array. Feature is a single map element. It carries a geometry (the shape) and a properties object, which holds the join key. geometry has a type (Point, LineString, or Polygon) and its coordinates . The coordinates hold a single [longitude, latitude] position for a Point , and an ordered list of positions for a LineString . Configuring the Quick Sight dataset and its GeoJSON In Quick Sight, when you configure a layer in a layer map visual, there are two primary settings to consider. The first is the Geometry type to visualize , which sets which geometry from the GeoJSON file renders: Points, Lines, or Polygons. A layer renders one geometry type at a time, so when a file mixes types like the preceding example, only Features of the selected type appear on the map. The second is matching the Shape file key field to the Dataset key field , which links each Feature in the GeoJSON to a row in your Quick Sight dataset. The field names don’t need to be identical, but the values do. The following two examples show this end to end, first a LineString layer and then a Point layer. Example: LineString layer Consider example data showing a flight from JFK to a destination city like Los Angeles. The GeoJSON structure for a single datapoint is configured as follows: { "type": "Feature", "geometry": { "type": "LineString", "coordinates": [ [-73.7781, 40.6413], [-85.5627, 40.6407], [-97.1415, 39.4569], [-108.1612, 37.1753], [-118.4085, 33.9416] ] }, "properties": { "route_id": "JFK-LAX" } } The corresponding row in the Quick Sight dataset contains the following information: Figure 1: Dataset row for the JFK-LAX route, keyed by route_id The route_id field is used to join the Quick Sight dataset with the GeoJSON file. The GeoJSON holds one such feature per route, and the dataset one row per route. The Geometry type to visualize is set to Lines. Figure 2: The JFK-LAX route drawn as a LineString layer Example: Point layer Consider example data showing a retail store location like Long Island City. The GeoJSON structure for a single datapoint is configured as follows: { "type": "Feature", "geometry": { "type": "Point", "coordinates": [-73.9490, 40.7447] }, "properties": { "store_id": "S-109" } } The corresponding row in the Quick Sight dataset contains the following information: Figure 3: Dataset row for a store, keyed by store_id The store_id field is used to join the Quick Sight dataset with the GeoJSON file. The GeoJSON holds one such feature per store, and the dataset one row per store. The Geometry type to visualize is set to Points. Figure 4: A store plotted as a Point layer Lines on layer map visuals Layer map visuals now support LineString geometry, connecting an ordered list of coordinates into a single path. As covered in the data structure section, each route is one feature, and its coordinates are the ordered positions the map connects in sequence. Use lines when the relationship between locations is what you want to show, such as flight paths, delivery routes, shipping lanes, or pipeline segments. The visual draws each path from the coordinates in your GeoJSON file rather than generating it from your data at load time. A field from your joined dataset can determine the line color encoding, so you can group routes by whatever that field represents. In addition to color, you can customize lines with width and opacity controls to adjust visual prominence and clarity on the map. The join key in the GeoJSON properties object ties each LineString to the dataset row behind its tooltip and color. For example, an airport operations team might map the flights leaving New York (JFK) on a given day. The GeoJSON file holds one LineString per route, keyed by a route ID that joins to the dataset. Each line starts at JFK and ends at its destination, such as Los Angeles, Chicago, or Miami. The dataset supplies the origin, destination, and carrier that show up in the tooltip. Figure 5: Flights leaving JFK drawn as LineString routes to multiple destinations Points on layer map visuals Amazon Quick Sight offers a native point map visual type that geocodes location names automatically and refreshes with your SPICE schedule or Direct Query connection. It supports dynamic point sizing, color encoding, and point styles such as cluster points and heatmap density gradients. It works best with data that changes frequently and where you want the map to respond to those changes visually. With the added support for GeoJSON point layers in layer map visuals, Quick Sight now offers a second point mapping capability with a few key differences. Layer map visual points use a uniform marker size and don’t support geocoding, so you provide explicit coordinates in the GeoJSON file. In return, you can control the viewport precisely, locking the map to an exact geographic region, and disabling panning and zooming. The following table summarizes the key differences: Feature Point map Layer map visual points Data source Latitude/longitude values or geolocation names in your dataset GeoJSON Point features joined to your dataset by a shared key Geocoding Recognizes city, county, state, country, and postal code automatically Not available. Must provide explicit coordinates in the GeoJSON file Location updates Mapping updates automatically with SPICE refreshes or Direct Query as location values change Visual uses a static GeoJSON file for point locations. Requires manual re-upload or API call to update geometry Viewport Auto-fits to your data, panning and zooming always enabled Auto-fits by default, can configure if panning and zooming is allowed Appearance Size and color can be encoded from the dataset. Point style configuration available (basic, cluster, heatmap) Customizable uniform marker size, fill opacity, border color and thickness. Color can be encoded from the dataset Choose layer map visual points when: You require a locked, non-scrollable viewport. Your locations are fixed and curated (such as regional offices, distribution centers, retail stores) rather than changing with each data refresh. You plan to combine points with other geometry types (covered in the advanced use cases section). Consider a retail brand whose regional managers use a Quick Sight dashboard to track store performance across a metro area. The GeoJSON file contains a Point feature for each store with a store ID property that joins to the dataset. The dataset holds the metrics (store type, monthly revenue, daily foot traffic) that drive the tooltip and color encoding. You position the map at the zoom level covering the metro area, then disable map navigation so the map renders at a consistent view on every load. Managers can’t accidentally zoom out to a national or global view. Figure 6: Store locations as points with map navigation disabled to lock the metro-area view Advanced use cases The previous sections cover a standard layer map setup. Use the following techniques when you need more control over what readers see, want to combine geometry types in a single view, or need geometry that changes over time. Controlling the viewport When you need to control the viewport in layer map visuals, you can pan and zoom to the view you want manually. Then disable map navigation to lock it in place. For use cases where you need more precise boundaries or programmatic control, you can set the exact viewport coordinates through the visual definition using the Quick Sight APIs. The layer map visual stores its viewport configuration in the MapState property within ChartConfiguration . This property accepts two fields: Bounds : The geographic coordinates defining the minimum visible area (North, South, East, West). MapNavigation : ENABLED or DISABLED to control whether readers can pan and zoom. Although the bounds property is not exposed on the console, you can set these bounds when working with the dashboard definition JSON for programmatic asset management. For example, to define the bounds, modify the MapState block in the visual definition, then call the CreateDashboard or UpdateDashboard APIs. The bounds define the minimum area that is guaranteed to be visible. The map zooms to make sure this entire area fits within the visual container. For the tightest fit with minimal extra space added to the map, match the aspect ratio of your bounds to the shape of your visual container. Layering geometries For use cases that require combining multiple geometry types into a single view, you can layer visuals on top of each other. For example, the following screenshot demonstrates plotting customer locations as points within US regional boundaries defined by polygons. This composition shows which territories have the highest customer density and can be used to correlate with other metrics present in the dataset like performance. Figure 7: Customer points layered within polygon regional boundaries This second example demonstrates combining points as stops along a delivery route path. The LineString draws the planned route, and Point features mark each scheduled stop along the way. Figure 8: A delivery route drawn as a LineString with Point markers for each stop To layer geometries, you stack multiple layer map visuals on top of each other, following these steps: Use free-form layout: Change the sheet layout setting to free-form so that visuals can overlap and stack. Create two layer map visuals: Create the two layer map visuals that you combine into a single view, such as one using a Point GeoJSON file and one using a LineString GeoJSON file. Use matching bounds: Using the approach previously described for controlling the viewport, verify all layer map visuals use identical bounds to have the same underlying map view. Disable panning and zooming: For each layer map visual, disable the panning and zooming under Map options so that alignment stays the same. Hide the base map and background on upper layer: Set the upper visual’s background to hidden under Display settings and disable the base map under Map options. Stack the visuals: Move the top visual on top of the base layer using drag-and-drop or by matching precise size and position coordinates under Display settings. Layer ordering follows the visual stacking order in the free-form layout. To change a visual’s position in the stack, choose the menu icon (three dots) on the visual, then choose Send backward or Bring forward . Readers can access the tooltip of the topmost visual, so place the layer that readers need details from on top. Each sheet supports up to five layer map visuals. Dynamically updating GeoJSON Unlike other Quick Sight visuals where data refreshes through SPICE or Direct Query, layer map geometry lives in the GeoJSON file itself. When your dataset refreshes on schedule, the metrics update (for example, colors change and tooltip values refresh), but the geometry remains at its original position. To update what appears on the map, like a new route, new point locations, or updated boundaries, you need to update the GeoJSON file and republish the dashboard. You can replace a GeoJSON file manually through the Quick Sight console by editing the layer map visual within the Analysis and uploading a new file. This works for infrequent changes such as updating territory boundaries quarterly or adding a new store location. For automated, on-demand, or dynamic updates, the process involves Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and the Quick Sight APIs outlined in the following steps: Upload the new GeoJSON to Amazon S3: Generate your updated geometry and save it to an Amazon S3 bucket. Custom solutions can use other AWS services such as Amazon Location Service to create the GeoJSON files. Reference the file on the dashboard definition: The dashboard definition contains a StaticFiles array with a SpatialStaticFile entry for each GeoJSON file. Modify the file reference to the S3 location of your updated file entry for each GeoJSON file. Call the UpdateDashboard API: Submit the updated definition with the new file reference using the UpdateDashboard API. Call the UpdateDashboardPublishedVersion API: Publish the change so it is visible to dashboard readers with the UpdateDashboardPublishedVersion API. The following example uses this pattern to support on-demand map updates in an embedded dashboard to generate optimal routes between locations and waypoints. Although outside the scope of this post, this represents an advanced use case that combines each of the preceding approaches. Figure 9: On-demand route generation in an embedded dashboard Conclusion In this post, we showed how to use Point and LineString geometry in Amazon Quick Sight layer maps to plot specific locations and the routes between them. We covered the GeoJSON structure and dataset join that layer maps require, and compared layer map points with the native point map. We also walked through advanced techniques for controlling the viewport, layering separate visuals into one view, and refreshing GeoJSON files with Amazon S3 and the Quick Sight APIs. To learn more about layered maps, refer to the Amazon Quick Sight layered maps documentation . Visit the Amazon Quick Community to connect with peers and stay updated on the newest features and resources.   About the authors Amit Makashir Amit is a Software Development Engineer on the Amazon Quick Suite visualization team, where he helped build Quick Sight’s layer maps and the geospatial mapping stack behind them. His work spans the mapping visuals customers see and the geocoding, data, and service infrastructure that power them. Drawn to maps, places, and spatial problem-solving, he brings that curiosity to much of his work. Outside the office, he enjoys the outdoors—hiking, exploring new destinations, and taking long scenic drives. He helps customers design, implement, and scale Quick across their organization, from architecture to everyday use. title: How Bayer Crop Science built an agentic decision engine on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with AWS Unified Operations
summary: Bayer Crop Science built the Agentic Decision Engine (ADE), a multi-agent platform on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that lets breeders, analysts, and researchers ask natural language questions about their analytics platform. This post covers the ADE architecture, five design decisions, and how the team prepared it for production with AWS Unified Operations.
content: Plant breeding decisions depend on data that spans genomics, field trials, imagery, environmental conditions, and model outputs. Bayer Crop Science runs hundreds of machine learning (ML) model configurations against this data across crops, regions, and teams, and each run needs to be repeatable and governed. To meet that requirement, Bayer built the Connected Decision Engine (CDE), a system for deploying, orchestrating, monitoring, and reusing ML workflows. CDE gives breeders, analysts, researchers, data scientists, and data engineers a consistent way to run analytics while preserving execution history and operational controls. As adoption grew, the bottleneck moved from running workflows to understanding them. Explaining a result meant piecing together context from APIs, documentation, metadata stores, dashboards, and logs. A user who wanted to know why a workflow failed, what a model did, or where a result came from still had to know which system to inspect. To close that gap, Bayer built the Agentic Decision Engine (ADE), a multi-agent, natural language interface over CDE. A supervisor agent routes each question to a specialist agent, the specialist retrieves context from the relevant system, and the user receives an answer without navigating the operational stack. In its first phase, ADE resolves about 80 percent of user questions without an engineer in the loop. ADE runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , an AWS service to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. AgentCore let the team focus on agent behavior instead of building and operating its own agent hosting, session isolation, and tool access layer. Three AgentCore capabilities drove that choice: a managed runtime that isolates each user session, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)-scoped tool access through AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, that keeps authentication and authorization outside agent code, and a framework-agnostic design that let the team bring its own LangGraph orchestration and choice of models. To prepare for launch and to operate ADE afterward, Bayer engaged AWS Unified Operations . The engagement provided a designated Technical Account Manager (TAM) and a generative AI Domain Specialist Engineer (DSE), who worked as an extension of the ADE team from design through production. The TAM, as Bayer’s strategic advisor, brought an established understanding of Bayer’s operating model and business priorities. The DSE brought generative AI domain expertise on AWS. In three technical standups each week, the team reviewed and made design decisions. The DSE built working knowledge of the ADE workload and how the Bayer team operates, so technical guidance reflected both AWS service behavior and Bayer’s context. This post follows that journey: the ADE architecture, five design decisions made during the build, the work to prepare the platform for production, and how it is operated after launch. Architecture overview ADE is organized into four layers: the user experience, agent orchestration, specialist agents, and the tools and data sources those agents call (Figure 1). Users reach ADE through a React web front end, and requests pass through an identity proxy for Microsoft Entra ID before they reach the agents. GitHub Actions builds the agent container images, pushes them to Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) , and deploys them to AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime hosts the agents, and because the runtime is framework-agnostic, the team runs its own LangGraph-based orchestration on it directly. The team chose LangGraph for its explicit graph-based control flow and checkpointing for multi-step workflows. LangGraph orchestrates the workflow, with a Supervisor Agent as the entry point that classifies each request, selects a specialist, and combines results when a question spans domains. The data plane is separated by responsibility. Amazon DynamoDB stores LangGraph checkpoint state. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL stores session records, user feedback, and analytics. Amazon ElastiCache caches agent responses with a time to live (TTL). Domain content in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) is embedded with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 and indexed in Amazon OpenSearch Serverless for Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG). Amazon CloudWatch captures runtime and application telemetry. AgentCore Gateway exposes backend APIs to agents as Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools and keeps authentication and authorization outside agent code. Figure 1: Agentic Decision Engine architecture on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore ADE runs 22 specialist agents in production, each scoped to one domain with its own tools and data sources. For example, the Domain Expert Agent answers conceptual questions through RAG. The Operational Agent retrieves live workflow status and results from CDE. The Troubleshooting Agent analyzes operational telemetry. The Visualization Agent generates charts or returns existing dashboards. A customer-specific Models as Skill pattern converts model code and documentation into skill definitions stored in a central registry, so agents answer model-specific questions from the model’s implementation instead of generic model knowledge. When a breeder asks, “Why did my phenotyping workflow fail yesterday?”, the supervisor classifies the intent and routes the request to the Troubleshooting Agent. That agent reads the workflow’s telemetry in CloudWatch and its status from the CDE API through AgentCore Gateway, identifies the failure point, and returns a diagnosis through the supervisor (Figure 2). The breeder doesn’t search logs directly. With the Troubleshooting Agent, a diagnosis that once took over an hour of manual log-hunting and waiting for engineer support now takes under 10 minutes. Figure 2: ADE request flow: intent classification, cache lookup, specialist routing, and response Five design decisions on the path to production The Unified Operations TAM and DSE took part in the following decisions as members of the working team, not as an escalation point after the fact. That let Bayer test each design against AWS service behavior before committing to it, while keeping ownership of the architecture and the final call. 1. Externalize orchestration state without treating the runtime as stateless AgentCore runtime provides isolated sessions that preserve execution context across invocations within a session’s lifecycle. That context isn’t a durable store for a multi-step workflow. ADE writes LangGraph checkpoints to DynamoDB so the graph can resume after scale-out events, restarts, or session boundaries without depending on one execution environment remaining available. Principle: Use the runtime session for active execution, and persist the state required to resume or reconstruct the workflow in a durable service. 2. Separate enterprise identity, gateway access, and downstream authorization Bayer standardizes on Microsoft Entra ID for user identity, while ADE’s services authorize each other with AWS-native mechanisms. Rather than force one token across every trust boundary, the team gave each boundary its own mechanism. Entra ID remains the source of user identity. AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) authorizes service-to-service calls. AgentCore Gateway outbound authorization handles access to downstream CDE services. A request interceptor AWS Lambda function performs custom validation and passes the authorization attributes that downstream tools require. The team worked through the token contract at each hop with the DSE. Principle: Identity failures in agent systems cluster at the transitions between user identity, agent identity, and tool identity. Define the issuer, audience, claims, scopes, and credential lifetime at every hop instead of reusing a token that is valid for one boundary at the next. 3. Treat model selection as an interface contract During the build, the team evaluated a newer model version with reasoning mode enabled. For that version, the combination of tool use and structured output that ADE depends on was not compatible with how its agents were implemented. The DSE confirmed the constraint, and the team retained the current model for the release. Principle: For tool-using agents, model choice is constrained by the full interface: tool calling, structured output, streaming behavior, reasoning features, latency, quota availability, and model-specific request semantics. A newer model is not automatically a drop-in replacement. 4. Control the tool surface before it controls the prompt CDE manages more than 500 model configurations. A dedicated MCP server per API would have added deployment, authentication, and version management overhead. ADE instead registers OpenAPI specifications with AgentCore Gateway, which exposes the REST operations as MCP tools. Adding or changing an API becomes a schema and gateway configuration change instead of a new server deployment. Tool schemas and descriptions also consume input tokens and compete with the user’s request and retrieved context. ADE scopes tools by specialist agent instead of giving every agent the full catalog. For larger catalogs, AgentCore Gateway supports semantic tool search, so an agent can find relevant tools without loading the entire catalog on every turn. Principle: Scope the tool catalog per agent. Every tool definition adds tokens and widens the model’s decision space. 5. Promote complex capabilities from tools to agents Visualization started as a tool invoked by other agents. As it grew, it needed its own data retrieval, chart selection logic, retries, error handling, and a decision about whether to generate a chart or return an existing dashboard. The team moved it into a specialist Visualization Agent. The agent generates on-demand charts with matplotlib and Plotly in AgentCore Code Interpreter, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that provides a sandboxed code execution environment, and exchanges data with it through Amazon S3. When a prebuilt dashboard is the better answer, the agent returns the existing Amazon Quick or Power BI asset. Principle: A tool performs a bounded operation. When a capability starts to own state, retries, planning, policy, or presentation decisions, model it as an agent. Preparing ADE for production As the build moved toward launch, the focus shifted from design to operability: detecting agent failures, attributing inference cost, and hardening the deployment. Observability: Measure task failures, not only exceptions A supervisor architecture turns one user request into a chain of model calls, tool calls, and agent handoffs. The final answer can be wrong even when every HTTP request succeeded. ADE encountered this directly: application exception handlers caught agent errors and returned responses that monitoring counted as successful. After reproducing the issue with the DSE, the team added custom CloudWatch metrics inside failure paths and alarms on agent-specific conditions: tool call errors, throttling, model timeouts, and structured output validation failures. Traces and invocation logs follow each request across the supervisor and specialists. Principle: Distinguish transport success from task success. Agent observability should show whether the task completed, which agent or tool changed the outcome, and whether the response used the expected source. Cost attribution: Combine billing attribution with request-level telemetry One ADE request can invoke several models and tools, so account-level Amazon Bedrock spend doesn’t explain unit economics. The team designed the attribution approach with the DSE using three mechanisms that answer different questions. Amazon Bedrock application inference profiles attribute billed model usage to an application or workload. Request metadata and model invocation logging associate token usage with a specific agent, feature, or request. IAM principal attribution adds an identity dimension. Together they let the team estimate cost per interaction, identify expensive agents, and determine whether prompts, retrieved context, or tool definitions drive token use. In practice, the Visualization and Operational agents, which rely on MCP tools and multiple tool calls, consumed the most tokens. The same telemetry surfaced a workload during launch preparation with a large repeated input prefix and no prompt cache activity. For supported models, placing stable instructions and tool definitions in a cacheable prompt prefix reduces repeated input processing, which lowers latency and token cost. For ADE, caching the stable prompt prefix cut input-token cost by 20–30 percent. Security and launch readiness IAM roles are scoped to each agent’s responsibility. The Troubleshooting Agent can read the operational data it needs for diagnosis but can’t modify workflows. The Domain Expert Agent can query its retrieval index but cannot call unrelated CDE APIs. In production today, ADE’s agent responses are governed by least privilege, read-only tool access scoped to each agent, structured output validation on agent responses, and answers grounded in retrieved CDE data and telemetry rather than open-ended generation. Bayer also plans to evaluate Amazon Bedrock Guardrails as an additional layer on these controls, complementing the custom safety checks already used in CDE multi-turn workflows. Before launch, Unified Operations ran a Critical Workload Review and a Well-Architected review with the Generative AI Lens alongside the ADE team. Because the DSE already knew the workload, both reviews targeted ADE’s specific failure modes, capacity risks, and deployment gaps rather than generic best practices. Findings included gaps in failure visibility across the supervisor and specialist agents, mutable container image tags, limited image traceability, and missing vulnerability scanning. The team responded with stronger alarms, immutable versioned images, scan on push in Amazon ECR, and lifecycle policies for unused images. The DSE also reviewed scaling and quota requirements with the team. Load testing validated both the application and its service quotas and exposed a networking failure mode that returned empty responses, which the team fixed before the production event. By launch, the team had tracked 35 blockers to resolution with Unified Operations. Launch, operations, and next steps Bayer launched ADE to a gated group rather than opening it to the whole organization at once. Since launch, more than 100 users across Bayer Crop Science have used ADE, including breeders, analysts, researchers, data scientists, and engineers. Alongside its 22 specialist agents, ADE exposes about 20 API tools and can host third-party agents as it expands. Exposing those APIs through AgentCore Gateway rather than a dedicated server per API cut per-API integration overhead by more than 99 percent. In its first phase, ADE has resolved about 80 percent of user questions without an engineer in the loop. CDE remains the governed execution layer for analytics. ADE adds a natural language layer over it, so users can ask about workflow status, results, model behavior, and failures without learning the location or interface of each underlying system. The engagement then shifted from launch readiness to ongoing operations. The DSE continues to meet with the team, so issue triage and operational reviews start from existing knowledge of ADE instead of a new ramp-up. ADE’s critical CloudWatch alarms, including the agent-specific alarms described earlier, are onboarded to AWS Incident Detection and Response. When one fires, AWS Incident Management Engineers engage within 5 minutes and start from the workload’s context rather than from scratch. On the security side, AWS Security Incident Response engineers support the team during potential or active security events, so ADE has AWS monitoring and response coverage for both operational and security issues. With agent-to-agent communication already in place, Bayer is focusing next on hybrid cloud agent interoperability. The team is exploring how agents running in different environments can discover and communicate with each other without manual configuration. Conclusion Bayer didn’t replace its analytics platform with ADE. It made CDE easier to query and operate. Most of the production work sat outside the prompts: durable state, identity boundaries, tool scoping, task-level observability, cost attribution, and launch readiness. Bayer owned the architecture and each of those decisions. Working with a designated DSE and TAM through AWS Unified Operations, the team tested those decisions against AWS service behavior during design and carried the same context into production. To learn more, explore Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , Amazon Bedrock cost attribution , AWS Well-Architected Generative AI guidance , and AWS Unified Operations . The authors would like to thank Sijie Shi, Jorge Gomes, Naveen Reddy, Iago Fonseca, Mateus Silva, and Sushimitha Jarugula for their contributions to the design, development, and launch of ADE. About the authors Subbu Dandamudi Subbu is Head of MLOps for R&D at Bayer. He leads the development of scalable platforms and AI capabilities and has played a key role in building the Connected Decision Engine (CDE) and its evolution into the Agentic Decision Engine (ADE) to accelerate AI-driven innovation across R&D. Dr. Leo de Melo Leo is a Staff ML Engineer at Bayer Crop Science, where he helps shape the future of AI-powered R&D through scalable platforms, agentic systems, and advanced analytics. With a background in Computer Science and Computational Mathematics, he specializes in building AI and data platforms that enable researchers to transform complex data into actionable insights and accelerate scientific discovery. Mahnoor Hussain Mahnoor is a Senior Solutions Architect specializing in Generative AI and cloud architecture. She helps customers operationalize GenAI by translating emerging capabilities into production-ready solutions across agentic systems, governance, security, and cloud operations. Her work focuses on helping organizations move from experimentation to enterprise adoption. Outside of work, Mahnoor enjoys spending time with family and traveling. Ram Pamidimukkala Ram is a Senior Technical Account Manager at AWS, specializing in Generative AI, agentic workloads, data analytics, multi-cloud, and cloud operations. He helps organizations design, modernize, and migrate workloads to the AWS Cloud efficiently and securely. As part of Unified Operations his work focuses on building resilient architectures that balance performance, cost optimization, and long-term sustainability. Sai Pavan Kasani Sai is a Domain Specialist Engineer for Generative AI at AWS. As a technical advisor and customer advocate, he helps teams move generative AI proofs of concept into production, with particular focus on agentic AI workloads. He also works with customers on inference optimization and cost efficiency as their generative AI applications scale. title: Better speech synthesis for audiobooks
summary: “Controllable text to speech” makes speech more expressive, character voices more distinct and consistent.
content: Text-to-speech systems — which convert written text into synthetic speech — display impressive naturalness in applications such as chatbots and virtual assistants, where interactions last seconds. But they tend not to fare as well with longer-form content. When applied to audiobooks, for instance, conventional text-to-speech (TTS) models fail to reliably change speaking style between characters, as a human narrator would. This creates two problems for listeners: (1) distinguishing narration from dialogue and (2) identifying which character speaks which lines. To address this problem, the Audible technology team is using controllable TTS, meaning the ability to control dialogue delivery with natural-language speech descriptions (e.g., "speak in an enthusiastic, high-pitched voice"). This allows the TTS model to leverage the deep textual understanding of large language models (LLMs) to synthesize high-quality speech. Our approach involves three key innovations. First, we developed a novel data synthesis pipeline to produce speech data captioned with high-quality descriptions of speech characteristics. Training on this data enables our model to understand captions and produce audio consistent with them at inference time. Second, we created a system that automatically profiles characters in books and identifies their dialogue with 97% accuracy. It also provides captions for that dialogue, which act as stage directions for the model. Third, we used the first two techniques to synthesize audiobooks featuring distinct character voices, improving dialogue differentiation by 3.7 points on a MUSHRA (multiple stimuli with hidden reference and anchor) test, a standardized method where listeners rate audio quality on a scale from 0 to 100. Across tests in both English and Spanish, we observe statistically significant improvement in listening experience for eight out of ten voices. TTS for audiobooks Subtle defects in synthetic speech, such as unnatural prosody or monotone delivery, are tolerable for short stretches but become increasingly grating over time — and audiobook listeners engage with the same voice for 10 to 15 hours per book. This is why off-the-shelf TTS models often fail to produce enjoyable, natural audiobook narrations. Furthermore, general-purpose TTS models are designed to process individual utterances with minimal context. That’s a reasonable approach when responding to questions like "What's the weather today?", but it’s inadequate for audiobooks, where narrative coherence depends on understanding the surrounding story context. A TTS model reading dialogue needs to know whether the speaker is the protagonist confronting an antagonist or a minor character making small talk, information that may only be available in earlier chapters. Finally, general-purpose models struggle to produce character voices in a consistent and natural way across the span of an entire book, often voicing a character in a markedly different way in chapter 1 than in chapter 10. Controllable text-to-speech I. The data synthesis pipeline Whereas conventional TTS models are trained on text-speech pairs, a controllable-TTS model also requires annotations that describe how the speech sounds. The speech in the training set also needs to be highly expressive, covering the wide variety of dimensions — pitch, speaking rate, character voices, emotions, speaking styles, etc. — the model must control. Previous TTS models couldn't handle that kind of expressivity, so most existing training data is neutral in tone. We expanded the training sets through two approaches: new recordings and human captioning of existing audio data. While there are some datasets that include descriptions of prosodic features, each has its own description format: some are long, some are short, and some use single tags. This limits the flexibility of model inputs and tends to make the model overfit the formats of specific datasets. To improve generalization, we use LLMs to rewrite the original prompts into different formats, varying length, verbosity, and structure (single tags vs. free-form natural language). Second, the human-in-the-loop data collection procedures do not scale to the size of the datasets we need. Therefore, we complement the collected data with a large amount of synthetic data. We use two approaches: 1. Expert-model pipeline. This approach uses expert models and signal-processing algorithms such as pitch extraction, speaking rate extraction, and emotion detection to extract numerical features from audio data. We then feed these features and classification labels into an LLM to generate speech captions. 2. Speech captioner. We developed a model that performs a task opposite that of controllable TTS: it takes speech and outputs a description of prosodic features. Using this speech captioner, we can annotate larger amounts of data. We use the annotated data as seed data to train the initial controllable-TTS model, and we also use it to continue training the speech captioner itself. We then use these models to generate synthetic data, and we improve them both iteratively to create a synthetic-data flywheel. II. BookLLM: Adapting to the audiobook domain The audiobook domain presents additional challenges for a controllable-TTS system, since different characters need to have distinct but consistent voices. For this, we developed BookLLM, a separate component that leverages off-the-shelf LLMs to identify unique characters and uses information in the book — for instance, age, gender, personality, and role — to define their voice characteristics. Then the model determines which character speaks where and captions dialogue with descriptions of how it should be spoken. We evaluated BookLLM on 25 English and Spanish books in the mystery, sci fi, and romance genres. We collected ground truth annotations using two human annotators. In English and Spanish, the system achieved 97% and 94% accuracy, respectively, in identifying which character speaks where, including distinguishing between narration and dialogue III. Bringing it all together Bringing the two components together yields a complete audiobook-synthesis pipeline. Given a new book, BookLLM first reads the entire text to build a cast list: it determines the unique characters, ranks them by importance, and derives a voice description for each. Rather than inventing an unbounded set of voices, it assigns each character a distinct profile from a curated voice catalogue, deliberately maximizing the contrast between the most prominent characters so that listeners can tell them apart. Minor and one-off characters fall back to the default narrator, avoiding a proliferation of barely used voices. BookLLM then walks through the book and attributes every passage to a speaker — the narrator or a specific character — and, for each line of dialogue, writes a caption describing how it should be delivered, such as "whispering nervously" or "shouting in anger". These captions are exactly the kind of natural-language speech description that the controllable-TTS model was trained to follow. At synthesis time, each unit of text is passed to the TTS model, together with its speaker's voice profile and, if necessary, its stage direction caption. Because a character's voice profile is fixed once at the book level, the model renders that character consistently from beginning to end, avoiding general-purpose models’ tendency to drift, or voice a character differently in chapter one than in chapter ten. The per-line captions layer moment-to-moment expressivity on top. The result is a full-length audiobook in which characters sound distinct, consistent, and expressive that ultimately provides a more delightful listening experience.

Also in the window, undocumented here on purpose: Nous sign-in reworked (every sign-in is the plain device login, the free-tier guest hands over to your account, the result shows who signed in, connectors offer sign-in instead of opening a guest), hermes update holding back a stable release it refuses instead of offering it, Windows hermes update no longer stuck on the old launcher after a Python repin, usage-window plan support (plan gauges, limit cards and model-switch recovery for window-based plans), pluggable delegation backends (route subagents by model map or profile, switchable per session), plugin slash commands that can ask you to pick an option, hermes import-agent , OpenClaw migration, hermes mcp serve and the Singularity backend moving out of core into plugins (setup offers the importer when it finds another agent), Desktop drag-to-pin in the sidebar and one-click plugin installs with tier badges, the Electron 44 upgrade, Pillow 13 and a batch of dependency security bumps, a clear message when a chat's working folder is gone, hermes update recovering paused gateways after a damaged .git , long Claude DirectSDK answers no longer cut off by the stall timer, Desktop group chats showing which bot is working again, and the experimental webhook-mode MCP events client. content: New Features Save reusable prompts and slash commands in ten numbered /presets slots, with a keyboard menu for quick access. ( #54380 , #54381 ) Set model, reasoning effort, speed, and permission profiles directly with inline /model and /permissions arguments. ( #54378 , #54383 ) Preview viewed and generated images in the fullscreen transcript on terminals supporting Kitty or Sixel graphics. ( #54216 ) Authenticate enterprise MCP connections using eligible Codex account grants or dedicated sign-in, including OAuth clients requiring secrets. ( #55334 , #55859 , #56001 ) Mask credentials during supported remote Bash commands and Zsh snapshot sessions, including credentials from custom providers. ( #54309 , #54432 , #56049 ) The Amazon Bedrock setup wizard is now enabled by default, with API key entry grouped alongside other AWS sign-in methods when credentials are detected. ( #56033 , #56023 ) Bug Fixes Failed compaction no longer leaves partial summaries in conversation history, and background compaction failures fall back without panicking. ( #53932 , #55581 ) Resuming sessions now finds compressed histories and restores saved thread settings instead of replacing them with global defaults. ( #54008 , #55923 ) Windows HTTPS and WebSocket connections now handle proxy authentication challenges using the signed-in user’s Negotiate or NTLM credentials. ( #55994 , #56000 ) CLI configuration overrides are preserved when -c or --config appears at multiple subcommand levels. ( #56022 ) Queued prompts now wait for pending permission selections to resolve before continuing. ( #55682 ) Hardened sandbox checks for case-variant metadata paths on macOS and replaceable symlinks used to locate executables. ( #54273 , #55384 ) Chores Reduced disk usage by pruning unused installations, cleaning abandoned marketplace checkouts, and bounding daemon logs. ( #53827 , #55149 , #55689 , #55690 , #55856 ) Updated the embedded JavaScript runtime with safety checks for optimized Array.sort operations. title: Kazakhstan Expands Compute for Its AI Future
summary: Kazakhstan’s AI ecosystem is moving from infrastructure plans to deployment. The shift is visible across the full AI stack — from infrastructure to models to applications. The announcements below — coinciding with a visit to Astana by NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang — point to the nation’s increasing supply of accelerated computing, along with […]
content: Kazakhstan’s AI ecosystem is moving from infrastructure plans to deployment. The shift is visible across the full AI stack — from infrastructure to models to applications. The announcements below — coinciding with a visit to Astana by NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang — point to the nation’s increasing supply of accelerated computing, along with its growing demand for what comes next. On Friday, Oct. 23, NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang visited Astana, meeting with President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev at the Akorda Presidential Palace and joining Deputy Prime Minister Zhaslan Madiyev — Kazakhstan’s minister of AI and digital development — for a public fireside chat at the Alem.AI program. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements Jensen Huang and Kazakhstan’s AI Minister Speak at Alem.AI In their fireside chat at Alem.AI, Kazakhstan’s international center for artificial intelligence, Madiyev and Huang discussed the country’s push to become an AI nation — building the energy and computing infrastructure to support homegrown AI and applying it across the economy. Madiyev said Kazakhstan wants AI that reflects its language and culture. “We want AI that understands and speaks Kazakh and captures cultural contexts and cultural specifics,” he said, describing the country’s work on Kazakh-language models. Huang said Kazakhstan could turn its energy resources into a foundation for AI production — and a new kind of export. “Instead of just exporting energy, in the future, you could transform energy into intelligence and export intelligence,” he said. He also argued that local data is central to that ambition: it embodies a country’s culture, history and values. “Your country’s data is your natural resource. It belongs to you.” The conversation also turned to physical AI. Madiyev pointed to Kazakhstan’s factories, mines, agriculture, transport and logistics as potential areas for development, asking how the country could become a hub for training models for robots and other physical systems. Huang called the idea “fantastic,” saying physical AI could transform industries from mining and mineral processing to agriculture. Huang said AI and robotics can help people do more, but ambition will shape how fully they seize that opportunity. He applied the idea to Kazakhstan, saying AI could help lift the country and its people. “If you have ambition, and I believe you do, AI will lift your nation,” Huang said. “AI will lift your people.” Huang also praised the founders of Higgsfield AI, the Kazakhstan-founded startup, and it was announced NVIDIA is making an investment into the startup during the event. “The first thing and the last thing is you invest in people, not companies,” he said, describing the founders as visionary and pointing to their effort to compete globally. Asked about AI security, Huang said the technology must be developed and deployed responsibly. He described NVIDIA’s OpenShell as a way to contain AI agents by limiting their access to files and tools and monitoring their activity. For young people entering a fast-changing field, Huang recommended learning how AI works — not just how to use it. He said aspiring AI programmers should understand the technology’s principles, strengths and weaknesses, combining technical knowledge with the ability to work effectively with AI. “I envy being 18 years old today… because the world is changing so rapidly, and there’s a complete reset because of technology.” The Infrastructure Layer Is Scaling The visits coincided with a signing ceremony marking Firebird’s investment agreement with the government of Kazakhstan, held at the presidential palace. Building on its first AI factory in Armenia, Firebird is expanding into Kazakhstan, where it has secured a U.S. export license for 45,000 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs. The first phase is under construction with Kazakhtelecom at Data Center Valley, targeting commercial launch in the third quarter of 2027. A planned second phase would bring Firebird’s total potential AI infrastructure capacity in Kazakhstan to approximately 500 megawatts. Firebird also plans to establish Firebird Labs Kazakhstan to support local AI startups, research and talent development through funding, access to compute and research partnerships. Firebird cofounder and CEO Razmig Hovaghimian attended the signing ceremony at the Akorda Presidential Palace alongside government officials. “What began as a seed of an idea 180 days ago has grown into a major investment in Kazakhstan’s AI future,” said Razmig Hovaghimian, co-Founder and CEO of Firebird. “President Tokayev’s vision gave us the confidence to think bigger about what we can build together. With Jensen Huang here today, that ambition feels more tangible than ever. We’re building the infrastructure for Kazakhstan’s talent and ideas to reach the world.” Kazakhtelecom , the nation’s largest telecommunications company, has already deployed 400 NVIDIA H200 and 480 NVIDIA B300 GPUs in Astana and Almaty. Next year, the company plans to deploy more than 1,000 GPUs in the Data Center Valley , along with more than 1,000 NVIDIA Vera Rubin GPUs in the Ekibastuz region, serving diverse workloads with infrastructure that enterprises, developers and institutions can use at scale. An Honorary Black Belt for Huang At the end of their meeting, President Tokayev presented Huang with the Order of Dostyk, First Class, for his contribution to the development of artificial intelligence in Kazakhstan. Dostyk means friendship and the Order honors peace, friendship and cooperation. Later that day, President of the International Judo Federation (IJF) Marius Vizer and Timur Kemell, IJF director of promotion and development and a member of the IJF Executive Committee, presented Huang with an honorary black belt in Judo. The belt, embroidered in gold stitching, was a special thanks for Huang’s support of Kazakhstan’s AI ambition and for leadership aligned with the spirit and rigor of the martial art. AI-Native Companies Scale With Compute And that development is accelerating. The nation’s AI-native companies are also building out their compute capacity — and the applications that run atop them. Higgsfield is expanding its AI infrastructure with NVIDIA Vera Rubin running on cloud service providers, giving the company additional capacity as models, products and customer demand for its generative media applications grow. inDrive and Pony.ai are also collaborating to explore robotaxi services in Kazakhstan, with Astana as the first deployment city. The companies will assess the feasibility of bringing Pony.ai’s seventh-generation robotaxis to the inDrive app, supported by NVIDIA AI infrastructure, built on the NVIDIA Hyperion sensor and compute platform with the NVIDIA Halos safety system. More local capacity gives developers and companies room to train, fine-tune and serve increasingly capable models. Successful applications, in turn, create demand for more compute. Kazakhstan’s AI opportunity isn’t defined by GPU counts alone. Connecting that infrastructure with developers, universities, startups and industries can turn accelerated computing into useful applications. That was at the core of the discussion the NVIDIA team had with hundreds of developers from across Kazakhstan during a reception later in the evening. The gathering in this self-proclaimed AI nation was inspiring because of the ideas shared, the clear drive to build and a collective ambition to share it with the world. Today’s announcements represent different layers of the AI stack in Kazakhstan— infrastructure deployment, access to compute and AI-native product development — where the AI foundation is reaching new scale. Watch the fireside chat between Jensen Huang and Deputy Prime Minister Zhaslan Madiyev, streamed live from Alem.AI in Astana .
