Unstructured path (policy and medical records documents) → Amazon S3 bucket (ACL-aware KB source) → Amazon Quick Knowledge Base (document-level ACLs, fail-closed at query time) Structured path (claims) All claims data currently resides in a lake (Amazon S3). → Glue ETL (curate) → Glue DataBrew (de-identify) → Lake Formation (row/column grants and AWS Glue Data Catalog ) → Amazon Quick Sight dataset ( Amazon Athena ) (row-level and column-level security, run-as role) Both of the preceding data flows for structured and unstructured data converge into an Amazon Quick chat agent with federated SSO, least-privilege space, guardrails, and CloudWatch vended logs. Here is how AnyCompany’s administrator implements the solution: Sign the BAA and provision through the AWS Management Console . The admin accepts the AWS BAA in AWS Artifact against the AWS account, then provisions Amazon Quick from the AWS Management Console with IAM Identity Center. AnyCompany records the agreement ID, timestamp, and account in its compliance register. Only the web version of Amazon Quick, provisioned through the AWS Management Console, can be brought under a signed BAA through AWS Artifact, which is a necessary component for customers building HIPAA-compliant workflows that touch PHI, subject to proper configuration and the customer’s own compliance responsibilities. Set the irreversible controls on day zero. Because AnyCompany’s security policy calls for control of its own encryption keys, the admin chooses to register a customer managed key as the account default before any Amazon Quick AI data is created. The data key is set once and can’t be changed later. (Default AWS managed encryption is also HIPAA-eligible. Using customer managed keys is not a prerequisite for the service to be HIPAA eligible.) The admin also settles the identity model on IAM Identity Center so that inactive-user detection applies. The Amazon Quick data key is set once on first data creation and can never be changed. If the key is deleted, the only recovery is to unsubscribe and resubscribe, which permanently removes all Amazon Quick data. Prepare the structured path outside Amazon Quick. Before Amazon Quick Sight touches claims, AnyCompany’s data team uses AWS Glue to build the curated claims tables and Glue DataBrew to produce a de-identified extract for the operations dashboards. AWS Lake Formation grants row- and column-level access on those tables through the AWS Glue Data Catalog. As a result, Amazon Quick never sees raw PHI that it does not need. Create an ACL-aware knowledge base for the documents. The admin connects the policy-and-appeals S3 bucket as a knowledge base with document-level ACLs enabled at creation. Because ACLs can’t be turned on later, this needs to be configured when you create the S3 bucket. Amazon Quick evaluates each user’s identity at query time and returns no documents when it can’t confirm access. Build a dedicated space and a custom chat agent. AnyCompany creates a PHI space with restricted membership, separate from general-productivity spaces. The care-management chat agent is scoped to only the ACL-aware knowledge base, with open web search disabled and guardrails configured. Read-only connectors are implemented for anything PHI-adjacent. Connect the dashboards with query-time security. The operations dashboards read the de-identified Amazon Quick Sight dataset over Athena, with Amazon Quick Sight row-level and column-level security and a run-as role layered on top of the Lake Formation grants. Turn on the audit signals before onboarding users. The admin creates a CloudTrail trail and configures CloudWatch vended log delivery (CHAT_LOGS, FEEDBACK_LOGS, KB_FILE_SYNC_LOGS, and the rest) to a retained, masked destination. Feedback is treated as a PHI surface. Validate, then scale from non-PHI to PHI. AnyCompany starts with non-PHI workflows, such as policy Q&A and document search, to confirm governance, tests with adversarial prompts to verify fail-closed ACL behavior, reviews the logs to confirm the events are captured, and only then expands the care-management team into PHI-adjacent work. Amazon Quick enforces identity, retrieval, guardrails, and the audit trail. But the de-identification, the ETL, and the lake-level grants happen upstream in Glue, Glue DataBrew, and Lake Formation. This division is the recommended pattern, and is the practical answer to augmenting Amazon Quick in a federated environment. How to make it compliant: Best practices Eligibility gives you a platform that can handle PHI. You still must configure it so that it does. This section helps you understand the shared-responsibility decisions involved. Because a few of these decisions are irreversible, make them before you create resources or onboard users. Start with the security model for agentic AI Amazon Quick agents don’t wait for instructions at every step. They invoke tools, modify data, and interact with external systems on their own. That changes how you approach securing your environment. AWS published four security principles for agentic AI in April 2026, and they apply directly here. Principle 1 — Layer agent safeguards onto your existing security framework. Don’t stand up a parallel security posture for Amazon Quick. Add agent-specific measures (guardrails, topic blocking, and PII redaction) on top of the IAM, network, and encryption policies you already enforce. Principle 2 — Trust deterministic controls over prompt-based ones. A well-crafted adversarial input can circumvent a prompt instruction. AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies, document-level ACLs, network boundaries, and admin-configured guardrails can’t be talked around. Use those as your primary enforcement. Agent instructions are your second layer, not your only one. Principle 3 — Apply defense in depth across perceive, reason, and act. Map every agent capability to one of three layers: Perceive: knowledge bases, uploaded files, web search, connector inputs, MCP tool outputs. Reason: the LLM processing context, controlled by guardrails and topic controls. Act: Connectors, Quick Flows, Quick Automate, scheduled tasks, MCP tool calls. Apply controls at each layer independently. A gap in one shouldn’t cascade into the others. Note that HIPAA BAA obligations extend to supporting services and solutions like MCP tools. Principle 4 — Expand autonomy progressively. Start agents in read-only mode against non-PHI data. Add capabilities one at a time. Test for data leakage, prompt-injection resilience, and permission-boundary adherence at each step before moving to the next. Decide before you deploy Because these three choices are permanent, make these decisions before implementation. Register your KMS key first. If your organization requires control of its own encryption keys, register a customer managed key as the account default before creating any Amazon Quick AI resources. The data key is set the first time Quick AI data is created in the account. After that, it can’t be changed. Customer managed key support requires an Enterprise subscription. Note that a customer managed key disables chat memory. Accounts configured with a customer managed key do not support this feature. Choose your identity model deliberately. You have four options: IAM Identity Center, Active Directory, IAM federation, and Quick local users. They differ in provisioning, offboarding, and governance behavior. Inactive-user detection, for instance, works only with IAM Identity Center or Active Directory. Switching identity providers after deployment means reprovisioning every user’s permissions and space memberships. Pick once. Make PHI knowledge bases ACL-aware at creation. For supported sources (Amazon S3, Google Drive, SharePoint, Confluence Cloud, and OneDrive), you decide at creation whether a knowledge base enforces document-level ACLs. That setting is permanent. You can’t enable ACLs on a knowledge base that was created without them. For anything PHI-adjacent, create it ACL-aware from the start. Warning: Misconfigured user-store mappings can silently expose restricted documents to the wrong users, without errors or alerts. It’s critical to validate your identity-to-ACL mapping before you ingest PHI content. AWS Region, network, and account boundaries Plan your deployment Region based on the following factors: Data residency: Amazon Quick processes and stores data in the Region where you provision it, and you need to confirm that Region satisfies your organization’s data-localization requirements. Note that Amazon Quick is a single-Region service: it benefits from multi-AZ resilience within a Region, but it doesn’t fail over across Regions. If you support business-critical workflows that require cross-Region resilience, provision a separate Amazon Quick deployment in a second Region, along with its supporting data, for example, replicating S3-based knowledge base sources across Regions. Service availability. Features are at times launched in different Regions at different times. Verify that everything your agents need, such as knowledge bases, connectors, and Amazon Quick Sight capabilities, is available where you plan to deploy. Multi-account strategy. Place Amazon Quick in a dedicated workload account in AWS Organizations. Use Service Control Policies (SCPs) to enforce Region restrictions and block accidental provisioning in out-of-scope Regions. For network boundaries: Amazon Quick is a managed service accessed over HTTPS. You don’t deploy it into a virtual private cloud (VPC). But your data sources (S3 buckets, databases, on-premises systems) might sit behind VPC boundaries. Use VPC endpoints and AWS PrivateLink where available. Make sure DNS resolution and firewall rules let Amazon Quick’s connectors reach your authorized data sources without opening the network wider than necessary. Minimize the agent’s attack surface Amazon Quick’s own documentation frames adversarial risk as a two-condition problem: risk exists when (1) an agent can read content from outside your trust boundary, and (2) it can take a consequential action. Narrow either condition and you reduce exposure. Constrain what agents can read (Perceive layer). Know every source that feeds an agent’s context: knowledge bases, uploaded files, web search, third-party research providers, connector responses, MCP tool outputs, and retained conversation memory. For PHI workflows: Scope agents to trusted, ACL-aware knowledge bases. Turn off open web search where it isn’t needed. Turn off file upload if the agent doesn’t require it. Limit conversation-history retention to the minimum useful window. Constrain what agents can do (Act layer). Inventory every outbound path: connectors, MCP tools, web queries, Quick Flows, Quick Automate workflows, scheduled agent runs. For PHI-adjacent agents: Prefer read-only connector access. Be cautious with automated and scheduled workflows, because they run without anyone watching. Block write actions unless explicitly justified and approved by your security team. Use connector-level permission scoping to restrict which operations an agent can invoke. Know the identity an action runs as. On-demand actions authenticate as the invoking user, bounded by that user’s connector permissions. Automated workflows run without an interactive session. Match the autonomy level to the sensitivity of the action, and document which agents operate in which identity mode. Enforce least privilege and data segregation Separate PHI-containing knowledge bases and spaces from general-productivity ones. Restrict membership. Grant space and agent access on a need-to-know basis. Review both sharing permissions (who can use a knowledge base) and source-document ACLs (which indexed documents an authorized user can actually retrieve). The default knowledge-base refresh cycle is 24 hours. Shorten it when your access-change requirements demand faster propagation. Refresh ACLs before reassigning or recycling email addresses. A PHI agent shouldn’t share a space with general-purpose productivity tools. This means you need to isolate use cases at the space level. Review connector permissions regularly. Rotate credentials stored in AWS Secrets Manager on a schedule that matches your credential-management policy. Practice data minimization AWS recommends against entering confidential data into resource names or tags, to avoid accidental mention in billing or diagnostic logs. Prefer de-identified data wherever the use case allows it. When ingesting structured data from databases or APIs, filter columns and rows at the source before indexing. Configure agent guardrails to redact PII in responses, hiding Social Security numbers (SSNs), medical record numbers (MRNs), and dates of birth, using the built-in PII detection filters. Configure audit logging and retention Amazon Quick provides several distinct audit signals. None of them flow by default and you might need to turn them on. Signal Source What it captures API operations CloudTrail Admin actions, configuration changes Chat interactions CloudWatch CHAT_LOGS — full conversation records User feedback CloudWatch FEEDBACK_LOGS — thumbs up/down with context KB sync events CloudWatch KB_FILE_SYNC_LOGS — ingestion status Operational metrics CloudWatch Latency, error rates, invocation counts Usage analytics Quick console Adoption, top queries, user activity Here is how to set them up: Create a CloudTrail trail for the accounts and Regions in scope. Configure CloudWatch vended log delivery (CHAT_LOGS, FEEDBACK_LOGS, KB_FILE_SYNC_LOGS) shortly after you turn on Amazon Quick’s AI features. Apply CloudWatch Logs data-protection masking to chat logs so PHI isn’t stored in cleartext. Set a retention period of at least six years. Consider S3 Object Lock on the log archive. Add CloudWatch alarms for anomalous activity. Enable AWS Security Hub for continuous compliance checks. Route critical alerts to your security information and event management (SIEM) or incident-response platform. Validate before you scale Before expanding scope, check the following: BAA acceptance is recorded in your compliance register. Data classification is documented: Which knowledge bases and spaces contain PHI, which agents can reach them. Adversarial queries and prompt-injection scenarios have been tested. Logs are being captured and masking works correctly. A tabletop breach exercise has been completed. InfoSec has signed off. Known limitations Here are some known limitations of Amazon Quick. No BAA on the Free or Plus path. You must use the path provisioned through the AWS Management Console to get BAA coverage. No cross-Region replication. Disaster recovery (DR) is constrained to a single Region. Guardrails are probabilistic, not deterministic. They reduce risk. They don’t eliminate it. Supplement with the infrastructure-level controls described earlier. Third-party connectors extend your BAA obligations. When a connector sends data to an external system, your compliance responsibility follows the data. Conversation memory might contain echoed PHI. Set retention policies and apply masking. Implementation guide The AnyCompany Health Plan example showed how to roll out Amazon Quick. This section turns that pattern into a step-by-step project plan you can hand to your platform team. Step 1: Execute the BAA (Day 1) Sign in with AWS Artifact permissions and accept the BAA. Record the agreement ID, timestamp, principal ARN, and account ID. Notify your legal and compliance team. Step 2: Set foundational, irreversible controls (Days 1–2) Register a customer managed key as the account default. Verify the key policy grants the required permissions: Encrypt, Decrypt, GenerateDataKey, DescribeKey. Configure your identity model (IAM Identity Center is recommended). Confirm the account sits in a dedicated workload organizational unit (OU) with Region-restricting SCPs. Step 3: Create ACL-aware knowledge bases (Days 3–7) Classify your data sources: PHI, PHI-adjacent, and non-PHI. Create knowledge bases with ACL awareness turned on for PHI and PHI-adjacent sources. Map the identity store to source permissions and validate with multiple test users. Verify sync logs confirm successful ingestion. Keep PHI knowledge bases separated from general content. Step 4: Create spaces (Days 5–8) Separate PHI-adjacent spaces from general-productivity spaces. Attach knowledge bases, dashboards, and action connectors. Restrict membership. Confirm that unauthorized users are blocked. Step 5: Create custom agents with guardrails (Days 7–12) Define each agent’s purpose narrowly. Attach only the knowledge sources it needs. Configure PII redaction, blocked topics, content filters, and grounding controls. Test with normal queries, boundary queries, and adversarial prompts. Document results and remediation steps. Step 6: Configure action connectors (Days 10–14) Start with read-only mode for PHI-adjacent data. Scope each connector to specific resources. Store credentials in AWS Secrets Manager with rotation turned on. Document the justification for any write access. Get security sign-off before turning it on. Test scope limits to confirm connectors can’t reach resources beyond their intended scope. Step 7: Configure audit, retention, and monitoring (Days 12–16) Enable CloudTrail and CloudWatch vended logs. Apply data-protection masking. Set retention to at least six years. Enable S3 Object Lock. Configure alarms, enable Security Hub, and integrate with your SIEM. Step 8: Validate with InfoSec (Days 14–21) Compile the evidence package: BAA confirmation, KMS configuration, identity setup, data classification, test results, and log samples. Run a tabletop breach exercise. Present to your InfoSec team. Remediate findings. Obtain sign-off. Expansion phase (Weeks 4–8) Start with non-PHI workflows: policy Q&A, document search, meeting prep, workflow automation. These let your team build confidence with the platform before PHI enters the picture. Then expand to PHI-adjacent workflows: clinical documentation assistance, claims processing, prior authorization, regulatory Q&A, patient communication drafting with human review in the loop. Monitor closely: review chat logs weekly, track guardrail trigger rates, and watch access patterns for 30 days after each new workflow goes live. Conclusion Amazon Quick gives regulated healthcare organizations, and the business associates who serve them, a managed AI workspace that is HIPAA-eligible across its full range of capabilities: agentic AI, knowledge retrieval, business intelligence, automation, and research. The path to a compliant deployment follows a clear sequence: Understand the difference between eligible and compliant, and own your side of shared responsibility. Execute the BAA on an account provisioned through the AWS Management Console. Set the irreversible controls first: KMS keys, identity model, ACL-aware knowledge bases. Minimize the agent’s read and action surfaces, enforce least privilege, and mask PHI in logs. Validate with your InfoSec team, then scale from non-PHI to PHI-adjacent workflows. The compliance expectations are moving as fast as the technology. AWS published its four security principles for agentic AI in April 2026 and the Well-Architected Agentic AI Lens in June 2026. Organizations that build on deterministic, infrastructure-level controls today will likely be well positioned as regulatory expectations catch up to what agentic AI can do. What to do next If you’re evaluating Amazon Quick: Request a compliance-focused briefing from your AWS account team. Ask about BAA scope, shared responsibility for agentic AI, and the latest HIPAA-eligible service additions. If you’re ready to deploy: Use the implementation guide as your project plan. The irreversible decisions in Step 2 deserve a dedicated architecture review before you start creating resources. If you’re already running Amazon Quick: Audit your deployment against the best practices in this post, especially the agentic security principles and the known limitations list. For architecture guidance, reach out to your AWS Solutions Architect or the AWS Healthcare and Life Sciences team. About the authors Meena Menon Meena is a Senior Customer Success Manager at AWS with over 20 years of experience delivering enterprise customer outcomes and driving digital transformation. At AWS, she partners with strategic ISVs across the Security, Observability, and Healthcare segments, helping them launch and scale AI workloads on AWS. She brings deep cross-industry experience working alongside these ISVs to accelerate cloud adoption, modernize platforms, and turn emerging technologies into measurable business impact. Shailesh Doshi Shailesh is a Senior Customer Solutions Manager at AWS with over 30 years of experience across multiple industry verticals, helping organizations turn cloud and AI investments into measurable business value. Currently he focuses on Healthcare and Life Sciences, partnering with providers, payers, and life sciences innovators to achieve their strategic goals and unlock enterprise value through Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, and Analytics, driving multi-fold growth in GenAI adoption. Shailesh works alongside executive and technical teams to accelerate GenAI investments, drive adoption, and modernize mission-critical platforms.

title: Stream low-latency speech from AI agents using Kokoro TTS on Amazon SageMaker AI
summary: Voice agents often wait for an agent's full response before starting speech synthesis, adding latency users feel directly. This post shows how to stream each sentence to a Kokoro-82M text-to-speech model on Amazon SageMaker AI as the agent produces it, and how to get that audio back to a browser over Server-Sent Events or a unified binary transport.
content:
A customer asks an AI voice agent a question and waits. The agent already has an answer, it’s midway through generating a long, multi-paragraph response, but the customer hears nothing for five seconds. By the time an answer arrives, the customer is frustrated, confused, and no longer paying attention. Text-to-speech integrations create exactly that gap. A one-sentence response might generate in 600 milliseconds, but the full response takes five seconds, and the integration waits for all of it before synthesis starts. This post shows how to close that gap. We stream each sentence to a hosted Kokoro-82M text-to-speech (TTS) model on Amazon SageMaker AI as soon as an agent produces it, so synthesis begins on sentence one instead of the finished response. Getting that audio back to a browser needs its own solution too, so we also cover both transports for doing it and what each costs in practice. Solution overview This solution closes the gap by streaming synthesis alongside generation instead of waiting for it to finish. As the agent produces each sentence, that sentence streams immediately to a hosted Kokoro-82M text-to-speech model, so audio playback can start before the agent finishes speaking its full response. Kokoro-82M holds only 82 million parameters, small enough to run cheaply on a single mid-tier GPU instance. That keeps both latency and inference cost low for a voice agent handling real traffic. Kokoro-82M runs in a custom container on a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint, on an ml.g5.xlarge GPU instance. The container exposes two routes: POST /invocations , which streams a response for one complete input, and WS /invocations-bidirectional-stream , which keeps one connection open across many messages in both directions. The following diagram shows the request path from client to model: Figure 1: Request path from the client to the SageMaker AI real-time endpoint over a bidirectional stream Prerequisites Before you begin, you need: An AWS account with permissions to create SageMaker AI endpoints; AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore; AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles; and an Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repository, including at minimum the sagemaker:CreateEndpoint , sagemaker:CreateEndpointConfig , sagemaker:CreateModel , sagemaker:InvokeEndpointWithBidirectionalStream , and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream actions. The sample container pins an older PyTorch with a known advisory ( PYSEC-2026-2286 , fixed in torch 2.10.0). Review and upgrade the pin before any non-proof-of-value use. AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) v2 , installed and bootstrapped in your target account and AWS Region. A SageMaker AI real-time endpoint deployed from a container that declares the com.amazonaws.sagemaker.capabilities.bidirectional-streaming=true Docker label. Python 3.12 or later, uv , and Docker to build the container image (the underlying HTTP/2 client only ships pre-built wheels for Python 3.12 and newer). The AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) with support for invoke_endpoint_with_bidirectional_stream . Familiarity with WebSockets and Starlette or a comparable ASGI framework. The deployment code from the GitHub repository referenced in this post. Walkthrough The walkthrough first deploys the endpoint and agent, then works through the client-side changes that make incremental streaming work end to end. Deploy the endpoint and agent The Kokoro-82M endpoint and the agent runtime deploy through two CLI tools, each wrapping its own AWS CDK stacks: uv run speech-infra deploy kokoro-82m uv run agent-infra deploy --bedrock-model-id speech-infra deploy provisions the Kokoro-82M endpoint. This includes the foundation and model-cache stacks that create the underlying IAM roles and sync the model’s weights into Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). The endpoint stack then builds the container image and creates the SageMaker AI model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint. agent-infra deploy provisions the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime hosting the Strands agent, which calls the endpoint you just deployed, so deploy the endpoint first. Step 1: Handle the WebSocket frame type SageMaker AI actually sends The bidirectional transport SageMaker AI uses delivers every piece of a client’s message to your container as a binary WebSocket frame. A common way to write a Starlette WebSocket handler is calling receive_text() , which reads message["text"] and raises KeyError if that key isn’t present. Because every message this client sends arrives as binary, that handler fails on every request. The failure is commonly misdiagnosed. A generic exception handler that forwards str(e) to the client turns KeyError('text') into an error frame reading 'text' , which looks like a missing field, not a framing issue. The endpoint itself reports InService throughout, since it accepts connections and responds to every message, with an error each time. Accept either frame type explicitly instead of assuming one will show up: from starlette.websockets import WebSocket, WebSocketDisconnect async def _receive_message(websocket: WebSocket) -> str: message = await websocket.receive() if message["type"] == "websocket.disconnect": raise WebSocketDisconnect(message.get("code", 1000)) payload = message.get("text") if payload is None: payload = message.get("bytes", b"").decode("utf-8") return payload This decodes bytes as UTF-8 when no text field is present, rather than assuming one frame type. Test it by sending a binary frame, because this failure mode produces a well-formed error frame and a healthy endpoint status, not an obvious crash. Step 2: Keep the session open between messages After your container finishes synthesizing one message’s audio, the instinct is to close the session, the way an HTTP cycle ends. That’s wrong here. After sending a message’s audio and a synthesis_complete control frame, the container loop should go back to waiting on receive() for the next message on the same, still-open session. Close the connection only when the client sends an explicit {"type": "close"} message. The following diagram shows one session carrying two sentences in sequence, closing only at the end: Figure 2: One bidirectional session carrying two sentences in sequence, closing only at the end This way, you can send several sentences, one after another, on one persistent session, with no reconnection cost between them. Closing eagerly after one response would force a new connection per sentence, undoing most of the latency benefit. Step 3: Stream sentences as the agent produces them With the session behavior in place, the client-side fix for the latency problem is a class that normalizes text arriving in two shapes: a complete string known up front, or a live token stream. It produces the same output either way: complete sentences, ready to send as soon as each one is complete. import re _SENTENCE_RE = re.compile(r"(? None: self._buffer = "" def feed(self, fragment: str) -> list[str]: self._buffer += fragment parts = _SENTENCE_RE.split(self._buffer) if len(parts) == 1: return [] self._buffer = parts[-1] return [s.strip() for s in parts[:-1] if s.strip()] def flush(self) -> str | None: remainder = self._buffer.strip() self._buffer = "" return remainder or None Call feed() once per fragment of text as it arrives. It returns any newly completed sentences, holding back trailing text. Call flush() once, at the end of input, to release whatever partial text remains even without trailing punctuation. This keeps a stream that ends before a period arrives from dropping a final sentence. This isn’t concurrent synthesis. Every bidirectional handler is a strictly sequential loop: receive a message, synthesize its audio, send that audio, send synthesis_complete , then receive the next message. Sentence two’s audio isn’t generated while sentence one’s still transmits. What incremental sending buys is narrower: synthesis on sentence one begins the instant it exists, rather than waiting for the full response. For a multi-sentence response with real generation time between its first and last sentence, that’s the entire latency win. We verified this against a live endpoint sending a three-sentence input over one session. All three chunks arrived with audio matching the text sent for each: Chunk Text Audio bytes Duration (s) 1 “Hello there.” 73,200 1.525 2 “This is a post deployment check.” 108,000 2.250 3 “It has three sentences.” 98,400 2.050 Step 4: Choose a transport for getting audio back to the client Streaming text into the model incrementally solves half the problem. The other half is getting the resulting audio out to whatever renders it, commonly a browser. Most agent and chat frontends already stream text over Server-Sent Events (SSE): one-directional, and supported natively by most browsers. SSE is a text protocol, not built to carry a raw binary payload. A team adding voice to an existing SSE pipeline naturally reaches for the pattern it already has: base64-encode the audio and wrap it in a JSON event. We measured the cost of that approach across 24 clips, confirmed with Amazon Transcribe that quality didn’t differ across encodings, and compared MP3 against AAC: Candidate Raw bytes Base64 bytes Bitrate Raw PCM 2,396,400 3,195,200 384 kbps MP3 48k 308,304 411,072 49.5 kbps AAC 32k fMP4 258,039 344,084 41.6 kbps Base64 inflates every payload by close to the expected 33%. The subtler cost is frame alignment. SSE events are delimited by a blank line, but the audio inside is delimited into MP3 frames. The two schemes don’t necessarily align with how the transport chunks the data. In one measured response, four logical MP3 frames arrived as six delivery chunks, two ending mid-frame. A consumer that treats each delivery chunk as one complete unit fails on ordinary, healthy traffic. The fix buffers incoming bytes and acts only once a delimiter is found: buffer = b"" for event in resp["Body"]: if "PayloadPart" not in event: continue buffer += event["PayloadPart"]["Bytes"] while b"

" in buffer: frame, buffer = buffer.split(b"

", 1) handle(frame) The alternative used today for the model-facing leg skips base64 and SSE framing entirely. It multiplexes raw binary audio and JSON control frames over the same bidirectional session already carrying incremental text input, and tells them apart with one rule. import json def _decode_control_frame(chunk: bytes) -> dict | None: try: decoded = json.loads(chunk.decode("utf-8")) except (UnicodeDecodeError, json.JSONDecodeError): return None return decoded if isinstance(decoded, dict) else None A chunk that fails to decode as a JSON object is audio, forwarded as received, with no encoding step anywhere in the path. One edge case matters: raw PCM audio can legitimately begin with byte 0x7b , the ASCII character { , the same character that opens a JSON object. This rule avoids misclassifying that audio because it requires the entire chunk to parse as valid JSON, not its first byte alone, something a PCM frame will essentially never do. Note: If your frontend already has a working SSE pipeline for text, base64-encoded audio inside an SSE event is the pragmatic choice. It costs roughly 33 percent extra payload and a buffer-and-reassemble step, but reuses infrastructure you already operate. If you’re building the voice path fresh, or latency is the priority, the unified binary and JSON approach avoids both costs and reuses the connection already carrying text. Step 5: Put it together in a real agent The fuller, end-to-end case is a live, generative agent composing its response one token at a time, with no way to know sentence four until sentence one exists. This example runs as a Strands agent, backed by Amazon Bedrock, deployed to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, calling the Kokoro endpoint with the pattern from Step 4. Three communication legs connect in this design: the browser-facing leg carrying Server-Sent Events back to the caller, the agent’s streaming call to Amazon Bedrock for text generation, and the agent’s bidirectional session with the Kokoro endpoint for synthesis. The following diagram shows those three communication legs, and where the overlap between generation and synthesis happens: Figure 3: The three communication legs connecting the caller, Amazon Bedrock, and the Kokoro endpoint The request payload carries a mode field, either "bidi" or "batch" , dispatched to two code paths inside the same entrypoint function. A benchmark between them changes exactly one variable: when synthesis starts. In run_bidi , two tasks run concurrently. One drains the Bedrock text stream and feeds completed sentences into the chunker. The other drains the Kokoro session and emits audio chunks as they arrive. Both push into one shared queue, so a consumer yields events in true arrival order: audio for an early sentence can reach the caller while Bedrock still generates a later one. run_batch is the deliberate opposite: it waits for the full response before one synthesis call, kept as a fair baseline. Going the other direction, the leg from the agent container back to the caller does use base64, for a different reason than Step 4 describes. BedrockAgentCoreApp ’s entrypoint must yield plain, JSON-serializable dictionaries, which its SDK turns into data: {json}

 frames automatically. There’s no way to hand it a raw binary frame. That’s a consequence of the JSON-native managed runtime, not the choice Step 4 measured and moved away from. Both run_bidi and run_batch pay that identical cost on this leg, so the measured difference between them is purely timing: when the first audio chunk is emitted. Testing and validation We isolated the TTS transport’s own contribution to time to first audio by sending the same 267-character, four-sentence block of text two ways: as one message (batch), and as only its first sentence (incremental). We ran five trials each against the live endpoint. As measured earlier, sending only the first sentence cut mean time to first audio byte from 329.3 ms to 156.7 ms, a 52.4 percent relative improvement, isolated to the TTS transport itself. We then measured the fuller, end-to-end case with a real language model producing the text, running the identical prompt through run_bidi and run_batch against the same live Bedrock model and endpoint, so the only variable is when synthesis starts. Using that same methodology, bidi mode’s time to first audio measured 2.4 times faster than batch mode against a local container, and 3.5 times faster against the deployed AgentCore runtime. The following chart shows that gap across both environments: Figure 4: Relative time to first audio for batch and bidi modes, locally and on the deployed runtime The gap widens, rather than narrows, for the deployed case once a real network hop is added. run_bidi absorbs that hop inside the overlap it’s already exploiting between generation and synthesis. run_batch has no equivalent overlap to hide that cost in, since it does one thing at a time, so every added millisecond of network overhead lands directly on its serial wait. To reproduce this comparison against your own deployment, run the same bidi-vs-batch test the agent container exposes: uv run agent-infra demo --endpoint-url --prompt " " This sends the prompt through both modes and reports the timestamp of the first audio_chunk event against agent_start for each. If you see errors instead, check for the KeyError: 'text' symptom from Step 1. An endpoint reporting InService while every request fails signals that bug, not a deployment issue. Clean up To avoid ongoing charges, tear down the resources this walkthrough creates in reverse deployment order, agent first, then endpoint: uv run agent-infra destroy --bedrock-model-id uv run speech-infra destroy kokoro-82m agent-infra destroy removes the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime resource. speech-infra destroy removes the SageMaker AI model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint. Neither empties the Amazon S3 bucket that caches model weights or deletes the Amazon ECR repository holding the container image, since both can be shared across models. If you no longer need them, empty and delete the Amazon S3 bucket and remove the Amazon ECR repository manually, since a stored model checkpoint and container image continue to incur small storage charges until removed. Conclusion We showed how to remove one source of avoidable latency from a voice agent, waiting for an agent’s full response before starting speech synthesis, and how to quantify a second, quieter cost: base64-encoded audio inside SSE inflates payload by about a third and can misalign with MP3 frame boundaries if you don’t buffer for it. Streaming each sentence into a SageMaker AI bidirectional endpoint as soon as an agent produces it cut time to first audio by more than half in isolation, and by 2.4 to 3.5 times in a deployed agent. Multiplexing binary audio and JSON control frames over that session, instead of encoding audio as text, removes the size inflation and frame-realignment work a naive SSE relay requires. If you’re adding voice to an agent that already streams text over SSE, start with the base64 approach in Step 4 and revisit the unified transport once latency becomes the priority. To learn more, see the Amazon SageMaker AI real-time inference documentation and the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation . If you’d like help applying this pattern to your own architecture, contact your AWS account team.   About the author Joseph Cottingham Joseph is a Machine Learning Engineer with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, where he designs and delivers AI systems that move organizations from idea to production. His technical background spans firmware, software, and machine learning, with deep expertise in high-throughput, event-driven architectures that keep AI workloads performant at scale. Joseph focuses on the intersection of state-of-the-art research and operational reality, delivering solutions that materially transform organizations and the systems they operate.

title: Stop guessing auto scaling targets for TTS on Amazon SageMaker AI
summary: Teams deploying custom text-to-speech models on Amazon SageMaker AI often guess at autoscaling thresholds, and a wrong guess either wastes GPU spend or breaches a latency SLO. This post deploys Kokoro-82M as a custom container and derives a measured autoscaling policy from two live-endpoint measurements, Q_max and T_total, instead of guesswork.
content: A traffic spike hits your self-hosted text-to-speech (TTS) endpoint, and requests start queueing. Latency climbs past your service level objective (SLO) right when the most callers are listening. The auto scaling policy behind that endpoint was supposed to prevent this, but the target value it scales on was a guess, and guesses like that fail silently until real traffic proves them wrong. Get that number wrong, and it’s paid for in one of two ways, and neither shows up as an alarm. Guess too conservative, and the fleet runs GPU instances that sit mostly idle. That cost lands on every invoice but never trips an incident report. Guess too aggressive, and the fleet carries a risk nobody sees. Each instance holds more concurrent requests than it can serve inside its latency promise. Nothing looks wrong until a real traffic spike pushes queueing time past the SLO. That happens right when the most callers are listening. That’s the hidden gap. A policy that looks fine on the console can already be failing the people it’s supposed to serve. In this post, we deploy Kokoro-82M , an 82-million-parameter TTS model, as a custom container on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) stacks handle the deployment. We replace guesswork with two measurements taken against the live endpoint. Q_max is the highest concurrency one instance sustains before breaching the SLO, and T_total is how long a scale-out takes end to end. We derive the scale-out threshold, scale-in threshold, and both cooldowns from those two numbers by arithmetic. Every number in this post comes from an actual deployment and measurement run of the aws-samples repository referenced in this post. Why default auto scaling metrics don’t work for TTS Most public guidance on Amazon SageMaker AI auto scaling targets short synchronous request/response calls, or large language model (LLM) serving, where the natural metric is tokens generated per second. TTS synthesis fits neither pattern: a single request holds a connection open for several seconds with no token-generation loop to attach a metric to. Kokoro-82M is non-autoregressive, a StyleTTS2 derivative with an ISTFTNet decoder, trained adversarially rather than by autoregressive next-token prediction or iterative denoising. It produces a full utterance from one duration-aligned pass. There’s no generation loop to instrument with a per-token metric in the first place. What determines whether a TTS instance is overloaded is simpler than it sounds: how many requests are queued and executing on it right now. The deployed policy scales on ConcurrentRequestsPerModel , a native metric Amazon SageMaker AI publishes itself rather than one this project’s own container code has to emit. Scaling on a metric Amazon SageMaker AI publishes removes an entire class of failure where a custom metric configuration looks correct on paper but nothing is actually publishing to it. ConcurrentRequestsPerModel publishes a Maximum statistic over a 10-second window, a different quantity from the mean in-flight count a benchmarking client measures directly. The tooling accounts for this. At every rung of the concurrency ladder it measures both quantities against the same load and records the ratio between them. It then uses that ratio to convert the client-measured threshold into Amazon CloudWatch units before writing it into the deployable configuration. For the Kokoro-82M run in this post, the measured ratio came out to exactly 1.0 at every rung, so the client-measured and Amazon CloudWatch-reported thresholds match directly. Solution overview This solution deploys Kokoro-82M in a custom container on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint, then replaces a guessed auto scaling target with one derived from two measurements taken against that live endpoint: Q_max , the concurrency ceiling one instance serves inside the SLO, and T_total , how long a real scale-out takes. A synthesis request flows through four layers: a client, the Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint, a custom container on a GPU instance behind that endpoint, and the Kokoro-82M model inside the container. Figure 1: The Kokoro-82M request path, from client through the Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint and custom container to the model The container supports two wire transports: response streaming ( InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream ), which streams audio back as it’s synthesized so playback starts before the utterance finishes, and bidirectional streaming ( InvokeEndpointWithBidirectionalStream ), which holds one long-lived session open for multiple messages. Running Kokoro-82M in a custom container, rather than behind a managed inference toolkit, is what makes the rest of this post possible. A container you control can enforce its own admission limits and expose the exact concurrency signal Amazon SageMaker AI already publishes, instead of retrofitting a borrowed metric onto a workload it wasn’t built for. The AWS CDK stacks that deploy this endpoint only attach auto scaling resources once a real, measured plan exists for the model, so a guessed configuration can never reach production silently. The rest of this post is that measurement. Prerequisites To follow this walkthrough, you need: An AWS account with permissions to create AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) buckets, Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repositories, and Amazon SageMaker AI resources. Note: the sample container pins an earlier PyTorch with a known advisory ( PYSEC-2026-2286 , fixed in torch 2.10.0). Review and upgrade the pin before any non-proof-of-value use. AWS CDK v2 , installed and bootstrapped in your target account and region. Python 3.11 or later, uv , and Docker to build the container image. A ml.g5.xlarge service quota with at least one spare slot above your baseline before running the scale-out measurement in this post. The deployment code from the GitHub repository referenced in this post. Walkthrough By the end of this walkthrough, you will have a live Amazon SageMaker AI auto scaling policy for Kokoro-82M, derived entirely from two measurements taken against your own endpoint rather than from a guess. Deploy the endpoint stacks The endpoint deploys through three AWS CDK stacks, applied in order: SpeechFoundationStack creates the IAM roles and the Amazon S3 bucket that caches model weights, SpeechModelCacheStack syncs a model’s Hugging Face weights into that bucket once, and SpeechEndpointStack builds the container image, pushes it to Amazon ECR, and creates the Amazon SageMaker AI model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint. Figure 2: The three AWS CDK stacks and the gate that decides whether auto scaling resources get synthesized The gate on the third stack keeps a default, unmeasured scaling configuration from reaching production. scaling_enabled is a static flag, true whenever max_instances is configured greater than min_instances , and it says nothing on its own about whether the numbers behind it were ever measured. The stack adds a second, independent check at synthesis time: does a real, feasible plan artifact exist for this model? Only when both conditions hold does the stack synthesize scaling resources: an EndpointAutoscaling construct that wires the scaling policy and alarms, and an EndpointObservability construct that adds the dashboards and alarms used to monitor it. A model with scaling_enabled=True but no measurement behind it gets the same no scaling resources output as one with scaling_enabled=False . The project’s CLI wraps the three stacks behind a single command, applying them in dependency order: uv run speech-infra deploy kokoro-82m SpeechModelCacheStack runs an AWS CodeBuild project that syncs the model’s Hugging Face weights into the cached Amazon S3 bucket once. A cold endpoint start doesn’t need to pull them from the internet. Gated by the preceding scaling_enabled check, SpeechEndpointStack builds the container image, pushes it to Amazon ECR, and creates the Amazon SageMaker AI model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint. The methodology packages as a command-line tool chain, run in a fixed order: Figure 3: The tool chain, run in order, each command handing an artifact to the next Step 1: Check for drift drift runs first, every time, before anything that costs money or holds an endpoint under load. It’s a read-only reconciliation between what’s actually deployed (scalable targets, scaling policies, alarm states) and what the config file says should be deployed. An orphaned policy from an earlier model, or a stopped or canceled qmax or ttotal run, would otherwise silently move capacity mid-measurement and corrupt the numbers being measured. uv run tts-bench drift A clean result reports no mismatches and exits with a preflight-ok status, clearing the way for qmax . A stopped or canceled qmax or ttotal run is the most common source of a reported mismatch, because it can leave auto scaling frozen on a single instance. uv run tts-bench thaw --endpoint speech-kokoro-82m restores the deployed policy before you proceed, since qmax and ttotal both assume the deployed state matches the config file exactly. Step 2: Measure Q_max, the concurrency ceiling Q_max is the largest concurrency, requests queued plus requests executing on one instance, at which a request still reaches first audio byte inside the SLO at the 95th percentile. It’s measured with a closed-loop load ladder: hold a fixed concurrency N exactly, and walk N upward one rung at a time until the SLO breaks. A closed loop avoids coordinated omission, the flaw in fixed-arrival-rate tests where a slowing server makes the client send fewer requests instead of surfacing real queueing delay. uv run tts-bench qmax --model kokoro-82m --dry-run uv run tts-bench qmax --model kokoro-82m --dry-run prints the schedule and a wall-clock estimate with zero AWS calls, so you can budget the roughly 36-minute cost of a live run first. The live command freezes auto scaling and pins capacity to one instance for the duration, restored automatically on exit, so the number it produces is a genuine per-instance ceiling. The load ladder recorded the following results: Concurrency p95 TTFAB (ms) Meets 3,000 ms SLO? 1 65.4 yes 5 286.2 yes 10 568.5 yes 20 1,129.3 yes 30 1,689.8 yes 40 2,245.0 yes 50 2,805.7 yes ( Q_max ) 60 3,374.8 no (breach) Figure 4: p95 time-to-first-audio-byte against concurrency, with the SLO line and the breach point at concurrency 60 Q_max = 50 , and it’s a bracketed result: rung 60 actually crossed the SLO, which makes 50 a real ceiling rather than a lower bound. The same run measured the uncontended service time, the time one request takes with no queueing at all: mean 61.3 ms, p95 66.1 ms. That number drives a second, independent alarm described later in this post. Step 3: Measure T_total, the real scale-out time T_total is how long it takes, wall clock, from the moment more capacity is requested to the moment that capacity serves healthy traffic. It’s measured by forcing a scale-out directly, bypassing the deployed policy’s own detection logic, then timestamping every distinguishable stage. uv run tts-bench ttotal --model kokoro-82m --qmax ttotal requires the qmax artifact as input, since its recovery judgment reads off that ladder’s own measured rungs, and refuses to run against a ladder measured on a different wire transport. The forced scale-out broke down into eight measured stages: Stage Duration Share of T_total capacity requested to desired_set 30.0 s 9.4% desired_set to instance visible in logs 180.8 s 56.5% (dominant) instance visible to container started 3.7 s 1.2% container started to framework_init 0.0 s 0.0% framework_init to weights_ready 6.5 s 2.0% weights_ready to warmup_done 1.0 s 0.3% warmup_done to in_service 20.7 s 6.5% in_service to traffic recovered 47.4 s 14.8% measured total (t_total_s) 260.2 s + policy detection lag, bounded (not measured) 60.0 s T_total, planned against 320.2 s Figure 5: The eight measured stages of a real scale-out, from capacity request to recovered traffic The dominant stage is Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance provisioning plus the container image pull, at 181 seconds, 56 percent of the planned-against total. The highest-impact way to reduce T_total isn’t application code, it’s reducing image size or using warm capacity pools. Everything downstream of “instance visible in logs” is a comparatively small 79 seconds combined. The 60-second addition on top of the measured 260.2 seconds isn’t measured in this run. It’s bounded from the policy’s own configuration (alarm evaluation period times evaluation periods, plus cooldown), because this run bypassed the policy’s detection logic on purpose to isolate pure provisioning time. plan sizes surge headroom against the full 320.2-second total, because that reaction time is a real part of any production scale-out even though this measurement excluded it. Step 4: Derive the deployed policy with plan plan is the only command that never touches AWS. It reads the qmax and ttotal artifacts, combines them with two operator-chosen inputs, an SLO of 3,000 ms p95 TTFAB and a surge ratio of 1.25x (the fleet tolerates traffic growing 25 percent within one scale-out cycle without breaching the SLO), and does the following arithmetic. It then prints a report with a verdict for each finding: ok , warn , or, for a genuinely infeasible plan, stop . uv run tts-bench plan --qmax --ttotal --peak-rps 5000 The --peak-rps flag (5,000 requests per second here, alongside an assumed trough of 10) sizes the fleet’s instance count. It doesn’t factor into the threshold arithmetic below. h = surge_ratio - 1 = 1.25 - 1 = 0.25 C_scale_max = (1 - h) x Q_max = 0.75 x 50 = 37.50 C_scale_min = (1 - 2h) x Q_max = 0.50 x 50 = 25.00 W_max = SLO - S_p95 = 3.000s - 0.066s = 2.934s C_scale_max is the concurrency at which one more instance is added, below Q_max by the surge fraction h , so the fleet still has queue headroom when it asks for more capacity. C_scale_min is the concurrency at or below which one instance is removed, set at (1 - 2h) of Q_max so scale-in triggers only once load has fallen well below where scale-out would trigger again. The final deployed configuration, exactly as produced by the tooling: "kokoro-82m": ModelEndpointConfig( model_name="kokoro-82m", instance_type="ml.g5.xlarge", min_instances=1, # trough 10 rps; 3 is the smallest safe floor for scale-in max_instances=9, # peak 5000 rps scaling_target_value=37.500, # C_scale_max, in Amazon CloudWatch units (ratio measured as 1.0) scale_in_threshold=25.000, # C_scale_min, in Amazon CloudWatch units ttfab_slo_ms=3000, queue_max_depth=50, # enforced by the container's own admission gate scale_out_cooldown_s=30, # short: one instance added at a time scale_in_cooldown_s=960, # long: see below ) The two cooldowns are asymmetric on purpose. Scaling out is cheap to be wrong about: worst case, you paid for one instance you didn’t need for thirty extra seconds. Scaling in isn’t symmetric in cost, since capacity removed and later needed again costs a full T_total (320 seconds) to replace. The scale-in cooldown is set to roughly three times T_total , so a scale-in decision only fires once load has genuinely, sustainedly dropped. The container’s own admission control separately enforces queue_max_depth=50 , equal to Q_max : past that depth, a request is refused immediately with a 503 queue_saturated response rather than left to queue past the point it could meet the SLO. A FirstChunkLatencyP95 alarm, thresholded at 65 ms (the measured p95 service time at concurrency 1), watches service time on an instance already serving, tighter than the end-to-end SLO, which includes queuing. Two findings from the Kokoro-82M run are worth including, because they’re the tool correctly surfacing a known, accepted trade-off rather than a defect: surge_survival (warn): Holding C_scale_max (37.5) against Q_max (50) puts one instance at 97.4% utilization the moment a scale-out triggers, and a replacement takes a full T_total to arrive. The surge ratio reserves extra queue slots, but surviving a real surge is about flow, how fast the queue drains, and there’s little flow headroom left at 97.4 percent utilization. scale_in_safety (warn): Removing one instance from a fleet of N multiplies every remaining instance’s concurrency by N / (N-1) . Scale-in stays stable only once that ratio holds under C_scale_max / C_scale_min (1.5 here), which requires N >= 3 . With a floor of 1 instance, a scale-in from 2 to 1 lands the survivor at exactly Q_max , right back at the ceiling that triggers another scale-out. The long cooldown damps this flapping without eliminating it. Raising the floor to 3 would remove it structurally, at the cost of standing capacity during low traffic. Every qmax or ttotal artifact’s file name encodes the configuration it was measured against, instance type and container image digest condensed into a slug (for example, g5xlarge-8b1b96bc ). ttotal and plan both refuse to pair artifacts whose fingerprints disagree. That’s downgradable to a warning with --allow-config-mismatch , but refusal is the default. Step 5: Confirm the deployed policy with validate validate is the last command in the chain, and the second one, alongside drift , that never mutates anything. It compares the scaling policy actually deployed against the values in the plan artifact, confirming the two match before you treat the configuration as live. uv run tts-bench validate --model kokoro-82m --plan A clean result confirms scaling_target_value , scale_in_threshold , and both cooldowns on the deployed scalable target match what plan derived. Any mismatch means the deployed policy and the measured plan have drifted apart, and should be resolved before relying on the endpoint’s auto scaling behavior. Testing and validation Every qmax , ttotal , and plan artifact referenced in this post is a committed file in the repository, not a one-off local output. The preceding worked example, including every number, is independently reproducible by re-running plan against the two committed measurement files, with zero AWS calls and zero new spend: $ uv run tts-bench plan --qmax --ttotal --peak-rps 5000 scaling_target_value : 37.500 (C_scale_max) scale_in_threshold : 25.000 (C_scale_min) surge_survival : warn scale_in_safety : warn Clean up To remove the resources created in this walkthrough, tear down the stacks in reverse order with a single command: uv run speech-infra destroy kokoro-82m speech-infra destroy removes the Amazon SageMaker AI model, endpoint configuration, endpoint, and any auto scaling or Amazon CloudWatch resources attached to it. It doesn’t empty the Amazon S3 bucket that caches model weights or delete the Amazon ECR repository holding the container image, since both can be shared across models. If you no longer need them, empty and delete the Amazon S3 bucket and remove the Amazon ECR repository manually, since a stored model checkpoint and container image continue to incur small storage charges until removed. Conclusion Deploy Kokoro-82M as a custom container on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint, and replace guesswork with two measurements taken against the live endpoint: Q_max , the highest concurrency one instance sustains before breaching the SLO, and T_total , how long a real scale-out takes. You derive the scale-out threshold, scale-in threshold, and both cooldowns from those two numbers by arithmetic. Scaling on ConcurrentRequestsPerModel , a native, AWS-published metric, and measuring its unit conversion directly rather than assuming it, is what keeps this configuration tied to real concurrency. The result is an auto scaling policy where every number traces back to a real measurement against your own endpoint, not an assumption carried over from a different workload shape. That distinction is what turns a config-file guess, one that silently overpays or silently breaches its SLO, into a policy you can defend with a specific concurrency ceiling and a specific scale-out time, both measured, not asserted. Nothing about this four-number model, SLO and surge ratio chosen, Q_max and T_total measured, the rest derived, is specific to TTS. It generalizes to latency-sensitive, concurrency-bound, real-time Amazon SageMaker AI endpoints. For example, a real-time image-embedding endpoint that holds each request open through a GPU forward pass is bound by the same concurrency ceiling, not by a throughput metric. The same qmax / ttotal / plan chain applies unchanged. The real bottleneck there is concurrent in-flight requests rather than a throughput metric borrowed from a different workload shape. The specific numbers here, Q_max=50 and T_total=320s , are true for Kokoro-82M on ml.g5.xlarge . They will differ for a different model or instance type. The methodology and tooling that produce them don’t. The five-command tool chain, drift , qmax , ttotal , plan , and validate , carries over unchanged to the next model you deploy this way. Clone the sample repository , then run the five-command chain, drift , qmax , ttotal , plan , and validate , against your own endpoint to produce a measured policy. Review the Amazon SageMaker AI auto scaling documentation to adapt the thresholds to your SLO, and open the SageMaker AI console to watch the policy react to live traffic. If you’d like help building a similar measurement-driven deployment, contact your AWS account team.   About the author Joseph Cottingham Joseph is a Machine Learning Engineer with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, where he designs and delivers AI systems that move organizations from idea to production. His technical background spans firmware, software, and machine learning, with deep expertise in high-throughput, event-driven architectures that keep AI workloads performant at scale. Joseph focuses on the intersection of state-of-the-art research and operational reality, delivering solutions that materially transform organizations and the systems they operate.

title: How Rescale built an AI triage agent with Strands Agents and AI-DLC
summary: Rescale used the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC) framework on AWS, with Strands Agents and Amazon Bedrock, to build an intelligent test-triage agent in weeks. Learn how AI-DLC structures AI-assisted development and how Rescale is scaling the practice across its engineering organization.
content: Every engineering team knows the ritual, and Rescale was no exception. A nightly test suite fails. An on-call engineer pulls the logs, classifies the root cause, and routes it to the right team, only to repeat the process the next morning. At scale, across distributed services and dozens of repositories, this ritual becomes a full-time job hiding inside an on-call rotation. Rescale is the digital engineering platform built for the AI era. R&D and engineering teams across aerospace, automotive, energy, life sciences, semiconductor, and manufacturing use the Rescale platform to accelerate innovation, bringing intelligent HPC, advanced modeling and simulation, agentic digital engineering, and AI physics together on a single platform. Beyond coding, Rescale uses AI across the engineering lifecycle, from planning and design through implementation, testing, review, and operations, while keeping engineers accountable for the result. AI can propose and execute, but people define scope, validate the work, and approve production changes. Engineers can then focus on architecture, product judgment, and the context required to operate complex distributed systems. In this post, we show how Rescale used the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC) framework on AWS to build an intelligent triage agent. They went from problem definition to staging deployment in five days, and to production within weeks. The post also covers how Rescale is extending AI-DLC across their engineering organization. The challenge As Rescale’s platform grew, so did the operational overhead of keeping it running. Engineers were spending significant time on a repetitive but critical task: classifying automated end-to-end test failures. Hundreds of test cases run in the suite, and when failures appeared, every alert, bug report, and escalation needed to be classified, prioritized, and routed to the right team. After routing, engineers would need to gather evidence from multiple logging and monitoring systems, along with several source repositories before debugging could even begin. Passing end-to-end tests were required to deploy services to production and thus debugging these system failures was in the critical path to getting new changes to production. In the manual workflow, engineers moved from the test report to logs, historical patterns, and source code to classify failures and identify the likely owning team. Because these integration tests gate weekly production releases, unresolved failures could pull several teams into hours of coordination before a deployment was allowed to proceed. The team had a clear idea of what a solution looked like: an intelligent agent that could classify and route issues automatically. What they were looking for was a structured way to go from that understanding to a working system in production, with enough structure to extend the approach to other use cases afterward. Why Rescale chose AI-DLC Rescale’s triage agent was a well-scoped problem with a tight timeline. The team needed a development approach that could move at that pace without skipping the architectural decisions that would determine whether the system worked in production. The AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC) is an open source, AI-centric methodology for software development built around two ideas: AI executes, humans decide: AI generates work plans, writes code, and proposes architecture, but it surfaces decision points and asks clarifying questions rather than guessing. Humans validate and steer at each step. Team sessions replace async handoffs: Instead of one person building alone and requesting review later, AI-DLC uses focused group sessions: Mob Elaboration (defining requirements together) and Mob Construction (building together while AI handles implementation). Decisions happen in real time. AI-DLC fit because the hard part wasn’t writing code. It was making sure the AI understood what the team wanted to build. In mob sessions, Rescale engineers answered the AI’s questions together and approved each plan before the AI moved on, so nothing was left to assumptions. Solution overview Rescale’s triage agent automates the classification and routing of nightly end-to-end test failures. It runs as a step within Rescale’s existing Argo Workflows continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipeline on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). When a nightly Playwright suite of hundreds of test cases produces failures, the pipeline triggers the triage agent pod. The agent performs the following steps: Invokes Claude Opus 4.8 on Amazon Bedrock to classify each failure into a root cause category: infrastructure issue, code bug, flaky test, or environment problem. Retrieves relevant historical failure patterns from a knowledge base for additional context. Queries pod logs through Model Context Protocol (MCP) for runtime evidence supporting the classification. Generates a structured remediation report with specific file references, function names, and recommended fixes for engineer review before any action is taken. The agent completes this workflow in seconds and outputs directly into the team’s existing reporting pipeline. The following diagram shows how these components fit together: Figure 1: Architecture for Rescale’s AI triage agent, running on Amazon EKS with Amazon Bedrock for classification, a knowledge base for historical failure patterns, and MCP-based log retrieval through Amazon CloudWatch integration The AI-DLC workshop experience The engagement was structured as a five-day, in-person workshop. AWS architects guided the build while Rescale engineers worked hands-on-keyboard, co-building in real time. Inception phase (days 1–2): From vision to validated requirements The team started by scoping requirements, capturing the intent in a vision document and a technical environment document that grounded the work before any building began. That intent began as a single statement, “We want AI-powered test triage that classifies failures and recommends remediation”. Working collaboratively in mob format, the team answered 20+ clarification questions generated by AI. This produced a scoped requirements document with Phase 1 boundaries explicitly defined and Phase 2 items deferred. Five user stories were consolidated into four units of work: Knowledge base for historical failure patterns. AI triage agent as the core classification and remediation engine. Argo Workflow Integration for trigger, infrastructure, and deployment. Evaluation Harness for accuracy measurement and regression gating. Human decisions drove the critical boundaries: what belongs in Phase 1 versus Phase 2, priority ordering, and deferred features like automated pull request (PR) generation. Construction phase (days 2–4): Architecture to running code The team defined interface contracts and data schemas, completed functional and non-functional design questions, and signed off on the architecture. Two architecture pivots emerged during the build, and the team validated each one before changing course. First, the team planned to host the agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, then moved it to Amazon EKS, where Rescale already runs its Argo Workflows CI/CD pipeline. Keeping the agent in the existing cluster meant no new runtime to operate and a direct trigger path from Argo. Second, in the early build the agent pulled log evidence from a third-party logging service through MCP. The team moved log retrieval to Amazon CloudWatch, which simplified the dependency chain. The MCP pattern stayed the same. Only the source behind it changed. Because AI-DLC keeps requirements and design decisions in shared documents, the team updated them in place and kept building without losing context. The agent was built using the Strands SDK, supporting concurrent failure analysis with structured output in JSON and HTML, containerized on Amazon EKS. By Day 4, the full pipeline was running in staging: Argo workflow trigger, triage agent pod, MCP log query, knowledge base retrieval, and structured triage output. Operations phase (day 5): Evaluation and handoff The team built a PyTest-based evaluation framework with live and stubbed test modes, establishing an initial classification-agreement baseline to measure the agent against and improve from. The agent was demoed live to Rescale’s CTO and VP of Engineering, correctly classifying both an infrastructure failure and a real code bug with specific file-level fix recommendations. How AI-DLC scaled rigor to complexity Not every unit of work gets the same treatment. The knowledge base needed minimal design and deployed using Terraform in hours. The Triage Agent got full rigor: architecture review, interface contracts, 12 design questions, and iterative code review. Argo Integration focused on infrastructure contracts and IAM. The Evaluation Harness used lightweight design but heavy implementation. AI-DLC matched depth to complexity automatically. By the end of Day 5, the agent was live in staging, processing real test failures with a measured accuracy baseline and a clear path to production. Production outcomes The triage agent has been running in production since the workshop. It automatically classifies nightly end-to-end test failures, replacing manual first-pass triage with an automated first pass that engineers validate. For each failure, the agent generates a structured remediation report with actionable next steps rather than raw logs. The agent’s classification agreement with human triage has risen from 44% at initial deployment to 68% today. It continues to improve as the team iterates on the golden dataset and prompt engineering. Since the triage agent entered production, the team has measured a 20% decrease in time blocking production deployment while test failures are analyzed. Because these tests gate Rescale’s weekly production releases, that reduction shows up directly in how quickly changes reach production. Engineers also spend less of the on-call rotation on repetitive classification. Life after the workshop: From one agent to an AI-first practice The workshop delivered one production agent, but its larger effect was on how Rescale approaches engineering work. The triage agent is part of a broader push at Rescale to deliver digital engineering capabilities for the AI era. Internally, Rescale is applying these same benefits realized from AI across its own engineering organization. AI-DLC gave Rescale’s engineers a structured, repeatable way to put that direction into practice. Scaling AI-DLC across the organization Rescale is evaluating an internal AI-DLC Center of Excellence , a small group that codifies best practices and helps other teams adopt the methodology independently. The engineers who participated are already applying what they learned. One of the engineers noted that the process “will be part of my workflow going forward,” not only for building agents, but for any complex development work where AI can contribute. Broader AI-native development Rescale is now incorporating AI-DLC into the standard software development lifecycle for new engineering simulation products. The framework brings simulation-domain expertise, product requirements, platform architecture, validation, and operations into one structured design process. Teams resolve key questions early, capture reviewed decisions in executable specifications, and give coding agents focused work with clear acceptance criteria. This shortens the path from product concept to validated implementation while engineers remain accountable for product correctness. The same approach is already being used in product-enabling platform work and agent systems: HPC simulation application catalog management. Container vulnerability tracking and remediation for government compliance requirements. Workflow-based cloud coding agents. Conclusion For the triage agent, the most useful output of AI-DLC was not the code itself. It was the structured path from an initial idea to a reviewed system design: clarifying questions, scoped requirements, and evaluation criteria. That specification gave coding agents a narrower, better-defined problem to solve. Instead of asking an agent to infer the architecture while implementing it, the team could use agents for focused construction against decisions that humans had already reviewed. The result was more focused, reviewable output that was easier to integrate and improve. For Rescale, that is the repeatable pattern: use AI-DLC to structure the design conversation, turn the decisions into a specification, and then use coding agents to accelerate implementation. Key takeaways Start with a real problem. Rescale’s triage agent succeeded because it solved an engineering challenge. The problem drove the solution, not the other way around. Human oversight accelerates, not decelerates. Every architecture pivot that improved the system came from human validation of AI proposals. The mob format, where AI generates and humans validate, is faster than working alone. The AWS stack provided each layer the agent needed. Amazon Bedrock supplied foundation-model access for classification in an environment Rescale was already using, so the team could build the triage workflow without taking on additional model-infrastructure overhead. The Strands SDK provided the agent framework, and Amazon EKS hosted the containerized agent within Rescale’s existing pipeline.
