title: Train Qwen3 on AWS Trainium with torchtitan
summary: Train Qwen3 on AWS Trainium with torchtitan three ways on a single trn2.48xlarge: the Hugging Face Transformers v5 modeling backend, torchtitan's native Qwen3, and NKI mixture-of-experts kernels. The same torchrun launcher and config structure work unchanged across all three paths, including loading and saving published Hugging Face safetensors.
content: Using torchtitan on AWS Trainium means using it the way you always have. TorchNeuron registers Trainium as a native PyTorch device, which lets torchtitan use it through standard PyTorch interfaces. You can use these configurations to pre-train from random initialization or fine-tune published weights. You can also customize the model implementation and kernels for your workload. In this post, you train Qwen3 three ways on a single trn2.48xlarge . The first method uses Transformers v5 as a modeling backend in torchtitan. It runs Hub models through AutoModelForCausalLM and reads and writes published safetensors directly. The second method switches to torchtitan’s native Qwen3 by changing config.model_spec . The third adds Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) mixture-of-experts (MoE) kernels from the torchtitan-neuron recipes and then uses torchtitan’s override registry to attach your own kernel. All three configurations use the same torchrun launch pattern and config structure. Prerequisites To follow this walkthrough, use a single trn2.48xlarge with either the AWS Deep Learning AMI for Neuron or a Neuron PyTorch training container. Both environments provide the Neuron driver, runtime, and compiler required to train on Trainium. Before you install torchtitan-neuron , check whether your environment already includes it. The following command prints the installed version and package path: python3 -c "import torchtitan, torchtitan_neuron; print(torchtitan.__version__, torchtitan_neuron.__file__)" This walkthrough uses the versions in the following table. To reproduce the examples, pin these versions. The Transformers v5 integration and Trainium-specific override modules can change between torchtitan releases. Component Version Instance trn2.48xlarge, 16 Trainium2 accelerators, 128 physical NeuronCores Logical NeuronCores 64 at LNC=2 torch, torch_neuronx 2.14.0, 2.14.3 transformers 5.16.0 torchtitan-neuron release-2.33 (0.2.2+neuron.1) When torch_neuronx is installed, TorchNeuron registers Trainium as the neuron device and torchtitan detects it at startup. In eager mode, Neuron compiles operations as they execute. With torch.compile , Neuron compiles the captured graph. This same launch pattern works across all three configurations. For the versions used in this walkthrough, install torchtitan-neuron and torchtitan’s remaining dependencies with --no-deps to preserve the Neuron build of torch: git clone https://github.com/aws-neuron/torchtitan-neuron cd torchtitan-neuron pip install -r requirements.txt Before you start training, get the Qwen3 model artifacts from Hugging Face Hub. Store them in a local directory that you can pass to the training config: hf download Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 \ --local-dir "$PWD/assets/hf/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507" Each training configuration is a Python config function. The three examples start from a base config that you update for each step. Train with Hugging Face Transformers v5 In the first configuration, Transformers v5 builds Qwen3 through AutoModelForCausalLM . The Hub model definition supplies the implementation used for the forward and backward passes. You select the model by setting its Hub ID in the config. Start with transformers_modeling_backend_full() . It leaves the fields that map to Hugging Face configuration keys unset, so AutoConfig.from_pretrained() loads the model architecture from the Hub. Create neuron_qwen3.py in the torchtitan-neuron repository root, where you run the training command. Add the imports, model artifact path, and base config: import os from torchtitan.experiments.transformers_modeling_backend.config_registry import ( transformers_modeling_backend_full, ) from torchtitan.experiments.transformers_modeling_backend.configs import ( TransformersBackendConfig, ) ASSETS = os.path.abspath("./assets/hf/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507") def v5_qwen3_4b() -> TransformersBackendConfig: config = transformers_modeling_backend_full() config.hf_model = "Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507" config.hf_assets_path = ASSETS config.dataloader.dataset = "c4_test" config.training.steps = 10 config.training.local_batch_size = 1 config.parallelism.data_parallel_shard_degree = -1 return config torchrun --nproc_per_node=64 --rdzv_backend c10d --rdzv_endpoint localhost:0 \ --local-ranks-filter 0 --role rank --tee 3 \ -m torchtitan.train --module neuron_qwen3 --config v5_qwen3_4b This command launches 64 training processes, one for each logical NeuronCore. --module neuron_qwen3 imports the local config module. --config v5_qwen3_4b selects the configuration function. The data parallel setting shards the model across all 64 ranks. Load and save Hugging Face checkpoints To fine-tune from published weights, enable checkpoint loading and point initial_load_path to ASSETS . The state-dictionary adapter adjusts the leading model. prefix and handles tied embeddings. It saves the final checkpoint as Hugging Face safetensors. def v5_qwen3_4b_finetune() -> TransformersBackendConfig: config = v5_qwen3_4b() config.checkpoint.enable = True config.checkpoint.folder = "checkpoint_qwen3_4b_ft" config.checkpoint.initial_load_path = ASSETS # absolute path required config.checkpoint.initial_load_in_hf = True config.checkpoint.initial_load_model_only = True config.checkpoint.last_save_in_hf = True config.checkpoint.last_save_model_only = True return config Use the first training-step loss as a quick check that torchtitan loaded the published weights. For Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 , the verified run produced a step 1 loss of 6.54 from published weights and 12.43 from random initialization. After training, load the exported checkpoint with AutoModelForCausalLM and load_state_dict . A successful round trip reports no missing or unexpected keys other than lm_head.weight , which Qwen3-4B ties to the token embeddings. This confirms that the files remain a standard Hugging Face checkpoint. Figure 1: The published checkpoint starts with a loss of 6.54, and the exported weights load without missing or unexpected keys Train with torchtitan’s native models In the second configuration, torchtitan builds its native Qwen3Model . Add the native Qwen3 imports and config function to neuron_qwen3.py : This example starts from qwen3_32b() because the tested torchtitan build does not provide a generic qwen3_4b() config builder. The next line replaces the 32B model specification with the 4B specification. The remaining fields reproduce the tested run. from torchtitan.models.qwen3 import model_registry from torchtitan.models.qwen3.config_registry import qwen3_32b from torchtitan.trainer import Trainer def native_qwen3_4b() -> Trainer.Config: config = qwen3_32b() config.model_spec = model_registry("4B", attn_backend="sdpa") config.hf_assets_path = ASSETS config.dataloader.dataset = "c4_test" config.training.steps = 10 config.training.local_batch_size = 1 config.training.global_batch_size = 64 config.parallelism.data_parallel_shard_degree = -1 return config torchrun --nproc_per_node=64 --rdzv_backend c10d --rdzv_endpoint localhost:0 \ --local-ranks-filter 0 --role rank --tee 3 \ -m torchtitan.train --module neuron_qwen3 --config native_qwen3_4b config.model_spec selects the model class and defines how torchtitan shards the model and maps its checkpoint keys. Here, model_registry("4B", attn_backend="sdpa") selects torchtitan’s native Qwen3 implementation with scaled dot product attention (SDPA). Add NKI kernels for mixture of experts In the third configuration, torchtitan runs mixture-of-experts layers with kernels written in NKI, the Neuron kernel language. Add the required imports and Qwen3 MoE config function to neuron_qwen3.py : from torchtitan.config import CompileConfig from torchtitan_neuron.models.qwen3.config_registry import qwen3_nki_moe_config def nki_qwen3_30b_a3b() -> Trainer.Config: config = qwen3_nki_moe_config( "30B-A3B", compile_config=CompileConfig(enable=False, backend="neuron"), n_layers=4, num_experts=64, top_k=4, ) config.hf_assets_path = ASSETS return config torchrun --nproc_per_node=64 --rdzv_backend c10d --rdzv_endpoint localhost:0 \ --local-ranks-filter 0 --role rank --tee 3 \ -m torchtitan.train --module neuron_qwen3 --config nki_qwen3_30b_a3b This configuration uses data parallel sharding across 64 ranks with a tensor parallel degree of 1. It does not use expert parallelism. num_experts=64 sets the number of experts in the model, not the expert parallel degree. Setting CompileConfig(enable=False) runs this example in eager mode. TorchNeuron supports registered NKI operators in both eager execution and torch.compile . In the torchtitan build used for this walkthrough, qwen3_nki_moe_config() replaces the MoE block with the NKI grouped-experts implementation. It also selects SDPA and the gather-free rotary embedding. When you enable torch.compile , add "grad_clip" to CompileConfig.components to compile gradient-norm clipping. NKI kernels enter training as PyTorch operators. wrap_nki makes an NKI kernel callable from PyTorch, and nki_op registers the operator. register_autograd attaches its backward pass using routing metadata saved during the forward pass. The example reduces Qwen3-30B-A3B to 4 layers and 64 experts so it fits on one trn2.48xlarge . It routes each token to 4 experts with top_k=4 . Attach your own NKI kernel In some cases, you might want to optimize an operation for the tensor shapes in your model. A specialized kernel can tailor its tiling and data movement to those shapes. It can also replace a performance-critical sequence of PyTorch operations with one optimized operator. You can write the kernel yourself or start with one from nkilib . This example uses rope_hf from nkilib.core.embeddings , which expects the Hugging Face tensor layout and supports its own backward mode. This example demonstrates kernel registration and autograd integration, not a performance improvement. Create my_neuron_kernels.py in the repository root, where you launch training. torchtitan stores query and key as [batch, seq, heads, head_dim] , whereas rope_hf expects [batch, heads, seq, head_dim] . Convert the layout inside the operator and allocate the output tensors with torch.empty_like() : import torch from nkilib.core.embeddings.rope_hf import rope_hf from torch_neuronx import nki_op from torch_neuronx.nki_hop import wrap_nki from torch_neuronx.utils import get_logical_neuron_cores LNC = (int(get_logical_neuron_cores()),) wrapped_rope = wrap_nki(rope_hf) @nki_op("my_kernels::rope_fwd") def rope_fwd(query, key, rope_cache): q = query.permute(0, 2, 1, 3).contiguous() k = key.permute(0, 2, 1, 3).contiguous() cache = rope_cache.reshape(-1, rope_cache.shape[-1]) q_out, k_out = wrapped_rope[LNC]( q, k, torch.empty_like(q), torch.empty_like(k), rope_cache=cache, ) return ( q_out.permute(0, 2, 1, 3).contiguous(), k_out.permute(0, 2, 1, 3).contiguous(), ) rope_hf computes gradients when you call it with backward=True . Register a second operator for that mode. Save the rotary cache during the forward pass so the backward pass can reuse it. Return None for the cache gradient because the cache is not differentiable. @nki_op("my_kernels::rope_bwd") def rope_bwd(grad_query, grad_key, rope_cache): gq = grad_query.permute(0, 2, 1, 3).contiguous() gk = grad_key.permute(0, 2, 1, 3).contiguous() cache = rope_cache.reshape(-1, rope_cache.shape[-1]) out_q, out_k = wrapped_rope[LNC]( gq, gk, torch.empty_like(gq), torch.empty_like(gk), rope_cache=cache, backward=True, ) return ( out_q.permute(0, 2, 1, 3).contiguous(), out_k.permute(0, 2, 1, 3).contiguous(), ) def _setup_context(ctx, inputs, output): ctx.save_for_backward(inputs[2]) def _backward(ctx, grad_query, grad_key): (rope_cache,) = ctx.saved_tensors grad_q, grad_k = rope_bwd(grad_query, grad_key, rope_cache) return grad_q, grad_k, None rope_fwd.register_autograd(_backward, setup_context=_setup_context) Because rope_hf requires a supported sequence length, validate that constraint before calling the kernel. Subclass CosSinRoPE and call rope_fwd from apply_rotary_emb : from dataclasses import dataclass from torchtitan.config import derive, override from torchtitan.models.common.rope import CosSinRoPE class NKIRoPE(CosSinRoPE): @dataclass(kw_only=True, slots=True) class Config(CosSinRoPE.Config): pass @staticmethod def apply_rotary_emb(query, key, rope_cache): stride = 128 * LNC[0] if query.shape[1] % stride: raise ValueError( f"rope_hf requires a sequence length that is a multiple of " f"128 * LNC={stride}, got {query.shape[1]}" ) q_out, k_out = rope_fwd(query, key, rope_cache) return q_out.type_as(query), k_out.type_as(key) Register NKIRoPE as the replacement for CosSinRoPE . derive() copies the shared configuration fields into the replacement config: @override( "nki_rope", target=CosSinRoPE.Config, exact=True, description="nkilib rope_hf kernel in place of the PyTorch rotation", ) def _nki_rope(cfg: CosSinRoPE.Config) -> NKIRoPE.Config: return derive(cfg, NKIRoPE.Config) To load the custom override, pass its module name to --override.imports . torchtitan imports the registry entry before it builds the model: torchrun --nproc_per_node=64 --rdzv_backend c10d --rdzv_endpoint localhost:0 \ --local-ranks-filter 0 --role rank --tee 3 \ -m torchtitan.train --module neuron_qwen3 --config native_qwen3_4b \ --override.imports my_neuron_kernels Before training starts, torchtitan logs each config node that the override replaces. Confirm that the output contains one nki_rope entry for each Qwen3 layer: [Override] nki_rope: model_spec.model.layers.0.attention.rope CosSinRoPEConfig -> NKIRoPE.Config [Override] nki_rope: model_spec.model.layers.1.attention.rope CosSinRoPEConfig -> NKIRoPE.Config Set the sequence length to a multiple of 128 * LNC , which is 256 when LNC is 2. Reshape the rotary cache to [seq, head_dim * 2] , with cosine values in the first half and sine values in the second. The kernel validates these constraints before training begins. For a complete torchtitan example, see torchtitan_neuron/models/gpt_oss/nki_attention.py . It connects nkilib flash-attention kernels through the same operator and override mechanisms. It also handles DTensor inputs for tensor parallelism. Before you train with a custom kernel, compare its outputs with the implementation it replaces. In the numerical test with float32 inputs, rope_hf and torchtitan’s PyTorch rotary embedding produced a maximum absolute difference of 0.0 for both query and key. When you register multiple overrides, limit each one to the intended module instances with fqns . For example, fqns=["layers.1[0-9].attention.rope"] targets the rotary embedding in layers 10 through 19. torchtitan stops when two overrides claim the same node and warns when an override matches no nodes. Review the training output At startup, confirm that torchtitan reports 64 ranks and the expected model. The first step includes compilation and takes longer than later steps. Each training step reports the loss, gradient norm, high-bandwidth memory (HBM) usage, throughput, and model FLOPs utilization (MFU). For the checkpoint run, confirm that the first-step loss is near 6.54. For the custom kernel run, confirm that the nki_rope override appears once for each Qwen3 layer. Scale across the instance The same parallelism settings apply to the Transformers and native model configurations. A trn2.48xlarge exposes 64 logical NeuronCores at LNC=2. Set data_parallel_shard_degree = -1 to shard the model parameters, gradients, and optimizer state across every rank that torchrun starts. Set config.parallelism.tensor_parallel_degree to shard each layer’s weights across a group of ranks. Each rank computes a slice of every matrix multiplication. With sequence parallelism enabled by default, normalization layers run on activations sharded along the sequence dimension. torchtitan combines tensor parallelism with Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) on a multidimensional DeviceMesh . Watch per-rank HBM as you increase the model size, sequence length, or local batch size. These values determine how much memory each rank requires. Clean up If you want to keep your checkpoints, copy them to persistent storage before you clean up. If you plan to reuse the instance, stop it . When you no longer need the instance, terminate it . Conclusion AWS Trainium works as a supported torchtitan device across all three configurations in this walkthrough. You can train Qwen3 through Hugging Face Transformers v5 and load or save published safetensors directly. You can also train with torchtitan’s native Qwen3 implementation by setting config.model_spec . For mixture-of-experts models, use the torchtitan-neuron NKI recipes. For custom kernels, use the override registry to attach NKI operators through the same launch flow. For setup guidance, see the AWS Neuron documentation . For current source and training recipes, see the torchtitan repository. About the authors Josh Longenecker Josh is a Solutions Architect on the Annapurna Labs ML accelerator team at AWS. He helps customers design, optimize, and deploy distributed AI training and inference workloads on AWS Trainium. His technical interests include distributed PyTorch, large language model training and inference, and NKI kernels. Alex Hoffman Alex is a Software Engineer working on distributed training at AWS Annapurna Labs. He enables end-to-end training experiences for AWS Trainium customers on TorchNeuron with torchtitan-neuron.

title: How U.S. Hunger connects leaders and data using Amazon Quick
summary: U.S. Hunger, a nonprofit addressing food insecurity, uses Amazon Quick to connect organizational data with leadership decisions. Leaders explore applicant data directly, share KPI definitions and financial context in Quick Spaces, and investigate policy questions with Quick Research.
content: For U.S. Hunger, feeding families takes more than delivering food to them. It takes understanding the people behind each request, the pressures they face, and the business that makes the mission possible. That means connecting information across the organization. Its mission is to feed families today and unite them to a healthier tomorrow. U.S. Hunger reports delivering more than 250 million meals. Its work has reached 59 countries historically and is now concentrated primarily in the United States. The organization reports approximately 500 percent growth over four years, compared with only 15–20 percent headcount growth. For a lean team at that scale, every hour and every decision matters. With Amazon Quick , U.S. Hunger can explore organizational data directly, colleagues can work from shared definitions, and leaders can examine financial information alongside the circumstances families report. U.S. Hunger’s experience shows how those capabilities fit into the daily work of a lean nonprofit. From banking to feeding families Rick Whitted spent 30 years in banking before making the leap to lead U.S. Hunger. His connection to food insecurity, however, began long before that career change. When Rick and his wife were in their mid-twenties, he left his career to start a business. They lost everything. Even though he went to work every day, they relied on help from family to get by. He remembers coming home to find a pantry box on the table, left by aunts or grandparents. Seeing that box broke him. More than 20 years later, when the board chair asked him to consider leading U.S. Hunger, his wife reminded him of those days, when their own family needed help putting food on the table. To her, leading U.S. Hunger was a chance to help families going through what they had experienced themselves. Rick cried, called the chair back, and accepted. “The families we serve today, their stories are my story.” — Rick Whitted, President and CEO, U.S. Hunger More than six years into the role, that personal connection remains at the heart of Rick’s leadership. From data requests to direct exploration U.S. Hunger first learned about Quick through an AWS Social Entrepreneur Accelerator event led by Kat Esser. Rick saw an opportunity to explore the organization’s data directly, following questions as they arose without asking the technology team for a new data pull each time. Chief technology officer (CTO) Ezekiel Brooks helped make that possible by giving Rick access to core datasets from Full Cart, U.S. Hunger’s food-assistance program. Full Cart delivers donor-funded food directly to households in need. Quick gave Rick room to explore the information at his own pace and ask follow-up questions. The organization’s data became his sandbox. The data comes from Impact Manager, U.S. Hunger’s proprietary cloud-based data platform supporting its food-assistance work. Quick pulls data from SQL Server into its in-memory engine, SPICE , through scheduled refresh jobs at 2 AM ET each night. The technology team and a colleague working with research data prepare the datasets and provide definitions to help Rick interpret the information. Figure 1: U.S. Hunger refreshes SQL Server data into SPICE at 2 AM ET each night for analysis in Amazon Quick Direct exploration was the starting point, but the moment when everything clicked came with a different discovery: Quick Spaces . The moment Quick became an enterprise tool For Rick, Spaces changed the role Quick could play in the organization. A Space gives colleagues a shared place to work with documents, definitions, and analyses relevant to a particular area of the business. That matters when leaders need to understand one another’s work and make decisions together. Shared definitions of key performance indicators (KPIs) help them agree on what a measure means. Financial documents and planning tools provide context for discussions about the organization’s resources. Rick sees this as his a-ha moment: using Quick to help the leadership team run the organization together. “Quick provides a live connection to how leadership thinks through problems. I can pick up where our CEO left off in a financial model or see how he’s framing a KPI, without scheduling another meeting.” — Sarah Aranguibel, Chief of Staff, U.S. Hunger The leadership team brings together a shared document of KPIs, developed over more than a year while working across NetSuite, Salesforce, Impact Manager, and its payroll system. The document records definitions, where measures come from, and goals. Rick also uses Quick to develop definitions for client tiers and shares them in the same Space. “With all the knowledge and data we have, Space reduces as much noise as possible and narrows my discussion.” — Rick Whitted, President and CEO, U.S. Hunger Selecting the Space relevant to a question keeps the conversation focused on the right documents. The financial Space is shared with the CTO, chief operating officer (COO), and finance leadership, giving colleagues access to the tools and business context behind an analysis. Together, these materials show colleagues what the organization measures and the business logic behind it. What Quick does for the team, day to day U.S. Hunger has given 17 colleagues access to Quick across its executive leadership, technology team, Full Cart program, Finance, Compliance, and supporting functions. For its CEO, chat is the primary day-to-day artificial intelligence (AI) workspace, and Spaces is the capability he uses most. Improving call reporting Using a Space containing Salesforce call reports, Rick is drafting instructions for the technology team: which measures to include, where the data comes from, and what each measure means. In Quick, he can comment directly on the generated draft and regenerate it with multiple changes incorporated. He can review and refine the instructions alongside the source reports, without spending time moving documents and comments between Word and chat. After completion, the instructions will guide reporting improvements for the member-engagement team, helping the program’s operational leaders and COO monitor the team’s work. Research and policy U.S. Hunger uses Amazon Quick Research to investigate current events, inform communications, and connect policy questions with its survey data. The CEO is also exploring how that data could serve a wider audience. With the version history in Quick Research, he can revisit earlier versions as he refines an investigation. Understanding food insecurity requires information about who is struggling and the circumstances behind that struggle. In September 2025, the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) announced that it would end future Household Food Security Reports. With that longstanding reporting series ending, access to other sources of evidence becomes especially important. U.S. Hunger wants to make the information it collects available beyond its own organization. It envisions a national hunger-data resource where researchers and the public can explore the experiences of families seeking assistance. Alongside that access, the organization plans an enterprise offering that companies can purchase, helping fund its mission. As Rick puts it, the goal is for “ the very data we’re using to help people ” to become “ the flywheel that feeds the very people we’re trying to help .” Executive insight and financial planning The national dashboard brings food insecurity together with income, education, health, and social needs. Filters help leaders examine different populations and use those findings in conversations with prospective partners about why families need help. For financial planning, Rick uses a Space containing audits, cash-flow information, and board budget views. A debt-service calculator and nonprofit financial-health worksheet help him share his banking experience with the COO. The financial documents provide context for drafting audit footnotes. With over a decade of financial documents available in the Space, Rick can ask Quick to compare patterns over time and explore questions about current operations. His familiarity with the source material helps him check the answers and challenge conclusions the evidence doesn’t support. Together, these workflows help Rick use Quick to explore both sides of the organization’s mission: understanding the families who need support and planning the finances that help U.S. Hunger provide it. Technology as social impact Putting food in an empty pantry meets an immediate need. Understanding what keeps that pantry empty means looking at the circumstances inside the home and the pressures around it, including income, housing, employment, and health. U.S. Hunger combines structured survey responses with narrative testimony collected since 2020. Its records include more than 300,000 applicants. Behind those records are lives, lived experiences, and families. Figure 2: U.S. Hunger records 304,348 applicants since 2020 (left) and 91.2 percent of applicants report skipping meals (right) Affordability is a central theme. Among respondents to the questions shown, 90.1 percent say they sometimes or often can’t afford balanced meals. Separately, 97 percent report difficulty paying for basics such as food, housing, medical care, and heating. Figure 3: Food insecurity frequency (top left), ability to afford balanced meals (top right), worry about food running out (bottom left), and difficulty paying for basics (bottom right) “In reality, it’s about affordability.” — Rick Whitted, President and CEO, U.S. Hunger The team supplies business definitions alongside the data. U.S. Hunger uses classification codes known as Z codes to categorize reported social and economic circumstances, including food insecurity, low income, and housing difficulties. Together, these views form what Rick calls “ an EKG reading on hunger. ” Food insecurity is the most frequently recorded Z code in this view, followed by low income. The other leading categories concern housing or financial circumstances. Leaders can examine the pressures accompanying requests for food, rather than looking at food needs in isolation. Figure 4: Food insecurity, low income, and housing or financial circumstances are the leading Z-code categories in this view. Applicants can have multiple codes, so the percentages are not mutually exclusive and need not total 100 percent Another view shows 44.7 percent of all applicants reporting illness and 79.1 percent enrolled in health insurance. In the employment view, 64.4 percent say they don’t need or want help finding or keeping work. These findings show why requests for food assistance need to be understood alongside families’ wider circumstances. Having health insurance doesn’t necessarily remove financial pressure, and help finding work is not what every applicant is seeking. Figure 5: Separate dashboard measures show reported illness and health insurance enrollment U.S. Hunger has been working to organize its data to better understand the pressures families face. Quick helps the team visualize patterns in that information. Rick describes one pattern as an early warning signal: periodic difficulty obtaining enough food, before families reach daily or weekly food insecurity. “We were on that journey, but [Quick] really helped us visualize that and lay that out much faster.” — Rick Whitted, President and CEO, U.S. Hunger For Rick, this is where technology becomes a form of social impact. Quick helps U.S. Hunger look past a request for groceries to the pressures behind it. Feeding a family meets today’s need. Understanding those pressures is part of helping that family toward a healthier tomorrow. A message to other nonprofits “501C is a tax designation. You’re still a corporation, which means you’re a business. And if you’re a business not embracing technology, you will get left behind – or your mission will cost you more.” — Rick Whitted, President and CEO, U.S. Hunger A nonprofit still has a business to run. Its leaders need to understand cash flow, agree on what performance measures mean, and connect operational decisions to their mission. U.S. Hunger uses Quick to bring that work together. Financial documents give Rick context for planning. Shared KPI definitions give colleagues a common reference. Dashboards help leaders examine the circumstances behind requests for food. Getting started didn’t require every system to be connected. Historical financial documents and questions Rick already needed to answer gave him a practical starting point. Other nonprofits can begin with a question that matters to their work and relevant information they have available. The people who know the organization remain the subject matter experts. They supply the context, check the answers, and decide what action makes sense. Quick helps them examine the evidence and bring it into those decisions. “This is not about bringing humans into the AI loop. It’s about bringing AI into the human loop.” — Rick Whitted, President and CEO, U.S. Hunger What comes next for U.S. Hunger and Amazon Quick U.S. Hunger is developing an enterprise KPI framework during Q4 2026. Boomi already connects NetSuite, Salesforce, and Impact Manager. The organization plans to use Boomi to bring research data, historical analytics, and enterprise KPIs into Amazon Redshift , which will supply data to Quick through scheduled SPICE jobs. Figure 6 shows the architecture supporting that planned expansion. Figure 6: U.S. Hunger’s planned enterprise KPI architecture brings data from business systems through Boomi into Amazon Redshift for analysis in Amazon Quick The diagram shows a planned pipeline bringing information from Impact Manager, NetSuite, Salesforce, Paylocity, ThriveLink, and iQpay through Boomi into Amazon Redshift. Scheduled SPICE jobs then supply the data to Quick. The next step for U.S. Hunger is to explore how its hunger data could become a national resource for researchers, the public, and companies. Rick has asked AWS for help shaping that work. The ambition extends the role of technology beyond internal analysis: Knowledge gathered while helping families could support research and generate revenue to help feed more families. Conclusion U.S. Hunger’s goal remains to feed families today and unite them to a healthier tomorrow. Direct data exploration, shared executive context, research, and financial analysis help its leaders understand both the organization they run and the families at the center of its mission. Watch the video Hear more from Rick Whitted in episode 8 of the Quick-witted podcast, “From Silos to Solutions.” He discusses how U.S. Hunger uses Amazon Quick and the role technology plays in its mission. Learn more about U.S. Hunger and explore Amazon Quick capabilities and customer stories . About the authors Rick Whitted Rick is CEO of U.S. Hunger, leading its evolution into a national platform addressing food access, health outcomes, and Social Drivers of Health. Under his leadership, the organization delivers more than 20 million meals annually while advancing data-informed, partnership-driven solutions at scale. Michelle Ye Michelle is a Product Marketing Manager at Amazon Web Services, focused on Amazon Quick. She works with customers across industries to share how they’re using AI to transform daily work. Sinisa Mikasinovic Sinisa is a Senior Solutions Architect at Amazon Web Services, where he has worked for 10 years, helping customers turn business challenges into practical cloud solutions. His work spans cloud architecture, data analytics, and generative AI, with a focus on helping teams adopt technology that supports their business goals.

content: Hermes Agent v0.22.4 Release Date: October 21, 2026 Patch release. Desktop stops showing suggestion pills above the composer, plus small plugin and dashboard fixes, for the CLI and installer, the Microsoft Store app, Docker and Hermes Cloud. Fixes Desktop no longer shows suggestion pills above the composer. The pills appeared for no clear reason, mostly nudging you to set up MCP servers. They and the helpers that only they used are gone. ( #142559 ) Plugins that install nothing skip the dependency consent step. A plugin that declares no dependencies, or whose pyproject.toml installs nothing, now enables without an empty consent prompt. ( #142569 ) Dashboard: WhatsApp can be safely re-paired after logging out. ( #142439 ) Desktop plugin review: the surface lint no longer flags prototype writes; reviewers check them by hand. ( #142586 ) Desktop: the approval-mode chip follows the active profile's mode. ( #142565 ) Release builds: the desktop bundle's pre-build check gets enough time to verify archived build inputs when storage is slow. ( #142623 ) Also new in the plugin catalog: bubblewrap (bwrap terminal backend on Linux), Singularity/Apptainer, mcp-serve (Hermes as an MCP server), agent-importers ( hermes import-agent , now with Cursor), inbox and workflow-record from Hermes Labs. Telegram Business moves to the Hermes Labs community tier. About this release Measured at commit 4d04303818b , the window since v0.22.3 contains 14 non-merge commits across 82 changed files (+1,475 / −3,022) and 13 merged PRs . Updating Microsoft Store app: updates through the Store. Desktop app installed from the installer (.exe / .dmg): no change in this release; it updates with the next bundled release. CLI: hermes update , or re-run the installer one-liner. Docker / Hermes Cloud: nousresearch/hermes-agent:stable (or :latest ). Full Changelog : v0.22.3...v0.22.4

content: Hermes Agent v0.22.3 Release Date: October 21, 2026 Patch release. This tag rolls up the ~620 PRs merged since v0.22.2 into a stable release for the CLI and installer, the Microsoft Store app, Docker and Hermes Cloud. Full curated notes for this window ship with v0.23.0. About this release Measured at commit 5b147ab036d , the window since v0.22.2 contains 2,911 non-merge commits across 4,206 changed files (+360,278 / −64,308), about 620 merged PRs and 326 closed issues . Also in the window, undocumented here on purpose: MCP progress notifications streamed as live tool progress, a refreshed classic CLI layout (glyph transcript, status line under the composer, two-line header), OAuth clients that plugins declare and Hermes signs in and refreshes, hermes plugins update offering every available plugin update plus an Update button for git-installed plugins in Desktop, steering and editing a queued prompt from Desktop, a guided subagent model and provider picker in Desktop, a live /loop countdown row in the CLI and TUI, opt-in Telegram DM topic transfer, a post_compaction plugin hook, a capabilities catalog, the Microsoft Store build going live automatically when a release publishes, session auto-prune back to opt-in with a one-time prompt when disk runs low, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt and one-slot DFlash drafts in the local runtime, and dozens of new plugin catalog entries. Full curated release notes for this window ship with v0.23.0 , which will document everything from v0.22.0 onward — highlights, feature areas, and complete contributor credits. Nothing in this window is skipped. Updating Microsoft Store app: updates through the Store. Desktop app installed from the installer (.exe / .dmg): no change in this release; it updates with the next bundled release. CLI: hermes update , or re-run the installer one-liner. Docker / Hermes Cloud: nousresearch/hermes-agent:stable (or :latest ). Full Changelog : v0.22.2...v0.22.3

title: Bringing the Spark to Europe: Local Intelligence Powers Next Wave of Agents
summary: At GTC Berlin, NVIDIA is showcasing its full lineup of local AI hardware. RTX Spark, which launched last week, powers personal agents on Windows PCs; DGX Spark supports developers building and scaling applications on Linux; and DGX Station serves enterprise teams running frontier workloads on Linux, with a Windows version arriving in December. Announcements include: […]
content: At GTC Berlin, NVIDIA is showcasing its full lineup of local AI hardware. RTX Spark , which launched last week , powers personal agents on Windows PCs; DGX Spark supports developers building and scaling applications on Linux; and DGX Station serves enterprise teams running frontier workloads on Linux, with a Windows version arriving in December. Announcements include: Underdog Desktop Agent now available for RTX Spark DGX Spark 64GB available on Friday, Oct. 23 NVIDIA Sync to support eight DGX Sparks and add Model Launcher this month October DGX Spark software update adds Wi-Fi Assistant and updates DGX Spark Skills DGX Station improves manageability with seven new integrations DGX Station for Windows launches in December with support for many manufacturing apps and agent harnesses Three new open source reference workflows for robotics on DGX Station NVIDIA Cloud Functions is coming in early access to DGX Station Recursive Flint, a new local coding model, is now available for NVIDIA local hardware Day-0 support for new Nemotron, GLM, DeepSeek, Qwen, MiniMax and FLUX.3 AI models New accelerations for llama.cpp and vLLM inference engines and a new collection of checkpoints optimized for local AI hardware. Learn more about these local AI announcements below, and check out the demos and sessions at GTC Berlin . Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements   RTX Spark Brings Personal Agents to the Windows PC RTX Spark is a new beginning for the PC — running personal agents, accelerated content creation and 1440p 100 frames-per-second gaming with up to 128GB of unified memory and 1 petaflop of AI compute. Here’s what early reviewers are saying about the platform since its October 16 release: “A dream machine for serious creators … ” — CGMag “Designed for the future of AI … ” — The Verge “An extremely capable, surprisingly portable and efficient machine … ” — PCMag Underdog , a new desktop agent app built for fully local, private AI, is also bringing its experience to RTX Spark. Powered by its Husky model-specific inference engine, Underdog runs models entirely on device, so personal agents can get work done without user data ever leaving the PC. Underdog is available now for download . To better enable developers and enthusiasts to build and customize local agents, many RTX Spark laptops come with an unlocked bootloader. During the GTC keynote, NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang showed off how AI agents running on RTX Spark can be used to train Hugging Face’s Microduck robot using NVIDIA Isaac Lab, Hermes Agent and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B. ASUS , Dell Technologies , HP , Lenovo, Microsoft and MSI laptops are available today, with Acer coming soon. Learn more about RTX Spark , and get started with the latest RTX Spark playbooks . DGX Spark Gives Developers Room to Build New DGX Spark 64GB systems — that can run models including Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B 24GB, Qwen3.8 27B and Gemma 4 26B-A4B — start rolling out from partners on Friday, Oct. 23. When workloads require more capacity, developers can connect multiple DGX Spark systems via built-in NVIDIA ConnectX-7 networking and NVIDIA Sync Cluster Assistant . This allows users to run advanced coding models like Qwen 3.8 Flash Next, DeepSeek v4 Flash 0731 and GLM 5.3 Flash. Now, DGX Spark supports clusters of up to eight units in manual configuration, enabling larger models, longer contexts, concurrent agents and distributed development. Ideal for small teams sharing a single cluster as a backend, with each developer running concurrent sessions against the same model, it delivers 1TB of unified memory — enough to run frontier-class models like GLM 5.3. Get started with the DGX Spark cluster playbook . NVIDIA Sync Model Launcher will also be available later this month. It simplifies access to local AI on a single DGX Spark or a cluster. With a few clicks, Model Launcher downloads a model and container suited to the configuration and connects the model to OpenCode. It automatically loads DGX Spark Skills for troubleshooting, device maintenance, access to official documentation and other workflow guidance. The October DGX Spark software update brings a new Wi-Fi Assistant that lets users switch networks when DGX Spark is running in appliance mode. Plus, DGX Spark Skills provide workflow-focused guidance in troubleshooting and device maintenance directly into NVIDIA Sync via OpenCode. DGX Spark systems are available directly from Acer , ASUS , Dell Technologies , GIGABYTE , HP , Lenovo, MSI and NVIDIA. DGX Station Puts Frontier Intelligence at the Desk For larger teams, DGX Station offers 748GB of coherent memory and up to 20 petaflops of AI performance, enabling developers to run advanced models like GLM 5.3 and serve 30+ users at speeds comparable to those provided by cloud models. Adding scale, NVIDIA Sync now supports DGX Station, simplifying connections between two Linux-based systems. New integrations with Absolute Security , Splunk by Cisco , Fleet Device Managemen t , Microsoft Intune , Perforce Puppet , Progress Software Chef and Tanium let IT teams manage DGX Station systems through enterprise setup, management and conformity processes, helping accelerate approvals and reduce deployment risk while minimizing time to first token. With the upcoming Windows-based systems, developers can build workflows that harness professional applications, run on NVIDIA RTX PRO GPUs and operate from agents that run their large language models (LLMs) on NVIDIA GB300 systems — all in one machine. DGX Station for Windows , expected from system manufacturer partners in December, extends local AI into the applications and operating environment enterprises already use. Engineers can run local models and agents in Windows-native software with access to AI models, tools and agents on the same system. DGX Station for Windows will feature support for manufacturing applications from nTop , Dassault Systèmes , Keysight Technologies , MathWorks , Rockwell Automation , Siemens , Synopsys , Unity and Altera for AI-guided design, simulation, validation and engineering automation. Users will be able to run agents using Hermes Agent , Perplexity or Aible on premises for agentic control in enterprise environments. The same local, controlled computing model extends to robotics. DGX Station gives robotics teams dedicated compute for post-training, simulation and evaluation, shortening iteration cycles without waiting for shared infrastructure. NVIDIA released three open source reference workflows that bring GPT-6 Astra, NVIDIA Isaac Lab, Isaac Lab-Arena and Cosmos to NVIDIA DGX Station. Developers can use them to refine GR00T 1.7 models with reinforcement learning, train dexterous manipulation skills and post-train Cosmos world models for synthetic data generation. NVIDIA Cloud Functions is coming in early access to Linux-based DGX Station. Teams can register local model endpoints in a shared catalog and access them through one OpenAI-compatible entry point. Developers can upgrade the model behind an endpoint without changing application code, while teammates can use shared models without direct machine access. This turns a DGX Station into a locally controlled inference service for a team. DGX Station brings local iteration to AI factory development. On the show floor at GTC Berlin, NVIDIA is previewing DSX OS running on DGX Station to simulate AI factory operations before full infrastructure is available. Another demo will showcase DGX Station systems powering a local token factory for more than 30 software developers. DGX Station systems are shipping today from ASUS , Dell Technologies , GIGABYTE , HP , MSI , Supermicro and Exxact . DGX Station for Windows systems are expected to begin shipping later this year from ASUS , Dell Technologies , GIGABYTE , HP , MSI and Supermicro . Introducing Recursive Flint — A New Local Coding Model Optimized for RTX Spark Today, frontier AI lab Recursive Superintelligence released Recursive Flint , a local LLM built for fast, accurate coding. A 40-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 2.5 billion active parameters, Recursive Flint delivers fast inference and performs well in agentic coding benchmarks like S WE-Bench Pro v2, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-bench verified. Recursive Flint was built using Recursive’s Eureka Machine, a system for large-scale automated AI research. It automates the full research loop: proposes ideas, implements them, runs experiments to validate ideas and uses the results to decide what to try next — creating specialized kernels that boosted Flint’s generation speed on RTX Spark by 55% without changing the model’s weights. Developers can download the open weights on Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 license and run the model on RTX Spark and DGX Spark systems, as well as GeForce RTX and RTX PRO GPUs. Developers can also post-train the model with NeMo Automodel for supervised fine-tuning and low-rank adaptation, or LoRa, as well as NeMo RL for group relative policy optimization. New Models With Day-Zero Support NVIDIA is also adding day-zero model support for NVIDIA Nemotron Bolt E4B 4B, GLM, DeepSeek, Qwen, MiniMax, Liquid AI’s LFM2.5-24B-A2B, plus the FLUX.3 Klein diffusion model. Nemotron Bolt E4B 4GB packs natural conversation and multi-turn agentic skills into as little as 4GB of memory, powering fast local voice assistants, interactive game characters and embedded interfaces on NVIDIA GeForce RTX GPUs, NVIDIA Jetson devices, and RTX and DGX Spark. Bolt E4B 4GB releases on Friday, Oct. 23. Black Forest Labs’ FLUX 3 Image Klein is a 5.6-billion-parameter open weights image model for generation and editing. NVIDIA-optimized builds let it run on GeForce RTX GPUs with as little as 8GB of VRAM and create a 1-megapixel image in about four seconds on an RTX 5090 GPU. MiniMax M3.1 Flash is a new open model built for NVIDIA DGX Station and DGX Spark, bringing long-context AI to the desktop. Liquid AI’s LFM2.5-24B-A2B is an open weights reasoning model that activates just 2 billion of its 24 billion parameters per token, making it fast enough to run private, tool-calling AI agents directly on PCs. Plus, NVIDIA has released a new collection of model checkpoints optimized for RAM efficiency on local AI hardware, enabling frontier-class open models to run with sufficient memory left over for KV cache. Each checkpoint is quantized while staying close to full-precision accuracy, starting with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP4-Local on a single DGX Spark 128GB or RTX PRO 6000 and GLM-5.3-Flash-FP4-Local on two systems. Developers can post-train on day zero with NeMo AutoModel on both DGX Spark and RTX Spark, with example recipes for Nemotron Bolt E4B , Flux 3 Image Klein and more. Accelerated AI Inference NVIDIA continues to work with the llama.cpp and vLLM open source communities to accelerate agentic workloads on local hardware. In llama.cpp, new speculative decoding support with MTP for Qwen 3.8 Flash Next makes end-to-end agentic tasks up to 1.4x faster on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell. In vLLM, faster speculative decoding and new FlashInfer prefill kernels for Qwen’s linear-attention layers make agentic tasks with Qwen3.8 27B up to 1.3x faster on DGX Spark. On DGX Station, GLM 5.3 Flash gets up to 1.2x higher throughput. Check out NVIDIA’s local AI inference recipes to try these latest optimizations. Follow NVIDIA RTX Spark on X , Instagram , TikTok and Facebook — and stay informed by subscribing to the NVIDIA Local AI newsletter . Follow NVIDIA Workstation on LinkedIn and X . title: Google Cloud and NVIDIA Announce General Availability of NVIDIA Vera Rubin Infrastructure
summary: General availability of the instances is coming next month, with planned expansion of availability to Europe — bringing an integrated platform for training, inference and large-scale reinforcement learning to cloud customers. A5X instances bring together NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72, NVIDIA ConnectX-9 SuperNICs, Google Cloud Virgo Network and Google Cloud’s fourth-generation advanced liquid-cooling technology for demanding […]
content: General availability of the instances is coming next month, with planned expansion of availability to Europe — bringing an integrated platform for training, inference and large-scale reinforcement learning to cloud customers. A5X instances bring together NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72, NVIDIA ConnectX-9 SuperNICs, Google Cloud Virgo Network and Google Cloud’s fourth-generation advanced liquid-cooling technology for demanding agentic inference and reinforcement learning workloads at scale. Google Cloud plans to scale its Vera Rubin-based infrastructure to as many as 960,000 Rubin GPUs across multiple sites. Ineffable Intelligence , a London-based technology company founded by AlphaGo creator David Silver, was the first customer to access A5X. Ineffable is using the platform to advance large-scale reinforcement learning and shape “superlearner” systems that learn continuously from experience. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements   Learning through interaction requires a continuous cycle of generating experience, evaluating outcomes and updating models, requiring infrastructure that can support the entire process at scale. A5X brings Vera Rubin into Google Cloud’s AI Hypercomputer as an integrated system, combining compute, networking and storage to support experience-driven learning at scale. “We’re building superlearners that continually improve through their own experience,” said David Silver, founder and CEO of Ineffable Intelligence. “That demands both substantial compute and a tight connection between generating experience and training on it, so each improvement in the agent can quickly shape its next experience. Vera Rubin’s combination of compute performance and high-bandwidth connectivity, between the Vera CPU and Rubin GPUs and between the Rubin GPUs within the rack, allow us to push the scale and ambition of our reinforcement learning research further.” WPP , a London-based marketing and communications company, has also demonstrated its creative agent reference architecture on NVIDIA Vera Rubin-based A5X instances using NVIDIA Nemotron models and NVIDIA OpenShell, part of the NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture for safe AI agents. The agents turn conversational requests into multistep creative workflows, such as video generation, upscaling and restyling, with human approval before execution. OpenShell provides governed sandboxes for agent execution, helping control access to sensitive brand assets and creative tools. In WPP’s initial tests, workloads that typically required a multi-node cluster ran on a single A5X instance. As organizations deploy agentic systems, they need to protect the proprietary models and sensitive data that power these systems — even when running on infrastructure they don’t own. Google Cloud will be among the first cloud providers to offer NVIDIA Confidential Computing at rack scale on bare metal instances such as A4X Max instances powered by NVIDIA GB300 NVL72. Additionally, Google Cloud is making Confidential Computing generally available on G4 VMs powered by NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs, offering a flexible platform for confidential inference and fine-tuning. Customers including Vertebrae , Polaris Cloud and Confidential Core AI are using Confidential G4 for conversational privacy, verifiable agent execution and policy-governed enterprise intelligence. To support energy-efficient deployment at scale, Google Cloud and NVIDIA are exploring NVIDIA DSX MaxLPS capabilities for Vera Rubin-based infrastructure to help optimize performance per watt and expand capacity within available data-center power budgets. Learn more about NVIDIA Vera Rubin and Google Cloud A5X instances. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements

title: NVIDIA Cloud Partners Scale Across Europe — Sovereign, Open and Built for Safe AI Agents
summary: Demand from AI-natives is pulling the European AI cloud ecosystem forward faster than ever. Developers need compute closer to their data, open models they can customize and serve at scale, and full-stack infrastructure that is secure by design. NVIDIA Cloud Partners across Europe, the Nordics, Africa, and Central Asia are expanding regional compute capacity for […]
content: Demand from AI-natives is pulling the European AI cloud ecosystem forward faster than ever. Developers need compute closer to their data, open models they can customize and serve at scale, and full-stack infrastructure that is secure by design. NVIDIA Cloud Partners across Europe, the Nordics, Africa, and Central Asia are expanding regional compute capacity for model training and inference, helping developers build agentic and physical AI applications, and establishing boundaries around what agents can access and do. Together, they’re turning Europe’s energy, data, research and industrial expertise into productive intelligence — supporting new models, applications, organizations and jobs while giving people more control over where and how they develop and deploy AI. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements   Sovereign: AI Clouds Building European AI Infrastructure Europe is home to world-class research, engineering talent, industrial expertise, data, the next generation of models and applications that requires large-scale computing close to where that knowledge resides. Regional AI clouds provide the infrastructure foundation on which model builders, enterprises and entire industries can grow. As AI factories scale, power becomes a constraint which makes it critical for every watt to produce more intelligence. Nscale is using the NVIDIA DSX Platform to coordinate power allocation with workload requirements. In tests using NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 systems, Nscale demonstrated that NVIDIA DSX MaxLPS enabled 37% more GPUs and nearly 50% higher aggregate inference throughput within the same provisioned power budget. Nscale also plans to deploy NVIDIA Vera Rubin infrastructure for frontier-model training and production workloads to support leading model and application builders using its full-stack, vertically integrated platform with expansion across five European markets. Crusoe is developing Spark, its liquid-cooled modular AI factories designed for the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform, to bring Crusoe Cloud capacity closer to users for low-latency AI inference. Crusoe Cloud serves leading model and application builders across EMEA, including Base44, Gradium, LTX and Wonderful. Aleria, Cassava Technologies , Firebird , G42 , Radiant, SWI Compute and Vultr are also developing and expanding NVIDIA-powered AI infrastructure across Europe, the Nordics, Africa and Central Asia. Regional capacity from AI clouds combines the full-stack NVIDIA DSX AI Factory platform , including NVIDIA Vera Rubin, NVIDIA BlueField and NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet networking, giving customers greater choice and control over where workloads and data reside while advancing sovereign computing services and economic growth. Open: Models and Libraries, From Training to Inference Across the ecosystem, AI clouds are expanding NVIDIA-powered infrastructure and services for developers to build applications with open models and libraries. This new capacity supports model training, fine-tuning for specialized tasks and inference at scale, including applications deployed at the edge. For production inference, Nebius has adopted NVIDIA Groq 3 LPX, using Spectrum-X Ethernet networking to integrate it with Vera Rubin NVL72 on Nebius Token Factory. The combination will bring faster token generation to latency-sensitive applications and agentic systems through the platform’s managed serverless and dedicated endpoints and familiar application programming interfaces. For robotics and physical AI, Nebius offers a purpose-built AI cloud solution that includes its full-stack Physical AI Workbench. Robotics companies including Rhoda AI , RoboForce and Sereact are building on the platform. The company also launched three NVIDIA retail agent blueprints — covering inventory, store operations, and fine-tuning —- into early access on Nebius infrastructure. Nebius is expanding its cloud services widely across the continent with its Physical AI Living Lab, and in Germany as a computer supplier for the Next Frontier Challenge of SPRIND, the Federal Agency for Breakthrough Innovation. Baseten has developed a specialized model for code-review routing with Nemotron 3.5 Lightning used by CodeRabbit. Through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, CodeRabbit improved routing agreement from 75.8% to 80.7% while reducing estimated inference costs by 50% for the evaluated workload. The results demonstrate how AI developers can customize NVIDIA open models for specialized tasks while improving accuracy and inference efficiency. Fireworks and Era4 are partnering to bring open models to enterprises across the U.K. and Europe. The collaboration combines Fireworks ’ model training and inference platform with direct liquid-cooled capacity powered by NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra GPUs at Era4’s Chesterfield facility, supporting plans for enterprise AI solutions in financial services, insurance and life sciences. Mistral is expanding its NVIDIA accelerated computing infrastructure to support model training, customization and inference. The expansion includes NVIDIA Vera Rubin infrastructure planned for delivery in 2027. Trained on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in Mistral -operated European data centers, Mistral Large 4 is the company’s latest frontier multimodal model, advancing capabilities across coding, agentic workflows and multimodal understanding. Verda plans to deploy NVIDIA Vera Rubin, continuing to promote open weight models with NVIDIA Nemotron and NVIDIA Cosmos already in production, and using the NVIDIA Dynamo open source framework for inference optimization. Safe: Secure Boundaries for AI Agents, From Silicon to Software As developers connect models to tools and business systems, they also need controls over what agents can access and do. Announced at GTC Berlin, the NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture with support from AI cloud ecosystem partners. Built on the foundation of NVIDIA OpenShell secure runtime software, the architecture is designed to give organizations full-stack control to deploy AI agents with clear boundaries around what agents can access and do. NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 for model inference, NVIDIA Vera CPUs with OpenShell for agent harnesses and tool use, and NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPUs running NVIDIA Sentry for in-silicon enforcement. Each play a distinct role in delivering that control, working together so agents can achieve what they’re meant to do without moving beyond the boundaries people set for them. Partners including Aleria , Baseten , Cassava , CoreWeave , Crusoe , DigitalOcean , Firebird , Fireworks, Firmus , G42 , GMI Cloud , IREN , Lambda , Lightning AI, Nebius , Nscale , Radiant Verda and Vultr are supporting the OpenShell Reference Architecture to enable secure agentic deployments for their customers. Together, European AI clouds are connecting regional infrastructure investment with the work of building and deploying AI. Expanded capacity gives builders more places to run workloads. Model and inference services help them put that capacity to use. Agent controls address what applications are allowed to do as they move into production. Explore NVIDIA Cloud Partners for infrastructure and services, and the OpenShell Reference Architecture for agent deployment controls. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements

title: Europe’s Industrial Leaders Reinvent Engineering and Manufacturing With NVIDIA
summary: To increase productivity, accelerate innovation and create new opportunities for economic growth, Europe’s industrial leaders are tapping NVIDIA CUDA-X and Omniverse libraries, as well as NVIDIA Cosmos and Nemotron open models, across the engineering and manufacturing lifecycle. Bringing those capabilities together on the factory floor, the NVIDIA Factory Operations Blueprint (FOX) is now available in […]
content: To increase productivity, accelerate innovation and create new opportunities for economic growth, Europe’s industrial leaders are tapping NVIDIA CUDA-X and Omniverse libraries , as well as NVIDIA Cosmos and Nemotron open models, across the engineering and manufacturing lifecycle. Bringing those capabilities together on the factory floor, the NVIDIA Factory Operations Blueprint (FOX) is now available in early access on GitHub , providing a path for developers to build and deploy always-on factory manager agents that coordinate work across machines, and specialist agents focused on use cases such as visual inspection, root cause analysis, report generation and fleet management. These agents can connect to frontier models, including NVIDIA Cosmos and Nemotron, and foundational knowledge including computer-aided design, product lifecycle management, simulation software, and IT and operational technology systems. Building on the FOX blueprint enables the ecosystem to build industrial agents that monitor factory operations in real time, correlate visual findings and machine logs to investigate problems, and coordinate responses. With Cosmos in-context learning, these agents can adapt using examples and documentation, without fine-tuning. Siemens is integrating agents built using FOX into Intelligence Center X, its agentic enterprise system, to help identify root causes and coordinate factory operations, for estimated cost savings of 20%. Siemens’ Process Preparation X agents use NVIDIA Cosmos Data Factory tools and skills to generate defect images for circuit-board inspection. At its Erlangen electronics factory, Siemens used this approach to reduce calibration time of inspection processes by 40%. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements   Accelerating Engineering From the First Design NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries accelerate simulation, giving engineers faster feedback to explore design alternatives before committing to physical prototypes. At GTC Berlin, NVIDIA is releasing cuDSS for general availability , accelerating the demanding calculations behind the complex simulations of structural stress, fluid flow, electromagnetic fields and semiconductor device behavior. Mercedes-Benz uses Siemens’ Simcenter STAR-CCM+ running on NVIDIA GPUs to compare vehicle designs through faster aerodynamic simulations. In factories, the company applies NVIDIA Cosmos 3 and the Metropolis VSS blueprint to build agents for vehicle inspection and windshield assembly verification, detecting deviations and ensuring consistently high quality. Cadence is benchmarking automotive fluid-dynamics workloads on NVIDIA GPUs to assess opportunities for faster design iteration, while Autodesk brings the NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo and Warp frameworks into NavPack, integrated with Autodesk Alias, to help designers like those at Bentley’s predict vehicle performance and iterate faster using simulation-trained AI. imec and Infineon are accelerating semiconductor simulation with Synopsys software and NVIDIA accelerated computing. Benchmarks of S-Litho on imec’s model show up to 40x speedup, while Infineon uses Sentaurus Device with NVIDIA CUDA libraries to achieve a 12x speedup in 3D breakdown simulation for next-generation power devices. Leonardo is working with Neural Concept on AI-driven aircraft design, tapping NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to bring aircraft geometry and aerodynamic simulation results together. Video courtesy of Neural Concept and Leonardo. Car manufacturers use Dassault Systèmes ’ LEO & AURA Virtual Companions, powered by NVIDIA Nemotron, and orchestrating CATIA AI Agents & SIMULIA AI Agents with SIMULIA solvers, accelerated by NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries, to rapidly design and virtually test vehicle doors before building physical prototypes. UniversalAGI is working with Saab to protect sailors from life-threatending wave impacts at sea, using UniversalAGI’s Latent Interaction Field Transformer physics AI foundation models with accelerated processing by NVIDIA Warp to evaluate thousands of wave conditions and headings in real time instead of days. These capabilities enable vessels to anticipate dangerous motion and autonomously select safer routes to avoid putting sailors at risk, while NVIDIA Omniverse libraries help visualize vessel behavior at sea. PhysicsX is working with GB1, Britain’s America’s Cup team , on AI-powered yacht design, using NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to visualize hull geometry and pressure fields, while Fermioniq ’s Sofia agent helps Deltares and Dutch ministries model river flow by translating natural-language requests into simulation solvers built on NVIDIA Warp. Mistral plans to use CUDA-X, Warp and Omniverse libraries to accelerate physics simulation and generate training data for engineering AI models. Testing Factories and Robots Virtually NVIDIA Omniverse and Isaac libraries enable digital twins and robotics simulation , helping manufacturers evaluate production systems and robot behavior before making changes on the factory floor. Video courtesy of Agile Robots, Audi and Dassault Systèmes. Audi uses a battery-production digital twin built with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to test production concepts before physical equipment is available. The company is also working with Dassault Systèmes and Agile Robots to simulate and validate mobile humanoid robots and logistics processes in DELMIA virtual twins built with Omniverse libraries. Schaeffler is integrating digital twins of its humanoid actuators — components that move robot joints — with NVIDIA Isaac simulation frameworks, helping its robotics partners evaluate component behavior in simulation and reduce physical testing. At Volkswagen Sachsen’s Transparent Factory, Wandelbots uses NOVA with Isaac Sim , built on Omniverse and OpenUSD, to validate assembly workflows digitally and prepare applications for physical robots. Falkor , a KONGSBERG company, is integrating agents and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries into its platform. With Microsoft Azure NCv6 virtual machines powered by NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs, agents with spatial intelligence combine engineering data, operating information and 3D equipment geometry to see, simulate and reason over industrial facilities, supporting inspection and maintenance use cases across the process and energy industries. Video courtesy of Falkor, a KONGSBERG company. The same simulation approach extends to AI infrastructure. Schneider Electric , together with AVEVA , is developing an AI factory digital twin built for Nscale with Omniverse libraries to help engineers compare power, cooling and equipment configurations before making physical changes.
