title: NVIDIA cuDSS Now Generally Available to Accelerate Engineering and Scientific Simulations
summary: NVIDIA cuDSS, launched today in general availability, is an NVIDIA CUDA-X library that shifts a critical part of engineering and scientific simulations onto GPUs. Complex engineering feats — from advanced chips to aircraft to industrial systems —– depend on simulation to predict how designs will perform before they’re built. As designs become more complex, simulations […]
content: NVIDIA cuDSS, launched today in general availability, is an NVIDIA CUDA-X library that shifts a critical part of engineering and scientific simulations onto GPUs. Complex engineering feats — from advanced chips to aircraft to industrial systems —– depend on simulation to predict how designs will perform before they’re built. As designs become more complex, simulations take longer to run, increasing computing demands and limiting the number of ideas teams can test. NVIDIA cuDSS accelerates solving large sparse systems — the math-heavy step that repeats throughout engineering and scientific simulations and often limits how many designs a team can test — by tapping into GPUs. This lets applications reduce time to results and increase simulation throughput, enabling end users to explore larger more realistic models, more accurate representations and a wider design space at a reduced cost.   Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements   Industry leaders are already integrating NVIDIA cuDSS into their tools to transform workflows for their end customers: Applied Materials: With cuDSS, Applied Materials accelerated sparse solves in Ginestra, its physics-based, defect-centric simulation platform, by up to 10x versus CPU-only approaches, speeding exploration of semiconductor materials and device reliability. COMSOL: Using COMSOL Multiphysics with NVIDIA cuDSS on NVIDIA accelerated computing, ZEISS SMT achieved a measured 4x speedup in an EUV lithography plasma simulation benchmark, completing the full simulation in six days and 14 hours. Cadence : Uses cuDSS in its Celsius software to accelerate simulations of heat, structural stress and warpage in advanced chips and 3D chip designs, helping customers including Nokia analyze complex designs faster. Dassault Systèmes : Dassault Systèmes reports an 8-10x speedup using cuDSS within its Abaqus structural and computer simulation technology electromagnetic solvers for performance-critical simulations across industries. Siemens : Siemens uses cuDSS in Simcenter STAR-CCM+ to accelerate simulations of structures in fluid-structure interaction workflows. Synopsys : Synopsys uses cuDSS in its Sentaurus Device simulator tool to accelerate simulations of advanced logic, memory and power chips, helping Infineon model increasingly complex devices faster. Accelerated Simulation at Scale As simulation workloads grow in size and complexity, cuDSS can scale out of the box from individual workstations to large computing clusters. Developers can integrate cuDSS into existing engineering, scientific and optimization software offerings, bringing GPU acceleration to tools already used by engineers and researchers. They can use cuDSS through C, C++, Python and Fortran interfaces. Learn more about cuDSS by visiting the NVIDIA demo booth and Dassault Systèmes booth at GTC Berlin. Featured image courtesy of Dassault Systèmes.   Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements

title: NVIDIA Confidential Computing Expands, Enabling Frontier Model Builders to Securely Scale Across Global Infrastructure
summary: NVIDIA builds tools to enable safe agents across the stack. The NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture, announced today, is part of NVIDIA’s growing portfolio of technologies that enables organizations to safely deploy agents at scale. NVIDIA Confidential Computing is the infrastructure layer that protects the models and data those agents depend on while running. Today, NVIDIA […]
content: NVIDIA builds tools to enable safe agents across the stack . The NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture, announced today , is part of NVIDIA’s growing portfolio of technologies that enables organizations to safely deploy agents at scale. NVIDIA Confidential Computing is the infrastructure layer that protects the models and data those agents depend on while running. Today, NVIDIA is expanding that layer with Confidential Bare Metal, a new deployment option with NVIDIA Confidential Computing that enables frontier model builders to run sensitive workloads on dedicated third-party infrastructure while retaining control of their models and data. NVIDIA is introducing new platform security controls that protect data in transit, measure platform integrity and enforce hardware-level access restrictions. These new controls let frontier model builders use bare-metal instances to own and operate their bespoke software stack, including host and platform infrastructure software, when operating on NVIDIA accelerated computing infrastructure across third-party cloud, neocloud and enterprise infrastructure. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements   NVIDIA Confidential Computing now offers a converged security architecture with three deployment options: Confidential Bare Metal for bare-metal infrastructure Confidential Containers for Kubernetes environments Confidential Virtual Machines for virtualized environments Organizations can match the right model to their trust boundaries and operating requirements. NVIDIA Confidential Computing is also expanding across NVIDIA Grace Blackwell and Rubin systems and will integrate with NVIDIA DSX OS as a reference architecture for cloud providers building AI factories. Model Builders Tap Global Capacity Confidential Bare Metal gives supported providers a path to serve high-value workloads that require strong model and data privacy protections. For model builders, the expanding ecosystem offers more geographic, sovereign and operational options for scaling training and inference worldwide. Cohere plans to integrate Confidential Bare Metal into Cohere Model Vault, using NVIDIA Confidential Computing trusted execution environments to extend hardware-rooted security directly to the GPU — protecting models and data in memory and across interconnects during execution. “Enterprises trust Cohere to provide a secure and confidential platform for inference,” said Phil Blunsom, chief technology officer at Cohere. “With NVIDIA Confidential Computing in Cohere Model Vault, we’re extending hardware-rooted security directly to the GPU, protecting customer data in memory and across interconnects during execution.” Google Cloud is extending support for Confidential Bare Metal to A4X Max instances powered by NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 systems. These will combine non-virtualized NVIDIA accelerated computing with cryptographic protection for training data and model intellectual property. “Google Cloud introduces Confidential Bare Metal to provide AI labs with hardware-isolated, non-virtualized compute environments and end-to-end cryptographic protection. Our A4X instances, built using NVIDIA Confidential Computing, preserve the privacy of user data, protect model IP, provide top-line serving performance,” said Andrés Lagar-Cavilla, distinguished engineer and AI infrastructure security lead at Google Cloud. Confidential Computing Expands Across the NVIDIA Platform NVIDIA Confidential Computing uses hardware-rooted isolation and cryptographic attestation to help protect models and data during execution. Support now extends to NVIDIA Grace Blackwell NVL72 — bringing Confidential Computing to NVL72 rack-scale systems — as well as x86-based NVIDIA HGX Rubin NVL8 and NVIDIA DGX Rubin NVL8 systems. CoreWeave , Firmus , GMI Cloud , Google Cloud , IREN , Lambda , Microsoft Azure Infrastructure, Nebius , Nscale and Vultr support NVIDIA Confidential Computing deployments. Global systems partners including Cisco , Dell Technologies , HPE , Lenovo, Supermicro and Bull will support these capabilities with NVIDIA-Certified Systems . NVIDIA DSX OS will support all NVIDIA Confidential Computing modes, giving cloud providers a software foundation for building and operating AI factories that support confidential workloads. Learn more about NVIDIA Confidential Computing . Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements

title: NVIDIA Agent Toolkit Expands, Grounding Enterprise Agents in Company Data
summary: Agents are only as useful as what they know, and only as trustworthy as the boundaries they run within. Leading enterprises are using the open source NVIDIA Agent Toolkit — now expanded with new tools — to customize and control agents, use company data to inform their answers and actions, monitor what they do and […]
content: Agents are only as useful as what they know, and only as trustworthy as the boundaries they run within. Leading enterprises are using the open source NVIDIA Agent Toolkit — now expanded with new tools — to customize and control agents, use company data to inform their answers and actions, monitor what they do and govern how they operate. NVIDIA Agent Toolkit comprises: The new NVIDIA Agent Knowledge Foundation with NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries NVIDIA open models including Nemotron Retriever and the new Kumo family NVIDIA OpenShell secure agent runtime NVIDIA NemoClaw secure agent blueprints Tools and skills, like NeMo Relay and NeMo Compass Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements   To develop agents that accomplish real work and are trustworthy from development to deployment, builders need an open agent stack that brings together the models, harness, runtime, data and tools. NVIDIA Agent Knowledge Foundation helps enterprises turn data into company intelligence agents can use. Agents can find relevant information, understand what it means for the business and use it to make predictions and help people decide what to do next. Companies can use Agent Knowledge Foundation without moving data, rebuilding existing workflows or changing governance controls. The foundation features NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries , including cuDF, cuGraph, cuML, cuOpt and cuVS, and the new Auto-Ontology library, which translates raw company data into familiar business concepts — like customers, products and orders — and maps how they relate. It also includes NVIDIA Nemotron Retriever and Kumo Structured open models — Kumo Tabular, Kumo Relational, Kumo Time Series and Kumo Forecast — which help agents find relevant company information to answer questions and make predictions. OpenShell provides the secure runtime boundary, giving enterprises control over what agents can access and do. NVIDIA NemoClaw blueprints provide reference designs for building secure, specialized agents. The newest NemoClaw blueprint for agent optimization provides a step-by-step starting point for improving agent intelligence — making them better at their jobs over time. Enterprises Adopt NVIDIA Agent Knowledge Foundation The new NVIDIA Agent Knowledge Foundation is already at work across enterprises. With Palantir , NVIDIA’s supply chain organization is using Agent Knowledge Foundation through Palantir Foundry, Ontology and AIP to deploy specialized agents, create actionable intelligence from proprietary data, predict outcomes and optimize decision-making. Databricks pairs NVIDIA Kumo Anomaly with Databricks Genie Ontology to power context-aware agents. Snowflake is enabling customers to use the NVIDIA Kumo Engine and Kumo Relational open models in their Snowflake Notebook environments to unlock more predictive capabilities. NVIDIA Nemotron Retriever models make search faster and more accurate. Using the embedding model, Amazon OpenSearch Service improved relevance with fewer search steps and virtually no added latency. SAP ’s fine-tuned reranker ran nearly 3x faster. ServiceNow improved reranking quality while cutting latency by nearly a quarter. Zoom is using Nemotron Retriever models to improve document understanding, search relevance and context retrieval for Zoom AI Services. Amazon Web Services (AWS) , ClickHouse , Cloudera , Cohesity , Dassault Systèmes , Dell , Elastic , Exa , IBM , NetApp , Oracle , Perplexity , Starburst and VAST Data are also among those building on Agent Knowledge Foundation. Learn more by joining this GTC Berlin session on building, deploying and optimizing specialized agents in production . Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements

title: NVIDIA Open Models Advance Europe’s Sovereign Intelligence Across Industries
summary: NVIDIA is expanding its family of open models across language, robotics, biology, and quantum computing, giving developers, researchers and enterprises what they need to build applications tailored to local languages and industries The portfolio includes the new NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt models; new NVIDIA Nemotron Retriever models for embedding, reranking […]
content: NVIDIA is expanding its family of open models across language, robotics, biology, and quantum computing, giving developers, researchers and enterprises what they need to build applications tailored to local languages and industries The portfolio includes the new NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt models; new NVIDIA Nemotron Retriever models for embedding, reranking and document parsing; the new NVIDIA Kumo family open weight foundation models and libraries for structured business data; NVIDIA Cosmos 3.5 world models; NVIDIA Alpamayo 2 Edge for autonomous vehicles; NVIDIA BioNeMo for healthcare and scientific discovery; and NVIDIA Ising for quantum computing. The open models give organizations a foundation they can customize with local data and deploy on infrastructure they control. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements   NVIDIA Nemotron Powers Post-Training Across Industries NVIDIA Nemotron brings open language models, datasets and recipes to developers building agents. The models support text and images, helping agents orchestrate workflows, reason through complex problems and complete specialized tasks at a lower cost. Nemotron models are built with data, research and expertise from the NVIDIA Nemotron Coalition , including European partners Black Forest Labs , H-Company and Mistral . Nemotron provides a foundation for enterprises to build applications based on their own knowledge and expertise. Dassault Systèmes , Domyn , Dream , Palantir’s customers , Salesforce , SAP , Shopify , Synopsys and WPP , as well as professional services providers like Accenture and EY, are working with Nemotron models and datasets to create custom models and build domain-specific agents. A broad ecosystem of post-training partners, including AfterQuery , AgileRL , AI21 , Alice , Applied Compute , Baseten , CoreWeave , Distil Labs , EON , Fastino , Fireworks , Google Cloud, Mercor , Multiverse Computing , Nebius , Handshake AI , Plurai , Prime Intellect , River.AI, Scale AI , Trajectory and TNG, is helping enterprises customize Nemotron for domain-specific workloads. NVIDIA Kumo Speeds Agents’ Work With Structured Enterprise Data NVIDIA Kumo open foundation models, libraries and tools help agents and applications forecast outcomes, score fraud risk and recommend actions from structured business data. Part of NVIDIA Agent Knowledge Foundation , Kumo shortens time to prediction and reduces the cost and complexity of building a separate machine learning pipeline for every task. Developers can use pretrained Kumo models to bring predictions to more applications quickly, then fine-tune them using proprietary data when higher performance is critical. The portfolio includes NVIDIA Kumo Structured , with models for relational and tabular prediction, forecasting and anomaly detection, and NVIDIA Kumo Engine , an open library stack for developing and deploying structured data foundation models. Cognite , Coinbase , Databricks , DoorDash , Revolut and Tubi are among the first to work with Kumo models to accelerate development. Snowflake customers are already using Kumo models to accelerate AI development in industries including advertising, energy, financial services and retail. NVIDIA Cosmos Accelerates Robotics Training and Simulation NVIDIA Cosmos is a family of open world foundation models that helps developers build robots, autonomous vehicles and vision agents that understand and interact with the physical world. NVIDIA is introducing new Cosmos post-training and optimization tools to help developers improve world models using less compute, along with simulation checkpoints for evaluating behavior in interactive driving and robotic manipulation scenarios before real-world testing. NVIDIA is also introducing Cosmos Data Factory — comprising blueprints and core agent skills — to help developers curate, label, generate and evaluate training data for driving scenarios, product defects, image augmentation and event generation. Developers can use complete workflows or individual capabilities with agents coordinating the process. Porsche with Voxel51 , ANYbotics with Encord , Zalando and CEVA Logistics with Sereact , and Siemens are using Cosmos Data Factory to create high-quality, diverse training datasets and improve model precision. NVIDIA Alpamayo 2 Brings Real-Time Reasoning to Autonomous Vehicles NVIDIA Alpamayo 2 Edge is a compact reasoning model that brings real-time scene understanding and motion planning directly into autonomous vehicles. Built on NVIDIA Cosmos and optimized for the NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor platform, it helps developers bring advanced driving capabilities into vehicles with lower computing requirements. NVIDIA BioNeMo RFD4-Proteina Advances Protein Design NVIDIA BioNeMo RFD4-Proteina is an open protein design model from NVIDIA and the Baker Lab at the University of Washington’s Institute for Protein Design. The model generates protein sequences and 3D structures to help researchers design proteins that bind to difficult targets, assemble into complex structures and bind to small molecules. NVIDIA BioNeMo RFD4-Proteina delivers leading performance across more than 10 protein design tasks and generates designs about 13x faster than RFdiffusion3 in a benchmark of 200 amino acid proteins. Researchers can use the model through agents to generate and evaluate candidates against design goals and molecular constraints, then choose which designs to test in the lab. NVIDIA Ising Accelerates Quantum Development The NVIDIA Ising family of open models provides a common, extensible foundation to speed the breakthroughs needed to develop useful quantum supercomputers, from real-time hardware calibration to error correction, across different qubit modalities and tailored to individual hardware needs. IQM Quantum Computers is using Ising to calibrate its quantum processors, showcasing how specialized open calibration models outperform large general-purpose models. SEEQC is combining the NVIDIA NVQLink platform and Ising with its unique Digital Link to meet the low-latency requirements needed for real-time quantum error correction. AWS is making NVIDIA Ising readily available to researchers by integrating the model family into AWS Parallel Computing Service (AWS PCS). While decoding is typically performed on classical hardware colocated with the quantum processor due to latency requirements, the AWS PCS integration lets researchers build on Ising prior to deployment. Availability NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is available on Hugging Face , ModelScope , OpenRouter and build.nvidia.com as an NVIDIA NIM microservice, as well as through NVIDIA cloud, post-training and inference partners. Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB is expected to be available on Friday, Oct. 23. NVIDIA Nemotron Retriever open models are available on Hugging Face , various partner platforms, and as an NVIDIA NIM microservice on build.nvidia.com . NVIDIA Kumo open models are available on Hugging Face and optimized and packaged as an NVIDIA NIM microservice for production inference on build.nvidia.com . NVIDIA Cosmos is now openly available on Hugging Face and GitHub , and through select inference partners. NVIDIA Alpamayo 2 Edge will be available for download on GitHub and Hugging Face later this month. The NVIDIA BioNeMo open model RFD4-Proteina is available on build.nvidia.com and as an NVIDIA NIM microservice, as well as on GitHub, Hugging Face and through select inference partners. NVIDIA Ising is available on GitHub, Hugging Face and build.nvidia.com . See notice regarding software product information. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements

title: GTC Berlin 2026: Live Updates From NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang’s Keynote
summary: Founded in a tent near the Berlin Wall in 1980, the Tempodrom moved several times before settling near Anhalter Bahnhof in 2001. Its permanent home has since hosted concerts, galas and political events. Today, it hosts a different kind of spectacle. GTC Berlin runs three days, with more than 100 sessions on agentic AI, robotics, […]
content: Founded in a tent near the Berlin Wall in 1980, the Tempodrom moved several times before settling near Anhalter Bahnhof in 2001. Its permanent home has since hosted concerts, galas and political events. Today, it hosts a different kind of spectacle. GTC Berlin runs three days, with more than 100 sessions on agentic AI, robotics, physical AI, open models and accelerated computing underway at STATION-Berlin down the road. Here, journalists, analysts and partners have gathered for the main event: NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang’s keynote. Huang Takes the Stage Huang opened with a question: What do L’Oréal, Revolut, Spotify, Merck, Vodafone, Zara, Porsche, Nestlé and HSBC have in common? They’re all European companies and they’re all working with NVIDIA on AI, he said. The keynote comes on the heels of NVIDIA’s weeklong road across Europe — Paris, London, Stockholm, Dublin — with the company committing nearly $10 billion to the technology ecosystem across Europe and working with 12,000+ partners. “After decades of advancement in the computer industry, we are now at the beginnings of a new industrial revolution,” Huang said.   Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements   AI is a five-layer cake , Huang explained. Energy powers advanced computers that are part of an AI factory, which generates tokens and digital intelligence from the models that run on it, which are then integrated into every application. “Long before the AI models emerge, the infrastructure has to exist,” he said, highlighting how, similarly, the internet first needed networking, and electricity first required the grid. “To be part of this AI economy, you don’t want to just be consuming the AI; you want to be producing the AI,” Huang said. “We could do all of that here in Europe, and in fact, we’ve already started.”   The AI Factory Gets a New Form Factor Huang framed NVIDIA’s full-stack AI factory — spanning hardware, system software, CUDA-X libraries and models — as a broad platform for building and operating AI infrastructure. “This now represents the breadth of technology necessary to create the AI factory,” Huang said. “This is what NVIDIA builds today, and this is the foundation by which we can enable Europe to be part of the AI ecosystem, the AI economy.” He said Vera Rubin, in full production, extends NVIDIA’s computing platform beyond models and large language models to process the entire AI agent. He also showed several of NVIDIA’s latest rack-scale hardware offerings. Next, Huang announced NVIDIA DSX POD , a reference design for complete NVIDIA Vera Rubin AI factories built by partners inside modular containers, integrated and validated before delivery. With DSX POD, onsite deployment can shrink from six months to just 14 days once site utilities are ready. “This is a complete transformation of the world supply chain,” Huang said. “This will change the way that people install and build data centers, and hopefully, as a result, velocity goes up.” The NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform enables companies to reduce water consumption for cooling by up to 100% and generate the same AI output with up to 30% less power. Agents Are the New Computing Platform — and Safety Is an Engineering Problem Huang said agents think, reason, iterate and use tools, driving token consumption as they become more useful. He described an agent as comprising five elements: a model, a harness that orchestrates its work and memory, a sandbox that isolates the harness, knowledge and tools. In that framing, an agent is more than a model answering questions; it can draw on knowledge and act through tools. “The most important thing is to make sure the agent is secure,” Huang said. The autonomous agent can access files, resources, networks and tools, so its privileges should be minimal and it should be monitored. NVIDIA’s answer is the new NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture for Safe AI Agents , a full-stack design built on NVIDIA OpenShell — an open source, policy-controlled runtime with kernel-level sandboxing that sits between an agent and the systems it can affect. That means privileges, policy enforcement and monitoring must adapt dynamically. “Every single time an agent is launched, the privileges are different,” Huang said. Open Models Turn Expertise Into an Advantage Huang presented NVIDIA’s open models as a starting point for building AI tailored to specific needs. NVIDIA’s frontier, open models are available for use across industries: Nemotron for language, Cosmos for world foundation models, GR00T for humanoid robotics, Alpamayo for autonomous vehicles, Ising for quantum-classical computing and Earth-2 for physics AI. “We are the frontier,” Huang said. “So in all of these different areas, we offer you all of the models, and we’re continuously working on it. We’ve been working on it for a decade, and we’ll continue to work on this forever.” NVIDIA provides the models, data and scripts to reproduce them, and companies can post-train a model on their own data for a particular use case — turning proprietary data into what he called “sovereign intelligence.” “You could start with an open model, something that’s incredibly good like Nemotron, and with your own data, post-train it for your use case and achieve, of course, super intelligence,” Huang said. “That is a very sensible thing to do, and all the technology exists today.” NVIDIA Gives Agents a Knowledge Layer Huang then introduced the NVIDIA Agent Knowledge Foundation as a set of models and libraries for connecting agents to enterprise data, whether it’s unstructured information in documents or structured data in databases. He highlighted Nemotron tools for parsing documents, embedding queries and reranking relevant information, along with new NVIDIA Kumo models for making predictions from structured data. “Ultimately, what turns these super agents, these agents into super agents, is that you give them access to your company’s knowledge,” Huang said. NVIDIA CUDA-X — Accelerated Tools for Agents Huang then described NVIDIA CUDA-X as a collection of accelerated libraries used across science, engineering, research and creative work. NVIDIA’s accelerated computing platform has more than 11 million developers building on it. Huang said those libraries can accelerate simulators, solvers and data-processing engines — the kinds of tools agents may draw on to do useful work. “CUDA-X tools are what gives agents the tools of the trade,” Huang said. Agents Go to Work in Labs, Factories and Engineering A video showcased NVIDIA Agent Toolkit bringing company knowledge, models and tools together in three industry examples: At Lila Sciences, agents help design a potential B-cell lymphoma therapy, using virtual experiments to guide work in an automated lab. At Siemens’ Erlangen factory, agents help prepare new products for production, testing plans in a digital twin before changes reach the factory floor. And at Dassault Systèmes, engineering agents adapt vehicle design, using simulation to identify a problem and refine the design. “And [all this] knowledge and tools belong to you,” Huang said after the video rolled. “That’s your expertise, and so all of this is now possible to do.” Telcos as Distributed AI Infrastructure Huang said AI is transforming telecommunications, improving spectrum efficiency and turning cell towers into distributed AI infrastructure. He cited 100,000 sites and about 100 gigawatts of distributed data centers, and said NVIDIA has made its first commercial phone call on T-Mobile’s network with Nokia after nearly eight years of work. “Now CUDA makes phone calls,” Huang said. “AI will revolutionize the way we do telecommunications. It will enhance our spectrum efficiency tremendously.” AI Moves Into the Treatment Room Healthcare and life sciences leaders are building on NVIDIA technologies to advance drug discovery and expand patient care. For example, NVIDIA and Siemens Healthineers are developing AI-enabled radiation therapy. Nemotron agents coordinate treatment planning, the Isaac for Healthcare platform and Omniverse libraries create a digital twin of the device and patient anatomy to simulate tumor targeting. Holoscan with IGX Thor connects live imaging and sensor data to enable real-time adaptive delivery as the patient moves. Huang described adaptive radiotherapy as a physical-AI application: as the patient’s body and tumor change during treatment, the system must track the changes and adjust the radiation targeting. “The tumor is changing in shape. The physical body is changing while you’re in therapy,” Huang said. “The robot, this radio adaptive radiotherapy system, has to perceive the changing environment, understand where the tumor is, segment it just perfectly and direct the radiotherapy accordingly.” The Road Ahead: Mobility Leaders Join NVIDIA’s Automotive Ecosystem Huang said the NVIDIA Hyperion computing platform is being designed into more vehicle fleets , with autonomous-driving software connecting robotaxis to ride-hailing services. Bolt with Lucid, Mercedes-Benz, Volkswagen Commercial Vehicles and Einride are showcasing selected autonomous-mobility use cases on the NVIDIA Hyperion computing platform, demonstrating potential applications for level 3 and level 4 vehicles as well as future robotaxi fleets. In addition, Volvo Cars is adopting Hyperion and NVIDIA Alpamayo Stack software for safe automated driving. NVIDIA also introduced new AI and safety technologies to help developers build, validate and deploy autonomous vehicles at scale. Volkswagen’s van, JLR, Volvo and Mercedes-Benz’s next-generation vehicles will be Hyperion-compatible, Huang announced, saying, “Welcome to Hyperion.” A Reference Humanoid for Robotics Researchers Huang then announced Agile ONE SN , a reference humanoid built on Isaac GR00T — a 31-degree-of-freedom body, expected to be available next year, designed to cut researcher setup time from weeks to days. The platform is modular: researchers can use the full workflow or pull in selected components. “This is a great starting point,” Huang said. It builds on NVIDIA’s open physical AI stack — Isaac Capture for data collection, GR00T models for robot intelligence, Isaac Lab for simulation-based training, Isaac OS for runtime — and NVIDIA’s open physical AI dataset. Partners including Agility Robotics, Figure, KUKA and NEURA Robotics are already building on the same platform. Personal AI Gets a New Machine Huang closed by discussing RTX Spark laptops , which launched last week , bringing together RTX graphics and NVIDIA’s full-stack AI platform in slim, premium Windows PCs for accelerated creation, immersive gaming and powerful local AI. He compared its 1 petaflop of performance and 128GB of memory with the DGX-1 he delivered to OpenAI in 2016 — then made the difference in size the punchline: “In the year 2016, I delivered 1 petaflop and 128GB … to a small company called OpenAI,” Huang said, holding up the compact machine in front of the audience. “This is 1 petaflop and 128GB. The only difference, of course, is that I can hold this like this, and DGX-1 took two people to carry upstairs.” Huang then showed a video of an agent helping train Hugging Face’s Microduck: it set up a course and simulated the robot in Isaac Sim, sent training jobs to the cloud, then brought the learned policy back to RTX Spark for evaluation before deploying it to the physical robot. A flock of four Microducks joined Huang onstage, sitting down, standing up and even taking a nap on cue. He explained that they were created on RTX Spark, trained in the cloud and learned their skills in simulation. “You were created on RTX Spark … [we] trained you in the cloud on a whole bunch of NVIDIA supercomputers, and you learned your skills right here on RTX Spark and the digital twin,” Huang told them. The Full Lineup With the Microducks gathered around him, Huang recapped the keynote: Europe is building its AI economy, AI factories are evolving to run agents and physical AI is the next frontier. “So that’s it,” Huang said. “Everybody can build agents. Every company in Europe will become an AI company … and we’re going to have a thriving AI economy here in Europe.” To close, Huang had one more surprise: a Eurovision-style musical send-off that turned the keynote’s themes into a comic recap. The lyrics raced from OpenShell’s guardrails — “No credentials. Access dismissed” and “Sentry on BlueField never clocks off” — to physical AI, where robot training was likened to “college for robots without student loans.” The punchline: “You can’t spell fungible without fun.” A saxophone solo led into a rousing “We are Europa” chorus. “Let’s work together to build Europe’s AI economy and put AI to work,” Huang said, closing out his talk. “Have a great GTC.” Explore NVIDIA GTC Berlin blogs and press releases in the online press kit .   Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements

content: Minor Changes #4294 3f80896 Thanks @liruifengv ! - Add a confirmation dialog when switching models in a session with conversation history: start a new session, compact and continue, continue directly, or cancel. Shown only when enabled by cloud configuration. #4188 3f0857e Thanks @oocz ! - List plugin skills under their qualified : name so same-named skills from different plugins all stay visible and invocable; invoking a plugin skill by its bare name no longer works, use the qualified name instead. #4214 ef727e5 Thanks @sailist ! - Support streaming large requests and responses through remote control, raising the transfer limit from 10 MiB to 100 MiB, with concurrent transfers bounded to protect memory. #4288 df0ff3c Thanks @github-actions ! - When the same session is open in multiple clients, sending from a second one now shows an occupancy prompt with retry/cancel, or reloads updates made elsewhere first and resends your message. #4200 5bab748 Thanks @7Sageer ! - Automatically generate a session title after the first turn and show it as the terminal window title. Patch Changes #4250 6e7cc90 Thanks @sailist ! - Setting [permission] dangerous_command_guard = false now turns off every built-in confirmation guard — dangerous commands, sensitive-file access, and git control-path access — instead of only the dangerous-command guard. #4281 5710c54 Thanks @sailist ! - Fix session events stopping after a session is archived and restored. #4201 83a39b4 Thanks @Grapedge ! - Stop blocking the terminal while the footer reads git status. #4230 b260326 Thanks @kimi-agent-bot ! - Report a clear error when thinking effort is set to off for Gemini 4 models. #4208 20b5991 Thanks @SeleneXX ! - Fix Gemini 4 requests always failing with a 400 error. #4242 c1459a6 Thanks @wbxl2000 ! - Run hooks such as PreToolUse and Stop in the session's project directory, as documented, instead of the directory the server was started from. #4210 f28c51c Thanks @sailist ! - Add the [mcp] default_deferred config key: when the experimental tool-select flag is on, set default_deferred = true in config.toml to load every MCP server's tools on demand by default; a server can opt out with deferred: false. #4171 0327e8e Thanks @7Sageer ! - Support custom-registry model upgrade metadata in model configuration. #4188 3f0857e Thanks @oocz ! - Allow uppercase letters, dot-separated segments, and @ suffixes in plugin names when installing plugins. #4294 3f80896 Thanks @liruifengv ! - Queue /compact while the agent is busy: the command now joins the message queue and runs in order instead of failing with an error; it is skipped if the context was auto-compacted while it waited. #4190 e4c99a3 Thanks @starquakee ! - Clarify unavailable tools, announce when no tools can be loaded, and discourage repeated failed tool selections. #4272 ce0834a Thanks @Grapedge ! - Move the session rating opt-out from tui.toml to config.toml. #4066 85077a4 Thanks @7Sageer ! - Keep subagent tool descriptions aligned with currently available tools. #3799 7e58f2d Thanks @kimi-agent-bot ! - Fix the latest reply disappearing from the transcript after a background task completion notification arrives; the fold boundary is now anchored to the notification turn itself instead of the asynchronously mounted task card. #4239 da5918c Thanks @RealKai42 ! - Remind the agent to update its todo list after 5 steps without an update instead of 10, only while the list still has unfinished items, and ask it to bring the list up to date before its final reply. #4248 8fcd332 Thanks @kimi-agent-bot ! - Show a single overflowing preview line in full instead of swapping it for a same-height expand hint. #4304 d36071e Thanks @kimi-agent-bot ! - web: Improved interactions and fixed known bugs.

( #174257 , #175007 , #176783 , #172671 ; related #174120 and #176669 ) Thanks @RomneyDa , @kazuyuki-eguchi , and @PennyVibe . ( #177716 , #177564 , #172705 , #171528 ) Thanks @jjjhenriksen and @RomneyDa . Background tasks: completions are no longer dropped when the config changes mid-turn. ( #169529 ; related #169054 ) Thanks @wangmiao0668000666 , @RomneyDa , and @Oldrich333 . Discord: restore native slash commands in channels and threads. Thanks @montrellcruse and @RomneyDa . Agents: keep the prompt cache when a rate-limited run retries, and preserve steering messages that arrive without an explicit target. Thanks @montrellcruse , @RomneyDa , and @obviyus . Cron/CLI continuity: preserve CLI chat sessions across cron announce wakes instead of resetting their provider session. ( #176218 ; related #176208 ) Thanks @eliavb43 and @RomneyDa . CLI tools: invalidate reused CLI sessions when the available tool catalog changes, restoring tools such as exec after Gateway restarts and preventing stale catalogs from reaching spawned agents. ( #176577 ; related #175670 ) Thanks @RomneyDa , @jackylecalvez2 , and @vincentkoc . GMI: omit unsupported reasoning_effort values on GPT-5.6 tool turns so the provider no longer rejects them with HTTP 400. ( #176709 ) Thanks @RomneyDa . Windows updates: recognize Scheduled Task permission denials in every Windows display language, keep Windows plugin dependency links across Doctor phases, and clean up backup scratch directories without EPERM failures. ( #174718 , #167756 , #169945 ) Thanks @RomneyDa and @Stronggenetics . Nodes: synchronous node exec output is no longer repeated as a separate Exec finished wake after the waiting caller already received it. ( #164511 ) Thanks @holgergruenhagen and @obviyus . macOS: long exec commands through the macOS app node no longer fail after 20 seconds. ( #172117 ; related #139706 ) Thanks @holgergruenhagen , @RomneyDa , @ylcn91 , and @Colton-Harris . Control UI: offer desktop setup instead of Retry when Host Desktop is off, model pickers refresh when the catalog changes mid-read, and locale refresh works again after adding a source-only locale. title: Physicist Christopher Stubbs joins Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust
summary: Dr. Christopher Stubbs, an experimental physicist and former Dean of Science at Harvard University, has joined Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust. He brings to the Trust decades of scientific expertise across observational cosmology and precision measurement. content: Dr. Christopher Stubbs, an experimental physicist and former Dean of Science at Harvard University, has joined Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust. He brings to the Trust decades of scientific expertise across observational cosmology and precision measurement. He has also advised the US government on national security and arms control. “I am honored to join Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust and to help the company deliver on its public benefit mission,” said Stubbs. “I use AI tools in my research every day and see what they make possible, and as an educator I have confronted some of the hard questions they raise. As a grandfather, I want to help ensure that AI is developed and deployed for the long-term benefit of humanity.” Stubbs is the Samuel C. Moncher Professor of Physics and of Astronomy at Harvard, where he served as Dean of Science from 2018 to 2024. In 1998, as a member of the High-Z Supernova Search Team, he helped discover the accelerating expansion of the universe, work that later earned the team the Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics. He was also the inaugural project scientist for what is now the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which started a 10-year survey of the southern sky in June. One of its aims is to study the accelerating expansion he helped discover. More recently, he’s written about how to keep AI-assisted research reproducible when models can give different answers to the same question. He’s a member of JASON, an independent group of scientists who have advised the US government on defense and technology since 1960. "When Chris found evidence that the universe was expanding at a rate no one expected, he and his team followed the data even when it went against the prevailing wisdom of the field. As AI starts to transform how science itself is done, Chris’s intellectual honesty, rigor, and commitment to the truth are the values we want shaping the future of this technology, and I’m grateful he’s bringing his deep expertise to the Trust," said Daniela Amodei, Co-founder and President of Anthropic. Anthropic is a Public Benefit Corporation, which means we’re structured to balance commercial growth with our public benefit purpose. The Trust exists to help us hold that balance over the long term. It has the authority to appoint a majority of Anthropic’s board, and Trustees advise the board and our leadership on critical decisions, particularly those involving risks and societal impacts of AI. This week we published our first Public Benefit Report [link], a public account of how we’re working toward our mission and where we’re falling short. The Trustees helped define the five mission pillars it measures us against, and the report closes with their assessment of our progress to date. Subject to stockholder approval, we’ve also committed to setting aside a portion of Anthropic’s shares to Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a new entity with a structure that increases the stake as the company grows. “Anthropic's Public Benefit Report sets out what we’re all working toward: helping the world build powerful AI safely, and making sure the technology drives advances that meaningfully improve people’s lives and society as a whole,” added Neil Buddy Shah, Chair of the Long-Term Benefit Trust. “Both goals depend on a deep understanding of frontier science and leading with integrity. Not only has Chris worked on some of the hardest problems in science, but he has consistently been a high-integrity leader of large, complex, collaborative scientific endeavors across academia, government, and the national laboratories. That will be of great value to the Trust as we support Anthropic in developing AI for the long-term benefit of humanity.” Stubbs, the Trust’s first physicist, joins Shah, national security expert Richard Fontaine, and former Federal Reserve Chair Ben Bernanke. Trustees are independent of the company’s management and investors.

title: Beyond the KV cache: Training and serving i14’s Laplace 3B linear attention model on AWS Trainium2 with native PyTorch
summary: Learn how i14 trained and served Laplace 3B, a linear attention model, on AWS Trainium2 using native PyTorch. Its recurrent state stays fixed at 29.5 MB per sequence regardless of context length, avoiding the growing key-value cache of transformer models and keeping serving memory predictable.
content: Most large language models (LLMs) use transformer architectures with softmax attention. During inference, their key-value (KV) cache grows with the conversation or document context. This can reduce concurrency, increase serving cost, and force agentic applications to discard useful history. i14 designed Laplace 3B as a linear attention alternative. Its recurrent state stays at 29.5 MB per sequence, independent of context length. Working with AWS, i14 used native PyTorch support through TorchNeuron Native to bring this custom architecture to AWS Trainium2 . This preserved its Gated Linear Attention (GLA) design and Muon optimizer. On one trn2.48xlarge instance, Laplace 3B trained at about 120,000 tokens per second. The model served 11,544 output tokens per second across 1,280 concurrent sequences. This post explains the model design, the changes i14 made for Trainium2, and the training and inference results. About i14 i14 is an AI research and technology company that develops model architectures, components, and runtimes. Its work draws on AI, computational cognitive science, and research into how biological systems learn over time. i14 applies these ideas to models that can retain long-range context without allowing serving state to grow with every token. Why linear attention models? Transformer softmax attention compares tokens across the context. During training, this computation grows quadratically with sequence length. During inference, the KV cache grows as the model processes more tokens. Linear attention reorganizes the computation around a recurrent state that is updated for each token. Laplace 3B uses GLA to compress prior context into a fixed-size matrix state. This changes training attention from O( T 2) to O( T ) and keeps inference state fixed at 29.5 MB per sequence. Consideration Transformer softmax attention Laplace 3B with GLA Training attention Builds pairwise token scores with O( T 2) scaling Updates chunked recurrent state with O( T ) scaling Inference memory KV cache grows with context Recurrent state remains fixed in size Longer contexts Each sequence consumes more accelerator memory Context length does not increase recurrent-state allocation Implementation Uses widely optimized attention kernels Requires architecture-specific kernels and compiler tuning Linear attention compresses history rather than retaining every key and value. You must therefore evaluate retrieval quality for your workloads. The fixed state can benefit long-running agents, large-document analysis, and applications that need persistent memory with predictable serving requirements. How i14 adapted Laplace 3B for AWS Trainium2 The original implementation of Laplace 3B used GPU-optimized Triton kernels. The AWS Generative AI Innovation Center (GenAIIC) team first rewrote the GLA kernel with standard PyTorch operators for Trainium2. After comparing both approaches, the team chose the beta version of TorchNeuron Native, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium , because it performed better. The implementation required three changes: Using native PyTorch for the GLA attention kernel. The team replaced the GPU-specific fused_chunk_simple_gla Triton kernel with standard PyTorch operators, using 16 chunks of 128 tokens to match the 128 partitions of the NeuronCore on-chip buffer. Redesigning how Muon communicates. Two all_to_all collectives in MuonFSDP2 cut per-rank traffic by 24 times and raised throughput by 1.63 times. Compiling the sequential backward pass. The team statically unrolled the 16 chunk steps of the GLA recurrence to fit the graph-size and on-chip memory limits of the compiler. The engineering challenges section describes each change in detail. Why AWS Trainium accelerators? AWS Trainium is a family of AWS machine learning (ML) accelerators designed for model training and inference. A trn2.48xlarge instance combines 16 Trainium2 chips, 64 logical NeuronCores, high-bandwidth memory, and NeuronLink-v3 connectivity. These resources support the distributed training and inference configurations described in this post. Three properties of Trainium2 shaped the implementation: software-managed on-chip memory (Challenge 1), a fast chip-to-chip interconnect (Challenge 2), and a static compiler (Challenge 3). The compiler traces the GLA recurrence as a fixed graph. Software-managed on-chip memory. Each NeuronCore has a 28 MiB State Buffer (SBUF) with 128 partitions and a 2 MiB partial-sum buffer (PSUM). The PSUM is wired to a 128×128 systolic Tensor Engine, alongside separate vector and scalar units. The SBUF is not a cache: the compiler schedules every HBM-to-SBUF transfer ahead of time, so the data is in place with no evictions or misses (Figure 1). Figure 1: NeuronCore-v3 internal architecture. Software-managed SBUF (28 MiB, 128 partitions), Tensor Engine (128×128 systolic array), Vector Engine, Scalar Engine, and GPSIMD cores. i14 and the Laplace 3B architecture Laplace 3B is the 24-layer i14 decoder, where every layer replaces softmax attention with Simple GLA. Figure 2 follows one layer from the input x t at the top to the output x t + 1 at the bottom. This section explains each module: normalization and convolution, the QKVG projection, the GLA mixer, and the feed-forward channel mixer. Normalization and convolution. Each token’s residual-stream vector x t ∈ ℝ D ( D = 3, 072 ) passes through a LayerNorm and a depth-wise causal Conv1d of width k = 4 with SiLU. This gives every position a 4-gram summary before the mixer. The GLA mixer then does content-based retrieval over the whole history through its decaying state. QKVG projection. The post-conv output goes through one fused matrix W q k v g ∈ ℝ 9, 216 × 3, 072 , where 9, 216 = H × (2 d k + 2 d v ) . It splits into four per-token streams: queries q t , keys k t , values v t , and a gate g t ( H = 16 , d k = 96 , d v = 192 ). The gate is used after the mixer. Figure 2: Laplace decoder layer architecture. Green = fixed (no params), gray = learned, yellow = recurrent state, blue = projection. GLA mixer. Each head h keeps a matrix state S t ( h ) of size d k × d v (96 × 192), a compressed, decaying record of past key-value pairs. At each token, it updates as: GLA recurrent-state update equation Here λ h is the fixed per-head decay, and k t v t ⊤ is the rank-1 outer product that writes the current key-value pair into the state. The readout queries the state: GLA state-readout equation Next, a self-augmentation step adds a gated copy of the value to each head’s output: GLA self-augmentation equation Here σ is the sigmoid and ⊙ is the element-wise product. The gate is the query dotted with a learned per-channel rescaling of the key, where a is the learned scale (aug_balance). At initialization, a = 0 , which gives a half-strength skip of the value. The per-head outputs pass through a Head RMSNorm within each decay tier, are concatenated, gated by S i L U ( g t ) , and projected by W o u t ∈ ℝ D × D back to the residual stream. Decay schedule. The per-head decay rate λ h controls how fast a head forgets past tokens. It is fixed at initialization (not learned) and set by a geometric schedule. The schedule gives the 16 heads a spread of memory lengths and defines each head’s log-decay rate γ h : GLA decay schedule equations Decay schedule’s reach. For this model, T min = 1 and T max = 2, 048 . Head 0 therefore has λ 0 = 0.5 (half-life of one token), and head 15 has λ 15 ≈ 0.9997 (half-life of 2,048 tokens). Heads are grouped into tiers, each sharing a Head RMSNorm. Channel mixer (FFN). After the attention block and its residual, a second LayerNorm feeds a GLU (SiLU) FFN with inner dimension 8,192. Its three matrices are two up-projections W 1 , W 2 ∈ ℝ 8, 192 × D and one down-projection W 3 ∈ ℝ D × 8, 192 . A second residual follows. The state S ( h ) is fixed at d k × d v = 96 × 192 per head regardless of sequence length. As a result, inference is O (1) per token, and training is O ( T ) rather than O ( T 2 ) . Parameter Value Parameters 3.028B total (2.718B Muon + 309.6M AdamW) Layers 24 decoder layers, D = 3, 072 hidden dim Heads 16 heads, d k = 96 (half-width Q/K), d v = 192 (full-width V) Mixer Simple GLA with fixed geometric decay ( T min = 1 , T max = 2, 048 ) Conv Depth-wise causal Conv1d, kernel width 4, SiLU FFN GLU (SiLU), inner dim 8,192 Norm LayerNorm pre-attn + Head RMSNorm (per tier) + LayerNorm pre-FFN Vocab 50,304 (padded to multiple of 64) Sequence 2,048 Training data 100B tokens, FineWeb-Edu Optimizer Muon for 2D weight matrices; AdamW for embeddings, norms Batch size 524,288 tokens/step, cosine LR, 3,815-step warmup Engineering challenges Each of the three changes raised its own engineering challenge. Challenge 1: Using native PyTorch on Trainium for GLA On GPU, GLA runs as the fused Triton kernel fused_chunk_simple_gla from the flash-linear-attention library. The GenAIIC team re-expressed it with standard PyTorch operators running through TorchNeuron Native , as explicit loops over fixed-size chunks. The chunk count is fixed at compile time and sets the backward-unroll depth. The team uses fla_num_chunks = 16, so each chunk holds C = 128 tokens. Within each chunk c , the intra-chunk output is masked linear attention, and the running state S adds earlier context: Chunked GLA intra-chunk output The state then advances to the next chunk: Chunked GLA state update Here λ C is the per-head decay compounded over the chunk. The 16 intra-chunk computations run in parallel, and only the state update is sequential (Figure 3). Figure 3: GLA chunked recurrence with parallel intra-chunk attention and a sequential state chain. Because the SBUF has 128 partitions, each 128-token chunk maps one token per partition, with no padding or cross-partition movement. This alignment increased measured throughput by 14 percent (Figure 4). Figure 4: Chunk size C = 128 maps one-to-one onto the 128 SBUF partitions. Challenge 2: Distributed Muon orthogonalization under FSDP2 Muon orthogonalizes each gradient before the update. For each of the 96 two-dimensional weight matrices (2.718 billion parameters), it runs five Newton–Schulz iterations (Algorithm 1). The Newton-Schulz algorithm The distributed problem. The Gram matrix A = X X ⊤ correlates every row of the weight with every other row. Under Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP2), each of the 64 ranks holds only 1/64 of the rows. A shard-local X X ⊤ therefore yields only a diagonal block and drops every cross-shard term (Figure 5). Figure 5: Newton–Schulz under FSDP2: the shard-local Gram block, and gather/broadcast compared with all_to_all. Naive approach: Gather and broadcast. Every rank gathers the full gradient (5.44 GB), one rank runs Newton–Schulz, and it broadcasts the result. This moves 10.87 GB per step while the other 63 ranks wait. Production approach: all_to_all transposition. In MuonFSDP2, one all_to_all gives each rank a few complete matrices, all 64 ranks run Newton–Schulz in parallel, and a second all_to_all returns the results. Per-rank traffic drops to 0.45 GB, 24 times less. Throughput rises from 73,378 to 119,934 tokens per second, 1.63 times higher, with a bit-identical loss curve (Figure 6). Figure 6: Per-step communication volume: 10.87 GB with all_gather compared with 0.45 GB with all_to_all. Communication cost. Newton–Schulz is only about 2 percent of the FLOPs in a training step ( 1.95 × 10 14 of 9.53 × 10 15 ), so communication was the bottleneck. Over NeuronLink-v3 at 1.28 TB/s, the 0.45 GB exchange takes under 0.4 ms of the roughly 4.4-second step. Challenge 3: Backward-pass unrolling for a sequential recurrence The backward pass differentiates through all 16 sequential state updates. On GPU, autograd builds this graph at runtime. On Trainium2, the compiler must see the whole unrolled 16-step graph in advance, which creates three constraints. Graph depth grows with chunk count: at 32 chunks ( C = 64 ), the graph overflowed the scheduler. Per-chunk memory grows with chunk size: at 8 chunks ( C = 256 ), intermediates spilled into HBM. Every shape is fixed at trace time, so each loop intermediate needs its own static allocation. Sixteen chunks ( C = 128 ) satisfy all three: the unroll fits the scheduler, intermediates stay on chip, and tiles align with the 128 SBUF partitions. Training results The GenAIIC team trained Laplace 3B on one trn2.48xlarge instance using all 64 logical NeuronCores and the all_to_all Muon path. The full recipe is 190,735 steps (100 billion FineWeb-Edu tokens). The following results are through step 84,210, about 44 billion tokens. Throughput. After compilation warmup, throughput settles at roughly 120,000 tokens per second and holds there through step 84,210. Loss and gradient stability. The loss (Figure 7a) drops smoothly from about 11.4 to 2.3729 at step 84,210. The gradient norm (Figure 7b) shows the expected early spike then a steady decline to about 0.05, with no post-warmup spikes, divergence, or NaN/Inf values. Figure 7: Training dynamics. (a) Loss 11.4 → 2.3729. (b) Gradient norm from TensorBoard data. Inference optimization on Trainium2 Through an unmodified vLLM engine, the GenAIIC team served 11,544 output tokens per second at 1,280 concurrent sequences on one trn2.48xlarge instance. Constant serving state. The 29.5 MB recurrent state per sequence is roughly 82 times smaller than a comparable KV cache at 8,192 tokens. Increasing the prompt from 2,048 to 8,192 tokens added only 0.5% to the cost per output token. Unmodified vLLM. A wrapper replaces one attribute per decoder layer, the token mixer, to read and write the recurrent state in the vLLM pool. Because the model declares itself attention-free, vLLM allocates one fixed page per sequence. Outputs matched the i14 reference token for token (48/48 steps on 3/3 prompts in BF16). Finding the bottleneck. A linear fit of decode time against the number of decoder layers L gives: Decode-time linear fit equation At L = 24 , that is 168.1 ms per step, 96.9 percent of it inside the decoder layers. The large projections cost 13.27 ms, near the 12 ms HBM-streaming floor. Most time went to small operators dispatched one at a time under eager PyTorch. Scaling to a full instance. Without tensor parallelism, throughput scales through replicas, with one engine and 20 sequences per logical NeuronCore. Eager throughput grew from 133 output tokens per second on one replica to 6,772 on 64, where host CPU usage reached 82 percent. Compiling the decode step removed per-operator dispatch and raised throughput 1.7 times, to 11,544 (Figure 8). Figure 8: Whole-instance inference throughput. (a) Replica scaling on eager and compiled decode. (b) Compiled decode lifts throughput from 6,772 to 11,544 output tokens per second. What fixed-batch benchmarks hide. Under real traffic, each new decode batch width is a separately compiled shape whose first use costs about 11 seconds. These steps were only 1.1 percent of the total but consumed 47.5 percent of decode time. Padding to fixed widths removed this cost with bit-exact results. Compiled decode then improved per-replica throughput 3.52 times under staggered arrivals, compared with 1.46 times on fixed batches. Because BF16 reassociation makes compiled output differ slightly from eager, use eager decode when exact reproducibility matters. Key takeaways The project produced lessons across both training and inference: Native PyTorch can support custom architectures on Trainium2. i14 retained the GLA architecture and used TorchNeuron Native for the final implementation. Communication design matters for custom optimizers. The Muon all_to_all design reduced per-rank traffic by 24 times and increased training throughput by 1.63 times. Fixed state keeps inference memory predictable. Each sequence uses 29.5 MB regardless of context length. Profile before compiling. Operator dispatch, rather than arithmetic or HBM bandwidth, accounted for most decode time. Benchmark realistic arrival patterns. Fixed batches hid the cost of compiling new shapes for changing batch widths. Conclusion Laplace 3B shows that AWS Trainium2 can support model architectures beyond standard transformers. Using native PyTorch through TorchNeuron Native and the AWS Neuron SDK, i14 trained and served its GLA-based model while preserving a fixed recurrent state. For agentic systems, this changes a basic serving constraint. Longer histories don’t require a larger per-sequence state, which can help teams retain more context while keeping memory use predictable. If growing context is increasing serving cost, reducing concurrency, or limiting agent memory, try i14 or contact your AWS account team to evaluate Laplace 3B on AWS Trainium2. Resources Try i14 AWS Trainium and Trainium2 AWS Neuron SDK documentation Native PyTorch support on AWS Trainium with TorchNeuron Native Gated Linear Attention Transformers with Hardware-Efficient Training Muon optimizer reference implementation AWS Generative AI Innovation Center   About the authors Kevin Shabahang Kevin is VP of AI Research at i14, where he researches different model architectures. His work centers on applying insights from cognitive science and computational neuroscience to develop more efficient large language models. Massimo Bardetti Massimo is CTO of i14.ai , an AI research startup. He has led engineering teams at Amazon Web Services, Microsoft, and startups in AI, neurotechnology, and entertainment. He also creates interactive art installations featured at festivals worldwide. Iman Abbasnejad Iman is an Applied Scientist at AWS, working with customers to design, develop, and deploy generative AI solutions. His work bridges AI research and practical applications, with a focus on large language models, agentic AI systems, model fine-tuning, and performance optimization to build reliable, efficient, and cost-effective AI solutions on AWS. Xiaodong Yu Xiaodong is a Machine Learning Engineer at AWS who focuses on generative AI, large language models, and machine learning performance optimization. His work covers efficient training and inference on AWS purpose-built machine learning accelerators, including AWS Trainium. Daniel Wirjo Daniel is a Solutions Architect at AWS focused on AI and SaaS startups. As a former startup CTO, he works with founders and engineering leaders to build and grow on AWS. Outside work, Daniel enjoys walking with a coffee, spending time in nature, and learning new ideas.
