Workflow context for AI agents with Smartsheet MCP on AWS
summary: The Smartsheet Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server lets AI agents read, update, and act on live data. This post shows two ways to connect it on AWS: Amazon Quick for business teams and Kiro for developers, so your agents can work with Smartsheet without switching tools.
content: AI agents are most useful when they can act on the real work happening across your organization. Running projects and operations involves complex, cross-functional tasks such as updating project timelines, reassigning tasks, and surfacing status. AI agents can support you with these without anyone switching tools. Smartsheet has launched a generally available Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server. With the Smartsheet MCP Server , AI assistants can read, write, and manage Smartsheet data through a standardized protocol. The protocol spans more than 40 tools for exploring, creating, and managing sheets, rows, columns, and automations. You can update task statuses, create rows, and modify project structure directly through natural language. In this post, we walk through two ways you can connect it to your existing workflows. Amazon Quick is an agentic AI workspace built for business users, project managers, and operations teams. They can ask questions, update sheets, and build dashboards through natural language without writing code. Kiro is an agentic IDE where developers connect to Smartsheet through MCP to reference project specs, update task status, and track dependencies without leaving their coding workflow. Architecture overview The following diagram shows how the Smartsheet MCP Server sits as the central integration layer connecting to AWS services. Amazon Quick and Kiro connect directly as MCP clients. Amazon Quick serves knowledge workers, project managers, and operations teams who want to query, update, and automate Smartsheet through natural language. With Kiro, developers can reference project specs, update task status, and track dependencies without leaving their coding workflow. The following architecture diagram illustrates these integration paths: the Smartsheet MCP Server in the center, with Amazon Quick and Kiro as MCP clients on the left, and Smartsheet’s API and data layer on the right. Figure 1: Smartsheet MCP Server architecture showing MCP client connections from Amazon Quick and Kiro through the server to the Smartsheet API layer Sprint management with Amazon Quick and Kiro Consider a software engineering team that tracks their sprint in Smartsheet. Tasks, owners, statuses, and blockers all live in a project sheet. Here’s what each path looks like for the same team: When a user such as a project manager wants to check which sprint tasks are blocked this week, they can ask Amazon Quick through natural language. The Amazon Quick chat agent queries the Smartsheet MCP Server, pulls the relevant rows, and surfaces a summary with owner names and due dates. The response is generated from live Smartsheet data without building a report or dashboard. For developers who are fixing bugs or working through features, they can ask Kiro to pull the current sprint sheet and show them the open backend tasks assigned to them. Kiro queries Smartsheet through MCP and surfaces the list inline. When the fix is committed, a Kiro hook automatically updates the corresponding row status to Complete. Prerequisites Smartsheet MCP Server delivers precisely structured context, including row relationships, column types, cell history, and comments. This produces token-efficient payload sizes rather than returning raw API payloads. This engineering decision compounds into reduced cost and improved latency at scale when running hundreds of AI-assisted queries across a project portfolio. To learn how Smartsheet built their remote MCP server on AWS, see How Smartsheet built a remote MCP server on AWS . Before connecting the Smartsheet MCP Server to Amazon Quick and Kiro, verify that you have the following in place: An active AWS account with appropriate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions for the service you’re connecting (Amazon Quick, or Kiro) A Smartsheet account on a Business, Enterprise, or AWM plan. A Smartsheet Personal Access Token, or OAuth credentials if your client supports the OAuth flow. For Amazon Quick: Author or higher permissions in your Amazon Quick account. For Kiro: Kiro IDE installed from kiro.dev with Node.js available in your environment. The Smartsheet MCP Server is available at three regional endpoints. It uses Streamable HTTP transport (MCP spec versions 2025-06-18 and 2025-03-26) and is authenticated with either OAuth 2.0 or a Personal Access Token. Commercial US: https://mcp.smartsheet.com. EU: https://mcp.smartsheet.eu. AU: https://mcp.smartsheet.au. Both options expose the same Smartsheet toolset. The right choice depends on where your work gets done: Choose Amazon Quick if you need a fully managed, organization-wide solution your whole team can use: no app registration, only pre-built OAuth, and it scales across knowledge workers in your enterprise. Choose Kiro if you’re a developer who wants something lightweight: no infrastructure, only a config file and a personal access token, scoped to your own workflow. Amazon Quick integration Amazon Quick includes Smartsheet as a pre-built connector in its directory. That means reading project status, updating rows, creating discussions, and surfacing risks, all in the same interface your business users already work in. Amazon Quick makes that integration available across the organization, from project managers and operations teams to business users who manage work in Smartsheet. To add the Quick integration: In the Amazon Quick console , navigate to Connectors and find Smartsheet in the directory. Figure 2: The Smartsheet connector in the Amazon Quick Connectors directory Select the Smartsheet connector tile. Enter the following integration details: Name – Descriptive name for your Smartsheet integration. Keep the Connection type and Auth configuration settings as is. Base URL – https://mcp.smartsheet.com . Client ID – App client ID from your Smartsheet Developer Tools app registration. Client Secret – App secret from your Smartsheet Developer Tools app registration. Token URL – https://api.smartsheet.com/2.0/token . Auth URL – https://app.smartsheet.com/b/authorize . Figure 3: Entering the Smartsheet connection details in Amazon Quick Choose Next . On the Manage Tools & Permissions page, you see a list of available tools. Choose Next . Figure 4: The Manage Tools and Permissions page for the Smartsheet connector On the Publish page, choose who can access this connection, and then choose Publish . Figure 5: Choosing who can access the Smartsheet connection on the Publish page Choose Next . After you’re connected, your Amazon Quick chat agent can work with Smartsheet data through natural language: “What projects in our portfolio are currently At Risk?” “Update the status of the authentication task in the Backend API sheet to Complete.” “Create a summary of all overdue items across the Q3 Roadmap and send it to the team.” Figure 6: Amazon Quick chat response summarizing overdue tasks from a Smartsheet project sheet with key observations and recommended actions Kiro integration Kiro is the right path when developers want Smartsheet project context available directly in their development environment, alongside their code, without context-switching. Kiro is built around spec-driven development. It turns high-level prompts into structured specs, then into working code, docs, and tests. MCP servers are how Kiro gets real-world context by connecting to documentation, databases, APIs, and enterprise systems to ground its agent in live data rather than training-time knowledge. A Kiro feature called powers is a one-click installable bundle that packages a curated MCP server with steering files and hooks. It gives the Kiro coding agent a new capability out of the box. For Smartsheet, configuring the connection takes a single JSON configuration block and from that point, the Kiro agent can reference live project data as part of a development workflow. To connect the Smartsheet MCP Server to Kiro, add it to your Kiro MCP configuration ( .kiro/settings/mcp.json for workspace scope). For a full walkthrough, see Getting Started with Kiro and MCP Servers : { "mcpServers": { "smartsheet-us": { "type": "http", "url": "https://mcp.smartsheet.com", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer " } } } } This configuration uses the Personal Access Token (API key) approach. For production deployments, OAuth is recommended. Set SMARTSHEET_API_TOKEN to your Smartsheet Personal Access Token in your environment. Kiro loads MCP servers as background processes on startup. After it’s initialized, Smartsheet tools are available to the Kiro agent across all modes: chat, spec planning, and hooks-based automation. Full details in the Smartsheet MCP Server Documentation . From there, Kiro can reference Smartsheet data as part of development workflows: “Check the Backend API project sheet for any open bugs and generate a prioritized fix list.” Figure 7: Kiro generating a prioritized fix list from open bugs in the Backend API project sheet “Pull the Q3 Roadmap sheet and create a spec for the features marked In Progress.” Figure 8: Kiro creating a spec from the in-progress features in the Q3 Roadmap sheet Enterprise governance For builders deploying in regulated or enterprise environments, the Smartsheet MCP Server security model is built on the same infrastructure and permissions layer as the Smartsheet REST API. It’s not a new trust boundary: OAuth 2.0 and Personal Access Token authentication : choose the auth method supported by your MCP client. User-level permission enforcement : agents can only access data the authenticated user has permission to see. No privilege escalation through natural language prompts. Organization-level AI controls : system administrators can turn on or off AI features globally. Write-tool access is configurable by user group. Streamable HTTP transport : firewall allowlisting is done by fully qualified domain name (FQDN) (mcp.smartsheet.com), not IP address. For compliance architects, the MCP Server doesn’t store prompts, and prompt content stays between the AI client and the model. Smartsheet sees only the structured tool calls and their results. Clean up If you followed this walkthrough and want to remove the integration afterward, here’s how to undo each path: Amazon Quick In the Amazon Quick console, navigate to Connectors . Select your Smartsheet connector. Choose Delete to remove the connection. This revokes the OAuth token and stops agent access to Smartsheet data. Kiro Open your MCP configuration file ( .kiro/settings/mcp.json ). Remove the smartsheet-us entry from the mcpServers object. Restart Kiro to unload the server. Next steps For background on how the server works, see How Smartsheet built a remote MCP server on AWS . After you’ve connected the Smartsheet MCP Server to your system of choice, here are four actions we recommend trying: You can ask the chat agent to monitor your active project sheets, identify rows marked Blocked or At Risk. You can also ask to annotate projects with a discussion comment, and deliver a structured summary to your team through your preferred channel. This would be an example workflow that chains get_sheet_summary , search , and create_discussion_on_row . The agent can also retrieve data through the Smartsheet MCP Server to reconcile task statuses between your issue tracker and your Smartsheet project plan. It can flag drift between the two, and update the affected rows, using get_sheet_summary , get_columns , update_rows , and create_discussion_on_row in sequence. You can also try to aggregate project health signals across your reports and dashboards. You can use it to produce a structured briefing without manual data gathering, drawing on list_reports , get_report , list_dashboards , get_dashboard , and search . Lastly, you can use the agent to follow every write with a discussion comment explaining what changed and why. This creates a human-readable audit trail inside Smartsheet through the combination of update_rows and create_discussion_on_row . All four patterns work across the preceding paths: Amazon Quick for business-user-facing workflows, and Kiro for developer-initiated actions. Building something with Smartsheet MCP and AWS? Share what you’re working on in the comments, or connect with us in the Smartsheet Developer Community . About the authors Galina Jordanowa Galina is a senior product marketing manager II at Smartsheet. She translates complex AI and product capabilities into clear, strategic market narratives and go-to-market (GTM) motions. She brings 26+ years in B2B SaaS marketing and a dev background that means she actually gets how builders think. Throughout her career, she’s connected technical depth with business impact and stays genuinely energized by what’s next in AI and the new ways it’s reshaping how teams build and work. Pyone Thant Win Pyone is a Partner Solutions Architect at AWS, where she supports strategic ISV partners to bring AI-powered solutions to market. She works at the intersection of cloud infrastructure and partner networks, helping partners use AWS services from AI/ML capabilities to data integration patterns to build deeper, more intelligent product experiences. Her work bridges hands-on technical partnership and go-to-market strategy, delivering joint solutions and industry offerings that reach shared customers. Vishnu Elangovan Vishnu is a Worldwide Agentic AI Solution Architect with over a decade of experience in Applied AI/ML and Deep Learning. He loves building and tinkering with scalable AI/ML solutions and considers himself a lifelong learner. Vishnu is a trusted thought leader in the AI/ML community, regularly speaking at leading AI conferences and sharing his expertise on Agentic AI at top-tier events.

title: Strengthening AI safety evaluation through independent third-party review
summary: How Amazon partnered with AVERI to independently assess — and improve — our internal safety testing of Amazon models.
content: As frontier AI models grow in capability, so does the importance of ensuring that safety evaluations are rigorous and comprehensive. At Amazon, we invest heavily in internal safety testing for our models, spanning categories like harmful-content generation, cybersecurity risks, privacy protection, and copyright compliance. A core principle of robust quality assurance is that even rigorous internal processes are strengthened by external scrutiny. That's why we partnered with AVERI (AI Verification and Evaluation Research Institute), an independent nonprofit dedicated to third-party evaluation of AI systems, to conduct an independent review of our internal safety evaluation datasets. AVERI’s mandate wasn’t just to test model outputs but to examine the quality and rigor of our tests themselves — asking whether our evaluations stress-test safety boundaries. How the collaboration worked We provided AVERI with a random sample of prompts drawn from our internal safety-evaluation suite. AVERI's team — led by executive director Miles Brundage and including researchers Sean McGregor, A. Feder Cooper, and George Balston — examined the evaluation prompts for diversity, difficulty calibration, and methodological soundness. AVERI assessed the sample independently without input from our evaluation team, ensuring their findings reflected a genuine external perspective. What the review confirmed AVERI’s review validated several strengths of our evaluation process: Comprehensive topical coverage — aligned with publicly documented safety categories including self-harm, cybersecurity, and other risk areas; Diversity of testing approaches — variation in writing style (professional vs. informal), single-turn and multiturn conversations, and original content; Low contamination risk — content that appeared to be original rather than sourced from publicly available datasets, reducing risk of evaluation leakage through pretraining. Opportunities for improvement With any fresh review comes the opportunity to identify areas that internal teams — deeply familiar with their own work — may overlook. AVERI's external perspective surfaced several opportunities to further strengthen an already comprehensive suite: Expanding linguistic and stylistic diversity — While our evaluations include multilingual prompts, AVERI recommended extending multilingual coverage more evenly across risk categories and further varying prompt structures to broaden the range of scenarios tested; Calibrating attack sophistication — AVERI recommended adding more multistep, adversarial prompts to our existing set, so evaluations probe deeper model reasoning and better reflect sophisticated real-world misuse attempts; Maintaining evaluation freshness — AVERI identified a small number of prompts with time-limited references and a few edge cases where grading criteria could be made clearer; Ensuring evaluation signal quality — In some cases, models may refuse based on superficial cues in a prompt, so passing those tests doesn’t necessarily indicate reliable safety behavior in new situations. How we incorporated the feedback Concrete improvements made: Test set refresh: Updated evaluation datasets to address specific issues identified, removing redundant prompts and adding more-challenging adversarial scenarios Difficulty calibration framework: Introduced tiered difficulty levels to ensure that evaluations include prompts that genuinely push model safety limits, not just straightforward cases Quarterly review cadence: Established a regular evaluation maintenance process to catch staleness, reduce repetition, and incorporate emerging attack patterns Broader language coverage: Expanded multilingual prompts across all risk categories rather than concentrating them in specific areas A model for the field This collaboration represents what we believe is an emerging best practice: engaging independent third parties to evaluate not just model outputs, but the quality of the evaluation process itself. As the AI safety field matures, we expect this kind of meta-evaluation to become an important complement to traditional red-teaming and benchmarking. The benefits are mutual: Amazon gains an independent check on our evaluation quality, while AVERI gains practical experience with the real-world challenges of assessing internal evaluation processes — insights that can inform best practices for the field as a whole. We're grateful to AVERI for their thorough and constructive review, and we plan to continue engaging independent evaluators as our models evolve. Transparency about our safety processes — including where we can improve — is fundamental to building justified confidence in AI safety.

title: From data to decisions: Conversational supply chain intelligence with Amazon Quick and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
summary: Enterprise supply chains are data-rich but insight-poor, with the data to decide scattered across ERP, monitoring, procurement, and email. This post shows how Amazon Bedrock AgentCore exposes those systems as a governed tool layer, and how Amazon Quick turns them into one conversational experience for business users, with a deploy-it-yourself walkthrough.
content: Giving supply chain teams direct access to the systems behind their decisions. Every supply chain generates constant signals: orders in approval, shifting lead times, slowing ports, drifting prices, disruptions. The problem isn’t scarce data. It’s the distance between the data and the decision-maker. Answering “which top-revenue SKUs are exposed to the current port closure, and what will it cost?” used to mean knowing which system held each piece and stitching them together by hand while the domain expert waited. Could that manager instead ask in plain language and get an actionable, cross-system answer in seconds? Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is the intelligence layer, exposing enterprise Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers as a composable tool layer. Amazon Quick turns that into action for personas with no setup. Answers come from live systems of record and grounded documents, not model recall, and every change waits for a named human. In this post, we walk through this pattern end to end, from a conversational walkthrough in Amazon Quick to the AgentCore tool layer behind it, and we show you how to deploy it yourself. The problem: Data-rich, insight-poor Figure 1: Domain expertise sits with users while operational data is fragmented across ERP, monitoring, procurement, and email Each question needs its own tool: inventory from the enterprise resource planning (ERP) system, disruptions from email or news, a request for quotation (RFQ) from procurement, and compliance from a checklist. Correlating is manual. A day in the life A manager’s morning traditionally spans the ERP (inventory exceptions), monitoring tool (alerts), procurement (alternatives), email (RFQ), and a tracker: 45–60 minutes across five systems with a dozen-plus context switches. Conversationally it’s three prompts in one tool, “Any critical disruptions affecting my top-revenue SKUs?” → “Assess the TechComp halt and issue an emergency RFQ to approved alternatives” → “Looks good. Send it.”, in minutes. Figure 2: Traditional multi-tool flow versus a single conversational thread orchestrated by AgentCore Deep dive: Supply chain scenario walkthrough The following five steps follow one disruption from detection to an approved emergency RFQ, all in a single Amazon Quick conversation. Step 1: Discovery – “What tools do I have?” The user asks “What supply chain tools do I have?” and Amazon Quick lists the supply chain MCP servers published in AWS Agent Registry. Because an administrator has turned on the registry integration, the four business MCP servers already appear as connector cards, with connection details pre-populated and no URLs to enter by hand. The orchestration agent is added as its own MCP connector. Step 2: Querying – “Show me active disruptions” “Check active supply disruptions” calls the Disruption Alerts MCP ( assess_disruption_impact ): three disruptions with severity, region, and SKU counts. How we solve it: Quick routes the request through AgentCore to the MCP server, which queries backend monitoring and returns a structured result, no dashboard or export. Step 3: Drill-down – “Assess the critical one” The user opens the TechComp Production Halt. assess_disruption_impact(disruption_id="DISR-002") correlates order, customer, and inventory data: $750K at risk, 23 orders, three days of supply. How we solve it: one MCP tool call fans out across systems of record, so the manager gets a consolidated impact read without touching the ERP. Step 4: Action – “Get mitigation recommendations” The user asks for mitigation. recommend_mitigation(disruption_id="DISR-002") chains the Governance MCP (verify approved alternatives) and Quoting MCP (contract-aligned quote), one flow from one request. How we solve it: the agent plans and sequences the calls, so a single ask spans disruption, governance, and quoting with no manual hand-offs. Step 5: Automated follow-up The user then sets up proactive monitoring (“Alert me every morning if there’s a new critical disruption”). The same flow can run unattended from an inbound supplier email. How we solve it: the same agent and tools run on a schedule or email trigger, posting review-ready cards to the Activity Feed for a person to approve. Put end to end, those five steps are a single runtime sequence: Figure 3: Runtime sequence for the walkthrough, where every result returns to Amazon Quick for approval Solution architecture That’s the experience. Here’s how it is built: the pattern separates the intelligence layer from the interface layer, so each evolves independently, with Amazon Quick as the interface and AgentCore as the intelligence. Figure 4: End-to-end architecture from Amazon Quick to AgentCore (Gateways, Runtime, Identity, Policy) to backends, with AWS Agent Registry alongside Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: The intelligence layer Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a modular agentic platform for building, deploying, and operating agents securely at scale. It offers more than we use here. Four of its services are relevant to this pattern: Runtime – Serverless hosting for MCP servers and agents, with session isolation and built-in identity. Gateway – Turns APIs, AWS Lambda functions, and services into MCP-compatible tools behind a secure managed endpoint, standardizing tool access. Reasoning is the calling agent’s. Identity – Authentication and credential management, compatible with existing identity providers. Policy – Deterministic authorization rules, authored in natural language or Cedar, that intercept every tool call before execution, keeping an agent in its lane on procurement and financial data. The MCP protocol: How tools communicate MCP is an open standard for how AI models interact with external tools. Each server exposes tools with typed parameters: { "server_name": "sc-disruption-alert-gateway", "tools": [{ "name": "assess_disruption_impact", "parameters": { "disruption_id": {"type": "string"}, "context": {"type": "object"} // order, inventory, revenue data } }] // plus classify_severity, recommend_mitigation, get_escalation_chain } This means: AI clients (Quick, custom agents, other MCP apps) can consume the same servers. Backends (SAP, Oracle, custom microservices) can be wrapped as an MCP server. Tool discovery is automatic. Clients query the registry for schemas at runtime. AWS Agent Registry: The discovery layer The registry is the governed discovery layer: a publisher submits a record, a curator approves it, and only then is it discoverable through hybrid search, browsing, or the registry’s MCP endpoint. One scale reality worth noting: because schemas are discovered at runtime, treat each as a contract, versioning new alongside old for breaking changes. Figure 5: Publishing an MCP server record to AWS Agent Registry, a curator approving it, an administrator linking it to Quick, and approved records becoming connector cards Multi-step orchestration The reasoning layer is an agent on AgentCore Runtime, an agent record at its direct invocation URL through a Custom MCP connector, with no Lambda or gateway. Here, it’s the Order Fulfillment Agent. Given one request it plans which tools to call and in what order: User: "A supplier just went down. Find alternatives, verify compliance, issue an emergency RFQ." Disruption Alerts MCP -> identify the disruption Governance MCP -> approved alternatives + compliance + budget authority Quoting MCP -> contract-aligned quote -> one consolidated recommendation Security and governance architecture Every tool call passes through the same AgentCore control set before it reaches a backend. Figure 6: The uniform AgentCore control set before the backend (IAM auth, per-tool authorization, input validation, policy evaluation, rate limiting, data-boundary enforcement, audit logging) The MCP servers in this pattern MCP server Capabilities Example queries Quoting Engine ( sc-quoting-gateway ) Quote generation, pricing rules, validation “Contract-aligned quote for 500 units of SKU-A” Governance Engine ( sc-governance-gateway ) Supplier approval, budget authority, regulatory compliance, policy rules “Is SupplierCo on our approved vendor list?” Invoice Processing ( sc-invoice-gateway ) Invoice approval routing, AP aging, payment schedules “What invoices are pending approval this week?” Disruption Alerts ( sc-disruption-alert-gateway ) Active disruptions, severity, impact assessments, mitigation “Critical disruptions affecting our APAC suppliers?” Order Fulfillment Agent ( sc-order-fulfillment-agent ) Multi-step orchestration across all four business MCPs (AgentCore Runtime, direct invocation URL) “A supplier went down, find alternatives, check compliance, issue an RFQ” Amazon Quick: The enterprise AI assistant Amazon Quick puts AgentCore tools before business users through chat, agents, the Activity Feed, and automated workflows, with no technical setup. Key components used Component Role in this pattern How it works Agent Registry connection Surfaces MCP servers as connectors Admin links the registry once. Records become connector cards Quick Agent One SC agent that adapts to role Tailors to persona (manager, procurement, analyst) MCP connectors Expose MCP tools in chat A card connector exposes tools across Chat, agents, schedules Activity Feed Proactive alerts and actions Agents post cards. The user acts Schedules Recurring natural-language automation For example, “every morning” Outlook Integration Email into the feed Supplier replies parsed and validated Structured data connectors Query operational records Quick queries Space datasets (orders, inventory, suppliers, contracts) for the MCP rule check Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) knowledge base Retrieval over documents Invoices, contracts, policies in an S3 knowledge base, grounding answers through Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) CRM connector (optional) Reads customer records (optional) CRM (for example, Salesforce) accounts, opportunities, contacts. Can also load into datasets Automated Activity Feed and proactive monitoring The Activity Feed is the proactive surface of Amazon Quick, a unified inbox where agents post results, alerts, and recommendations. Feed items are: Actionable, each carries context and next-step actions. AI-triaged, with priority indicators (Reply needed, Follow up, Deadline). Cross-source, spanning email, schedules, agent runs, and external systems. Human-in-the-loop, where agents propose and humans decide. How automated monitoring works AgentCore tools plus the proactive capabilities of Amazon Quick give two paths, time-based and email-driven, through a common trigger → agent → output pipeline. Figure 7: Three-stage pipeline from trigger (schedule or email) to autonomous agent (assess_disruption_impact, check_supplier_approval, apply_approval_rules, validate_quote) to review-ready card Use case: Validate supplier responses from email Suppliers reply to an emergency RFQ by email with pricing. The agent validates each (approved supplier? within guidelines?) and stages the result. It does not author a quote, pick a winner, or issue a purchase order (PO). Phase 1: Setup (one-time, approximately 5 minutes) Connect Outlook : in Amazon Quick, choose Settings → Connections → Add Outlook . Configure Activity Feed : turn on email monitoring in feed preferences. Create SC Agent : build an agent with these instructions: Supply chain procurement assistant. On a supplier RFQ reply with pricing: 1) extract SKU(s), quantities, pricing; 2) validate approved vendor (Governance MCP); 3) check pricing within guidelines (Quoting MCP); 4) post a review-ready card (approved-supplier, within-guidelines); do NOT draft a PO or select a supplier. Create Schedule : “Every 2 hours during business hours, check for new supplier replies and validate them.” Phase 2: Runtime (fully automated) Schedule -> email from "TechSupply Co" (MCU-7200, 10,000 units @ $2.45/unit) -> Governance MCP: approved? | Quoting MCP: within guidelines? -> "Supplier Response - Ready for Review" card The feed card carries the validation results and decision-relevant facts: Supplier Response: Ready for Review Details Supplier TechSupply Co, approved vendor SKU / Qty / Price MCU-7200 · 10,000 units · $2.45/unit Price check within purchasing guidelines Actions Select for PO · Compare responses · Reject Phase 3: Human-in-the-loop The reviewer compares validated responses and either selects a supplier and issues the PO, or rejects with a logged reason. Selection and the PO stay with a person. Use case: Proactive disruption monitoring Schedule-triggered, the same pattern applies: a daily 8:30 AM agent checks for new critical or high-severity disruptions, assesses impact, flags anything under seven days of supply as URGENT, and posts an alert card with an Issue Emergency RFQ action. Where this fits alongside traditional BI Dimension Traditional business intelligence (BI) / dashboards AgentCore + Amazon Quick Access model Navigate, log in, find the dashboard/report Ask in natural language. The system finds the source Time to insight Minutes to hours (find → filter → export → correlate) Seconds (ask → answer with cross-system context) Multi-system correlation Manual: 3-4 tabs, copy-paste Automatic: the agent orchestrates across MCP servers from one query Action gap Insight in one tool → switch → act in another Insight → action in the same conversation Setup cost Weeks/months (dashboard design, ETL, permissions, training) Minutes to connect, once your MCP servers exist Run cost Fixed: pipelines cost the same whether or not anyone asks Usage-based: serverless scales to zero, cost tracks questions (Lambda + agent tokens) Trust & accuracy As fresh as the last ETL load Computed live from systems of record and grounded docs, every write human-gated This isn’t a “replace everything” argument. Dashboards remain superior for trend visualization, collaborative analysis, regulatory reporting, and exploratory analysis. Use conversational AI for real-time operational decisions and BI for strategic analysis. They complement, not compete. Personas and use cases One Quick Agent serves all three personas: the manager maintains continuity, procurement sources with compliance-awareness, the analyst correlates signals. Persona also bounds reach, through row/column-level security and per-persona MCP-tool scoping, so procurement does not see finance data. Persona Use case Tools invoked Outcome SC Manager Morning disruption check Disruption Alerts MCP Disruptions, revenue at risk, days of supply SC Manager Emergency procurement Governance → Quoting MCP Verified alternatives + RFQ, one flow Procurement Supplier verification, budget authority Governance MCP Approval, compliance, limits Procurement RFQ generation and response validation Quoting MCP RFQ issued + responses validated Ops Analyst Cross-system correlation SC Operations Agent Multi-MCP reasoning, one query Ops Analyst Payment queue, audit, disruption trends Invoice / Governance MCP AP aging, audit log, patterns Getting started Deploying the pattern takes three phases: provision the infrastructure, connect Amazon Quick to your data and the registry, and turn on monitoring. Prerequisites Before you begin: An AWS account with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and AWS Agent Registry. AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) v2, AWS Serverless Application Model (AWS SAM) CLI, and Docker (the agent runs as an arm64 container). Python 3.12 or later, with Boto3 1.43.94 or later for the registry step. Active credentials with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions to deploy and register ( aws sts get-caller-identity returns the target account). Data layer: a database (Snowflake, PostgreSQL/RDS, or a SQLAlchemy engine), an Amazon S3 bucket, optionally a Salesforce org. Amazon Quick set up for your organization. (Optional) An Outlook account for email automation. Setup uses two surfaces, so each of the following steps names where it happens: the Amazon Quick web console in a browser (Amazon Quick Sight permissions, Agent Registry linking, connectors, and agent settings) and the Quick Desktop App (connecting Outlook for email automation). The conversational experience in the Desktop App comes last, once setup is done. Deploy the infrastructure Everything is open source and scripted: clone the quick-for-supply-chain example in the aws-samples/sample-amazon-quick-suite-knowledge-hub repository and follow its README.md , or point a coding agent like Kiro at it. The README.md covers three phases. Phase 1 deploys the AgentCore stack: the identity layer (an Amazon Cognito user pool and app client, authorization-code OAuth flow, plus a test user), four business-rule MCP servers (each an AWS Lambda function fronted by its own AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, using CUSTOM_JWT authorization), the gateway targets mapping the tools of each Lambda function, and sc-order-fulfillment-agent on AgentCore Runtime as a container, with least-privilege IAM roles. Phase 2 uploads the synthetic dataset to Amazon S3. Phase 3 verifies gateways and runtime are Ready. Six Agent Registry records are approved. Figure 8: AWS Agent Registry console with six approved records (four MCP Server, one Agent, one Skills) Grant Amazon Quick access to your data In the Amazon Quick web console (browser): grant Amazon Quick access from the Amazon Quick Sight admin page (Manage Quick Sight → Security and permissions) to both the S3 bucket and Amazon Athena, since each table is served through an Athena source over an AWS Glue database. Without the Athena grant, dataset creation fails. Figure 9: Amazon Quick Sight Security and permissions, with Amazon Athena alongside Amazon S3 Link the registry and create connectors Linking the registry is one-time and administrator-level. Creating a connector is per-user. Both happen in the Amazon Quick console. See the AWS Agent Registry integration guide. Link the registry (administrator, one-time) An administrator links one Agent Registry to the Quick account. In the Amazon Quick web console (admin): go to Manage account → Permissions → AWS Agent Registry and turn on the registry ( sc-supply-chain-registry , one per account). Only registries in your account and Region, agent-registry namespace, AWS_IAM (SigV4) authorization, and READY status appear. The Quick-managed service role links it. Figure 10: Linking the registry, where only READY, AWS_IAM registries are selectable Create a connector After the registry is linked, approved MCP server records become connector cards: the four business MCPs as cards, the order-fulfillment agent added manually. At scale, federate connector authentication through your identity provider and provision connectors to groups, with the Cognito user pool as the seam. In the Amazon Quick web console (per user): the four cards appear on the Connectors page ( sc-quoting-mcp , sc-governance-mcp , sc-invoice-processing-mcp , sc-disruption-alert-mcp ). Authenticate through the OAuth authorization-code flow ( OAUTH2_AUTHORIZATION_CODE ) with client ID, secret, and token, authorization, and redirect URLs from the deploy script. Sign in as the test user, turn on tools, create and share. Figure 11: The four business-MCP connector cards, with the order-fulfillment agent added manually Registry-sourced connectors are Custom MCP connectors (relevant for custom permissions). Removing the link later doesn’t delete connectors already created. Figure 12: The Authenticate step using the authorization-code OAuth flow (OAUTH2_AUTHORIZATION_CODE) Add the order-fulfillment agent connector In the Amazon Quick web console: because it is an agent record, create its connector manually (Connectors → Create for your team → Model Context Protocol → Create new): name it sc-order-fulfillment-agent , point it at the AgentCore Runtime direct invocation URL from the deploy script, complete the same OAuth sign-in, create and share. Figure 13: Creating the sc-order-fulfillment-agent connector, pointed at the AgentCore runtime invocation URL Attach the connectors to your agent The deployment creates the Supply Chain agent: a Quick Space, imported datasets and S3 knowledge base, and the agent with instructions, starter prompts, and welcome message. What remains is attaching the connectors. In the Amazon Quick web console (agent settings): open the deployment-created Supply Chain agent (default id sc-supply-chain-agent ) and attach all five connectors (four business MCPs plus sc-order-fulfillment-agent ), or pass the five connector IDs to the setup script. Set up proactive monitoring To make it proactive, Quick runs the same agent on a schedule or on incoming email and posts results to the Activity Feed. Both paths reuse the agent and tools you configured. In the Quick Desktop App (Settings → Connections): connect Outlook and turn on email monitoring. Then, in Quick Chat, create two natural-language schedules, time-based (“Every morning, check for new critical disruptions”) and email-driven (“Every two hours in business hours, check supplier replies and validate”). The agent extracts pricing, runs the checks, and posts a card. Try it in Amazon Quick With the agent and connectors ready, ask in natural language in Amazon Quick Chat. Each prompt shows the data-then-rules pattern. Ask Amazon Quick What you get “What supply chain tools do I have?” The five MCP connectors (quoting, governance, invoice, disruption alerts, order-fulfillment agent), with status. “Show me active supply disruptions.” Active disruptions with severity, region, SKU counts (Disruption Alerts MCP). “Assess the impact of the TechComp production halt.” Revenue at risk, affected orders, days of supply, from your datasets. “Is this supplier an approved vendor, and do we have budget authority for a $72,000 PO?” An approval from the Governance MCP (vendor status, budget authority, compliance). “Generate a contract-aligned quote for 1,000 units for this customer.” A contract-aligned quote from the Quoting MCP, as a branded document. “A supplier just went down. Find alternatives, verify compliance, and issue an emergency RFQ.” The Order Fulfillment Agent chains disruption, governance, and quoting MCPs into one recommendation. Conclusion AgentCore and Amazon Quick are a repeatable enterprise-AI pattern: separate intelligence from interface. AgentCore turns fragmented backends into a composable, governed, AI-accessible layer through standard MCP interfaces. Amazon Quick democratizes access in natural language. The gain is the collapsed decision chain: detect, research, decide, act, and log once spanned five tools, now one conversation. The AI researches, correlates, validates. The person decides. Every call is authenticated, authorized, policy-checked, and audited, and a 45-60 minute routine across five systems can collapse to minutes. That is the shift from data-rich, insight-poor to data-rich, decision-ready. Start with one MCP server and one persona. The registry grows and the experience stays the same. About the authors Vineet Kachhawaha Vineet is a Sr. Worldwide Agentic AI Solution Architect at AWS, focused on Amazon Quick. He works closely with enterprise customers and partners to design, deploy, and scale AI-driven solutions. Vineet also co-led the AWS for Legal Tech initiative, helping legal and compliance organizations harness AI/ML to drive business value. He loves building and tinkering with agentic AI solutions and considers himself a lifelong learner. Vineet regularly speaks at AWS events and industry conferences, sharing his expertise on generative AI and agentic architectures. Kamlesh Mariwala Kamlesh is a Senior Specialist Solutions Architect for Generative AI at Amazon Web Services (AWS), focused on the automotive and manufacturing industries. He helps customers design scalable, secure, and cost-effective architectures that use generative AI, agentic AI, and machine learning to solve complex business problems and speed up time to value. Sachin Sathaye Sachin is a Head of Data and AI GTM and Architectures at AWS, where he advises enterprise leaders on their data and AI transformations.
