title: Fine-tuning GPT-OSS-20B for multilingual reasoning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod
summary: Learn how we fine-tuned GPT-OSS-20B for multilingual reasoning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, and how to decide between supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning with GRPO. SFT took reasoning-language accuracy from 22% to 100%, and GRPO added measurable gains where headroom existed.
content: GPT-OSS-20B is an open-weight reasoning model that thinks in English. Ask it to reason in French, German, Spanish, or Italian and it acknowledges the instruction, then produces its chain-of-thought in English anyway. On a 50-example multilingual reasoning test, the base model reasoned in the correct target language only 22 percent of the time. That 22 percent was almost entirely the English examples (English 100 percent, French 0 percent, German 10 percent, Spanish 0 percent, Italian 0 percent). For teams deploying reasoning models for non-English users, that gap matters. A user who asks a question in French expects the model to reason and answer in French, not to switch to English mid-thought. Closing that gap is a fine-tuning problem. It raises a question every team faces once they start customizing open-weight models: supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), or both? In this post, we walk through how we fine-tuned GPT-OSS-20B for multilingual reasoning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod . We show when SFT alone was sufficient and when GRPO added measurable value on top. To understand more broadly when GRPO helps, we also ran a controlled Qwen2.5-7B experiment across two tasks with different capability gaps. The short answer: SFT does most of the work, GRPO refines when there is headroom to refine, and matching the technique to the capability gap is what decides the outcome. Solution overview This section covers the multilingual reasoning task and dataset, how SFT and GRPO complement each other, and the training stack we ran on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod. The task and dataset The dataset is HuggingFaceH4/Multilingual-Thinking — a chain-of-thought reasoning dataset translated into French, Spanish, German, and Italian alongside English, roughly 949 training and 50 validation examples. The model receives a reasoning language: system-prompt instruction and must both reason and answer in that target language, overriding its strong English prior. The evaluation is 50 test cases: 10 math/logic problems across 5 languages (EN/FR/DE/ES/IT). Two metrics matter: Reasoning-language correct – is the chain-of-thought in the requested language? Answer-language correct – is the final answer in the requested language? How SFT and GRPO fit together The clearest way to think about the two techniques: SFT teaches a behavior the model doesn’t have. GRPO optimizes a behavior the model can already sometimes produce. GRPO works by sampling a group of responses per prompt and pushing the policy toward the above-average ones. If the desired behavior has zero probability in the base distribution, there is very little for GRPO to reinforce. That single idea explains almost every result in this post. The training stack We ran on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod with Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) orchestration. For the initial SFT and GRPO runs on GPT-OSS-20B, we used the PyTorch TRL library. For the Qwen control experiment, we switched to veRL as the trainer, with Ray and KubeRay for distributed orchestration and vLLM for fast rollout generation. Checkpoints and datasets lived on Amazon FSx for Lustre, and the inter-node fabric used Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA). All fine-tuning used Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), which is parameter-efficient and well-suited to both SFT and GRPO. The following diagram shows the training data path end-to-end. A submission from the user lands on the Amazon EKS control plane of the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster. Amazon EKS schedules a Ray head pod plus worker pods that run the veRL trainer and vLLM rollout workers. Both sets of pods mount Amazon FSx for Lustre for the base model, training data, and checkpoints. Inter-node collectives use EFA. Rollouts stream from vLLM back to the veRL trainer, and the trainer writes checkpoints back to Amazon FSx for Lustre. Figure 1: End-to-end training data path for SFT and GRPO fine-tuning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod with veRL, Ray, KubeRay, vLLM, and Amazon FSx for Lustre for Qwen control experiments The following describes each hop in more detail. The submitter starts the run from Amazon SageMaker Studio or the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI). The Amazon EKS control plane on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod places pods on GPU nodes and starts a Ray head with worker pods for the veRL trainer and the vLLM rollout workers. Amazon FSx for Lustre provides shared, high-throughput storage for the base model, the training data, and the checkpoints. When training completes, the trainer writes the LoRA adapter back to Amazon FSx for Lustre for downstream evaluation or serving. Prerequisites To follow along, you need: An Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster with Amazon EKS orchestration. GPT-OSS SFT used 4× ml.g6e.12xlarge (16× L40S 48GB). The Qwen control used 2× g6e.48xlarge (16× L40S). An Amazon FSx for Lustre file system mounted on the cluster with a PersistentVolumeClaim named fsx-claim at /fsx . EFA-enabled instances and a working NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) and aws-ofi-nccl stack for multi-node SFT. A container registry such as Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) to hold the training image built from the reference repository. A HuggingFace access token for openai/gpt-oss-20b and the HuggingFaceH4/Multilingual-Thinking dataset. The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), kubectl , docker , and envsubst available on your workstation. Set up the training environment All of the commands, manifests, and scripts referenced below live in the awsome-distributed-ai GitHub repository under 3.test_cases/pytorch/trl/gpt-oss-lora-grpo/ . Clone the repository and change into the test case directory: git clone https://github.com/awslabs/awsome-distributed-ai cd awsome-distributed-ai/3.test_cases/pytorch/trl/gpt-oss-lora-grpo Copy the environment template, then edit env_vars to set your ECR registry, image name, tag, and HuggingFace token: cp env_vars.example env_vars source env_vars Build the training image and push it to your registry. The image bundles PyTorch, TRL, HuggingFace Transformers, PEFT, and the training and inference scripts: cd artifacts && ./build_push.sh && cd .. Point kubectl at your cluster and apply the FSx storage manager pod. The storage manager gives you a shell into the shared file system for checkpoint conversion and eval-log inspection: aws eks update-kubeconfig --name --region us-east-2 envsubst '$REGISTRY $IMAGE $TAG $HF_TOKEN' \ Fine-tune GPT-OSS-20B with SFT and LoRA We begin by measuring the base model, then configure the SFT run and examine the results. The base-model gap Base GPT-OSS-20B on the 50-case eval scored 22 percent reasoning-language correct (11/50). Per-language: English 100 percent, French 0 percent, German 10 percent, Spanish 0 percent, Italian 0 percent. The model defaults to English reasoning regardless of the instruction. SFT configuration The SFT setup used LoRA r=8, α=16, trained for 1,000 steps on 4× ml.g6e.12xlarge (16× L40S 48GB) with Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) full-shard, bf16 precision, and gradient checkpointing. The job runs as an elastic HyperPodPyTorchJob managed by Kueue, launched with hyperpodrun . Apply the SFT manifest: envsubst '$REGISTRY $IMAGE $TAG $HF_TOKEN' \ Watch training progress: kubectl get pods -l app=gpt-oss-lora-elastic kubectl logs -f -l app=gpt-oss-lora-elastic Loss and gradient norm print each step. A healthy run looks like this: {'loss': 1.035, 'grad_norm': 0.163, 'learning_rate': 0.0002, 'mean_token_accuracy': 0.716, 'epoch': 3.25} {'loss': 1.003, 'grad_norm': 0.171, 'lr': 0.0002, 'acc': 0.722, 'epoch': 3.32} {'loss': 0.976, 'grad_norm': 0.159, 'lr': 0.0002, 'acc': 0.726, 'epoch': 3.57} When training completes, convert the FSDP checkpoint to the Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) format that TRL’s GRPO trainer and the inference scripts expect: kubectl exec -it fsx-storage-manager -- python /app/convert_fsdp_checkpoint.py \ --checkpoint /fsx/checkpoints/checkpoint-1000 \ --output /fsx/checkpoints/converted-peft/lora-checkpoint-1000-peft SFT results and the staged learning curve After SFT, the model reasons in the correct language 100 percent of the time (50/50) across all five languages. SFT learned this in two stages: Around step 200, the model learned to reason in the target language (reasoning-language metric hits 100 percent). Around step 1000, the model additionally learned to give the answer in the target language. Final SFT eval (step 1000): Reasoning-language correct: 100 percent (50/50). Answer-language correct: 62 percent (31/50). Both correct: 62 percent (31/50). Per-language answer accuracy: FR 60 percent, DE 60 percent, ES 30 percent, IT 60 percent, EN 100 percent. Takeaway: SFT is not optional here. The base model can’t follow the reasoning-language instruction at all, and SFT takes reasoning-language from 22 percent to 100 percent. The remaining gap is answer-language at 62 percent. That’s the harder half, because the final answer is short and the English prior is strongest there. Refine answer-language with GRPO Answer-language was the obvious target for GRPO. SFT already produced correct reasoning 100 percent of the time, and the model sometimes produced the answer in the right language, so there was a signal to reinforce. Run GRPO on top of the SFT checkpoint We ran GRPO with TRL’s GRPOTrainer , starting from the SFT checkpoint. The setup: load the SFT LoRA, call merge_and_unload , and add a new LoRA (r=8, α=16, about 0.068 percent trainable parameters, 13.6M of 20B). Training used K=8 generations per prompt, device_map=auto , learning rate 1e-6, and 10 epochs. The reward function scored answer-language (±5.0), reasoning-language (±1.5), and brevity (+0.5 or −1.0), for a combined range of −7.5 to +7.0. Launch GRPO from the converted SFT checkpoint: envsubst '$REGISTRY $IMAGE $TAG $HF_TOKEN' \ GRPO writes checkpoints to /fsx/checkpoints/grpo-singlenode/ . Pick the best checkpoint against your held-out eval (the answer-language metric peaked early in this run) and convert it to PEFT format for inference and evaluation. Result (from the SFT checkpoint): Reasoning-language correct: 100 percent (held: GRPO didn’t break what SFT taught). Answer-language correct: 62 to 70 percent (+8 points, 35/50). Both correct: 70 percent . Per-language answer: FR 70 percent, DE 80 percent, ES 60 percent, IT 40 percent, EN 100 percent. GRPO delivered a real +8 point gain on the answer-language metric while holding reasoning at 100 percent. The gain came where there was headroom to gain. Answer-language was the sometimes-correct behavior that SFT had not fully converged on, and GRPO reinforced it. Compare base, SFT, and GRPO inference side by side To see the qualitative difference, deploy three inference pods that share the same base model but load different adapters: envsubst '$REGISTRY $IMAGE $TAG $HF_TOKEN' \ Run the same French-reasoning prompt through each variant: kubectl exec -it inference-base -- python /app/inference_g6e.py \ --reasoning_language French kubectl exec -it inference-trained -- python /app/inference_g6e.py \ --checkpoint /fsx/checkpoints/converted-peft/lora-checkpoint-1000-peft \ --reasoning_language French kubectl exec -it inference-grpo -- python /app/inference_grpo_new.py \ --use_grpo \ --grpo_checkpoint /fsx/checkpoints/converted-peft/checkpoint-1470-peft \ --reasoning_language French The base pod reasons in English despite the instruction. The SFT pod reasons in French but often answers in English. The GRPO pod reasons and answers in French. To reproduce the full 50-case eval that generated the numbers earlier, run the evaluation manifest and read the result file from the FSx storage manager: envsubst '$REGISTRY $IMAGE $TAG $HF_TOKEN' \ To understand more broadly when GRPO adds value, we ran a controlled experiment on Qwen2.5-7B across two tasks with different capability gaps. Test the pattern with a Qwen2.5-7B control To test the “match technique to capability gap” thesis on a different model and different tasks, we ran controlled experiments on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. The first task is the same multilingual reasoning task (where headroom exists). The second task is GSM8K, where the model is already at peak accuracy. This is an internal experiment, and the public repo has not yet been released. Infrastructure: 2× g6e.48xlarge (16× L40S), EFA 100Gbps, FSx Lustre, Ray 2.44 + KubeRay 1.4.2, veRL v0.6.1, vLLM 0.8.4. Arms: A = base, B = SFT-only, C = SFT+GRPO. Multilingual reasoning (50 cases) Metric A base B SFT C SFT+GRPO Δ GRPO Structured format 0% 92% 98% +6 Reasoning language 0% 96% 98% +2 Answer language 0% 38% 44% +6 Both correct 0% 38% 44% +6 GSM8K, a task with no headroom On GSM8K, base Qwen2.5-7B already scores 90.5 percent (181/200). GRPO at step 30 also scores 90.5 percent. When most sampled groups are all-correct, the group-relative advantage collapses to zero, so there is no learning signal. This is the other half of the thesis: GRPO needs headroom (pass@k >> pass@1) to have anything to optimize. No headroom means no gain. Best practices Start with SFT. GRPO cannot teach a behavior with zero base probability. It can only reinforce responses the model already sometimes produces. SFT took reasoning-language from 22 percent to 100 percent, and every GRPO win in this work was built on that SFT checkpoint. Use LoRA for both SFT and GRPO. LoRA r=8/α=16 was parameter-efficient (0.068 percent trainable), and on the Qwen control it stayed numerically stable through GRPO (grad norm 0.23, about 11.7 GB per GPU). It’s a strong default when you want SFT and GRPO to share the same adapter shape. Match the technique to the gap. Use SFT for missing behavior. Use GRPO for refining an existing, sometimes-correct behavior. GRPO’s realistic ceiling here was +6 to +8 points. Check for reward headroom before spending GPU-hours. If most groups are all-correct (GSM8K 90.5 percent base), the group-relative advantage collapses to zero and GRPO gets no gradient. Verify there is headroom (pass@k >> pass@1) before starting a GRPO run. Clean up resources To avoid ongoing charges, delete the workload resources and then the underlying infrastructure: Delete the training and inference pods and jobs: kubectl delete hyperpodpytorchjob lora-hyperpod-elastic --ignore-not-found kubectl delete pod grpo-single inference-base inference-trained inference-grpo \ eval-grpo fsx-storage-manager --ignore-not-found Scale down or delete the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster or its node groups. Delete the Amazon FSx for Lustre file system once you have exported any checkpoints you want to keep. Delete any Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) buckets or objects used for training data or checkpoint archives. Conclusion We showed how to fine-tune GPT-OSS-20B for multilingual reasoning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, and how to decide between SFT and GRPO. SFT did most of the work: reasoning-language went from 22 percent to 100 percent. GRPO added a real, modest refinement on top (answer 62 percent to 70 percent) where headroom existed. A parallel Qwen2.5-7B control confirmed the pattern. GRPO added +6 percent on multilingual reasoning, where there was room to improve. It added no gain on GSM8K, where the model was already at peak accuracy (90.5 percent). Decision framework: Behavior the model can’t do at all: use SFT . Behavior it does sometimes, with headroom: use SFT then GRPO for a few points more. Model already at peak accuracy, or target has zero base probability: GRPO won’t help . To try this yourself, walk through the test cases in the awsome-distributed-ai repository. For more on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, see the service detail page and the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod documentation . For a walkthrough of Ray on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, see the related post Running distributed training on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod with Ray and Amazon SageMaker Studio . The link will be added after that post is published. Share your results in the comments.   About the authors Mijanur Palash Mijanur is a Specialist Solutions Architect on the AI/ML Infrastructure team at AWS. He focuses on distributed training and reinforcement learning workloads on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod for automotive, pharmaceutical, and generative AI customers. Outside of work, Palash enjoys hiking and photography. Mark Vinciguerra Mark was a Worldwide Specialist Solutions Architect for Generative AI at AWS, focused on distributed training and inference on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod. He works with strategic customers on large-scale foundation-model workloads across EKS and Slurm orchestration and contributes reference architectures and workshops for HyperPod, Ray, and SageMaker Unified Studio.

title: How Octave built a secure multi-tenant AI foundation on Amazon Bedrock
summary: Octave built a secure, multi-tenant AI foundation on Amazon Bedrock, using Cohere Embed v4 for embeddings and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for isolated agent execution, to power a Complaint Triage Assistant that searches 2 billion regulated documents without crossing tenant boundaries.
content: In quality management for regulated industries, the institutional memory that resolves a problem is almost always buried somewhere in a customer’s history. A similar defect investigated last year, a Corrective and Preventive Action (CAPA) that fixed the root cause, an audit finding that flagged the same gap. That knowledge sits in billions of documents no human can search by semantic similarity across languages and formats, so every investigation starts from scratch. Octave Reliance has helped each organization collect documents across multiple systems to help them search more easily and keep track of everything they have. The Octave Reliance team saw unlocking this history as its single largest opportunity to help customers work faster and stay compliant. The obstacle was equally clear: complaint records, audit findings, and corrective actions carry the platform’s strictest isolation requirements, and those were exactly the records the AI would need to read. In a platform serving over 14,000 customers across medical devices, pharmaceuticals, and food manufacturing, a single inadvertent disclosure from one customer to another would carry regulatory consequences far outweighing any AI benefit. Octave operates across 180 countries, serving more than 60% of the Global Fortune 500 . Its cloud-native quality management system, Reliance , supports over 650 enterprise customers with over 40 applications, from complaint management and CAPA tracking to audit management and supplier quality. Everyone generates regulated data that AI could reason over. Each customer is a separate tenant and no data can cross a tenant boundary. Faced with that, the Reliance team made an unusual call: rather than shipping one AI feature, it spent its first cycle building a foundation every future feature would sit on. That foundation has since cut deployment time per use case by 50 percent. If you are bringing AI to a software as a service (SaaS) platform where the data is valuable, but isolation is non-negotiable, the reasoning travels beyond quality management. In this post, we walk through the four tensions that shaped the design and the three-layer foundation Octave built with Cohere Embed v4 on Amazon Bedrock. We then follow the pipeline that embedded 2 billion documents and the Complaint Triage Assistant that proved it in production. Why a foundation, not a feature Envisioning workshops with AWS surfaced four high-impact use cases: complaint summarization and triage, audit readiness monitoring, incident narrative generation, and predictive quality risk scoring. They also surfaced the insight that shaped everything after dozens of applications, each with different document types and workflows. Building AI for one in a silo meant rebuilding the infrastructure for the next. So, the team inverted the plan: build the horizontal platform first, then cut vertical feature slices into it. Complaint summarization and triage went first, to prove the architecture before the rest followed. The four tensions Before selecting a single model, the team spent its time on four problems that pulled in different directions. None could be traded away. Making data available without risking inadvertent disclosure. Complaint records, CAPAs, standard operating procedures (SOPs), and audit findings belong to one tenant and must be unreachable by another. Not even an errant AI query could cross. Vector store, retrieval logic, and generation context all had to be scoped to a single tenant. Executing agents in isolation. The permissions governing an agent’s tools, data stores, and model endpoints had to be scoped to the requesting user rather than a shared service role, available only during execution, and respectful of that user’s access rights. A shared agent pool with static credentials failed all three. Reading content that cannot be trusted. Agents here ingest complaints, email attachments, scanned PDFs, and images from outside the organization. The OWASP Top 10 for large language model (LLM) Applications (2025) names the threats that apply directly: prompt injection through ingested content (LLM01), sensitive information disclosure (LLM02), improper output handling (LLM05), and excessive agency (LLM06). Hidden instructions in an attached PDF are not hypothetical at this volume. Embedding 2 billion documents without a quarter-long wait. Reliance hosts more than 2 billion documents, with individual tenants storing millions of Word files, PDFs, scanned forms, spreadsheets, images, and email. The team committed to onboarding even the largest tenant within a single working day. Because these documents inform regulatory decisions, quality could not be traded for throughput. A missed complaint erodes trust in the whole system. Where the architecture landed Holding four tensions at once narrowed the options considerably. Amazon Bedrock addressed them as one platform: multi-model access through a single API, the AWS Region residency and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) governance the AWS account already enforces, and Guardrails as production content controls rather than something to build. The foundation resolves into three layers, shown in Figure 1. Data preparation embeds quality documents with Cohere Embed v4 on Amazon Bedrock and writes them to a per-tenant vector store on Amazon OpenSearch Service . Secure execution passes a user request through AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , which applies authentication and policy before handing it to an isolated microVM session that calls an Anthropic Claude model on Amazon Bedrock. Wrapping both, content protection applies Amazon Bedrock Guardrails twice: input filtering on the way in, output filtering before anything reaches the handler. Retrieval, execution, and screening stay in separate stages, so each can be enforced and evidenced on its own. Figure 1: High-level architecture of the Reliance AI foundation Choosing how to represent the data Nothing else worked until the documents were retrievable. That meant accurately, across languages and formats, and not across a tenant boundary. The team evaluated embedding models against its own corpus rather than public leaderboards. The deciding questions were specific to this data: what a photo of a cracked housing has to do with the paragraph describing it, and a German complaint with an English CAPA. Cohere Embed v4 on Amazon Bedrock won on five counts and they weren’t independent of each other. What was decided first was how much of the pipeline was made unnecessary. Quality records carry photos of defective products, scanned inspection forms, and annotated diagrams alongside text. Embed v4 places both modalities in one vector space. A photo of a cracked housing and the paragraph describing that defect are retrievable from a single query, with no separate pipeline per modality. Native multilingual support does the same work along the other axis: documents arrive in multiple languages, often inside one tenant’s corpus, and need no translation preprocessing. Two pipelines the team never had to build, and two fewer places for a document to fall out of retrieval. The remaining three counts settled where the vectors could live and what they would cost. Customer data can’t leave its AWS Region, even for inference, so in-Region model availability on Amazon Bedrock was a precondition rather than a convenience. Embed v4 supports in-Region inference in the US East (N. Virginia) Region (us-east-1), Europe (Ireland) Region (eu-west-1), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo) Region (ap-northeast-1), covering three of Octave’s regional compliance requirements. Model and feature availability varies by Region and changes over time. For current coverage, see Regional availability by models in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. Within each Region, Amazon OpenSearch Service costs scale linearly with dimension count. That made Embed v4’s configurable output dimensions of 256–1,536 worth testing rather than accepting by default. Testing against representative production queries showed 512 dimensions holding target accuracy while cutting storage roughly 66 percent against the 1,536 default. The 128K token context window paid off elsewhere entirely: chunks of roughly 4K tokens pack many to a request, which is where the onboarding throughput came from. Keeping tenants apart at runtime The harder question was where to enforce tenant separation. Application code would have worked, but it would have meant every future feature team getting it right on every code path, where one missed check risks inadvertent cross-tenant disclosure. The team pushed isolation into the runtime instead. AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, enforces separation below the application layer, and because it stays framework- and model-independent, the agent framework and models chosen for the Complaint Triage Assistant were not constrained by the isolation decision. Each user session runs in a dedicated microVM with its own CPU, memory, and filesystem, stopped and sanitized when the session ends. That is hardware-level separation designed to hold regardless of how the agent behaves. AgentCore carries the authenticated user’s identity through the whole execution chain: per-user OAuth token vaults verify the agent acts for that specific user rather than a shared service identity, and credentials are scoped per-agent and live only during the session. AgentCore Gateway authorizes at the tool, operation, and parameter level. Automated reasoning provides formal verification against the defined rules. It’s the same discipline behind IAM and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) policy validation. Figure 2 traces that separation across two tenants. Figure 2: AgentCore session separation between tenants. Each microVM is stopped after use with memory sanitized. A complaint submitted by a quality handler at Tenant A therefore reaches only Tenant A’s token vault, tools, and sandbox in AgentCore Code Interpreter, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Tenant B’s session has no path to any of them. Treating ingested content as untrusted This tension had no clean answer. A complaint attachment is untrusted input, but it’s also the thing the agent exists to read, so suspicious content couldn’t be rejected. The team settled on defense in depth. Octave applied Amazon Bedrock Guardrails over the agent logic rather than inside it, at three points in the complaint workflow. The ApplyGuardrail API evaluates text extracted from attachments before embedding, retrieved documents and tool outputs before they enter the agent’s context, and the synthesized brief before the handler sees it. Attachment-derived content is passed with input tagging, marking it as data rather than instruction. That is what makes an injection buried mid-document detectable. Personally Identifiable Information (PII) is masked on the way in. Detection alone wasn’t sufficient, so bounded agency sits underneath. Whatever an agent is asked to do, AgentCore Gateway still governs which tools it can invoke, and document extraction runs in the AgentCore Code Interpreter sandbox with no network egress and no persistence beyond the session. A payload hidden in a PDF has to defeat every layer, not one. The effect: detection and masking rates are tracked per tenant, so what the screening caught is something Octave can evidence rather than assert. Getting 2 billion documents through the pipeline Ahead of the embedding model sat the harder problem: extracting usable content from Word files, spreadsheets, digital PDFs, scanned pages, photographs, and email threads. Several languages appear, sometimes inside one record. And it had to run fast enough that onboarding took a day rather than a quarter. Figure 3 traces the resulting pipeline end to end. Figure 3: Ingestion pipeline: event-driven document processing from the application platform through Step Functions orchestration to the per-tenant OpenSearch index. Document events fan out through Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) and Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) into an AWS Step Functions state machine. That state machine orchestrates parsing, chunking, and embedding across concurrent AWS Lambda executions inside a dedicated Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC). Because parallelism comes from fanning batches across executions rather than scaling one resource, throughput grows without rearchitecting. Parsing handles the heterogeneity: semantic hierarchy preserved from Word files and spreadsheets, optical character recognition (OCR) applied to scanned PDFs lacking a text layer, embedded images treated as first-class content. Chunks carry metadata: tenant, document type, source application, language, and a content hash. That metadata drives both retrieval filtering and per-tenant namespace enforcement. The throughput came from packing. Interleaving many 4K chunks into single requests against Embed v4’s 128K context window cut the API calls for a large corpus by about an order of magnitude. In Octave’s internal testing on Amazon Bedrock, Embed v4 delivered 28 million tokens per minute. After tuning batch sizes with Cohere’s solutions architects until memory bottlenecks cleared, the pipeline sustained 1.4 million documents per 24 hours per tenant workload. That is what made the single-working-day commitment real. The Complaint Triage Assistant A hospital reports defective syringes to a medical device manufacturer, and the record lands with email, photos of damaged units, and supporting documentation attached. A quality handler has to piece the context together across those formats, work out whether anything like it has been reported before, and find what resolved it. Only then can a priority be assigned, often inside a reporting window measured in days. The assistant is built with the Strands Agents SDK, open-sourced by AWS, which composes agentic workflows as graphs, with nodes as tool invocations or model calls and edges as the data dependencies between them. AgentCore runtime runs that graph and isolates it per session, and five stages carry a complaint from raw attachments to a finished brief. Document extraction comes first. PDFs, images, email attachments, and videos all enter AgentCore Code Interpreter, which parses each artifact into a structured intermediate representation. A Claude model on Amazon Bedrock then summarizes the record, and that summary, rather than the raw multi-thousand-token source, becomes the retrieval query. Retrieval runs it against the tenant’s OpenSearch index of Embed v4 embeddings, surfacing similar past complaints and their CAPAs, with AgentCore Gateway enforcing that only authorized namespaces are reachable. What comes back is not trusted on similarity alone. A separate model call scores results by confidence and discards matches that share vocabulary but differ in root cause. What survives goes to synthesis, where Anthropic Claude Sonnet on Amazon Bedrock assembles the output: key facts, sentiment, urgency indicators, the closest historical records with their outcomes, and a recommended triage priority. Completed briefs are cached in Amazon DynamoDB with a per-environment time to live (TTL), so repeated views cost nothing extra. The handler no longer starts from zero, but from institutional memory. Figure 4 places that engine behind a private API boundary. A portal request reaches AgentCore runtime through a private Amazon API Gateway and a Lambda function, and retrieval reads the document index through role-based access with pre-signed URLs while attachments stay in Amazon S3. Cached summaries and OpenTelemetry traces exit to the summarization table and the evaluation dashboard. Figure 4: Summarizing engine: the AgentCore-powered workflow handling document extraction, retrieval, reasoning, and synthesis within a private API boundary, with response caching and full observability. Figure 5 reduces the same path to a single line, with Guardrails filtering at both ends. Figure 5: Complaint Triage Assistant pipeline from ingestion to handler output Proving what the agent did Observability here is not only how the engineering team debugs but also how they integrate with system auditing capabilities to meet compliance requirements. An auditor can ask why a particular complaint was triaged the way it was, and “the model decided” will not survive that conversation. AgentCore captures OpenTelemetry-compatible traces across every node of the graph: each model call, retrieval, and AgentCore Code Interpreter run. Months later, Octave can show which retrieved documents and prompts produced a given brief. The model invocation logging of Amazon Bedrock adds a per-tenant record of every request and response, scoped through the IAM identity AgentCore propagates, with costs attributing to the initiating tenant in Amazon CloudWatch. Offline, AgentCore Evals reruns the workflow against expert-annotated ground truth after any change to prompts, models, or retrieval parameters, reporting summarization faithfulness, retrieval precision at K, and output completeness. A prompt that reads better but retrieves worse gets caught before users see it. Results The Complaint Triage Assistant has been running in production for three months, and the following numbers reflect that period. The handler who used to open an investigation with nothing now opens it with the relevant history already assembled. The 4–6 hours Octave measures per investigation is the work the pipeline absorbed: extraction across formats, the hunt for precedent, and the reading it takes to tell a genuinely similar defect from a coincidence of wording. The foundation also changed how quickly Octave ships. By its own accounting, development cycles for new AI capabilities went from months to weeks. Shared data preparation, secure execution, and retrieval are the three layers of Figure 1. They cut deployment time per use case by 50 percent, because each new capability inherits them rather than rebuilding them. That landed semantic search in Q2, two quarters ahead of the original Q4 target. Looking back The decision to build a foundation first was the one the team second-guessed most. Months of infrastructure work is hard to defend when stakeholders want an AI feature they can see. The next round of use cases has borne it out. Two choices carried it: isolation pushed into microVM sessions and identity propagation rather than application code, and embedding models evaluated against Octave’s own corpus, which surfaced the 512-dimension trade-off no benchmark would have shown. The team also drew a line it chose not to cross. The assistant surfaces context and precedent. The quality handler still makes the call. In an industry where that call carries regulatory weight, that boundary shaped what got automated and what did not. What’s next Octave is now extending the foundation across the Reliance suite. Audit readiness monitoring, incident narrative generation, and predictive quality risk scoring are next, each building on the same infrastructure. If your platform faces a similar tension: valuable data behind hard isolation requirements. Octave’s experience shows the trade-offs are workable. To learn more about the services behind this story, see Amazon Bedrock , the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation , and Cohere on Amazon Bedrock . For related architectural guidance, see AWS vector solutions: Build agentic AI where your data lives and Scaling agentic AI: Enterprise patterns without vendor lock-in . title: Access OpenAI GPT models on Amazon Bedrock from Canada with cross-Region inference
summary: Canadian organizations can now access OpenAI GPT-5.6, GPT-6, and GPT-6.1 models on Amazon Bedrock from the Canada (Central) and Canada West (Calgary) Regions using cross-Region inference. This post covers the models and inference profiles, how to set up permissions, and how to invoke them with the Responses, Chat Completions, and Converse APIs.
content: Canadian organizations building generative AI applications on Amazon Bedrock often need the latest foundation models (FMs), such as OpenAI GPT-6.1, OpenAI GPT-6, and GPT-5.6, accessible from the Canadian AWS Regions. With Amazon Bedrock cross-Region inference (CRIS), you can now access these models from Canada. OpenAI GPT-5.6 models (Sol, Terra, and Luna), GPT-6 (Astra, Sol, and Luna), and GPT-6.1 Sol are available from the Canada (Central) and Canada West (Calgary) Regions. Inference is processed in North America, with data-residency controls described later in this post. Cross-Region inference is a capacity mechanism. Your application calls the Amazon Bedrock Runtime endpoint in your source Region. Amazon Bedrock then routes the request to a supported destination Region for processing. With this approach, you get access to a broader capacity pool that can help your application sustain throughput during demand spikes. You don’t need to manage destination Region routing in your application. In this post, we walk through the GPT-5.6, GPT-6, and GPT-6.1 models available from Canada and the cross-Region inference profiles that serve them. We then show how to set up permissions and invoke the models with the OpenAI Responses API, Chat Completions API, and the Amazon Bedrock Converse API. For the Responses API, we include streaming and tool-use examples. Finally, we cover how to request quota increases, review the observability signals available in your source Region, and clean up when you are done. Models available from Canada With Amazon Bedrock, you can access three families of OpenAI models in Canada through cross-Region inference. The following table summarizes each model and its positioning. Model Positioning GPT-6.1 Sol Strong reasoning and coding for tasks where both performance and cost matter GPT-6 Astra Complex end-to-end reasoning and agentic tasks GPT-6 Sol Strong reasoning and coding for recurring tasks with economics suited to regular use GPT-6 Luna Fast, low-cost inference for high-volume repeated tasks with adjustable reasoning effort per request GPT-5.6 Sol High reasoning, coding, and agentic workloads GPT-5.6 Terra Balanced performance and cost for everyday production GPT-5.6 Luna Fast and affordable for high-volume, latency-sensitive applications These models accept text and image inputs, return text, and support a 1-million-token context window, reasoning mode, and tool calling. GPT-6.1 Sol supports the same context window and tool calling, with additional input and output modalities documented in its model card. GPT-5.6, GPT-6, and GPT-6.1 also support prompt caching on Amazon Bedrock (see the Prompt caching section). These models are available through the OpenAI Responses API, the OpenAI Chat Completions API, and the Amazon Bedrock Converse API on the bedrock-runtime endpoint. For pricing, see Amazon Bedrock pricing . For per-model Region availability, see the model cards in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide . Cross-Region inference profiles from Canada Amazon Bedrock inference profiles are logical identifiers you pass in place of a raw model ID. Each profile defines a model and the set of Regions to which Amazon Bedrock can route a request. Two profile types are available from Canada: US geographic (prefixed us. ) routes requests to your Canadian source Region and US Regions. Choose this profile when your workload requires inference processing to remain within North America (Canada and the US). Global (prefixed global. ) routes requests to supported commercial AWS Regions where the model is deployed. This draws on a broader capacity pool at the time of the request. Endpoint availability differs by model and source Region, as shown in the following table. Model US geographic profile Global profile GPT-6.1 Sol ca-central-1, ca-west-1 ca-central-1, ca-west-1 GPT-6 Astra / Sol / Luna ca-central-1, ca-west-1 ca-central-1, ca-west-1 GPT-5.6 Sol / Terra / Luna ca-central-1, ca-west-1 ca-central-1 Profile membership and model availability can change. The global profile for the GPT-5.6 models is available only from ca-central-1 . From ca-west-1 , use the US geographic profile for GPT-5.6. Verify the active profiles for your source Region before deployment, either with the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) or on the console (see the following section), or see the Cross-Region inference support documentation . Getting started The following sections walk through the setup and code needed to invoke these models from your Canadian source Region. Prerequisites Before you begin, confirm that you have the following: An AWS account with the Canada (Central) ca-central-1 or Canada West (Calgary) ca-west-1 Region enabled as your source Region. An AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role or user with permissions to invoke the inference profiles (see Set up permissions ). A service control policy (SCP) that allows the inference profiles in your source Region, if your organization enforces SCPs (see SCP considerations). Python 3.9 or later with the openai , boto3 , and aws-bedrock-token-generator packages installed. Set up permissions For quick exploration, attach the AWS managed policy AmazonBedrockLimitedAccess . For deployed workloads with stricter access controls, use a least-privilege custom policy. The following example grants access to the GPT-6 Astra global profile from ca-central-1 : { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["bedrock:InvokeModel*"], "Resource": [ "arn:aws:bedrock:ca-central-1::inference-profile/global.openai.gpt-6-astra" ] }, { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["bedrock:InvokeModel*"], "Resource": ["arn:aws:bedrock:*::foundation-model/openai.gpt-6-astra"], "Condition": { "StringLike": { "bedrock:InferenceProfileArn": "arn:aws:bedrock:ca-central-1::inference-profile/global.openai.gpt-6-astra" } } } ] } If you authenticate through the API-key path (bearer token for the OpenAI SDK), also grant bedrock:CallWithBearerToken . For the Responses API, add bedrock:InvokeModel on arn:aws:bedrock:ca-central-1:*:project/default . SCP considerations If your organization restricts Regions through SCPs, use the bedrock:InferenceProfileArn condition key to allow CRIS traffic while blocking direct calls to unapproved Regions. The following SCP denies Amazon Bedrock inference outside your approved source Regions unless the request uses a CRIS inference profile: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "DenyBedrockOutsideCanadaUnlessCris", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": ["bedrock:InvokeModel*"], "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringNotEquals": { "aws:RequestedRegion": ["ca-central-1", "ca-west-1"] }, "ArnNotLike": { "bedrock:InferenceProfileArn": [ "arn:aws:bedrock:*:*:inference-profile/us.openai.*", "arn:aws:bedrock:*:*:inference-profile/global.openai.*" ] } } } ] } With this condition, Amazon Bedrock can route to the profile’s destination Regions even when those Regions are otherwise denied by your SCP. Every destination Region in your chosen profile must be allowed for the request to succeed. For more detail, see Set up cross-Region inference in multi-account environments . Verify active inference profiles Before invoking a model, you can verify which profiles are active in your source Region with the AWS CLI. The following command lists the active OpenAI profiles from ca-central-1 . To run the same check from Calgary, replace ca-central-1 with ca-west-1 . aws bedrock list-inference-profiles \ --region ca-central-1 \ --type-equals SYSTEM_DEFINED \ --query "inferenceProfileSummaries[?contains(inferenceProfileId, 'openai')].[inferenceProfileId,status]" \ --output table The Amazon Bedrock console offers the same view. Open the console, choose Canada (Central) or Canada West (Calgary) as your Region, choose Cross-Region inference under Inference , and review the available profiles. The following screenshot shows the active OpenAI inference profiles listed on the Amazon Bedrock console for the Canada (Central) Region. Figure 1: Active OpenAI cross-Region inference profiles on the Amazon Bedrock console (Canada (Central)) Invoke the models through Amazon Bedrock Runtime GPT-5.6, GPT-6, and GPT-6.1 support three access paths on the bedrock-runtime endpoint: the OpenAI Responses API, the OpenAI Chat Completions API, and the Amazon Bedrock Converse API. The OpenAI-compatible APIs are called on the /openai/v1 paths of the endpoint. The endpoint accepts either AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4) or an Amazon Bedrock API key . The following examples use the Amazon Bedrock token generator for Python to create a short-term Amazon Bedrock API key from your current AWS credentials, so your application does not need to store a static key. OpenAI Responses API For applications that already use the OpenAI SDK with the Responses API, point the client at the Regional Amazon Bedrock Runtime endpoint and pass the inference profile ID as the model. from aws_bedrock_token_generator import provide_token from openai import OpenAI region = "ca-central-1" # Use "ca-west-1" for Calgary client = OpenAI( base_url=f"https://bedrock-runtime.{region}.amazonaws.com/openai/v1", api_key=provide_token(region=region), ) response = client.responses.create( model="global.openai.gpt-6-astra", input="What are the key considerations for AI governance in Canadian financial services?", max_output_tokens=1024, ) print(response.output_text) For streaming output, set stream=True and iterate over the response events, printing text as it arrives: stream = client.responses.create( model="global.openai.gpt-6-luna", input="List five generative AI use cases for Canadian healthcare.", max_output_tokens=512, stream=True, ) for event in stream: if event.type == "response.output_text.delta": print(event.delta, end="", flush=True) OpenAI Chat Completions API The OpenAI Chat Completions format works through the same endpoint. response = client.chat.completions.create( model="global.openai.gpt-5.6-terra", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize recent AI regulatory trends in Canada."}], max_completion_tokens=1024, reasoning_effort="low", ) print(response.choices[0].message.content) For the full list of supported parameters, including reasoning effort levels, see the model cards in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. Amazon Bedrock Converse API Use the Converse API when your application calls Amazon Bedrock through an AWS SDK. Boto3 resolves credentials through the standard AWS credential chain. import boto3 bedrock = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name="ca-central-1") response = bedrock.converse( modelId="us.openai.gpt-5.6-terra", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Summarize recent AI regulatory trends in Canada."}]}], inferenceConfig={"maxTokens": 1024}, ) # GPT-5.6 and GPT-6 may return a reasoningContent block alongside the text. # Select the block that contains the text output. text_output = next(block["text"] for block in response["output"]["message"]["content"] if "text" in block) print(text_output) The same call works for GPT-6 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, and GPT-6.1 Sol by changing the inference profile ID. The following example uses the US geographic profile for GPT-6 Sol and the global profile for GPT-6 Luna. Both were validated from ca-central-1 . # GPT-6 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, and GPT-6.1 Sol are called the same way. Swap the inference profile ID, and choose a us. (US geographic) or global. profile to match your data boundary. # For example, GPT-6.1 Sol via the US geographic profile: modelId="us.openai.gpt-6.1-sol" # GPT-6 Sol via the US geographic profile: strong reasoning and coding for complex work. response = bedrock.converse( modelId="us.openai.gpt-6-sol", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Summarize recent AI regulatory trends in Canada."}]}], inferenceConfig={"maxTokens": 512}, ) # GPT-6 Luna via the global profile: fast, low-cost inference for high-volume tasks such as classification. response = bedrock.converse( modelId="global.openai.gpt-6-luna", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Classify this ticket as BILLING, TECHNICAL, or OTHER: ..."}]}], inferenceConfig={"maxTokens": 256}, ) Tool use These models support client-side tool use (function calling) . Define tools in the tools parameter, and the model returns a structured tool-call request for your application to execute. response = client.responses.create( model="global.openai.gpt-6-astra", input="What's the current exchange rate from CAD to USD?", tools=[{ "type": "function", "name": "get_exchange_rate", "parameters": { "type": "object", "properties": { "from_currency": {"type": "string"}, "to_currency": {"type": "string"} } } }], ) # The model returns a tool-call request rather than text. for item in response.output: if item.type == "function_call": print(f"Tool: {item.name}, Args: {item.arguments}") Prompt caching GPT-5.6, GPT-6, and GPT-6.1 support prompt caching on Amazon Bedrock to reduce the cost and latency of repeated prompt prefixes. Implicit caching requires no changes to your code: Amazon Bedrock automatically caches eligible prefixes of 1,024 tokens or more. Cached tokens read on subsequent requests are billed at a discounted rate and do not count against your tokens-per-minute quota. Cached tokens appear in the response usage object and in Amazon CloudWatch metrics so you can track usage. For cache-write pricing, minimum prefix sizes, and support for explicit cache breakpoints, see the prompt caching documentation and the individual model cards . Quota management Cross-Region inference quotas on the bedrock-runtime endpoint are measured in tokens per minute (TPM) per model. Each quota combines input and output tokens against a single limit. US geographic and global inference profiles have separate quota allocations, so switching between them changes the pool you draw from. Token consumption combines input tokens, cache-write input tokens, and output tokens. Output tokens are multiplied by the model’s burndown rate, so output-heavy workloads consume quota faster than raw token counts suggest. Before a production rollout, request quota increases early and monitor quota utilization. Test with representative prompts, output lengths, streaming behavior, concurrency, and peak traffic. To request a quota increase, follow these steps: Open the Service Quotas console in ca-central-1 or ca-west-1 . Choose Amazon Bedrock , then select the quota named “Cross-Region InvokeModel tokens per minute” for the model that you need. Choose Request increase at account level , enter your target value, and submit the request. For details on how token usage and costs are tracked, see Track usage and costs in Amazon Bedrock . Observability Because these models run through the Amazon Bedrock Runtime API, requests made through an inference profile appear in your observability tooling the same way on-demand requests do. Invocation logs and Amazon CloudWatch metrics are recorded in your source Region. This holds regardless of where the request was processed. Your observability stays in one place. AWS CloudTrail logs every request, recording which destination Region served it in the additionalEventData.inferenceRegion field. For example: "additionalEventData": { "inferenceProfileArn": "arn:aws:bedrock:ca-central-1:111122223333:inference-profile/global.openai.gpt-6-astra", "inferenceRegion": "us-west-2" } Amazon CloudWatch metrics are published per inference profile, covering invocation count, token count, latency, throttles, and errors. Model invocation logging delivers full request and response payloads to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) or Amazon CloudWatch Logs. To activate it on the Amazon Bedrock console, choose Settings , then choose Model invocation logging . You can also call the PutModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration API. It is off by default. AWS Data Exports itemizes spend by model and profile. Amazon CloudWatch Coding Agent Insights If you use these models to power AI coding assistants such as OpenAI Codex, Amazon CloudWatch Coding Agent Insights provides a dedicated dashboard. It surfaces token usage, API request counts, active users, and cost attribution across dimensions such as department, team, and environment. To activate it, configure your coding agent to export telemetry to Amazon CloudWatch. For the setup steps, see Set up OpenTelemetry for OpenAI Codex . Clean up To avoid ongoing charges after testing, remove the resources you created: Turn off model invocation logging. On the Amazon Bedrock console, choose Settings , then choose Model invocation logging , or call DeleteModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration . This stops delivery of logs to Amazon S3 and Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Delete or detach the IAM policies and any Amazon Bedrock API keys that you created for testing. The inference profiles themselves are system-defined and incur no cost when they aren’t in use. Security and compliance Cross-Region inference is designed to protect your data in transit and at rest. Requests travel over the AWS private backbone encrypted with TLS 1.2+ rather than the public internet. For Canadian customers, your data at rest stays in your source Region by default. This includes invocation logs, knowledge bases, and configurations. Only the transient inference computation happens in the destination Region, and by default model providers don’t have access to your prompts or completions. There’s one consideration specific to OpenAI models. Content flagged by automated abuse classifiers might be retained for up to 30 days in the destination Region for review. If you want to constrain processing to North America (Canada and the US), you can choose the US geographic profile. We recommend reviewing Amazon Bedrock abuse detection with your compliance team. For a more detailed look at Canadian data residency patterns, see Cross-Region Inference and Canadian Data Residency: A Technical Architecture Guide . Conclusion In this post, we showed how to access OpenAI GPT-5.6 (Sol, Terra, and Luna), GPT-6 (Astra, Sol, and Luna), and GPT-6.1 Sol from Canada. These models are available from the Canada (Central) and Canada West (Calgary) Regions using cross-Region inference on Amazon Bedrock. We covered the available inference profiles, how to set up permissions and an example SCP, and how to invoke the models with the Responses, Chat Completions, and Converse APIs. For the Responses API, we included streaming and tool-use examples. We also showed how to request quota increases, review usage, and clean up your test resources. To get started, review the OpenAI model cards in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide , then open the Amazon Bedrock console and send a test prompt through an inference profile. For pricing, see the Amazon Bedrock pricing page . If you have questions or feedback, leave a comment on this post. About the authors Roopesh Ramklass Roopesh is a Specialist Principal Solutions Architect for AI/ML at AWS, based in Vancouver, Canada, where he helps customers design and scale generative AI solutions. He brings deep expertise across the AI/ML spectrum, partnering with organizations to turn ambitious AI ideas into reliable, high-impact solutions. He advises customers on recommended practices and practical solutions for cloud and AI-related governance, risk, and compliance. Dan specializes in helping AWS customers navigate financial services and privacy regulations applicable to the use of cloud and AI technology in Canada with a focus on digital sovereignty, third-party risk management, and operational resilience. Prasoon Gupta Prasoon is a Solutions Architect at Amazon Web Services (AWS) Canada. He enjoys helping public sector customers modernize and get the most value from the cloud. Outside of work, he enjoys building full-stack, AI-based tools on AWS for fun, spanning serverless architectures, agentic AI, and developer platforms.
