These techniques complement push-down capabilities in use cases where pre-calculating complex transformations may be necessary, while preserving access control rules and data lineage. Publish for discovery A semantic view that only exists as a queryable endpoint leaves a discoverability gap. The next team that needs a “ customer lifetime value ” measure has no way to know lifetime_customer_value already exists, what it’s built on, or who else depends on it. Publishing customer_360 and lifetime_customer_value to the Denodo Data Marketplace turns them into reusable, governed enterprise data products and closes that gap: both objects appear with their VQL definitions, ownership, business descriptions, custom properties, and lineage back to the base views. Consumers search by business meaning rather than by knowing the schema. The Denodo Data Marketplace also provides other features focused on self-service for non-technical users, including data preparation wizards, endorsements and deprecations notes from the administrators, and the capability to make requests and ask questions to data product owners. Denodo extends this with the 360 graph , a relationship view around a business concept. This graph attaches the reports, dashboards, notebooks, or agent tools that already use customer_360 , along with glossaries that define the meaning of the data in the table or conditions of use, for instance. Consumers can inspect the surrounding context of the dataset before writing a query. Figure 5: customer_360 graph view listing in the Denodo Data Marketplace. The detail panel shows a BI tool in Tableau consuming the view and the glossary definition linked to the view A note on interoperability The semantic model in Denodo is defined in VQL, but Denodo natively exposes any view over multiple open protocols. The same customer_360 view can be reached as SQL through JDBC, ODBC, or ADBC, as GraphQL through the Denodo GraphQL Service, as OData 2.0 or 4.0 through the Denodo OData Service, or as MCP tools through the Denodo MCP Server. Choosing MCP for this walkthrough is a fit for AgentCore. The same view is available to a Power BI dashboard, a Tableau workbook, or a Java application without additional modeling. Denodo also joined Apache Ossie (incubating), formerly Open Semantic Interchange (OSI), in March 2026, a vendor-neutral open-source specification for semantic metadata. Apache Ossie is at an early stage, but the intent is portability of semantic definitions across applications that adopt it. That said, Denodo already offers integration through Denodo Connects to share metadata with other data catalogs such as SageMaker Catalog, Collibra, Purview, and others. Governed access: Identity propagation and runtime enforcement Broad reach across data sources is one of the core characteristics of an enterprise-wide semantic layer, but that same reach creates a real risk when runtime access control is missing. If per-user filtering lives in the agent’s code, it’s one prompt injection away from being bypassed. If it lives in the LLM, it doesn’t really live anywhere. If it is enforced only in individual source systems, policies can be inconsistent and may not account for business meaning created across sources. Aurora doesn’t know what “ top spender ” means in the semantic layer, and neither does an on-premises PostgreSQL cluster behind a bastion host. And very often, especially in hybrid scenarios that blend on-premises and cloud systems, Identity Providers across all of them are not even an option. The approach in this architecture is to enforce access at the semantic layer, using the identity of the human user who initiated the request, propagated end-to-end from the IdP through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to Denodo Virtual DataPort. The identity propagation chain Figure 6 zooms into the identity portion of the reference architecture in Figure 1, expanding the outbound path from the app to Denodo VDP into an eight-hop sequence. The following numbered steps correspond one-to-one to the numbered arrows in the figure. Figure 6: Identity propagation and query flow from the user’s login through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to Denodo (MCP Server and VDP) and the underlying data sources. Black arrows show the outbound identity and query path. Green dashed arrows show the return path with the filtered result set The user authenticates to the app against the enterprise IdP. The IdP returns a JWT carrying the user’s identity and attribute claims — role, region, department, and whatever else the IdP is configured to emit. The app calls the agent through AgentCore Gateway with the user’s JWT as the bearer token. Gateway routes the request to AgentCore runtime, which hosts the Strands agent process. When the agent invokes an outbound tool call, AgentCore Identity performs an On-Behalf-Of token exchange and returns a new access token whose sub claim is the human user and whose aud claim is Denodo. The agent presents the new access token to the Denodo MCP Server as Authorization: Bearer on the MCP request. Denodo VDP validates the JWT against the configured JWKS URL, checks the issuer and audience, extracts the scope claim, and maps the caller to a Denodo role. VDP evaluates Global Security Policies at query time and returns a filtered result set to the agent. VDP queries the data sources to satisfy the request and combines the results before returning them. Gateway JWT validation at step 2 is optional because VDP re-validates the token in step 6. With Gateway validation on, malformed tokens fail earlier in the request path. The token exchange at step 4 uses either the RFC 8693 token-exchange grant or the RFC 7523 JWT-bearer grant, based on the credential provider configuration. The credential itself does not enter agent code. AgentCore Identity injects it at call time. The caller-identity passthrough option at step 8 is enabled per data source and requires Denodo and the source to share the same IdP. When it applies, the caller’s identity is forwarded end-to-end, giving full auditing at the source. Applying access policies in Denodo Customer 360 data is regulated. For example, some users (HR, fraud analysts) may need to see PII like a Social Security number (SSN) and full credit card number. But most users (marketing, analytics) must not. Denodo’s mechanism for this is Global Security Policies with attribute- and role-based access control. A Global Security Policy is a rule that applies to views or columns carrying a specific tag, evaluated against the caller’s role and session attributes at query time. The underlying view is not restructured. To illustrate this, we’ve tagged two columns ( ssn and card_num ) as PII on the base views over Aurora. We create a Global Security Policy mask_pii_columns . Audience: The caller’s role is not hr_user . Elements: Applies to columns with the pii_sensitive tag. Action: Mask with asterisks ( **** ). We then define two Denodo roles. hr_user : Has Execute on customer_360 . Sees every column. marketing_user : Has Execute on customer_360 . Will see ssn and card_num as **** because the policy applies. When marketing_user runs the VQL query: SELECT cid, first_name, last_name, state, ssn FROM customer_360 WHERE state = 'WI'; VDP evaluates the Global Security Policy before planning the query. It sees that ssn carries the pii_sensitive tag and the caller’s role is not hr_user , so it rewrites the projection to return *** for ssn . For row-level filtering (a US-East analyst who should only see east-coast customers, for example) the same mechanism scales. The policy condition can even depend on session attributes mapped from the JWT token, or pulled dynamically from an external table. A note on Responsible AI Denodo’s Global Security Policies filter PII at the semantic layer, so the model never sees ssn or card_num for callers who shouldn’t. Even then, agent responses can echo customer identifiers, locations, or spending patterns in natural language. Treat agent outputs with the same handling and retention policy you apply to the underlying regulated data: scope logging and transcript storage, apply Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for content and sensitive-topic controls, and limit who can read the responses. For broader guidance, see Responsible AI in Amazon Bedrock . Audit and observability across layers Each layer of the request path logs independently. AgentCore runtime emits invocation records to Amazon CloudWatch . AgentCore Gateway logs inbound MCP requests, including the caller’s JWT sub claim. The Denodo MCP Server records tool calls to its own log. Denodo VDP’s audit log captures the full VQL request, the mapped Denodo role, the resolved federated plan, and policy evaluation outcomes. These logs can also be incorporated into Amazon CloudWatch . When per-source audit tied to the human user is required (for HIPAA or SOX compliance, for example), configure pass-through session credentials on the base views for those sources so Denodo forwards the caller’s identity to the source system where the source supports it, instead of relying on service accounts. Expose the layer through the Denodo MCP Server The Denodo MCP Server is an add-on component that sits between MCP clients and VDP: download the distribution, extract it, edit config/application.properties , and start it. The server listens for streamable HTTP MCP requests at http:// :8080/ /mcp and forwards them to VDP over JDBC. Three configuration values matter for this walkthrough. mcp.security.oauth2.enabled=true : accepts OAuth 2.0 bearer tokens on inbound MCP requests. Paired with VDP’s OAuth authenticator configuration, the token forwards to VDP for validation and role resolution (see also the Governed access section). vdp.datasource.jdbcUrl=jdbc:vdb:// :9999/ : the JDBC URL where VDP is reached. The specific database targeted per request comes from the MCP endpoint path. mcp.visibility.tags=mcp controls which views are visible from the MCP Server. If defined, only views tagged with at least one of these tags will be visible. The server implements the MCP OAuth 2.0 authorization flow, including RFC 9728 Protected Resource Metadata and RFC 7591 Dynamic Client Registration. A note on IdP compatibility The Denodo MCP Server documents support for the automatic Dynamic Client Registration flow with Okta, Ping Identity, and Keycloak. For other identity providers, the MCP Server also accepts manual client configuration where the OAuth token is obtained out of band and forwarded as a static Authorization header on the MCP request, as described in the Denodo MCP Server User Manual . Front the server with an Application Load Balancer If the Denodo MCP Server runs on Amazon EC2 or Amazon EKS in the same VPC as VDP, expose it through an Application Load Balancer with an HTTPS listener and a certificate from AWS Certificate Manager . This gives AgentCore Gateway a stable HTTPS endpoint and offloads TLS termination from the MCP Server process. Target group: HTTP, port 8080. The health check path should accept both 200 and 404 as healthy responses, since the root path returns 404 and /health returns 200 when the server is up and connected to VDP. Register as an AgentCore Gateway target The full step-by-step walkthrough, including AgentCore Gateway creation, IAM service role configuration, and Gateway target validation, is in Denodo’s Integrating Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with Denodo via MCP Server integration guide. Add Denodo VQL skill in the harness The Denodo VQL skill acts as a system prompt extension for the LLM within the agent framework (such as Strands or Bedrock AgentCore). When registered in the agent harness, it instructs the model on VQL syntax rules and how to help prevent SQL errors. Deploy and run the agent The Denodo AgentCore documentation reference has the full agent code in the Denodo KB. The pattern is short: a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock, an MCP client pointed at the Denodo MCP Server, and an AgentCore runtime entrypoint that wires them together. Verification To confirm the semantic layer, the agent, and the identity flow work as intended, we run three query categories through the agent, plus one governance rerun that demonstrates the same-query-two-users property from the Governed access section. We can use Denodo’s Data Marketplace assistant, which relies on equivalent tools behind the scenes, to get a quick validation on our scenario. Query 1, Aurora-only “List our customers in Wisconsin, with their city.” The agent generates and runs: /* The query needs to retrieve first_name, last_name, and city from the customer_360 view where state = 'WI', ordered by last_name. The output will be multiple rows with 3 columns. The table is at customer granularity (one row per customer). No obligatory columns are present, so a simple WHERE filter on state suffices. */ SELECT "first_name", "last_name", "city" FROM "customer_360"."customer_360" WHERE "state" = 'WI' ORDER BY "last_name" VDP’s optimizer determines that only Aurora-side data is needed for the projection and filter, and pushes a single query down to Amazon Aurora. Based on a probe query, the agent can translate the filter from Wisconsin to the predicate state = 'WI' . Amazon Redshift and the on-premises cluster are not touched. Query 2, Redshift-only “What are our top 10 products by units sold?” The agent generates: /* The user wants top 10 products by total units sold from a metric view. I need to use EVALUATE_METRIC for units_sold, GROUP BY product_name, ORDER BY the metric descending, LIMIT 10. The output will be multiple rows (up to 10) with two columns: product_name and total_units_sold. */ SELECT "product_name", EVALUATE_METRIC("units_sold") AS "total_units_sold" FROM "customer_360"."lifetime_customer_value" GROUP BY "product_name" ORDER BY "total_units_sold" DESC LIMIT 10 Figure 7: VDP pushes the entire query (join, aggregation, ordering, and limit) to Amazon Redshift because both the product and order data live there. Aurora and the on-premises cluster are not touched Query 3, three-way federation “Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime value haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet?” The agent generates: /* This is a metric view, so I need to use EVALUATE_METRIC for lifetime_spend and order_count. The query needs to: 1. Aggregate by first_name, last_name, state, rewards_since to get total lifetime_spend and order_count 2. Rank top 20 by total lifetime_spend 3. Filter those top 20 where rewards_since IS NULL I'll use a CTE with ROW_NUMBER() to get top 20, then filter for NULL rewards_since in outer query. */ WITH "ranked_customers" AS ( SELECT "first_name", "last_name", "state", "rewards_since", EVALUATE_METRIC("lifetime_spend") AS "total_lifetime_spend", EVALUATE_METRIC("order_count") AS "total_order_count" FROM "customer_360"."lifetime_customer_value" GROUP BY "first_name", "last_name", "state", "rewards_since" ORDER BY "total_lifetime_spend" DESC LIMIT 20 ) SELECT "first_name", "last_name", "state", "rewards_since", "total_lifetime_spend", "total_order_count" FROM "ranked_customers" WHERE "rewards_since" IS NULL ORDER BY "total_lifetime_spend" DESC Figure 8: Agent result for the three-way federated query, listing the top customers by lifetime value who have not enrolled in the rewards program VDP plans across the three engines as described in the Build the semantic layer section: profile from Aurora, aggregated spend from Amazon Redshift, enrollment records from the on-premises cluster, and the final join and top-N inside VDP. The top result in the POC data was Marcus Chen from Milwaukee, WI, with $47,832 in lifetime spend, a customer with high spend and no rewards enrollment, exactly the auto-enrollment target from the example question in The example . Note that the LLM didn’t need to come up with the definition of lifetime_spend , since the formula is part of the semantic model as defined in the metric view. Governance rerun We run Query 1 with ssn added to the projection, as two different callers: SELECT cid, first_name, last_name, state, ssn FROM customer_360 WHERE state = 'WI'; As hr_user , the result includes the ssn values. As marketing_user , the result returns the same rows with ssn with asterisks as a masked value. No changes to the query text, the agent code, the MCP Server, VDP, or Aurora between the two runs. The Global Security Policy mask_pii_columns from the Governed access section evaluates against the caller’s role at query time, and VDP rewrites the projection accordingly. The same behavior applies to card_num . Figure 9: The governance rerun of the same query, with ssn returned in full for hr_user and masked for marketing_user Extending to other sources Adding a source outside AWS to customer_360 , whether that’s Salesforce for CRM records, ServiceNow for customer service data, or SAP for ERP tables, is the same modeling exercise as Aurora, Amazon Redshift, and the on-premises cluster. Create a base view, join it into the derived view on cid , and tag sensitive columns. The metric views, the Global Security Policy, and the agent’s VQL don’t change. What changes is the wrapper VDP uses to reach the source. For example: Salesforce connects through the Denodo Salesforce connector with OAuth 2.0 authentication and VQL-to-SOQL translation over the REST or Bulk API. ServiceNow, Microsoft Dynamics 365, and other SaaS tools use Denodo’s SaaS wizard templates , pre-configured for common APIs. SAP ERP connects through BAPI sources using the SAP Java Connector. VDP calls SAP RFCs and shapes the response into rows. The agent doesn’t know which of these sits underneath. It queries customer_360 in VQL. Denodo’s wrapper handles the source-native translation, and Denodo’s Global Security Policy applies uniformly whether the row comes from a JDBC engine, a REST API, or an RFC call. One deployment-time decision varies by source: whether to pass the caller’s identity through to the source or connect as a service account. Pass-through gives end-to-end audit at the source when the source supports it (Kerberos to SAP or OAuth to Salesforce, for example). Service-account connections are simpler, and the source’s audit shows the query as coming from Denodo. Deployment: Denodo Agora versus self-managed Denodo on AWS runs in one of two shapes. Both use the same Virtual DataPort, same VQL, same Global Security Policies, same MCP Server. The choice is operational. Agora: Fully managed Denodo Agora is Denodo’s fully managed cloud service, available on the AWS Marketplace . Agora runs on a split-plane architecture. The Control Plane (Solution Manager, Design Studio, Scheduler admin, Monitoring/Diagnostics) runs in Denodo’s cloud accounts, and the Execution Plane (VDP, Scheduler, Data Catalog) runs inside the customer’s AWS account. The compute that touches the data lives in the customer’s VPC. The management surface is operated by Denodo. Choose Agora when you don’t want to operate the application and the update cadence Denodo publishes works for your organization. Self-managed on Amazon EC2 or Amazon EKS Self-managed deployments install Denodo Platform entirely in the customer’s AWS account. Denodo publishes VM images on AWS Marketplace and ships container images with Helm charts for Amazon EKS. You handle the cluster, upgrades, and backups. Choose self-managed when compliance requires a specific deployment posture, when you want to control the version cadence, or when the reference architecture calls for a Denodo cluster inside a specific VPC. Reaching sources outside AWS Both deployment shapes place VDP in the customer’s AWS account. Reaching an on-premises source is the same problem in both cases: a network path from the VPC that hosts VDP to the on-premises cluster, provisioned through whichever hybrid connectivity option the organization already uses. For SaaS sources like Salesforce or ServiceNow, no additional setup is needed, since the Execution Plane has outbound internet access by default, which is sufficient for OAuth 2.0 authentication and REST API calls. Conclusion and where to start Reliable agentic access to enterprise data needs three things working together: a foundation model that can plan and generate queries, a semantic layer that presents business-meaningful data over live source systems, and a runtime that hosts the agent and manages the identity flow. Amazon Bedrock, Denodo Platform, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore each play one of those roles. The agent talks to the semantic layer, not directly to the underlying databases. Base views, derived views, metric views, tags, and Global Security Policies live in VDP. When a source schema drifts, when a new source comes online, or when a governance rule changes, the update happens in the semantic layer and every consumer picks it up at the next query. The additional metadata the semantic layer carries (documentation, descriptions, metric formulas, and the 360 graph) gives the model more grounded business context to reason over, rather than raw schema alone. Where to start Try Agora on AWS and follow the instructions to deploy. Agora is Denodo’s fully managed cloud service for deploying an AI data layer on AWS, providing live, governed access to distributed enterprise data. Most teams get this working by starting narrow and expanding. Pick one agentic workflow that spans two or three distinct source systems that takes longer than it should to answer today. Write three to five specific questions the workflow needs to answer. These are the queries the semantic layer must support on day one. Connect data sources and create base views over the source tables the workflow touches. Tag PII columns during creation. Build the derived views and metric views the questions require. Implement Global Security Policy to help protect PII, protected health information (PHI), payment card industry (PCI), or other sensitive information. Register the Denodo MCP Server as an AgentCore Gateway target and wire a Strands agent to it using the pattern in the earlier section. Deploy with agentcore deploy . Further reading Integrating Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with Denodo via MCP Server : Denodo Community reference implementation. Denodo MCP Server User Manual . Denodo VQL Guide , including Defining a Metric View . Denodo Global Security Policies . Amazon Bedrock AgentCore developer guide . About the authors Suntosh Murthy Suntosh is a Partner Solutions Architect at Denodo, where he collaborates with strategic partners to design and implement cloud data architecture, semantic layer solutions, and enterprise reference architectures that help customers make data-driven decisions. Pablo Alvarez-Yañez Pablo is the Global VP of Product Management at Denodo, where he defines the offering strategy, sets direction and priorities for the product portfolio, and translates customer needs into requirements. He is responsible for formulating the product strategy, gathering customer feedback, and coordinating with engineering, marketing, and sales to execute on that strategy. His current priorities revolve around cloud deployments, big data, and data science. JP Boreddy JP is a Senior Solutions Architect at AWS, where he partners with enterprise customers on cloud architecture, data, and AI workloads. Sahil Thapar Sahil is a Principal Solutions Architect at AWS, where he works with ISV customers to build highly available, scalable, and resilient applications on the AWS Cloud. He specializes in containers, machine learning, and generative AI, helping enterprises architect production-grade solutions.

title: Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with Strategy Mosaic and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
summary: The third post in our semantic-layer series builds a customer 360 across Amazon Redshift and Amazon Aurora with Strategy Mosaic, exposes it to a Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore through the Mosaic MCP server, and enforces per-user row and column security end-to-end.
content: This post is co-written with Zhili Cheng, Principal Product Manager, George Earle, Director, AI Engineering, and Kyler K, Sales Engineer of Strategy. In the first post in this series , we built a semantic layer on AWS using Stardog’s knowledge graph over Amazon Aurora and Amazon Redshift and ran a Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore against that layer. The second post kept the same customer 360 (C360) pattern and swapped in Denodo’s data virtualization platform, extending the source mix to include an on-premises PostgreSQL cluster. This post uses the same C360 pattern again, with Strategy Mosaic as the semantic layer. Stardog’s semantic layer is ontology-based: concepts and relationships modeled as RDF, with IRIs as the unit of federation and SPARQL as the query language. Denodo’s is data virtualization: base and derived views composed in VQL. Mosaic’s is dimensional: attributes, hierarchies, facts, and metrics composed through Strategy’s metric expression syntax, with linked models as the unit of federation. That model serves four native protocols from one definition: Model Context Protocol (MCP) for AI agents, JDBC/ODBC over Trino for SQL clients, XMLA for Power BI and Excel, and REST for custom applications. Behind those protocols is a long list of certified data sources . Supported systems include cloud warehouses such as Snowflake and Databricks. Operational databases include Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) , Oracle, and SQL Server. Analytical engines include Amazon Athena , Trino, and SAP HANA, and software as a service (SaaS) sources include Salesforce. The linked-model pattern extends beyond the Amazon Redshift and Amazon Aurora pair this walkthrough uses. In this walkthrough, a Strands agent hosted on AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, reaches Mosaic through the MCP endpoint. The joins, metric definitions, and per-caller row and column filters live inside Mosaic, not in the agent prompt. We assume you’re familiar with the semantic-layer architecture from the first post in the series. If any of it is new, the Stardog post covers the ground. By the end of this post, you will know: How to model a C360 domain in Strategy Mosaic across Amazon Redshift and Amazon Aurora using two linked models, with no ETL. How Mosaic’s metric syntax (base, advanced with named filter objects, level qualifiers, and compound) captures the business definitions the agent must reason over. How to expose the model to an AgentCore-hosted Strands agent through the Mosaic MCP server, and how user identity propagates so per-user Row-Level Security (RLS) and Object-Level Security (OLS) hold end-to-end. How to choose between live pushdown and in-memory execution for agent traffic. How to publish the same governed definitions to Power BI, Tableau, notebooks, and custom apps, and how to export them in Apache Ossie format for tools outside Mosaic. The source of truth for the walkthrough is Strategy One (March 2026) , the release when Mosaic access through the MCP server became available by default. Strategy Mosaic terms used in this post A short reference before we get to the model. Mosaic Schema and Mosaic Models . Two modeling paths within one universal semantic layer. Mosaic Schema is the centrally governed enterprise model. Mosaic Models is the self-service, AI-assisted modeling path in Mosaic Studio. Models can map to Schema attributes and inherit dimensions, object ACLs, and RLS. This walkthrough uses Mosaic Models. Model . The top-level artifact within either modeling path. Publishes attributes, metrics, hierarchies, and security rules over physical tables. The walkthrough uses two Mosaic Models, one over Amazon Redshift and one over Aurora, linked together. Attribute . A business entity such as Customer. Carries multiple forms: an ID form for joining and a display form for reading. Mosaic uses forms to resolve names like “Carolyn Inworth” to the underlying cid . Hierarchy . A parent-child relationship between attributes. Category rolls up through parent to Department. Address rolls up to City to State. Fact and metric . A fact is a numeric column. A metric aggregates it. Purchase Amount = price * quantity is a base metric. Metrics can also be advanced (an aggregation qualified by a named condition) or compound (a formula over other metrics). Filter object . A named condition referenced from metrics in angle brackets. [Large Orders] is a filter whose qualification is Purchase Amount > 500 . A metric references without inlining the predicate. Level qualifier . Metric expression syntax that pins aggregation grain. {~+, !Customer+} sets the grain to Customer regardless of how the query is sliced. Model linking . Composition across models on shared attributes (Customer, Time). Mosaic pushes aggregates to each source and joins intermediate results on the linking attributes. Certified model . Only certified models are reachable through the MCP server. Live or in-memory . Two per-model execution modes: live pushdown to the source, or answers from a Mosaic-resident cube. Details later in this post. The example: Customer 360 across Amazon Redshift and Amazon Aurora The C360 pattern from the first two posts stays in place. The schema is adapted from Stardog’s C360 Knowledge Kit , so a reader following the series sees the same entities, keys, and anchor question answered by a different semantic layer. A retail organization has customer records, addresses, credit cards, and rewards enrollment sitting on the operational side, and orders, products, and product categories sitting in the warehouse. Business users want answers that span both without knowing which system holds which fact. Where this post differs is how Mosaic reaches the two sources. Mosaic does not federate rows across engines at query time. It plans one query per source, pushes native SQL down, and joins the intermediate result sets in the Mosaic engine on the shared attributes declared through model linking. The C360 walkthrough models the analytical side as a Purchase model over Amazon Redshift and the operational side as a Customer model over Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-compatible edition. The schema across the two databases: Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-compatible (operational) Table Key columns customer cid (PK), first_name , last_name , email , ssn , phone , location address id (PK), city , state , zip , street_name credit_card id (PK), cid , card_num , card_type rewards_account id (PK), cid , account_id , create_date Amazon Redshift (analytical) Table Key columns purchase id (PK), cid , pid , date , quantity , price , card product id (PK), name , brand , price , dept category id (PK), dept_name , parent vendor id (PK), vendor_name , industry The shared ID is cid , an integer that appears as the primary key in customer on Aurora and as a plain column in purchase on Amazon Redshift. There is no SQL constraint linking them, and there can’t be, because they live in different engines. Every question that joins a customer to their orders must reconcile that integer somewhere. Mosaic absorbs it through model linking rather than a materialized cross-engine join. A representative question that exercises the whole model: Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime spend haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet? This is the auto-enrollment question from the Denodo post . It needs customer profile from Aurora, aggregated spend from Amazon Redshift, and enrollment status from Aurora, ranked and filtered on definitions that live in the semantic layer. Reference architecture Figure 1 shows the end-to-end runtime. The inbound authentication path runs from the client through AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and the runtime. The outbound query path runs from the Strands agent through the Mosaic MCP endpoint to Amazon Redshift and Amazon Aurora. Figure 1: Reference architecture. Inbound authentication path and outbound query path between the client, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore components, the Strategy Mosaic MCP endpoint, the Mosaic engine, and Amazon Redshift plus Amazon Aurora. The runtime splits into an inbound path and an outbound path. Inbound. A client sends the user’s question through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway. Gateway validates the JSON Web Token (JWT) that identifies the human user against the enterprise identity provider (IdP). It then routes the request to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, which hosts the Strands agent. The agent invokes Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock to interpret the prompt and plan the query. Outbound. When the agent decides to query the semantic model, its MCP tool connects directly to the Mosaic MCP endpoint at https:// /collaboration/mcp/mosaic over HTTPS. The agent presents an OAuth 2.0 access token in the Authorization: Bearer header. Mosaic validates the token against its bundled OAuth authorization server and resolves the caller to a Strategy user. It then applies the Use MCP Server privilege and certified-model gate, evaluates row-level and column-level security for that user, and plans the query across the linked Purchase and Customer models. Amazon Redshift and Amazon Aurora respond to source-native SQL that the Mosaic engine emits per source. Two properties matter for the rest of the walkthrough. Cross-source joins happen because a modeler declared a link, not because two sources happen to be reachable. The agent can only traverse links that exist in the model. The token that reaches Mosaic represents the human user, not a service account, so RLS and OLS evaluate against the caller’s identity end-to-end. AWS Secrets Manager holds the caller’s refresh token between calls, and the Governed access section walks the full identity chain. Build the semantic layer The walkthrough uses two Mosaic Models, the self-service AI-assisted modeling path in Mosaic Studio, linked on shared attributes. Mosaic Studio is the authoring suite, and the screenshots in this post come from its Design Center modeling workspace. Three passes: datasets and joins on each side, attributes and hierarchies, then metrics that carry the business logic. A team with an existing centrally governed Mosaic Schema can map the model’s attributes to it and inherit dimensions, object ACLs, and RLS from the enterprise schema without a parallel security review. Do this early if your data architects already maintain a governed schema. Two linked models Each Mosaic model connects to one live source. Model linking composes them. Purchase : Live against Amazon Redshift. Facts on the purchase table ( price * quantity ), dimensions on product , category , vendor , and the purchase date. Customer : Live against Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-compatible. Dimensions on customer , address , credit_card , rewards_account . Inside each model, the physical joins are declared once against the source schema. The Purchase model resolves purchase.pid = product.id , product.dept = category.id , and product.brand = vendor.id , plus a self-reference on category.parent = category.id for the department rollup. The Customer model resolves customer.location = address.id , customer.cid = credit_card.cid , and customer.cid = rewards_account.cid . These are the relationships Mosaic uses to plan the source-native SQL it pushes down. Nothing physical crosses between Purchase and Customer. The two models link on Customer and Time. When a question needs both (for example top spenders in Wisconsin pulls state from address and spend from purchase ), Mosaic pushes the appropriate aggregation to each source and combines the results on the linking attributes. No ETL, no third copy. Domain ownership follows the model boundary. The CRM team owns Customer, and the data system team owns Purchase. Neither hands over its source. They agree on the linking attributes, and security propagates from the underlying models automatically. There’s no materialized cross-engine join and no shared physical schema between Amazon Redshift and Amazon Aurora. The join is the linking-attribute agreement. Attributes and hierarchies Attributes carry multiple forms. Customer uses cid as the ID form and first_name + last_name as the display form, so an agent can ask about “Carolyn Inworth” and Mosaic resolves it to the right key on both sides of the link. Figure 2 shows the Customer attribute authored in Mosaic Studio, with cid as the ID form and Full Name, First Name, and Last Name as display forms. Figure 2: Customer attribute definition in Design Center. cid is the ID form used to join on the underlying key. Full Name, First Name, and Last Name are display forms. Two hierarchies matter for C360: The Category hierarchy rolls up through parent to Department. The category.parent self-reference means a department-level question aggregates consistently. Address rolls up through City to State in the same pattern. That makes State = 'WI' a single attribute qualification rather than a join the agent must construct. Figure 3 shows the geography hierarchy authored in Design Center, chaining State through City and ZIP Code down to Customer. Figure 3: Geography hierarchy in Design Center for the Customer model. State rolls up through City and ZIP Code to Location, and Location links to Customer. The agent asks for State = 'WI' , not for address.state . Physical column names don’t leave the model. Every consumer of the semantic layer sees the attribute form and its display forms, and the hierarchy carries the rollup automatically. Metrics: Base, advanced, compound, time-intelligence A base metric applies a group function to a fact. Purchase Amount is Sum(price * quantity) on the purchase table. Figure 4 shows the Purchase Amount base metric authored in Mosaic Studio: the formula Price * Quantity, with a description field that tells the agent what the metric means in business terms. Figure 4: Purchase Amount metric authored in Design Center. The formula multiplies price by quantity, and the description tells the agent what the metric means in business terms. The interesting C360 concepts are advanced metrics: an aggregation qualified by a named condition. In Strategy, conditions are references to filter objects in angle brackets, not inline predicates. Filter objects are model objects with their own name, description, and permissions, so they are reusable and auditable across metrics that share a definition. Define the filters once: Filter object Qualification [Large Orders] Purchase Amount > 500 [Sports Category] Category = "Sports" [Rewards Members] Rewards Account is not null [Card Present] Purchase Card is not null [Big Spender] Customer Lifetime Spend > 10000 Each filter object carries a name, description, qualification, and access permissions. The shape a modeler authors or exports for [Large Orders] looks like this: name: [Large Orders] description: Purchases whose net line amount exceeds $500. Referenced by Large Order Spend and any metric that scopes to high-value transactions. qualification: Purchase Amount > 500 permissions: read: Everyone modify: Data Modelers Then reference the filters in metric expressions. Each of these is an advanced metric: a base aggregation qualified by a named filter. Large Order Spend Sum([Purchase Amount]) {~+} Sports Spend Sum([Purchase Amount]) {~+} Rewards Spend Sum([Purchase Amount]) {~+} Figure 5 shows the Design Center view of an advanced metric with a filter condition applied. It uses the same authoring pattern as the preceding Large Order Spend . Figure 5: Advanced-metric authoring in Design Center, showing the base formula and the filter condition referenced from the Large Orders filter object. Customer Lifetime Spend also needs a level qualifier, because lifetime means the whole history regardless of how the current question is sliced: Customer Lifetime Spend Sum([Purchase Amount]) {~+, !Customer+} The ! before Customer sets grouping to none, so the metric returns each customer’s full total on every row rather than collapsing to one row per customer. See Strategy Metric Level Symbols for the full syntax. Notice that [Big Spender] in the filter table qualifies on a metric expression rather than an attribute predicate. Filter objects can gate on either. Share of wallet is a compound metric, built from other metrics: Sports Share of Wallet [Sports Spend] / [Customer Lifetime Spend] Levels and conditions carry through from the components unchanged. Share of wallet is a ratio, so it doesn’t add or average. The share across an AWS Region isn’t the average of each customer’s share, and the metric description tells the agent that. See Strategy Conditional Metrics . Beyond base, advanced, and compound, Mosaic ships governed time-intelligence metrics as first-class expressions. Previous Year , Previous Quarter , Year-to-Date , and Quarter-to-Date are declared once on the model and preserved through slice, so a question like how does Sports spend this year compare with last year becomes an attribute pick and two metric references rather than a hand-written SQL date filter. Custom calendars attach at the model level, so the same year-over-year expression works for a fiscal year that ends in September and a calendar year that ends in December. See Governed Time-Intelligence Metrics in Mosaic . Edit the filter object once and the Power BI dashboard, the SQL extract, and the agent all move together. That is what a named, governed model artifact gets you that an inline SQL predicate cannot. How Mosaic plans and executes queries The Mosaic engine parses each MCP query call as Trino-dialect SQL, resolves the dimensional references to the underlying Purchase and Customer models, applies the RLS or OLS that the caller is subject to, and plans physical SQL per source. The dialect matches what Strategy publishes for the MCP query tool , so the SQL the agent emits is portable across MCP clients connecting to the same certified model. For the auto-enrollment question, planning unfolds like this: Push down to Amazon Aurora: a join of customer and rewards_account on cid , projecting profile and rewards_account.create_date , filtered where enrollment is null. Returns one row per unenrolled customer. Push down to Amazon Redshift: SUM(price * quantity) grouped by cid . Returns one row per customer with total spend. Combine inside Mosaic: join the two intermediate result sets on cid (the linking attribute), rank by lifetime spend, and return the top 20. Aurora runs a transactional profile join. Amazon Redshift runs the fact aggregation. Mosaic handles the cross-engine join on a small intermediate set (one row per customer, not one row per order). A hand-written pipeline approximates the same shape and then must be kept in sync forever. One SQL detail matters. Metrics are governed values, but Trino treats them as selected columns, so when a query uses GROUP BY , metrics need an aggregation wrapper such as SUM(metric_name) . The metric’s definition, conditions, and join paths are still resolved by Mosaic. The outer aggregation is the caller’s. A non-additive ratio like share of wallet therefore needs to say so in its description. Live pushdown or in-memory Every Mosaic model runs in one of two modes. Mode Behavior Best fit Live Pushdown to Redshift or Aurora at query time Consistently-current data. Source security applies directly In-memory Answered from a Mosaic-resident cube Bounded recent windows. Predictable latency. No per-query warehouse compute Both modes enforce the same security rules. RLS and OLS are set once on the model and evaluated regardless of where the answer comes from. The choice is a performance and cost question. Agent traffic is repetitive and bursty. An agent decomposing top spenders in Wisconsin into several exploratory follow-ups fires many small queries over the same recent slice. Serving that from memory turns variable per-query warehouse spend into fixed Mosaic capacity, and it’s usually faster. For interactive agent workloads over a bounded window, in-memory is often both quicker and cheaper. Configure Mosaic-side entitlements before switching a model to in-memory, and validate them in the same test pass you use to validate the numbers. One definition, four interfaces The metrics, attributes, hierarchies, and security rules built in the previous section reach every consumer through native protocols. No connector translation, no metric re-implementation, no drift. Protocol Typical consumer What it uses Mosaic for MCP AI agents (Strands, Claude, Copilot, ChatGPT, Gemini) Semantic discovery + governed query SQL / JDBC / ODBC (Trino) Tableau, SQL clients, Python notebooks Flexibility and ad-hoc analysis DAX / XMLA Power BI, Excel PivotTables Semantic fidelity for BI REST Custom applications, data science Programmatic access The same certified Mosaic model that the Strands agent in this walkthrough consumes also serves a business analyst working in Amazon Quick , which registers Mosaic MCP as an OAuth-authenticated connector. No second integration is required. Governed access: Identity propagation and runtime enforcement Mosaic enforces access in the semantic layer, before a query reaches Amazon Redshift or Aurora. HR and fraud roles see personally identifiable information (PII) fields like ssn and card_num . Marketing and analytics roles do not. Enforcement is identical whether the caller is a Strands agent over MCP, an analyst in Excel over XMLA, or a notebook over JDBC. One set of RLS and OLS objects, one certified-model gate, one privilege check. Attributes and metrics marked as sensitive also feed Mosaic Sentinel Risk Management , which alerts on queries that touch flagged objects and detects behavioral anomalies as a defense-in-depth layer next to OLS. Figure 6 shows the identity propagation chain across two lanes: the front-door OAuth handshake that runs once per user, and the per-request path that runs on every agent tool call. Each lane carries the user’s identity end-to-end so Mosaic can enforce RLS and OLS on the caller rather than a service account. Figure 6: Identity propagation chain. The front-door OAuth handshake runs once per user, or on refresh-token renewal (steps 1-4). The per-request path runs on every agent tool call (steps 5-10). Nothing in the chain re-scopes to a service account. Mosaic evaluates governance on the caller’s Strategy user identity. The chain follows two lanes. Front-door OAuth handshake (once per user). The human user authenticates against the enterprise IdP. The application starts an OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code flow against Strategy Library at /collaboration/authorize with scope offline_access . Strategy Library, federated to the same IdP through SAML or OIDC, returns a refresh and access token pair at /collaboration/token . The app persists the refresh token to AWS Secrets Manager, keyed by the user’s IdP sub claim. Per-request path (every agent tool call). AgentCore Gateway validates the IdP JWT and routes to AgentCore runtime, which hosts the Strands agent invoking Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock. The agent’s MCP tool retrieves the user’s refresh token from Secrets Manager, exchanges it for a fresh access token, and presents Authorization: Bearer to /collaboration/mcp/mosaic . Mosaic resolves the token to a Strategy user, enforces the Use MCP Server privilege, certified-model gate, and RLS and OLS, then plans and executes against Purchase and Customer. A marketing analyst doesn’t see ssn or card_num . A fraud analyst does. Nothing in the chain re-scopes to a service account. Governance evaluates on the caller’s identity from IdP to Mosaic engine. Expose the layer through the Mosaic MCP server Strategy Library exposes two MCP endpoints: Endpoint Path What it does Agents MCP /collaboration/mcp/agent Routes a question to a certified Strategy agent, which answers using its own data and instructions Mosaic MCP /collaboration/mcp/mosaic Queries Mosaic models and AI-enabled cubes directly, no Strategy agent required Both work independently. This walkthrough uses Mosaic MCP . Putting the semantic layer directly in front of the Strands agent skips an inference hop. The tool chain Four tools, chained from project to model to semantics to query. Tool What it does Parameters get_projects Lists Strategy projects the caller can access none get_models Lists certified Mosaic models and datasets in a project project get_semantics Returns a model’s full definition: attributes and metrics with data types, descriptions, and metric formulas model query Runs a read-only Trino SQL query. Writes and DDL rejected with MOSAIC_SQL_WRITE_REJECTED sql The agent chains these calls automatically. get_projects and get_models narrow to the right model by description before the agent reads a column name. get_semantics returns the governed definitions the agent then uses to compose SQL against real object names: Sports Share of Wallet as a compound metric, Customer Lifetime Spend scoped to Customer, the Category hierarchy, and the formula for every metric. Two Mosaic-specific SQL conventions matter. Column identifiers follow a __ pattern and must be wrapped in double quotes ( "customer__customer name" ). Time attributes are exposed both as base columns and as pre-bucketed interval columns ( (day interval) , (month interval) ), and the docs explicitly say to use the interval columns for time-grouped aggregations rather than date_trunc . Metadata is what makes it accurate get_semantics returns definitions, but the agent still must choose the right metric. Without descriptions, Total Spend and Customer Lifetime Spend look interchangeable, and they aren’t. Four properties do most of the work: object descriptions (what the metric means and when not to use it, including aggregation behavior for non-additive metrics), semantic definitions (how compound metrics compose), relationships (which attributes are valid slices), and governance context (so the agent can say what it can’t see rather than presenting a filtered number as complete). The model description is the first thing get_models returns and it’s how the agent picks the right model. Mosaic can import metadata from upstream catalogs, so column descriptions already maintained flow in rather than being retyped. Deploy the agent Strands is a small framework for building agents. A short Python entry point wires Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock to the Mosaic MCP endpoint as a tool source. The AgentCore runtime hosts the process. AgentCore Gateway terminates inbound requests and forwards the human user’s JWT. The system prompt matters. Give the agent explicit instructions to follow the three-step call pattern before writing SQL: get_projects , then get_models , then get_semantics on the target model. Tell it to reference only attribute and metric names that get_semantics returned. Include a short section on the business terminology in the target model ( Customer Lifetime Spend is the customer’s total across their history regardless of the current slice. Sports Share of Wallet is a ratio. And so on). This is the prompt engineering that pays the most in accuracy. Turn on Amazon Bedrock prompt caching for the reused portion of the system prompt. The get_semantics payload runs to a few thousand tokens and doesn’t change within a model version, so caching drops the input-token cost per call on repeated invocations. Agent traffic against a stable semantic layer is exactly the repetitive, bursty pattern that benefits most. Two effects compound on the MCP path. First, get_semantics returns compressed business context (metric definitions, hierarchies, attribute forms) instead of raw schema DDL, so the model reasons over a smaller, higher-signal payload. Strategy’s published benchmark measures the input-token and per-query cost impact of serving semantic context versus raw schema. Second, Bedrock prompt caching keeps that already-compressed payload warm across calls. For repetitive agent traffic, both effects apply per call: the model reasons over compressed context, and repeat calls hit the cache. Verification To confirm the semantic layer, the agent, and the identity flow work as intended, we ran three query categories through the agent and then a governance rerun of one of them as a different role. Query 1, Aurora-only. List our customers in Wisconsin, with their city. The agent generates a query against the Customer model that projects the display forms of Customer and City and filters state to WI: SELECT "customer__customer name", "city__city name" FROM "Customer" WHERE "state__state name" = 'WI' ORDER BY "customer__customer name" Mosaic pushes a single query to Aurora and returns the rows. Amazon Redshift is not touched. Query 2, Amazon Redshift only. What are our top 10 products by units sold? SELECT "product__product name", SUM("Units Sold") AS "total_units" FROM "Purchase" GROUP BY "product__product name" ORDER BY "total_units" DESC LIMIT 10 The entire query pushes to Amazon Redshift. Aurora is not touched. Query 3, cross-model. Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime spend haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet? SELECT "customer__customer name", "state__state name", SUM("Customer Lifetime Spend") AS "lifetime_spend" FROM "Customer" WHERE "rewards_account__account_id" IS NULL GROUP BY "customer__customer name", "state__state name" ORDER BY "lifetime_spend" DESC LIMIT 20 Mosaic plans across both models. Profile and enrollment status come from Aurora, spend aggregation from Amazon Redshift, joined on the Customer linking attribute inside the Mosaic engine, then filtered and top-N’d. The agent did not need to define Customer Lifetime Spend . It referenced the metric by name and Mosaic resolved the formula, level qualifier, and linking paths. Governance rerun. We ran Query 1 with ssn added to the projection as two callers. As a fraud analyst, get_semantics returned the SSN attribute and the query returned the values. As a marketing analyst, get_semantics returned a Customer attribute without ssn at all, so the agent had no attribute to project. Same request, same query text, two correct answers from one definition. Cross-interface confirmation. We opened the same certified Customer model in Excel through the Mosaic XMLA endpoint and dragged State and Customer Lifetime Spend onto a PivotTable. The state-level totals matched the agent’s numbers exactly. Early in the run, the agent averaged share of wallet across customers, the classic non-additive mistake. Adding one line to the metric description ( “ratio metric. Do not average across customers, recompute from components” ) stopped it. That’s the case for writing metric descriptions in the first sprint rather than the last. Extending across data sources The same linking mechanism extends to a third source: clickstream events in Amazon Simple Storage Service ( Amazon S3 ) queried through Amazon Athena, tables in Apache Iceberg on Amazon S3 Tables , a capability of Amazon S3, or a SaaS source such as a CRM. Model the source in Mosaic, link it on Customer and Time, and browse-to-buy questions compose into the same customer view without a third pipeline. Adding a source doesn’t change the metric definitions that already exist. The agent can only travel paths a modeler declared. AWS Lake Formation governs access to the underlying lake tables. Mosaic’s RLS and OLS apply on top. The same live-source pattern applies to every system in Strategy’s supported data source catalog , covering on-premises databases such as PostgreSQL and MySQL alongside the warehouses and engines already named in this post. Interoperability with Apache Ossie Some tools will not take a dependency on a single semantic layer. Apache Ossie (incubating) is the open specification for that gap, launched as the Open Semantic Interchange on September 23, 2025 and now in the Apache Incubator as Apache Ossie (incubating). It defines a vendor-neutral format for metrics, dimensions, relationships, and business concepts so definitions move between tools without being retyped. Strategy participates alongside Snowflake, Dremio, dbt Labs, Salesforce, and others. Mosaic exports and imports Ossie artifacts. Metric and dimension definitions modeled over Amazon Redshift publish as Ossie YAML consumable by Ossie-aware tools without a Mosaic connector. Definitions authored elsewhere (a metric maintained in dbt, a dimension standardized in a catalog) flow into Mosaic instead of being re-implemented. The artifacts are plain text, so they live in Git and promote through environments like other code. Apache Ossie is early. Use it where portability matters most and fidelity matters least, for example formulas, dimensions, descriptions, and ownership metadata, while keeping governance policy, execution strategy, and security configuration native to Mosaic. Deployment: Strategy Cloud Mosaic runs as a managed service on Strategy Cloud. Strategy operates the application. Connections to Amazon Redshift and Amazon Aurora go over the network from Strategy Cloud egress. You allow-list the Strategy Cloud CIDRs on the source security groups. Observability Two observability planes cover the path from question to answer. Sentinel and Platform Analytics cover the query side. Sentinel captures near real-time query duration, slow queries, and usage by user, tool, and model. AgentCore Observability , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, covers the agent side: planning steps, tool calls, latency per turn. Sentinel and Platform Analytics show what happened once the request reached Mosaic. AgentCore Observability shows what the agent was doing before it got there. Conclusion Reliable agentic analytics combines strong reasoning, trusted business context, and secure execution. Amazon Bedrock provides the model, Strategy Mosaic provides the governed semantic layer over live data, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore hosts the agent and terminates authentication. The agent talks to the semantic layer, not to Amazon Redshift or Aurora directly. Schemas evolve, the semantic model absorbs the change, and the same definitions serve Power BI, Tableau, notebooks, the Strands agent, and Amazon Quick. Through Apache Ossie, they also reach tools that do not connect to Mosaic. Where to start Pick one metric currently argued about (NRR, contribution margin, active customer are common candidates). One metric with more than one definition in circulation. Write three to five business questions about it. These become your acceptance tests. Model your primary source in Mosaic and get the metric returning a defensible number. Link additional sources incrementally, one at a time, on the attributes that already exist in the model. Author descriptions on every metric and attribute the agent will see. This is where accuracy moves most. Connect the Strands agent over Mosaic MCP and run your acceptance questions. Observe real query patterns for a couple of weeks, then move what’s hot to in-memory. Export stable definitions to Apache Ossie and put them under version control. Further reading Strategy Mosaic – Universal Semantic Layer Interact with Agents, Mosaic Models, and Cubes Using an MCP Server Strategy Advanced Metrics: Report Data and Calculations Strategy Conditional Metrics Strategy Metric Level Symbols Strategy Compound Metrics Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide Amazon Bedrock prompt caching Apache Ossie (incubating) Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with Stardog and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with Denodo and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore About the authors Zhili Cheng Zhili is a Principal Product Manager at Strategy, leading Mosaic, the universal semantic layer from Strategy, with 17+ years spanning engineering and product. George Earle George is the Director of AI Engineering at Strategy, where he leads the company’s AI engineering efforts. Kyle K Kyle is an experienced Sales Engineer in enterprise software, specializing in pre-sales, solution architecture, and proof-of-concept engagements. He holds a B.S. in Computer Science from Eastern Washington University. JP Boreddy JP is a Senior Solutions Architect at AWS, where he partners with enterprise customers on cloud architecture, data, and AI workloads. Sahil Thapar Sahil is a Principal Solutions Architect at AWS, where he works with ISV customers to build highly available, scalable, and resilient applications on the AWS Cloud. He specializes in containers, machine learning, and generative AI, helping enterprises architect production-grade solutions.

title: Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with AtScale and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
summary: The third post in our semantic-layer series builds a governed customer 360 model on Amazon Redshift with AtScale, then exposes it to a Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore through the AtScale MCP server. Identity propagation, RBAC, row security, and full query audit are enforced at the semantic layer, not the prompt.
content: In the first post in this series , we built a semantic layer on AWS using Stardog’s knowledge graph over Amazon Aurora and Amazon Redshift . We ran a Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore against that layer. The second post kept the same customer 360 (C360) pattern and swapped in Denodo’s data virtualization platform, extending the source mix to include an on-premises PostgreSQL cluster. This post uses the same C360 pattern again, with AtScale as the semantic layer. AtScale takes a different shape from the first two. The semantic model is dimensional (dimensions, hierarchies, and measures) rather than a graph of triples or a set of views. AtScale authors the model in the Semantic Modeling Language , an open, YAML-based specification versioned in Git, and exposes it simultaneously, from a single deployed model, over three protocols: SQL, XML for Analysis (XMLA), and the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The Strands agent and the business intelligence (BI) tools the enterprise already uses get the same computed answer from the same definitions. The rest of the pattern carries over from the earlier posts. A foundation model on Amazon Bedrock (Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 for the walkthrough) plans and writes queries. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore hosts the Strands agent and manages the outbound credential the agent presents to AtScale. The joins, metric definitions, and row and column filters that apply to the caller live inside the semantic layer rather than the prompt. We assume you’re familiar with the semantic-layer architecture from the first post in the series: what a semantic layer is, what it’s for, and why the model plans queries without owning the joins. If any of that is new, the first post covers the ground. By the end of this post, you will know: How to model a C360 domain in the Semantic Modeling Language (SML): datasets, dimensions and hierarchies, facts, measures, calculated measures, and perspectives, versioned in Git. How AtScale plans a dimensional query against Amazon Redshift, and how AtScale’s autonomous aggregate management accelerates the query patterns an agent generates. How to expose the model to an AgentCore-hosted Strands agent through the AtScale MCP server, and how to register that MCP server with AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. How the human user’s identity propagates from the enterprise identity provider through AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to AtScale, and how AtScale enforces role-based access control (RBAC), row security, and perspectives at query time. How to deploy AtScale on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) using the AtScale Helm chart and the AtScale K8S Blueprints repository. The source of truth for the walkthrough is the AtScale C2026.7 release . Where a specific tool name or endpoint applies, we cite the AtScale documentation . The example: Customer 360 on Amazon Redshift The customer 360 pattern from the first two posts stays in place. A retail enterprise has customer records, orders, products, and rewards enrollments spread across systems, and business users want to ask cross-cutting questions without knowing which system holds which fact. The Stardog C360 Knowledge Kit we adapted for the first post in the series models this scenario with Customer, Order, Product, and Address entities joined on an integer cid that appears as a primary key in the customer table and as a plain column in the purchase table. Where this post differs from the first two is where the data physically sits. Stardog and Denodo federate at query time across two engines. AtScale plans a dimensional query as native warehouse SQL and pushes it to one engine per query, so cross-engine data is consolidated upstream. For this walkthrough, all analytical C360 data lives in Amazon Redshift Serverless . Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL remains the operational system of record, and a replication path ( AWS Database Migration Service or Amazon Aurora zero-ETL to Amazon Redshift ) keeps the analytical copy current. The agent queries a single AtScale model that maps to the Amazon Redshift tables. The schema in Amazon Redshift: Table Key columns customer cid (PK), first_name, last_name, email, ssn, phone, location address id (PK), city, state, zip, street_name credit_card id (PK), cid, card_num, card_type rewards_account id (PK), cid, account_id, create_date purchase id (PK), pid, purchase_date, quantity, price, cid, card product id (PK), name, brand, price, dept category id (PK), dept_name, parent vendor id (PK), vendor_name, industry Nine columns of interest across eight tables. cid links customer records to purchases. pid links purchases to products. dept links products to categories. Everything analytical is in Amazon Redshift, so joins push down to native SQL rather than being resolved in the semantic layer or in an extract, transform, and load (ETL) pipeline. A representative question that exercises the whole model: Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime spend haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet? This is the auto-enrollment question from the Denodo post, carried over so a reader following the series can see the same request answered by a different semantic layer. It touches customer profile, address, purchase history, and enrollment status: one row per customer across four logical entities. AtScale terms used in this post AtScale implements the semantic layer as a dimensional model over a warehouse. The AtScale documentation and the SML specification use a specific set of primitives that come up throughout this post. A short reference is useful before we get to the walkthrough. Semantic Modeling Language (SML) –  An open, YAML-based specification for describing semantic models. Every SML object (model, dataset, dimension, hierarchy, metric, calculation, perspective, row security) is a YAML file. The specification lives at github.com/semanticdatalayer/SML . Model –  The top-level artifact. A model references datasets, dimensions, facts, and metrics, and exposes them through the AtScale query engine. Dimension and hierarchy –  A dimension groups related attributes (customer, product, date). A hierarchy inside a dimension organizes those attributes into levels (product → category → department, or year → quarter → month → day). Fact and measure –  A fact is a dataset that holds measurable events joined to dimensions on key columns. A measure is a quantity aggregated from a fact column, for example SUM(price * quantity) for revenue. Calculation –  A derived measure expressed as a formula against other measures. Perspective – A publishable subset of the model exposed to a specific role or group. Perspectives are how AtScale controls which dimensions and measures a caller can see. Row security – A model object that filters rows returned to the caller based on the caller’s identity or attributes. Autonomous aggregate management –  AtScale watches query patterns across consumers and materializes summary tables in the warehouse when a pattern is expensive enough to justify one. Subsequent queries that match the pattern route to the aggregate transparently. Design Center –  The AtScale authoring surface. A modeler edits SML through a visual canvas or a text editor. Either way the artifact on disk is SML YAML in Git. AtScale MCP server – The in-product MCP endpoint at /mcp that exposes the semantic model to any MCP client. Where more detail is useful, the AtScale documentation and the SML specification are the authoritative references. Reference architecture The runtime splits into an inbound path and an outbound path, following the same shape as the Stardog and Denodo posts. Inbound. A client sends the user’s question to the Strands agent through AgentCore Gateway. Gateway validates the JSON Web Token (JWT) that identifies the human user against the enterprise identity provider (IdP), then routes the request to AgentCore runtime (a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore), which hosts the agent process. The agent invokes Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock to interpret the prompt and plan the query. Outbound. When the agent decides to query the semantic model, it invokes a tool call to the AtScale MCP server. AgentCore Gateway serves as the outbound proxy: the AtScale MCP server is registered as an MCP target on Gateway, so tool calls route through Gateway and AgentCore Identity injects the credential at that hop. AtScale’s MCP endpoint accepts either a bearer token (for development and single-identity scenarios) or an OAuth 2.0 access token issued by AtScale’s bundled Keycloak instance (the production path). The AtScale engine validates the token, resolves the caller to an AtScale role, and plans the query against the deployed C360 model. The query request travels down through the AtScale engine, and the results travel back up. There’s no ETL job that pre-materializes cross-database joins. The analytical copy in Amazon Redshift is the source of truth for the semantic model, kept fresh from Aurora by the upstream replication path. Figure 1: Inbound authentication path and outbound query path between the client, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore components, the AtScale MCP server, the AtScale engine, and Amazon Redshift Serverless The architecture is deliberately opinionated on identity. Gateway and Identity hold the tokens at the runtime edges. The agent doesn’t see them and only orchestrates the conversation and the tool calls. Build the semantic layer AtScale’s semantic model is a collection of SML objects (datasets, dimensions, facts, measures, calculations, perspectives, row security) versioned in Git. A working model has a shape a data engineer will recognize from a star schema, but every object is expressed as YAML rather than data definition language (DDL), and every object is a separate file. Building the C360 model happens in three passes: datasets over the Amazon Redshift tables, dimensions and hierarchies with the joins between them, and measures and calculations that express the business logic. Datasets. Each Amazon Redshift table becomes an SML dataset. A dataset declares the physical connection, the schema, the table, and the columns AtScale will surface. Datasets can be authored visually in Design Center or edited directly as YAML. Either surface writes the same SML file to Git. Dimensions and hierarchies. The C360 model has seven dimensions. dim_customer holds customer profile attributes and joins to dim_address through the location key and to dim_rewards through cid . dim_product holds product attributes and organizes them into a hierarchy through dim_category . dim_date supports date-based analysis. dim_vendor groups products by supplier. dim_rewards holds one row per enrolled customer with account_id and create_date , and snowflakes off dim_customer so that never-enrolled customers surface as null in the enrollment attributes. AtScale’s hierarchy primitive is the concise expression of the product-to-category relationship. A query against the model can navigate product → category → parent category without a recursive SQL common table expression, and the large language model (LLM) sees a single dimensional path rather than a join graph. A representative SML fragment for the product hierarchy: # dim_product.yml unique_name: dim_product object_type: dimension label: Product hierarchies: - unique_name: product_category label: Product Category levels: - unique_name: department dataset: category key_columns: [dept_name] - unique_name: category dataset: category key_columns: [id] - unique_name: product dataset: product key_columns: [id] secondary_attributes: - unique_name: brand - unique_name: product_name key_column: name Facts and measures. The fact table for C360 is fact_purchase , mapped to the Amazon Redshift purchase table. It joins to dim_customer on cid , to dim_product on pid , and to dim_date on purchase_date . Measures come off the fact: total_revenue as SUM(price * quantity) , order_count as COUNT(id) , and units_sold as SUM(quantity) . Calculated measures. Business logic that lives in the model rather than in the query. customer_lifetime_value is total_revenue evaluated at customer grain, the same formula applied to a coarser slice of the fact. Segments like big_spender and spend_tier are calculated measures with conditional expressions: # big_spender.yml unique_name: big_spender object_type: metric expression: | CASE WHEN SUM(price * quantity) > 10000 THEN 'Yes' ELSE 'No' END The expression is evaluated at query time. A column would hold one answer at one grain. The expression recomputes for whatever slice the query asks about, by customer, by customer and year, or by region. When the definition changes (the threshold moves from $10,000 to $15,000), the update happens in one YAML file, gets reviewed as a pull request, and deploys through the AtScale CI hook. Each consumer picks up the new definition on the next query, whether that is the agent, Excel over XMLA, or Tableau over Multidimensional Expressions (MDX). Figure 2: The C360 model in AtScale Design Center. dim_customer, dim_address, dim_rewards, dim_product with the product-to-category hierarchy, dim_date, dim_vendor, and fact_purchase connected by orange lines that indicate dimension-to-fact and snowflake relationships. Calculated measures (customer_lifetime_value, big_spender, spend_tier) appear as separate nodes referenced from the fact Figure 3: The same model as side-by-side SML YAML, one file per dimension, metric, and calculation, versioned in a Git repository The artifact on the right of Figure 3 is not a description of the model. It is the model. Design Center’s visual canvas and the YAML editor are two views of the same file, and the Git diff is the authoritative record of every change. The files conform to the open-source SML specification, so the repository can be read without the engine. After it’s deployed, the model is simultaneously reachable over SQL (for JDBC-based BI tools and notebooks), XMLA (for Excel and Power BI), and MCP (for the agent). The total_revenue calculation returns the same number to Claude Sonnet 4.6 as it does to an Excel PivotTable pointed at the same XMLA endpoint. We confirm this match in Verification. How AtScale plans and pushes down queries When the agent asks a question against the semantic model, AtScale’s AI Computation Engine (ACE) does the planning. The steps a query goes through are the same for a dimensional SQL request from the MCP run_query tool and for an XMLA request from Excel. Only the parser at the front differs. Take the auto-enrollment question: Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime spend haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet? The agent, prompted with the model context returned by describe_model , composes a dimensional SQL query against the C360 model. ACE parses that query into a logical plan, resolves the dimensional references to the underlying fact_purchase , dim_customer , dim_address , and dim_rewards datasets, applies any row security the caller is subject to, and then plans the physical query against Amazon Redshift. Two things happen at the physical-planning stage that separate AtScale from a hand-written pipeline. First, the join is pushed to Amazon Redshift as a native SQL join rather than materialized in the semantic layer. The Amazon Redshift optimizer sees a single SQL statement with a filter and an aggregate, and executes it accordingly. Second, AtScale’s aggregate manager checks its registry for a pre-built aggregate that matches the query pattern. If a summary table exists that groups purchases by customer at the right grain, AtScale rewrites the query to hit the aggregate instead of scanning fact_purchase . The query returns in a fraction of the time it would take against the raw fact table, without the agent or the modeler doing any manual work to route it. Figure 4: The agent’s dimensional query enters the AtScale planner. The planner checks its aggregate registry, finds a matching aggregate for the query pattern, rewrites the query to hit the summary table in Amazon Redshift, and returns the result. The lower path shows the same query without a matching aggregate hitting fact_purchase directly The aggregate manager is what makes an agent-driven workload economically feasible. LLM-driven analysis fires more queries than a human analyst would, and open-ended prompts like Tell me something interesting about our sales can spawn a dozen. AtScale watches the query pattern, materializes aggregates in the warehouse itself (not a separate cache), and routes matching queries transparently. Aggregate creation is demand-defined against observed traffic across consumers, not only the agent. The audit record for the query captures both the dimensional SQL the LLM wrote and the warehouse-native SQL AtScale rewrote it into, along with whether an aggregate served the query. That record is available to an operator through the AtScale Queries page in Design Center, and it’s what the following governance section builds on. A note on multi-source and interoperability AtScale connects to warehouses over JDBC. The C360 walkthrough targets Amazon Redshift Serverless. The same SML model works over Snowflake, Databricks, and Google BigQuery, and AtScale documents the connection pattern for each. What changes when you swap the connection is the SQL dialect AtScale emits, not the SML in Git. One architectural property is worth stating explicitly because it differs from the first two posts in this series. A single AtScale query resolves in one warehouse engine. If the C360 model spans two warehouses (dimensions on Snowflake, facts on Amazon Redshift, say), a query that touches both must be reconciled in one of two ways. The first is upstream, by consolidating an analytical copy in one warehouse through a replication path. The second is by the warehouse itself, using engine-level federation such as Amazon Redshift Spectrum for querying Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) , or Apache Iceberg tables that both engines can read. AtScale plans a dimensional query and pushes it to one engine. The cross-engine story lives one layer down. That choice cuts both ways. It rules out the live cross-engine federation Stardog and Denodo perform at query time, but it lets AtScale’s planner and aggregate manager work against a single-engine execution model, which is what makes the aggregate story load-bearing at scale. Enterprises that already run a warehouse-centric analytical architecture with change data capture (CDC) pipelines from operational systems reuse that architecture. Enterprises whose answers require live federation across engines are better served by the semantic layers in the first two posts. Governed access: Identity propagation and runtime enforcement Customer 360 data is regulated. Some users (HR, fraud) need to see personally identifiable information such as Social Security numbers and card numbers. Most users (marketing, analytics) must not.
