Row-level filters restrict analysts by geography, and a per-user audit trail must survive from the human’s browser through to the warehouse. AtScale enforces these requirements at the semantic layer, before any query reaches the warehouse. Enforcement happens identically whether the caller is the Strands agent over MCP, an analyst in Excel over XMLA, or a notebook over JDBC. One row-security object in SML, one perspective, one set of role bindings, applied to each consumer of the model. Identity propagation from the user to AtScale The chain follows the same shape as the one in the Denodo post, with the terminal hop landing at the AtScale engine rather than continuing to the warehouse. The human authenticates to the application against the enterprise IdP and receives a JWT. The application forwards the JWT as a bearer token to the Strands agent through AgentCore Gateway, which validates it (issuer, audience, signature) and routes the request to AgentCore runtime. When the agent invokes a tool call to the AtScale MCP server, AgentCore Identity supplies the OAuth 2.0 access token issued by AtScale’s bundled Keycloak, mapped to the human user’s identity. The AtScale credential does not enter agent code. The AtScale MCP server accepts the OAuth token. The AtScale engine validates it against Keycloak, resolves the caller to an AtScale role, and plans the query with the caller’s row-security constraints and perspective bindings applied. The warehouse is reached with the AtScale connection identity from AWS Secrets Manager. Figure 5: The identity chain from human user through AgentCore Gateway, AgentCore runtime, AgentCore Identity, the AtScale MCP server, and the AtScale engine, terminating at the semantic-layer enforcement point. The warehouse hop is a service-account connection with the AtScale credential RBAC, row security, and perspectives AtScale expresses access control as three composable primitives. RBAC assigns roles to callers based on Keycloak claims. Row security is a model object that filters rows returned to the caller based on the caller’s identity or attributes. A perspective is a publishable subset of the model exposed to a specific role or group. For the C360 walkthrough, we define two roles. hr_user : sees the full C360 model, including ssn and card_num . marketing_user : sees the Marketing perspective, which hides ssn and card_num at the model layer. When marketing_user asks a question that references ssn , the agent’s describe_model call returns the Marketing perspective, one that does not include ssn . The agent has no attribute to project. Row-level filters compose the same way: an SML row-security object that scopes customers by state restricts a caller to a specific set of rows without any change to the agent’s prompt. Audit fidelity Queries through the AtScale engine are logged with the caller’s identity, the model, the LLM-generated dimensional SQL, the AtScale-translated pushdown SQL that Amazon Redshift saw, the security policies applied, whether an aggregate served the query, and the row count returned. Because the record captures both the query the model wrote and the query the warehouse executed, an auditor can trace an answer from the human question to the SQL that produced the number. Neither the first nor the second post in this series captures both forms of the query in one record. An audit record for a governed query looks like this: { "timestamp": "2026-08-31T10:34:56Z", "user_identity": "mary_major@example.com", "user_role": "marketing_user", "semantic_model": "Customer_360", "question": "Top 10 customers by revenue in California", "generated_sql": "SELECT full_name, total_revenue FROM ...", "translated_pushdown_sql": "SELECT ... FROM redshift ...", "security_policies_applied": ["regional_row_security"], "served_from": "aggregate", "execution_time_ms": 850, "rows_returned": 10 } The generated_sql and translated_pushdown_sql fields are the ones that make the trail complete: an auditor sees both the query the LLM composed against the semantic model and the query the warehouse actually ran. Expose the layer through the AtScale MCP server The AtScale MCP server is a component of the AtScale distribution, exposed at /mcp . It’s generally available in the AtScale C2026.7 release and speaks the standard Model Context Protocol . Any MCP-compatible client (the Strands agent in AgentCore runtime, Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, VS Code) can connect to the same endpoint against the same deployed model. The server exposes a set of tools scoped to querying the semantic model. The AtScale documentation publishes a tools reference per release. The tools that matter for an agent-driven workload are: list_models : Enumerate the models the caller can see, along with the column groups that describe how dimensions map to facts. describe_model : Return the dimensions, hierarchies, measures, calculations, and business descriptions for a chosen model. This is the payload the agent’s system prompt is loaded with before it starts composing queries. search_columns : Keyword search over the model’s columns. Useful when a full describe_model payload would use too much of the LLM’s context window. validate_query : Check that a dimensional SQL statement is compatible with the model without executing it against the warehouse. This lets the agent iterate on its query cheaply before firing anything Amazon Redshift will bill for. run_query : Execute a dimensional SQL statement against the model and return the rows. run_queries : Run multiple statements in a batch, useful for open-ended prompts where the agent fires several exploratory queries in parallel. get_version : Report the MCP server version, so a client can decide whether to cache the model schema. The AtScale MCP endpoint accepts two authentication modes. The bearer-token path uses an API token minted from Design Center. Every request runs as the token owner, and this path suits a proof-of-concept or a single-identity service. The OAuth 2.0 path uses AtScale’s bundled Keycloak with a pre-provisioned client whose ID is exactly atscale-mcp , documented on the AtScale Connecting with Claude page. AgentCore Gateway presents the access token on the agent’s behalf, the AtScale engine validates it against Keycloak, and downstream policy evaluation uses the human user’s identity. Registering the AtScale MCP server as an AgentCore Gateway target follows the standard Gateway MCP target flow. The tools listed earlier appear to the agent as ordinary tools, with AgentCore Identity handling the credential at the Gateway hop. Sidebar: Extending the model with AI-assisted modeling The AtScale MCP server exposes tools scoped to querying, and AtScale has been extending the MCP surface with author-side tools that let an agent introspect a warehouse schema, generate a candidate SML model from source metadata, validate the SML against the specification, and commit the result to Git. This pattern, in which an agent shapes the semantic model rather than only reading from it, is a natural fit for Claude Code and Cursor workflows. In those workflows, a data engineer collaborates with the LLM to bootstrap a model over a new dataset. AtScale groups this direction into three capabilities. A Semantic Discovery Engine scans warehouse schemas, query history, and lineage to infer candidate joins, hierarchies, and metric definitions. A Model Recommendation System suggests dimensions, measures, and relationships based on observed query patterns. A Governed Feedback Loop keeps human review of AI suggestions in the SML-and-Git workflow, so changes are versioned and auditable. The specific tools available at the time of publication are documented in the AtScale MCP tools reference. Check the current release notes for what is generally available and what is still in preview. The rest of this post covers the consumer path, an agent querying a deployed model, which is what a production C360 workflow relies on today. Deploy and run the agent Strands Agents is a small framework for building agents. A short Python entry point wires Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock to the AtScale MCP server as a tool source. AgentCore runtime hosts the process. AgentCore Gateway terminates inbound requests and holds the outbound AtScale credential through AgentCore Identity. Foundation model availability on Amazon Bedrock varies by AWS Region. For the current list, see Regional availability by models . The system prompt matters. The AtScale documentation and the reference demos in the AtScale corpus consistently recommend a three-step call pattern for the agent: list_models to see what is available, then describe_model on the target model to load the dimensions and measures into context, and only then run_query (or validate_query first, if the query is expensive to iterate on). The reasoning is that the LLM should not fabricate column names or metric names. It should reference only what describe_model returned. The system prompt should say so explicitly, and it should include a short section on the business terminology in the target model ( total_revenue means sales dollars, not units) so the agent maps user questions to the right measure. Turn on Amazon Bedrock prompt caching for the reused portion of the system prompt. The describe_model payload runs to a few thousand tokens and does not change within a model version, so caching it drops the input-token cost per query on repeated calls. The cache-point configuration is a request parameter on the BedrockModel object. See the Strands documentation for the current parameter name. Verification To confirm the semantic layer, the agent, and the identity flow work as intended, we ran three queries through the agent and then a governance rerun of one of them under a different role. The following behavior is what should reproduce in a working deployment. Query 1, single dimension List our customers in Wisconsin, with their city. The agent generates a dimensional SQL query against the C360 model that selects first_name , last_name , and city from dim_customer and dim_address where state = 'WI' . AtScale’s planner resolves the dimensional path to the customer and address tables in Amazon Redshift, pushes a single SQL statement down, and returns the rows. Query 2, aggregation with aggregate hit What are our top 10 products by units sold? The agent aggregates units_sold by product and orders descending. AtScale’s aggregate manager finds a matching demand-defined aggregate and rewrites the query to hit the summary table in Amazon Redshift rather than scanning fact_purchase . The Queries page shows both the LLM-generated dimensional SQL and the aggregate-routed warehouse SQL side by side. Query 3, cross-domain Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime spend haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet? The agent generates a query that joins dim_customer , dim_address , dim_rewards , and fact_purchase , and aggregates customer_lifetime_value by customer. The query restricts to customers where dim_rewards.account_id is null. The left join to dim_customer on cid keeps never-enrolled customers, who surface with a null enrollment record. The agent returns the top 20 by lifetime spend. AtScale’s planner resolves the joins to native SQL against Amazon Redshift and returns the ranked list. The customer_lifetime_value formula is not something the LLM had to invent. It’s a calculated measure defined once in customer_lifetime_value.yml and referenced by name in the query. Governance rerun We run a variant of Query 1 that adds ssn to the projection ( Show me our customers in Wisconsin, with their SSN ) as two different callers. As hr_user , describe_model returns the full C360 model, the agent composes the query, and the result set includes the SSN values. As marketing_user , describe_model returns the Marketing perspective, which does not expose ssn . The agent has no attribute to project, so it returns an answer without SSN. Nothing changes between the two runs except the caller’s identity. The query text, the agent code, the MCP server, the AtScale engine, and Amazon Redshift are all untouched. Cross-consumer confirmation We opened the same C360 model in Excel through the AtScale XMLA endpoint and dragged Customer.State and Total Revenue onto a PivotTable. The state-level totals match the ones the agent returned for equivalent questions, to the exact number. Extending across data sources Adding a new data source to the C360 model is a modeling exercise, not an integration one. Suppose the customer support team asks that the model include ticket volumes so an agent can answer Which of our top spenders opened a support ticket in the last 30 days? The steps are: Land the support-ticket data in Amazon Redshift alongside the other C360 tables, using the same replication pattern used for the operational tables. Add an SML dataset that maps the new table to a logical object. Add or extend a dimension ( dim_ticket ) and add the join to dim_customer on cid . Add any new measures the model needs ( open_ticket_count , avg_resolution_time ). Commit the SML changes, review them as a pull request, and deploy through the AtScale CI hook. Nothing changes in the agent code or the AgentCore configuration. The next time the agent calls describe_model , it sees the new dimension and measures, and it can compose questions against them. The same pattern applies to a different warehouse. If a source lands in Snowflake or Databricks rather than Amazon Redshift, the connection is a new SML dataset with a Snowflake or Databricks connection, and queries resolve in that engine per the earlier multi-source note. Deployment: AtScale on Amazon EKS AtScale runs on Kubernetes, and the reference deployment on AWS is Amazon EKS . AtScale ships an official Helm chart at oci://docker.io/atscaleinc/atscale , and the AtScale K8S Blueprints repository provides infrastructure as code (IaC) scaffolding for standing up an EKS cluster with the components AtScale expects: an ingress controller, a persistent store for the AtScale metadata database, a Redis instance for query caching, and an AtScale-configured Keycloak instance for identity federation. The AtScale deployment on EKS runs across a small set of Kubernetes pods. atscale-engine is the core query planner and executor. atscale-mcp-server is the MCP endpoint the agent talks to. atscale-keycloak is the bundled identity provider that federates to Amazon Cognito, Okta, Azure Active Directory, and other OpenID Connect (OIDC)-compliant IdPs. Supporting pods handle the SML API and the Design Center UI ( atscale-sml-api , atscale-sml-web ), PostgreSQL metadata storage ( atscale-db ), the query cache ( atscale-redis ), and ingress ( atscale-ingress , typically fronted by an AWS Network Load Balancer). The C360 application (a chat UI or a client library that calls the agent) can run in the same EKS cluster in its own namespace. It uses an IAM role for service account (IRSA) to reach Bedrock and AWS Secrets Manager without embedding credentials. Networking is standard: AtScale reaches Amazon Redshift through the virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoint or a security-group rule that permits the AtScale namespace’s egress to Amazon Redshift, and the human user reaches the application through the ingress load balancer. AtScale offers cloud deployment options beyond self-managed EKS. Check the AtScale website for current offerings and AWS availability. The rest of this post assumes the self-managed pattern described earlier. Conclusion Agentic access to enterprise data needs three things working together: a foundation model that can plan and generate queries, a semantic layer that computes governed, business-meaningful answers over the live warehouse, and a runtime that hosts the agent and manages the identity flow. Amazon Bedrock, AtScale, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore each play one of those roles. The agent talks to the semantic layer, not directly to the warehouse. Dimensions, hierarchies, measures, perspectives, and row security live in SML in Git. When a schema drifts or a governance rule changes, the update happens in one file, and each consumer (the agent, Excel, Tableau, Power BI) picks it up on the next query. Where to start Most teams that get this working start narrow and expand. Pick one workflow that spans two or three data sources and takes longer than it should to answer today. Write 3–5 questions the workflow needs to answer. These are the queries the semantic layer has to support on day one. Consolidate the analytical data into Amazon Redshift (or the warehouse of your choice), using AWS Database Migration Service or Amazon Aurora zero-ETL for operational data. Bootstrap the SML from the warehouse schema in Design Center, then refine it against the competency questions. Deploy AtScale on Amazon EKS with the AtScale Helm chart and the AtScale K8S Blueprints, register the AtScale MCP server as an AgentCore Gateway target, and wire a Strands agent through it. Further reading AtScale MCP server documentation: Connect to AtScale with AI AtScale C2026.7 release notes: documentation.atscale.com AtScale MCP tools reference (published per release with the AtScale documentation) AtScale K8S Blueprints: github.com/AtScaleInc/atscale-k8s-blueprints Semantic Modeling Language specification: github.com/semanticdatalayer/SML Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide Amazon Bedrock prompt caching Strands Agents on AWS Prescriptive Guidance Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with Stardog and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (first post in this series) Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with Denodo and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (second post in this series) About the authors Frank Lapolito Frank is a Solutions Engineer at AtScale who helps organizations simplify their data architectures and connect technical complexity to business value. JP Boreddy JP is a Senior Solutions Architect at AWS, where he partners with enterprise customers on cloud architecture, data, and AI workloads. Sindhu Jambunathan Sindhu is a Senior Solutions Architect at AWS with 13+ years of experience, helping ISV customers build scalable, secure, cost-effective data and generative AI solutions. Before AWS, she was a Senior Software Engineer at Microsoft and holds an MS in Computer Engineering from the University of Florida. Sahil Thapar Sahil is a Principal Solutions Architect at AWS, where he works with ISV customers to build highly available, scalable, and resilient applications on the AWS Cloud. He specializes in containers, machine learning, and generative AI, helping enterprises architect production-grade solutions.

content: Nebius and Nscale are among global technology partners looking to NVIDIA Vera CPUs to build the next wave of infrastructure. Their momentum reflects rapid advancements in agentic computing. Agents do more than generate answers: they retrieve information, run software tools, execute code and evaluate results. Each step depends on fast CPU processing. Vera accelerates that work, helping agents respond faster and enabling data centers to make better use of computing capacity. Vera is designed to sustain that speed even when running thousands of tasks simultaneously, helping organizations expand services without trading responsiveness for scale. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements   Building Europe’s Computing Capacity AI cloud providers Nebius , Nscale and Verda are building with Vera to support the growing computing needs of businesses and developers. High-performance, energy-efficient CPUs help these providers scale the data processing and software execution behind services, alongside the GPUs running models. The broader sovereign AI ecosystem also includes Aleria , a sovereign AI infrastructure and platform provider, supporting demand for infrastructure that keeps data and operations under customers’ control. More Ways to Put Vera to Work Server manufacturers Bull , Dell Technologies , HPE , Lenovo and Supermicro are building Vera-based systems, giving customers more deployment options for their high-performance computing and AI data centers. Vera can power standalone CPU servers or work alongside NVIDIA GPUs in accelerated systems, supporting different workloads and deployment needs. Data processing companies ClickHouse , Cloudera , Duck Labs , Elastic , Polars , Redpanda , SAP and Starburst observed strong results on Vera for analytical, extract-transform-and-load and semantic search workloads in early testing. Vera’s per-core performance, LPDDR5X memory bandwidth and NVIDIA Scalable Coherency Fabric help achieve performance gains across the board. Software and developer-platform companies Atlassian, Inherent and Nous Research are adopting Vera for environments where AI agents work alongside developers and researchers. Atlassian is looking to Vera to accelerate the data processing that builds semantic search indexes for its AI-powered products; Inherent has tested Vera and is looking to adopt it for environments where AI agents work alongside engineers on novel scientific research; and Nous Research uses Vera to authenticate agent identities and validate every action before it executes, keeping deployments secure as agent fleets grow. Baseten-Blaxel , Daytona, E2B, Modal, Prime Intellect and Vercel provide cloud-based sandboxes, which serve as computers for AI agents, and are building on Vera to power the infrastructure agents depend on to execute code, run tools and test results. Every agent needs a secure, isolated sandbox that can be provisioned instantly, and because sandboxes spin up millions of times a day, the speed of each individual startup cycle compounds at scale. Vera’s fast per-core performance and high-bandwidth memory make it well suited to this pattern, giving sandbox providers the throughput not only to spin up sandboxes but to run agentic workloads at maximum scale without interruption. title: Spain-Based Startups Advance Regional Innovation With Barcelona Supercomputing Center
summary: The Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC)’s AI Factory Accelerator Programme, now in full operation following a pilot initiative, gives startups access to sovereign compute, technical support and training to support innovation across industries. Many of these companies are also members of the NVIDIA Inception program for cutting-edge startups — and as of today, access to some […]
content: The Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC) ’s AI Factory Accelerator Programme, now in full operation following a pilot initiative, gives startups access to sovereign compute, technical support and training to support innovation across industries. Many of these companies are also members of the NVIDIA Inception program for cutting-edge startups — and as of today, access to some of the BSC AI Factory services are available through the NVIDIA Inception portal . NVIDIA Inception complements the BSC AI Factory Accelerator Programme by providing members with training through NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute open courses, business mentoring, venture capital connections and other resources. An upcoming extension of MareNostrum 5 — BSC’s public infrastructure serving scientific and technological innovation, powered by NVIDIA accelerated computing — will deliver supercomputing access through the BSC AI Factory and other AI Factories across Europe. BSC AI Factory is among Europe’s first AI factories and the first in Spain, and has delivered more than 800 services to private and public-sector clients since its April 2025 launch. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements   Three Inception members were recently named the BSC AI Factory Accelerator Programme’s AI Champions at the pilot initiative’s demo day: Qatium ’s water-network platform — already used by more than 250 utilities in 16 countries — is now in early production with its Neural Water Intelligence technology, powered by proprietary AI models trained on MareNostrum 5. title: Structured outputs for Anthropic Claude models on Amazon Bedrock
summary: Amazon Bedrock now supports structured outputs for all Anthropic Claude models on both the bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle endpoints. Receive schema-compliant JSON that conforms to a defined structure, without custom parsing, retry logic, or post-processing, using JSON Schema output format and strict tool use.
content: Amazon Bedrock now supports structured outputs for all Anthropic Claude models, on both the bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle endpoints, where the model is available. Whether you call Claude through Boto3 and the bedrock-runtime APIs or through the Messages API and the bedrock-mantle endpoint, you can now receive schema-compliant JSON responses that conform to a defined structure. You no longer need custom parsing, retry logic, or post-processing. Practical applications With structured outputs for Claude on Amazon Bedrock, you can automate reliable, schema-compliant tasks across industries. Examples include extracting every required field from financial earnings reports and compliance documents, parsing clinical notes into Electronic Health Records (EHR), and enriching product catalogs with consistent, validated results. You can also analyze contracts for key terms, parties, and obligations, or power intelligent support ticket routing where intents, sentiments, and entities always match your application’s data model. What changes with structured outputs on Amazon Bedrock Structured outputs use constrained decoding to enforce your JSON schema during token generation, not after the fact. The model doesn’t produce tokens that would violate your schema. This changes output formatting from probabilistic to deterministic. Two complementary mechanisms are now available on both Amazon Bedrock endpoints: Feature Purpose Use case JSON Schema output format Control the model’s response structure Data extraction, report generation, API responses Strict tool use Validate tool parameters against schemas Agentic workflows, function calling, multi-step automation What this means for you Each response is a valid JSON, so you no longer encounter JSON.parse() errors or parsing exceptions. Responses are also type safe: field types are enforced, and required fields are always present. Because outputs always conform to your schema, you don’t need retries to handle schema violations, making your integration more reliable. Structured outputs also constrains responses to only the fields your schema defines, which reduces output token count and can lower inference costs for high-volume workloads. These properties make structured outputs production ready, so you can deploy at scale without additional schema-validation code. Supported models and availability Structured outputs works with batch inference , so you can process large volumes of requests asynchronously while still receiving schema-compliant outputs. On the bedrock-runtime endpoint, it also works with cross-Region inference, so you can use it across AWS Regions without additional setup. If you need responses in real time, you can stream structured responses as typed events. How it works When you make a request with a JSON schema, here’s what happens behind the scenes: Schema validation –  Amazon Bedrock validates your JSON schema against the supported JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 subset. Grammar compilation –  For new schemas, Amazon Bedrock compiles a grammar artifact (the first request might take slightly longer). Caching –  Compiled grammars are cached for 24 hours, making subsequent requests faster. Constrained generation –  The model generates tokens that produce valid JSON matching your schema. Performance considerations For performance, the first request with a new schema might take longer because Amazon Bedrock compiles a grammar artifact before generation begins. After that initial compilation, subsequent requests using the same schema run with minimal overhead because the compiled grammar is cached. This cache is scoped to your account and lasts for 24 hours from first access. Changing the structure of your JSON schema invalidates the cache and triggers a fresh compilation, while changing only the name or description fields leaves the cached grammar intact. Getting started: Structured outputs with the InvokeModel API (bedrock-runtime) The InvokeModel API takes the Anthropic-native request body, so the schema goes in output_config.format as a JSON object rather than a JSON string. The following example shows how to extract the structured lead data from a customer email using boto3 with an Anthropic Claude model: Python import boto3 import json REGION = "us-east-1" # Choose your preferred region bedrock_runtime = boto3.client(service_name="bedrock-runtime", region_name=REGION) # Define the JSON schema for structured output schema = { "type": "object", "properties": { "name": {"type": "string", "description": "Customer name"}, "email": {"type": "string", "description": "Customer email address"}, "plan_interest": {"type": "string", "description": "Product plan of interest"}, "demo_requested": {"type": "boolean", "description": "Whether a demo was requested"} }, "required": ["name", "email", "plan_interest", "demo_requested"], "additionalProperties": False } # Make a request with structured outputs via the InvokeModel API # (reusing the schema defined for the Converse example) response = bedrock_runtime.invoke_model( modelId="global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5-5", body=json.dumps({ "anthropic_version": "bedrock-2023-05-31", "max_tokens": 512, "messages": [ {"role": "user", "content": ( "Paulo Santos (paulo@example.com) is interested in our Enterprise plan " "and wants to schedule a demo for next Tuesday at 2pm." )} ], "output_config": {"format": {"type": "json_schema", "schema": schema}} }) ) body = json.loads(response["body"].read()) # Check the stop reason before parsing if body["stop_reason"] == "end_turn": result_text = next(b["text"] for b in body["content"] if b["type"] == "text") print(json.dumps(json.loads(result_text), indent=2)) elif body["stop_reason"] == "max_tokens": print("Response truncated: increase max_tokens and retry.") JSON { "name": "Paulo Santos", "email": "paulo@example.com", "plan_interest": "Enterprise", "demo_requested": true } The response conforms to your schema. No additional validation is required. For additional API usage examples, including the Messages API, see the accompanying sample notebook . Strict tool use for agentic workflows Amazon Bedrock Mantle is designed for agentic applications with server-side tools, background inference, and stateful conversations. With strict tool use on the bedrock-mantle endpoint, you can now guarantee that tool parameters match your input schema exactly. The following example shows how to define a tool with strict schema enforcement: Import json from anthropic import AnthropicBedrockMantle # Reusing the client created in the Messages API example client = AnthropicBedrockMantle(aws_region="us-east-1") message = client.messages.create( model="anthropic.claude-sonnet-5", max_tokens=512, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What's the weather like in San Francisco?"}], tools=[ { "name": "get_weather", "description": "Get the current weather for a specified location", "strict": True, "input_schema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "location": { "type": "string", "description": "The city and state, e.g., San Francisco, CA" }, "unit": { "type": "string", "enum": ["celsius", "fahrenheit"], "description": "Temperature unit" } }, "required": ["location", "unit"], "additionalProperties": False } } ] ) #Tool inputs conform to the schema for block in message.content: if block.type == "tool_use": print(f"Tool: {block.name}") print(f"Input: {json.dumps(block.input, indent=2)}") Setting strict: true constrains the model’s tool input to match your schema exactly. The location field is always a string, and the unit field is always either celsius or fahrenheit. The model can’t add fields outside your schema, so the tool input contains only what your schema specifies. This is especially valuable for agentic use cases on Amazon Bedrock Mantle, where models orchestrate multi-step workflows with server-side tools like web search and code interpreter. Top use cases for Claude structured outputs Structured outputs reduce error-handling complexity the most in three common patterns: Data extraction: Extract fields from invoices, contracts, email, and transcripts into JSON that always matches your schema, ready to load into databases or customer relationship management (CRM) systems. Reliable agent tool calls: Validate tool arguments against their schemas at generation time, so multi-step agent workflows run without failures from malformed input. Classification at scale: Classify tickets, leads, or content by intent, priority, and sentiment for routing, moderation, and evaluation. Claude Haiku 5.5 reliably handles quick and repetitive workloads such as summaries, compactions, database queries, and classification requests. The following example shows how to classify and route incoming data using the Invoke API and Haiku 5.5: import boto3 import json REGION = "us-east-1" # Choose your preferred region bedrock_runtime = boto3.client(service_name="bedrock-runtime", region_name=REGION) # Classification schema: enums restrict output to a fixed set of labels schema = { "type": "object", "properties": { "category": { "type": "string", "enum": ["billing", "technical", "account", "sales", "other"], "description": "Primary ticket category" }, "priority": { "type": "string", "enum": ["low", "medium", "high", "urgent"], "description": "Urgency based on business impact" }, "sentiment": { "type": "string", "enum": ["positive", "neutral", "negative"], "description": "Customer sentiment" }, "escalate": {"type": "boolean", "description": "Whether a human should review immediately"}, "reason": {"type": "string", "description": "One-sentence justification for the classification"} }, "required": ["category", "priority", "sentiment", "escalate", "reason"], "additionalProperties": False } ticket = ( "Our production API calls have been failing with 500 errors since this morning. " "We're losing orders every minute. This is the second outage this month!" ) # Make a request with structured outputs via the InvokeModel API response = bedrock_runtime.invoke_model( modelId="global.anthropic.claude-haiku-5-5", body=json.dumps({ "anthropic_version": "bedrock-2023-05-31", "max_tokens": 512, "system": "You are a support ticket classifier. Classify the ticket accurately.", "messages": [ {"role": "user", "content": f"Classify this support ticket:\n\n{ticket}"} ], "output_config": {"format": {"type": "json_schema", "schema": schema}} }) ) body = json.loads(response["body"].read()) # Check the stop reason before parsing if body["stop_reason"] == "end_turn": result_text = next(b["text"] for b in body["content"] if b["type"] == "text") result = json.loads(result_text) print(json.dumps(result, indent=2)) # Route the ticket based on the guaranteed-valid labels if result["escalate"]: print(f"Escalating to on-call: {result['category']} / {result['priority']}") elif body["stop_reason"] == "max_tokens": print("Response truncated: increase max_tokens and retry.") Requirements and best practices To use structured outputs effectively on Amazon Bedrock, follow these guidelines: Set additionalProperties: false on all objects : This is required for structured outputs to work. Without it, your schema won’t be accepted. Use descriptive field names and descriptions : Models use property names and descriptions to understand what data to extract. Clear names like customer_email outperform generic names like field1 . Use enum for constrained values : When a field has a limited set of valid values, use enum to constrain options. Start basic, then add complexity : Begin with the minimum required fields and add complexity incrementally. Basic schemas compile faster, are easier to debug, and keep your request payload lean because the schema counts toward the Converse API payload size. Reuse schemas to benefit from caching : Structure your application to reuse schemas across requests. The 24-hour grammar cache improves performance for repeated queries. Check the stop reason in every response : Two scenarios can produce non-conforming responses: refusals (when the model declines for safety reasons) and token limits (when max_tokens is reached before completing). Handle both cases in your code. Test with realistic data before deployment : Validate your schemas against production-representative inputs. Edge cases in real data often reveal schema design issues. For additional best practices and schema design recommendations, see Structured outputs in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. Supported JSON Schema features All basic types: object , array , string , integer , number , boolean , null . enum (strings, numbers, booleans, or nulls only). const , anyOf , allOf (with limitations). $ref , $def , and definitions (internal references only). String formats: date-time , time , date , duration , email , hostname , uri , ipv4 , ipv6 , uuid . Array minItems (only values 0 and 1). Not supported The following are not supported: Recursive schemas. External $ref references. Numerical constraints ( minimum , maximum , multipleOf ). String constraints ( minLength , maxLength ). additionalProperties set to anything other than false. Conclusion Structured outputs for Anthropic Claude models on Amazon Bedrock provides the reliability that production AI applications require. It is available now on both the bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle endpoints. By combining JSON Schema output format and strict tool use, you can build data pipelines that need no additional validation. You can also create reliable agentic workflows and production AI applications without custom parsing or retry logic. Structured outputs for Claude on Amazon Bedrock is now generally available. To learn more, see the Amazon Bedrock documentation and explore our sample notebook . What workflows could validated, schema-compliant JSON improve in your organization? Share your feedback and questions in the comments. About the authors Anshika Saxena Anshika is a Generative AI Data Scientist at AWS, focused on Amazon Bedrock. She helps enterprise customers accelerate their generative AI and agentic AI adoption by guiding them through building and implementing solutions on Amazon Bedrock. She also works with ISVs and startups to enable them with the latest Anthropic services on Amazon Bedrock. title: Developers can now access SageMaker Studio through the new AWS experience
summary: New Amazon SageMaker AI customers can now land in a fully configured SageMaker Studio environment in only a few steps. Sign up with an identity you already have, such as Amazon, Apple, GitHub, or Google, with no advanced AWS account or credit card required for most customers, plus $100 in AWS Free Tier credits.
content: Today, we’re excited to announce that new Amazon SageMaker AI customers can now land inside a fully configured Amazon SageMaker Studio environment in only a few steps after signing up for AWS. You can use a sign-in method that you already have, such as Amazon, Apple, GitHub, Google, or an email address. You don’t need to set up an advanced AWS account, enter a credit card (for most customers), or configure an environment manually. New customers also receive $100 in AWS Free Tier credits that work across SageMaker AI, including model customization, training jobs, Studio notebooks, and endpoint deployments. This post follows on from our previous post, From Hugging Face to Amazon SageMaker Studio in One Click , which introduced deep links from Hugging Face model pages directly into SageMaker Studio workflows. Earlier this year, we also sped up Studio environment creation time from 2 minutes to about 20 seconds and pre-configured model customization permissions in every new Studio domain. Together, these changes removed much of the friction after a developer reached Studio. One major hurdle remained before they got there: creating an AWS account. New customers had to verify an email address, enter contact information, verify a phone number, provide payment details, and select a support plan before they could start building. For individual developers and small startup teams used to signing in and building within a few minutes, that was still a significant barrier. What’s new With this launch, SageMaker Studio is now integrated with the updated AWS sign-in and sign-up experience , which introduces new options for creating and managing AWS accounts along with simplified collaboration. New customers can create an account using an identity that they already have and start building in SageMaker Studio right away. New sign-in experience New customers can now sign up using their Google, GitHub, Apple, or Amazon account, or with an email address, in 2–3 steps. You don’t need to complete the advanced AWS account sign-up, verify a phone number, or enter a credit card (for most customers): Figure 1: The Sign up for AWS page with social sign-on options After you sign up, SageMaker AI automatically creates your Studio environment in about 20 seconds. You then land on the page that matches where you started. For example, you might discover and select a model from Hugging Face for deployment through Deploy on SageMaker AI . Studio then opens the Deployment page with the model pre-configured for endpoint creation: Figure 2: Deploying a Hugging Face model on Amazon SageMaker AI Figure 3: Configuring endpoint settings in SageMaker Studio Up to $200 in Free Tier credits, no credit card required for most customers New customers receive $100 in AWS Free Tier credits that work across SageMaker AI, including endpoint deployments, model customization, Studio notebooks, and model training. You also have the chance to earn an additional $100 worth of credits. Credits are applied automatically to your usage, and you receive an email notification as you approach your limit. The Free Tier period ends after 6 months or when you’ve used all your credits, whichever comes first. At that point, resource usage stops automatically, so you won’t be surprised by unexpected charges. You can upgrade to a paid plan at any time by adding payment details. Built on the foundations of previous launches New environments created through the new sign-in experience include the improvements from earlier launches. Permissions for model customization, training, evaluation, and deployment are pre-configured, so you don’t need to create AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles. Eligible accounts get default access to G5, G6, and G4dn GPU instances for endpoints, training jobs, and Studio notebooks. Additionally, the instance selection menu in Studio shows quota availability, so you can quickly see which instance types are available for use. Getting started You can try the new sign-in experience today: Browse models on Hugging Face , choose Deploy , select Amazon SageMaker AI and then choose Customize on SageMaker AI or Deploy on SageMaker AI  on a supported model. Alternatively, visit the Amazon SageMaker Studio page and choose Get started with Amazon SageMaker AI . On the AWS sign-in page, choose Google , GitHub , Apple , or Amazon , or enter your email address, and follow the prompts to create your account in a few steps. Land in your fully configured SageMaker Studio environment and start building with your Free Tier credits. The new sign-in experience is available for new AWS accounts. If you already have an AWS account, there’s no change to how you sign in. Conclusion The new sign-in experience removes the last major hurdle between discovering and building with Amazon SageMaker AI. Combined with faster environment creation, pre-configured permissions, deep links from Hugging Face, and default GPU access, individual developers can get started quickly. Startup teams can now go from finding a model to customizing or deploying it in minutes, using an identity they already have. To get started, visit aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/studio or explore models on Hugging Face .   About the authors Hazim Qudah Hazim is a Specialist Solutions Architect at AWS based in Dallas, TX. He enjoys helping customers build and adopt AI/ML solutions using AWS technologies and best practices. Prior to his role at AWS, he spent many years in technology consulting with customers across many industries and geographies. In his free time, he enjoys running and playing with his dog Nala. Paul Hargis Paul has focused his efforts on machine learning at several companies, including AWS, Amazon, and Hortonworks. He enjoys building technology solutions and teaching people how to use them. Paul likes to help customers expand their machine learning initiatives to solve real-world problems. Prior to his role at AWS, he was lead architect for Amazon Exports and Expansions, helping amazon.com improve the experience for international shoppers. Naidile Murali Naidile is a Product Manager at AWS based in Bellevue, WA. She focuses on enhancing the AI/ML developer experience on Amazon SageMaker AI, including new customer onboarding to Studio, SageMaker JumpStart model hub, and GPU capacity management for IDEs. Prior to AWS, she worked as a software engineer at HSBC and holds an MBA from Georgetown University.

summary: What's changed Added a transcript line when a plugin that runs first skips one of your mod's hooks, naming the event and the plugin Added decider: "person" to a mod's tool.check answer: only the permission dialog or a host's callback can approve the ask, and it is refused with the mod's reason where nobody can be asked Added e.isReadOnly to a mod's tool.check event, set when the tool call is read-only Added /auto-mode-setup : a guided setup that reads your project and recent sessions to...
content: What's changed Added a transcript line when a plugin that runs first skips one of your mod's hooks, naming the event and the plugin Added decider: "person" to a mod's tool.check answer: only the permission dialog or a host's callback can approve the ask, and it is refused with the mod's reason where nobody can be asked Added e.isReadOnly to a mod's tool.check event, set when the tool call is read-only Added /auto-mode-setup : a guided setup that reads your project and recent sessions to teach auto mode about your environment, now also available on Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry, Claude apps gateway and telemetry-disabled sessions Added /claude-api managed-agents-secure , which compares a Managed Agents agent's settings with Anthropic's published security guide, without changing anything Added the names of the tools called earlier to the compaction summary in the transcript view (Ctrl+O) Added a warning on Pro and Max plans when resuming an inactive conversation would use a noticeable share of your 5-hour usage limit: resume anyway, or start a new conversation and Claude can look up the previous one if you refer to it Fixed the organization policy not refreshing until the hourly check after approving an ANTHROPIC_API_KEY at startup or switching "Use custom API key" in /config Fixed sandboxed commands failing to start on Linux when a sandbox.filesystem.denyRead glob contains brackets that are not a character class, such as a [user-id] route folder Fixed rm -r of a mounted drive or a folder at its top level ( /Volumes , /media , WSL's /mnt/c ) not getting the safety prompt that rm -rf /Applications gets Fixed CLAUDE_CODE_TRANSCRIPT_LOCAL_GC dropping messages from the saved transcript when the disk filled up while the file was being trimmed Fixed a plugin keeping a headless run going past --max-turns , Stop, or ended input by spawning subagents or re-running a finished one Fixed a failed mod reload removing the tools and commands of the version that stays loaded, and its messages being wrong or silent about whether the previous version is still loaded Fixed a click on a mod's button being lost when buttons with the same label and no key were redrawn unchanged Fixed mod sharing in the built-in plugin-authoring skill stopping at the secret scan on machines with managed settings and on Team and Enterprise plans Fixed scheduled Cowork cloud sessions waiting five minutes again for each subagent whose WebFetch needed a URL approval that nobody was there to give Fixed Write results and rejected edits showing a file outside the working directory as ../../… ; they now show ~/… or the full path Fixed a claude.ai Directory plugin's skills not running as commands when picked from the "/" menu in Cowork cloud sessions Fixed Remote Control permanently withholding a desktop conversation's history when a different account was signed in to the terminal Fixed Remote Control failing to start from Claude Desktop when DISABLE_TELEMETRY or DO_NOT_TRACK is set on a paid plan Fixed model switches, messages and interrupts waiting behind a context usage check in SDK and desktop sessions Fixed context_management: Extra inputs are not permitted errors behind LLM gateways; Claude Code now resends the request without that field Fixed OpenTelemetry settings delivered through server-managed settings being ignored for the whole session after signing in during first-run setup or the first start after /logout Fixed unsandboxed Bash commands in Claude Desktop Code tab sessions on macOS and Linux not seeing environment variables exported in shell startup files such as ~/.zshrc Fixed the Consumer Terms notice being skipped for a day or longer after a server error Fixed /privacy-settings offering choices that may not apply to you after a network or server error Fixed a "Context limit reached" or "Prompt is too long" error after stopping a turn while Claude Code was compacting a conversation the API had rejected as too long Fixed subagents sometimes forgetting their most recent work when they were messaged or resumed right after finishing Fixed claude --help text for --tools , --resume , --debug , --json-schema , --disable-slash-commands , --system-prompt-snapshot and claude update to match actual behavior Fixed claude --worktree removing the worktree and its branch without asking at exit when HEAD was detached or on another branch, which could lose commits Fixed resumed and cloud sessions sending Claude the whole skill list again each time plugins reloaded at startup Fixed an interrupt not ending a Read that waits on an idle pipe or device named like an image Fixed /effort status , /effort ultracode and the prompt's effort indicator showing a guessed effort level when CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL is auto or unset and no level is sent Fixed a PreToolUse hook's deny reason being replaced by a timeout error when an Agent SDK callback hook on the same tool call timed out Fixed Bash and PowerShell deleting a large command's output file when it could not be copied to the session's tool-results folder, unless the disk is full Fixed notes typed into a multiple-choice question with previews being cut off with "…" in terminals under about 100 columns, hiding what was typed ( #82768 ) Fixed self-paced /loop wakeups scheduled at the 1-hour maximum firing just after the 1-hour prompt cache expired, so those wakeups no longer re-read the conversation uncached Fixed agent teams: approving a shutdown request from the main session no longer exits the whole CLI Fixed a skill's once hook also removing another skill's identical hook after it ran Fixed transcript mode's { and } landing the prompt on an inconsistent row, or off screen, instead of the transcript's first row Fixed CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW=200k silently setting a 100K window: the variable now accepts k and M suffixes like --autocompact , and warns when a value is out of range or ignored Fixed Ctrl+C in the agents view clearing a text selection without copying it when pressed before the mouse button was released Improved /usage to say when a rate limit on usage data ends instead of "try again in a moment" Improved the lines shown when a mod written in the session loads, reloads or fails to load Improved artifacts with several views: when you ask for links to them, Claude now writes out each view's link and explains that the address bar stays the same as you switch views Improved cloud sessions: a new conversation's first turn no longer waits for the local (stdio) MCP servers of plugins synced from claude.ai, unless a server sets alwaysLoad: true Improved how a remote session recovers its status when the server refuses a status update that carried other session data Improved session file size in auto mode: the safety classifier's context is no longer stored with every request Improved the claude -p invalid-settings warning: a file that did not load lists only what stopped it, and long lists are capped per file Improved resume of large compacted sessions in SDK and headless mode: the first request after resuming is sent sooner Improved responsiveness and throughput when many subagents are running at the title: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart: 2026 year-to-date in review
summary: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart onboarded over 100 new models from 30 providers in the first three quarters of 2026. This recap covers the model-onboarding highlights and JumpStart enhancements, including the simplified Model Hub, pre-configured deployment options, and Hugging Face deep link integration.
content: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart is a machine learning (ML) hub within Amazon SageMaker AI that provides access to a curated catalog of AI models, solution templates, and example notebooks. It reduces the time it takes to go from model selection to deployment. You can use it to evaluate open source large language models (LLMs), deploy a vision model for document understanding, or fine-tune a compact model on your own data. SageMaker JumpStart serves three primary use cases: Model discovery and evaluation — Browse hundreds of foundation models (FMs) from providers like Alibaba (Qwen), NVIDIA, Google, Mistral, Cohere, IBM, and more. Each model card includes architecture details, benchmarks, licensing information, and sample notebooks. One-click deployment — Deploy your choice of model to a SageMaker real-time inference endpoint with pre-configured settings optimized for your workload (low cost, low latency, throughput, or balanced). No manual container or instance configuration required. Model customization — Fine-tune models directly from the console or SDK using techniques like low-rank adaptation (LoRA), supervised fine-tuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Serverless customization options reduce infrastructure management. You can access SageMaker JumpStart through the SageMaker Studio console (Models → JumpStart models), programmatically through the SageMaker Python SDK, or directly from Hugging Face using the recently launched deep link integration. 2026 onboarding at a glance From January through September 2026, SageMaker JumpStart onboarded over 100 new models across 30 distinct providers. This represents a significant expansion of the catalog, driven by the accelerating pace of open source model releases and growing customer demand for choice across model architectures, sizes, and capabilities. Here’s a breakdown of the leading contributors and a link to our SageMaker JumpStart page : Alibaba (Qwen): 29 models spanning reasoning (Qwen 3.8-27B), large-scale mixture-of-experts (Qwen3.5-122B-A10B), agentic workflows (Qwen-AgentWorld-35B-A3B), code generation (Qwen3-Coder-Next, Qwen 3 Coder 30B), speech recognition (Qwen3-ASR-1.7B), text-to-speech (Qwen3-TTS), embeddings (Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B), and reranking (Qwen3-Reranker-4B). NVIDIA: 17 models including the Cosmos3 world foundation model family (Super, Edge, Nano), Cosmos Reason 7B, MSA-Search, Nemotron 3.5 Lightning , Nemotron-3-Super-120B (FP8 and BF16), Nemotron3 Ultra, Nemotron-Nano-12B-v2, Nemotron 3 Nano Omni (multimodal) , and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for vision-language. Mistral: 7 models including the Ministral-3 family (3B, 8B, 14B in standard and BF16) and Voxtral-Mini-4B-Realtime for speech. Google: 6 Gemma 4 variants, including gemma-4-31B-it, E2B-it, E4B-it, 26B-A4B-it, assistant, and NVFP4 quantized. IBM: 4 models including Granite 4.0 h-micro/small/tiny and granite-speech-4.1-2b for multilingual automatic speech recognition (ASR) across 6 languages. Cohere: 4 models including Command A (A100) and Rerank v3.5, v4.0 Fast, and v4.0 Pro for retrieval augmentation. Others: 33 models from MiniMax, Zhipu AI (GLM), DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Allen AI, Microsoft, Meta (Muse Spark) , Reflection (Beam) , Black Forest Labs, JetBrains, OpenBMB, BharatGenAI, Kakao, OpenFold, and more. Model onboarding highlights The models onboarded in 2026 reflect several focused priorities in how we expand the SageMaker JumpStart catalog. These aren’t only industry trends. They represent the areas where we see strong customer demand and significant opportunity to help customers build production AI applications on SageMaker. Expanding the NVIDIA open-model portfolio NVIDIA is one of our significant model providers, and in 2026 their contribution extended well beyond language models. The Cosmos3 world foundation models, available in Super, Edge, and Nano tiers, bring video generation, physics simulation, and action planning into a single architecture for physical AI applications such as robotics, autonomous systems, and digital twins. Combined with Nemotron models spanning from efficient edge inference (Nano-12B) to large-scale reasoning (Super-120B), SageMaker JumpStart now offers a broad portfolio of NVIDIA open models. If you build on NVIDIA hardware, you can deploy these models on SageMaker with optimized containers and pre-configured endpoints. Closing the multimodal gap Customer workloads increasingly require models that process more than text. In 2026, we prioritized onboarding models that handle vision, speech, and document understanding natively. NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano Omni processes text, vision, and speech in a single model. Google Gemma 4 adds vision-language capabilities across multiple sizes. IBM granite-speech-4.1-2b handles speech recognition and translation across six languages. Mistral Voxtral-Mini supports real-time speech understanding. These additions mean customers can avoid chaining separate preprocessing models for multimodal workloads. Making creative AI accessible Image and video generation moved from niche to mainstream in 2026. We onboarded FLUX.2 Small Decoder and FLUX.2-klein-base-4B from Black Forest Labs for fast text-to-image generation, Meta Muse-Glimmer-30B for multimodal agentic workflows, and NVIDIA Cosmos3 for video generation. With these models, you can access creative AI capabilities with the same one-click deployment experience you use for language models. Prioritizing efficient and quantized models Not every workload requires a frontier-scale model, and many customers are focused on optimizing inference costs as they move to production. We onboarded multiple quantized and compact models: Zhipu AI GLM-5.2 FP8 delivers strong performance with a reduced memory footprint. JetBrains Mellum2-12B uses a mixture-of-experts architecture with only 2.5B active parameters for code generation. OpenBMB MiniCPM5-1B packs multimodal capabilities into 1 billion parameters. Microsoft Phi-4-mini-instruct and IBM Granite 4.0 h-tiny demonstrate that compact models serve production workloads on instance types like ml.g5.xlarge. These models can optimize latency and total cost of ownership (TCO) for targeted use cases. Onboarding purpose-built models for targeted tasks General-purpose LLMs are versatile, but purpose-built models are optimized for specific tasks. In 2026, we onboarded Qwen-AgentWorld-35B-A3B for autonomous AI workflows with native tool-calling. GLM-OCR, LightOnOCR, and DeepSeek-OCR handle document text extraction. Qwen3-Reranker-4B and Cohere Rerank v4.0 improve retrieval precision in Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines. langcache-embed-v3-small provides lightweight embedding for semantic search. Qwen3-ASR and Qwen3-TTS bring speech recognition and synthesis. OpenFold3 supports protein structure prediction for scientific computing. With these models, you can build pipelines where each stage uses the specialized tool for the job, rather than forcing a single model to do everything. Broadening provider diversity Reducing concentration risk in model selection is important for enterprise customers. In 2026, we expanded the catalog to include 30 providers, up from a more concentrated set in prior years. Alibaba Qwen is the single largest contributor with 29 models spanning reasoning, coding, speech, and retrieval. Zhipu AI and DeepSeek add competitive LLMs and specialized OCR. MiniMax and Moonshot AI contribute emerging architectures. Cohere brings reliable reranking. BharatGenAI and Kakao expand regional model coverage. This breadth gives customers more options for performance, cost, licensing, and language support. SageMaker JumpStart enhancements in 2026 Beyond model onboarding, SageMaker JumpStart also shipped significant improvements in 2026 that reduce friction across the model lifecycle, from discovery to deployment. Simplified Model Hub on the SageMaker AI console Previously, discovering SageMaker JumpStart models required navigating into SageMaker Studio and finding the SageMaker JumpStart section in the left navigation. The new Model Hub experience surfaces the full SageMaker JumpStart catalog directly on the SageMaker AI console landing page. You can browse models by category and filter by input/output modality, publisher, model size, license, and framework. You can also view sample notebooks and open models inside Studio with a single click. This avoids the multi-step navigation that slowed initial exploration. Pre-configured endpoint deployment options Choosing the right instance type, serving container, and optimization settings for a model deployment typically required manual benchmarking across dozens of combinations. SageMaker JumpStart now offers named deployment configurations, with optimization options for: Balanced — An even tradeoff between cost, latency, and throughput for general-purpose workloads. Throughput optimized — Maximum tokens per second using techniques like Speculative Decoding, ideal for high-volume batch processing. Latency optimized — Lowest Time to First Token (TTFT), prioritizing speed for interactive applications. Cost optimized — Lowest infrastructure cost per request, suitable for workloads that can accept higher latency. These configurations include Neuron-optimized setups for AWS Inferentia and AWS Trainium instances, reducing deployment complexity and infrastructure costs. You can deploy a model with a single click and the right optimization profile, rather than spending weeks benchmarking configurations manually. Hugging Face deep link integration A new integration with Hugging Face connects model discovery directly to SageMaker Studio, for onboarded models. When browsing models on Hugging Face, you can choose Deploy on SageMaker AI or Customize and Deploy on SageMaker AI . You land directly in a configured Studio environment with the model pre-loaded, permissions pre-configured, and GPU quota visibility built in. This avoids the need to set up AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles, create a domain, or configure permissions before experimenting. Getting started There are three ways to get started with SageMaker JumpStart: SageMaker Studio console — Open SageMaker Studio, navigate to Models → JumpStart models, and browse the catalog. Choose a model to view its details, then choose Deploy or Customize . SageMaker Python SDK — Deploy models programmatically using the SageMaker Python SDK. Visit the SageMaker JumpStart model catalog for SDK examples and deployment guides. Hugging Face deep link — Browse the HuggingFace Model Hub and choose Deploy on SageMaker AI  to land directly in Studio for SageMaker JumpStart onboarded models. Each model on SageMaker JumpStart includes deployment configurations, sample notebooks, and documentation. For a hands-on walkthrough, see our related blog post on “ Deploy and evaluate models with Amazon SageMaker JumpStart ”. Conclusion The first three quarters of 2026 have been a period of significant progress for Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. With over 100 new models onboarded from 30 providers, the catalog now spans a wide range of capabilities. These include frontier reasoning models, multimodal vision-language models, creative AI for image and video generation, speech recognition and synthesis, optical character recognition (OCR) and document understanding, embedding and retrieval models for RAG, agentic workflow models, and specialized scientific computing models. These onboarding priorities reflect where we see the strongest customer demand and the greatest opportunity to accelerate AI adoption on AWS. They include expanding the portfolio, closing the multimodal gap, making creative AI accessible, prioritizing efficiency and quantization, onboarding purpose-built models, and broadening provider diversity. Combined with the enhancements like simplified Model Hub, pre-configured deployment options, and the Hugging Face deep link integration, SageMaker JumpStart continues to lower the barrier between model discovery and production deployment. Visit the SageMaker JumpStart model catalog to explore the full lineup. Next steps There are many ways to get started with SageMaker JumpStart. Try one of these out for yourself! Evaluate models and choose the right one for you Learn how to Deploy from HuggingFace to SageMaker Studio Use pretrained models in case-based deployments Design a Physical AI model factory on SageMaker HyperPod   About the authors Vamsi Goparaju Vamsi leads Go-to-Market (GTM) and Revenue Acceleration initiatives at AWS, enabling Inference and ModelOps workloads for our customers, and driving OSS Use Cases and Product features for Amazon SageMaker AI, JumpStart and Generative AI. With over 16 years of experience spanning AWS, Dell, and Infosys, he brings a unique blend of technical depth and business knowledge across cloud, high-performance computing (HPC), artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and analytics. He holds an MBA from Texas A&M University’s Mays Business School. Naidile Murali Naidile is a Product Manager at AWS based in Bellevue, WA. She focuses on enhancing the AI/ML developer experience on Amazon SageMaker AI, including onboarding, IDE connectivity, and GPU capacity management. Prior to AWS, she worked as a software engineer at HSBC. Naidile holds an MBA from Georgetown University. Dan Ferguson Dan is a Solutions Architect at AWS, based in New York, USA. As a machine learning services expert, Dan works to support customers on their journey to integrating ML workflows efficiently, effectively, and sustainably. Gula Nurmatova Gula is a Software Development Manager at AWS based in New York, USA. She leads the engineering teams behind Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, making foundation models from providers like NVIDIA, Meta, and Mistral easy to discover, evaluate, and deploy across SageMaker and Amazon Bedrock. Prior to AWS, she held engineering and engineering management roles at RTX and GE, and holds a Master’s degree in Computer Science

title: Germany Wants to Lead the World in Industrial AI: How NVIDIA Will Help
summary: In the cavernous hall of Kraftwerk, a former power station in Berlin, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang sat down to discuss Germany’s AI roadmap, and in particular, the industrial applications of AI. Huang opened by tracing NVIDIA’s longstanding relationship with German industry, beginning with gaming systems, workstations and automotive […]
content: In the cavernous hall of Kraftwerk, a former power station in Berlin, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang sat down to discuss Germany’s AI roadmap, and in particular, the industrial applications of AI. Huang opened by tracing NVIDIA’s longstanding relationship with German industry, beginning with gaming systems, workstations and automotive design in the early 2000s and leading to today’s partnerships in autonomous vehicle development and digital twins for manufacturing. The conversation focused on how Germany can make the most of the AI revolution by playing to its strengths in manufacturing and automotive — and by encouraging AI adoption across the country’s ecosystem of small and medium-sized companies. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements   Earlier in the day, as part of the Invest in Germany Summit, Chancellor Merz, the Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy and the Federal Ministry for Research, Technology and Space signed a Joint Declaration of Intent with NVIDIA. The German federal government’s aim is to merge traditional German engineering and manufacturing expertise with cutting-edge research and AI technology. The declaration sets out an agreement to work on a joint initiative with NVIDIA to advance cutting edge AI models for physical AI. Formalizing and expanding NVIDIA’s collaboration with Germany’s federal government and its “Industry 4.0 Platform,” which is comprised of representatives from politics, industry, research and trade associations, helps achieve the government’s stated goal to “systematically bring industrial AI into widespread use and to establish a state-of-the-art industrial AI ecosystem in Europe.” Germany’s Ambition to Integrate AI With Industry Merz and Huang dug into industrial AI and how NVIDIA can help Germany lead the way. The German Chancellor first laid out his government’s ambition. “We are fully committed to be one of the most advanced places in the world, not just in the European Union, but in the world to work with AI, to integrate AI into our industry,” Merz said. “I’m really optimistic that we will be one of the leading, if not the leading, country in the world in terms of the spread of AI for all the companies — our manufacturers, machinery, automotive industry and suppliers of the automotive industry. I think this is a great opportunity.” Merz called out the leaders of the small and medium businesses — the Mittelstand — in the audience. “The biggest advantage we have in Germany is our so-called Mittelstand,” Merz said. “Please open your doors for AI to make use of your data. This is a real secret and a real advantage for Germany to make use of all the data which is already available in our companies.” Huang agreed, and praised Germany’s world-class expertise in manufacturing companies both large and small, as well as its math and science excellence. That national expertise and knowledge is what sets the German economy apart, he said, and AI will only amplify it. “That knowledge belongs to you,” Huang said. “It cannot be replaced. AI can only augment your capability, it will not replace your capability. Take advantage of the technology. It’s a new instrument.” Germany’s expertise with physical technologies is a differentiator, Huang and Merz agreed, and a powerful accelerator for the German economy when AI is included. “If we are successful in bringing these two aspects and parts of the business of the future together,” Merz said. “I’m really very optimistic that Germany can be one of the most successful economies in the world.” Huang described AI’s impact across virtually every industry as a new industrial revolution. “This industrial revolution is so mighty, so powerful,” Huang said. “In the Chancellor’s words, you are re-engineering Germany. This is your chance to do it well.” Merz envisioned a regular reunion with Huang to assess the progress Germany is making with AI. “I would like to see him regularly, let’s say at least once a year, and discuss the progress we made,” Merz said, “And see a guy sitting in my office being extremely happy about Germany as a place to invest.” NVIDIA’s Investments in Germany Huang also announced new investments in four German startups, part of a nearly $10 billion commitment by NVIDIA to support companies, universities, research institutions and more across Europe. NVIDIA has been investing across Germany’s startup ecosystem, supporting leading technology companies including n8n, Neura Robotics and Black Forest Labs . Today, Huang announced new planned investments in Agile Robots, Avelios Medical, Mirelo and Reflex Aerospace. Agile Robots, a Munich-based robotics company, builds AI-powered robots, from robotic arms to its Agile ONE humanoid, for manufacturing, logistics and healthcare. Avelios Medical, a Munich-based healthcare technology startup, develops an AI-native hospital information system that serves as the core system of record for clinical and administrative workflows, integrating AI directly into hospital operations to free up doctors and nurses to deliver better patient care. Mirelo , a German startup, develops AI models that generate sound effects, speech and music for video, helping creators and production teams produce high-quality audio that perfectly matches their visuals on screen. Reflex Aerospace, a Berlin-based space scaleup, designs and builds high-performance satellites ready for launch in about 12 months instead of years. Siemens and NVIDIA Advance Autonomous Manufacturing; Record-Breaking Quantum Simulation Earlier in the day, Siemens announced it’s partnering with NVIDIA to advance AI-driven, autonomous factories. Siemens showcased new AI solutions at its Erlangen factory , advancing its role as a global blueprint for autonomous manufacturing. Fully virtual production ramp-up reduces engineering effort by up to 85%, while agent-based production planning enables more adaptive manufacturing and cost savings of up to 20%. NVIDIA researchers used JUPITER, Europe’s largest supercomputer at the Jülich Supercomputing Centre, to run a record-breaking simulation of a fault-tolerant quantum computer. The 104-qubit simulation is the largest and most detailed of its kind to date.   Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements
