title: Pegasus 1.5 from TwelveLabs is now available in Amazon Bedrock
summary: TwelveLabs Pegasus 1.5 is now available in Amazon Bedrock. The video language model turns long-form video into structured, timestamped metadata: define the moments that matter and get every matching segment back as JSON, with new video segmentation, multimodal prompting with reference images, and on-the-fly processing of up to two hours of video.
content: On Oct 9, 2026 we announced the availability of TwelveLabs’ Pegasus 1.5 on Amazon Bedrock . Pegasus 1.5 is a video language model that turns long-form video into structured, timestamped metadata. You describe the moments that matter to your workflow, and the model returns every matching segment as JSON. Video represents a significant and complex category of unstructured data, yet most of it remains unsearchable and underutilized. Extracting structured, actionable insights from that content has historically required labor-intensive manual review or fragmented toolchains. With earlier versions of Pegasus, you can point the model at a clip, ask a question, and get an answer. Now, Pegasus 1.5 analyzes the entire video, finds every segment that matches user-defined criteria, and returns structured, timestamped metadata. It also introduces video segmentation, multimodal prompting with reference images, and on-the-fly processing. With Pegasus 1.5 on Amazon Bedrock, you can analyze videos directly from an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) URI or a base64 string with no pre-indexing required, and your data remains within the AWS data boundary. In this post, we cover what’s new in Pegasus 1.5, how the model is packaged on Amazon Bedrock, and how to send your first request. We then walk through video segmentation, structured JSON output, and multimodal prompting. What’s new in Pegasus 1.5 Pegasus 1.5 has the following changes compared to previous versions: Time-based metadata generation. You define the segments, events, or domain-specific cues that matter to your workflow, such as editorial segments, sports plays, speaker changes, or brand appearances. Pegasus 1.5 returns every matching segment as JSON, with start and end times and the requested fields populated. Multimodal prompting. A segment definition can combine a text description with a visual reference. This makes it possible to locate a specific product, logo, or person, along with what they are doing on screen. On-the-fly processing. No ingestion pipeline or pre-indexing step is required. Videos are sent directly from Amazon S3 and results are returned in the response. Extended processing capacity. Pegasus 1.5 analyzes videos up to two hours long in a single request, up from one hour in Pegasus 1.2. Pegasus 1.5 retains and enhances the core capabilities that made Pegasus 1.2 a powerful tool for video understanding, including: Video-to-text generation : Creates detailed textual descriptions based on video content. Granular visual comprehension : Analyzes objects, on-screen text, and numerical content within video frames. Temporal grounding : Accurately identifies timestamps of specific events within videos. Multimodal understanding : Combines visual, audio, and textual information for comprehensive analysis. Multilingual support : Full support for English, with partial support for Arabic, Chinese, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, Thai, and Vietnamese. How Pegasus 1.5 works on Amazon Bedrock Pegasus 1.5 takes a video and either a text prompt or a set of segment definitions, and returns text or JSON. You call it on the bedrock-runtime endpoint with the InvokeModel API, or with InvokeModelWithResponseStream when you want the response streamed as it’s generated. Setting Value Model ID twelvelabs.pegasus-1-5-v1:0 AWS Region US West (Oregon), us-west-2 Inference On-demand APIs InvokeModel , InvokeModelWithResponseStream Each request runs in one of two analysis modes, chosen with the analysisMode field: Analysis mode analysisMode You send You get back General general (default) A text prompt in inputPrompt A text answer in message , or JSON when you supply a schema Time-based metadata time_based_metadata Segment definitions in responseFormat A segments list with start and end times and the fields you asked for You can point the model at video in two ways. An S3 location ( s3Location ) takes the object’s uri and the bucketOwner account ID, and suits long-form video. A base64 string ( base64String ) embeds the video in the request body, up to 25 MB, and suits short clips. To track cost by application, create an application inference profile from the Pegasus 1.5 model, tag it, and call it by its Amazon Resource Name (ARN) in place of the model ID. Getting started with Pegasus 1.5 The following section outlines how to get started with Pegasus 1.5. Prerequisites Before you begin, make sure you have: An active AWS account with Amazon Bedrock access. Python 3.10 or later, with the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) installed. AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions for bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream . Model access enabled for TwelveLabs Pegasus 1.5 in the Amazon Bedrock console . Videos stored in an Amazon S3 bucket, or short clips you can send inline. The following policy grants both invoke actions on Pegasus 1.5. { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "bedrock:InvokeModel", "bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream" ], "Resource": [ "arn:aws:bedrock:us-west-2::foundation-model/twelvelabs.pegasus-1-5-v1:0" ] } ] } Boto3 signs requests with your usual AWS credentials. You can also authenticate with an Amazon Bedrock API key by setting it in the AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK environment variable. For production, prefer a short-term key generated from your IAM credentials with the aws-bedrock-token-generator package, because it expires automatically. Bearer-token authentication also requires the bedrock:CallWithBearerToken permission. Send your first request Install Boto3: pip install boto3 The following example analyzes a video stored in Amazon S3 in general mode. This example uses the global Cross Region Inference (CRIS) endpoint. To target the US geographic endpoint instead, replace “global.” with “us.” in the endpoint URL. import boto3 import json from botocore.config import Config AWS_REGION = "us-west-2" MODEL_ID = "global.twelvelabs.pegasus-1-5-v1:0" bedrock_runtime = boto3.client( service_name="bedrock-runtime", region_name=AWS_REGION, config=Config( # keep a longer read_timeout for lengthier invocations such as video segmentation read_timeout=900, retries={"max_attempts": 0}, connect_timeout=10, ), ) # Analyze a video stored in Amazon S3 payload = { "inputPrompt": "Summarize this video and identify the key topics discussed.", "mediaSource": { "s3Location": { "uri": "s3://amzn-s3-demo-pegasus-15/your-video.mp4", "bucketOwner": "your-account-id" } }, "temperature": 0.2, "maxOutputTokens": 4096, "includeMetering": True } response = bedrock_runtime.invoke_model( modelId=MODEL_ID, body=json.dumps(payload) ) result = json.loads(response["body"].read()) print(result["message"]) The response carries the answer in message , the token counts in input_tokens and output_tokens , and the reason generation ended in stopReason . A stopReason of length means the answer reached maxOutputTokens before it finished, so check it before you rely on the output: if result["stopReason"] == "length": print("The answer was cut off. Raise maxOutputTokens and try again.") print("Tokens in:", result["input_tokens"], "out:", result["output_tokens"]) Request fields for general mode: Field Required Description inputPrompt Yes The question or instruction about the video mediaSource.s3Location.uri One video source is required S3 URI of the video mediaSource.s3Location.bucketOwner With uri AWS account ID that owns the bucket mediaSource.base64String One video source is required Base64-encoded video, up to 25 MB temperature No Randomness of the output, from 0 to 1. Default 0.2 maxOutputTokens No Maximum tokens to generate, from 512 to 98,304 responseFormat No A JSON Schema the answer must follow analysisMode No general (default) or time_based_metadata For a short clip, you can send the video inline instead of from S3: import base64 with open("your-video.mp4", "rb") as f: video_b64 = base64.b64encode(f.read()).decode("utf-8") payload["mediaSource"] = {"base64String": video_b64} response = bedrock_runtime.invoke_model(modelId=MODEL_ID, body=json.dumps(payload)) print(json.loads(response["body"].read())["message"]) Note that the preceding example uses the optional includeMetering attribute. includeMetering: True makes Pegasus 1.5 add two billing-usage fields to the non-streaming response: outputTokenCount and inputVideoSecond (the analyzed video’s duration in seconds). Stream the response For interactive applications, InvokeModelWithResponseStream returns the answer in chunks as it’s generated. Each chunk carries the next piece of text in message : response = bedrock_runtime.invoke_model_with_response_stream( modelId=MODEL_ID, body=json.dumps(payload) ) for event in response["body"]: chunk = json.loads(event["chunk"]["bytes"]) print(chunk.get("message", ""), end="", flush=True) print() Return structured JSON In general mode, you can constrain the answer to a JSON Schema so downstream code can parse it directly. Set responseFormat.type to json_schema and put the schema under jsonSchema . The answer arrives in message as a JSON string: payload = { "inputPrompt": "Analyze this video and return a structured summary.", "mediaSource": { "s3Location": { "uri": "s3://amzn-s3-demo-pegasus-15/your-video.mp4", "bucketOwner": "your-account-id" } }, "temperature": 0, "maxOutputTokens": 2048, "includeMetering": True, "responseFormat": { "type": "json_schema", "jsonSchema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "summary": {"type": "string"}, "key_scenes": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}}, "setting": {"type": "string"} }, "required": ["summary", "key_scenes", "setting"] } } } response = bedrock_runtime.invoke_model(modelId=MODEL_ID, body=json.dumps(payload)) summary = json.loads(json.loads(response["body"].read())["message"]) print(summary["summary"]) for scene in summary["key_scenes"]: print(" -", scene) Video segmentation: Turning video into structured data Time-based metadata generation is where Pegasus 1.5 differs most from earlier versions. Instead of a prompt, you send one or more segment definitions, and the model returns every segment of the video that matches each one. Set analysisMode to time_based_metadata and responseFormat.type to segment_definitions . The definitions take the place of inputPrompt , so leave that field out. Each definition has: id : a name for the definition, returned on every segment it matches. description : what a matching segment looks like. fields : the values to extract for each segment, each with a name , a type ( string , boolean , number , integer , array , or timestamp ), and a description . The following example identifies each editorial section in a news broadcast and returns a title, summary, and key topics for each one: payload = { "analysisMode": "time_based_metadata", "mediaSource": { "s3Location": { "uri": "s3://amzn-s3-demo-pegasus-15/news-broadcast.mp4", "bucketOwner": "your-account-id" } }, "responseFormat": { "type": "segment_definitions", "segmentTimeFormat": "hh:mm:ss", "segmentDefinitions": [ { "id": "editorial_section", "description": "A distinct editorial section of the broadcast, " "such as a new story, topic, or segment of the program.", "fields": [ {"name": "segment_title", "type": "string", "description": "A descriptive title"}, {"name": "summary", "type": "string", "description": "A brief summary of the segment content"}, {"name": "key_topics", "type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}, "description": "Main topics discussed"} ] } ] }, "temperature": 0, "maxOutputTokens": 32768, "includeMetering": True } response = bedrock_runtime.invoke_model( modelId=MODEL_ID, contentType="application/json", accept="application/json", body=json.dumps(payload) ) result = json.loads(response["body"].read()) for segment in result["segments"]: print(segment["start_sec"], "-", segment["end_sec"], segment["segment_title"]) print(" ", segment["summary"]) print(" topics:", ", ".join(segment["key_topics"])) The previous sample code when tested against a sports clip may produce an output like the following sample. { "segments": [ { "start_sec": "00:04:24", "end_sec": "00:05:22", "segment_title": "Substitutions and Added Time", "summary": "The referee announces three minutes of added time, and both teams make substitutions in preparation for a potential penalty shootout.", "key_topics": ["Substitutions", "Added time", "Penalty shootout preparation", "Tactical changes"] }, { "start_sec": "00:05:22", "end_sec": "00:08:57", "segment_title": "Last Gasp Attempts and Final Whistle", "summary": "The final minutes of the match see intense action from both sides, with several close calls before the referee blows the final whistle, ending the game in a 3-3 draw.", "key_topics": ["Final whistle", "Draw"] }, { "start_sec": "00:08:57", "end_sec": "00:09:29", "segment_title": "Match Conclusion and Penalty Shootout Setup", "summary": "The match concludes with a 3-3 draw, leading to a penalty shootout. Players from both teams shake hands and prepare for the decisive moments.", "key_topics": ["Match conclusion", "Penalty shootout", "Player handshakes", "Final"] } ], "definition_errors": [], "input_tokens": 249408, "output_tokens": 802, "stopReason": "stop", "finish_reason": "stop" } Each segment carries start_sec , end_sec , and the fields you defined. segmentTimeFormat controls how the times are written: seconds returns numbers you can do arithmetic on, while hh:mm:ss and hh:mm:ss.fff return readable timestamps as strings. The response also includes a definition_errors list, which is empty when every definition was processed. A single request can include multiple segment definitions, for example one for editorial sections and another for on-screen brand appearances. Pegasus 1.5 returns the matches for all of them in one segments list, and tags each segment with _definition_id so you can tell them apart. The following example adds a second definition to the previous request and groups the results: from collections import defaultdict payload["responseFormat"]["segmentDefinitions"].append({ "id": "brand_appearance", "description": "A shot where a company logo or branded product " "is clearly visible on screen.", "fields": [ {"name": "brand", "type": "string", "description": "The brand shown"}, {"name": "is_prominent", "type": "boolean", "description": "Whether the brand is the main focus of the shot"} ] }) response = bedrock_runtime.invoke_model(modelId=MODEL_ID, body=json.dumps(payload)) result = json.loads(response["body"].read()) by_definition = defaultdict(list) for segment in result["segments"]: by_definition[segment["_definition_id"]].append(segment) for definition_id, segments in by_definition.items(): print(definition_id, len(segments), "segments") Because the schema is defined once, the same definitions can be applied across an entire video library, producing consistent metadata for every asset. Multimodal prompting: Adding visual context to your queries Pegasus 1.5 introduces multimodal prompting, so you can include reference images alongside your text prompts. This is useful when you want to ask the model about specific objects, people, or scenes that are easier to show than describe. For example, you can provide a product image and ask the model to identify every moment where that product appears in a video. Or you can provide a reference image of a specific logo and ask the model to detect brand appearances and their timestamps. This capability enhances the precision of video analysis, and opens up use cases such as visual brand monitoring, product placement analysis, and image-guided content search. Reference images attach differently depending on the mode. In general mode, put them in promptV2.mediaSources , alongside the question in promptV2.inputText . In segmentation mode ( analysisMode: time_based_metadata ), attach them to the mediaSources of each segment definition inside responseFormat.segmentDefinitions . A definition can then match a visual reference as well as a text description. Each image needs a name , a media_type of image , and exactly one source: either an inline base64String or an s3Location with uri and bucketOwner . A single request can carry up to 30 reference images. A general-mode request asks the model about an object shown in a reference image. The following sample payload and response provide an example in general mode. payload = { "analysisMode": "general", "mediaSource": {"s3Location": {"uri": "s3://...", "bucketOwner": "..."}}, "promptV2": { "inputText": "Does the object in the reference image appear in this video?", "mediaSources": [ {"name": "ref1", "media_type": "image", "base64String": "..."} ] } … } { "input_tokens": 144, "output_tokens": 11, "message": "Yes, the green canoe appears in the video.", "stopReason": "stop" } In segmentation mode, the reference image lives inside the definition, so Pegasus returns only the segments where that product appears. The following sample payload and response provide an example in segmentation mode. payload = { "analysisMode": "time_based_metadata", "mediaSource": {"s3Location": {"uri": "s3://...", "bucketOwner": "..."}}, "responseFormat": { "type": "segment_definitions", "segmentTimeFormat": "hh:mm:ss", "segmentDefinitions": [ { "id": "product_appearance", "description": "A shot showing the product in the reference image", "fields": [ {"name": "what", "type": "string", "description": "what is on screen"} ], "mediaSources": [ {"name": "ref1", "media_type": "image", "s3Location": {"uri": "s3://...", "bucketOwner": "..."}} ] } ] } } { "segments": [ {"start_sec": "00:00:00", "end_sec": "00:00:02", "what": "A family of four in a green canoe, paddling on a calm river surrounded by towering red rock formations."}, {"start_sec": "00:00:09", "end_sec": "00:00:10", "what": "The family back in the canoe, paddling away from the shore, with the children smiling and enjoying the serene surroundings."} ], "definition_errors": [], "input_tokens": 4498, "output_tokens": 292, "stopReason": "stop", "finish_reason": "stop" } Monitoring usage Pegasus 1.5 publishes Amazon CloudWatch metrics in the AWS/Bedrock namespace under its model ID, including Invocations , OutputTokenCount , InvocationLatency , and InvocationClientErrors . Use them to track volume and latency. Pair them with application inference profiles when you need usage broken down by application. Use cases Pegasus 1.5 is designed for organizations that manage large volumes of long-form video: News and broadcast archives : Teams can define editorial segments, topics, and speaker changes once, then catalog years of footage that was previously searchable only by transcript keywords. Sports broadcasters and leagues : Detect plays, scoring events, and other key moments across full-length game footage, speeding up highlight production. Streaming applications : Scene-level metadata supports moment-based recommendations, contextual ad placement, and segment-level brand safety review. In each case, people remain part of the workflow. Their work shifts from finding and tagging every moment by hand to reviewing and refining the metadata generated by the model. Input requirements Pegasus 1.5 supports the following video specifications: Duration : Up to 2 hours. File size : Up to 2 GB from Amazon S3, or up to 25 MB as a base64 string. Resolution : 360×360 to 5184×2160. Aspect ratio : Between 1:1 and 2.4:1, or their inverses. Formats : FFmpeg-supported formats. title: How Deepgram optimized voice AI at scale with AWS Trainium
summary: Deepgram worked with the AWS Forward Deployed Engineering team to port its Nova-3 speech-to-text model to AWS Trainium2 for offline batch inference. This post covers porting to the AWS Neuron stack, kernel-level tuning, a data-parallel Rust runtime, and the throughput and cost results on batch transcription.
content: As voice becomes a first-class modality for AI, Deepgram’s models span speech-to-text, text-to-speech, and voice agents. They now process quadrillions of audio tokens a year for more than 200,000 developers and 1,400 organizations. Customers use them through the Deepgram API or run them in their own environments, including on Amazon SageMaker AI. For Deepgram, serving efficiency determines how much audio the system can process for a given infrastructure budget. High-volume batch workloads put heavy pressure on that budget, so the more efficiently each accelerator hour is used, the more audio Deepgram can serve on the same fleet. That made inference efficiency a natural target and Deepgram turned to AWS AI chips to improve it. They worked with AWS to bring its Nova-3 speech-to-text model to AWS Trainium2 for offline batch workloads such as contact-center analytics and medical transcription. The engagement began with Deepgram delivering Nova-3 as standard PyTorch code. Over several months, Deepgram and the AWS Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE) team ported Nova-3 to AWS Trainium2 in PyTorch reconstruction and tuned it for the new hardware. The final configuration runs eight model replicas on a single Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) trn2.3xlarge instance. On Deepgram’s offline, throughput-oriented batch workloads, that setup processed 11–70 percent more audio per dollar than the compute options Deepgram had been running. We measured this using instance pricing at the time of the evaluation. These gains help Deepgram scale efficiently, keep shipping better models, and bring them to customers at lower prices. These benefits can extend to customers who self-host Deepgram models in their own virtual private cloud (VPC) on Amazon SageMaker AI. There, Deepgram and AWS continue to improve ease of setup, reliability, and observability. In this post, we walk through the full inference optimization effort on Trainium: porting Nova-3 to the AWS Neuron software stack, the kernel-level tuning that followed, the data-parallel Rust runtime that lets Deepgram’s own model server call Trainium, and the throughput and cost results we measured on batch transcription. Optimizing Nova-3 to Trainium2 with native PyTorch Starting with standard PyTorch code, we used TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch integration of the Neuron Compiler, which supports both eager execution and torch.compile . We ran Nova-3 in eager mode on Trainium2 first and checked which operations fell back to the CPU, then compiled with torch.compile . The compiled path ran every model operation on Trainium2 with no CPU fallbacks detected. We compiled the encoder and decoder as separate static-shape graphs using torch.compile . Throughout, we checked numerical accuracy at two levels: layer-level output consistency against CPU, and the end-to-end Word Error Rate (WER), which had to stay in line with Deepgram’s reference values and target. From that working baseline, we kicked off the optimization work by replacing several layers with fused kernels from the public NKI Library (NKILib), a collection of pre-built reference kernels written with the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI). The kernels covered operations such as fused QKV projections, fused feed-forward network (FFN) layers, and depthwise 1D convolution. We optimized for throughput and, by extension, cost efficiency, targeting Deepgram’s offline inference workloads. Throughput is reported as a relative gain over a baseline configuration rather than as absolute audio processed per second, and we swept batch sizes 1–128 to find the throughput-maximizing batch size. Kernel-level tuning with Neuron Explorer and NAD Enabling kernels is only the first step of an optimization flywheel: enable an NKI kernel (custom or from NKILib), profile the workload, then either tune the existing kernel or replace it with a new one based on the profiling insights. This cycle repeats until the performance target is met. At each step, a different part of the Neuron stack accelerates the work: NKILib provides drop-in replacement kernels, Neuron Explorer is the go-to tool for profiling Neuron workloads, and the Neuron Agentic Development (NAD) toolkit speeds up profiling analysis and kernel tuning through its profiling and kernel-writing skills. In our case, the NKILib kernels got us most of the way, and profiling showed where a hand-written kernel would do better. Each time, the NAD profiling skills took us from a Neuron Explorer profile to a root cause, and the NAD kernel-writing skills helped produce the replacement kernels. Layer What we found and changed Gain FFN The reference kernel’s tiling schedule reloaded the full set of projection weights from off-chip memory for every token tile, so memory bandwidth limited throughput as the token count grew. Our hand-tuned kernel loads each weight tile once, reuses it across multiple token tiles, and pipelines weight reads with on-chip compute. 2.0x lower latency compared to the reference kernel at batch size 96 Depthwise conv1d The experimental NKILib kernel framed the operation as an implicit general matrix multiply (GEMM), which left Tensor Engine utilization low. We rewrote it as a broadcast multiply-accumulate loop on the Vector Engine, reaching full engine utilization, enough to more than offset the Vector Engine’s lower peak throughput. 1.5x speedup compared to the reference kernel at batch size 96 Conv2d The model’s conv2d layers hit a compilation bottleneck: beyond batch size 32, these layers prevented the model from compiling as a single graph. Since NKILib had no conv2d kernel, we wrote one from scratch in NKI. The kernel went through several profiler-informed iterations following the flywheel described earlier, unlocking batch sizes above 32. Up to 50x on the convolution module at batch sizes ≤32 Data-parallel runtime in Rust Each Trainium2 device features eight physical NeuronCores, exposed by default as four logical NeuronCores (LNC2). Because each Nova-3 model instance fits comfortably on a single physical core, we reduced the number of physical cores per logical core to one (LNC1). This configuration lets us host eight model replicas (DP8) per Trainium2 device. Inputs are processed concurrently while maximizing per-device throughput. The data-parallel runtime is driven by a work-stealing queue with one thread per replica. Deepgram’s production serving stack is written in Rust, so porting Nova-3 to Trainium2 required more than compiling the model: it also had to run without Python or PyTorch in the serving path. We therefore built a lightweight runtime in which Rust coordinates model replicas through a shared work-stealing queue. A C layer loads and executes ahead-of-time-compiled Neuron Executable File Format (NEFFs) directly through the Neuron Runtime API ( libnrt ). The runtime integrates directly with Deepgram’s serving architecture and reproduced the reference token sequences exactly at every tested batch size. We benchmarked it against multithreaded (MT) and multiprocessing (MP) Python data-parallel runtimes. Compared with the MP baseline, the Rust runtime removes the overhead of the Python interpreter entirely. Compared with the MT baseline, it further alleviates global interpreter lock (GIL) serialization, so dispatch calls from concurrent worker threads are no longer contended within a single process. These gains matter because Nova-3 performs a sequence of small decoder calls for each audio chunk, making host-side dispatch the bottleneck at low batch sizes. The throughput improvement is therefore largest there, and remains meaningful even at the throughput-maximizing batch size. There, the Rust runtime delivered a 7.5% throughput gain over the multiprocessing Python baseline. Figure 1: Deepgram Nova-3 on AWS Trainium2, compiled ahead of time and served from Rust Cost saving impact We measured price-performance as audio processed per dollar. On Deepgram’s offline, throughput-oriented batch workloads, the single-device Trainium2 setup (trn2.3xlarge) processed 11–70 percent more audio per dollar than the compute options Deepgram had been running. Conclusion In this post, we demonstrated how Deepgram and the AWS FDE ported the Nova-3 speech-to-text PyTorch model to Trainium hardware using TorchNeuron, which provides native PyTorch framework integration for AWS Trainium. We improved performance by replacing layers directly with pre-built kernels from NKILib. We then assessed performance using Neuron Explorer and used the Neuron Agentic Development (NAD) profiling skills to query profiling data and accelerate performance troubleshooting. Building on these insights, we adapted kernel source code using the NAD kernel-writing skills. Finally, we built a lightweight Rust data-parallel runtime for AWS Trainium, calling the Neuron Runtime API from Rust. Our setup demonstrated cost savings in offline, throughput-oriented scenarios, validating AWS Trainium as a viable and efficient option for Deepgram’s inference workloads. To try this approach on your own models, start with the AWS Neuron documentation , which covers the compiler, the runtime, and the supported frameworks. The Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) guide explains how to write the kernels described in this post, and the NKI samples repository holds the reference kernels we started from. The Neuron developer tools documentation covers the profiling and agentic tooling we used here, including Neuron Explorer and Neuron Agentic Development. For instance sizes and pricing, see Amazon EC2 Trn2 Instances . For help scoping a similar port, contact the AWS Forward Deployed Engineering.   About the authors Pierre Lienhart Pierre is a Senior Machine Learning Engineer with the AWS Forward Deployed Engineering team in London. He partners with model providers and AI companies to unlock the full potential of their inference workloads across a range of compute types, helping them serve models faster and at lower cost in production. Victor Wang Victor is a Staff Software Engineer at Deepgram and Technical Advisor to the VP of Engineering. Before joining Deepgram, Victor held multiple roles at AWS, including Sr. Solutions Architect, Technical Program Manager, Proserve Consultant, and Software Developer. His passion is learning new technologies and traveling the world, and he has flown over 2 million miles. Andre Gomes Andre is a Solutions Architect at Annapurna Labs ML, AWS, with experience helping startups run large-scale training and real-time inference. A former startup co-founder and CEO, he works with founders to scale their workloads on Trainium and Inferentia. Andre earned his PhD at UFMG, including research at the University of Cambridge, where he applied large language models and neural topic modeling to large-scale data analysis and decision making. Elyse Zhang Elyse is a Senior GenAI Strategist in AWS, where she helps enterprise and startup customers with their model customization journey. She focuses on translating business requirements into effective customization strategies across industries. Haotian An Haotian is a Machine Learning Engineer with the AWS Forward Deployed Engineering team, where he specializes in customizing foundation models and optimizing inference at scale. He works closely with customers to adapt generative AI to their specific use cases, helping them unlock new capabilities and drive measurable business outcomes. Niraj Chaudhari Niraj is a Deep Learning Architect with the AWS Forward Deployed Engineering team. He works with enterprise customers to customize foundation models through supervised and reinforcement fine-tuning, build agentic systems, and optimize AI workloads. He also helps customers take generative AI applications from proof of concept to production on Amazon SageMaker AI and Amazon Bedrock. Rohit Thekkanal Rohit serves as Senior Manager, ML Engineering for Model Customization at the AWS Forward Deployed Engineering team, where he leads the development of scalable generative AI applications focused on model optimization. With nearly a decade at Amazon, he has contributed to machine learning initiatives that significantly impact Amazon’s retail catalog. Rohit holds an MBA from The University of Chicago Booth School of Business and a Master’s degree from Carnegie Mellon University.

title: Push-based KV transfer to improve TTFT and TPOT for disaggregated inference in vLLM
summary: vLLM's prefill-decode disaggregation splits LLM inference across engine instances but must transfer the KV cache between them. This post introduces a push-based NIXL connector that moves transfer coordination off the critical path, delivering up to 3x better TTFT and 30% better TPOT in benchmarks on Amazon EC2 P5en instances with AWS EFA.
content: vLLM is an open-source inference and serving engine for large language models (LLMs). LLM inference has two distinct phases: prefill, which processes the input prompt and builds the key-value (KV) cache, and decode, which uses that cache to generate output one token at a time. These phases have different compute, memory, and scaling characteristics. Prefill-decode (P-D) disaggregation runs them on separate engine instances, allowing each phase to scale and be optimized independently. This can improve resource utilization, throughput, and latency under load. However, it also requires transferring the KV cache from the prefill instance to the decode instance before token generation can begin, making efficient KV transfer critical to time-to-first-token (TTFT). One of the ways vLLM performs this transfer is through the NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library (NIXL) connector , which moves KV blocks over interconnects that support Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA), such as AWS Elastic Fabric Adapter ( AWS EFA , the low-latency RDMA network used across servers in AWS). On supported instance types , AWS EFA supports GPUDirect RDMA and Neuron Direct RDMA. NIXL can therefore transfer KV blocks directly between GPU or AWS Trainium device memory without staging through host memory. The default mode for NIXL connector is pull-based : After the prefill instance finishes computing the prompt KV cache, the router relays the source metadata, including the prefill block IDs, to the decode instance. The decode instance then allocates destination blocks, prepares the NIXL transfer, and initiates NIXL READ to pull the KV blocks from the prefill instance. Because these coordination and setup steps occur sequentially after prefill and before decoding can begin, they extend the TTFT critical path, as shown in the following timeline. Figure 1: Pull-mode KV transfer timeline, where the router relay, decode-side allocation, and NIXL READ run serially on the path to the first token This post introduces a push-based NIXL connector that moves post-prefill transfer coordination and setup off the critical path. If you run disaggregated prefill/decode inference with vLLM, push mode can improve application responsiveness by reducing TTFT and TPOT, particularly at high request rates. In our benchmark on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) P5en instances connected with EFA, push mode delivered up to 3x better TTFT and up to 30 percent better time-per-output-token (TPOT) compared to pull mode (see the Performance data section) for the Qwen3-32B model. Results depend on workload and configuration. We built and validated the feature on AWS Trainium instance clusters connected with EFA, and then we contributed it to vLLM as an accelerator-agnostic feature. The results here are from an Amazon EC2 P5en (GPU) cluster with EFA, showing the gains carry over to GPUs. This post explains the push-based architecture, transfer flow, threading model, performance results, and how to reproduce the benchmark. Push-based KV transfer This section explains the push-based design: its architecture, the transfer protocol, and the threading model that keeps KV transfer off the critical path. Architecture overview Push-based transfer improves TTFT and decode throughput for two reasons: It removes the serialization of the pull model by overlapping producer and consumer work. The decode instance registers its target blocks in advance while the producer is still computing KV. The transfer then begins as soon as the producer’s blocks are ready, rather than after a consumer-side ID-discovery round trip, removing that round trip from the path to first token. It moves the transfer-setup time off the decode instance. That setup runs on the prefill side and on a background thread. It prepares the NIXL descriptors and submits the transfer, so the decode instance does not spend those cycles during its latency-critical token-generation phase. The net effect is lower TTFT and higher output-token throughput on the decode instance. The push connector coordinates three actors: the decode instance registers its target blocks up front, the prefill instance matches each request and issues the transfer, and a dedicated background thread carries the KV write off the engine’s forward-pass loop. The following diagram shows how these pieces fit together. Figure 2: Push-based KV transfer architecture, showing how the decode instance, prefill instance, and background transfer thread coordinate Implementation details The protocol has three logical steps. 1. Registration (decode side). When the decode instance allocates local blocks for a request requiring remote prefilling, it prepares a registration describing where the prefill instance should write the KV: its own identity and the block locations it has just reserved. Within the same engine step, the worker transmits this registration to the prefill instance as a NIXL notification. Because registration happens at allocation time, the connector knows the destination blocks before the prefill instance completes prefill. 2. Rendezvous (prefill side). The registration from the decoder and the completion of prefill on the producer can arrive in either order, and the connector handles both. If the registration arrives first, the producer holds it until its own prefill finishes. If prefill finishes first, the producer holds the request’s blocks until the registration arrives. Whichever event happens second triggers the transfer. The connector pairs requests by ID, and the matching accounts for reissued requests, correctly associating preempted or retried requests. 3. Transfer (prefill side). Once a request is matched, the producer establishes a connection to the decode instance (if one does not already exist) and issues an NIXL WRITE that copies the KV blocks directly into the decoder’s registered memory, addressing each destination tensor-parallel rank. The producer and consumer may use different internal block layouts. Each side maps block locations to its own physical layout at transfer time, allowing different block sizes on each side. Each WRITE carries a completion notification that NIXL delivers to the decode instance once the data arrives. The decoder counts these notifications, one per producer rank that writes into it. It treats the KV as received only after all expected notifications have arrived, at which point the request proceeds to decode. Threading model The push connector separates model execution from KV-transfer preparation by using a dedicated background transfer thread on each prefill worker. At the start of a request, the decode main loop allocates its destination KV blocks and registers them with the prefill instance while the prefill main loop computes the prompt KV cache. After both the destination registration and prompt KV are ready, the prefill main loop hands the KV blocks to the background thread and quickly returns to model execution. The background thread establishes or reuses the NIXL connection, maps the request’s KV block IDs to memory descriptors, merges contiguous blocks into larger transfer regions, and submits the NIXL WRITE to the decode instance. When NIXL completes the transfer, it sends a completion notification to the decode instance, which then begins token generation. Keeping descriptor preparation and transfer submission off the latency-critical main loops prevents this per-request work from delaying model execution. The following diagram shows these main-loop and background-thread handoffs for a single request. Figure 3: Main-loop and background-thread handoffs for a single request in the push-based threading model Timing comparison of pull and push The following diagram summarizes the pull and push transfer flows described in the preceding sections and highlights their effect on TTFT. Although both modes use the same NIXL and EFA/RDMA data path, pull performs the metadata relay and decode-side setup after prefill, while push overlaps decode-side setup with prefill. As a result, push removes these operations from the post-prefill critical path, allowing decoding to begin sooner. Figure 4: Pull and push transfer flows compared, highlighting how push overlaps decode-side setup with prefill The two modes also involve a routing tradeoff. Pull mode allows the router to select a decode instance after prefill completes, which provides greater flexibility for load-aware routing and quality-of-service management. Push mode selects the decode instance earlier so that destination setup can overlap with prefill. In return, under comparable load, the prefill instance can release its KV blocks sooner because the transfer starts as soon as both the prompt KV and destination registration are ready. Performance data For evaluation, we used Qwen3-32B model on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with EFA. To isolate P→D transfer performance, we configured the benchmark to disable prefix caching with --no-enable-prefix-caching . This configuration makes the decode node retrieve the full KV cache from the prefill node for every request. Otherwise, overlapping prompts could reuse the decode node’s local cache and bypass the transfer, which would produce misleading comparison results. The following chart compares TTFT for push and pull KV transfer. We sweep input lengths 1k–16k and request rates of 1–8 queries per second (QPS). At low load and short prompts, the two modes perform almost identically. As QPS and input length grow, pull mode degrades sharply, reaching about 1,744 ms at 8 QPS and 16k. Push mode stays far lower at roughly 540 ms, around 3x reduction. The gap opens because pull mode posts NIXL descriptors inline on the decode worker, synchronously within its engine loop, so that work stalls token generation. Push mode moves it to a background thread, off the critical path. Figure 5: TTFT for push compared to pull KV transfer across input lengths and request rates (1P1D topology, 128 output tokens, prefix caching disabled on the decode node) This chart shows TPOT under the same conditions. The pattern mirrors TTFT. At light load, push and pull are close, around 5.6–5.8 ms. As load and input length rise, pull climbs to about 10.4 ms at 4–8 QPS and 16k, while push holds near 7 ms. The reason is that push offloads descriptor preparation and transfer submission from the decode worker. Token generation is not starved, so per-token latency stays flat even at high concurrency and long contexts. Figure 6: TPOT for push compared to pull KV transfer across input lengths and request rates (1P1D topology, 128 output tokens, prefix caching disabled on the decode node) How to run benchmark To reproduce our 1P1D benchmark configuration, one prefill node and one decode node, using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with EFA, refer to the detailed instructions in the Reproducing our results guide. The guide covers environment setup, launching the vLLM prefill and decode servers, running the benchmark, and collecting results. The feature can run on other supported configurations, but performance results will vary depending on the hardware, model, workload, and network configuration. Conclusion In this post, we showed how the push-based KV connector overlaps prefill computation with decode-side block allocation and registration, removing the post-prefill router round trip and decode-side transfer setup from the critical path. This reduces TTFT and TPOT, particularly at high request rates. In our Qwen3-32B benchmark on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with EFA, push mode provided up to a 3x improvement in TTFT and 30 percent improvement in TPOT compared with pull mode. Results vary by workload and configuration. To use push mode, configure both the prefill and decode servers to use NixlPushConnector instead of NixlConnector . Choose the push-based connector when early decode node selection is acceptable and lower TTFT is the priority. The pull-based connector remains the better fit for workloads that require bidirectional KV transfer or defer decode-instance selection until after prefill for load-aware routing. vLLM supports both push- and pull-based KV connectors, so you can select the approach that best fits your deployment. As a future improvement, we are exploring bringing the background NIXL threading model to the pull-mode connector, moving NIXL setup off the critical path so that pull-mode workloads could benefit from the same optimizations. We have opened a pull request to explore this. Related resources vLLM disaggregated serving guide AWS EFA Push-mode NIXL KV connector Acknowledgments We thank the vLLM community for their support in maintaining this feature.   About the authors Sunita Nadampalli Sunita is a Principal Engineer and AI/ML expert at AWS. She leads AWS Trainium and AWS Graviton software performance optimizations for AI/ML workloads. She is passionate about open-source software development and delivering high-performance and sustainable software solutions. Nicolò Lucchesi Nicolò is a Research Engineer at Mistral, where he leads the Inference Foundation team. He is a vLLM maintainer, with a background in fast inference for LLMs and Computer Vision.

title: Improve TTFT for multi-turn agentic workloads with bi-directional KV transfer in vLLM
summary: Multi-turn agentic workloads reprocess growing conversation context each turn, driving up latency. See how bi-directional KV cache transfer lets prefill and decode nodes reuse previously computed context across turns, cutting time to first token by up to 1.6x for Qwen3-32B and 3.3x for GLM-5-FP8 on Amazon EC2 P5en instances with EFA.
content: Multi-turn agentic workloads build on accumulated context as an agent reasons, invokes tools, and incorporates earlier results. With each new turn, the client resends the conversation history, including system instructions, prior prompts, tool results, and model responses, causing the growing context to be processed repeatedly. In Prefill-decode (P-D) disaggregation , each request is split across specialized nodes: the prefill node processes the prompt and builds its key-value (KV) cache, then the decode node retrieves those KV blocks and generates the response. Conventional disaggregated serving, however, only transfers KV cache in one direction: from prefill to decode node. This one-directional flow creates two inefficiencies for multi-turn workloads. First, after generating a response, the decode node holds KV cache entries for both the prompt and the newly generated tokens. When processing the next turn, the prefill node cannot retrieve those entries, so it must recompute the KV projections for the previous response tokens. Second, the decode node maintains the session state while the prefill nodes don’t, increasing the probability of cache eviction for active sessions on the prefill nodes. On a full cache miss, the prefill node must recompute KV projections for the entire conversation history, including system instructions, prior user requests, tool results, and model-generated responses. As the conversation grows, this redundant work consumes more accelerator capacity and increases time to first token (TTFT). When you build conversational assistants and agentic applications, longer interaction histories can increase latency and consume accelerator capacity through repeated prefill computation. In this post, we show how bi-directional KV cache transfer lets prefill and decode nodes reuse previously computed context across turns, which improves accelerator utilization and helps applications sustain responsive TTFT as conversations grow. In our multi-turn benchmarks on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) P5en instances, bi-directional KV transfer reduced TTFT by up to 1.6x for Qwen3-32B and up to 3.3x for zai-org/GLM-5-FP8 (see the Performance data section). Results vary with workload and configuration. The instances are connected with AWS Elastic Fabric Adapter ( AWS EFA ), a low-latency remote direct memory access (RDMA) network used across servers in AWS. On supported instance types , AWS EFA supports GPUDirect RDMA and Neuron Direct RDMA to move KV blocks directly between GPU or AWS Trainium device memory on the prefill and decode nodes. We originally built and validated the feature on AWS Trainium instance clusters connected with EFA and contributed it to vLLM as an accelerator-agnostic capability. The results presented here are from an Amazon EC2 P5en GPU cluster with EFA, showing that the benefits also carry over to GPUs. This post explains the bi-directional KV transfer architecture, router metadata flow, KV-block retention and recompute controls, performance results, and how to reproduce the benchmark. Bi-directional KV transfer Bi-directional KV transfer is a mechanism in which a decode node returns previously computed KV to a prefill node on subsequent turns of a conversation. This avoids recomputing shared context on the prefill node and is governed by a configurable KV recompute threshold. It mitigates both computational-redundancy scenarios described earlier. To make it work, the KV must survive past the turn that produced it and travel in the reverse direction, coordinated by a KV-cache-aware router. NIXL KV connector enhancements for bi-directional transfer We extended the NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library (NIXL) KV connector to let prefill nodes consume remote KV blocks, similar to how decode nodes already consume KV blocks that the prefill node provides. This is not a trivial change, because the two node types are architecturally different: prefill nodes compute KV representations for new prompt tokens and can provide complete prompt KV blocks. Decode nodes lack the capability (or efficiency) to generate complete KV representations and can only serve previously cached KV blocks. As a result, prefill and decode nodes still carry their own roles and logic for computing the metadata of remote and local KV blocks. The actual KV transfer mechanism (a NIXL READ), however, is common to both the P->D and D->P directions. The following diagram first shows the existing flow in blue. The router sends the request to prefill node, prefill node computes the prompt KV and returns its block metadata, and the router forwards the request and metadata to decode node for the standard P→D NIXL READ. The numbered red path illustrates the bi-directional KV transfer additions: (1) decode node retains eligible KV blocks after generation, (2) returns their metadata in the streaming response, and (3) the router caches that metadata for the next prefill request. Prefill node then (4) checks the remotely reusable KV after it applies local cache matches, (5) queues an asynchronous receive when the reusable token count meets the threshold, and (6) performs a D→P NIXL READ before computing the remaining suffix. Figure 1: Standard prefill-to-decode flow (blue) and the bi-directional KV transfer additions (red) KV-cache-aware router vLLM includes connector-side support for bi-directional KV transfer, while coordinating KV reuse across conversation turns requires a KV-cache-aware router. vLLM GitHub provides an example proxy that implements the flow used in this post which can be adapted for your environment. The KV-cache-aware router is a lightweight, stateful control-plane component between the client, prefill, and decode nodes. It maintains an in-memory mapping from the client-provided conversation_id to decode’s kv_transfer_params . The router stores only block-location metadata, not KV tensors, and obtains that metadata from the response stream rather than separately querying decode node. The following diagram shows how the router manages KV metadata across conversation turns. On the first turn, the cache lookup misses and the request follows the standard P→D flow. The router then saves decode’s metadata from the response stream. On later turns, the router retrieves that metadata using the conversation_id so prefill can reuse KV from decode. It then refreshes the metadata after generation for the next turn. Figure 2: KV-cache-aware router metadata flow across conversation turns Block retention TTL Normally a decode instance frees a request’s blocks as soon as generation finishes. Under bi-directional KV transfer mode, it holds them for a configurable lifetime ( decoder_kv_blocks_ttl , default 480 seconds) and publishes their location and expiry. The conversation’s KV, both prompt prefix and generated response, then stays available for the next turn. For a turn that arrives before the time to live (TTL) expires, prefill node reuses the KV. One that arrives later falls back to normal prefill. Because this TTL is fixed and not renewed, tune it to the expected time between turns to balance KV reuse against accelerator-memory usage. A natural next improvement is to extend the heartbeat-renewed lease to the decode side. A decode instance could then reclaim blocks as soon as a conversation goes idle rather than at the end of a fixed timer. KV recompute threshold KV reuse isn’t always faster than local recomputation. For a short reusable prefix, interconnect and coordination overhead can exceed the time needed to recompute the tokens. The kv_recompute_threshold setting, which defaults to 64 tokens, controls this decision. Prefill node recomputes when the token count to compute is below the threshold and pulls KV from decode node when it is at or above the threshold. Deployments can tune this value based on model computation time, KV size, and interconnect performance. Performance data For evaluation, we used Qwen3-32B and GLM-5-FP8 models on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with EFA. To emulate scenarios in which the prefill node has evicted its local cache or the router selects a different prefill node that does not have the conversation’s KV blocks, we disabled prefix caching on prefill node with --no-enable-prefix-caching . Across both the models, turning on bi-directional KV transfer reduces prefill computation on multi-turn conversations, and the benefit typically grows with prompt length. With the feature OFF, the prefill instance recomputes the entire grown context each turn, so TTFT rises steeply. Qwen3-32B climbs from 158 ms at 2k to 778 ms at 24k, and GLM-5-FP8 from 500 ms at 2k to 2,334 ms at 20k. With it ON, the decode instance’s retained KV is reused instead of recomputed, keeping TTFT far flatter. Qwen3-32B rises only from 122 ms to 460 ms over the same range (about a 1.6x reduction at the longest prompt), while GLM-5-FP8 rises from 358 ms to 702 ms and runs up to 3.3x below the recompute path at long prompts. The prefill-duration breakdown explains why. Bi-directional transfer adds a small KV-transfer time (about 30 ms to 130 ms for Qwen3-32B; about 29 ms to 110 ms for GLM-5-FP8), but the prefill compute it removes far outweighs that KV-transfer time. As a result, the total prefill duration with transfer ON (Qwen3-32B: 128 ms to 414 ms; GLM-5-FP8: 316 ms to 541 ms) stays well below the recompute-only path (Qwen3-32B: 153 ms to 744 ms; GLM-5-FP8: 500 ms to 2,331 ms). The larger GLM-5-FP8 model shows a bigger absolute and relative gap, since its higher per-token recompute time makes KV reuse pay off even more as models and contexts scale. Qwen3-32B The following chart plots TTFT against prompt length for Qwen3-32B, comparing bi-directional KV transfer ON versus OFF. Figure 3: Qwen3-32B TTFT versus prompt length with bi-directional KV transfer on and off The next chart breaks the prefill duration for the same runs into its recompute and KV-transfer components. Figure 4: Qwen3-32B prefill duration split into recompute and KV-transfer components Together the charts show TTFT staying nearly flat with the feature ON while the OFF path climbs steeply as context grows, because the small KV-transfer time is far outweighed by the recompute it removes. zai-org/GLM-5-FP8 The same two views follow for GLM-5-FP8. The first plots TTFT against prompt length with the feature ON versus OFF. Figure 5: zai-org/GLM-5-FP8 TTFT with KV reuse on and off The second breaks the prefill duration into its recompute and KV-transfer components. Figure 6: zai-org/GLM-5-FP8 prefill duration breakdown GLM-5-FP8 shows a much larger gap than Qwen3-32B, up to about 3.3x lower TTFT at long prompts, because its higher per-token recompute time makes KV reuse pay off even more as context length grows. How to run benchmark To reproduce our 1P1D benchmark configuration, one prefill node and one decode node, using Amazon EC2 P5en instances with EFA, follow the step-by-step instructions in the Reproducing our results guide . The guide covers environment setup, launching the vLLM prefill and decode servers, running the benchmark, and collecting results. The feature can run on other supported configurations, but performance results will vary depending on the hardware, model, workload, and network configuration. Conclusion In this post, we showed how bi-directional KV cache transfer can reduce TTFT as an agent’s conversation history grows. In P-D disaggregated deployments, the feature lets prefill node reuse KV blocks retained by decode node across turns, reducing repeated computation. Configurable block-retention and recompute thresholds determine when reuse occurs. On a 1P1D deployment using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with EFA, at the longest prompt lengths tested, we observed TTFT reductions of 1.6x for Qwen3-32B and 3.3x for zai-org/GLM-5-FP8. Results depend on the workload and deployment configuration. To implement this in your environment, use vLLM v0.21.0 or later with NixlConnector, enable bidirectional_kv_xfer on both prefill and decode servers, use a kv-cache-aware router, and follow the GitHub reproduction guide . Related resources AWS EFA Prefill-Decode (P-D) disaggregated serving Benchmark KV Cache Offloading with Multi-Turn Conversations Acknowledgments We thank the vLLM community for their support in maintaining this feature. About the author Sunita Nadampalli Sunita is a Principal Engineer and AI/ML expert at AWS. She leads AWS Trainium and Graviton software performance optimizations for AI/ML workloads. She is passionate about open-source software development and delivering high-performance and sustainable software solutions.

title: NVIDIA Advances Agentic Security for Media, From European Public Service Broadcasting to Global Content Production
summary: At a creative industry event that took place today in Berlin — hosted in collaboration with Adobe, Bertelsmann, NVIDIA and UFA — the latest advancements in intelligent media were on display. Key to the news: the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) is collaborating with NVIDIA to expand its sovereign framework with cloud, open models and integration […]
content: At a creative industry event that took place today in Berlin — hosted in collaboration with Adobe , Bertelsmann , NVIDIA and UFA — the latest advancements in intelligent media were on display. Key to the news: the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) is collaborating with NVIDIA to expand its sovereign framework with cloud, open models and integration partners, while Adobe Frame.io is accelerating video agent search capabilities with NVIDIA GPUs, helping German TV and film producer UFA find the right moments faster. Read more about both announcements below. Sovereign Clouds and Open Models Built for European Broadcasters The EBU and NVIDIA are expanding the sovereign standards they introduced last year for European public service media. The initiative now brings in sovereign cloud providers, open model developers and systems integrators to define how broadcasters can deploy agents while keeping control of their data, infrastructure, models and security. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements   The EBU is the world’s leading alliance of public service media, with over 115 member organizations in more than 55 countries reaching over 1 billion people. As agents move into newsrooms, production and audience services, those broadcasters need a foundation that protects editorial independence, data sovereignty and national resilience. The expanded initiative is turning those principles into deployable services. It’ll define requirements and reference architectures for where workloads run, how data is governed, which models power services and how systems stay secure throughout their lifecycle. “These standards give EBU members a shared foundation to strengthen resilience, retain control and deliver accountable advanced services that sustain audience trust,” said Annsofi Eriksson, chief technology officer at the EBU. Cloud providers will map the standards to sovereign deployment options: Microsoft will bring expertise from Microsoft Sovereign Cloud, including Azure Local and Foundry Local, so broadcasters can process sensitive editorial material locally and keep critical services running when external connectivity is down. Nebius offers a platform for broadcasters to train, fine-tune and run their own models on European infrastructure. Open models give broadcasters the visibility to inspect, evaluate and adapt AI for local languages, archives and editorial policies. NVIDIA Nemotron open models provide a foundation broadcasters can customize for domain-specific applications and public-service requirements. “Sovereign cloud infrastructure and open models can help Europe’s public service media innovate while protecting data, editorial independence and cultural diversity,” said Delphine Ernotte, CEO of France Télévisions and president of the EBU . Media-specific consulting and systems integration provided from Qvest and other system integrators to ensure that reference architectures are practical, interoperable and deployable in real world broadcast environments. Adobe Frame.io Speeds Video Search With NVIDIA Accelerated Computing Also at the event, Adobe is highlighting its latest enhancements that help creatives search through video data faster. Adobe is using NVIDIA accelerated computing to help creative teams find and work with video content faster. Its GPU-accelerated search pipeline uses NVIDIA NVDEC for video decoding, TensorRT for optimized AI inference and the CUDA platform for preprocessing and embedding generation. Adobe is also advancing GPU-accelerated media ingest using NVIDIA NVENC and NVDEC to accelerate video encoding and decoding, helping production teams process growing media libraries more efficiently. The results: about 5x faster embedding generation, up to 4x higher throughput and up to 5x lower latency for search processing. A new two-frame-per-second proxy, about 80% smaller than the 360p version it replaces, cuts storage and transfer while keeping the visual detail search needs. That speed matters for UFA , one of Germany’s leading film and TV producers. It delivers more than 3,500 hours of programming a year, including the daily drama “Gute Zeiten, schlechte Zeiten.” When editors build a recap or flashback, they may need a specific reaction or unresolved exchange from as far back as 15 years — something file names and folders can’t surface. Frame.io semantic search finds moments inside videos by concept, action or setting, and hybrid search adds notes, transcripts and approval status. An editor can search for “a character looking concerned,” narrow by character name and filter to approved footage, then move straight into review. The work is part of a broader Adobe and NVIDIA collaboration that also spans Adobe Substance 3D, Firefly Foundry and 3D digital twin workflows for enterprises. Learn more about NVIDIA technologies for media and entertainment .   Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements

title: RTX Spark Ignites Global Celebration as New Windows PCs Arrive
summary: NVIDIA RTX Spark laptops are now available, bringing NVIDIA Blackwell RTX graphics, up to 128GB of unified memory and the full NVIDIA AI platform to slim, premium Windows PCs. content: NVIDIA RTX Spark laptops are now available, bringing NVIDIA Blackwell RTX graphics, up to 128GB of unified memory and the full NVIDIA AI platform to slim, premium Windows PCs. Starting at $2,399, laptops from ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft and MSI bring powerful local AI, content creation and gaming capabilities to a portable device, with additional systems on the way. NVIDIA celebrated the launch with events around the world, including one in Berlin, where NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang made a surprise appearance. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements   A New Generation of Windows PCs Has Arrived RTX Spark brings decades of NVIDIA accelerated computing innovation into a single superchip, combining an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU and NVIDIA Grace CPU with up to 1 petaflop of AI compute and up to 128GB of unified memory. Read more in the press release . RTX Spark Launch Celebrations Light Up Berlin The arrival of RTX Spark brought fans, creators and PC enthusiasts together in Berlin during the Festival of Lights, an annual autumn art festival that transforms the German capital’s most famous landmarks, streets and squares into glowing canvases. This year, the festival featured RTX Spark-themed lighting on the Berlin TV Tower. Berlin sparked something special, indeed. Fans gathered hours ahead in anticipation for the launch celebration at XPERION, the gaming venue inside Saturn at Alexanderplatz, where attendees got hands-on with RTX Spark laptops from leading PC makers, exploring the latest gaming experiences, content-creation workflows and local AI capabilities. Even this Geralt cosplayer waited to get his hands on RTX Spark. The celebration included a special appearance by Huang, who greeted an enthusiastic crowd, passed out popcorn and posed for selfies. He also gave out five personally signed RTX Spark laptops. You get a signed RTX Spark. You get a signed RTX Spark. Berlin held one of six RTX Spark retail launch celebrations worldwide. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements   From San Francisco to Seoul: How the World Welcomed RTX Spark A massive crowd gathered at the JD MALL Shuangjing Store in Beijing to celebrate the highly anticipated launch, enjoying a night of innovation and community connection. Crowds gathered to demo RTX Spark at the Beijing RTX Spark launch party. Attendees at Vatan Bilgisayar Topkapı in Istanbul experienced a lively event filled with interactive demonstrations and specialized programming led by local creators. Attendees witnessed local celebrities speak at the RTX Spark launch party in Istanbul. Seoul’s COEX East Lobby transformed into a bustling hub of creativity, hosting an eager crowd for engaging hands-on demos and captivating evening sessions dedicated to gaming and AI. Hands-on demos at the RTX Spark launch party in Seoul. Tech enthusiasts in San Francisco visited the local Best Buy store for an unforgettable morning of hands-on RTX Spark demos, fireside chats with local founders and a special appearance by tech influencer iJustine. Lines were long but lively at the San Francisco RTX Spark launch party. The energy at Muse Garden in Taipei was electric as the local AI community came together for a vibrant evening of music, engaging discussions and incredible product showcases. Incredible atmosphere at the Taipei RTX Spark launch party. Developers and AI enthusiasts can explore NVIDIA-tested recipes, playbooks and resources for running local AI on RTX Spark . Follow NVIDIA RTX Spark on X , Instagram , TikTok and Facebook — and stay informed by subscribing to the NVIDIA Local AI newsletter . Follow NVIDIA Workstation on LinkedIn and X . See notice regarding software product information.

content: OpenAI-compatible requests for GPT-6 models ( gpt-6-sol , gpt-6.1-sol , gpt-6-1-sol , and later gpt-5 through gpt-9 ids) send max_completion_tokens instead of max_tokens , so OpenAI and Azure no longer reject them. Azure's gpt-35-turbo keeps max_tokens The hub daemon records which client started it ( CLINE_HUB_LAUNCHER_CLIENT , CLINE_HUB_LAUNCHER_VERSION , CLINE_HUB_LAUNCHER_TRANSPORT ) and publishes that as OTel resource attributes. SSH remote hubs report the local client with transport ssh . @cline/shared adds withHubLauncherIdentity , claimHubLauncherIdentity and readHubLauncherIdentity The telemetry self-check report includes traces_exporter Refreshed the model catalog (6,952 → 7,041 models). Adds the CommandCode and Reflection providers. The Cline recommended list leads with Claude Sonnet 5.5 again, so the cline provider's bundled default goes back to Claude Sonnet 5.5 from Gemini 4 Argon. content: 2026.10.10-beta.2 Highlights Changes Fixes Workspace safety: reject a multi-file apply_patch before changing files when a later update target is missing or its context does not match, preserving the original workspace for the next attempt. Commit-time I/O failures can still leave partial effects. ( #160409 ; related #117742 and #127496 ) Thanks @masatohoshino , @obviyus , and @yetval . Tool policy: run plugin before_tool_call hooks in standalone openclaw agent exec sessions so plugin tool guards take effect. ( #159333 ; fixes #158824 ) Thanks @joseairosa and @obviyus . Buzz: reconnect when a relay closes during NIP-42 authentication without terminating the Gateway or interrupting other channels and sessions. ( #170591 ; fixes #147269 ) Thanks @masatohoshino , @obviyus , @jarvis-modern-mail , and @RomneyDa . macOS downloads: save dashboard and conversation attachments through the native Save dialog while keeping the current page open. ( #173654 ) Thanks @Patrick-Erichsen . OpenRouter onboarding: accept valid API keys with the default openrouter/auto model instead of rejecting setup with a route mismatch. ( #173292 ; related #162798 ) Thanks @chandraveshchaudhari and @obviyus . macOS setup: let fresh native profiles start the Gateway and complete automatic setup, including when supervised startup needs a retry. ( #173246 ) Gateway startup: follow a replacement model-runtime refresh instead of exiting when initial preparation is superseded. ( #173366 ; related #173357 ) Thanks @Jackten and @RomneyDa . Gateway logging: keep serving and shut down normally when a deleted temporary-directory backing path makes daily log rollover fail. ( #160433 ; fixes #130807 ) Thanks @masatohoshino , @obviyus , @WadeOwenWatts , and @Patrick-Erichsen . Gateway stability: stop session diff capture from opening live SQLite and hard-linked files, preventing SIGBUS crash loops when the shared-memory file is truncated. ( #174017 ) Native app updates: let Doctor finish agent database upgrades on native-first profiles instead of reporting success while the Gateway refuses to start on an older schema. ( #174297 ) Cron: plan history maintenance from run identities and load full payloads only for rows it updates, so large cron histories no longer exhaust the SQLite worker's memory and take channels down. ( #174530 ; fixes #174078 ) Thanks @wangmiao0668000666 , @RomneyDa , and @asikorskiy . Windows Claude CLI: stop every turn with a stored Anthropic credential from stalling until the no-output watchdog when Claude Code never reads the credential pipe. ( #174571 ; fixes #174204 ) Thanks @RomneyDa and @scalesmart . Plugins: restore the SDK facade exports that published external plugins still import, so those plugins load again. ( #173777 ; fixes #173386 ) Thanks @RomneyDa and @FtlC-ian . Chat tools: keep the chat usable after removing a tool server that failed to start, cleaning up its failed startup before reporting the launch error. ( #171397 ) Thanks @joelagnel . Updates: bound the post-activation Doctor step by the update's allowance instead of waiting indefinitely with the Gateway down. ( #173862 ) Updates: keep Gateway-managed source updates from failing with missing backup modules after the runtime is replaced. ( #173587 ) Thanks @vishnusenthil-16 . Updates: make openclaw update --no-restart honest for npm, pnpm, and bun installs, which restart themselves after the package is replaced, record the update as successful, and keep a still-serving older build unverified.
