content: 2026.10.4 Highlights The Gateway keeps running after the computer sleeps or the system clock jumps, instead of restarting itself because its ownership heartbeat looked stale. ( #170790 ) Thanks @AnvinaLI , @sgh6688 , @waynegault , and @RomneyDa . Gateway shutdown and restart no longer hang on a stalled transcript worker or in-flight session lifecycle events. ( #170493 , #170555 ) Thanks @Oldrich333 . Tlon group DMs no longer treat other participants as the owner, closing an owner-impersonation path. ( #165801 ) Thanks @eleqtrizit . Headless browser pages keep responding to clicks while a site waits for a passkey. ( #170857 ) Thanks @trukhinyuri . Manual /compact settles the active run before compacting instead of aborting it and dropping the pending request. ( #166163 ) Thanks @holny and @alexph-dev . Changes Stability patch for 2026.10.3 with no new features or configuration changes. Thanks @RomneyDa . Fixes Gateway: stays responsive during long reply-tagged streams, and long replies that quote tool-call XML no longer re-parse Markdown on every token. ( #166782 , #171573 ) Thanks @boeingchoco . Gateway: blocked durable context-engine turns are logged once instead of on every run. ( #167595 ) Thanks @jalehman . Control UI: delayed application heartbeats no longer force a reconnect. ( #171253 ) Gateway: recover state ownership after sleep and wall-clock changes, and allow openclaw gateway restart from verified external macOS terminals. ( #170790 , #170354 ) Thanks @AnvinaLI , @sgh6688 , @waynegault , and @RomneyDa . Gateway: bound transcript-worker shutdown waits and wait for session lifecycle publication during shutdown. ( #170493 , #170555 ) Thanks @Oldrich333 . Gateway: start enabled standalone plugin files with the Gateway, and keep worker heap limits enforced when the managed service sets a process-wide heap flag. ( #171330 , #166581 ) Thanks @holgergruenhagen , @valkyriweb , @xydigitLybnnnn , @goslingmanagment , @waynegault , and @obviyus . Agents: launched plugin turns no longer fail with writer-claim errors, and Claude CLI sessions no longer fork history across message routes. ( #170077 , #167241 ) Thanks @cmatrx0 . Agents: manual compaction settles the active run instead of aborting it. ( #166163 ) Thanks @holny and @alexph-dev . OpenAI: tool turns for reasoning models on api.openai.com Completions routes no longer fail with a 400. ( #166182 ) Thanks @obviyus and @AsTutoAI . Updates: agent databases are no longer flagged as changed during snapshot capture, the success summary stops repeating settled plugin data/settings upgrades as pending, and metadata inventory keeps running under progress-output backpressure. ( #170351 , #170413 , #168493 ) Thanks @DonnieFi , @RomneyDa , and @vincentkoc . Updates: slow host admission no longer holds the database writer and disrupts Gateway work, progress keeps reporting through temporary Doctor maintenance, snapshot failures get an accurate headline and recovery advice, and Linux updates can clean up abandoned runtime directories under protected systemd user managers. ( #171493 , #171454 , #171457 , #171488 , #170783 , #166335 ) Thanks @RomneyDa , @DonnieFi , and @vincentkoc . Updates: candidate validation no longer amplifies private SQLite snapshots on live installs, older drivers stop reading candidate-migrated state and stale restart verdicts clear, and optional cron inspection or snapshot cleanup failures no longer stall updates. ( #167451 , #170130 , #170754 ) Thanks @angeliti999 and @RomneyDa . Updates: openclaw update repair turns no longer time out before running tools on slower hosts; nested authority checks reuse the current state snapshot instead of copying the database again. ( #166847 ) Doctor: updates no longer refuse unreferenced retired OAuth sidecars, and offline state repair works for app-owned Gateways. ( #165420 , #170768 ) Thanks @obviyus and @RomneyDa . Tailscale: an interrupted start stops its serve process, local access stays available when the tailnet denies Serve, and Doctor checks configured Tailscale startup prerequisites. ( #167514 , #171509 , #166947 ) Thanks @pandysp and @RomneyDa . macOS: app recovery keeps compatible newer Gateways instead of downgrading them, and repair accepts a verified LaunchAgent bootstrap that is already in progress. ( #170766 , #170740 ) Thanks @RomneyDa . Sessions: equivalent POSIX path aliases such as /tmp and /private/tmp no longer restart channels. ( #166462 ) Thanks @ericcaiwx-star . MCP: OAuth login completes when the authorization server registers loopback redirect URIs without a port. ( #170876 ) Thanks @9fw2pq8sgb-art . Browser: headless pages accept clicks while a site waits for a passkey. ( #170857 ) Thanks @trukhinyuri . Control UI: updated chats recover through the serving document. ( #168941 ) Tlon: never treat group DM authors as the owner. ( #165801 ) Thanks @eleqtrizit . Telegram: polling workers resolve in both source and package builds. ( #154286 ) Thanks @xydt-juyaohui and @markfietje . Discord: agent consults keep working after voice changes. ( #171029 ) Thanks @ericcaiwx-star and @brainmonger . Feishu: config hot-reload no longer orphans conversation bindings. ( #169226 ) Thanks @ruel225 , @junniar , and @obviyus . IRC: long non-ASCII replies are no longer lost when the server relays them. ( #159730 ) Thanks @rodricksz4h5 . Release: plugin npm publish tolerates repeated artifact pagination entries, Linux builds trigger after automatic requests with hosted-runner credentials, and ratchet checks read large Git baselines. ( #171044 , #167087 , #167237 , #164743 ) Thanks @RomneyDa and @shakkernerd . content: New Features Open /config to search preferences across categories, change supported settings immediately, and see which changes require a restart. ( #52990 , #53429 ) Send a follow-up while Codex is responding to steer it immediately. Interrupting a turn also stops active Code Mode cells and their nested tool calls. ( #51812 , #51835 ) Configure a leader key in /keymap . The default is Ctrl+X , shortcut hints stay open until you choose or cancel, and voice mute moves to F9 . ( #52273 ) Restart a managed background server from /daemon . Codex warns about work the restart could interrupt, then reconnects automatically. ( #53173 ) Codex can run independent read-only tools in parallel, including skill, memory, and conversation-history lookups. ( #52245 ) Daybreak is enabled by default for eligible accounts. codex exec can also select it with an OpenAI API key when the server offers access. ( #53701 , #53717 ) Bug Fixes Resuming a saved thread restores its permissions and network approvals, while respecting explicit overrides and current managed policy. ( #53150 , #53419 , #53424 ) The network proxy now checks permission before a DNS lookup, rejects duplicate Host headers, and prevents credential aliases from bypassing inspection hooks. ( #51650 , #52661 , #53506 ) Return to an existing side conversation with /side after switching threads. Answers to pending prompts also go back to the thread that asked. ( #52184 , #53436 ) On Windows, Ctrl+V and Shift+Insert paste text as well as images. On WSL, repeated pastes reuse the clipboard reader, and copy attempts time out instead of hanging. ( #53224 , #52967 , #53453 ) Local commands finish promptly when a child keeps an output pipe open. Remote commands preserve late-arriving output so the final poll can still collect it. ( #52652 , #53331 , #53622 ) codex exec no longer prints the same file diff again after an unrelated command. ( #53444 ) Documentation Updated the bundled OpenAI Docs guidance for migrations to the GPT-6 family, including model-specific reasoning, tool use, and data residency considerations. ( #51768 ) Clarified how the Linux sandbox uses bubblewrap for filesystem isolation and seccomp for syscall filtering. ( #52610 ) Chores Codex now uses its standard shell executor and no longer bundles a patched zsh . Configurations using the retired shell flags receive a migration notice. ( #52160 , #52213 ) Reduced Linux and macOS release package size by stripping symbols from packaged binaries while preserving them in the original build outputs. summary: What's changed Added CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG_MAX_USAGE_LIMIT_WAIT_MS so unattended retry mode ( CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG ) ends a request at a usage limit that resets too far away instead of waiting Added OpenTelemetry tracing guidance to the claude-api skill, including setting up trace destinations with the ant CLI Added the % motion to vim mode: jump to the matching bracket, alone or with d/c/y Added rows to a mod's Input : a text field of several lines in the terminal, where Enter...
content: What's changed Added CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG_MAX_USAGE_LIMIT_WAIT_MS so unattended retry mode ( CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG ) ends a request at a usage limit that resets too far away instead of waiting Added OpenTelemetry tracing guidance to the claude-api skill, including setting up trace destinations with the ant CLI Added the % motion to vim mode: jump to the matching bracket, alone or with d/c/y Added rows to a mod's Input : a text field of several lines in the terminal, where Enter submits and Shift+Enter or a backslash before Enter starts a new line Added classifier_verdict and permission_mode to OpenTelemetry tool_decision events, so auto mode classifier decisions can be told apart from permission rules Added classifier_category to OpenTelemetry tool_decision events, naming the built-in rule a classifier block matched, when OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1 Fixed quitting removing a worktree made by a WorktreeCreate hook without asking when it may hold unpushed commits Fixed the fable (and best ) model alias erroring on the Anthropic API when the newest Fable model is not available to your organization: Claude Code now retries once on the previous Fable model Fixed a misleading "Please run /login" error when a full disk keeps the login from being refreshed; the error now names the disk and says to delete files Fixed Grep and Glob reporting no matches when the search program failed unexpectedly before returning any results; they now return an error saying the search failed Fixed workflow agents sometimes skipping their step, and the run still reporting success, after reading the harness note that their task text carries no user authority Fixed artifact updates being refused where a PreToolUse hook covers Edit or Write; Claude now edits the file and then republishes instead of changing it in the publish call Fixed skills and commands with very many or very long argument names stalling for seconds when invoked; only the first 64 names, each up to 64 characters, are now filled in Fixed skills, commands and hooks using very large amounts of memory when their arguments fill many placeholders Fixed stray characters such as >0q covering the folder trust prompt, and >4m before the shell prompt at exit, in terminals built on VTE older than 0.53 such as MATE Terminal on RHEL 8 Fixed stray GOK text appearing in the prompt at startup in some versions of iTerm2 Fixed switching to a model whose name contains application-inference-profile running your awsAuthRefresh command and delaying model-switch hooks when the provider is not Bedrock Fixed sign-in refresh timeouts and unexpected sign-outs after a short command such as claude auth status or claude plugin list exited in the middle of a token refresh Fixed a tool call cut off by a message sent mid-turn during its permission check being reported to the model as rejected by the user Fixed a case where switching to a model with a smaller context window could spend usage credits on a summary by the previous model without asking first Fixed conversations being compacted over and over, on a model you didn't pick, behind an LLM gateway whose responses name a different model than the one requested Fixed vim mode sometimes staying in INSERT after Escape on a slow or busy machine Fixed Esc discarding a typed AskUserQuestion answer in vim mode: the free-text field now supports vim NORMAL mode, and Esc cancels only from NORMAL Fixed the Read tool reading binary files such as .xlsm, .parquet, .epub and .heic as text Fixed a Markdown table with only a header row drawing nothing when too wide for the terminal, including in plans on the plan approval card Fixed the /claude-api skill saying CMEK external-key endpoints aren't available on Claude Platform on AWS Fixed skills no longer being listed to the model after using /rewind Fixed the compaction row in a resumed session offering ctrl+o for history that is not loaded; it now says where the earlier messages are saved, and also shows in fullscreen Fixed the "new task? /clear to save tokens" hint coming back right after you interrupt a response Fixed the permission prompt for a plugin or skill hook's ask decision not showing which plugin or skill the hook comes from Fixed /diff not noticing a conflicted cherry-pick or revert in reftable repositories when one of its git checks timed out or failed Fixed workflow scripts asking for permission or being refused when read, edited or re-run after a Bash cd in the same session Fixed dim text on the dark ANSI theme and 16-color terminals: faint inside filled boxes, not faint under selection and search highlights, and list descriptions dimmed like other secondary text Fixed a mod's $.model.fork returning nothing-to-fork when called before the first response of a new Claude Code process had finished, as in claude -p runs and cloud sessions Fullscreen mode: Fixed /compact and auto-compact briefly freezing the UI while the visible transcript is rebuilt Self-hosted runner: Fixed sessions started from Slack being unable to find or attach a repository when managed settings restrict MCP servers; use deniedMcpServers to keep those tools off Self-hosted runner: Fixed sessions being reported as having a deleted source branch, and not retried, when an unrelated setup or session failure quoted git's missing-ref wording Self-hosted runner: Fixed the log promising a retry of a failed or declined session release for a session that is ending; repeated failures now show a count Windows: Fixed stopped background PowerShell commands missing the closing [killed] line in their output file Improved switching to a model with a smaller context window: a conversation too long for the new model is now summarized by the previous model first Improved rendering performance while a long-running subagent works: its progress trail now updates incrementally instead of being reprocessed in full on every render Improved artifacts: pages Claude writes now paint the band above a sticky header, so scrolled text no longer shows there in the mobile apps Improved mods: in VS Code and the desktop and mobile apps, a tree drawn above the question dialog can now hold Markdown and up to 48 rows; the terminal keeps 12 plain rows Changed a mod hook's .catch handler to run only when the hook throws or times out; events raised beneath the hook's own calls now skip that hook without asking its .catch Changed a mod's $.env.set to resolve with {} once the variable is set or unset, or with { deny } saying why when the write is not made [VSCode] Added LaTeX math rendering in Claude's responses, including $$ and multi-line \[ … \] blocks and inline $…$ and \(…\) math [VSCode] Added a "Get more usage" link to the usage-limit banner for Pro and Max plans in the VS Code and JetBrains panels [VSCode] Fixed a conversation that crashes or freezes the panel being reopened on every reload [VSCode] Fixed the chat panel slowing down during long thinking: it no longer re-parses the whole thinking text on every update [VSCode] Fixed diagnostics showing "[object Object]" instead of the rule code (e.g. MD013) for some language servers [VSCode] Fixed the native dictation audio module being loaded, to check microphone permission, where dictation is not offered (non-claude.ai sign-ins, remote windows)

content: 2026.10.10-beta.1 Highlights Faster, steadier Gateway: chat turns, session lists, startup, and idle Gateways do far less SQLite and main-thread work, with more database work moved onto worker threads, so busy hosts and large agent fleets stay responsive. ( #167965 , #168002 , #168093 , #169005 , #169164 , #171685 , #170151 , #169871 , #168649 , #170612 , #171371 , #171805 , #168992 , #169543 ) Thanks @obviyus , @609NFT , @Leon-SK668 , @chelsealong , @RomneyDa , and @joshavant . Updates that finish: upgrades from 2026.10.1 and earlier betas complete, busy Gateways and slow Doctor steps no longer refuse or roll back a good update, failed updates no longer leave a half-installed version, and macOS, Windows, and Bun installs recover from their platform-specific failures. ( #168849 , #172249 , #172196 , #172151 , #172247 , #171101 , #170519 , #172640 , #171936 , #170940 , #171077 , #172494 ) Thanks @RomneyDa , @homeworld520 , @Yolo521-bot , @giulianoaccorsi , @AntaresGG , @stop-time , @davidcittadini , and @SBC2016 . Restart-safe replies: interrupted and unfinished replies resume after a Gateway restart, and watched child results, queued turns, accepted agent updates, and operator tasks survive restarts instead of disappearing. ( #172234 , #172412 , #169489 , #171717 , #170697 , #170858 , #170384 , #172356 , #172023 ) Thanks @jeanmonet . Cloud sessions: move sessions between local and cloud from the session menu, organize cloud environments by repository with environment recipes and verified Node toolchains, and see snapshot progress while sessions start before the first snapshot finishes uploading. ( #171690 , #170892 , #170862 , #170796 , #170875 , #170895 , #171729 ) Local Gateway in the desktop apps: the Windows desktop app and fresh Tauri installs can run a local Gateway, fresh macOS installs start in guided dashboard setup, and first-run setup chooses inference automatically. ( #169522 , #169512 , #169568 , #169628 ) New models: Gemini 4 Argon becomes the default Gemini model alongside Gemini 3.8 Flash, Nemotron 3.5 Super VL and xAI Imagine Image 2.0 arrive, Meta models run through Muse Code, and pickers stop offering retired models. ( #171852 , #172339 , #172449 , #172445 , #170487 , #171526 , #171879 ) Thanks @nv-kasikritc , @jacobtomlinson , @JFLeonM , and @obviyus . Newer Apple platforms required: OpenClaw now requires macOS 26.2, iOS 26.2, and Safari 26.2 or newer. ( #168595 ) Changes Apple platform requirement: require macOS, iOS, and Safari 26.2 or newer for the native apps and Control UI. ( #168595 ) Cloud sessions: move sessions between local and cloud from session menus, organize cloud environments by repository, support repository environment recipes with verified Node toolchains, save suggested cloud profiles on first use, show snapshot startup progress, start sessions while the first snapshot uploads, ready workers for empty-workspace sessions, report slow dispatch phases, and keep cloud setup secrets behind scoped egress grants. ( #171690 , #170892 , #170862 , #170796 , #170875 , #170895 , #171729 , #170929 , #171749 , #171073 , #170810 ) Thanks @VACInc . Desktop apps and first run: support local Gateways in the Windows desktop app, start fresh Tauri installs with a local Gateway, start fresh macOS installs in guided dashboard setup, guide missing native permissions in chat, and choose inference automatically during first-run setup. ( #169522 , #169512 , #169568 , #169635 , #169628 ) Local setup: offer optional memory embedding setup, add managed llama.cpp OCR and vision setup, and allow non-interactive llama.cpp embedding-only setup. ( #163693 , #148193 , #170153 ) Thanks @PollyBot13 , @duyufansh2008 , and @dh-js . Bun runtime: build standalone OpenClaw executables with Bun, add an opt-in pinned Bun runtime that rejects unpinnable paths before changing anything, and start the Gateway faster on Bun. ( #172384 , #168832 , #168982 , #169543 ) Thanks @vincentkoc . Experimental PostgreSQL: add an experimental PostgreSQL engine for the Workboard store, select the shared-state engine at its owner, generate PostgreSQL DDL from canonical SQLite schemas, add PostgreSQL migrations with capability admission and exact schema-drift checks, preserve PostgreSQL stores in backups and updates, and add verified offline database port tooling. ( #169214 , #171962 , #168219 , #169933 , #172265 , #170828 , #170518 , #171368 , #171265 , #170037 , #170055 , #170059 , #171350 , #171484 , #171518 , #171795 , #172046 , #171545 ) Thanks @vincentkoc and @joshavant . Conversations: organize and archive nested conversations explicitly, choose when sessions can send and receive messages, opt in to sessions_send thread targets, run sessions in existing folders on paired devices, and snooze sessions until a custom time. ( #168076 , #162316 , #168846 , #169722 , #171255 ) Thanks @VACInc , @obviyus , and @jacobtomlinson . Session personalization: personalize session backgrounds, add per-session speech bubbles and prompt reactions, show session-specific previews for public links, and match public conversation pages to the chat design with copy buttons. ( #168301 , #168861 , #169527 , #168156 ) Thanks @vyctorbrzezowski and @VACInc . title: Meta’s Muse Spark Open now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
summary: Muse Spark Open, Meta's coding-optimized open-weight model, is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. Deploy it to a SageMaker AI endpoint in your own AWS account using SageMaker Studio or the SageMaker Python SDK, and run your first inference request.
content: Muse Spark Open, Meta’s coding-optimized open-weight model, is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart , the machine learning (ML) hub of Amazon SageMaker AI . The model was trained on real developer workflows, such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions, and it supports a context window of 1 million tokens. You can deploy it to a SageMaker AI endpoint in your own AWS account in a few steps, without managing the serving infrastructure yourself. SageMaker JumpStart offers two variants: BF16 ( Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B ) and NVFP4 quantized ( Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 ). In this post, we introduce Muse Spark Open and show you how to deploy the model with Amazon SageMaker Studio and the SageMaker Python SDK , send it a first inference request, and clean up. Overview of Muse Spark Open Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained for agentic coding workflows, with a focus on first-attempt accuracy, tool calling, and understanding of large codebases. It’s a reasoning model, and it accepts text, images, documents, audio, and audio-video as input and returns text. Muse Spark Open uses a mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture with 816 billion total parameters, of which 42 billion are active for each token. The model holds the capacity of a very large network, while the compute it spends on each token is closer to that of a much smaller dense model. Meta releases the weights under the Muse Model License, which includes the Muse Spark Usage Policy. The following table summarizes the model. Attribute Muse Spark Open Provider Meta Architecture Mixture of experts (MoE), reasoning model Parameters 816B total, 42B active Context length 1M tokens Input modalities Text, image, document, audio, audio-video Output modalities Text Variants in SageMaker JumpStart BF16 and NVFP4 License Muse Model License, including the Muse Spark Usage Policy Built for long-running coding agents Meta trained Muse Spark Open on the way developers work in real repositories: code generation, debugging, multi-file refactors, and tasks that run for a long time. With the 1 million-token context window, the model can take in a whole project, including its dependencies, legacy code, and thousands of files. You don’t need to split a task into smaller pieces to fit the context. Meta also designed Muse Spark Open as an agentic model from the start. Meta says the model plans, acts, observes the result, and corrects itself over long horizons, rather than making single tool calls. As a reasoning model, it works through a task before it acts, and the SageMaker AI endpoint returns that reasoning alongside the answer, so you can follow what an agent is doing and why. Meta trained the model to browse the web, coordinate subagents for work that can be split up, and operate computers across desktop, mobile, and browser environments. These are capabilities of the model. On SageMaker AI, your application or agent framework provides the tools, browser, and computer-use environment that the model calls. Beyond code, Meta reports that Muse Spark Open reasons across images, documents, audio, and video. Two properties of the model shape how you serve it. First, sparse activation keeps per-token compute low, but serving still requires enough GPU memory to hold all 816 billion parameters, so the instance choice comes down to memory capacity. Second, the NVFP4 variant stores weights in NVIDIA’s 4-bit floating point format, which needs roughly a quarter of the memory of the BF16 weights. On SageMaker AI, that difference decides the instance: the NVFP4 variant runs on ml.p5e.48xlarge , and the BF16 variant runs on ml.p6-b300.48xlarge . That makes NVFP4 the variant to try first when you size for cost. Evaluate it on your own workloads to confirm the quality fits your use case. With open weights on SageMaker AI, you also control the deployment. The endpoint runs in your AWS account, so your source code and prompts are processed on infrastructure that you configure and control. You can attach the endpoint to your own Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) , encrypt its storage volume with a key from AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) , and turn on network isolation for the container. You also choose the instance type and scaling limits, and you pin the model version, so the model only changes when you redeploy. Use cases You can use Muse Spark Open for a wide range of applications. Meta’s focus on coding and agentic workflows suits it to the following use cases: Coding assistants over private repositories : Answer questions about large codebases, refactor them, and debug them with the full project in context, while the code is processed on an endpoint in your account. Long-running coding agents : Run agents that plan a change, edit across multiple files, run tests in your own sandbox, and correct course based on the results. Multimodal engineering workflows : Turn screenshots, design documents, or a recorded bug report with audio and video into a reproduction plan or a draft fix. Getting started with SageMaker JumpStart You can deploy Muse Spark Open from SageMaker Studio or with the SageMaker Python SDK. Each path creates a real-time SageMaker AI endpoint in your account. Prerequisites Before you start, make sure that you have the following: An AWS account with permissions to create SageMaker AI models and endpoints. An AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) execution role for SageMaker AI. For this walkthrough, the AmazonSageMakerFullAccess managed policy is sufficient. For production, scope the role to the actions and resources that your deployment needs. For details, refer to How to use SageMaker AI execution roles . A SageMaker AI domain with access to SageMaker Studio, for the Studio path. For setup instructions, refer to Use quick setup for Amazon SageMaker AI . Service quota for the endpoint instance type: ml.p5e.48xlarge for endpoint usage for the NVFP4 variant, or ml.p6-b300.48xlarge for endpoint usage for the BF16 variant. To raise a quota, refer to Requesting a quota increase . For the SDK path: Python 3.10 or later and SageMaker Python SDK v3 ( pip install --upgrade sagemaker ). An AWS Region where Muse Spark Open is available in SageMaker JumpStart. At launch, Muse Spark Open is available in US East (N. Virginia) and US East (Ohio). To check availability in other Regions, open SageMaker JumpStart in your Region. The instances that host Muse Spark Open are multi-GPU instances, and you pay for an endpoint for as long as it runs, whether or not it serves requests. Delete the endpoint when you finish, as described in the clean-up section of this post. For rates, refer to Amazon SageMaker AI pricing . Deploy using SageMaker Studio The SageMaker Studio path suits a first evaluation: you find the model, review its license, and deploy it from one model detail card. To find Muse Spark Open in SageMaker JumpStart Open SageMaker Studio. In the navigation pane, choose JumpStart . In the search box, enter Muse Spark Open. Choose Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B for the BF16 variant or Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 for the NVFP4 variant to open its model detail card. Figure 1 shows the model detail card, which lists the model description, license, and the Deploy option. Figure 1: The Muse Spark Open model detail card in SageMaker JumpStart To deploy the model On the model detail card, choose Deploy . Muse Spark Open is a gated model, so SageMaker Studio shows its end-user license agreement (EULA). Review the agreement and accept it to continue. For Endpoint name , keep the generated name or enter your own. For Instance type , select ml.p5e.48xlarge for NVFP4 or ml.p6-b300.48xlarge for BF16. SageMaker Studio lists only the instance types that the model supports. For Initial instance count , enter 1. (Optional) Under Advanced options , select a VPC and an AWS KMS key, or turn on network isolation. Choose Deploy . Figure 2 shows the deployment settings for the NVFP4 variant. Figure 2: Deployment settings for Muse Spark Open Deployment typically takes 15–20 minutes while SageMaker AI provisions the instance and loads the weights. When the endpoint status changes to InService , the endpoint is ready for requests, as shown in Figure 3. Figure 3: The Muse Spark Open endpoint in service Deploy using the SageMaker Python SDK SageMaker JumpStart identifies each variant by a model ID: BF16: meta-vlm-muse-spark-open-816b-a42b . NVFP4: meta-vlm-muse-spark-open-816b-a42b-nvfp4 . The following code deploys the NVFP4 variant with SageMaker Python SDK v3. You can run it in a SageMaker Studio notebook, which uses your domain’s execution role. In any other Python environment with AWS credentials, pass your SageMaker AI execution role with the role_arn parameter. Muse Spark Open is a gated model, so you must set accept_eula=True to deploy it. To pin a specific model version, add model_version to JumpStartConfig . from sagemaker.core.jumpstart.configs import JumpStartConfig from sagemaker.serve import ModelBuilder from sagemaker.train.configs import Compute # NVFP4 variant; for BF16, use "meta-vlm-muse-spark-open-816b-a42b" with ml.p6-b300.48xlarge model_id = "meta-vlm-muse-spark-open-816b-a42b-nvfp4" jumpstart_config = JumpStartConfig( model_id=model_id, accept_eula=True, # Confirms that you accept Meta's license terms ) model_builder = ModelBuilder.from_jumpstart_config( jumpstart_config=jumpstart_config, compute=Compute(instance_type="ml.p5e.48xlarge"), # role_arn=" ", # Required outside SageMaker Studio ) model = model_builder.build(model_name="muse-spark-open-nvfp4") endpoint = model_builder.deploy(endpoint_name="muse-spark-open-nvfp4") Run inference When the endpoint is in service, send it a request with the invoke method. The endpoint accepts an OpenAI-compatible chat payload with a messages list and returns a chat completion. The final answer is in message.content , the model’s reasoning is in message.reasoning_content , and usage.reasoning_tokens reports how many tokens the reasoning used. Because Muse Spark Open is a reasoning model, leave enough room in max_tokens for its reasoning and the final answer. import json payload = { "messages": [ { "role": "user", "content": "Write a Python function that validates ISO 8601 dates, and add pytest unit tests for it.", } ], "max_tokens": 4096, } response = endpoint.invoke( body=json.dumps(payload), content_type="application/json", ) result = json.loads(response.body.read().decode("utf-8")) message = result["choices"][0]["message"] print("Reasoning:", message.get("reasoning_content")) print("Answer:", message["content"]) The endpoint also supports streaming. To receive tokens as they’re generated, add "stream": true to the request body and call endpoint.invoke_with_response_stream instead of invoke . Clean up To stop incurring charges, delete the endpoint when you no longer need it. If you deployed with the SDK, delete the model, the endpoint, and the endpoint configuration: from sagemaker.core.resources import EndpointConfig endpoint_config = EndpointConfig.get(endpoint_config_name=endpoint.endpoint_name) model.delete() endpoint.delete() endpoint_config.delete() If you deployed from SageMaker Studio, delete the endpoint in the SageMaker AI console: choose Inference , then Endpoints , select the endpoint, and choose Actions , Delete . Conclusion In this post, we showed how to deploy Muse Spark Open, Meta’s coding-optimized open-weight model, from SageMaker JumpStart to an endpoint in your own AWS account. You used SageMaker Studio or the SageMaker Python SDK and sent the model a first inference request. Benchmark both variants on your own repositories before you choose an instance for production. To get started, search for Muse Spark Open in SageMaker JumpStart in SageMaker Studio. For more deployment options, such as inference components and optimized deployment configurations, refer to JumpStart foundation model usage in the Amazon SageMaker AI Developer Guide. Before you deploy, review the Muse Model License, which SageMaker JumpStart shows when you deploy the model. For help planning a production deployment, contact AWS .   About the authors Aris Tsakpinis Aris is a Senior Specialist Solutions Architect for Generative AI focusing on open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock and the broader generative AI open-source ecosystem. Alongside his professional role, he is pursuing a PhD in Machine Learning Engineering at the University of Regensburg, where his research focuses on applied natural language processing in scientific domains. Liam Neal Reilly Liam is a Software Engineer on the Amazon SageMaker JumpStart team at AWS, where he focuses on deploying and optimizing open-weight AI models. He received his undergraduate degree from the University of Massachusetts Amherst, where he researched human-robot interaction, and he continues to follow developments in robotics and world models. Outside of work, he enjoys cooking and rock climbing.

content: A new beginning for Windows PCs starts tomorrow with the launch of NVIDIA RTX Spark — one PC built for creators, gamers and AI agents. All are invited to celebrate with NVIDIA and partners at launch events around the world. Share Your Spark Every PC has a story. What was your first Windows PC, and what did it spark a love for? Join the celebration online by sharing responses with #ShareYourSpark for a chance to win an ASUS ProArt P14 RTX Spark laptop signed by NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang. See the campaign and official rules . See What Reviewers Are Saying From local AI workflows to creative apps and gaming, see what reviewers are saying about RTX Spark — then experience it at a launch celebration. “The fact that NVIDIA, Microsoft and their partners have delivered such a capable, compatible and polished platform even in its first at-bat should put the rest of the PC industry on notice.” — Tom’s Hardware “I tested NVIDIA’s RTX Spark for gaming and local AI – the performance absolutely stunned me.” — TrustedReviews , UK “I’m very happy to report that performance is actually looking really good when it comes to AI, gaming and creative workflows.” — Microcenter “[RTX Spark] is a different species of computer that has arrived early. It is a statement of intent from NVIDIA about where computing is going — trading raw benchmarking crowns for the ability to carry a self-rewriting, fully autonomous, CUDA-accelerated digital brain in your backpack.” — Tom’s Guide “One of the most impressive parts of the launch is how many apps NVIDIA has worked with to ensure optimisation with the Spark technology.” — Creative Bloq Independent testing from Artificial Analysis offers an early look at the powerful local AI performance RTX Spark brings to a laptop. Join the Launch Celebrations On Friday, Oct. 16, get hands on with RTX Spark at launch events around the world. title: Trust in Depth: Giving agents more autonomy without losing control
summary: Enterprise leaders want AI agents to take on more work but don't fully trust them to act correctly every time. Trust in Depth is AWS's layered approach-scope, know, bound, observe, and prove-that lets agents act on their own when their actions can be verified, reserving human judgment for the decisions that need it.
content: In every conversation I have with enterprise leaders, they say the same thing. They want agents to do more, but they don’t trust them to do it right all the time. That’s fair. The same creativity and autonomy that makes agents useful makes them hard to trust. Give an agent a task and it finds its own path to finish it, picking tools and sequencing steps no developer scripted. Run the same task twice and it might take a different route each time. A test that passes today tells you little about what the agent does tomorrow. The usual answer is a person in the loop, approving everything the agent does. That works at small scale, but as agents take on more work, human approvals pile up and review fatigue sets in. People asked to check everything stop catching the things that matter. Caution becomes a bottleneck, and agents capable of far more sit idle on the valuable work that could be making more of an impact. The fix is to let the agent act on its own when its actions can be verified, and reserve human judgment for the decisions that need it. As agents take on higher stakes work, like financial transactions, a wrong action becomes increasingly harmful. Organizations need the confidence to hand an AI agent important work, knowing it will stay within the limits set, even when no one is watching. That confidence must be built. Content filtering, testing, and monitoring each serve an important purpose, but none of these capabilities alone can promise an agent will behave correctly the next time it runs. Trust comes from independent layers that reinforce one another, the same layered discipline the industry has practiced for two decades as Defense in Depth, turned to a new purpose. Where Defense in Depth limits what can go wrong, this expands what you can safely allow. AWS calls it Trust in Depth. Trust in Depth: Trust you can verify You build trust by answering a set of questions at different moments in the agent’s lifecycle: Scope, before it runs: What is this agent for, what capabilities does the job require, and what must it never do? Know, at deployment: Who authorized it, what identity does it carry, and can you account for every agent acting on your behalf? Bound, while it runs: Do its actions stay within the limits you set, and can it still do the job? Observe, after each run: Can you reconstruct what the agent did and why, and learn from it? Across these questions, some requirements can be expressed as precise rules, while others call for judgment. A company might require that only a manager can approve access, or that an employee’s sign-in must be blocked before their mailbox can be shared. Other expectations, such as keeping a friendly tone or handling a sensitive situation appropriately, depend on context and human judgment. For precisely defined rules, testing shows whether the controls work in the cases you anticipate, but an agent takes paths you didn’t. The technology that goes further is automated reasoning, the mathematical logic that checks whether a rule holds in every possible case. It can establish that a rule holds on every path covered by a precise description of the system and its assumptions, or uncover the exact case where it fails. That result is a proof, and it is only as good as the rules and assumptions behind it, which is why the hardest work comes before the agent runs. AWS has run automated reasoning in production for more than a decade , from Identity and Access Management (IAM) at more than 2.1 billion requests per second to critical systems like the AWS Nitro Hypervisor, Amazon S3 Block Public Access, and VPC Reachability Analyzer. Now we are bringing it to agents. Wherever an agent’s rules can be stated precisely, automated reasoning can check them. However, not every rule can be stated precisely. “Only a manager can approve access” can be proven. “Keep a friendly tone” cannot. Where proof does not apply, limit the agent’s access and actions, evaluate its behavior, and send genuine ambiguity to a person to apply judgment. Grant more autonomy as you establish that the relevant rules are enforced, the agent performs reliably on the task, and failures can be detected and handled. Here is what each Trust in Depth layer asks of you, and how AWS helps you answer it. Scope your agent to only what the job requires Trust begins before an agent runs, and this is where to invest the most effort. Problems caught here are cheap to fix. Scoping means deciding what work the agent owns, which tools, data, and services it may reach, the rules it must follow, and which decisions stay with a person. “Resolve the customer’s issue” says what to achieve, not how the agent may act to achieve it. The agent still needs limits on what it may see, what it may do, and when it must stop and ask. Give it only the access its job requires, and no more. Watch for capabilities no one granted on purpose, the ones bundled with a tool or a role. Grant an admin role for one task, and the agent can inherit permissions across your whole environment. Scoping starts at the build stage, with how you define the agent. Kiro , the agentic coding system, brings rigor and mature engineering practices to the build stage of agents. It turns high-level intent into structured, spec-driven requirements and uses automated reasoning to surface contradictions, ambiguities, and gaps before any code is written. Kiro also derives property-based tests that check the implementation against those requirements across a wide range of inputs, catching bugs that are hard to detect. Strands provides an open-source tool kit for defining an agent’s model, instructions, and tools, and a managed runtime for operating it. Whatever framework you choose, the responsibility to define the agent’s job and its boundaries is the same. The next step is turning those boundaries into rules you can hold the agent to. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides governance controls to scale agents safely and governs what the agent does. Using Policies in Bedrock AgentCore, you describe in plain language which tools, APIs, and data the agent may reach, and automated reasoning checks the policy for gaps, like catching a rule that grants too much access, and checks for contradictions that make a rule unable to ever be satisfied, before it takes effect. Scoping your agent is the hard part, because turning human intent into durable, enforceable policy requires precision and completeness. However, it is also the part that pays off most. Everything that builds on what you set here, and the more precise the policy, the more your agent can safely do on its own. Know every agent acting on your behalf, and under whose authority You can’t govern what you can’t see. Teams are creating agents faster than anyone can track them, and an agent no one knows about is an agent no one controls. Every agent needs its own identity, checked every time it acts. No action should be orphaned. When something goes wrong, you can tell which agent did what, and who authorized it. AWS Agent Registry provides a managed, approved catalog of the agents, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, tools, and skills across your organization. Administrators use approval workflows to gate what becomes discoverable and remove what no longer meets the bar for security, compliance, and quality. Both people and agents can find and reuse what already exists instead of rebuilding it. But a catalog only tells you what exists. Once the agents are known, AgentCore issues each agent its own identity and checks it on every request, so every action traces back to a specific agent operating under a known authority. That is how you know every agent acting on your behalf. Bound what your agent says and does, within the limits you set Setting boundaries matters because an agent can take 10 steps you approved and still reach an outcome no one intended. It can expose sensitive data, drift off topic, or combine permitted actions in ways your policies forbid. Limits can fail in both directions. Too loose, and the agent can do what it shouldn’t. Too tight, and it can’t do its job at all. So let the agent choose how to pursue its task but never rely on it to enforce its own limits. Those limits define the agent’s boundaries and belong in the environment around the agent, enforced deterministically and evaluated across the full sequence of actions, not one step at a time. This is where the policy you defined in Scope takes effect. Policy in AgentCore enforces it on every tool call routed through AgentCore Gateway , a secure entry point for agents, tools, and models. Because enforcement sits outside the agent’s reasoning, the same checks can hold even when the agent is buggy, manipulated, or hit with a prompt injection: it cannot turn off a control it does not run. Authority does not have to stay fixed either. Because a task’s risk changes as it proceeds, temporal policies weigh what has already happened in a session and adjust permissions as the work continues. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails governs what the agent says and is told. It filters harmful or off-topic content and redacts sensitive data. Automated Reasoning checks go further, proving a response is consistent with the policy you set, not the model’s interpretation of it. Boundaries also govern what an agent can reach in the first place: which files it can touch, which services it can call, and which credentials it can use. Strands Box , an open-source sandbox, enforces those boundaries from outside the agent’s instructions, so the agent can work with real tools and data but reach only what you allow. The same boundaries hold from a developer’s first local session through to production, so an agent can’t do in production what it couldn’t in development. Observe what your agent did, then improve it Even with scoping, identity, and boundaries in place, an agent can respond in milliseconds, with no errors and every dashboard green, and still do the wrong thing. It may have retrieved the wrong information, chosen the wrong tool, or followed a path no one expected. A healthy system is not the same as a successful task. To tell the difference, you must reconstruct what the agent actually did: the context it received, the tools it called, the policy decisions applied, and the result. Testing before deployment remains essential. Production adds evidence about behavior under real conditions and gives operators what they need to investigate, intervene, and improve. Amazon CloudWatch Omni is built for continual observation. It captures every trace and lays out each step an agent took, from model calls to tool invocations, on a timeline a team can investigate. Its built-in evaluators score agent responses for qualities standard monitoring misses, such as correctness, faithfulness, and whether the agent chose the right tool. And the traces where an agent went wrong become the dataset you test the fix against, so operating an agent and improving it draw on the same evidence. What Trust in Depth looks like in practice A manager asks a help desk agent to offboard Sam, an account manager who is leaving the company. The agent needs to remove Sam’s access, transfer his mailbox to his successor, and free up the license the company no longer needs. But Sam’s emails may also contain evidence needed for a client dispute. The wrong sequence could leave Sam with access after he leaves or put that evidence at risk. Security, messaging, legal, and finance each have requirements the agent must follow, even though no one has scripted the full workflow. Two rules govern the sequence. Sam’s sign-in must be blocked before his mailbox can be converted and shared with his successor. Before changing his email license, the agent must check for a legal hold, a requirement to preserve records for a dispute, and confirm the change keeps those records protected. Scope . Before the agent runs, the team writes these rules as policies in AgentCore. Each policy requires that the prerequisite step already succeeded for Sam’s account before the next step can run. The agent gets exactly six tools: block sign-in, check for legal holds, place a hold, convert a mailbox, give the successor access, and change a license. It gets no tool to delete the account, because the shared mailbox needs the account to survive. Know . The agent carries its own identity, so every change to Sam’s account traces back to it. Bound . The agent tries to convert Sam’s mailbox to a shared one for Priya, the successor. Policy in AgentCore, enforced at the AgentCore Gateway, blocks the call: Sam can still sign in, and converting the mailbox wouldn’t change his password, so his old credentials would still open it. The agent blocks Sam’s sign-in, then converts the mailbox and gives Priya access. Next it moves to the manager’s actual request, freeing up the license, but the gateway blocks that too, because no one has checked Legal’s hold list. The agent checks and finds that Legal requires Sam’s emails to be preserved for a client dispute. It places the hold, confirms it is in effect, then changes Sam’s license to one that supports that protection. The company can reclaim the broader license while keeping the evidence intact. Observe . Every step is recorded: what the agent tried to do, what the rules decided, the hold, and the outcome. The agent completed the task without a person approving every step. Its permissions limited what it could change, its identity made those changes traceable, and policies stopped it from acting before the required safeguards were in place. The recorded steps let the team verify that Sam’s access was blocked, his successor could use the mailbox, and the required evidence remained protected. What becomes possible when agents are trusted AWS brings these layers together so you can scope an agent to its job, know which agents are acting for you, bound what they do and say, see what they did and improve over time, and prove your rules hold wherever they can be stated precisely. No one layer earns that trust on its own. Together, they are Trust in Depth, and they are what turns a capable agent into an agent that can be trusted to do important work. You draw the lines: what an agent may do on its own, what needs a person’s approval, and when it must stop. That frees your people for what only people can do: weigh the hard calls, resolve the gray areas, and own the decisions you choose to keep in human hands. As evidence builds that an agent stays inside those lines, you can widen its responsibilities or narrow them. At AWS, we believe every organization deploying agents, on any platform, should be able to answer these four questions with evidence, and with proof wherever it applies. That is the bar AWS is building for our customers, and the one we invite the industry to hold itself to. Defense in Depth made it safe to connect systems to the world. Trust in Depth makes it safe to let agents act autonomously within it. Start with one agent, one workflow, and one boundary you can prove. Then expand as the trust is earned. To begin implementing enforceable rules, explore Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and Automated Reasoning checks in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails . About the author Shawn Bice Shawn is Vice President of AI Services at Amazon Web Services (AWS), where he leads the Automated Reasoning Group. The team’s core mission is advancing AI agent safety. Shawn drives science and product teams to bring neurosymbolic AI, which combines large language models with formal verification, into developer tooling so every builder can create trustworthy AI agents whose key behaviors are mathematically proved. Over nearly 30 years, Shawn has led security, data, and product organizations at AWS, Microsoft, and Splunk. He began his career as a U.S. Army officer in the 25th Infantry Division.

title: Open From Data Center to Desktop: NVIDIA Expands Nemotron Family With Highest Efficiency Super VL and Bolt Models
summary: NVIDIA today released Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, an open 120-billion-parameter model that delivers the fastest task completion and highest accuracy for specialized always-on agents. Joining it are two new edge models: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, optimized to balance intelligence and speed per GB for local agentic workloads, and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, optimized […]
content: NVIDIA today released Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, an open 120-billion-parameter model that delivers the fastest task completion and highest accuracy for specialized always-on agents. Joining it are two new edge models: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, optimized to balance intelligence and speed per GB for local agentic workloads, and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, optimized for intelligence per GB for fast conversational agents. Super VL and Bolt 74B-A9B are available now, with Bolt E4B coming Oct. 23. The three open models together cover the full range of agent deployments, from large enterprise servers down to edge devices and local hardware. Any organization that wants to run agents on NVIDIA infrastructure now has an open, optimized model for their tier, without having to choose between capability and deployability. Super VL and Bolt join the Nemotron family alongside Lightning and Ultra. Lightning, released in August, handles high-throughput workloads; Ultra handles the hardest reasoning tasks; and Bolt brings intelligence to the edge. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL: Frontier Accuracy at One-Fifth the Size Super VL, built in collaboration with the Nemotron Coalition , delivers leading accuracy on multimodal agentic tasks — instruction following, tool use, multistep business workflows, and visual understanding — comparable with NVIDIA’s largest reasoning model at roughly one-fifth the parameter count. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL delivers frontier-level intelligence in its class for high-volume agentic workflows. As the fastest open agentic model in its class — 5x faster than the next best — it helps enterprise agents complete high-volume tasks faster across workflows that span days or weeks. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, on Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index leadboard, achieves up to 5x faster throughput compared to other models in its class. Unlike closed frontier models, organizations can post-train Super VL on their own data, deploy it on their own infrastructure and oversee what they build. Nemotron 3.5 Bolt: Agentic Intelligence at the Edge Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is designed to run everyday agentic tasks locally on NVIDIA RTX/DGX Spark, using a native 2-bit quantization to fit in 24GB of memory and run alongside other applications. Relative to other models with a similar memory footprint, it provides a good balance of intelligence and speed: smart enough to get most jobs done, yet much faster than the smartest models.   With Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, users can delegate their projects to popular local agent harnesses — from researching the web to writing to debugging code — all without sending those workloads to the cloud. It is the #1 open model in its class on PinchBench , and the #2 open model for BrowseComp . Bolt E4B 4GB is built for physical and conversational agents on GeForce RTX, Jetson, and RTX/DGX Spark. It combines natural conversation with multi-turn agentic capabilities to power fast local voice assistants, interactive characters and embedded interfaces. Adoption of Custom Super Intelligence Dozens of organizations across industries are post-training Super VL on their own data, tools, policies and workflows to push accuracy higher on the specialized tasks that define their agent deployments. Super VL is being post-trained and customized by organizations across industries. Scale AI post-trained the model for Skydance’s vendor credit finance agent and for EY’s M&A due diligence agent. AfterQuery customized the model for Hebbia for credit agreement analysis. AI21 and Alice post-trained the model for cybersecurity attack resilience. Mercor post-trained the model on APEX-SWE coding benchmark, for coding agents that plan, write and debug code. ModelScope enables developers to fine-tune the model through its ms-swift framework for specialized multimodal applications. Additional organizations customizing Nemotron 3.5 Super VL include Ramp for financial document intelligence; Dream , sovereign AI-powered cybersecurity research and vulnerability analysis; Lila Sciences for scientific discovery and search, and R1 for medical claims analysis and revenue cycle management. TrainLoop post-trained the model with dermatology data from Nolla, which just became the first company approved for AI to write initial patient prescriptions. Software platform companies integrating Nemotron 3.5 Super VL include: Atlassian , for tasks like agentic search across apps such as Jira and Confluence. CrowdStrike , which is customizing the model for agentic blue teaming in enterprise security. Dassault Systèmes , powering engineering design and simulation. Perplexity , for search and agentic tasks in Perplexity Search and Computer. Salesforce , which is customizing Nemotron to power AI agents that digitize and automate complex government workflows in secure customer environments through Missionforce Operations. Synopsys software for semiconductor design verification interoperates with the model. What Nemotron 3.5 Super VL Actually Sees Nemotron 3.5 Super VL’s vision language strengths are targeted at what agents encounter in practice: optical character recognition, tables, charts and structured information in visual documents. It processes a web page, extracts text, reads graphs and charts, and returns insights from what it finds. The same applies to PDFs and other documents agents commonly work with. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL understands images, webpages and PDFs and acts on that understanding. Combining text and visual understanding in one model means agents don’t need to route tasks between separate systems — context carries through as work moves from document to data to decision. Open for Maximum Control, Security, and Privacy Openness and customizability reinforce each other. The model ships with open weights, open datasets and training recipes. Control runs in two directions. Organizations can run the model wherever their security and data-residency requirements dictate. They also choose to adopt a model they can adapt, rather than one subject to a provider’s restrictions. In insurance, for example, a customized agent can scan claims for fraud markers on repeat. In financial services, an agent can review credit scores and flag activity against an organization’s own lending criteria. The model stays on premises. The data stays private. Customization is supported through NVIDIA NeMo, Python-based pipelines and open datasets. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL was trained on about 26 trillion tokens across pretraining and continued pretraining, then post-trained with roughly 3.8 million samples and reinforcement learning across dozens of environments. NVIDIA is also releasing open datasets on Hugging Face spanning agentic tool use , finance, instruction following, long context, fairness and vision-language understanding, along with the reinforcement learning environments in NeMo Gym. NVIDIA NIM packages the model as a production-ready microservice with performance-optimized, validated configurations and enterprise-grade support, refreshed every two weeks with security patches and performance improvements. And with the model running on NVIDIA Dynamo, organizations can serve up to 8x more users with 85% lower latency. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is available now on Hugging Face, Open Router, ModelScope community and as NVIDIA NIM. Runs on DGX Spark, DGX Station, and RTX Nemotron 3.5 Super VL runs across NVIDIA’s full hardware stack: on DGX Spark , DGX Station , RTX PRO and RTX systems for local intelligence at the desktop, on NVIDIA Jetson at the edge, and across data center and cloud environments. Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24G B is available now on Hugging Face, with support for llama.cpp , Ollama , LM Studio , Unsloth , Canonical and vLLM . Built for NVIDIA RTX Spark laptops arriving Oct. 16, it also runs on GeForce RTX PCs , DGX Spark , DGX Station and RTX PRO workstations . Download the open weights , explore customization resources with NVIDIA NeMo, or read the technical blog for the full architecture breakdown. Stay up to date on agents, NVIDIA Nemotron and more by subscribing to NVIDIA news , joining the community , and following NVIDIA AI on LinkedIn , Instagram , X and Facebook . Explore self-paced video tutorials and livestreams . See notice regarding software product information.

title: Dial Up the Cloud: NVIDIA DLSS 4.5 Controls Arrive on GeForce NOW
summary: Dial in the next gaming session this GFN Thursday. Then, step into the Shroud as Keen Games’ Enshrouded leaves early access with its 1.0 release, or let the bolts […]
content: Dial in the next gaming session this GFN Thursday. New NVIDIA DLSS 4.5 controls give GeForce NOW members more choice over how supported games look and perform in the cloud, even without the latest hardware. Then, step into the Shroud as Keen Games’ Enshrouded leaves early access with its 1.0 release, or let the bolts fly in Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 . Both are streaming on GeForce NOW at launch. With 10 new games joining the cloud this week, members can put the new controls to work in supported titles and keep playing across supported devices without downloads, installs or expensive hardware upgrades. Fine-Tune the Cloud With DLSS 4.5 Controls More control, more cloud power. NVIDIA DLSS 4.5 controls are now available on GeForce NOW, giving members more choice over how supported games look and perform in the cloud, even without the latest hardware. DLSS Super Resolution sharpens image quality, while Dynamic Multi Frame Generation delivers lower latency and reduces stutter for smoother streaming, and Ray Reconstruction enhances ray-traced visuals. In addition, Ultimate members streaming on GeForce RTX 5080-powered cloud rigs benefit from the maximum available options, including Dynamic Multi Frame Generation up to 4X. From James Bond’s globe-trotting missions in 007 First Light — now with path tracing support — to CONTROL Resonant ’s reality-bending Manhattan and the shadowy scares of Resident Evil Requiem , the controls help fine-tune supported games for image quality, responsiveness or a preferred balance between the two. These new settings are available in the GeForce NOW app under settings, for Windows, macOS, Chrome OS and Steam OS platforms. Members can read here for more details on using the feature with their membership tier, and more information on how to get the smoothest cloud game streaming for some games on GeForce NOW. Rise, Flameborn Enshrouded 1.0 brings the co-op survival action role-playing game out of early access and into its full release. Rise as a Flameborn, the last ember of hope of a dying race, and venture into a vast world of survival, action and role-playing, where a corrupting fog has consumed a once-beautiful kingdom. The title brings improvements to existing systems, alongside expansions in combat with nine new spells, new mage and archer skills, reworked wands and upgradeable Eternal spells and arrows. New enemy variants keep encounters fresh, while a new biome raises the player level cap to 50 and equipment cap to 55. GeForce NOW offers Enshrouded 1.0 ready to play in the cloud at launch across supported devices. Skip the 60GB local install to save precious storage space, then step into the Shroud without waiting for downloads or needing to make room for the update. Let the Bolts Fly Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 is now streaming on GeForce NOW. The brutal, fast-paced sequel to the retro first-person shooter brings more enemies, more weapons and new ways to purge. Picking up directly after the original game, a branching single-player campaign sends the fight to grimdark new worlds. Choose between the formidable Sternguard Veteran Malum Caedo and the swift Sister of Battle Nyra Veyrath, each with distinct abilities, weapons and play styles. From towering hive cities to jungle mangrove swamps, new enemy types await in every biome. GeForce NOW keeps the campaign ready in the cloud. No local rig upgrades or game installs stand between members and the fight — the Emperor’s work waits for no loading bar. In addition, members can look for the following joining the GeForce NOW library : Deep Dish Dungeon (New release on Steam , Oct. 13) Planet Zoo 2 (New release on Steam , Oct. 13) Total War: SHOGUN 2 – Complete Edition (New release on Steam , Oct. 13) Valor Mortis (New release on Steam , Oct. 13) Among the Trolls (New release on Steam , Oct. 14) over the hill (New release on Steam , Oct. 14) Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 (New release on Steam , Oct. 14) Beyond These Stars (New release on Steam and Xbox , Oct. 15), available on Game Pass Tenebris Somnia (New release on Steam , Oct. 16) The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Remastered ( Xbox ), available on Microsoft Store Also this week, the performance of DLSS 5’s 3D-Guided Neural Rendering model is improving by 2X, enabling even more gamers to enjoy DLSS 5’s transformative uplift in lighting and materials at high frame rates and settings. The new, more performant DLSS 5 model will debut in NBA 2K27 on Oct. 16 on GeForce NOW, GeForce RTX 50 Series GPUs and RTX Spark laptops. Dates listed above reflect when games are released on their respective stores. GeForce NOW availability may vary, as games are onboarded after they’re released and added throughout the week. Keep an eye on GeForce NOW channels and GFN Thursdays for availability updates to announced titles. Gamers who want to test out the new 4.5 controls and high-performance GeForce NOW cloud gaming can start with a day pass to try premium cloud gaming before committing to a membership. Better yet, the cost of the day pass can be applied toward a first monthly membership — making it easy to try GeForce RTX-powered cloud gaming with the latest releases, then level up for more. What’s on the playlist this weekend? Let us know on X or in the comments below.

content: This is a gateway-only extended-stable release, which is our current equivalent to LTS. title: NVIDIA Expands Advanced Technology Access for Europe’s Scientific Community Through Open Learning Resources, Collaborations and Compute
summary: Much of today’s scientific progress begins with computation. But turning accelerated computing’s potential into scientific progress — modeling climate systems, designing molecules, simulating materials and more — depends on more than breakthrough technology. Especially for smaller labs, early-career scientists or science-based startups, the hardest part of research can be everything that comes before the science: […]
content: Much of today’s scientific progress begins with computation. But turning accelerated computing’s potential into scientific progress — modeling climate systems, designing molecules, simulating materials and more — depends on more than breakthrough technology. Especially for smaller labs, early-career scientists or science-based startups, the hardest part of research can be everything that comes before the science: assembling tools, finding compute and building the expertise to use both. At the AI in Science Summit in Dublin today, the European Commission launched the AI in Science Enablers Initiative, a shared framework connected to RAISE — the Resource for AI Science in Europe — that brings private-sector support closer to Europe’s research community. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements NVIDIA is joining the campaign , providing: Access to accelerated tools, models and platforms Compute, cloud resources, data and scientific resources Skills, training and technical support Collaborative projects and pilots along with support for researchers and talent Support for startups and ecosystem development “Europe’s ambition in AI in science can only become reality if we bring together the strengths of our research community, industry and other partners,” Ekaterina Zaharieva, European Commissioner for Startups, Research and Innovation. “Through the AI in Science Enablers campaign, we are turning this ambition into concrete commitments that give researchers access to the tools, expertise and resources they need to innovate.” Open Models NVIDIA’s pledge begins with open source technology. NVIDIA has released more than 250 open models, 250 open datasets and over 1,400 open source software projects spanning large language models, healthcare, robotics, climate science, physical AI, autonomous vehicles and scientific research. The models and datasets are available on Hugging Face and GitHub. Building on this open ecosystem, researchers can build agentic reasoning capabilities with NVIDIA Nemotron — a family of architectures, open weights, open source models, training data and recipes — and scientific software including NVIDIA BioNeMo Agent Toolkit , NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo libraries, NVIDIA Earth-2 models and NVIDIA ALCHEMI NIM microservices to accelerate research across biology, chemistry, molecular design, weather and climate, energy, engineering, physics and material sciences. Skills and Training Building advanced intelligence capability across Europe requires knowledge that travels as freely as compute. The NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute has launched a new open source courseware hub with hands-on course materials covering accelerated computing and deep learning — freely downloadable and openly licensed, with no enrollment, fees or deadline. Modular by design, the courses can be adapted for university curricula, supercomputing center bootcamps or developer community events, and serve as a direct bridge to NVIDIA’s broader training and certification programs . Access to Compute NVIDIA is collaborating with cloud infrastructure partners and European national AI factories — including in France , Spain and Sweden — to open new routes for startups and small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to access sovereign European compute and services. The NVIDIA Inception program for startups provides access to compute resources and technical support, lowering the barrier to entry for startups seeking high-performance infrastructure and technological education. AI2F in France is the first AI factory to have collaborated with the Inception program for four months, demonstrating strong results. The BSC AI Factory ran a pilot initiative and is now rolling out its first full accelerator program, with growing interest from other European national AI factories in replicating the model in 2027. Beyond startup support, this program is designed to contribute to a broader strategic objective: building self-sustaining AI ventures in Spain and Europe. Sweden AI Factory , one of Europe’s 19 EuroHPC-funded AI factories, announced a collaboration with NVIDIA to open its infrastructure and expertise to Inception startups and SMEs enterprises across sectors including life and material sciences, autonomous systems and gaming. Finally, EuroHPC supercomputing centers such as CINECA and JSC provide academia and startups with free access to NVIDIA GPU infrastructure and services for open research. NVIDIA complements this access with office hours, bootcamps and hackathons that help researchers fine-tune models on their own datasets. As an example, NVIDIA is co-organizing an European AI hackathon this month alongside Austrian Scientific Computing , the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre , the High-Performance Computing Center Stuttgart and The Cyprus Institute, for Pharos-CY . AI Infrastructure Expansion To top it all off, NVIDIA is powering Europe’s most ambitious expansion of AI infrastructure to date, with 35 supercomputers currently in development across the continent — the largest single-year buildout of supercomputing capacity Europe has ever seen. Together, these systems will equip over 3 million researchers with next-generation infrastructure, accelerating discovery across domains from climate science and drug development to materials research and beyond. Explore NVIDIA technologies for science and open source courseware , and find hands-on training through the NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute . Follow the European Commission’s RAISE Pledging Initiative . Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements

content: Hermes Agent v0.22.2 Release Date: October 15, 2026 v0.22.1 was built from the wrong commit. It shipped unreleased gateway work, and the Microsoft Store app could stick on "Connecting." 0.22.2 is the release 0.22.1 was meant to be. Known issue: Sessions that ran under the 0.22.1 gateway can't be deleted in 0.22.2. Highlights The gateway starts after a reboot again. After a restart, Linux can hand an early PID to an unrelated process, and the gateway could mistake it for a running gateway, so a supervised gateway (systemd, launchd, Docker) refused to start. Hermes now records the boot it started in, and when it can't tell, it asks the host lock, which only a live gateway holds. ( #138594 , fixes #133744 ) Long local-model turns survive on laptops. Local requests always stream with prompt-reading progress (shown in the status line), stall timers skip time the machine was asleep, a recovered local server gets another try instead of a breaker that failed every later message, and compression no longer times out while the server is still reading a long conversation. On Windows unified-memory machines, model launch and the prompt cache are sized to free memory. ( #138560 ) Below is everything in the 0.22 release line since v0.22.0: the fixes 0.22.1 was meant to ship, plus the two above.
