title: The Nordics and NVIDIA Show What’s Possible When a Region Commits to Advanced Computing
summary: The Nordic countries have become the European leader in unicorn startup density, producing the most emerging companies valued at $1 billion or more per capita on the continent. Now, a new chapter for the region is unfolding as countries race to build one of Europe’s most consequential technology ecosystems. The many computing advancements already underway […]
content: The Nordic countries have become the European leader in unicorn startup density, producing the most emerging companies valued at $1 billion or more per capita on the continent. Now, a new chapter for the region is unfolding as countries race to build one of Europe’s most consequential technology ecosystems. The many computing advancements already underway in the Nordics, combined with the opportunity that lies ahead, signal a region moving from ambition to application. NVIDIA’s Investments in the Nordics Over the past year, NVIDIA has invested in the technology ecosystem in the Nordics, including Sweden’s leading startups Lovable and Legora.   Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements   Lovable , a Stockholm-based startup, provides a software creation platform that enables anyone to build and run software using plain language. In collaboration with NVIDIA, Lovable is optimizing inference for open models and training its models using NVIDIA Dynamo software and Nemotron tools. Legora provides an agentic operating system for legal work, supporting lawyers in research, review and drafting across complex matters. Nordics Emerge as Infrastructure Hub The foundation for establishing the Nordics as a technology powerhouse is already being built and the region holds a structural advantage: abundant renewable energy, rigorous data governance and a research tradition that bridges academia and industry. The Nordics are one of Europe’s fastest growing hubs for infrastructure. AI clouds are expanding with a projected 1 gigawatts of capacity to be deployed across the region by the end of 2027. Among these cloud providers are Bitdeer, CoreWeave , Crusoe , Hyperstack, Nscale , Verda and Volta . In Sweden, a consortium anchored by Ericsson, AstraZeneca, Saab, SEB and Wallenberg Investments, with SKF as strategic partner, launched Sferical One — a shared supercomputer running on two NVIDIA DGX SuperPODs with 16 racks of NVIDIA DGX GB300 systems and 1,152 GPUs. The consortium will build services using NVIDIA Nemotron open models, which allow researchers to customize and deploy their models in a secure environment. Nordic-Built Intelligence Some of the Nordics’ leading technology companies are now building proprietary intelligence on NVIDIA infrastructure. Spotify , which personalizes music, podcasts and audiobooks for hundreds of millions of listeners, uses NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM inference software to run AI-powered podcast recommendations faster and cheaper at scale. The deployment is a case study in inference efficiency: delivering the same recommendations to a global audience at a lower cost per query. ABB Robotics developed RobotStudio HyperReality using NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to bridge the gap between robot simulations and real-world performance. By combining NVIDIA’s advanced simulation capabilities with ABB Robotics’ virtual controller, running the same firmware as its physical robots, the solution enables engineers to train, test and validate robots virtually, while using real-world data to continuously improve the digital model. According to ABB Robotics, the solution delivers up to 99% simulation accuracy and reduces commissioning time by up to 80%. Finnish telecom company Elisa is launching a beta of Moontalk AIRI, a real-time enterprise agentic assistant that retrieves information, captures insights and documents decisions during meetings and calls. Built on NVIDIA Nemotron open models and distributed infrastructure, it uses company data and low-latency networking to deliver fast, context-aware responses. Nordic Startups Scaling on NVIDIA Sweden’s startup ecosystem raised $2.8 billion in the first half of 2026 and is projected to reach $5 billion for the year. This next generation is building fast — and on open models. Stilta is reinventing how companies protect their inventions with intellectual property. The Stockholm-based startup is post-training NVIDIA Nemotron open models to scale patent analysis from a single patent to entire portfolios — work that was previously out of reach. Nemotron gives Stilta the language model accuracy for continuous portfolio monitoring at scale, across the thousands of patents that large industrial and technology companies hold. ConfidentialMind’s SampoTron , built on NVIDIA Nemotron-3-Embed, delivers more than 20% improvement in cross-lingual retrieval accuracy across English, Finnish and Swedish. Agaton , a platform that analyzes customer conversations in real time, is using NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning to speed up Revenue Mining solution on live sales calls. By routing knowledge retrieval to Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, Agaton can cut response latency to deliver fast responses that inform customers’ buying decisions. Klang , a Swedish speech lab, fine-tuned the NVIDIA Parakeet v3 model to create Pianissimo — a Swedish transcription model that reduces errors by 75% while being 64x faster than the most accurate alternative. Built on over 50,000 hours of Swedish speech using the open source NVIDIA NeMo framework, the model is freely available on Hugging Face. Embedl , founded in Gothenburg and a member of the NVIDIA Inception program for cutting-edge startups, and Space Cargo Unlimited unveiled an onboard prototype that monitors protein crystallization, flags anomalies and recommends actions on a single NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX module, without continuous ground connectivity. Sweden AI Factory — one of Europe’s 19 EuroHPC-funded AI factories — announced a collaboration with NVIDIA to open its infrastructure and expertise to Inception startups and small- and medium-sized enterprises across industries, including life and material sciences, autonomous systems and gaming. Autonomous Machines on Nordic Roads and Factory Floors In Sweden, advanced computing is also powering vehicles on the road and machines in factories. Volvo Cars is combining its industry-leading vehicle safety systems and engineering expertise with NVIDIA Hyperion , Halos OS and Alpamayo Stack to enable future Volvo cars to safely navigate complex real-world environments from door to door. Autonomous freight company Einride is building its next-generation Einride Driver on NVIDIA Hyperion for autonomous freight trucks, using the NVIDIA Halos safety system and NVIDIA Cosmos open world models. Meanwhile, Toyota Material Handling Europe — the world’s leading forklift manufacturer — is bringing autonomous machines to factory floors. In a collaboration with NVIDIA and SoftServe, Toyota Material Handling Europe is adopting a simulation-first approach to autonomous material handling, cutting autonomous solution deployment time by up to 50% across its global engineering, manufacturing and innovation teams. Norrsken Foundation and NVIDIA are opening the Stockholm AI Lab, a physical hub for AI-native founders working on global challenges, set to open in 2027. Quantum Meets Accelerated Computing Finally, Swedish companies are advancing quantum research using NVIDIA’s quantum computing platform. Stockholm-based FirstQFM used NVIDIA accelerated computing to train a model that reduces the execution time of quantum processors by 33% without sacrificing performance. Validated on a QuantWare quantum processor unit, this model optimizes how the operations needed by quantum algorithms are turned into detailed hardware instructions, accounting for detailed updates on how the hardware is calibrated. Tune in to NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang’s GTC Berlin keynote on Wednesday, Oct. 21, at 11 a.m. CEST. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements

title: v2.1.300
summary: What's changed Added virtualText to a mod's prompt decorations: text drawn in the prompt box that never enters the draft or the submitted prompt Added cache_creation_5m_tokens and cache_creation_1h_tokens to the OpenTelemetry api_request event, splitting cache writes by lifetime Added $.ui.view({ agentId }) for mods: shows an agent's transcript in the main view when you ask, and $.ui.view({}) goes back Added a dir prop on a mod's Text for right-to-left text: on Windows and in VS Code's...
content: What's changed Added virtualText to a mod's prompt decorations: text drawn in the prompt box that never enters the draft or the submitted prompt Added cache_creation_5m_tokens and cache_creation_1h_tokens to the OpenTelemetry api_request event, splitting cache writes by lifetime Added $.ui.view({ agentId }) for mods: shows an agent's transcript in the main view when you ask, and $.ui.view({}) goes back Added a dir prop on a mod's Text for right-to-left text: on Windows and in VS Code's terminal its rows read in that direction and sit flush right Added /advisor on Claude Platform on AWS; no advisor runs until you pick one with /advisor , advisorModel or --advisor , and CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ADVISOR_TOOL=1 turns it off Added OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic-convention attributes to trace spans, such as gen_ai.provider.name , gen_ai.conversation.id , gen_ai.tool.name and error.type Added support for rewriting a workflow agent's prompt and model in the agent.spawn mod hook, which could only refuse workflow agents before Added the prompt.change mod hook, raised when the prompt box's text changes without a typed edit: a recalled history entry, a clear, an undo, or a plugin's fill Fixed cloud sessions telling Claude that an organization policy blocked a host when the session's own network settings did Fixed /autocompact warning about high token usage when you choose a smaller auto-compact window Fixed SessionEnd hooks sometimes not running when you exit while a background command is still running Fixed claude --help naming a removed tool in its description of --restricted Fixed claude agents not refreshing any pull request's status when the data for one of them came back incomplete Fixed Claude being told a background agent was lost, not resumable, after a cloud session's container was replaced, when the agent had already been resumed once Fixed subagents you had typed messages to disappearing from /tasks shortly after finishing, leaving no way back to the conversation Fixed a completed parent agent dropping off the breadcrumb (its child shown re-rooted at top level) while you were viewing the child Fixed the agents view taking a typed word such as "up", "down" or "escape" for that key when input arrived in a burst, which could move the peek mid-reply or clear a draft Fixed automatic tool search ( ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=auto ) turning off part-way through a conversation, for example while MCP servers reconnect after a resume Fixed a login refused by forceLoginOrgUUID leaving the refused organization's token stored, or live after /login Fixed the diff view in Claude Desktop and Remote Control sessions not noticing a conflicted cherry-pick or revert in reftable repositories Fixed the Artifact tool's verbose and ctrl+o line reading Artifact("(unprintable path)") while a call's input arrives; its row now shows "Waiting…" and "Running…" as Bash's does Fixed the first transcript entry written after resuming a session being lost when a crash had cut the transcript's last line short Fixed /branch dropping messages, and claude purge skipping subfolder projects, when they contain a Unicode line or paragraph separator (U+2028, U+2029) Fixed plugin WorktreeCreate and WorktreeRemove hooks not running when Claude Code starts with --worktree (not yet with --tmux ) Fixed OpenTelemetry tool_result events missing git_commit_id after git commit -q in repositories using reftable ref storage Fixed a prompt that a mod's prompt.submit hook rewrote or dropped still being recorded as typed in the OpenTelemetry user_prompt event and interaction span, and in session title requests Fixed a note meant for Claude about mod hot-reloading appearing in the transcript as if you had typed it Fixed agent hooks ignoring their model : aliases like haiku now resolve, a subagent's model no longer overrides it, and an unavailable model falls back to the caller's instead of allowing the action Fixed --worktree sessions sometimes starting from the wrong commit when a tag or branch was named like a commit ID, and their starting git status naming a branch other than the new worktree's Fixed the branch showing as ".invalid" and --worktree failing to reopen a worktree in repositories using git's reftable ref storage Fixed Claude naming files in the session scratchpad by a bare filename or relative path instead of their full path Fixed claude remote-control servers giving up on renewing their connection after a brief sign-in error, such as a locked keychain; they now retry, and warn when you need to run claude /login Fixed --worktree failing in a worktree of a bare repository when origin's default branch can't be fetched; the fallback base is now the current checkout's HEAD, not the main repository's Fixed starting Claude Code in a VS Code, Cursor or Devin Desktop integrated terminal launching the editor's command-line tool twice to check for the extension; it now launches it once Fixed a mod's prompt.edit hook not being raised for a newline entered with the chat:newline keybinding (Ctrl+J, or a rebound Enter) Fixed a conversation failing on every turn with a 400 error when the API rejected an MCP tool's input schema; Claude Code now sends that tool without parameters for the rest of the conversation Fixed resuming a headless or Agent SDK session losing the recent messages a compaction had kept, when the compaction followed a reply cut at the output token limit (compactions from this version on) Fixed Claude not being told about an MCP server's tools and instructions until its next tool call, when the server finished connecting after a compaction Fixed Remote Control sessions being marked stopped while still running, on a computer serving several sessions at once Fixed resuming a headless or Agent SDK session losing its compaction summary or bringing back pre-compaction history, when the compaction followed a retried or unfinished reply in the same turn Fixed Claude polling a background command's output file or sleeping while it runs Fixed feature flags and staged rollouts staying stale behind a TLS-inspecting proxy whose certificate is trusted only through the OS certificate store Fixed claude daemon stop --any printing "stopped" while a stuck background service kept running: it now waits, force-kills the service, and says so with exit 1 if it is still there Fixed claude daemon stop exiting with no output, and leaving sessions listed as running, when telemetry is turned off Fixed Write, Edit and NotebookEdit in Cowork cloud sessions reporting success for a path on your own computer, where the file never arrived Fixed Claude searching for deferred tools already loaded earlier in the conversation when a session resumes a history that never listed them Fixed secondary (dim) text looking the same as normal text under the dark ANSI theme and on 16-color terminals Fixed cloud sessions hanging 5 minutes per turn when the organization's policy can't be read; the turn now ends promptly and says why Fixed a cloud session sometimes running an already answered message a second time after the session restarted during a long reply Self-hosted runner: Fixed the runner and orchestrator freezing (no polls, /healthz or SIGTERM shutdown) while nobody reads their output; logs keep the latest 256 KiB and count drops (not on Windows) Improved WebFetch in Cowork cloud sessions to tell Claude that a page failed moments ago instead of fetching it again Improved mod sharing in the built-in plugin-authoring skill: Claude scans a mod's files for keys before opening them, and asks before scanning a folder outside the project Improved the note Claude 3 models get about an @-mentioned PDF, so they less often answer without reading it Improved artifact updates: Claude now applies a small change and republishes the artifact in one call, and makes larger edits and republishes within a single response Changed CLAUDE_CODE_PROVIDER_MANAGED_BY_HOST sessions to ignore CA-bundle, tool-proxy, git TLS and git config variables like SSL_CERT_FILE in settings; under Claude Desktop, only in project settings Changed exit to force-kill background commands still running 1.5 seconds after being asked to stop; in fullscreen mode they could previously be left running Changed Claude Desktop's Code tab to apply managed settings when forceLoginGatewayUrl names an Anthropic-operated gateway that serves the session's hostname; that gateway must be reachable at start Changed claude gateway to stop at start, naming the key, on a desktop: policy key that Claude Desktop cannot use from a gateway, where it earlier started with a warning Changed large requests to api.anthropic.com to use gzip compression even when telemetry is disabled; set CLAUDE_CODE_GZIP_REQUEST_BODIES=0 to turn it off Changed the claude-api skill to leave Managed Agents sessions in place unless you ask to archive or delete them Changed background sessions to resume a carried workflow through the Workflow tool's approval instead of running it from the handoff file Changed local session transcripts to also record each API request's system prompt, tools and parameters, so a transcript you choose to share can reproduce a request exactly Changed the /sandbox mode options to read "Sandbox commands" instead of "Sandbox BashTool" Changed PermissionRequest hooks in Cowork cloud sessions: a setMode update in a hook's allow is now ignored; the rest of the approval still applies Changed hooks: updatedInput from PreToolUse and PermissionRequest hooks is now validated like Claude's own input: unknown keys are dropped, and input the tool rejects denies the call Removed the --sandbox and --no-sandbox flags from claude remote-control , which had no effect; passing either now exits with an error. Set sandbox.enabled in settings to sandbox sessions [VSCode] Added the claudeCode.attachSelection setting to stop text selected in the editor from being added to your messages [VSCode] Fixed fast mode staying on after usage credits ran out, which made each request be refused and re-sent; it now turns off until you turn it back on, with an error notice [VSCode] Fixed the Thinking toggle switching to Off on models that always think; the toggle is no longer shown for those models [VSCode] Fixed "Edit prompt" on a flagged message opening the file or command menu over the restored prompt; Enter now sends it as written [VSCode] Fixed Shift+dragging a file onto the prompt on Windows inserting an unreadable /c:/… path instead of a mention relative to the working directory [VSCode] Fixed changes to VS Code's chat font size settings needing a window reload or being undone by a theme change; diffs and the plan preview now follow them too [VSCode] Fixed "Resume session" and tabs restored after a reload opening an empty new conversation instead of one that had moved into a git worktree [VSCode] Fixed ↑ then Enter on a recalled slash command running it without its arguments; the command and file menus no longer open over a recalled prompt until you edit it [VSCode] Fixed Shift+dragging a file from the Explorer or an editor tab onto the prompt inserting nothing in WSL, SSH and Dev Container windows [VSCode] Fixed Ctrl+Alt+F toggling Focus view instead of opening Find in the Explorer, other tree views, or the Debug Console on Windows and Linux [VSCode] Fixed the check for sessions open in other windows or terminals creating extra processes on macOS: it now starts /bin/ps directly instead of searching PATH for ps on every check [VSCode] Windows: Fixed a conversation showing "still open somewhere else" after a crash or power loss, when Windows had since restarted and given the old process ID to another program [Cloud sessions] Fixed "Allow for this task" missing from Cowork's approval prompts for connector tools where an organization turns off "Always allow" (regression in 2.1.292) [Cloud sessions] Fixed most commands in the / menu losing their descriptions in cloud sessions once you sent a second message [Remote Control] Fixed the diff view in Remote Control sessions on claude.ai and the desktop app showing deleted and renamed files as modified; requires Claude Code v2.1.296 or later on your machine [Claude Tag] Added support for Slack Connect channels: an Owner or Claude Tag admin can let Claude in Slack answer in channels shared with another organization; it's off by default [Claude Tag] Added a private Allow once / Deny card in Slack threads for connector actions that need your approval, so Claude asks instead of refusing; others only see that it's waiting on you [Claude Tag] Added support for Slack voice clips in Claude in Slack: Claude reads Slack's transcript of a clip when Slack has one [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude in Slack not answering another app that tags it in a thread under a message Claude itself posted to the channel [Claude Tag] Changed access bundles an admin attached to a Slack channel to keep applying once the channel becomes a Slack Connect channel, with no need to remove and re-attach them [Code Review] Fixed Code Review ignoring @claude review comments from people with write access whose GitHub organization membership is private; their comments now start a review [Code Review] Fixed Code Review's "paused for this repository" comment sending admins to Code Review settings; it now says who can fix it and links the Git providers page

title: Build self-improving document processing using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
summary: Learn how to build an agentic intelligent document processing (IDP) system using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that classifies, extracts, validates, and learns from business documents with minimal human intervention, automatically handling new document formats without manual template configuration.
content: IDC research shows that document-related challenges cost organizations $19,732 for each information worker annually and reduce productivity by 21.3 percent. Organizations receiving invoices from hundreds of suppliers often face layouts that vary by issuer and change without notice. Template-based systems require constant maintenance at this scale. Staff can spend up to 30 percent of their time on document-related tasks, and manual data entry error rates range from 1–4 percent . Conventional intelligent document processing (IDP) solutions address some of this burden, but they require extensive upfront configuration for each document format and break when layouts vary across vendors. In this post, you learn how to build an agentic IDP system using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that classifies, extracts, validates, and learns from business documents with minimal human intervention. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Your agents automatically handle new document formats, such as supplier invoices, purchase orders, insurance claims, and loan applications. By the end of this post, you can: Deploy a multi-agent IDP system, often in under 20 minutes. Process new document types without manual template configuration. Let agents train themselves on each new document format and reuse what they learn, so later documents of that type go straight to extraction without retraining. Challenges with rule-based document processing Many IDP pipelines require you to define templates, extraction rules, and validation logic for every document format upfront. When a new vendor sends a purchase order with a different layout, the pipeline breaks. This creates three core challenges: Template rigidity: Each new document format requires manual configuration, and even minor layout changes can cause extraction failures. No learning: The same extraction errors repeat across similar documents because the system doesn’t retain knowledge from previous corrections. Scaling burden: Each new vendor or document variant multiplies the maintenance effort, and organizations processing documents from hundreds of sources face ongoing operational costs. An agentic approach addresses these challenges. Instead of static templates, AI agents analyze each document, generate extraction instructions, validate results, and learn from corrections automatically. Over time, your system builds a knowledge base of document formats, so you process similar documents with minimal additional configuration. Solution overview In this solution, eight specialized agents collaborate across two graph-based workflows running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The following diagram shows the multi-agent workflow graph built using Strands Agents , an open source SDK for building AI agents. Figure 1: Multi-agent orchestration workflow graph Identification workflow : The Analyzer agent extracts text using Amazon Textract and identifies the document type and sender. The Matcher agent searches for similar documents using vector similarity in Amazon S3 Vectors , a capability of Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). Training workflow (new document types): When no match is found, the Instructions agent generates extraction prompts, the Extractor agent extracts structured data, and the Validator agent checks results against schemas and business rules in Amazon Aurora DSQL . If validation fails, the Instructions Fixer agent refines the prompts and retries. On success, the Save Instructions agent persists the instructions for reuse. Automation workflow (known document types): When a match is found, the Extractor agent uses existing instructions. If validation fails, the Troubleshooter agent fixes the extracted data directly without modifying instructions. How it works The following diagram shows the infrastructure architecture for the solution. Figure 2: Agentic IDP infrastructure architecture on AWS Business documents arrive in Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) or direct upload to Amazon S3. Amazon EventBridge triggers an AWS Lambda function that creates a tracking job in Amazon DynamoDB and invokes AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. AgentCore runtime orchestrates document processing through Strands Agents. Your agents securely access AWS resources through machine-to-machine credentials managed by AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Amazon Cognito . Your Lambda functions become agent-compatible tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) interface of AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Agents extract text using Amazon Textract, classify documents using vector embeddings in S3 Vectors, and validate data against business rules in Aurora DSQL. Agents access enterprise data through MCP servers to validate extracted content against business rules. You monitor status and troubleshoot issues through a chat-enabled dashboard hosted on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS). You gain visibility into agent performance through AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Amazon CloudWatch telemetry. Deploy the solution Follow these steps to deploy the solution infrastructure and web UI to your AWS account. Prerequisites To deploy this solution, you must have: An AWS account . Access to Amazon Bedrock with Amazon Nova and Anthropic (Claude) models enabled. For model availability by AWS Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock . Access to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (Runtime, Gateway, Identity), S3 Vectors, and Amazon Aurora DSQL in a supported Region . AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) v2 installed. Docker installed and running (required for building and deploying container images). Python 3.11+ and Node.js 18+. AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions to create S3 buckets, Lambda functions, DynamoDB tables, Cognito user pools, Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repositories, and Amazon ECS services. Clone the repository and set up the environment: git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/agenticidp-guidance.git cd agenticidp-guidance uv venv source .venv/bin/activate uv pip install -r requirements.txt cd ui/orchestrator npm install cd ../.. Deploy the stacks: uv run deploy.py --admin-email your-email@example.com This deploys six AWS CloudFormation stacks: Core (S3, Cognito, DynamoDB), Gateway (Lambda tools, AgentCore Gateway), Aurora (Amazon Aurora DSQL), Agent (AgentCore runtime, containers), UI Orchestrator (API endpoints), and Modern UI (React app on Amazon CloudFront ). Deployment takes approximately 15–20 minutes. Verify deployment by checking that each stack shows CREATE_COMPLETE in the CloudFormation console. Process files and review results After deployment, you receive an email with the CloudFront URL, username, and temporary password. Process a document Sign in to the web UI and choose Process Document . Upload a sample purchase order from infrastructure/sample_data/purchase_orders/training/ . The document enters the agent workflow: The Analyzer agent extracts text and identifies the sender and document type. The Matcher agent searches for similar documents in the vector store. For a new document type, the training workflow generates extraction instructions, extracts data, validates it, and saves the instructions for future use. For a known document type, the automation workflow extracts data using existing instructions and validates it. Review results in the Review Jobs and Instructions tab to verify extracted data, validation results, and generated instructions. Example: A new document type (training workflow) Suppose you upload the first purchase order from a new retailer, Two Wheel Store. The Matcher agent searches the vector store, finds no similar document, and routes the job through the training workflow. The Analyzer agent uses Amazon Textract to extract the raw document text: # PURCHASE ORDER FROM: Two Wheel Store Order #: PO-2026-0102-2584 Date: 2026-01-02 ## Items Ordered AC-021 Advanced Computer Qty: 1 $75.61 Colors: cr4321 @ $75.61 ... SB-004 Folding Classic Qty: 8 $9634.32 Colors: cb8901 I Sizes: S @ $1204.29 TOTAL: $14931.54 The Instructions agent generates extraction prompts from the schema, and the Extractor agent produces structured JSON: { "po_number": "PO-2026-0102-2584", "retailer_name": "Two Wheel Store", "order_date": "2026-01-02T00:00:00Z", "line_items": [ { "sku": "AC-021", "product_name": "Advanced Computer", "quantity": 1, "unit_price": 75.61, "line_total": 75.61 }, { "sku": "SB-004", "product_name": "Folding Classic", "quantity": 8, "unit_price": 1204.29, "line_total": 9634.32 } ], "order_total": 14931.54 } The Validator agent checks the result against the schema and fails : validation_status: INVALID error: 'SB-004' does not match '^AB-[A-Z]{2}-\d{3}$' The vendor’s SKU format ( SB-004 ) doesn’t match Acme Bikes’ internal format ( AB-SB-004 ). The Instructions Fixer agent diagnoses the mismatch and adds an explicit SKU transformation rule to the extraction prompt: prefix vendor SKUs with AB- . On the second pass, the seven line items validate successfully, and the Save Instructions agent persists the refined prompt to the vector store. End-to-end time for this first run: 3 minutes 49 seconds. Example: A known document type (automation workflow) When a second purchase order from Two Wheel Store arrives, the Matcher agent finds the stored instructions from the first run with a confidence score of 3.946 (threshold: 3.7) and routes the job through the automation workflow: The Extractor agent applies the stored instructions directly, so the orchestrator skips prompt generation. The SKU transformation rule learned during training applies automatically ( EL-002 → AB-EL-002 , HB-071 → AB-HB-071 , PD-002 → AB-PD-002 ). The three line items validate on the first pass with an order total of $5,979.19. End-to-end processing completes in 1 minute 30 seconds, down from 3 minutes 49 seconds on the first run. Use the interactive chat The dashboard includes a chat interface for troubleshooting: Ask what tools do you have to see available agent capabilities. Ask list instructions to view stored extraction instructions. Ask what is the status of job XXXX to check processing progress. Ask what went wrong with job XXXX, how can we update the instructions? to diagnose failures. Understand how accuracy improves over time The system improves over time through two feedback loops: Training loop : When the Instructions Fixer agent refines extraction prompts after validation failures, the improved instructions are saved and reused for similar documents. Processing loop : When the Troubleshooter agent fixes extraction errors, it provides detailed analysis that helps identify patterns in document format variations. When changing models, use AgentCore Evaluations , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to confirm that extraction quality remains acceptable. The solution already uses AgentCore Observability, so it has the required instrumentation. Estimated cost You pay only for what you use, because the solution runs on serverless and on-demand resources with no idle costs. For a workload of 10 training documents and 1,000 processed documents each month in US East (N. Virginia), the estimated cost is approximately $58 per month. Foundation model (FM) inference through Amazon Bedrock represents approximately 85 percent of the total cost, at roughly $0.055 per document. Actual cost depends largely on the models assigned to each agent. Model choices are centralized in agents/orchestratorgraph/utils/config.py , so you can use lower-cost models for simpler tasks and stronger models where needed. For detailed pricing, refer to the Amazon Bedrock pricing page. Customize the solution for your use case You get a purchase order processing use case with a synthetic bike company dataset, a pre-built JSON schema, and a validation Lambda function that checks extracted data against product and vendor records in a mock ERP database. To process your own documents, you must replace the included schemas and validation logic with your own. Define your document schema Create a JSON schema that defines the fields you want to extract for each document type. The sample purchase order schema in agents/orchestratorgraph/doc_schema/purchase_order_schema.json provides a reference. Your schema should specify field names, data types, and whether each field is explicitly stated in the document or inferred from context. Build your validation process The included validator checks purchase order data against synthetic vendor and product tables in Aurora DSQL. Your production implementation requires a validation process tailored to your business rules. For example: An invoice validator might check vendor IDs against your accounts payable system and verify line item totals match the invoice total. A contract validator might verify that the document contains required clauses and that dates and party names match your records. A claims validator might check policy numbers, coverage limits, and claimant information against your policy management system. To add a new validator, create a Lambda function that accepts extracted JSON and returns a pass/fail result with detailed error messages, then register it as a tool in AgentCore Gateway. Refer to gateway/tools/po_validator_tool/ for the implementation pattern. Update agent prompts The agent prompts in agents/orchestratorgraph/prompts/ reference purchase order terminology. Update these prompts to reflect your document types and extraction requirements. The Orchestrator agent, Validator agent, and Instructions agent each contain document-type-specific language that you should adapt. Best practices Keep these recommendations in mind as you train and operate your agentic IDP system. Start with representative samples : Upload 5–10 documents per type during training, including edge cases with format variations, to build reliable extraction instructions. Use business rule validation : Connect validators to your reference data (vendor lists, product catalogs) in Aurora DSQL to catch extraction errors early. Monitor agent performance : Use AgentCore Observability and CloudWatch to track execution paths, identify bottlenecks, and measure extraction accuracy over time. Add document types incrementally : Create a JSON schema for each new document type and a corresponding validation Lambda function. The agents handle the rest. Add guardrails for production : Apply Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to enforce content filtering and grounding checks on agent outputs. This is especially important when you process sensitive document types such as insurance claims or loan applications. Review the OWASP Top 10 for LLMs : Consult the OWASP Top 10 for LLMs and Generative AI Apps for security considerations when building applications that use large language models (LLMs). Clean up Important: Before running cleanup, export the data you want to retain. The destroy.py script permanently deletes processed documents (S3), job history (DynamoDB), validation data (Aurora DSQL), and learned extraction instructions (vector store). To avoid ongoing charges, remove the deployed resources: uv run destroy.py Verify that the six CloudFormation stacks are deleted on the console: AgenticIDP-Core-Dev, AgenticIDP-Gateway-Dev, AgenticIDP-Aurora-Dev, AgenticIDP-Agent-Dev, AgenticIDP-UIOrchestr-Dev, and AgenticIDP-ModernUI-Dev. Conclusion In this post, you learned how to build a self-improving document processing system using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, where specialized AI agents collaborate to classify, extract, validate, and learn from business documents. This agentic approach adapts to new document formats automatically and improves accuracy over time through feedback loops, replacing manual template configuration with autonomous learning. As next steps: Deploy the sample solution and test with the included purchase order samples. Add your own document types by creating JSON schemas and validation rules. Explore how to integrate extracted data with downstream systems such as ERP, CRM, or content management tools. To learn more about the services and patterns used in this post, refer to the following resources: For a deep dive into the agent framework used in this solution, refer to Strands Agents SDK: A technical deep dive into agent architectures and observability . To understand how AgentCore Gateway transforms APIs into agent-compatible tools, refer to Introducing Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway: Transforming enterprise AI agent tool development . For background on the Model Context Protocol and how it integrates with AWS services, refer to Unlocking the power of Model Context Protocol (MCP) on AWS . To learn how agents can retain context across sessions, refer to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory: Building context-aware agents . For details on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore capabilities, refer to the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation . For expert guidance on building document processing solutions, AWS Professional Services and AWS Partners can help. About the authors Erik Cordsen Erik is a Solutions Architect at AWS serving customers in Georgia. He is passionate about applying cloud technologies and machine learning to solve real life problem. When he is not designing cloud solutions, Erik enjoys travel, cooking, and cycling. Vivek Mittal Vivek is a Solution Architect at Amazon Web Services, where he helps organizations architect and implement cutting-edge cloud solutions. With a deep passion for Generative AI, Machine Learning, and Serverless technologies, he specializes in helping customers harness these innovations to drive business transformation. He finds particular satisfaction in collaborating with customers to turn their ambitious technological visions into reality. Sourabh Jain Sourabh is a Senior Solutions Architect with over 8 years of experience developing cloud solutions that drive better business outcomes for organizations worldwide. He specializes in architecting and implementing robust cloud software solutions, with extensive experience working alongside global Fortune 500 teams across diverse time zones and cultures.

title: Generate presentations with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
summary: This post walks you through building an AI agent system with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that automates PowerPoint presentation creation from enterprise documents. A supervisor agent, Retrieval Augmented Generation, and Amazon Bedrock Guardrails generate grounded presentations in under 90 seconds.
content: A financial services team spends significant time each week manually creating client PowerPoint presentations from quarterly reports, compliance documents, and market analyses. Each presentation requires reading hundreds of pages, extracting key data points, structuring slides, and generating supporting visuals. This post walks you through building an AI agent system using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that automates this workflow, completing in under 90 seconds in our internal testing. This approach reduces presentation creation time while grounding content in source documents. The solution deploys a supervisor agent on AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, using the Strands Agents framework to orchestrate document generation and summarization tools. Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 (available on Amazon Bedrock) handles content creation, Amazon Titan Text Embeddings v2 powers vector search, and Stability AI Stable Image Inpaint (available on Amazon Bedrock) generates slide images. This post includes a public repository with the code assets. Solution overview The solution deploys a single supervisor agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime that selects between document generation and summarization tools based on user requests. A Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline uses Amazon OpenSearch Serverless for vector storage and semantic search across multimodal content. The solution includes a REST API built with .NET 8 minimal APIs, so you can integrate with existing enterprise applications through standard HTTP calls. AWS Lambda offers serverless compute, including containerized functions for PowerPoint generation. The solution secures the implementation with Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) isolation, AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption, and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) least-privilege access control. Key concepts This section covers AgentCore runtime, RAG, and content safety guardrails as they apply to this solution. Agent orchestration with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore A single AI agent generating documents from large knowledge bases must retrieve content, structure outlines, generate text, create images, and assemble files. Rather than implementing these competing responsibilities in a monolithic function, the solution uses a tool-based architecture where a supervisor agent routes requests to specialized tools. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime provides a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. The agent code runs in an isolated container with session management, built-in identity, and observability. The solution uses the Strands Agents framework (an open source SDK for building AI agents) to implement the supervisor logic. The supervisor agent exposes two tools: generate_pptx: Creates PowerPoint presentations by invoking the PPTX Generator Lambda function, which retrieves content from the knowledge base, generates slide outlines, creates AI images, and assembles the final document. generate_summary: Extracts and synthesizes information from the knowledge base using RAG to deliver accurate, grounded responses. The agent determines whether a request requires document generation, content summarization, or both, then invokes the appropriate tool. You can add new capabilities by defining new tools in the agent code without modifying existing ones. Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) for enterprise knowledge RAG addresses a fundamental challenge in AI systems: delivering accurate, up-to-date information grounded in enterprise data rather than relying solely on the model’s training data. The implementation uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases , which combine vector search with large language models (LLMs) to retrieve relevant context before generating responses. The RAG pipeline works as follows: You upload enterprise documents to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) . The system chunks and parses documents, applying special handling for multimodal content including tables, charts, and images. Amazon Titan Text Embeddings v2 converts each chunk into high-dimensional vectors that capture semantic meaning. Amazon OpenSearch Serverless stores the vectors, creating a searchable vector database. At query time, the system converts the user’s request into an embedding and performs similarity search to retrieve relevant document chunks. Retrieved chunks supply context to the language model, which generates responses grounded in the source material. This approach is designed to help reduce hallucinated content by grounding generated documents in source information from the enterprise knowledge base. Note: The Amazon OpenSearch Serverless collection data plane must remain publicly accessible because Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases accesses Amazon OpenSearch Serverless from AWS-managed infrastructure, not through customer VPC endpoints. IAM data access policies protect the collection, and VPC-only access restricts the Amazon OpenSearch Serverless dashboard. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for content safety Enterprise AI applications require content moderation to meet organizational standards and compliance requirements. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails offers built-in content filtering and safety mechanisms integrated throughout the document generation pipeline. Guardrails operate at multiple stages: Input processing: Filters user requests to help prevent injection issues and inappropriate content. Output generation: Monitors model outputs to verify compliance with content policies. Personally identifiable information (PII) handling: Detects and anonymizes or blocks PII. The implementation creates custom guardrails through AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) , configured with specific policies tailored to enterprise document creation. The agent applies guardrails at the model invocation level, providing consistent content safety without requiring manual configuration for each deployment. Solution architecture The following diagram illustrates the agent-based document generation system. Figure 1: Architecture of the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore RAG presentation generation system The data flow begins with user requests arriving through Amazon API Gateway , which routes them to a .NET-based Chat API running on AWS Lambda . The API maintains conversation state in Amazon DynamoDB . It then invokes the supervisor agent hosted on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime. The supervisor agent analyzes the request and selects the appropriate tool. For document generation, it invokes the PPTX Generator Lambda (a containerized Python function). For summarization, the supervisor invokes the Summary Generator Lambda, which queries the knowledge base through the retrieve_and_generate API. The system processes, chunks, and embeds documents stored in Amazon S3 using Amazon Titan Text Embeddings v2. Amazon OpenSearch Serverless indexes the embeddings for fast semantic search. When tools query the knowledge base, Amazon OpenSearch Serverless retrieves relevant chunks, which are then supplied as context to Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 (on Amazon Bedrock) for generating grounded responses. The system stores generated documents in Amazon S3 and returns presigned URLs for secure download. Security measures include: AWS WAF with managed rule sets and IP-based rate limiting on Amazon API Gateway. Amazon Cognito with the Plus feature plan and advanced security mode for threat protection. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails provisioned through AWS CDK for consistent content filtering. Amazon DynamoDB with point-in-time recovery, deletion protection, and customer-managed AWS KMS encryption. Amazon S3 buckets with versioning, server access logging, and block public access. AWS X-Ray tracing on Lambda functions for distributed debugging. Input validation with regex-based tenant ID and session ID verification. Tenant isolation through AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) role assumption per tenant. Prerequisites Before deploying, you need the following tools and access configured in your environment: AWS environment: An active AWS account with permissions for deploying infrastructure. AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) configured with credentials. IAM role with appropriate service access policies. Development tools: .NET SDK 8 with Amazon.Lambda.Tools installed globally. Python 3.12 or later for AWS CDK and Lambda functions. Node.js and AWS CDK CLI for infrastructure deployment. Docker or Finch for building container images (ARM64 support required). AWS services access: Amazon Bedrock with model access for Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6, Amazon Titan Text Embeddings v2, and Stability AI Stable Image Inpaint (available through Amazon Bedrock). For model availability by Region, see Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock . Amazon Bedrock AgentCore access enabled in your account. Amazon API Gateway Regional REST API integration timeout configured to at least 300 seconds. The default is 29 seconds. For more information, see API Gateway quotas . An existing Amazon VPC with private subnets. An Amazon S3 bucket for deployment artifacts. Set up the solution The setup process includes configuring deployment parameters and initializing the AWS CDK environment. Clone the repository and navigate to the project directory: git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/sample-generating-powerpoint-presentations-with-amazon-bedrock.git Create the configuration file pipeline-params.ini at the repository root: environment=dev awscliprofile= ContainerRegistry=lambda-pptx-gen AgentContainerRegistry=agentcore-supervisor BucketDev= VpcId= ParsingInferenceProfileId=us.anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5-20251001-v1:0 AgentInferenceProfileId=us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6 EmbeddingModelId=amazon.titan-embed-text-v2:0 ImageGenerationModelId=stability.stable-image-inpaint-v1:0 PPTXGenImageTag=latest AgentImageTag=latest Set awscliprofile to your AWS CLI profile name, or leave empty to use environment variable credentials. Bootstrap AWS CDK (one-time per account and Region): cdk bootstrap This creates the AWS CloudFormation CDKToolkit stack required for AWS CDK deployments. Make build scripts executable: chmod +x ./pipeline-build.sh chmod +x ./pipeline-deploy.sh chmod +x ./deploy-agentcore.sh Build and deploy The deployment consists of three phases: building artifacts, deploying infrastructure, and deploying the AgentCore runtime agent. Build phase The build phase compiles application code and packages deployment artifacts. Run the build script: ./pipeline-build.sh This compiles the .NET projects (Chat API) and packages them as Lambda deployment packages. It builds the PPTX Generator container image using Docker or Finch and authenticates with Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) . It then pushes the container image and stores build artifacts in the asset-output directory. Infrastructure deployment phase The infrastructure deployment creates AWS resources and configures service integrations. Run the deployment script: ./pipeline-deploy.sh The deployment creates four AWS CloudFormation stacks in dependency order: VPCEndpointsStack: Configures Amazon VPC endpoints for AWS services including Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. OpensearchStack: Provisions Amazon OpenSearch Serverless collection for vector storage. AgentCoreStack: Creates guardrails, Lambda functions, IAM roles, and stores configuration in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store . ChatApiStack: Deploys Amazon API Gateway and Chat API Lambda. AgentCore runtime deployment After the infrastructure stacks are deployed, deploy the supervisor agent to AgentCore runtime: ./deploy-agentcore.sh This script builds the supervisor agent container (ARM64), pushes it to Amazon ECR, creates the AgentCore runtime and endpoint, and updates the Systems Manager parameter with the endpoint Amazon Resource Name (ARN). The Chat API references this endpoint ARN to route requests to the agent. After deployment, AWS CloudFormation outputs include the Amazon API Gateway endpoint URL and resource identifiers. Configuration The solution offers several configuration points: Agent instructions Edit agent/app.py to modify the supervisor agent’s system prompt and behavior. The agent uses Strands Agents with two tools defined in agent/tools.py : generate_pptx: Invokes the PPTX Generator Lambda for document creation. generate_summary: Invokes the Summary Generator Lambda for knowledge base queries. Model selection In pipeline-params.ini , adjust model identifiers: ParsingInferenceProfileId : Model for knowledge base document parsing (Anthropic Claude Haiku 4.5 recommended for cost efficiency). AgentInferenceProfileId : Model for agent reasoning (Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 recommended). EmbeddingModelId : Embedding model for vector search (Amazon Titan Text Embeddings v2). ImageGenerationModelId : Model for slide image generation (Stability AI Stable Image Inpaint). With inference profiles instead of direct model IDs, requests draw on a broader multi-Region capacity pool, which increases throughput and helps maintain consistent performance under load. Lambda configuration Adjust compute resources in the stack files: Chat API: 128 MB memory, 29-second timeout, 100 reserved concurrency (in api.py ). PPTX Generator: 900 MB memory, 300-second timeout, 50 reserved concurrency (in pptx_gen.py ). Summary Generator: 512 MB memory, 300-second timeout, 50 reserved concurrency (in sum_gen.py ). Results In internal testing with a 90-page Amazon 2024 Annual Report PDF, the solution produced the following performance metrics: Presentation generation time: 70–90 seconds end-to-end (including knowledge base retrieval, content generation, image creation, and file assembly). Slide count: Six slides with title, bullet points, image+text, image-only, and takeaway formats. Image generation: Two AI-generated images per presentation using Stability AI Stable Image Inpaint. Cost per generation: Approximately $0.04 in model invocation costs at time of writing in us-east-1 (text and image generation, with image generation accounting for the majority of cost). Knowledge base ingestion: Under 2 minutes for a single 1.3 MB PDF document. PowerPoint presentations The following figures show example slides from a generated presentation. Figure 2: Generated title slide with customizable branding Figure 3: Generated content slide with bullet points Figure 4: Generated slide combining text with an AI-generated image Figure 5: Generated content slide summarizing profitability metrics Figure 6: Generated image-only slide with an AI-generated visual Figure 7: Generated takeaways slide Generated presentations include: Title slides with customizable branding. Content slides with bullet points and structured text. Image slides with AI-generated visuals from Stability AI Stable Image Inpaint (on Amazon Bedrock). Speaker notes with presentation guidance. Consistent formatting based on corporate templates. Summaries Summary outputs provided to the knowledge base include: Concise synthesis of knowledge base content. Citation tracking to source documents. Structured formatting with key points highlighted. API responses The Chat API returns: Streaming responses for real-time user feedback. Because internal testing showed that presentation generation takes 70–90 seconds (exceeding the default Amazon API Gateway 29-second integration timeout), the Chat API uses an asynchronous invocation pattern. Use streaming or polling to receive the final result rather than waiting on a synchronous REST call. Conversation context maintenance across multiple turns. Amazon S3 presigned URLs for document downloads (5-minute expiration). Generated content undergoes Amazon Bedrock Guardrails validation to verify compliance with content policies before delivery. Clean up To avoid ongoing charges, delete the deployed resources: Delete the AgentCore runtime and endpoint: aws bedrock-agentcore-control delete-agent-runtime-endpoint \ --agent-runtime-id \ --agent-runtime-endpoint-id aws bedrock-agentcore-control delete-agent-runtime \ --agent-runtime-id Turn off Amazon DynamoDB deletion protection (required before stack deletion): aws dynamodb update-table --table-name chat-sessions-dev --no-deletion-protection-enabled aws dynamodb update-table --table-name tenant-table-dev --no-deletion-protection-enabled Delete AWS CloudFormation stacks in reverse dependency order: aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name ChatApiStack aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name AgentCoreStack aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name OpensearchStack aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name VPCEndpointsStack Empty Amazon S3 buckets before deletion (AWS CloudFormation cannot delete non-empty buckets): aws s3 rm s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket --recursive Delete Amazon ECR repositories containing container images: aws ecr delete-repository --repository-name lambda-pptx-gen --force aws ecr delete-repository --repository-name agentcore-supervisor --force Delete tenant knowledge base sub-stacks (created by the tenant provisioner): aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name bedrock-kb- Security considerations This solution uses Lambda environment variables for configuration values such as model IDs, Amazon S3 bucket names, and guardrail IDs. These are resource identifiers, not secrets. For production deployments, use AWS Secrets Manager for sensitive configuration values such as API keys and database credentials. The AgentCore runtime agent runs in an isolated container with session-level isolation. Each user session operates in a dedicated environment, helping to prevent cross-session data contamination. Conclusion In this post, you built an AI agent system with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that automates enterprise document generation. The supervisor agent deployed on AgentCore runtime routes requests to specialized tools for document creation and summarization, reducing presentation creation to about 90 seconds in an internal test. The RAG pipeline grounds generated content in source documents, and Amazon Bedrock Guardrails verifies content compliance. You can adapt this architecture for automated report generation in financial services, technical documentation for engineering teams, or proposal creation for sales organizations. To get started, clone the GitHub repository and follow the setup instructions.
