title: How Tamnoon built AI-powered cloud security remediation with Amazon Bedrock
summary: Learn how Tamnoon built Tami, an agentic cloud remediation orchestrator on Amazon Bedrock that autonomously investigates and safely remediates cloud security findings from CNAPP and cloud-native sources. The approach drove a 90%+ reduction in critical cloud exposure in 90 days with zero production issues.
content: Critical cloud exposures pile up faster than security teams can close them. Cloud-native application protection platforms (CNAPP), cloud providers, and posture scanners generate more findings than any team can triage, and risk accumulates in the gap between detected and fixed. Most findings sit untouched, not because they’re hard to fix. Someone must investigate context, identify the owner, confirm the fix won’t break production, and then do it at a volume that outpaces headcount. In this post, we share how Tamnoon built Tami, an agentic cloud remediation orchestrator on Amazon Bedrock , to close that gap. Tami autonomously investigates findings ingested from CNAPP and cloud-native sources and assesses whether remediation is safe. It then generates and orchestrates the fix with guardrails and governance wherever a change touches a customer’s cloud. The approach drove an over 90 percent reduction in critical cloud exposure in 90 days with zero production issues. About Tamnoon Tamnoon is an AI-powered cloud security remediation platform that works alongside CNAPPs. Its AI assistant, Tami, helps human cloud security experts investigate, prioritize, and safely remediate misconfigurations and issues across customer environments in AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and other cloud providers. Tamnoon integrates with the CNAPPs and cloud-native tools teams already use and turns their findings into validated, production-safe fixes. Most of the work including investigation, prioritization, and remediation planning happens before anything touches a live environment, which is what makes automated remediation trustworthy at scale. Cloud security remediation challenges A security engineer can spend hours investigating a single finding. Often, it traces back to the same root cause as dozens of other alerts. Alert volume overwhelms headcount: CNAPPs and scanners generate thousands of findings. Teams can’t triage them all, so critical exposures sit unresolved while risk compounds for months. Investigation is manual and repetitive: Each finding requires context gathering on who owns the resource, what depends on it, whether the fix is safe. This eats hours of senior engineer time, repeated across every item in the backlog. Fear of production impact blocks automation: Teams hesitate to automate remediation because they can’t risk taking down production. Without confidence that a fix is safe, nothing moves. Reactive prioritization: Without a way to cluster related findings or score remediation confidence, teams work through alerts linearly rather than addressing root causes that resolve many issues at once. Tamnoon’s solution addresses the full pipeline from finding ingestion to validated fix. The platform treats these challenges as interconnected rather than isolated problems. Solution overview Tamnoon takes you from initial finding to executing the fix. The platform ingests findings from CNAPP, Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) providers, and other security tools and normalizes them into a unified schema. It then enriches them with asset and exposure context and prioritizes them. From there, the agentic layer takes over using a set of specialized AI agents, each running in an event-driven, serverless architecture on AWS, so every stage scales independently and fails safely. Agentic architecture on Amazon Bedrock The platform delegates work to four specialized agents, each responsible for a distinct phase of the remediation pipeline: An investigation agent draws on training from millions of real customer cloud environments to determine context, filters that context through a large language model (LLM)-as-a-judge validation layer. It reasons through the remediation goal, operational scope, and cloud-provider-specific verification, producing read-only investigation steps and a complete investigation plan. A safety-scoring agent builds an evidence chain per asset, combining automated verification results with analyst findings. It classifies each finding’s remediation as SAFE, RISKY, or AWAITING DATA with a deliberately conservative bias. When in doubt, it downgrades. A remediation agent activates only for findings that the safety agent has deemed safe. It reasons through ordering, dependencies, and conditions, then produces a remediation plan in which every step follows a backup, remediate, and verify structure and includes rollback guidance. A code-generation agent turns plan steps into executable remediation, but only after an input guardrail screens for relevance and prompt injection. Every artifact passes an automated generate-and-review loop in which a separate reviewer agent must approve the output. Why Amazon Bedrock When the Tamnoon team set out to build Tami, the choice of foundation model (FM) platform was going to shape everything that followed. Tamnoon’s remediation agents don’t all do the same kind of work. Some perform deep investigative reasoning to understand the root cause of a security finding. Others handle high-volume validation, checking proposed fixes quickly and cheaply. Still others review generated code, balancing quality against cost on every task. Matching each of these jobs to the right model, without stitching together a different integration for each one, was a core requirement. That requirement is what made Amazon Bedrock the natural fit. Through a single API, each agent can call the foundation model best suited to its task. The most capable models handle the hardest reasoning. More efficient models take on the repetitive, high-throughput work. Review-focused models optimize the trade-off between output quality and cost. Because it’s one integration rather than many, models can be swapped or upgraded as the landscape evolves, without re-plumbing the architecture each time. Operational overhead at scale was another factor in the decision. As request volume grew, Tamnoon wanted to avoid building and maintaining its own logic to distribute traffic across regional capacity. Amazon Bedrock Cross-Region inference handles this automatically. It automatically routes inference requests to the optimal AWS Region within a defined geographic boundary, maintaining throughput without requiring any custom routing code to operate. Security was the final consideration, and for a cloud security company it was non-negotiable. With Bedrock, inference runs inside Tamnoon’s own AWS environment under AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)-scoped permissions. Sensitive customer data never leaves the trust boundary. That gave the team confidence that the platform underpinning Tami met the same standard Tamnoon holds its own service to. How Tamnoon integrates with CNAPPs and cloud security tools Tamnoon sits downstream of the detection tools security teams already run. CNAPPs like Wiz, CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Cortex, Upwind, SentinelOne, Orca, and Cyera along with cloud-native services like AWS Security Hub and Amazon GuardDuty are the source of truth for what’s wrong in the environment. Tamnoon connects through API-based integrations and normalizes findings into a common format, so a misconfiguration looks the same whether it came from Wiz or GuardDuty. The detection tools remain the foundation. Tamnoon delivers the end-to-end remediation that follows. For every finding it works, Tami assigns a Remediation Confidence Indicator (RCI) of SAFE, RISKY, or AWAITING DATA. That rating tells teams what can be automated and what needs human review first. Figure 1: Tamnoon in action Tamnoon AWS architecture Tamnoon runs entirely within its own AWS accounts, isolated per environment. Users access the platform through a single secure entry point built on Amazon API Gateway, with encryption managed by AWS Certificate Manager and sign-in handled by Amazon Cognito. Everything behind that entry point runs in private networks across multiple Availability Zones, so the core platform is never directly exposed to the internet. Inside that environment, Tamnoon combines two kinds of compute. Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) runs the always-on services behind the dashboard, while AWS Lambda powers the event-driven work of collecting findings, analyzing them, and executing remediations. A set of AWS messaging and workflow services, including Amazon EventBridge, Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS), and AWS Step Functions, coordinate these steps so large volumes of findings are processed reliably and in parallel, with no single bad record stalling the rest. The AI layer runs on Amazon Bedrock. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model, gives Tamnoon’s agents a governed way to take action instead of open-ended access. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails then review both the request and the generated code before anything moves forward. Supporting services handle the rest of the platform: managed databases and caching for state, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) for playbooks and artifacts, and AWS Secrets Manager for credentials, so sensitive keys never live in application code. On the customer side, everything to the left of the AWS Cloud boundary is what customers connect into Tamnoon. They can link their own AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud accounts, plug in the security tools their findings come from, and connect the destinations where they want outcomes delivered, such as Slack, Jira, ServiceNow, and GitHub. Figure 2: Tamnoon AWS architecture How Tamnoon maintains zero production issues Zero production issues is a reality for Tamnoon’s customers, and it is no accident. Autonomy at Tamnoon sits inside a defense-in-depth safety architecture, where each layer assumes the one before it might miss something. It starts before any fix is even drafted. No remediation is written until an independent safety assessment, focused on scope and deliberately biased toward caution, concludes that the change is safe to make. From there, the platform draws a hard line between reading and writing. Investigation steps are validated as strictly read-only, so the work of understanding a problem can never alter it. Only the remediation path is allowed to change anything, and every change it makes carries its own backup, verification, and rollback steps. That discipline is reinforced by constant self-critique. Each generation step is paired with a reflection step that checks the output and feeds its critique back into regeneration, so the system is always reviewing its own work rather than trusting it outright. Those recommendations are also kept grounded in reality. Agent output is validated against automation results, user feedback, and training data drawn from real fixed alerts, and when the model cannot reach an accurate result on its own, a human is brought into the loop. The final safeguard is at the moment of execution. The AI never holds cloud credentials. Instead, execution is brokered through short-lived, tenant-scoped credentials under customer-controlled trust, running in an isolated environment kept separate from the agents that plan the work. Wrapping all of this is human governance: remediations flow through an approval workflow with a full audit trail, and every AI capability is proven internally before it ever reaches a customer. Data security and compliance Tami reasons over sensitive customer data: alert payloads, resource identifiers, misconfigurations, and remediation context. That data must stay inside the AWS trust boundary, run with least privilege, and stay auditable. Standardizing on Amazon Bedrock makes that possible. Sensitive content stays inside AWS Every Tami workload invokes Anthropic Claude on Amazon Bedrock through the ChatBedrockConverse interface, rather than calling a third-party LLM endpoint. That single choice puts the full AI supply chain under one AWS native service, which has real consequences for how customer data is handled. Inference runs entirely within Tamnoon’s own AWS account in US commercial Regions, so data never leaves AWS. For information about model availability by Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock . Because Bedrock doesn’t retain or train on prompts or completions, customer data never reaches an external vendor in the first place. That boundary holds even as workloads scale. Bedrock Cross-Region inference automatically routes requests to Regions within the US geographic boundary, increasing the throughput available to the application. The compute behind it stays private as well. Each service runs as an AWS Lambda function attached to a virtual private cloud (VPC), in private subnets with an explicit security group, no public ingress, and tightly controlled egress. Guarding what reaches the model Payloads can carry sensitive detail, so Tami applies Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to every request and response. The policy is enforced at the Bedrock layer, which means it covers all three services uniformly and no individual function’s prompt logic can bypass it. That single enforcement point does several things at once. First, it protects sensitive data. PII and secret-like content is masked before it is ever persisted or surfaced, so nothing sensitive lingers where it doesn’t belong. It also guards against prompt injection, which matters because Tami reasons over untrusted findings that an unauthorized user could influence. Filtering at the guardrail layer stops a crafted payload from hijacking the model or exfiltrating context. Finally, denied topics and content filters keep the model’s output scoped to security remediation and nothing else. Every intervention is logged alongside AWS CloudTrail, giving enterprise customers a clear trail of governance evidence. Least-privilege access Access across the platform runs through a dedicated per-service IAM execution role, so each function can reach only what it needs and nothing more. That principle is easiest to see in how Tami touches Amazon Bedrock. Its only Bedrock permission is bedrock:InvokeModel , scoped to specific inference-profile and foundation-model ARNs. It has no ability to manage, train, or export models. The same discipline extends to every other dependency. Access to AWS Secrets Manager is limited to the two secrets a function actually uses, SQS access is confined to its own input queue, and Amazon CloudWatch writes are restricted by namespace. There are no broad, catch-all roles anywhere in the design. Functions attach only to the managed AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole and AWSLambdaVPCAccessExecutionRole policies, and nothing wider than that. Multi-tenant isolation and governance Keeping tenants separated is a foundational requirement, and it is enforced from the very first call. Service-to-service calls use OAuth2 client credentials through Cognito, scoped per application, and work is processed one SQS message at a time with its tenant context attached. As a result, a single invocation only ever touches one tenant’s data. Much of this assurance comes from treating the entire platform as code. IAM policies, network placement, model IDs, and alarms all live in versioned AWS CloudFormation and SAM templates, so every permission and model version is reviewable in source control with no manual console changes to drift out of sync. Model versions in particular are pinned to dated identifiers, for example claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929 , which means a model change is always an explicit, reviewed code change rather than a silent upgrade. That transparency carries through to runtime. Every inference call lands in AWS CloudTrail, attributable to the invoking role, and deterministic decoding with temperature set to zero keeps scoring and planning consistent from one run to the next. Failure handling is governed with the same rigor. Each service has an input queue with redrive, an error-handler function, a dead-letter queue, and CloudWatch alarms on timeouts and DLQ depth wired to on-call. Failures are contained and observable, and never silently dropped. Results and impact Tami has analyzed more than 14 million cloud alerts across Tamnoon’s customer base, a number tracked in Tamnoon’s 2026 State of Cloud Remediation report . The decisions Tami makes reflect patterns learned from these real-world environments. For a typical customer, the results show up fast, usually within 90 days. Metric Before After Critical cloud exposure Compounds for months as alerts outpace headcount Up to 90% reduction in 90 days ( source ) Remediation efficiency Thousands of raw alerts, no clear prioritization Up to 100x efficiency through root-cause clustering ( source ) Production issues Teams avoid automation because of risk Zero production issues across millions of workloads Engineer time Hours per finding, repeated across backlog 13,000+ hours saved per week across customer base ( source ) The compression and zero-issue figures come from Tamnoon’s research. The pattern is consistent, showing fewer open exposures, far less manual work, and no downtime from the fixes themselves. Conclusion Building an agent that can reason about a cloud finding is the straightforward part. Building one you’d trust to act on production is the hard part. Amazon Bedrock is a fully managed service that provides access to high-performing foundation models along with the tooling to build agentic applications: orchestration, tool use, and guardrails, through a single API. That combination matters here for a specific reason: acting on production cloud infrastructure demands both strong reasoning and hard safety boundaries. Four things make that possible: Your exposures actually close: Tamnoon operates on live cloud infrastructure, not on tickets or workflow automation. The backlog goes down instead of sideways. Autonomy scales without production risk: Every proposed action carries a confidence rating. SAFE actions can auto-execute while AWAITING DATA or RISKY actions pull in Tamnoon’s embedded cloud engineers. Runs on the stack you already bought: Tamnoon works on top of popular CNAPPs and cloud security tooling. Every detection tool you already pay for starts paying off because its findings finally get closed. Team capacity scales without growing: Fast, safe adoption of frontier AI means more exposures closed per analyst, with no added headcount. Next steps To get started with a similar architecture, consider the following: Explore Amazon Bedrock and the models available through it. Review the Amazon Bedrock documentation to plan your architecture. Book a demo with Tamnoon to find out how much of your critical cloud exposure you can close in the next 90 days. About the authors Ishara Premadasa Ishara is a Solutions Architect on the AWS Startups team, where she helps startup customers build and scale with the right architecture on AWS. She specializes in AI/ML, Data Intelligence, and Analytics, helping startups build strong data foundations and bring generative AI solutions into production. Outside of work, Ishara enjoys the outdoors and loves travel, reading, and baking. Adi Milner Adi is Head of Engineering at Tamnoon, where he leads engineering and product teams building AI-powered cloud security and remediation solutions. With more than 20 years of experience in software engineering and technology leadership, his work spans cloud infrastructure, distributed systems, developer platforms, and agentic AI. He is passionate about applying AI to complex engineering and security problems and building products that deliver measurable value to customers. Maya Levine Maya is Head of Product and Technical Product Marketing at Tamnoon. Maya previously led product management at Sysdig, and before that held security engineering, cloud technical marketing, and cybersecurity evangelist roles at Check Point Software Technologies. A frequent speaker at conferences such as AWS re:Invent and RSAC, she is passionate about building AI products that security teams trust to act on their behalf.

title: Deploy and evaluate models with Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
summary: Learn how to deploy an available model from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, run a lightweight and repeatable performance test using the SageMaker Python SDK, and delete the endpoint when testing is complete.
content:
Choosing the right model for a specific application requires a practical way to test it with representative inputs. Amazon SageMaker JumpStart provides access to a broad catalog of already pretrained models. In this post, we show how to deploy an available model from SageMaker JumpStart, run a lightweight and repeatable performance test using the SageMaker Python SDK, and delete the endpoint when testing is complete. For supported models and available capacity, this workflow provides a repeatable evaluation path, although deployment time varies by model, instance type, quota, and AWS Region. In 2026, SageMaker JumpStart introduced two improvements that simplify model discovery and deployment. In the Model Hub section of the Amazon SageMaker AI console, you can browse the SageMaker JumpStart catalog, view sample notebooks, and open them directly in SageMaker Studio. Pre-configured endpoint deployment options provide named configurations optimized for priorities such as low cost, low latency, or general-purpose workloads across a range of generative AI models, including Neuron-optimized configurations. Additionally, you can now go from Hugging Face model discovery to SageMaker AI deployment in a single click using the new deep link integration. Solution overview Our approach uses a reusable Python script that performs three steps: Discover and deploy a model from SageMaker JumpStart. Run model-specific sample prompts and measure latency, approximate output length, and single-request generation rate. Clean up the endpoint. This pattern works for many compatible SageMaker JumpStart models, although payload formats, required instance types, end-user license agreement (EULA) requirements, and response schemas may require model-specific adjustments. Prerequisites An AWS account with SageMaker AI permissions. Python 3+ with SageMaker Python SDK v3 installed ( pip install "sagemaker>=3, ). Sufficient GPU instance quota for the model you want to test or request a quota increase . Step 1.a: Discover available models UI path to find models in SageMaker JumpStart: Figure 1: Browsing the model catalog on the SageMaker JumpStart Models page in SageMaker Studio Code path using SageMaker Python SDK: from sagemaker.core.jumpstart.notebook_utils import ( list_jumpstart_models, ) REGION = "us-east-1" models = list_jumpstart_models( filter="task == textgeneration", region=REGION, list_versions=True, ) print(f"Found {len(models)} text generation models") for model_id, model_version in models[:10]: print( f" - {model_id} " f"(version {model_version})" ) Or search by model name: from sagemaker.core.jumpstart.notebook_utils import list_jumpstart_models ids = list_jumpstart_models( filter="model_id contains qwen", region=REGION, list_versions=True, ) print(f"{len(ids)} models matched in {REGION}
") for model_id, version in ids: print(f"{model_id: Step 1.b: Deploy the model UI path to deploy models from SageMaker JumpStart: Figure 2: Deploying a model from its SageMaker JumpStart detail page in SageMaker Studio Code path using SageMaker Python SDK: import time from sagemaker.core.jumpstart.accessors import JumpStartModelsAccessor from sagemaker.core.jumpstart.configs import JumpStartConfig from sagemaker.core.training.configs import Compute from sagemaker.serve import ModelBuilder MODEL_ID = "huggingface-vlm-qwen3-5-27b" MODEL_VERSION = "1.13.0" REGION = "us-east-1" ACCEPT_EULA = False # Set True only after reviewing the model terms def get_field(value, name, default=None): if isinstance(value, dict): return value.get(name, default) return getattr(value, name, default) # Resolve the JumpStart-recommended deployment configuration. specs = JumpStartModelsAccessor().get_model_specs( region=REGION, model_id=MODEL_ID, version=MODEL_VERSION, ) if isinstance(specs, list): if not specs: raise ValueError( f"No JumpStart specification found for {MODEL_ID}" ) specs = specs[0] recommended_instance_type = get_field( specs, "default_inference_instance_type", ) if not recommended_instance_type: raise ValueError( f"No recommended instance type found for {MODEL_ID}" ) print(f"Model: {MODEL_ID}") print(f"Region: {REGION}") print(f"Recommended instance: {recommended_instance_type}") start = time.time() jumpstart_config = JumpStartConfig( model_id=MODEL_ID, model_version=MODEL_VERSION, accept_eula=ACCEPT_EULA, ) model_builder = ModelBuilder.from_jumpstart_config( jumpstart_config=jumpstart_config, compute=Compute( instance_type=recommended_instance_type, instance_count=1, ), ) model = model_builder.build() endpoint = model_builder.deploy() deploy_time = time.time() - start print(f"Deployed in {deploy_time:.1f} seconds") print(f"Endpoint: {endpoint.endpoint_name}") Step 2: Run sample prompts and measure performance from sagemaker.core.payloads import retrieve_all_examples import json import time MODEL_ID = "huggingface-vlm-qwen3-5-27b" MODEL_VERSION = "1.13.0" REGION = "us-east-1" example_payloads = retrieve_all_examples( region=REGION, model_id=MODEL_ID, model_version=MODEL_VERSION, serialize=True, ) #you can re-create the endpoint pointer using the endpoint name: #from sagemaker.core.resources import Endpoint #endpoint = Endpoint.get(endpoint_name=" ",region=REGION) def read_response_body(result): body = result.body if hasattr(body, "read"): body = body.read() if isinstance(body, bytes): body = body.decode("utf-8") if isinstance(body, str): try: return json.loads(body) except json.JSONDecodeError: return body return body def extract_output(response): """Handle common JumpStart text-generation response formats.""" if isinstance(response, list): response = response[0] if response else "" if isinstance(response, dict): choices = response.get("choices") if choices: choice = choices[0] message = choice.get("message") if isinstance(message, dict): return message.get("content", "") return choice.get("text", "") for field in ( "generated_text", "output_text", "text", ): if field in response: return response[field] return response results = [] for payload in example_payloads or []: start = time.perf_counter() result = endpoint.invoke( body=payload.body, content_type=payload.content_type, accept=payload.accept, ) latency = time.perf_counter() - start response = read_response_body(result) output = extract_output(response) if not isinstance(output, str): output = json.dumps(output, indent=2) # This is an estimate based on whitespace-separated words. output_words = len(output.split()) results.append( { "request_preview": payload.body[:50], "latency_s": round(latency, 2), "estimated_output_words": output_words, "words_per_second": round( output_words / latency, 1, ) if latency > 0 else 0, } ) print("Input:
", payload.body, end="

") print("Output:
", output, end="

") print( f"Latency: {latency:.2f} seconds
" f"Estimated output words: {output_words}
" f"Estimated single-request output generation rate: " f"{output_words / latency:.1f} words/second
" ) print("-" * 80) print("
Summary:") for result in results: print(result) Result: Input: {"max_tokens": 256, "messages": [{"content": "What is deep learning?", "role": "user"}], "model": "/opt/ml/model"} Output: Here's a thinking process that leads to the explanation of deep learning: 1. **Deconstruct the Request:** * **Question:** "What is deep learning?" * **Intent:** The user wants a clear, comprehensive, yet accessible definition and overview of deep learning. * **Target Audience:** Likely someone looking for a general understanding, possibly a student, tech enthusiast, or professional exploring the field. The tone should be informative, structured, and not overly jargon-heavy (though key terms need explanation). 2. **Initial Brainstorming & Key Concepts:** * What is it? A subset of machine learning, which is a subset of AI. * Core mechanism: Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs). * "Deep" means many layers (hidden layers). * How does it work? Learning representations from data (feature learning). * Key applications: Image recognition, NLP, speech, self-driving cars. * Why is it popular now? Big data, GPU power, better algorithms. * Pros/Cons: High accuracy vs. black box, data hunger. 3. **Structuring the Answer:** Latency: 9.07 seconds Estimated output words: 153 Estimated single-request output generation rate: 16.9 words/second -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Summary: {'request_preview': '{"max_tokens": 256, "messages": {"content": "What', 'latency_s': 9.07, 'estimated_output_words': 153, 'words_per_second': 16.9} Step 3: Cleanup print(f"Deleting endpoint: {endpoint.endpoint_name}") endpoint.delete() endpoint.wait_for_delete() print("Endpoint deleted") Conclusion This pattern works for many available SageMaker JumpStart models, but the payload format, required instance type, EULA, and response parsing may require model-specific adjustments. By using consistent test prompts and measuring latency, throughput, and output quality across models, you can compare options and select the right fit for your workload. Try this approach with different models from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart to find the right balance of quality, speed, and cost for your applications. References SageMaker Python SDK Documentation Benchmark and Optimize SageMaker JumpStart Deployment (blog post) From Hugging Face to SageMaker Studio in One Click (blog post) Amazon SageMaker JumpStart About the authors Vamsi Goparaju Vamsi leads Go-to-Market (GTM) and Revenue Acceleration initiatives at AWS, enabling Inference and ModelOps workloads for our customers, and driving OSS Use Cases and Product features for Amazon SageMaker AI, SageMaker JumpStart, and Generative AI. With over 16 years of experience spanning AWS, Dell, and Infosys, he brings a unique blend of technical depth and business knowledge across cloud, high-performance computing (HPC), artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and analytics. He holds an MBA from Texas A&M University’s Mays Business School. Gula Nurmatova Gula is a Software Development Manager at AWS based in New York, USA. She leads the engineering teams behind Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, making foundation models from providers like NVIDIA, Meta, and Mistral easy to discover, evaluate, and deploy across SageMaker and Amazon Bedrock. Prior to AWS, she held engineering and engineering management roles at RTX and GE, and holds a master’s degree in Computer Science. Naidile Murali Naidile is a Product Manager at AWS based in Bellevue, WA. She focuses on enhancing the AI/ML developer experience on Amazon SageMaker AI, including onboarding, IDE connectivity, and GPU capacity management. Prior to AWS, she worked as a software engineer at HSBC. Naidile holds an MBA from Georgetown University. Dan Ferguson Dan is a Solutions Architect at AWS, based in New York, USA. As a machine learning services expert, Dan works to support customers on their journey to integrating ML workflows efficiently, effectively, and sustainably.

content: Across industries, the U.K. is putting the full stack to work. T he scale of deployment is growing fast, from enterprises transforming their businesses to startups solving some of the planet’s hardest problems. NVIDIA is putting that principle into practice, including through a five-year, $250 million compute commitment to strengthen the U.K.’s agentic safety and security research. NVIDIA’s Investments in the UK NVIDIA has been investing in the U.K. startup ecosystem, supporting companies including Basecamp Research , Ineffable Intelligence , Synthesia , Wayve and many more. Today, NVIDIA announced new planned investments in Boltz , Foresight , Hiverge, Prima Mente and Riverlane . Boltz , a London-based AI startup founded by MIT researchers, builds biomolecular models and AI agents that help scientists predict molecular structures and interactions, and design potential new medicines. Foresight, a London-based startup, helps owners of major infrastructure projects, including hyperscale data centers, predict completion dates, mitigate risks and accelerate time to revenue. Hiverge , a Cambridge-based AI startup founded by researchers from Google DeepMind and the University of Cambridge, builds an AI discovery engine that automatically writes and optimizes algorithms for tasks such as faster AI training and complex logistics planning. Prima Mente , a London-based AI biology startup, focuses on building biological foundation models to decode complex diseases and identify novel therapeutic targets, starting with Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s and ALS. Riverlane, a Cambridge-based quantum computing startup, builds real-time error correction hardware and software that work across all major qubit types, helping quantum computers become reliable enough for practical use. In addition, NVIDIA is partnering with the Earthshot Prize , joining as a Global Alliance Founding Partner to bring compute and technical expertise to innovators working on solutions for the world’s greatest climate and sustainability challenges.   Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements   Technology Leaders Pioneer Intelligent Solutions Across the UK In energy, Fuse Energy is moving its customer AI onto its own in-house infrastructure, built on NVIDIA B300 Blackwell Ultra, delivering faster, more responsive support to over 450,000 U.K. households. Meanwhile, sovereign AI company Locai Labs released Nemotron-Personas-UK — an open source dataset of one million synthetic personas representing the UK’s demographic, regional and cultural diversity — helping developers build fairer, more representative AI systems. Healthcare In healthcare, OneAdvanced is deploying what it calls the U.K.’s first and most advanced fine-tuned LLM for Primary Care AI-triage — built with NVIDIA Agent Toolkit software and open models — supporting millions of National Health Service patients. Heidi has now integrated NVIDIA Nemotron open models to give clinicians faster access to trusted medical evidence. Speechmatics is deploying Oak, a multilingual medical speech recognition model, using NVIDIA Triton Inference — giving healthcare organizations control over where sensitive patient audio is processed. Apian , Synnovis and NVIDIA are teaming up to use advanced computing and digital simulations using NVIDIA Cosmos to help hospital robots handle the heavy lifting of moving lab samples, freeing up medical staff to focus on patient care. Danaher and NVIDIA are collaborating to advance autonomous science and help accelerate the pace of discovery by bringing accelerated computing, scientific and physical AI into laboratory workflows and instruments. Danaher’s recently announced AI-powered autonomous lab — designed to deliver up to 8x faster discovery of affinity reagents — is using NVIDIA BioNeMo open models within its AI-driven protein design workflows, data and automation technologies that connect design with experimental feedback. Smart Cities On the civic side, Liverpool City Region is building an NVIDIA-powered “City Brain” — a sovereign AI strategy designed as a blueprint for dozens of Unitary Authorities across the U.K. Digital Jersey , Innovation City Belfast and Tees Valley Combined Authority are each exploring how trusted AI compute can serve communities and public services. Financial Services In financial services, LSEG and NVIDIA are bringing GPU-accelerated market analytics to global institutions. Revolut introduced PRAGMA earlier in the year — a foundation model for banking event sequences, pre-trained on 26 million anonymised user histories. PRAGMA has moved from research to real-time scaling. Lloyds Banking Group built ATUM , a transaction foundation model that converts billions of banking transactions into reusable AI. And Starling is developing a banking foundation model trained on Civo’s U.K. sovereign cloud infrastructure. NatWest is collaborating with NVIDIA on Nemotron Voice to better understand how banking customers across the U.K. speak, while Modulr is deploying a network of agents using Nemotron for distinct parts of payment operations. Quantum Quantum is moving from research to systems deployable alongside classical AI, and the U.K. is at the heart of this shift. Riverlane has shown how GPUs can accelerate decoder recalibration workflows used in quantum error correction, helping decoder performance keep pace with real-time changes in quantum hardware behaviour. The work forms part of a broader collaboration exploring how AI, accelerated computing and quantum error-correction technologies can work together to support future quantum systems. ORCA Computing unveiled PT-3, its latest photonic quantum accelerator, at the Digital Realty Innovation Lab , and used it to run the NVIDIA Proteina model for protein design. ORCA found that its hybrid quantum-classical extension improved identifying useful proteins by 20%. Together, these announcements showcase how enterprises, organizations and startups in the U.K. are fostering innovation across the nation. This includes more than 3,100 U.K. companies that are a part of the NVIDIA Inception program for cutting-edge startups. Tune in to NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang’s GTC Berlin keynote on Wednesday, Oct. 21, at 11 a.m. CEST.   Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements

title: European Cities Deploy NVIDIA-Powered AI Agents to Run Smarter Urban Operations
summary: Keeping a city running means making decisions that affect residents every day — from when to repair a road to how to use energy more efficiently. Across the EMEA region, cities and local software, infrastructure and integration partners are using NVIDIA accelerated computing to build physical AI agents and digital twins that help teams make […]
content: Keeping a city running means making decisions that affect residents every day — from when to repair a road to how to use energy more efficiently. Across the EMEA region, cities and local software, infrastructure and integration partners are using NVIDIA accelerated computing to build physical AI agents and digital twins that help teams make those decisions. These applications can anticipate maintenance needs, guide urban planning and make public services more responsive. Software partners including ABA Technology , Akila , Galene AI , Honeywell Technologies , K2K , Linker Vision , Milestone , Onetera , ThinkDeep and Younite AI are using NVIDIA physical and agentic AI to develop solutions for city operations and public services. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/linker-vision.mp4 Video courtesy of Linker Vision and MVRDV. NVIDIA Cosmos open models and the NVIDIA Metropolis Blueprint for video search and summarization (VSS) help agents interpret video and identify conditions, such as traffic congestion, equipment condition, underused spaces and safety hazards, that need attention. NVIDIA Nemotron open models enable developers to build agents that reason over information, respond in natural language and deploy digital twins with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Projects span Belgium, Finland, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Poland, Sweden, the U.K. and elsewhere. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements   In the U.K., the Liverpool City Region , K2K is exploring how to build AI factories using NVIDIA accelerated computing, Cosmos and the VSS blueprint that can support urban planning and public services — testing applications for mobility and safety. The Island of Jersey is working with K2K to strengthen decision-making, mobility and urban planning while advancing clean energy and public services. Innovation City Belfast is exploring a pilot with K2K focused on smart mobility, transport systems, citizen safety and event and response management. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/IKM®-�-Video-GTC-V.10.10.2-compressed.mp4 Video courtesy of K2K. In France, the Department of Côte-d’Or , Akila and ThinkDeep built operations agents that combine sensor, infrastructure and historical data in a sovereign digital twin using NVIDIA Nemotron, Omniverse and accelerated computing, with Cosmos adoption planned for video data. Across more than 500 public buildings, the agents support energy, compliance, safety and climate resilience, and cut document search time from weeks to minutes and reduce total operating costs by 10%, targeting 30% at scale. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Akila-CGCO-compressed.mp4 Video courtesy of Akila. In addition, Port Sud de France in Sète is working with ThinkDeep’s agentic platform that uses Cosmos and Nemotron to analyze cargo and safety data, coordinate operations and guide secure handling of hazardous materials. In Italy’s Milan region, Galene.AI , Dell Technologies and TD Synnex are deploying an NVIDIA-powered, locally operated AI factory, starting with Cinisello Balsamo and planning expansion to four additional municipalities. Services include real-time translation, citizen chatbots and assistance with procurement and funding. These applications aim to simplify administrative work and help people get access to municipal data in seconds versus hours, while keeping local governance of data. At Belgium’s Port of Antwerp-Bruges , Milestone and Dell Technologies are testing how agentic vision AI technologies, using NVIDIA Cosmos and the VSS blueprint, could support complex use cases such as oil-spill warnings by training models with synthetic data to prepare for incidents where real-world data is scarce. In the Nordics, Younite AI is developing a digital twin experience with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for Gothenburg in Sweden as a part of the EU’s Citiverse initiative, focused on helping cities simulate changes and improve accessibility by providing event entrance previews, seating and crowd conditions before arrival. These cities point toward a broader ambition: adapting agentic applications to local needs and extending them across departments and neighboring municipalities and countries such as Poland’s city of Wroclaw. Elsewhere in the region, Honeywell Technologies is deploying Forge Cognition, powered by NVIDIA Nemotron, Cosmos, Omniverse and the VSS blueprint, at the Dubai Fairmont Hotel to connect AI agents with building systems and improve reliability, energy efficiency and operations. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/honeywell.mp4 Video courtesy of Honeywell Technologies. Building the AI Infrastructure for European Cities For European cities, scaling from pilots to everyday operations requires infrastructure that can process local data, customize models and run AI agents. System builders and infrastructure partners including Cisco , Dell Technologies , HPE , Lenovo and Supermicro are packaging NVIDIA accelerated computing, networking and storage into locally operated AI factories. These systems let cities customize and run intelligent applications locally while retaining control of their data, models and operations. Nebius and Net Zero Compute are part of the broader ecosystem building AI factories designed to accelerate deployment and reduce costs for agentic services. EY and Accenture provide the integration and operational expertise to connect applications with city systems. Their work helps cities build repeatable deployment blueprints that they can adapt across departments and expand as local needs grow. Learn how NVIDIA and its ecosystem are bringing physical AI, agentic AI and local AI factories to cities worldwide at Smart City Expo World Congress , running Nov. 3-5 in Barcelona.   Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements

content: Hermes Agent v0.22.0 Release Date: October 13, 2026 Since v0.21.0: ~24,200 commits · ~6,080 merged PRs · ~15,600 files changed · ~2,045,000 insertions · ~1,140,000 deletions · ~7,180 issues closed · ~2,520 contributors The Threshold Release. Hermes was the god of thresholds: the doorway, the crossing, the boundary stone. v0.21.0 assembled the pantheon; v0.22.0 is about getting through the door. A fresh desktop install now opens on a guided setup chat that runs on a free trial model, so a newcomer is talking to Hermes before they own an API key. Connectors carry the agent across into the apps you already use, with no account needed to start. Local models bring it home to your own hardware with a one-click llama.cpp runtime. And the threshold itself got sturdier: tested SemVer stable releases that installs follow by default, signed desktop packages (including the Microsoft Store), and one package manager underneath everything. Around that spine: a 600-plugin catalog, the Claude 5.5 / GPT-6 model wave, password-manager sign-in for the browser, a bot screen you can take over, one backend and one gateway for every profile, and a codebase a third smaller. This is the largest window Hermes has shipped, about 2.5x the v0.21.0 cycle, and it rolls up and fully documents the v0.21.1–v0.21.7 patch releases. ✨ Highlights A first launch that sets itself up — Open the desktop app on a computer where you have never used Hermes and it starts a short setup chat instead of a settings screen. One card at a time it asks your name, an accent color and a layout, which apps to connect, which plugins to install, then gives a quick tour and offers up to four first tasks picked for you. It runs on a free trial model ( nous/welcome , once per OS user), so it needs no key; Skip setup ends it and Settings → Run onboarding again brings it back. The agent also gained set_theme , so "make it violet, dark mode" works in any desktop chat. ( #137429 , #137522 , #137807 , #134209 , #105258 — @alt-glitch , @OutThisLife , @ethernet8023 , @rewbs ) Connectors: Hermes works inside your apps — The agent can now act in hosted apps such as Linear and Notion through the Nous tool gateway: ask for an app, sign in once in your browser, and the tools are usable in the same turn. You do not need a Nous account to start; the first time you use an app, Hermes creates a free connectors-only identity. The desktop has a new Connectors page that puts hosted apps and your MCP servers in one list (it replaces the MCP tab), the same setup card appears in the TUI and CLI, and you can connect several named accounts of one app (a work and a home account) and manage them with /connectors or hermes connectors . ( #106842 , #111008 , #119074 , #135143 , #135072 , #135097 , #135151 , #135173 , #137426 — @alt-glitch , @rewbs ) Local models in one click — Hermes can now run open models entirely on your machine with nothing leaving it: no account, no API key. It installs and maintains llama.cpp with the right engine for your hardware (CPU, CUDA, Metal, Vulkan or ROCm), rates every catalog model against your GPU and RAM, and picks the highest-quality build that fits. Downloads pause and resume, the server starts and stops with Hermes, and engine updates are one click. Start from Settings → Providers → Local Models on Windows, macOS and Linux, or hermes model → Local models in a terminal. The catalog includes Qwen3.8 27B, Qwen3.8 Flash Next (with its MTP speculative head), Qwen3.6 35B-A3B and DeepSeek V4 Flash, plus any GGUF from Hugging Face. ( #100667 , #101823 , #128768 , #111423 , #133111 , #134116 — @jquesnelle , @ethernet8023 ) Stable release channels — Hermes now ships tested SemVer releases. Every release passes source CI, Docker, Nix, signed desktop builds and install/upgrade runs on every OS before it is published, and source installs now move from release to release by default instead of tracking every commit on main . Prefer the bleeding edge? hermes update --set-channel main , or the new channel switch in Desktop Settings → About . Moving to an older release is labelled a rollback and never happens without asking, and installer reruns keep you on the channel you chose. ( #102765 , #135847 , #135949 , #136313 , #137780 — @ethernet8023 , @KoNit-K ) Signed desktop packages, the Microsoft Store, and one package manager — The desktop app is now a sealed, signed package that carries its own Python and Node and updates itself, so first launch builds nothing. Windows gets a signed MSIX (x64 and ARM64) through App Installer or the Microsoft Store; macOS gets a signed, notarized build for Apple Silicon. Underneath, a new unified package manager ( hermes pm ) owns every pinned, hash-checked tool and Python environment: updates build a new environment and switch only once it passes its check, so a failed or killed update can no longer leave you half-applied. ( #102765 , #132361 , #132386 , #120339 , #122221 — @ethernet8023 ) The Plugin Catalog: 600 reviewed plugins — The plugin catalog launched this cycle and grew to 600 entries, each pinned to a reviewed commit and installable from Hermes Desktop or the CLI. Browse by category and star ranking with a page per plugin and per author; catalog rules keep listed plugins from patching Hermes internals or shipping unscannable binaries. Memory providers now live with their makers (Honcho, Supermemory, Hindsight, Mem0, OpenViking, Holographic), as do Home Assistant, Spotify and Langfuse: existing users are migrated automatically, and the default install got leaner. ( #69446 , #111415 , #117808 , #113381 , #114732 , #131267 , #132476 , #136436 — @itpartypattaya , @happy5318 , and 400+ plugin authors) The Claude 5.5 and GPT-6 model wave — Claude Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, Sol and Luna plus GPT-6.1 Sol, and Gemini 4 Argon are pickable on Nous Portal, OpenRouter and native routes where offered. Prior reasoning is now replayed by default on every provider that can read it, across resume, branches and compaction, so long multi-step work keeps its train of thought. And when a provider has a bad hour, Hermes waits out transient 503/529/timeouts in visible, bounded cycles instead of ending your turn. ( #100577 , #119304 , #126842 , #134759 , #128248 , #137955 , #136358 , #116353 — @kshitijk4poor , @unsupportedpastels , @100yenadmin , @mssteuer , @xxxigm ) Sign in to websites with your password manager — The browser agent can log into sites with logins from 1Password, Bitwarden or Hermes's own encrypted vault, and the model never sees the password. If nothing is saved, you get a masked prompt in the CLI, TUI or Desktop to save it, one-time codes are filled without entering the conversation, and card and address fills at checkout need your confirmation. ( #106480 , #107585 , #137084 ) Bot Screen: watch your bot work, take over when it needs you — A bot running on a Linux gateway can have its own desktop that Hermes Desktop streams live. When it hits a login, a 2FA prompt or a CAPTCHA, you take the screen, finish the step yourself, and hand control back while the bot carries on with your session. With a Docker, SSH or Singularity backend, the bot's screen, computer use and the browser run inside the sandbox, never on your host. ( #108914 , #121169 , #121110 ) One backend and one gateway for every profile — Hermes now runs a single messaging gateway and a single desktop backend per machine that serve all of your profiles, instead of one process per profile. Creating a profile makes its bots live without a restart, each profile keeps its own credentials, allowlists, cron jobs and sessions, and hermes update migrates existing per-profile setups automatically. Fewer processes, no token clashes, one thing to start and stop. ( #112854 , #108928 , #118273 , #117983 , #118246 , #118027 ) See and steer your subagents live — Running subagents now stay visible above the composer in the CLI (F6), TUI (Ctrl+T) and Desktop with each child's task, elapsed time and live transcript, plus Steer and Stop buttons. /stop reaches background children and hands back their partial work, and delegate_task can pass screenshots and mocks to vision-capable children. ( #105593 , #115616 , #97689 ) A model picker that knows your plans — Star your favorite models, see a subscription running low ("17% left · resets 3:00 PM") and when a rate limit lifts right in the picker, and pick reasoning effort as part of choosing a model in hermes model , /model ( /model X --reasoning high ) and Desktop. You switch before you hit the wall instead of after. ( #126535 , #133392 , #133408 , #110346 , #113117 — @OutThisLife , @anotherchu ) Hermes in your language, everywhere — Every user-facing string in the CLI, messaging gateway, TUI and Desktop now goes through one translation catalog with full coverage in all 16 bundled languages. New languages can ship as plugins, and any profile can override individual strings with a small YAML file. ( #126296 ) Leaner in every sense — The whole codebase was simplified with zero behavior change: source went from about 1.06M to 698K lines (−34%) and gateway/run.py shrank from 34,847 lines to 5,512. Prompts got lighter too: about 19 rarely used tools now load only when the agent searches for them, roughly halving the desktop tool schema sent on every call, and another ~2.1k tokens came off the fixed prompt. Local models prefill less on every turn. ( #102117 , #97979 , #106676 , #137084 — @alt-glitch ) Small comforts that add up — Opt-in vim keys in the CLI prompt, a git-branch field in the status bar, a bell and desktop notification when Hermes is waiting on you, Ctrl+C that clears your draft instead of killing the turn, an editable /queue , and hermes --native to let your own terminal handle TUI scrollback and search. On Desktop, a new Simple mode turns the app into a plain chat window, and errors now say what went wrong with a one-click fix. ( #106412 , #106434 , #101284 , #101320 , #137065 , #95999 , #121035 , #118587 , #111601 — @saforem2 , @TurgutKural , @glitchbunny0 , @harshmoney123 , @pierrenode , @abhinav11082001-stack , @OutThisLife ) ⚠️ Upgrade notes Python 3.14 is the runtime for managed installs (the package manager installs it for you). KittenTTS is unavailable on 3.14. ( #102765 ) Windows desktop is MSIX-only and needs Windows 11 22H2 or newer; the NSIS/MSI installers are gone. The macOS app is Apple Silicon only in default builds. ( #102765 , #136603 ) One gateway per machine is the default. hermes update folds per-profile gateways into the multiplexed default when nothing conflicts. ( #112854 ) Chats no longer reset on an idle/daily timer. session_reset idle/daily modes are retired (configs that still set them log a warning); /new or /reset starts fresh. ( #105021 , #126244 ) Old sessions are pruned automatically. sessions.auto_prune now defaults to on: ended sessions inactive for 90 days are deleted at startup. Pinned and open sessions are never touched; set sessions.auto_prune: false to keep everything. Memory providers moved to catalog plugins (Honcho, Supermemory, Hindsight, Mem0, OpenViking, Holographic), as did Home Assistant, Spotify and Langfuse. Existing users are migrated on update or first start, with data intact. ByteRover and RetainDB remain bundled. Plugin authors: the old plugin compatibility import layer is gone ( #126164 ), hermes sync (Skill Sync) was removed ( #132465 ), and the bundled tirith scanner was removed ( #133832 ). Several tools were renamed ( todo → todo_list , cronjob → cronjob_manage , process → process_manage ); the old names still work. ( #97979 ) 🚪 Onboarding, Free Tier, Connectors & Local Models First-run onboarding Guided setup chat on a fresh desktop install (see Highlights) . Existing installs and remote (SSH, URL, Cloud) backends don't get it automatically; the old setup-profile flow and /initiate-setup are deleted. ( #137420 , #134215 , #108292 — @alt-glitch , @ethernet8023 , @OutThisLife ) The agent can restyle the app — The new set_theme tool sets the accent (a swatch or any #rrggbb ), light/dark/system mode and layout, or shows a picker; "make it violet" works in any desktop chat. ( #137522 — @alt-glitch ) Nous free tier A free model for your first desktop launch — A first desktop install with no provider or Nous account gets the free nous/welcome model as a one-time trial (once per OS user), so onboarding needs no key. The CLI, TUI and gateway get no account or free model. HERMES_GUEST_ONBOARDING is gone. ( #137807 , #105258 , #105260 — @alt-glitch ) Sign in and keep your apps — hermes auth upgrade , or /login in any chat or messaging DM, upgrades the free identity to a full Nous account with your connected apps. ( #105259 , #105261 — @alt-glitch ) Clear limits — The free rate limit ends the turn at once with the reset time; every free-tier failure has a code and a plain sentence; the app handles the account service's browser check; free-tier users see a Terms and Privacy notice. Nous accounts without credits can pick models billed to a subscription they hold and get free managed fast web search. ( #134049 , #111970 , #133824 , #117079 — @alt-glitch , @kshitijk4poor , @rewbs ) Connectors Hosted app connectors, the Connectors page and several accounts per app (see Highlights) . Connector tools can also send your local files as attachments and save the files they return. nous.guest: false turns guest identities off; tools.connectors.enabled: false turns connectors off. ( #111238 , #138014 — @alt-glitch ) One connect flow everywhere — Hosted apps and local MCP servers share one setup card (desktop dialog, TUI callout or CLI panel), and the agent can use new tools in the same turn. On desktop, manage_connections can show a browsable app directory. ( #111008 , #109517 , #137426 — @alt-glitch ) Local models One-click local models (see Highlights) . Also: Hugging Face GGUF downloads with pause/resume, and a one-time setup offer after onboarding on machines that can run the recommended model. ( #129506 — @alt-glitch ) Engine updates and wider GPU support — An Update now prompt updates the engine in one click. NVIDIA on Linux gets CUDA, AMD and Intel GPUs get Vulkan sized by their own memory, and every backend runs llama.cpp b11370. ( #111423 , #133111 , #131782 — @jquesnelle , @skyecon , @mbeattietex1-star , @Belaquaa ) Better recommendations — Only models that fit fully in GPU memory are recommended, and the 27B no longer on hardware that runs it poorly. Qwen3.8 Flash Next with its MTP head fits 128 GB machines; NVIDIA Spark recommendations are tuned. ( #108429 , #135438 , #134116 , #112107 — @jquesnelle , @RyanUnderhill ) Your own local servers — LM Studio has a provider profile, Ollama pickers no longer flicker, a self-started llama.cpp server shows up in /model , and fallback to the desktop-managed model works. ( #134320 , #113129 , #116679 , #131795 — @kshitijk4poor , @DaxLee9988 , @fangliquanflq , @Finn763 , @albeight ) 📦 Stable Releases, Desktop Packages & Package Manager Stable releases & update channels Tested SemVer stable releases and the channel switch (see Highlights) . v0.21.6 and v0.21.7 were the first through the new gate; forks stay on main , and an install ahead of the newest release waits for the next. Lighter update checks — one GitHub API call a day replaces git fetch every 30 minutes. ( #107648 ) Desktop bundles & the Microsoft Store Sealed, signed desktop packages (see Highlights) . In a package, hermes update points to the right updater (App Installer, Store or macOS). ( #134911 ) Packaged installs work end to end — the agent's terminal runs hermes , Uninstall explains OS removal, and Python-dependency plugins install inside MSIX. ( #134051 , #135333 — @alt-glitch ) Unified package manager hermes pm (see Highlights) : pinned, hash-checked Python 3.14, uv, Node, ripgrep, FFmpeg, Chromium and Git/Bash on Windows, with hermes pm doctor|status|repair|gc . Contributors use source ./activate (or .ps1 / .fish ). Dependency environments are generations — new ones are checked before use, so a failed install keeps the working one; updates and hermes pm gc reclaim old ones (92 GB to 18 GB on one host). ( #124968 , #133808 — @JoaoMarcos44 ) Optional features install on first use — opt-in SDKs (Anthropic, Bedrock) load mid-session without a restart; security.allow_lazy_installs: false turns this off. ( #122221 — @ethernet8023 ) Plugins declare Python dependencies — resolved with core across profiles; conflicts are refused, and updates disable a plugin that no longer fits. Hindsight, Honcho, Supermemory, Mem0 and Home Assistant moved to the catalog and auto-install where used. ( #113851 , #122103 , #114569 , #132469 — @ethernet8023 ) Install & update Updates can't half-apply (see Highlights) . A killed update repairs itself on the next launch. ( #132361 , #120339 ) Faster updates, smaller checkouts — updates rebuild only what changed (16.5 s vs 32.5 s on macOS), clones are blobless, and partial-clone .git growth is fixed. ( #135092 , #133016 , #131679 — @kshitijk4poor , @ethernet8023 , @liuhao1024 , @whyyagswhy ) Small, hash-checked installers — install.sh / install.ps1 verify pinned uv and Git, hand off to PM, log to logs/install.log , and now work on musl Linux (Alpine, Void), Windows 10 and Unicode Windows paths. ( #124964 , #125598 , #132430 — @JoaoMarcos44 , @kshitijk4poor , @Finn763 , @OutThisLife ) Failures say why — with opt-in telemetry, install, update, skill and plugin failures record a reason. ( #133809 ) Docker / Nix / Termux / Windows Docker — pinned Debian 13 base with full Chromium; stable / latest move only on a published release; baked-in extras return after a restart. ( #135726 , #135084 — @unsupportedpastels ) Nix, Termux, Windows — Nix shares the pins; its desktop app gets Wayland; Termux moves to a signed APT package ( pkg upgrade hermes-agent ), though its docs still warn it is broken; Windows updates finish while the old runtime is in use. ( #128144 , #122146 , #131779 — @ethernet8023 , @janviernine ) CI & release engineering Release gates — E2E suites run on release builds, the full suite on native Windows, and SSH/Docker backends against real daemons. ( #135409 , #96458 , #136602 — @ethernet8023 ) 🧠 Providers & Models New providers Providers as plugins — ACP and CLI-driven providers install out of tree via hermes plugins install ; --provider chatgpt picks ChatGPT Codex OAuth. ( #101456 , #115761 — @AlexanderPrendota , @DarRahman ) Provider upgrades — Bedrock serves GPT-6 (1M) and enforces Claude Guardrails; Azure Foundry lists deployments; Gemini takes full JSON Schema tools; OpenCode Go routes Claude via Messages. ( #133573 , #107815 , #115770 , #98928 , #134848 — @victor-kyriazakos , @JoaoMarcos44 , @xxxigm , @thejpanganiban , @pandacooming ) New knobs — agent.text_verbosity sets Responses answer length; named custom providers run on the Codex app-server. title: v2.1.299
summary: What's changed Added CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_FILE_MENTIONS environment variable: Claude gets the paths of @ file mentions to read with its file tools, not the files' contents Added idle compaction in the terminal: a 200K+ token conversation left idle for about 54 minutes is compacted before its one-hour prompt cache expires, so your next message doesn't reprocess it all Added CLAUDE_CODE_IDLE_COMPACT_MIN_TOKENS to change idle compaction's 200K-token minimum; "idleCompaction": false in...
content: What's changed Added CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_FILE_MENTIONS environment variable: Claude gets the paths of @ file mentions to read with its file tools, not the files' contents Added idle compaction in the terminal: a 200K+ token conversation left idle for about 54 minutes is compacted before its one-hour prompt cache expires, so your next message doesn't reprocess it all Added CLAUDE_CODE_IDLE_COMPACT_MIN_TOKENS to change idle compaction's 200K-token minimum; "idleCompaction": false in settings.json turns it off. Both need v2.1.290 or later Added $.prompt.media so a prompt.submit hook of a mod installed by managed settings can read the bytes of an image or document attached to the prompt Added $.session.identity() for mods installed by managed settings: how the session is signed in, and its organization and email when managed forceLoginOrgUUID lists that organization Added size , weight , mono and tabular to a mod's Text and named spacing steps ( xs to xl ) to its Box ; bold is deprecated in favor of weight Added --shutdown-drain-sec to claude self-hosted-runner orchestrator : on SIGTERM it stops polling and gives the poll in flight and running spawn hooks up to that many seconds to finish Added the skill's frontmatter, source, plugin name and file path to what a mod's skill.prompt hook receives Added /effort and /fast in agent view to set what new sessions start with; a bare /model , /effort or /fast there now opens a picker Added a "safe mode" line to the agents view peek panel for background sessions started with --safe-mode Added a one-time note when plan mode won't ask before most edits or commands because bypass permissions is available Added --disallow-tools and a disallowed_tools case field to claude plugin eval to keep specific built-in tools, such as Agent, out of eval runs Added support for turning off the attribution block in Claude Desktop's Code tab: set CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER=0 in the env of a Claude apps gateway's code policy Added a field to the attribution block in Claude Code sessions behind a Claude apps gateway; remove the block with CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER=0 Added a queue door to the session.append mod hook, so a mod can make the transcript's queue records differ from the prompt as sent Added a note in /plugin and claude plugin validate naming a mod's hooks that are skipped where an organization manages Claude Code Added /usage warnings for max effort, workflows, always-on context and large tool results Fixed the error for a denied cloud session, which could point to the wrong organization when a key from apiKeyHelper was in use Fixed sessions on a gateway-specific model name behind a custom ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL ending with "Prompt is too long · automatic compaction failed" near 200K tokens instead of sending the request Fixed a mod that submits a prompt at the end of every turn keeping a headless run going past --max-turns , --max-budget-usd , an interrupt, or the end of the host's conversation Fixed cloud sessions sometimes showing the model's follow-up text after a tool group's one-line label Fixed the Write and Edit tools creating a mod in a session's mods folder without asking in accept-edits mode when the config directory's path has no .claude in it Fixed installed mods that kept running in an open session after being turned off remotely; they now unload between turns Fixed Edit and Retry in Cowork and claude.ai cloud sessions failing on a message stopped while its UserPromptSubmit or mod prompt.submit hooks were still running (regression in 2.1.296) Fixed an agent teammate started without a description keeping part of a credential from its prompt in the task description shown for it Fixed the claude.ai view of a Remote Control or cloud session freezing when a large batch of events could not finish uploading over a slow connection Fixed a sandboxed shell command being able to write into a --plugin-dir folder, whose code Claude Code reloads and runs outside the sandbox Fixed memory growth under heavy debug logging ( --debug , --debug-file ), and a hang on exit when the debug log is on a disk or network mount that stops accepting writes Fixed memory growing without bound when debug output goes to stderr and the parent process stops reading it Fixed rm prompts on shell -c scripts that don't run rm . An rm built at run time in a script Claude Code can't read no longer prompts unless CLAUDE_CODE_STRICT_INLINE_SHELL_RM_PROMPT=1 Fixed double-clicking a word in an expanded transcript row in fullscreen mode collapsing the row instead of selecting the word Fixed claude mcp list , claude doctor and /status reporting an empty .mcp.json as invalid Fixed /btw jumping the transcript to the bottom when asked while scrolled up in fullscreen Fixed sandboxed commands failing on WSL2 with bwrap: Can't mkdir /mnt/c/Program Files/ClaudeCode when the sandbox can write to the Windows drive Fixed scheduled wakeups (ScheduleWakeup) not firing while a background task was running in Agent SDK, IDE and claude remote-control sessions Fixed a mod's prompt.submit rewrite being silently dropped, sending the prompt as typed, for some prompts with a pasted image or an image that can't be read Fixed a Remote Control prompt being lost when another queued prompt in the same batch failed to deliver Fixed a Remote Control prompt that had passed its hooks being dropped from prompt history when Stop interrupted the next queued prompt's hook Fixed sign-in, MCP servers and project trust appearing lost on Linux after a sandboxed command left an empty .config.json in the config directory Fixed /sandbox reporting success when its setting could not be saved because the project folder is not writable; it now says nothing changed and why Fixed SDK and headless sessions staying in auto mode after the host switched to a model that doesn't support auto mode Fixed MCP servers named constructor or prototype in an MCP config never being connected Fixed tools of an MCP server named constructor or toString asking for permission in auto mode and bypass permissions mode Fixed a spurious "synced[0] commands mod's hot reload ignoring a fix saved right after a failed reload; saving a mod file without changing it no longer reloads the mod Fixed mods loaded from source files being refused when a hook hands $ queued prompts sent as content blocks over --input-format stream-json running together without a line break when merged into one turn Fixed self-hosted runner sessions shutting down MCP servers added grading and makes the suite exit 1 Fixed permission prompts cutting off or wrapping too early when the reason text contains keycap or joined emoji Fixed forceLoginOrgUUID and forceLoginMethod from MDM side questions in non-interactive sessions not being cancelled when the session ends, and running a second time when the same request arrived again mid-run Fixed sandboxed commands on macOS being able to read or write a denied path by its real location when the denied path passes through a symlink Fixed sandbox denyRead and allowRead globs with braces, parentheses or backslashes in a folder's name being read differently by Claude Code's settings checks than by the sandbox Fixed sandbox glob allowRead and allowWrite entries not being re-checked when the directory they start from is replaced by a symlink Fixed worktree-isolated sessions accepting some awk programs the isolation guard should refuse Fixed claude mcp add -- --background being started as a background session Fixed a prompt or reply of --bg or --background to a background session being taken for the flag, which could start new sessions over and over instead of delivering it Fixed a custom slash command's embedded shell line
