ref storage Fixed claude self-hosted-runner sessions using Anthropic-managed git showing tracked files as staged deletions when starting in a reused clone whose remote is still empty Fixed Ultracode not being announced to scheduled tasks and other delivered headless turns when ultracode is on in settings Fixed MCP OAuth sign-in, token refresh and sign-out not sending configured headers / headersHelper values, which broke servers behind an authenticating proxy Fixed the Artifact tool reporting a spurious one-line difference against the live page, and refusing the publish, when a large page with a line break after is published again unchanged Fixed $.ui.open reporting a mod's pane as placed in sessions where no surface draws it, such as Claude Code for VS Code and claude -p Fixed the agent.spawn mod hook not running when a finished subagent or a killed teammate is resumed: the hook's event now carries resume , and a mod can refuse it Fixed claude plugin validate rejecting a mod's $.state references when plugin.json has no types key and the contract is at ./types/index.d.ts Fixed a mod's dimColor text looking the same as plain text under the dark ANSI theme and on 16-color terminals Fixed plan mode running a write (an MCP tool's, a file's, a shell command's) that a PreToolUse hook or a mod's tool.check hook allowed Fixed background subagents in auto mode sometimes sending their final report twice, once as the result and once as a message Fixed SendMessage not finding a subagent by name after the CLI restarted and resumed the session (names given before the last compaction still need the agent ID) Fixed replies cut off at the output token limit ending the turn silently, with no retry or error, after a request fell back to non-streaming mode Fixed Read garbling UTF-16LE files with a byte-order mark, and Write dropping byte-order marks or silently converting Windows-1252, Shift-JIS, GBK or UTF-16BE files to UTF-8 (now refused) Fixed cloud sessions sometimes leaving a message unanswered when the worker was replaced right after a compaction Fixed cloud sessions and CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_INTERRUPTED_TURN sometimes answering a finished turn again after a restart, when a tool ended the turn and a skill loaded in the same step Fixed photos sent over Remote Control being dropped when their copy could not be saved on your computer; Claude now still sees the photo Fixed files sent over Remote Control sometimes not arriving in long-running sessions Fixed files of 30 to 35 MiB sent over Remote Control or to a cloud session not arriving Fixed a user-installed mod's $.env.set changing the environment or shell prefix that command hooks from managed settings start with Windows: Fixed the process-liveness check leaving orphaned PowerShell processes behind on busy machines until memory ran out Windows: Fixed PreToolUse and PermissionRequest hooks that set no shell failing open when Git for Windows isn't installed; a guard that fails now blocks the call Windows: Fixed Bash commands failing with "command not found" for a whole session when Git Bash did not report its PATH at startup Self-hosted runner: Improved what setup and doctor say when the runner's machine has no git credentials Self-hosted runner: Fixed sessions that wrote output before their first turn being left with no release timer, ignoring --retire-at and delaying shutdown Improved the error shown when a cloud session is refused because your claude.ai login was rejected or has expired: it now tells you to sign in again with claude auth login Improved enforcement of managed permission rules, managed hooks and organization MCP tool names against user-installed mods Improved memory and disk use when PDFs are @-mentioned: their bytes are no longer kept in the session transcript Improved sandboxed Bash on Linux: Esc and Ctrl-C now work while wildcard read rules are being expanded for a command Improved the startup warning for an unrecognized model ID: it is now one short line under the welcome banner with a docs link, instead of a long raw message Improved the plugin-authoring skill's steps for sharing a mod: Claude asks public or private and checks the files before creating a GitHub repository Improved the Skill tool's "Unknown skill" error to suggest a skill's listed name when Claude wrongly adds the anthropic-skills: prefix to it Improved /reload-skills to say it re-sends the full skill list to Claude, which is how to get skills back after compaction Improved the error shown when a worktree cannot be created because its base commit does not resolve: it now says how the lookup ended and the likely reasons, such as a repository without a commit Improved the error for creating a worktree at a bare-repository layout's root: it now explains the layout instead of an unrelated git error Improved artifact watching: a local session can now watch up to 25 published artifacts at once, up from 10 Improved background agent notifications: they now say when an agent is only waiting on its own background work, got a message too late for its result, or was stopped by a usage limit Changed plugin hooks and workflow scripts to refuse values they hand back that nest deeper than 28,000 levels, with an error naming the limit (workflow scripts allowed 100,000) Changed actions a plugin hook can block to be refused, not let through, when the hook cannot be handed them or cannot hand back its answer; a tool that already ran has its result withheld Changed requests to claude.ai's connector proxy and to Anthropic-hosted MCP servers to no longer follow HTTP redirects; redirects by a connector's own server are unaffected Changed MCP requests in cloud and self-hosted runner sessions to no longer follow HTTP redirects from the session's MCP proxy Changed skill and command loading: one whose file or folder name has hidden, direction-changing or blank-like characters, or > is no longer offered until renamed; such a name: is ignored Changed ui.render trees in claude plugin test : each mod's Box or Text root now carries part: { plugin } naming the mod, so exact-tree assertions must include it Changed WebFetch page reads to pick their effort as web searches do: the caller's level on the caller's own model, otherwise the level settings give the small model Changed claude plugin test to fail a call to a mod's served $ method that has not answered within ten seconds, as a session does Changed MCP allow rules to reach only the server they name: mcp__a no longer allows a server named a__b or a_ ; write mcp__ __* with the server's whole normalized name Changed agent tools: lists to take only the named MCP server's tools; list a server whose name contains __ as mcp__ __* Changed Claude in Chrome in Cowork cloud sessions outside auto mode: an approved-site action the safety classifier flags now asks you instead of being refused, unless managed settings apply Changed cloud session and Remote Control MCP connectors to negotiate MCP protocol version 2026-07-28 by default on installs that fetch no flags; MCP_PROTOCOL_NEGOTIATION=legacy opts out Changed MCP tool descriptions and server instructions from Anthropic's first-party MCP servers at api.anthropic.com to reach Claude in full instead of being cut at 4,096 characters Changed auto mode in Cowork cloud sessions: a PermissionRequest hook can no longer approve shell commands or subagents; those prompts wait or are denied Changed the resume command printed at exit: it names the session by its ID and no longer by its name, so that nothing in a session name can run when the line is pasted Changed the resume command printed at exit of a worktree session: it uses -w and -r if the long flags do not fit the terminal. If neither fits a kept worktree, rows above it say where to run it Changed /btw side questions in non-interactive sessions to return a timeout error when still unanswered after 11 minutes Changed UserPromptSubmit hooks to run before a skill or custom slash command expands, so a hook that blocks the prompt now also stops its embedded shell commands Changed a skill's own front-matter UserPromptSubmit hook to first run on the prompt after the one that invokes the skill Changed the turn.start mod hook to also hear subagents' and teammates' turns, not only the main loop's; tell them apart by e.agentId (absent on the main loop) Changed the errors shown when /ultrareview can't upload a repository to stop suggesting git add . , which could stage or commit untracked files such as .env Changed the cyber safeguard notice to no longer ask people to apply to the Cyber Verification Program [VSCode] Fixed an unsent prompt and its attachments being lost when switching to another session and back [VSCode] Fixed unused blank chats keeping a background Claude process running after starting a new conversation [VSCode] Fixed the mic button showing an internal error message when you are signed out of claude.ai; it now offers to sign you in [VSCode] Improved startup time in workspaces without a Python environment by starting Claude while the Python extension loads [VSCode] Improved startup: the model picker and slash command menu now fill in right away in a new window on a folder you've opened before [Cloud sessions] Fixed a memory spike that could crash a session when many of its existing output files were re-sent to it at once [Cloud sessions] Fixed saving an edited routine silently moving it to a different environment when its own had been deleted or wasn't in the list; the routine now keeps its environment [Cloud sessions] Fixed Sessions search in a self-hosted environment's admin details finding nothing when you paste the session ID from a session's link [Cloud sessions] Fixed the Sessions and Runners lists in a self-hosted environment's admin details saying the list is empty when a search just has no matches [Cloud sessions] Improved the deploy command shown when you create a self-hosted environment or environment key: it shows in full, wraps between arguments, and has a visible copy button [Cloud sessions] Changed deleting a self-hosted environment to turn off its routines right away, with the reason shown on each routine, instead of leaving their runs to fail [Remote Control] Fixed Remote Control sessions whose computer can't be reached still appearing to send your messages; your text now stays in the box and Send is off until it reconnects [Claude Tag] Added the ability for Claude in Slack to delete a canvas it created in a channel when someone asks it to [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude in Slack staying silent on untagged posts that a channel's own instructions tell it to answer, such as posts that tag someone else, in channels with guests [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude in Slack reporting a reply to another channel's thread as posted when it isn't a member there; it now says the reply wasn't delivered and how to fix that [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude in Slack sometimes ending a turn without posting its answer when a self-hosted runner's image has no python3 [Claude Tag] Changed how Claude in Slack corrects a message it got wrong: it edits the message in place and adds a short "Edited" note instead of striking through the old text [Claude Tag] Changed Claude in Slack to join channels with more than 100 members quietly, with no intro message [Code Review] Fixed Code Review's monthly spend-limit comment and check-run card sending admins to Claude Code settings; they now link the Usage page, where that limit is set

title: Building agents that transact with Anchor Browser and AgentCore payments
summary: Learn how the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center Partner Agent Factory and Anchor Browser built AI agents that autonomously pay for x402-protected web resources and APIs. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments checks budgets, signs transactions, and retries requests without exposing wallet credentials to the agent runtime.
content: AI agents increasingly need to access web resources that are priced per request. For example, premium datasets charge by the query, research APIs meter by the call, and paywalled publishers gate content behind payment. When an AI agent encounters one of these resources, the server returns HTTP 402 Payment Required. The agent has no built-in payment mechanism, no budget attached to the session, and no programmatic way to satisfy the request. The task stalls and requires manual intervention. Anchor Browser with Agentic Payments handles machine-to-machine payment workflows on behalf of the agent. Developed in collaboration with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center Partner Agent Factory , it’s now available on AWS Marketplace . This post covers how Anchor Browser integrates with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments so that AI agents can pay for x402-protected pages and APIs autonomously. The x402 protocol is an open standard for HTTP-based machine-to-machine payments. A server responds with 402 Payment Required along with the amount, accepted payment methods, and payment address that the agent uses to complete the transaction. Anchor Browser is a cloud-based browser automation solution purpose-built for AI agents. Each agent session runs inside a managed browser environment that maintains authentication state, handles navigation, captures network requests, and provides a live view of page interactions. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides capabilities to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments is a fully managed capability within AgentCore that AI agents can use to discover, access, and pay for APIs, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and web content autonomously. AgentCore payments manages wallet connectivity, enforces configurable spending limits at the infrastructure layer, and processes payments through the x402 protocol. It also provides observability into payment attempts, approvals, denials, and settlements through Amazon CloudWatch. When an agent running in Anchor Browser encounters a 402 response, AgentCore payments authorizes and completes the transaction within the configured budget. The workflow continues without interruption. Challenges When an autonomous agent encounters an x402-protected resource, the workflow stalls. The agent makes a request, such as fetching a premium research report or calling a paid data enrichment API, and the server responds with HTTP 402 Payment Required. Without a mechanism to pay, the task that was supposed to run autonomously now requires human intervention. Today, developers must build the entire payment stack. This effort spans four categories of complexity: Payment protocol handling Detecting and parsing the 402 challenge from the HTTP response, and distinguishing payment-required responses from other 4xx errors. Constructing the correct payment header with the cryptographic proof in the exact format the merchant expects. Supporting multiple payment schemes (exact, upto, and protocol variants) without hardcoding vendor-specific logic into the agent. Maintaining compatibility across x402 merchant implementations that might vary in challenge format, supported stablecoins, or settlement timing. Security and key management Storing a private key to sign payments, requiring secure key storage within an environment exposed to untrusted inputs. Managing wallet lifecycle operations, including key rotation, credential refresh, and provider failover. Operational resilience Resubmitting the original request with the payment header while preserving session state, cookies, and request context. Providing idempotency, which is essential for wallet operations. Enforcing per-session and per-transaction spend limits with real-time budget tracking across concurrent agent executions. Observability and compliance Capturing every payment attempt, approval, denial, and settlement in audit logs for compliance and reconciliation. Without a managed payment service, the agent must internalize the entire payment stack. On every x402-protected call that returns a 402 response, the agent must orchestrate the full payment flow internally, including: Signing the proof. Attaching the correct header. Retrying the request. Settling the transaction. Logging the result. Each of these steps requires custom code that developers must build, secure, and maintain. Figure 1 illustrates this architecture. The agent contains eight tightly coupled components (Wallet, Private Keys, Budget Controls, Sign Proof, Attach Header, Retry Logic, Settle Payment, and Logging). The agent connects to an x402 API with a 402 challenge flowing back and a retry flowing forward. Figure 1: Agent payment stack The security considerations extend beyond the engineering effort. Uncontrolled spending. Without hard spending limits enforced at the infrastructure level, a bug, retry loop, prompt injection, or inadvertent access can trigger unintended payments. An agent retrying a paid endpoint in a loop continues to authorize payments until manual intervention occurs. Key exposure. When private keys reside inside the agent runtime, they share an execution environment with untrusted web pages, third-party tools, and external dependencies. These vectors might inadvertently disclose the credentials that control real funds. Signing flow exposure. If the signing infrastructure is accessible from the runtime, a threat actor can attempt to access the key or redirect payments to an address under unauthorized control. Effective mitigation requires that the key doesn’t enter the runtime in the first place. Browser-based agents introduce an additional constraint: the payment must occur within the same browser session. Otherwise, session recordings and live view no longer match what actually executed. Solution Anchor Browser and AgentCore payments address this complexity by moving the entire payment stack into managed infrastructure. Unlike a stateless tool call, Anchor Browser provides a real cloud browser with persistent identity, repeatable and deterministic workflows, and the session context needed to log in, navigate, and finish tasks reliably. Authentication, navigation, network requests, recordings, and live view happen inside the same browser session. When a payment is required, the transaction happens within that session. The recording captures the full sequence from request to 402 to payment to content delivery. Anchor agents include a built-in x402 tool that handles paid API calls natively within the browser context. The built-in tool requires no changes to existing Playwright, Puppeteer, or Chrome DevTools Protocol-based workflows. AgentCore payments serves as the payment layer. At the center of the service is the Payment Manager, the top-level resource that coordinates payment operations for the AWS account. Creating a Payment Manager requires specifying an authorizer type and an IAM role. AgentCore then provisions a corresponding workload identity in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity. The remaining components connect the Payment Manager to external wallet infrastructure: A PaymentConnector integrates the Payment Manager with an external wallet provider, either Coinbase Developer Platform (Coinbase CDP) or Stripe Privy. A PaymentCredentialProvider stores wallet provider credentials securely in AgentCore Identity. A PaymentInstrument identifies the specific wallet address from which funds are drawn. Anchor Browser sets up wallets through AgentCore payments using a supported wallet provider, without placing wallet secrets or private keys inside the agent runtime. AgentCore payments handles wallet operations through the configured provider. For endpoint discovery, AgentCore provides a curated Coinbase x402 Bazaar MCP server through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway , so agents can discover available pay-per-use x402 endpoints programmatically. AgentCore payments restructures the payment architecture. Sensitive operations move out of the agent runtime and into a managed service layer. The Anchor Agent holds only two payment-related components: a budget session and the x402 tool. The infrastructure, including authentication, wallet secrets, payment limits, observability, and payment proof signing, resides in the AgentCore payments layer. Figure 2 shows the Anchor Agent connecting to the AgentCore payments managed layer, which handles wallet provider integration with Coinbase CDP or Stripe Privy. Figure 2: Anchor Browser integrates with AgentCore payments How the payment flow works The following steps describe what happens end to end, from the moment a browser session encounters an x402-protected resource to the moment the agent receives the response and continues the task. Anchor Browser creates a dedicated AgentCore PaymentSession for the browser session. When the session starts with x402 turned on, Anchor Browser provisions a PaymentSession through AgentCore payments, linking the browser session to a configured payment instrument and budget. The browser receives an HTTP 402 Payment Required response. The agent navigates to a URL or makes a fetch or XMLHttpRequest (XHR) request. The merchant responds with a 402 challenge specifying the amount, accepted payment methods, and payment address. The browser selects a compatible payment method. Anchor Browser reads the 402 challenge payload and matches the requested payment method against the instrument linked to the PaymentSession. AgentCore verifies the session budget and generates the cryptographic payment proof. AgentCore payments validates that the payment amount falls within the session spending limit. The service then signs the transaction using the configured wallet provider (Coinbase CDP or Stripe Privy) and returns the cryptographic proof. No key material enters the browser or agent runtime. The browser retries the original request with the payment header. The browser attaches the signed proof as PAYMENT-SIGNATURE for x402 v2 or X-PAYMENT for x402 v1, then retries the original request exactly once. The merchant verifies and settles the payment, then returns the protected resource. The merchant validates the cryptographic proof, settles the transaction on-chain, and serves the content. The agent continues the task. Wallet credentials remain with AgentCore and the configured wallet provider throughout this flow. Prerequisites Before you begin, make sure that you have a valid Anchor Browser API key ( ANCHOR_API_KEY ). To create one, see the Anchor Browser Quick Start guide. Setting up automatic x402 payments Setting up agentic payments for Anchor Browser requires one session property. Set session.x402 to true . The property defaults to false . When enabled, the browser session can automatically access x402-protected websites with payments signed by AgentCore payments and retried inside the same browser session. Enabling session.x402 authorizes the browser to make real payments from the configured payment instrument. The following examples show how to create a payment-enabled session for Anchor Browser using cURL and JavaScript: cURL curl --request POST --url https://api.anchorbrowser.io/v1/sessions --header "anchor-api-key: $ANCHOR_API_KEY" --header "content-type: application/json" --data '{"session":{"x402":true}}' JavaScript const response = await fetch('https://api.anchorbrowser.io/v1/sessions', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'anchor-api-key': process.env.ANCHOR_API_KEY, 'content-type': 'application/json', }, body: JSON.stringify({ session: { x402: true } }), }); const { data: session } = await response.json(); console.log(session.cdp_url); After connected through Chrome DevTools Protocol, the agent navigates normally. You don’t need to include a wallet key or payment header in your automation code. The browser handles 402 challenges, payment signing, and retries transparently for document navigation, fetch, and XHR requests. Payment session limits and behavior Anchor Browser enforces the following guardrails at the session level through AgentCore payments integration. Each payment-ready browser session operates within configured spending and time constraints. For specific limits, refer to the Anchor Browser technical documentation . If the merchant response is malformed, no compatible network is offered, the budget is exhausted, or AgentCore payments rejects the payment, the browser returns the original 402 response to the page unchanged. Your automation code can then handle the 402 as a standard HTTP error. The x402 session property controls payments to third-party resources only. The property doesn’t replace Anchor credits and doesn’t pay for the browser session. Automation code for Anchor Browser Your automation code for Anchor Browser remains unchanged. The following example demonstrates that no payment-specific code is required: const { chromium } = require('playwright'); // Connect to the x402-enabled session via CDP const browser = await chromium.connectOverCDP(session.cdp_url); const page = await browser.newPage(); // Navigate to an x402-protected resource exactly as with a free page await page.goto('https://premium-research.example.com/market-report'); // The page loaded, the payment was handled automatically // Extract content as normal const content = await page.textContent('article'); No wallet logic, no payment header construction, and no retry code. The agent navigates to the URL. If the server returns 402, Anchor Browser coordinates with AgentCore payments to sign the payment proof, retries the request with the appropriate payment header, and delivers the content to the page. Your automation code receives the final rendered page with no indication that a payment occurred. This pattern applies uniformly to paywalled journalism, licensed financial data, gated API documentation, metered research databases, and other resources that gate content behind a 402 challenge. Using the built-in x402 tool for API calls Paid resources aren’t limited to web pages. Many are APIs that expect POST, PUT, or other HTTP methods. Common examples include data enrichment services, premium inference endpoints, and licensed content APIs. For these use cases, Anchor Browser agents include a built-in x402 tool that you call like a standard HTTPS API within the browser context. Your agent makes the API call through fetch or XHR. If the server returns a 402 challenge, the browser coordinates payment signing through AgentCore payments and retries the request with the signed payment header. Your code receives the response as though the endpoint were free. The tool isn’t tied to a specific vendor, model, or framework. Payment operates as a session-level capability beneath your existing tooling, and no changes to agent code are required. // Fetch call to a paid API endpoint within the x402-enabled session const response = await page.evaluate(async () => { const res = await fetch('https://data-enrichment.example.com/api/v1/enrich', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify({ company_domain: 'example.com' }), }); return res.json(); }); // If the API returned 402, AgentCore handled payment automatically // The response contains the enriched data console.log(response); Your automation code doesn’t receive wallet credentials. Automatic payments are available only when session.x402 is set to true and remain subject to the spending and expiration limits described in the previous section. Key benefits This integration moves payment from application code to the infrastructure layer: No payment infrastructure to build. No wallet SDK to integrate, no 402 response parser to write, no retry loop to implement, no header construction logic to maintain, and no custom audit logging to build. AgentCore payments manages the entire payment stack. No changes to existing tooling. Playwright scripts, Puppeteer automations, Chrome DevTools Protocol commands, and agent flows in Anchor Browser continue to function exactly as before. Payment is a session capability attached to the browser, not a modification to agent logic, prompts, or tool definitions. Private keys don’t enter the runtime. Signing and settlement happen inside AgentCore payments. The service communicates with Coinbase CDP or Stripe Privy through secure credential storage in AgentCore Identity. The agent runtime doesn’t have access to key material that can move funds. Budgets are enforced at the infrastructure level. Every session operates within defined spend limits that AgentCore enforces before authorizing a payment. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Observability provides full payment audit trails through Amazon CloudWatch. When a session reaches the spending limit, AgentCore payments denies the payment. Paid tasks complete successfully. Paid GET pages load. Paid API calls return responses. The agent completes the workflow rather than stopping at a 402 response and requiring manual intervention. Billing is consolidated. Anchor Browser settles third-party x402 charges in credits on the same invoice as browser session time. There’s no separate crypto custody to manage, no USDC balance to monitor, and no on-chain settlement for the finance team to reconcile. Conclusion Anchor Browser, integrated with AgentCore payments, equips AI agents to handle x402 payment challenges autonomously for paywalled web pages and paid API endpoints. Wallet credentials stay out of agent code, and no custom payment infrastructure is required. As more of the web moves to per-request pricing, agents that lack a payment mechanism can’t complete tasks involving paid resources. This integration addresses that gap: agents complete paid workflows end to end, operating within defined budgets, with full observability through AgentCore Observability, and without cryptographic key material in the runtime. To get started, explore the following resources: Automatic x402 payments in Anchor Browser AgentCore payments developer guide AgentCore payments with browser integration Anchor Browser on AWS Marketplace About the authors Cher Simon Cher is a Principal Deep Learning Architect at AWS, where she helps customers, startups, and AWS Partners build large-scale, high-performance AI/ML solutions. A published author, she specializes in translating AI research into production-ready solutions. Guy Ben Simhon Guy is a Co-Founder and CPO at Anchor Browser, leading product and strategy. He focuses on building infrastructure that enables AI agents to reliably interact with the web and operate real computer environments at scale. Elay Gelbart Elay is a Founding and Lead Engineer at Anchor Browser, pioneering its browser infrastructure and core engineering. He specializes in large-scale browser infrastructure, distributed systems, and building reliable execution environments for AI agents. Chethan Shriyan Chethan is a Principal Product Manager – Technical at AWS. He has more than 12 years of experience in product and business management. Chethan is passionate about building and delivering technology products that create meaningful impact in customers’ lives. Peter Jiang Peter is a Senior Software Developer at AWS, based in Seattle, WA. He is a core member of the engineering team behind the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments initiative, which enables payment capabilities for AI agents. With over 8 years of experience in the financial and payments industry, Peter has launched multiple greenfield projects spanning banking, crypto, and agentic systems.

title: Manage private pricing offers for Amazon Bedrock with managed entitlements
summary: Managing AI model access across dozens or hundreds of AWS accounts creates friction when each account must accept AWS Marketplace Private Pricing Offers individually. This post shows two ways to activate MPPO entitlements in AWS License Manager: a lightweight script for a one-time fix, and CDK automation for ongoing event-driven processing.
content: Managing AI model access across dozens or hundreds of AWS accounts creates operational friction when each workload account must subscribe and accept AWS Marketplace Private Pricing Offers (MPPOs) individually. Amazon Bedrock with managed entitlements simplifies multi-account access to third-party AI models so you can subscribe once from a central account and distribute access across your organization. In this post, we show you two ways to activate AWS Marketplace Private Pricing Offer (MPPO) entitlements in AWS License Manager. Use the lightweight script when you want a one-time, no-infrastructure fix for received licenses you already trust. Use the CDK automation when you want ongoing event-driven processing that verifies sellers, creates and activates distributed grants. Why automate grant activation With AWS Marketplace Private Pricing Offers, you can negotiate custom rates for third-party models on Amazon Bedrock. After an eligible private offer is accepted, AWS Marketplace creates a license in AWS License Manager. In AWS Organizations with all features enabled, organization-level grants are auto-accepted but remain Disabled until you activate them. Teams often manage this by checking the AWS License Manager console and activating grants manually. Manual checks work, but they add effort and are easy to miss. Until someone activates the grant, negotiated pricing does not apply. The same effort appears as teams adopt new models or renew terms. Solution overview The sample repository provides two paths: Path 1 – The lightweight path is a standalone script that lists received licenses and prints a dry-run plan. It only creates and activates organization-wide grants when you re-run it with --apply --confirm-account-id . It has no seller allow-list, so use it only when you trust every received license in the management account. Path 2 – The event-driven path uses AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) to deploy ongoing automation in your AWS management account. Choose one of the following implementation paths. Use Path 1 for one-time activation without CDK. Use Path 2 for ongoing event-driven automation. Path 1: Lightweight script (one-time activation) Use this path when you need one-time activation without deploying CDK. The script lists every received license in the management account, so use the dry run as your review gate before applying changes. Clone the sample repository locally and move into the project directory. git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/sample-bedrock-managed-entitlements.git cd sample-bedrock-managed-entitlements Run the lightweight script in dry-run mode. python3 lightweight/distribute_licenses.py Review every listed license and confirm that the ISV Partner issuer and account scope match the private offer you expect. Apply the reviewed plan from the same AWS Organizations management account. python3 lightweight/distribute_licenses.py --apply --confirm-account-id ACCOUNT_ID After the grant is active, validate the billing path before you rely on the private offer in production. Billing data in AWS Cost Explorer can lag, so use it to compare the effective charge for covered Amazon Bedrock usage after charges appear. For a repeatable check, adapt the sample scripts/bedrock_discount_check.py utility to match your ISV Partner issuer and confirm the expected discount path. Path 2: CDK automation (ongoing activation) Use this path when you want new private pricing agreements handled automatically. The CDK stack listens for eligible AWS Marketplace agreement events, checks your seller allowlist, creates distributed grants, and retries activation when License Manager needs more time. The solution contains three components: Amazon EventBridge rule : The stack listens for AWS Marketplace agreement events on the default event bus in us-east-1 . The rule matches source aws.agreement-marketplace and detail type Purchase Agreement Created - Acceptor , then invokes the AWS Lambda function. AWS Lambda function : The function receives the AWS Marketplace agreement event, verifies the seller allow-list, discovers the license, creates the distributed grant, and requests activation with CreateGrantVersion(Status=ACTIVE) . The function logs the outcome to Amazon CloudWatch Logs for auditability. AWS License Manager entitlements : The grant targets your organization, selected organizational units (OUs), or specific accounts. Negotiated pricing applies only after the grant is activated and reaches ACTIVE or WORKFLOW_COMPLETED . The following diagram shows the event-driven flow. Figure 1: Sequence diagram showing AWS Marketplace sending a Purchase Agreement Created – Acceptor event to Amazon EventBridge, which invokes an AWS Lambda function. The function verifies the seller, discovers the received license, creates a distributed grant, requests activation with CreateGrantVersion(Status=ACTIVE), and writes the outcome to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Key benefits of this approach: Faster time to negotiated pricing. The negotiated rate applies after the distributed grant reaches ACTIVE or WORKFLOW_COMPLETED , without waiting for a manual console check. Consistent handling across accounts. The same AWS Lambda function and Amazon EventBridge rule pattern can be deployed for each organization that receives third-party model grants, so activation logic doesn’t vary by operator. Built-in audit trail. Every activation attempt or skip decision is logged to CloudWatch Logs, giving you a record of when each grant was activated, deferred, or ignored. Prerequisites Before you deploy this path, confirm these prerequisites: Use the AWS Organizations management account in us-east-1 with Python 3.12+, AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), and AWS CDK v2 configured. Confirm that AWS Organizations uses all features and that the private offer is for a License Manager-backed Bedrock model. Software as a service (SaaS) products are out of scope for this automation. Implementation steps Clone the sample repository locally and move into the project directory. git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/sample-bedrock-managed-entitlements.git cd sample-bedrock-managed-entitlements Verify or enable organization prerequisites. python3 scripts/bootstrap_prereqs.py --check --region us-east-1 Review any APPLY or MANUAL items before making changes. The bootstrap script can enable License Manager organization integration, License Manager trusted access, AWS Marketplace license-management trusted access, and required service-linked roles. python3 scripts/bootstrap_prereqs.py --apply --region us-east-1 --confirm-account-id ACCOUNT_ID Configure deployment inputs. python3 scripts/setup_config.py Review config/sellers.json . Configure your Organization ID, seller allow-list, notifications, and optional grant targets. By default, grants target the full organization. Use grantTargets to scope grants to selected OUs or AWS accounts. Deploy the CDK stack. cd cdk pip install -r requirements.txt cdk bootstrap aws://ACCOUNT_ID/us-east-1 cdk deploy Seed the Amazon DynamoDB seller allow-list from config/sellers.json . cd .. python scripts/seed_sellers.py --config config/sellers.json Treat the seller allow-list as a security boundary. Verify each seller account ID against your accepted AWS Marketplace private offer or received License Manager license before seeding the table. Don’t add broad or unverified seller entries, because matching sellers can trigger grant creation and activation across your configured grant targets. After deployment and seller seeding, the stack is ready to process eligible AWS Marketplace agreement events. Grant creation and activation happen only for verified sellers in the allowlist, and activation may be deferred until License Manager finishes processing the grant workflow. Validate the deployed automation. python scripts/e2e_validate.py --org-id o-xxxxxxxxxx --seller-account SELLER_ACCOUNT_ID --simulate Verify grant activation after an eligible AWS Marketplace agreement event. aws logs tail /aws/lambda/mppo-grants-handler --follow --region us-east-1 python scripts/bedrock_discount_check.py --issuer "ISV Partner" Activation and billing visibility can take hours or days. After the event-driven workflow accepts and activates the grants, confirm the grant state in AWS License Manager, then validate covered Amazon Bedrock usage in AWS Cost Explorer after billing data appears. For a repeatable check, adapt the sample scripts/bedrock_discount_check.py utility to match your ISV Partner issuer and target linked account. Clean up If you deployed this stack for testing, remove it to avoid the small ongoing Lambda and Amazon EventBridge charges: cdk destroy Voice of customer “As an AI Care Partner supporting millions of clinician consults every week, Heidi Health relies on third-party foundation models at real scale. Private pricing on AWS Marketplace gives us a cost-effective and efficient way to manage that growth: we can granularly attribute usage and pricing across AWS accounts and organizational units, and automate grant management as we adopt new models. That lets our platform team scale cost governance without scaling manual work.” — Marcus Lau , Head of Platform Engineering, Heidi Health Conclusion This post showed two ways to activate managed entitlements for Amazon Bedrock private pricing offers. Use the lightweight script for one-time activation of trusted received licenses, or deploy the CDK automation when you need ongoing event-driven processing for new AWS Marketplace agreements. Both approaches reduce manual effort and help negotiated pricing apply after distributed grants are activated. To get started, try the code sample in your AWS management account to automate model subscriptions. title: Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B
Natural language security queries at Orca Security using Amazon Bedrock
summary: Orca Security built Discovery AI, a natural language query agent on Amazon Bedrock that converts plain-English questions into Sonar queries. The post shares the multi-stage architecture and the results: 90% lower query cost, 93% fewer input tokens, and 75% lower latency than the initial baseline.
content: Security analysts need fast answers about their cloud infrastructure without deep familiarity with domain-specific query languages. Orca Security ’s tool covers over 900 cloud models (the resource types Sonar tracks, such as an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance or an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket). Querying that data required precise model names, nested relationship navigation, and selection from 18 operators (comparison functions like equals or contains used to filter results). To solve this, Orca Security partnered with AWS to build Discovery AI, a natural language query agent on Amazon Bedrock . Orca provides context-aware security for cloud, code, and AI, and Sonar is its domain-specific query system where users search, filter, and explore across the entire data graph. In this post, we share the architecture and results of Discovery AI, which converts a natural language question into a Sonar query. As a result, Orca reduced query costs by 90 percent, input tokens by 93 percent, and latency by 75 percent compared to the initial baseline. Bridging natural language and structured queries Orca Security’s Sonar query system supports 900+ cloud infrastructure and application models with complex relationships between them. To query this data, users construct JSON objects that specify exact model names, select from 18 operators, and navigate parent-child hierarchies across cloud providers. Doing this well requires deep familiarity with the Sonar schema. To build this capability, the Orca team set out to build a natural language interface that can generate valid Sonar queries from plain text. Their initial proof of concept loaded the full Sonar schema into a single prompt on the largest available model. This included over 900 model definitions, every relationship type, and a generous set of example queries. The output quality was strong (design partners and internal users responded positively) but three significant drawbacks emerged at production scale. Token consumption was inefficient, at roughly 2 million input tokens per workload, which drove up cost. Latency was high, with end-to-end response times of around 60 seconds per workload. Accuracy on complex, multi-model queries was limited because nested relationships and multi-condition queries often required additional refinement. The Orca team validated that the concept worked. The next challenge was making it cost-effective, fast, and accurate enough for production. To address this, the Orca team designed and deployed a solution that handles thousands of queries per day at 15-second response times using Amazon Bedrock. Solution overview Orca designed Discovery AI as a hybrid solution on Amazon Bedrock that combines Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) with schema-aware query construction. The system converts natural language questions into valid Discovery filters through a multi-stage pipeline, with each stage matched to the most appropriate Amazon Bedrock model. Orca chose Amazon Bedrock because it provides multi-model access through a single API, letting the team allocate different foundation models to each pipeline stage without managing separate integrations. Amazon Bedrock also inherits AWS governance controls through AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoints, and AWS CloudTrail, meeting Orca’s security requirements. The model-agnostic architecture meant the team could swap in newer model versions as they became available without rearchitecting the pipeline. The following diagram illustrates the nine-stage pipeline architecture. Figure 1: Multi-stage Discovery AI pipeline architecture showing the flow from natural language input to validated Discovery filter queries using foundation models on Amazon Bedrock The Discovery AI pipeline converts a natural language request into a validated Discovery filter through nine steps. Request Entry and Context Setup: The pipeline starts by combining the user’s natural language request with relevant context, including the user’s organization, connected cloud providers, and request metadata. This context helps the pipeline interpret the request accurately and generate a Discovery filter that matches the customer’s environment. Quick Deterministic Matcher: The Quick Matcher identifies structured inputs such as IP addresses, Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs), ARNs, file hashes, Amazon Machine Image IDs, Oracle Cloud Identifiers, EC2 IDs, URLs, and alert IDs. It uses regex and rule-based matching to detect high-confidence patterns.When a match is found, the pipeline can return a predefined Discovery filter through a fast path, without using large language model (LLM) inference. When no match is found, the request continues to the next step. LLM Guardrail Screening: The Guardrail component checks whether the request is safe, relevant, technical, and supported. It blocks prompt injection attempts, off-topic requests, and unsupported inputs before they reach the rest of the pipeline. Requests that fail the guardrail checks are rejected with an appropriate error. Approved requests continue to example retrieval. Embedding-Based Semantic Candidate Recall: The pipeline searches for relevant previously validated query examples using Amazon Titan Text Embeddings. It retrieves the 20 nearest examples from the vector store based on semantic similarity. These candidates provide the pipeline with examples of how similar natural language requests were previously translated into Discovery filters. Neural Relevance Reranking: The retrieved candidates are reranked using Cohere Rerank 3.5 on Amazon Bedrock. It identifies the examples that are most relevant to the current request and selects the five highest-signal examples. When an exact or high-confidence match is found, the pipeline can reuse the known-good filter directly. Otherwise, the reranked examples are passed to the generative stages. LLM-Driven Relevant Model Selection: Model Selection narrows more than 900 Sonar models to the small set relevant to the request. It considers the user’s request, connected providers, and retrieved examples when selecting the appropriate models. The selected models are provided to the Generator using the appropriate schema level, ranging from compact micro schemas to more detailed mini schemas. This reduces unnecessary context and makes generation more efficient. Tool-Augmented Agentic Filter Generation: The Generator uses a tool-augmented agent to construct the final Discovery filter. It reasons over the selected model schemas, retrieved examples, user context, and available tools. The agent can iteratively refine the filter as it works toward a valid representation of the user’s request. Static and API-Backed Validation: The generated filter is checked for syntactic and semantic correctness. The pipeline first applies static validation and then verifies the filter against Orca’s Sonar API. When validation fails, the validation error is returned to the Generator so the agent can correct the filter and try again. If the maximum number of retries is reached without producing a valid filter, the pipeline returns an invalid-filter response. The Generator is constrained to the reranked examples and selected schemas. Static validation resolves every model, field, and operator back to those schema definitions. Each validation error goes back to the agent with the offending element identified, so retries re-ground rather than re-guess. Post-Processing and Response: After a valid filter is produced, whether through the Quick Matcher, reuse of a known-good example, or agentic generation, the pipeline prepares the final response.The team allocated different foundation models on Amazon Bedrock across components based on each stage’s requirements. Anthropic Claude Haiku 4.5 powers the Model Selector and Generator. These components require strong reasoning for accurate query construction. Amazon Nova 2 Lite handles the Guardrail and Validator, where fast inference at lower cost is prioritized. Amazon Titan provides embeddings for semantic search in the Example Retrieval component. Cohere Rerank 3.5 reranks retrieved candidates to maximize relevance. For model availability by AWS Region, refer to Regional availability by models . Maximizing relevance and diversity in example retrieval Example retrieval emerged as the single biggest accuracy lever in the pipeline. Strong examples teach the Generator how to translate questions into Sonar queries more efficiently than schema alone, so the Orca team benchmarked several retrieval strategies on Amazon Bedrock. Each strategy traded off relevance, diversity, or speed in a different way, and comparing them directly showed which combination worked best. Pure top-K semantic search on Amazon Titan embeddings performed quickly, but it tended to return near-duplicate examples that starved the Generator of diversity. Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) improved diversity, but it traded off relevance when the top candidate was actually the right answer. Retrieving a larger candidate set and then reranking it pulled in a broader pool and used a reranker to select the most relevant subset, which pointed toward the winning approach. The winner was top-20 nearest-neighbor retrieval using Amazon Titan embeddings. Orca then reranked these results with Cohere Rerank 3.5 down to the top five. This approach gives the Generator a small, diverse, highly relevant set of examples without forcing a trade-off between coverage and precision at retrieval time. Loading over 900 models into context A core constraint shaped the architecture. It wasn’t feasible to include 900+ Sonar model schemas into every prompt. Even with long-context models, doing so degrades both cost and accuracy. The Model Selector resolves this. Running on Anthropic Claude Haiku 4.5, it works against compact, semantically rich representations of each model (name, purpose, key fields, and key relationships). Given the user’s question, it returns only the models the Generator actually needs. The Generator then receives full schema detail only for those selected models plus the relationships that connect them. Evaluation methodology To iterate confidently, the Orca team built a continuous evaluation harness early in the project. The harness combines a curated dataset, an automated scoring layer, and a slice-based measurement approach so the team can trust every change before it ships. Together these elements turn evaluation into a routine step rather than an afterthought. The curated evaluation dataset spans the question types, model families, and complexity tiers seen in production, so it reflects real usage. An LLM-as-judge scoring layer grades generated queries on correctness, completeness, and semantic equivalence to a reference query, which gives the team a consistent quality signal. The measurement methodology then breaks deltas down by slice, allowing the team to identify exactly where regressions occur and what to correct. Every change to a prompt, a model, a retrieval parameter, or an example flows through the harness before it ships to production. Domain-expert-in-the-loop labeling system for continuous improvement Sustaining accuracy as customer environments evolve and new question patterns emerge required more than a strong initial deployment. The Orca team built an internal labeling tool for product managers, support engineers, and security researchers. With the tool, they can flag queries, correct outputs, and push corrections into the example bank in one action. Furthermore, the system automatically collects production queries with low-confidence matching examples and routes them to the appropriate domain expert for daily labeling. The next pipeline run retrieves the new example through Cohere Rerank 3.5, and accuracy on that class of question improves the same moment, with no deployment. “The labeling UI is the single most important investment we made for long-term quality. It turns Discovery AI from a static deployment into a living system, with our domain experts continuously improving it inside their normal workflow.” — Or Gabay, Director of AI, Orca Security Combined with end-to-end pipeline observability and shared dashboards spanning product, engineering, and customer-facing teams, this feedback loop is what keeps Discovery AI improving after initial launch. Results After deploying Discovery AI to production, the new solution outperformed the initial baseline across cost, latency, and accuracy. Input token usage fell by 93 percent, from approximately 2 million tokens down to 140,000 per comparable workload. Overall cost fell by 90 percent, driven by that lower token consumption together with per-stage model allocation across Amazon Bedrock. Latency also improved, with end-to-end response times dropping by 75 percent, from approximately 60 seconds to 15 seconds. Accuracy on complex, multi-model queries also improved, measured continuously through the team’s evaluation harness. Discovery AI now handles thousands of queries per day in production since March 2026, with internal subject matter experts and customer feedback validating quality. Conclusion In this post, we shared how Orca Security built Discovery AI on Amazon Bedrock. The solution reduced query costs by 90 percent, input token usage by 93 percent, and latency by 75 percent compared to the initial baseline. The solution combines several key technologies. These include RAG-based example retrieval with Cohere Rerank 3.5, per-stage model allocation across Anthropic Claude Haiku 4.5 and Amazon Nova 2 Lite, and semantic search powered by Amazon Titan. Additionally, a continuous human-in-the-loop labeling system provides ongoing improvement. This combination allowed Orca to turn a working prototype into a production-grade solution that is both cheaper to run and more accurate. To get started building similar solutions, explore Amazon Bedrock for foundation model (FM) access, Cohere Rerank on Amazon Bedrock for retrieval optimization, and Amazon Titan for embeddings. To learn more about Orca Security’s cloud security tool, visit orca.security . To learn more about how Orca Security applies AI across its framework, see how Orca drives security outcomes with AI and how Orca secures AI adoption, including Amazon Bedrock . For more on the techniques used in this post, read related posts on the AWS Machine Learning Blog . About the authors Deniz Yilmaz Deniz is a Machine Learning Engineer at the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center. She partners with enterprise customers across EMEA to design and deploy production-grade generative AI solutions, from proof of concept through to scaled deployment. Her work focuses on agentic architectures, retrieval-augmented generation, and evaluation methodology for building reliable AI systems in production. Natalie Tarasova Natalie is a Machine Learning Engineer in the AWS Custom Model Optimisation team. She focuses on LLM fine-tuning, continued pretraining, and post-training. She is the author of SWE-InfraBench , a benchmark for LLMs on infrastructure-as-code. Julia Wagner Julia is a Senior AI Strategist at the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center. She partners with large enterprises and innovative startups across multiple industry verticals to define and implement generative and agentic AI strategies and products. With over a decade of product and technology leadership experience, she helps organizations automate complex workflows, accelerate R&D, and build the organizational capabilities needed for scaled AI adoption. Barak Tarab Barak is the AI Team Lead at Orca Security, driving the development of advanced artificial intelligence capabilities. His professional focus centers on building scalable AI solutions and robust infrastructure. Saurav Hiremath Saurav , Software Engineer at Orca Security. Lead and built API Security suite at Orca and now transitioned to building Agentic AI systems for enterprise customers. Occasionally spotted contributing to OSS (prev. Facebook’s Jest, React Hermes)

title: How ShipStation Global built an AI IT help desk on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
summary: ShipStation Global's engineering team built Deckhand, an AI IT help desk agent for Slack on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. It answers routine IT questions from a curated knowledge base, reads error-message screenshots, and files Jira tickets. In its first three months it resolved 97.5% of channel queries with a 96% positive feedback rating.
content: This post is co-written with Kenneth Salmon, Edward Boswell, Jack Armstrong, Robert Banh, and Nick Ciubotariu from ShipStation Global. Answering the same IT questions and clearing routine tickets drains time that IT teams could spend elsewhere. To reclaim it, the ShipStation Global Engineering team built Deckhand , an AI-powered IT help desk agent for Slack, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore . ShipStation Global is the leading intelligent shipping and logistics platform for small and mid-sized shippers, and it operates on a simple belief: the more efficient its teams are, the better it delivers for customers. Deckhand puts that belief to work. It answers routine IT and company questions from a curated knowledge base, reads error-message screenshots, and creates and updates Jira Service Management tickets. In this post, we discuss how ShipStation architected Deckhand, which resulted in resolving 97.5 percent of incoming channel queries while earning a 96 percent positive feedback rating by employees (Figure 1). Figure 1: 3-month channel coverage and positive feedback Business challenge The problem Deckhand solves is the one every IT team will recognize: the same questions are routinely asked, error messages are posted after business hours, and information needs to be gathered from different teams. At ShipStation Global, those conversations lived in a busy help desk Slack channel, where employees asked, and IT answered, one thread at a time. The answers usually already existed in a Confluence how-to article, on a company intranet page, or in a thread from eight months earlier. Finding them was the hard part. The channel data made the scale concrete. In the 12 months before launch: Employees posted more than 1,500 threads, and volume kept growing. With employees in the US, UK, Spain, Poland, Australia, and the Philippines, more than a fifth of questions arrived outside US business hours. Answers were split across different places: Confluence articles, intranet pages and PDFs, IT-maintained guides, and the channel’s own history. Repetitive questions consumed time that structured self-service steps could have handled. “We created Deckhand because getting help should be as simple as asking a question in Slack, not deciphering a ticket form or sending an email into the void. We believe that tickets are an indication of operational friction not productivity. Deckhand resolves common questions on the spot and, when it can’t, converts the conversation into a fully contextualized ticket with one click, improving the employee experience and freeing our team from endlessly repeating the phrase: ‘Please file a ticket.’” — Chris Collins, Senior Director IT at ShipStation Global Solution overview Deckhand works in Slack like any teammate—joining channels, reading the conversation, and drawing context from Slack profiles to answer IT questions in place. We run it on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, hosts the agent in isolated sessions, so we run no servers or containers. The solution has four main components, shown in Figure 2: Slack service:  A FastAPI and Slack Bolt application, hosted on AWS App Runner . It receives Slack events, decides whether the bot should respond, and builds a user-context payload from the requester’s Slack profile, including name, email, time zone, and manager. Agent service:  A Strands agent, deployed as a container on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime , manages the multi-turn tool agent loop using Anthropic’s Claude in Amazon Bedrock . Tools and knowledge:  A single AWS Lambda function, exposed as Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools through AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, classifies requests, creates and updates Jira tickets, and analyzes images. An Amazon Bedrock knowledge base indexes content from Confluence, the company intranet, Slack, and marketing pages, storing it in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) . Operations and feedback. Amazon DynamoDB stores feedback, AWS X-Ray traces request paths using OpenTelemetry, and the services log to Amazon CloudWatch . Figure 2: Architecture diagram showing Slack events entering the Slack service and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, with separate paths to an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base, AgentCore Gateway-backed Lambda tools, Jira Service Management, and DynamoDB feedback. When an employee posts in a channel where Deckhand is a member, the Slack service assembles the full thread history and user context. It then invokes the agent through the AgentCore runtime API. The agent searches the knowledge base and calls tools as needed. When it finds an answer, it returns a final response (Figure 3). When it doesn’t, it asks a clarifying question or offers to create a ticket (Figure 4). Figure 3: Deckhand responds with self-service steps Figure 4: Deckhand offers to create a ticket Deckhand workflow This section walks through how Deckhand is implemented, from prerequisites to a working deployment. Prerequisites To implement this pattern, you need the following: An AWS account with access to Amazon Bedrock, AgentCore runtime, and AgentCore Gateway. A Slack app with event subscriptions, a signing secret, and a bot token scoped to your use case. A container image registry such as Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR). An Amazon S3 bucket and an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base. AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles scoped to each runtime and tool, and AWS Secrets Manager entries for third-party credentials. Building the agent with Strands Agents and AgentCore The agent is intentionally lightweight. Using the open source Strands Agents SDK , an agent consists of a model, a set of tools, and a system prompt. The SDK manages the reasoning loop, allowing the model to select tools, process results, and iterate until it produces an answer. Deckhand’s agent service is implemented in a few lines of Python. from strands import Agent from strands.models import BedrockModel from strands.tools.mcp import MCPClient from strands_tools import retrieve from mcp.client.streamable_http import streamablehttp_client model = BedrockModel( model_id=MODEL_ID, max_tokens=2048, temperature=0.3, ) gateway = MCPClient(lambda: streamablehttp_client(url=GATEWAY_URL)) agent = Agent( model=model, tools=[gateway, retrieve], system_prompt=SYSTEM_PROMPT, ) The model ID is set through an environment variable, which allows switching models without modifying application code. Tools are integrated with the agent in two ways. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases retrieval is a native Strands tool that supports knowledge base search with a single import. Other functions, including classification, ticket management, user resolution, and image analysis, are handled by a Lambda function registered on AgentCore Gateway. The Gateway exposes these as MCP tools, and the Lambda routes each invocation by tool name. This separation allows tool logic to be updated independently, and the agent can access new tools from the Gateway without requiring a rebuild. AgentCore runtime hosts the agent as a container, avoiding the need for server or session management. The Slack service calls the agent synchronously for each message, providing the thread transcript and user context, and posts the final response. Since context, including the employee’s profile, is included with every request, the agent can complete ticket details automatically. Knowledge base design and answer routing Deckhand answers from a single Amazon Bedrock knowledge base with core S3-backed data sources: Articles synced from Confluence. Internal pages, PDFs, and events synced from the company intranet. Resolved support threads mined from Slack (covered in the next section). Each document includes metadata such as title, source URL, content type, and event dates. This allows the agent to filter content, for example, when users ask about upcoming events or weekly lunch menus in the Austin office. Mining Slack history with Recursive Language Models (RLMs) The most valuable data source is the archive of resolved support threads. Before Deckhand existed, Slack was where problems got solved: years of employees describing issues and IT walking them through fixes. That history is an organic knowledge base, validated by the best possible reviewer: the person whose problem got fixed. It’s also noisy: a raw export mixes banter, automated alerts, and threads that never actually got resolved. Indexing an unverified fix or a garbled summary means the knowledge base surfaces an incorrect answer with the same confidence as a correct one, so extraction needs to be precise. The mining process follows a three-stage pipeline (Figure 5): A script exports the channel’s full history via the Slack API, retrieving complete replies for every thread and writing a structured dump that includes thread markers, timestamps, and reply counts. DSPy’s Recursive Language Model (RLM), running Claude on Amazon Bedrock, treats that export as a navigable memory space inside a sandboxed Python read-eval-print loop (REPL) rather than a single prompt. Working iteratively over the data, it classifies each thread as resolved, unresolved, or escalated and filters out announcements and non-questions. Strict criteria keep quality high: a thread counts as resolved only when the full, workable fix is visible in the thread itself. For each resolved thread, the RLM orchestrates recursive sub-LLM (large language model) calls to extract structured fields, each validated against a Pydantic model. The fields include an issue summary, the original question, and the resolution. They also capture whether the fix is self-service or needs a ticket, the self-service steps, the application and system involved, error messages, and tags. When a sub-LLM call returns something that fails the schema, the RLM’s code-based loop catches the validation error in the interpreter and retries. The results are written as a markdown document organized by issue. The pipeline uploads it to Amazon S3 for the knowledge base to index. Figure 5: Export classification and extraction workflow of the Slack conversation We chose RLM because it maintains the entire Slack history in a persistent sandbox variable space, allowing iterative reasoning over the export and consistent output structure. As a result, when an employee encounters a problem previously solved by a colleague, Deckhand provides the proven solution, often as actionable, numbered steps. Knowing when not to answer An AI bot in a shared channel fails socially before it fails technically. Deckhand’s most refined logic decides when to stay quiet: The agent’s first decision on every message is whether it’s an announcement, a social message, or a conversation between people. If so, it outputs “SKIP,” and the Slack service suppresses the reply. In threads, it replies only to the original poster. If the last reply came from another human helper, it stays silent, because a person has taken over. If a reply starts by @naming a person, the message isn’t for the bot. Collecting feedback Each answer includes feedback buttons. A thumbs-up is recorded directly, while a thumbs-down prompts a brief “what went wrong” field. Ratings are stored in DynamoDB with the original question and the bot’s response. Negative feedback is a valuable dataset used to improve the system prompt and agent behavior, and to update incorrect knowledge base information. Security and validation Prompt rules enhance behavior but do not replace access controls. Enforcement is managed through code and infrastructure: Ticket creation requires explicit confirmation. When Deckhand offers to create a ticket, the Slack service adds a Create Ticket button, and selecting it sends confirmation through the agent. Ticket updates only accept valid keys matching the helpdesk project pattern and reject empty comments. Classification is validated before it acts. Request classification runs as a separate Amazon Bedrock Converse API call that returns structured ticket fields, validated with Pydantic before anything reaches Jira. The image tool is restricted to downloading only from Slack’s file host. It authenticates with the bot token, limits each request to five images of up to 5 MB each, and sends the files to a vision model using the Converse API. Credentials stay out of code. Slack tokens, the signing secret, and Jira credentials live in AWS Secrets Manager , and each service and tool runs under its own scoped IAM role. The prompt enforces behavioral safeguards: never request passwords or multi-factor authentication (MFA) codes, never write credentials in ticket comments, and never expose profile metadata used for ticket fields. Outcome Deckhand launched in April 2026. It started at about 30 messages a day and reached as many as 100 by early summer. In its first three months it handled 1,935 messages, started 1,221 agent conversations, and opened 409 Jira tickets. It replied to 97.5 percent of messages. A third of the questions came in after hours, when no one on the IT team was working, and Deckhand answered 94 percent of those. People who would have waited until the next morning got an answer that night. Feedback improved as the team worked on it. Positive ratings went from 82 percent in April to 96 percent in June, after they revised the system prompt and knowledge base to fix what people complained about. The clearest win was ticket deflection. An agent conversation is a question that would otherwise have become a Jira ticket. Of the 1,221 conversations, only 409 turned into tickets. The other 812 were handled in chat. Filing a ticket and then working and closing it runs about 30 minutes. Those 812 conversations add up to roughly 406 hours over three months, or around 1,600 hours a year. Employees kept that time for their own work, and IT never spent it on intake. Conclusion Deckhand took repetitive IT questions off people’s plates and gave the time back to employees and the IT team. It works because each part of the stack has one job and runs as a managed service: AgentCore runtime hosts the agent, AgentCore Gateway turns a Lambda function into MCP tools the agent can call, and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases handles retrieval. The team shipped it without standing up servers or maintaining orchestration code. To build a similar solution, begin with a well-maintained knowledge source and a clearly defined action. Refer to the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation and Strands Agents SDK for agent development, and the Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases documentation for connecting content sources. To discuss an agentic AI use case for your organization, contact your AWS account team. About the authors Kenneth Salmon Kenneth is a Software Engineer at ShipStation Global specializing in integrations, workflow automation, and AI-driven systems. His work centers on leveraging applied AI, large language models, and conversational agents to solve complex operational challenges. Edward Boswell Edward is a Senior Software Engineer at ShipStation Global specializing in AI applications and rapid prototyping. He is passionate about using AI to remove operational bottlenecks and improve team efficiency. Outside of work, Edward is a former professional magician who enjoys entertaining at meetings. Jack Armstrong Jack is a Senior Software Engineer at ShipStation Global. He is a polyglot programmer experienced with Python, TypeScript, and other languages, with vast knowledge in software engineering systems, especially Amazon Bedrock. Robert Banh Robert is a Director of Engineering at ShipStation Global, where he leads a SWAT team focused on deploying AI across departments. He is passionate about solving problems and leveraging data to drive actionable improvements. Nick Ciubotariu Nick is the Chief Technology Officer at ShipStation Global. He has spent over two decades shipping enterprise-scale software and AI systems used by hundreds of millions of people. Ravi Kashyap Ravi is a Senior Solutions Architect at AWS who works with retail and e-commerce companies to build, scale, and optimize their cloud and AI workloads. He focuses on automation and applied AI, and he gives back to the developer community as an active open source contributor.
