title: Build long-horizon agents with Grok 4.7 on Amazon Bedrock
summary: Grok 4.7 is now available on Amazon Bedrock. In this post, we build a tool-calling agent on Grok 4.7 and evaluate it on three reasoning tasks at four reasoning effort levels, measuring correctness and token cost per completed task. We show how to tune the trade-off per request and monitor it in production.
content: SpaceXAI’s Grok 4.7 is now available on Amazon Bedrock, which offers a choice of foundation models (FMs) from multiple providers. According to SpaceXAI, Grok 4.7 is trained to work longer on more difficult tasks and knows when to check its own work. That matters most for agents, which carry a task through many steps and must verify what they find along the way. An agent that works this way has to do more than look things up. It has to form a candidate answer, check it against what it has learned, and refine it until it fits. Grok 4.7 exposes a reasoning effort setting that controls how much deliberation happens before each response, and for agent workloads a practical question is which level to run. In this post, we build a tool-calling agent on Grok 4.7 and evaluate it on three tasks that require search rather than lookup. The tasks are diagnosing a two-service outage from its alerts, scheduling maintenance under interacting constraints, and choosing an optimal set of migrations under a budget. Each task has exactly one correct answer, verified by brute force. We ran all three at every reasoning effort level, six times each, for 72 agent runs. The agent answered 67 of the 72 runs correctly. At xhigh it answered all 18 correctly, and at low it answered 15 of 18 while using about an eighth of the output tokens. That gives a clear trade-off you can tune per request, and we show how to measure it on your own tasks and how to monitor it in production. We report token counts rather than currency throughout. Token prices change, and the counts are what your own costs are derived from, so a measurement expressed in tokens stays valid. What SpaceXAI reports about Grok 4.7 According to SpaceXAI, Grok 4.7 uses a larger base model than Grok 4.6 and was trained with a longer reinforcement learning run on a harder mix of tasks. This mix is weighted toward problems that take many hours to complete. SpaceXAI reports that the model is better at verifying its own work and at managing longer context. SpaceXAI’s published benchmark results follow that emphasis. The largest reported gains over Grok 4.6 appear in the categories that measure sustained work rather than single-turn answers. Benchmark Category Grok 4.6 Grok 4.7 Terminal-Bench 4.0 Multi-hour terminal work 20.3% 37.6% EEBench Electrical engineering 53.0% 64.0% Harvey Legal Agent Benchmark Legal work 15.8% 19.6% CursorBench 4.0 Longer-running coding 40.4% 46.3% HealthBench Professional Clinical reasoning 48.5% 56.7% AA Briefcase v1.1 Multi-hour office work 1,546 1,657 Source: SpaceXAI, Introducing Grok 4.7 ( https://x.ai/news/grok-4-7 ). Scores are as published by SpaceXAI at the time of the model launch. Benchmarks show how a model performs across standard tasks. For your own workload, the useful next step is to measure on tasks shaped like yours, which is what the rest of this post walks through. SpaceXAI lists a 500K token context window for Grok 4.7, with text and image input and text output. On Amazon Bedrock, the model supports configurable reasoning effort, tool calling, and structured output. How you access Grok 4.7 on Amazon Bedrock Grok 4.7 runs on the bedrock-runtime endpoint and is accessed through a cross-Region inference profile. Two profiles are available: Inference profile Routing Use when us.xai.grok-4.7 Within the US geography You have US data residency requirements global.xai.grok-4.7 Commercial AWS Regions You have no residency constraints and want the widest capacity Cross-Region inference routes requests across multiple AWS Regions, which gives you higher throughput without managing capacity Region by Region. Requests name one of the inference profiles rather than a bare model ID. The model supports the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions and Responses APIs, and the Amazon Bedrock Converse API. On Converse, reasoning is returned as a reasoningContent block alongside the text block. In inferenceConfig , set maxTokens only, and put model-specific parameters, such as reasoning effort, in additionalModelRequestFields . For the current list of supported Regions, service tiers, and token prices, see the Grok 4.7 model card in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide and the Amazon Bedrock pricing page ( https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/pricing/ ). Prerequisites An AWS account with access to Amazon Bedrock, and model access enabled for Grok 4.7. Python 3.9 or later, with openai , boto3 , and aws-bedrock-token-generator installed. AWS credentials configured in your environment. Your AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) identity needs bedrock:InvokeModel on both the inference profile and your account’s default project: arn:aws:bedrock:{region}::inference-profile/us.xai.grok-4.7 or the global. equivalent. arn:aws:bedrock:{region}:{account-id}:project/default . Include both resources in the policy statement. The default project permission is required in addition to the inference profile. Connect to the model For production use, we recommend generating a short-term bearer token from your existing AWS credentials, so authentication stays tied to your IAM identity and no long-lived secret is stored: from aws_bedrock_token_generator import provide_token from openai import OpenAI REGION = "us-west-2" MODEL_ID = "us.xai.grok-4.7" client = OpenAI( api_key=provide_token(region=REGION), base_url=f"https://bedrock-runtime.{REGION}.amazonaws.com/openai/v1", timeout=360, max_retries=0, # retries are handled explicitly, see "Build in retries" below ) Reasoning tokens count as output tokens and draw down max_completion_tokens before the answer text is produced, so size the limit to leave room for both. If the limit is reached during reasoning, the response returns without answer text, so check for empty content in agent code and raise the limit if you see it. Our runs used a limit of 32,768 tokens, which left headroom at every effort level. Grok 4.7 supports four effort levels: low , medium , high , and xhigh . Effort levels can change between model versions, so it is worth confirming them against the service rather than hardcoding a list: def supported_effort_levels(candidates=("none", "low", "medium", "high", "xhigh", "max")): supported = [] for level in candidates: try: client.responses.create(model=MODEL_ID, input="Say OK.", reasoning={"effort": level}, max_output_tokens=2048) supported.append(level) except Exception as exc: if "unsupported_value" not in str(exc) and "invalid_value" not in str(exc): raise return supported print(supported_effort_levels()) # ['low', 'medium', 'high', 'xhigh'] Design tasks that need reasoning Many agent evaluations test diligence: read a record, filter it, add it up. Those tasks are worth having, but to see what reasoning effort contributes, a task has to require search: the answer can’t be read off the data, it has to be proposed and then checked. We built a synthetic environment of 20 services, exposed through seven tools, and three tasks on top of it. Every task has exactly one correct answer, and each is built so that a quick heuristic is not enough to find it. Task What the agent has to do What makes it a reasoning task two_fault_diagnosis Two services failed silently at 03:00 and 12 others raised alerts. Identify the two that failed Failed services raise no alerts, so the answer is not among the alerting services. 190 possible pairs, and only one explains exactly the alerts observed maintenance_schedule Patch eight services over four nights, two per night, under ten constraints and a rule that two services from the same team never share a night 2,520 possible schedules, one valid. The team rule depends on data the agent has to look up migration_budget Choose candidates to migrate that maximize risk reduction within a budget, including transitive prerequisites 53 feasible sets, one optimal. Picking the best ratio first gives a set nine points short of the optimum Four practices keep a measurement like this trustworthy, and they apply to most agent evaluations. State every rule the grader relies on. If the prompt leaves an edge case open, a reasonable answer can be scored as wrong, and the evaluation ends up measuring the specification rather than the model. The diagnosis prompt, for example, says explicitly that a failed service raises no alert of its own. Prove each task has one answer. Each environment is small enough to enumerate, so we checked every candidate answer before running anything. For the schedule, that is a few lines: import itertools ALL_SLOTS = sorted(set(itertools.permutations([1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4]))) def valid_schedules(services, constraints): return [s for slots in ALL_SLOTS if satisfies(s := dict(zip(services, slots)), constraints)] assert len(valid_schedules(SERVICES, CONSTRAINTS)) == 1 # exactly one answer assert len(valid_schedules(SERVICES, CONSTRAINTS_WITHOUT_TEAM_RULE)) > 1 # the rule matters Grade a required final line, not the whole response. Each prompt asks the agent to end with a line such as FINAL: auth, checkout . The grader reads only that line, so a response that discusses other candidates while explaining its reasoning is graded on its conclusion: def final_line(answer): lines = [l for l in (answer or "").splitlines() if "FINAL" in l.upper()] return lines[-1] if lines else None Track format separately from correctness. A missing final line is a different signal from an incorrect one. In our runs, all 72 responses included a gradeable final line. Constrain tool parameters with an enum where the valid values are known, so every tool call targets a real resource: TOOLS = [ {"type": "function", "function": { "name": "get_dependencies", "description": "Services that one service directly depends on.", "parameters": { "type": "object", "properties": {"service": {"type": "string", "enum": SERVICE_NAMES}}, "required": ["service"], }}}, # The remaining six tools follow the same shape. ] The system prompt is deliberately short, and asks the agent to check its answer before giving it: AGENT_SYSTEM = ( "You are an infrastructure analyst agent. Use the tools to gather facts and never guess " "a value you can look up. Before answering, check your answer against every rule in the " "task. End with the FINAL line exactly as the task specifies." ) The agent loop is a standard tool-calling loop: call the model with reasoning_effort set, execute each returned tool call, append the result keyed by tool_call_id , and repeat until the model stops requesting tools. Tracking prompt_tokens and completion_tokens across the loop gives the token counts reported in the following section. Results Six runs of each task at each effort level, 72 runs in total. The agent answered 67 correctly. Task low medium high xhigh two_fault_diagnosis 5 of 6 6 of 6 6 of 6 6 of 6 maintenance_schedule 5 of 6 5 of 6 5 of 6 6 of 6 migration_budget 5 of 6 6 of 6 6 of 6 6 of 6 All three tasks 15 of 18 17 of 18 17 of 18 18 of 18 Per run low medium high xhigh Mean output tokens 1,184 6,430 6,778 9,147 Output tokens relative to low 1.0x 5.4x 5.7x 7.7x Mean tool calls 17.2 18.7 17.8 18.1 Median elapsed time 18s 98s 89s 106s Figure 1: Share of runs answered correctly at each reasoning effort level (left), and mean output tokens per run with median seconds per run overlaid (right) Three observations. xhigh answered every run correctly. All 18 runs across the three tasks were correct at xhigh , and medium and high answered 17 of 18 each. With six runs per task and level, the differences between levels are indicative rather than statistically conclusive, and the direction was consistent across all three tasks. Effort changes how much the agent reasons, not how much it explores. Tool calls were essentially flat, between 17.2 and 18.7 per run at every level. The agent gathered the same facts regardless of effort, and what changed was how much reasoning it applied to them, with output tokens rising from 1,184 at low to 9,147 at xhigh . low offers a strong cost-to-quality ratio. At low , the agent answered 15 of 18 runs correctly using about an eighth of the output tokens of xhigh , with a median run of 18 seconds. Where a slightly lower completion rate is acceptable, or where answers are reviewed downstream, low is an efficient choice. Where every answer needs to be right first time, higher levels are the safer default. How effort level shapes the answer The tasks were designed around a specific kind of difficulty, and looking at how each effort level handled them clarifies when the extra reasoning is worth it. Optimization. The migration task rewards considering combinations rather than ranking options one at a time. Selecting the candidates with the best individual ratios produces a reasonable answer that is nine points short of the optimum. At medium and above, the agent found the optimal set in all 18 runs. Hypothesis testing. The diagnosis task requires checking a candidate pair in both directions: every alert has to be explained, and every service that stayed silent has to be consistent with the answer. At medium and above, the agent identified the correct pair in all 18 runs. Constraint satisfaction. The scheduling task combines ten listed constraints with a team rule that depends on looked-up ownership data. xhigh produced the valid schedule in every run, and this was the task where the highest level made the clearest difference. The pattern across the three is that additional reasoning effort is most valuable where the agent has to weigh several candidate answers against each other, rather than follow a single path to the result. Monitoring reasoning in production In production you don’t have a known answer to grade against, but you do know how many output tokens and tool calls each run used. Those give you a useful operational signal. Correct runs at each level stay above a clear floor of reasoning volume. Every correct run at medium and above used at least 1,739 output tokens, and the typical run used several thousand. A run that makes no tool calls, or that produces far less output than is normal for its level, is worth flagging for review: def flag_for_review(run, baseline): """baseline: output tokens of graded, correct runs at the same effort level.""" reasons = [] if run["tool_calls"] == 0: reasons.append("made no tool calls") if run["output_tokens"] Calibrate the baseline from runs you have graded, per task and per effort level, then apply it to runs you have not. Treat a flag as a prompt to inspect or re-run. At low , where every run is brief, output volume is a weaker signal, so pair it with spot checks. Asking the agent to verify its answer in the system prompt is worth keeping, because it makes the agent’s reasoning straightforward to follow when you review a run. Pair it with automated grading wherever a known answer exists, so that quality is measured independently of the transcript. Choosing a reasoning effort These results suggest a few practical rules. Match effort to the kind of task. Tasks that involve search, optimization, or testing a hypothesis benefit most from medium or higher. Tasks that follow a single path, or whose answers are reviewed downstream, can run efficiently at low . Set effort per request, not per agent. Effort is a request parameter, so an agent can run its planning and verification steps at a higher level and its mechanical steps, such as formatting a tool result, at low . That combines much of the reliability of a higher level with a lower token cost. Measure on your own tasks, with repeats. A single run per configuration gives a single observation. Repeating each configuration several times shows how consistent it is. Monitor reasoning volume. Output tokens and tool calls per run, tracked by effort level, give you an early signal to review a run before its result is used. Limitations of this measurement Six runs per task and effort level. Enough to show a consistent direction across three tasks, not enough for a confidence interval. Treat the differences between levels as indicative. A synthetic environment. The tools read from data generated in code, which is what makes it possible to prove each task has exactly one answer and to grade automatically. Real tools add latency, partial results and errors, none of which are tested here. Minutes, not hours. Median run time ranged from 18 seconds at low to 106 seconds at xhigh . This is a scaled-down proxy for long-horizon work. The method transfers. The absolute figures do not. One model version, one Region, one prompt per task. Different phrasings of the same task may change the results, which is part of why stating every rule explicitly matters. Token counts, not costs. To convert to currency, apply the current rates for your inference profile and service tier from the Amazon Bedrock pricing page. The Global and US Geo profiles are priced differently, and the Flex and Priority service tiers apply multipliers. Operational controls for agent workloads Build in retries. Agents that issue a high volume of calls should treat retries as part of the design. Set a request timeout, retry only errors that are retryable, back off exponentially with jitter, and honor a Retry-After header when one is returned: import random, time RETRYABLE = {408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504} def call_with_backoff(fn, attempts=7, base=4.0, cap=180.0): for attempt in range(1, attempts + 1): try: return fn() except Exception as exc: status = getattr(exc, "status_code", None) retryable = status in RETRYABLE or "timed out" in str(exc).lower() if not retryable or attempt == attempts: raise time.sleep(random.uniform(base, min(cap, base * 2 ** attempt))) On-demand throughput scales up over time, so ramp a new high-volume workload gradually rather than starting at full rate. Auditing a run. Model invocation logging writes request and response data to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) or Amazon CloudWatch Logs. This gives you the full transcript of runs you want to review after the fact. Monitoring reasoning volume at scale. Amazon CloudWatch metrics give you the aggregate view of token usage, which is where the per-level baselines described earlier become something you can alarm on. Attributing spend across agents. Cost itemization in AWS Cost Explorer and the AWS Cost and Usage Report breaks usage out per model, which combined with per-task token counts gives you both unit economics and the aggregate bill. Matching cost to urgency. Service tiers are set per request, so one deployment can send an overnight analysis through the Flex tier and an interactive request through Priority. For a workload that runs at a higher effort level, tier selection is a further lever on cost. Choosing a routing profile. Cross-Region inference widens the capacity pool a long run draws from. The Global profile serves from your choice of commercial AWS Region and is typically priced lower per token than geographic routing. The US profile keeps processing within the United States. Choose based on your data residency requirements as well as cost. Clean up The examples in this post do not create billable AWS resources beyond per-request token usage. If you generated a long-term Amazon Bedrock API key, delete it in the Amazon Bedrock console when you are finished, because it remains valid until revoked. Short-term tokens generated from IAM credentials expire on their own. If you enabled model invocation logging to Amazon S3 while testing, review the bucket and remove objects you no longer need. Conclusion SpaceXAI trained Grok 4.7 to work longer on more difficult tasks and to know when to check its own work. On three tasks that required search rather than lookup, the agent answered 67 of 72 runs correctly, and every run at xhigh . Because reasoning effort is set per request, you can choose where each step of an agent sits on the trade-off between thoroughness and token cost. Three things are worth carrying into your own evaluation. Design tasks with one provable answer and state every rule the grader depends on. Repeat runs, so you see how consistent each configuration is. And monitor output tokens and tool calls by effort level, so you have an operational signal alongside your quality measurements. Further reading Introducing Grok on Amazon Bedrock Grok 4.7 is now available on Amazon Bedrock Route model inference requests across AWS Regions with cross-Region inference Getting started with Amazon Bedrock Chat Completions API Amazon Bedrock pricing Introducing Grok 4.7  (SpaceXAI) About the authors Suheel Farooq Suheel is a Principal Solutions Architect at AWS, specializing in artificial intelligence, machine learning, and generative AI. He helps Foundation Model Provider customers design, build, modernize, and scale their AI/ML and generative AI workloads on AWS — from bringing foundation models to Amazon Bedrock to optimizing training and inference and building Agentic AI solutions. His experience spans the AWS AI/ML and generative AI portfolio, particularly Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Amazon SageMaker AI. In his free time, Suheel enjoys working out and hiking. Anirban Gupta Anirban is a Principal Engineer at AWS based in Seattle, USA, where he focuses on the design of secure, high-scale model-serving infrastructure for Amazon Bedrock. He has driven the technical work behind several foundation-model launches on the platform. Prior to joining Amazon Bedrock, he was a Principal Engineer on AWS Outposts, building hybrid on-premises cloud infrastructure. James Wang James is Senior Product Growth Manager at SpaceXAI. Previously, he was Director of Product Marketing at Cerebras, where he launched Cerebras Inference and the CS-3 AI accelerator. Before that James was lead AI analyst at ARK Invest. He started his career at NVIDIA, launching the first CUDA-capable GPUs in the early days of deep learning. Ikenna Izugbokwe Ikenna is a Principal Solutions Architect at AWS specializing in networking, containers, and AI infrastructure. He guides model providers through scaling their training and inference systems while enabling rapid deployment of evolving frontier models on AWS. His work increasingly spans agentic AI – building reliable, cost-efficient multi-agent systems and the inference infrastructure behind them in production.

title: Mixture-of-Experts kernel engineering on Amazon SageMaker AI
summary: AWS engineers share kernel optimizations for fused Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models on Amazon SageMaker AI: Swap-AB for WGMMA utilization, Triton backend routing for FP8 quantization, and eliminating Triton JIT recompilation. Together they deliver up to 10% higher throughput and up to 9% faster Time to First Token on H200 GPUs.
content: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is a sparsely-activated architecture that scales large language model (LLM) capacity while keeping per-token compute low. Because its operations account for a large share of total compute time, inefficiencies there directly raise request latency and cost. Therefore, optimizing MoE operations through kernel engineering offers the largest opportunity for performance gains. Fused MoE is a key optimization technique for the MoE architecture. A fused MoE system merges token routing, data shuffling, and specialized network calculations into a single batched operation on the GPU. This replaces executing those routing and expert computations as separate, sequential loop operations. While this provides latency advantages, it also brings complexity in kernel implementations and debugging capability. High GPU utilization for this architecture requires hardware-specific optimizations. In this post, we describe the different kernel optimizations we implemented for fused MoE models and show you how you can benefit from this work. We used a representative MoE model as our primary example. Swap-AB for WGMMA utilization To maximize tensor processing throughput, the NVIDIA Hopper architecture relies on the Warp Group Matrix Multiply Accumulate (WGMMA) instruction protocol, which executes collectively across a cooperative warpgroup of 128 threads. This operand asymmetry is fundamentally an instruction set architecture (ISA)-level property. In the underlying wgmma.mma_async assembly definition, the hardware fixes the matrix row dimension (M) at a constant scale of 64 to define its parallel thread-mapping topology. The column dimension (N) remains highly variable. Operand A strictly maps across this fixed M dimension (using registers or shared memory), and Operand B maps across the variable N dimension (through a shared memory descriptor). These operand slots are therefore structurally non-interchangeable. Consequently, peak hardware tile utilization is governed by these rigid shape encodings, requiring that the M dimension equals or exceeds 64 to prevent compute execution lanes from sitting idle. This structural preference stems from how Hopper Tensor Cores partition memory blocks. The hardware enforces a fixed minimum layout shape for the leading dimension of the first operand, locking the block height to exactly 64 (M=64). When a mathematical matrix possesses a large, continuous leading dimension in this primary slot, Hopper’s internal hardware schedulers can cleanly map and distribute data across the physical computing grid. This structural asymmetry becomes a severe performance bottleneck during the decode phase of MoE networks. In a standard MoE layer, the linear algebra governing expert computation is formulated using traditional matrix notation: A[M,K] x B[K,N] —> C[M,N] Where (M) represents the token row count (or batch size), (K) represents the hidden feature dimension, and (N) represents the expansive expert output dimension. During the decode phase, the system processes only one token per user sequence at a time. Consequently, the batch space or token row size is profoundly thin, regularly dropping to a profile where (M Matrix (A) transforms into a thin, fragmented horizontal vector (for example, 1 x 4096). Matrix (B) (the core expert weights) remains in a large, dense vertical block (for example, 4096 x 8192). Because the row count (M) is tiny, Matrix (A) is physically incapable of filling the hardware’s fixed (64)-row layout bucket for Operand A. When the WGMMA instruction executes over this layout, it leaves a vast portion of the physical Tensor Core capacity completely starved. The silicon spends clock cycles processing empty spatial slots, leading to poor hardware utilization. In a standard dense LLM layer, weight matrices are static, unified, and perfectly contiguous. In an MoE layer, however, the workload is fractured across a fleet of independent subnetworks (experts). This creates unique memory and layout bottlenecks that make it hypersensitive to the WGMMA constraints of the Hopper GPU. In a standard dense layer, matrix multiplication multiplies a token vector by a single layer weight matrix. The output dimension (N) is the model’s hidden size (for example, 4096). In a Fused MoE kernel, the GPU isn’t only multiplying against one expert. It’s grouping and running math for all active experts simultaneously to avoid launching individual kernels for each expert. For a standard dense layer, N is the hidden size (4,096). For a fused MoE layer, N is the number of experts chosen multiplied by the expert intermediate size. For a model running a topk=8 routine, the effective N dimension inside the fused kernel explodes into tens or hundreds of thousands of parameters. Because the N dimension is so disproportionately large compared to the tiny decode token size (M=1), the layout asymmetry becomes extreme. Transposing the matrices moves this large, combined MoE dimension into the primary slot, unlocking hardware prefetching at a scale that standard dense layers cannot match. To resolve this hardware misalignment without altering the underlying mathematical integrity of the model, we exploit the algebraic property of matrix transposition: B T [N,K] x A T [K,M] —> C T [N,M] Figure 1: Swap-AB for WGMMA utilization By programmatically flipping the matrix multiplication before it reaches the PTX assembly layer, we realigned the software to match the exact topography of the Hopper silicon. This transposition triggers two immediate architectural advantages on the GPU. First, it saturates the physical layout. The expansive expert dimension (N = 8192) is promoted to the first operand position (B T ), and because (N) is large it easily floods the hardware’s mandatory (64)-row threshold. The Tensor Cores then operate at maximum local density with no wasted execution cycles. Second, it activates asynchronous prefetching. Hopper’s dedicated hardware copy engines can prefetch memory addresses asynchronously from shared memory straight into registers before the math execution block fires. Placing the continuous, large weight blocks (B T ) in the leading slot lets these engines trace the data layout smoothly and keep the compute pipeline saturated without CPU intervention. This produced a 2–4 percent end-to-end output throughput improvement across large-scale MoE models on H200. We upstreamed this optimization to vLLM, and it is available in version 0.24.0 or later. Backend routing for FP8 tensor quantization Beyond kernel internals, the choice of which backend executes the MoE computation has a large effect on performance. The vLLM MoE oracle routes different quantization schemes to Triton, FlashInfer+CUTLASS, or other backends. Profiling revealed that for FP8 tensor-quantized models on Hopper, the Triton backend consistently outperforms the default FLASHINFER_CUTLASS path. The Triton backend outperforms CUTLASS in low-concurrency MoE workloads primarily because it replaces rigid, framework-level matrix math configurations with custom, operator-level register fusion. CUTLASS relies on standard C++ template structures that treat FP8 tensor scaling, matrix multiplication, and expert aggregation as discrete mathematical operations. The Triton backend instead consolidates this entire pipeline into a single hardware pass. Data is pulled from global high-bandwidth memory (HBM) exactly once and processed entirely within the GPU’s ultra-fast local SRAM registers and compute execution files. It’s then streamed back to the final matrix destination. This removes the slow global VRAM read/write roundtrips that compromise CUTLASS when it is forced to constantly step through intermediate tensor scaling steps. Furthermore, this register-level fusion is specifically paired with dynamic scheduling layouts designed around variable token bucketing, resolving a severe structural flaw in traditional compilation templates. CUTLASS is natively optimized for dense, large, and predictable matrix dimensions. When it encounters the fluid, ultra-thin batch profiles (M Updating the routing policy is a pure configuration change with no kernel code modified. Still, it yielded a 10 percent end-to-end throughput improvement for FP8 quantized fused MoE models on H200. This improvement is available in the AWS Large Model Inference (LMI) v28 container. Triton JIT recompilation elimination One of the most impactful performance pathologies in GPU inference is also one of the least obvious: unnecessary kernel recompilation. Triton, the compiler framework underlying many of vLLM’s custom kernels, specializes integer arguments by default. Every time a kernel is invoked with a previously unseen value for a specialized parameter, Triton triggers a fresh just-in-time (JIT) compilation. In serving workloads where sequence lengths and batch sizes vary continuously, this creates a steady stream of compilation overhead that inflates latency, particularly Time to First Token (TTFT). In MoE model serving, the _fused_inv_rope_fp8_quant_per_head kernel (responsible for fused rotary position embedding and FP8 quantization) was recompiling on every new num_tokens value. Adding do_not_specialize annotations to the variable-length parameters removed these recompilations entirely, improving TTFT by 9 percent  on H200 at 8-way tensor parallelism (PR #42849). In a multi-GPU cluster, all 8 GPUs must execute their kernels in perfect, microsecond-level synchronization. If even one GPU must stop to recompile its local _fused_inv_rope_fp8_quant_per_head kernel because its local token batch count changed, the other seven GPUs sit idle and wait for it. By eliminating recompilations across the entire cluster, we smoothed out the multi-GPU coordination overhead, delivering a 9 percent speedup for the user’s initial response latency. The principle here is to treat the compiler as a first-class optimization surface. Understanding how Triton specializes semantics and recognizing when parameters are dead or variable unlocks latency improvements with minimal code change. We upstreamed this optimization to vLLM, and it is available in version 0.22.0 or later. Conclusion Through our collaboration with the vLLM community, we implemented and open sourced multiple kernel optimizations for fused MoE models. We apply these optimizations in the LMI Deep Learning Container on Amazon SageMaker AI. Together, these optimizations have delivered up to 10 percent higher throughput and up to 9 percent faster TTFT. To get started with custom model hosting, see the Amazon SageMaker AI hosting documentation .   About the authors Mona Mona Mona is a Specialist Solutions Architect at AWS, focused on machine learning infrastructure and AI/ML services. She helps customers design and optimize their ML pipelines using Amazon SageMaker. Sadaf Fardeen Sadaf is the SDM of Inference optimization charter for SageMaker, HyperPod and Amazon Bedrock. Her team develops GPU performance optimizations for open source large language models and are active contributors to vLLM. Sadaf also leads development of Model servers and optimized GenAI recommendation service. Xin Yang Xin is a Sr Software Development Engineer at AWS, specializing in large-scale deep learning inference and performance optimization. She works on building and optimizing model serving systems for large language models, with a focus on GPU performance, distributed inference, and open-source technologies such as vLLM.

summary: A new outline along the left edge of the conversation lists each prompt you sent. Hover a mark to preview the prompt, and click it to jump there Plugins that fail to load or error during a session now show a status line in the chat naming the plugin and the error, instead of silently losing their tools You can cancel a Cline Cloud sign-in while it is waiting for the browser Session titles renamed on the web now update in the app The Cloud setup card stays visible on smaller windows when...
content: A new outline along the left edge of the conversation lists each prompt you sent. Hover a mark to preview the prompt, and click it to jump there Plugins that fail to load or error during a session now show a status line in the chat naming the plugin and the error, instead of silently losing their tools You can cancel a Cline Cloud sign-in while it is waiting for the browser Session titles renamed on the web now update in the app The Cloud setup card stays visible on smaller windows when signed out Installing a skill without Git installed now says Git is required and how to fix it, instead of showing a raw clone error Scheduled routines: queued runs now start instead of staying pending forever, a run whose model call fails (for example, a retired model) is marked failed with the error, and after downtime only the latest missed occurrence runs instead of every one back to back. The routine editor now lists current models instead of retired ones With no model chosen, the Cline provider uses the first model in Cline's recommended list (Claude Sonnet 5.5) Turning reasoning off now works on every provider. Models that can't turn it off keep their default, and level-only Gemini models no longer reject the request with a thinking-budget error Screenshots and other images no longer inflate the token estimate, which made auto-compaction run long before the conversation was near its limit Auto-compaction uses the selected model's context window when the catalog entry has none Rule files that are symlinks now load Skills in .claude/skills are now discovered The editor tool no longer receives null in place of the text to replace from some models Refreshed the model catalog. Adds the AI/ML API, LowRouter, and Prime Inference providers. The v0 provider now offers only its default model, v0-1.5-md , and OpenCode Go uses its new https://opencode.ai/inference/go/v1 endpoint. The Cline free list adds Step 5 Preview. Default models change for 302.AI, CrossModel, Cortecs, DigitalOcean, NEAR AI Cloud, and Ofox (Claude Haiku 5.5), DevPass (LLM Gateway), LLM Gateway, and Meta (Muse Wonder 1.0), Aixy (GPT-6.1 Sol), CloudFerro Sherlock and Moark (GLM 5.3), Ambient, NanoGPT, Neuralwatt, and Novita AI Full Changelog : desktop-v0.0.45...desktop-v0.0.46

title: v4.1.24

content: Changed With no model chosen, the Cline and OpenRouter providers now use Claude Sonnet 5.5. For Cline, that's the first model in Cline's recommended list. Selecting ai& shows its own API key and model picker, instead of the generic OpenAI-compatible form with base URL and custom headers. Refreshed the model catalog. Adds Claude Haiku 5.5 and the AI/ML API, LowRouter, and Prime Inference providers. The Cline free list adds Step 5 Preview. The v0 provider now offers only its default model, v0-1.5-md , and OpenCode Go uses its new https://opencode.ai/inference/go/v1 endpoint. Default models change for 302.AI, Cortecs, CrossModel, DevPass, DigitalOcean, Eden AI, GitHub Copilot, Google Vertex AI, LLM Gateway, Meta, Moark, NanoGPT, NEAR AI Cloud, Neuralwatt, Novita AI, Ofox, OpenCode Go, Requesty, Vivgrid, and a few others (most now Claude Haiku 5.5 or Muse Wonder 1.0). If you use one of those providers without pinning a model, expect a different default. Fixed Turning reasoning off no longer fails with a 400 error on GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Fable 5 or Claude Opus 5.5, and now works on every provider. Level-only Gemini models no longer reject the request with a thinking-budget error. An MCP server or hook that exits before reading all of its input no longer crashes the extension host about 3 seconds later. A 404 from a stale or retired model id is no longer shown as a sign-in problem. Cline shows the real error instead of the logged-out card. Errors in the Cline output log keep their details. Production builds used to drop them, so a line like "Cline OAuth login failed:" showed no reason. Deleting a slash command from the input keeps the spacing of the text around it. Screenshots and other images no longer inflate the token estimate, which made auto-compaction run long before the conversation was near its limit. Auto-compaction uses the selected model's context window when the catalog entry has none. Rule files that are symlinks now load, and skills in .claude/skills are now discovered. The editor tool no longer receives null in place of the text to replace from some models. Settings migrated from older versions no longer add an empty SAP AI Core provider. Full Changelog : v4.1.23...v4.1.24

title: All Systems Go: Global PC App Ecosystem Ready for NVIDIA RTX Spark
summary: NVIDIA RTX Spark is a new beginning for the PC — a reinvention combining the capabilities of a gaming PC, a creative studio and a personal AI supercomputer into a single superchip. With up to 128GB of unified memory and 1 petaflop of AI compute, RTX Spark delivers the full stack of NVIDIA RTX and […]
content: NVIDIA RTX Spark is a new beginning for the PC — a reinvention combining the capabilities of a gaming PC, a creative studio and a personal AI supercomputer into a single superchip. With up to 128GB of unified memory and 1 petaflop of AI compute, RTX Spark delivers the full stack of NVIDIA RTX and CUDA technologies for creators, developers and gamers, while unlocking a new paradigm in personal computing via powerful local AI agents. Last week, NVIDIA and Microsoft announced that RTX Spark laptops will be available on Friday, Oct. 16 . Ahead of the launch, NVIDIA and its ecosystem partners are rolling out new software features and performance optimizations to expand what’s possible with local AI on RTX Spark. New and upcoming RTX Spark updates — among the thousands of apps, games and models available at launch — include: New agent features, models and tools that enhance local agents on RTX Spark: Updates to top agent apps including GitHub Copilot, Hermes, OpenClaw, Perplexity, Pi and WorkBuddy streamline setup on RTX Spark, improve security with OpenShell and Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC), and enable hybrid local and cloud AI routing. The NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B model, purpose-built for agentic AI on RTX Spark, releases on Thursday, Oct. 15. NVIDIA PAIR moves out of beta and adds llama.cpp support. Top creative apps optimized for RTX Spark: Up to 2x performance is coming soon to Adobe’s top apps. NVIDIA and Adobe have collaborated to rearchitect Photoshop for GPU-accelerated compositing and Premiere for playback, rendering, effects and more. The NVIDIA Broadcast 2.3 release brings new Video Super Resolution, Video Frame Generation, offline file processing and agent Model Context Protocol (MCP) controls to the app. NVIDIA RTX Video Frame Generation and high dynamic range (HDR) capabilities are available now in ComfyUI to accelerate AI generative video workflows. NVIDIA DLSS Ray Reconstruction will be available in Blender 5.3 in November to improve interactivity in the viewport. Developer tools are now ready for RTX Spark: Top developer frameworks are now available for RTX Spark, including PyTorch, Python and CUDA, as well as all CUDA libraries. GitHub Copilot, Pi and other coding agents are now optimized for RTX Spark. Llama.cpp adds support for decision models, and releases a Windows app. Hundreds of top games and anti-cheat are supported on RTX Spark, plus: A 2x faster DLSS 5 AI model arrives Friday, Oct. 16, and a new Performance Mode for DLSS Frame Generation is available today via the NVIDIA App beta . Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, the third-generation small language model (SLM) for NVIDIA ACE AI game characters, releases Friday, Oct. 23. The latest RTX Remix update, including DLSS 5 support, releases on Friday, Oct. 23. Advancing Local AI Agents With New Apps, Models and Tools AI is changing the way people interact with PCs. Agent popularity skyrocketed this year, with projects such as OpenClaw and Hermes topping popularity charts on GitHub. Local large language models (LLMs) surpassed the intelligence threshold to power agents, with models like Qwen 3.8-Flash-Next catching up to frontier cloud models released just a few months ago. As a result, local LLM downloads are already 5x higher than all of last year. From models to agent harnesses to security to tools, NVIDIA is partnering closely with the local AI ecosystem to make RTX Spark the ideal hardware to run local agents. Local AI Agents Made Easy On RTX Spark From the first boot of RTX Spark, users will be greeted with a “Getting Started” screen to choose and install their agent app. These agents will come with new, secure sandboxing technology thanks to NVIDIA OpenShell and MXC. MXC delivers operating system-level security, while OpenShell makes it simpler for agents to adopt MXC and adds advanced capabilities such as credential protection and security monitoring. Hermes Agent will integrate granular OpenShell controls and MXC by the end of the month. OpenClaw and GitHub Copilot now support MXC. After installing an agent, setting up local AI is also now seamless in GitHub Copilot, Hermes Agent, OpenClaw, Perplexity, Pi and WorkBuddy. The apps will recommend an optimized local model and settings configuration for RTX Spark, and set it all up for users in a few clicks. Many users want the best of both worlds — local models for free iteration, and cloud models for frontier intelligence. NVIDIA Switchyard, an open source model router library, enables agents to intelligently route queries between local and cloud LLMs, allowing the user to minimize cloud usage but still obtain similar results to just running on cloud. Hermes will be adding Switchyard later in October, and other agents like Perplexity Computer and GitHub Copilot have integrated their own routing solutions. Software providers have made it simple for agents to connect to top Windows apps, with easy-to-use MCP libraries and command line interfaces (CLIs). NVIDIA has also now made available MCPs for its applications, including NVIDIA App, Broadcast, PAIR, Omniverse, RTX Remix and a large library of CUDA-X Skills . NVIDIA is also releasing AI playbooks for RTX Spark, available on Friday, Oct 16. Users can set up their first agent, build an AI chief of staff, configure their system for development or design a creative assistant. Meet Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B: Built for Local Agents on RTX Spark NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, available Thursday, Oct. 15, is a new LLM purpose-built for running local agents on RTX Spark. This model is a 74B parameter, 9B-active-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, packed into 24GB using 2-bit quantization with advanced quantization-aware training techniques to retain quality. It aims to achieve the optimal balance between speed and intelligence, being faster than most popular dense models while smarter than most popular MoE models with a similar memory footprint. Users will be able to run Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B at launch through llama.cpp, vLLM, Ollama, Unsloth and LM Studio. It will also be directly accessible via agents such as Hermes and OpenClaw. Like other Nemotron models, Bolt 74B is fully open source — including training data, weights and recipes — so developers can fine-tune and customize their own agents. The Perfect PAIR Local AI doesn’t have to run on just one PC. NVIDIA PAIR , a personal AI router, is officially moving out of beta today, making it easier to tap into the total AI compute of compatible PCs on a local network. The free, open source software tool automatically discovers and connects devices, installs AI models and inference engines, and distributes AI workloads across available systems. The official release adds llama.cpp support, direct model downloads from Hugging Face, customizable inference engine settings and RTX Spark support, along with a variety of inference and user experience improvements. PAIR works on Windows, Linux and macOS. Developers can contribute to the open source project via Github — just one month after the initial PAIR release, the community has already contributed over 10 features and fixes to the release. Sparking Creativity RTX Spark brings over 130 accelerated apps, CUDA for fast video and image generation, and RTX technologies such as DLSS, NVENC and OptiX to advanced content creation workflows — all in a thin and light laptop with on-the-go performance. Adobe Accelerates Creative Applications for RTX Spark Adobe is optimizing its industry-leading creative applications, including Photoshop, Premiere and Substance 3D, for RTX Spark, delivering up to 2x faster AI, editing, color and effects across creative workflows. In Photoshop, GPU-accelerated compositing makes complex image editing faster and more responsive, with improvements to the Remove Tool and effects such as Light Leaks. Premiere accelerates demanding video editing tasks, including playback, rendering, color grading and AI-powered features such as Enhance Speech and Object Mask. Meanwhile, Substance 3D Painter speeds up texture creation workflows, from baking high-resolution mesh maps to opening, saving and exporting large projects. The updates will be rolling out in phases, with AI feature optimizations in Photoshop and Premiere now ready in beta, and with Adobe Substance 3D updates coming soon. Opt in to the beta to get access to the RTX Spark-optimized builds. Latest NVIDIA Broadcast Brings New AI Effects to Live and Recorded Content Available for download now, NVIDIA Broadcast 2.3 runs natively on RTX Spark, and adds new RTX Video Super Resolution and Frame Generation AI effects and Studio Voice profiles. A new Offline File Processor lets creators apply Broadcast effects to prerecorded content, with many effects running at higher quality since there isn’t a need to maintain real-time performance. The update also introduces a new MCP server and skill that lets local AI agents adjust effects, change settings and process files directly through the Broadcast app. RTX Video Brings Frame Generation and HDR to ComfyUI ComfyUI is expanding its RTX Video tools with two new nodes: RTX Video Frame Generation and RTX Video HDR. It’s also providing the ability to export EXR files, giving creators more ways to enhance AI-generated video. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/comfyui_nvidia_vfx_nodes_explainer_4k48_v4.mp4   RTX Video Frame Generation increases video frame rates for smoother motion for GeForce RTX 40 Series GPUs and newer, while RTX Video HDR converts standard dynamic range (SDR) footage to HDR for greater flexibility in color grading. Combined with RTX Video Super Resolution, these tools enable creators to upscale, enhance and refine video within a single ComfyUI workflow. For example, creators can combine LTX 2.5 with RTX Video Frame Generation and HDR to transform a 1080p, 30 frames-per-second (fps) SDR clip into a smoother 60 fps HDR video exported as EXR files ready for color grading. Blender Adds DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction Blender has released a beta version of its popular 3D editor, adding compatibility for RTX Spark. Download Blender version 5.3 to get access. Coming next month, Blender will also be adding support for DLSS Ray Reconstruction, allowing for real-time updates in the viewport so artists can navigate a scene while previewing it in real time. Code, Test and Deploy From RTX Spark Developers are moving from writing code to directing AI agents. This new development paradigm is requiring many to spread their work across their laptop, a cloud LLM and a cloud virtual machine, where they test and prototype. RTX Spark enables developers to work on one machine, running all their workloads and libraries, testing and prototyping, and deploying. They can now do so directly in Windows with the new Windows Developer Config, which enhances the user experience for devs and installs all the top developer tools — or via Windows Subsystem for Linux, where they can get access to the same packages they’ll use to publish to the cloud. Developer Tools Are RTX-Spark Ready NVIDIA has partnered with Microsoft to ensure that developer tools are ready for RTX Spark. Alongside RTX Spark, the community is releasing: The first PyTorch-CUDA build for Windows on Arm. The first Python build that is native by default on Windows on Arm, with Python 3.15. The first native Conda installer for Windows on Arm, with over 2,000 Conda packages. 97% of the top 15,000 Python wheels are ready, thanks to work with the ecosystem. NVIDIA will be working closely with the community to ready the remaining wheels. Development is now mostly done by agents. NVIDIA Skills — an open source GitHub repository that teaches agents how to use NVIDIA CUDA-X tools and libraries — lets users develop apps that are accelerated on NVIDIA technologies, even without knowing anything about CUDA. Coding Agents Are Ready for Local AI In addition to GitHub Copilot — one of the most popular coding agents, used by millions worldwide — adding support for MXC, it’s updating its model router HydraFusion with support for local models. This enables developers to use their local hardware to reduce token consumption while tapping into frontier intelligence. Microsoft is making coding models, such as MAI 1.1 Coding Flash, available locally , and adding llama.cpp as a backend to Windows ML — extending the supported models and enabling the latest NVIDIA performance optimizations. Get started with GitHub Copilot running locally when RTX Spark launches. Llama.cpp Adds Support for Decision Models, Releases a Windows App Decision models are the latest breakthrough in AI development. They give AI agents a near-instant way to make decisions, without lengthy reasoning loops. They can choose what to do next, from classifying requests to selecting the next action, up to 200x faster than traditional agents. Decision models are now supported in llama.cpp and Unsloth on RTX Spark and GeForce RTX GPUs. Llama.cpp is also releasing today Llama Windows , a Windows-native companion app for llama.cpp, enabling an easy-to-use user interface to download and run models locally, without having to go into the command line. This app, like llama.cpp, is optimized for RTX Spark. Learn more on the Hugging Face blog . Llama Windows runs from the Windows 11 system tray, with local models and recommended models from the Hugging Face Hub one click away. Game On: RTX Spark Launches With Hundreds of Top Games and DLSS 5 RTX Spark is ready for gaming, with hundreds of top titles available when laptops launch on Friday, Oct. 16, including CONTROL Resonant , Cyberpunk 2077 , Fortnite , Gears of War: E-Day , Genshin Impact , Hogwarts Legacy , Honkai: Star Rail , Marvel Rivals , NARAKA: BLADEPOINT , NBA 2K27 , World of Warcraft and many more. NVIDIA has worked to bring the full stack of RTX technologies, including DLSS, Reflex, Remix, G-SYNC and ray tracing, to the new platform, along with collaborating with game developers to enable anti-cheat support for popular multiplayer games. Learn more about gaming on RTX Spark . DLSS 5 Brings Neural Rendering to RTX Spark NVIDIA DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering is also coming to RTX Spark on launch day. The technology uses AI to enhance lighting and materials with lifelike detail, making game worlds and characters more realistic while preserving developers’ artistic vision. A new, 2x faster DLSS 5 AI model debuts in NBA 2K27 on Friday, Oct. 16, boosting frame rates by up to 1.4x. The faster model will also power DLSS 5 in Hogwarts Legacy starting Thursday, Nov. 5, and Where Winds Meet in late November. DLSS 5 is also coming to NVIDIA RTX Remix on Friday, Oct. 23, so modders can add better materials, lighting and shadows to classic characters and environments, as shown from modder Sparkles/Kim2091 in her in-development project, Fallout 4 RTX . Read more about DLSS 5 on RTX Spark on GeForce.com. Game Agents Running Locally on RTX Spark Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB is the third-generation SLM for NVIDIA ACE, the suite of technologies for building in-game AI agents that deliver next-generation gaming experiences. The first-generation model was in a public beta earlier this year for PUBG , allowing players to team up with AI teammates, while the more efficient second-generation model previewed in Aniimo at Gamescom, turning standard creatures into voice-responsive companions. Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B combines natural conversation with multi-turn tool use, instruction following and grounding in application state to power fast local voice and device assistants, interactive characters and embedded interfaces. Designed for a low memory footprint and fast time to first token, this model enables responsive local experiences while leaving headroom for applications and other AI models. Its new conversational mode helps keep responses concise and speech-ready, and developers can turn reasoning on or off as needed. Starting Friday, Oct. 23, test drive the third-generation Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB inside SkyrimNET, an AI nonplayable character (NPC) modding platform by MinLL for The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim. SkyrimNET transforms every NPC into an unscripted, interactive character equipped with personal memory, voice and autonomy for dynamic conversations and context-aware quests generated on the fly. Now compatible with RTX Spark, SkyrimNET supports both cloud and local inference across multiple models, with the latest Nemotron models delivering best-in-class performance for efficient and fast in-game interactions. Download the build on GitHub . Accelerating Modding Workflows in RTX Remix As AI agents continue to help modders make their favorite classic games compatible with the RTX Remix renderer , NVIDIA is streamlining asset updates with a major overhaul to its AI-powered texture generation workflow. Launching Friday, Oct. 23, as part of Remix 1.6, ComfyUI Version 2 replaces complex REST application programming interface (API) node connections with a dedicated AI tools layout directly in the sidebar. This update allows modders and artists to generate physically based rendering materials natively inside RTX Remix with zero API setup required. A new batch processing feature makes it easy to scale beyond single-texture experimentation to full modding projects, while an intuitive presets system lets non-technical creators adjust key settings without touching the node graph. Subscribe to the NVIDIA Local AI newsletter . Follow NVIDIA RTX Spark on X , Instagram , TikTok and Facebook . See notice regarding software product information.

content: 2026.10.5-beta.3 Highlights Updates leave the Gateway running: pnpm 12 installs keep their Gateway service and openclaw launcher on the durable install path, Windows updates accept qualified Scheduled Task accounts and their own verified driver, macOS accepts protected Bun service commands, and clean service-install refusals no longer leave the Gateway stopped. ( #170003 , #169059 , #170131 , #169244 , #169481 , #169563 , #170006 , #169662 , #169658 , #169915 ) Thanks @xilopaint , @k-sekula , @RomneyDa , @jokerman1302-eng , and @vincentkoc . Stuck updates recover: updates settle package-activation journals after filesystem remounts or device-number drift, ride out a briefly locked state database, stop reporting false post-install failures after migration, and reclaim retained updater runtimes that blocked npm recovery. ( #169410 , #170046 , #169050 , #169352 , #168210 , #170130 , #169422 , #170170 , #169463 ) Thanks @patrickschiller , @RomneyDa , @SergeiAug , @angeliti999 , and @Warhangel . Doctor keeps credentials and data: Doctor no longer deletes an OAuth profile when the legacy auth store is unreadable, refuses retired state before migrating the database, imports retained ACP metadata, and restores a stopped Gateway when cleanup fails. ( #170256 , #168959 , #170051 , #169918 , #169759 , #169783 ) Thanks @Yolo521-bot , @bautrey , and @RomneyDa . Turns survive restarts: interrupted turns, subagent work, automation turns, steered sessions, and node-hosted turns resume after a Gateway restart, and streamed replies from a killed worker stay in history. ( #168650 , #169144 , #170162 , #170252 , #170161 , #170223 ) Telegram never replays old updates: the first start after updating no longer re-dispatches months-old Telegram updates from the legacy spool as new owner instructions. ( #170068 , #169784 ) Thanks @angeliti999 . Codex and provider replies complete: Codex replies keep their last tokens and accept follow-ups after a failed thread preparation, ChatGPT turns retry a mid-stream WebSocket close, and DeepSeek tool markup no longer leaks into messages. ( #168400 , #169431 , #167512 , #167345 , #169728 , #159665 ) Thanks @RomneyDa , @jjjhenriksen , @ericcurtin , @obviyus , @mightyx , and @TOMUIV . Meta Muse Wonder: Meta users can select meta/muse-wonder-1.0 with tools, image input, streaming, reasoning controls, and a 1M-token context window. ( #170232 ) Thanks @RomneyDa . Plugin SDK compatibility: plugins built against 2026.10.1 and 2026.10.2 can import createSessionHeaderLink from openclaw/plugin-sdk/control-ui again. ( #169746 ) Thanks @RomneyDa . Changes Meta Muse Wonder: adds meta/muse-wonder-1.0 with text and image input, tools, streaming, encrypted reasoning replay, and a 1,048,576-token context window; Spark remains the onboarding default. ( #170232 ) Thanks @RomneyDa . Device joins: the CLI and Control UI join command now installs a background node service that can host agent sessions ( --service --session-host ), with a command-only service alternative, and already-paired devices get a working command to enable session hosting. ( #168623 ) Thanks @obviyus . Fixes Telegram: legacy spool updates older than 24 hours are imported as stale and never dispatched, so already-handled messages are not executed again after an update. ( #170068 , #169784 ) Thanks @angeliti999 . Plugin SDK compatibility: createSessionHeaderLink is restored in openclaw/plugin-sdk/control-ui as a deprecated export for plugins built against 2026.10.1 and 2026.10.2. ( #169746 ) Thanks @RomneyDa . Reply delivery: streamed text from a killed native worker stays in history with its real failure, steered messages behind subagent announcements are no longer dropped as interrupted, blocking questions from routed agent turns reach their conversation, live sends survive delivery recovery, WebChat no longer shows false attachment errors or duplicate file cards, Talk consultations no longer abort right after connecting, and deleting a session records its cancellation before draining retained replies. ( #170223 , #168077 , #170039 , #169010 , #169093 , #170083 ) Thanks @RomneyDa and @brokemac79 . Restart recovery: turns interrupted while a session was still preparing resume after a restart, interrupted subagents return to their parent with their history, automation turns, steered sessions, and node-hosted turns resume instead of failing with an active turn claim, a Gateway restarts cleanly when a stored cloud worker's machine is gone, and symlinked state directories keep working after a restart. ( #168650 , #169144 , #170162 , #170252 , #170161 , #168907 , #168361 ) Thanks @obviyus . Nodes and channels: node requests and events no longer fail with "pairing changed" during another device's pairing activity, and channel tools keep working after a config write restarts the account. ( #169486 , #169575 , #159396 ) Thanks @ceckert and @RomneyDa . macOS app: fresh app installs authenticate to their app-hosted Gateway and finish setup faster, and the Gateway reconnects automatically after a trusted TLS certificate renewal. ( #169403 , #168151 ) Codex and OpenAI: Codex replies keep their final tokens when a stream drops the last delta, Codex follow-ups work after a failed thread preparation, ChatGPT turns retry a mid-stream WebSocket close with code 1000, and personal-account quota rechecks no longer abort replies. content: Plugins now load inside the hub instead of a separate node or bun process, so the CLI no longer needs a JavaScript runtime on your PATH to run plugins. A plugin that fails to load no longer silently loses its tools: Cline prints a warning naming the plugin and the error, cline config tools --json lists it as a plugin_failure entry, and the new cline hub plugins shows each plugin's status and last error ( --reload re-imports one without restarting the hub). Set CLINE_PLUGIN_MODE=sandbox to keep the old subprocess behavior --thinking now applies in ACP mode ( --acp ). Before, ACP sessions always ran with reasoning off cline hook accepts agent_error events. Before, it exited with an error and no response A provider API key set in the environment (such as OPENROUTER_API_KEY ) now counts as configured at startup, for providers that read a single environment variable. Before, the TUI asked you to set up the provider anyway With no model chosen, the Cline provider now uses the first model in Cline's recommended list (Claude Sonnet 5.5) Turning reasoning off now works on every provider. Models that can't turn it off keep their default, and level-only Gemini models no longer reject the request with a thinking-budget error Screenshots and other images no longer inflate the token estimate, which made auto-compaction run long before the conversation was near its limit Auto-compaction uses the selected model's context window when the catalog entry has none Scheduled runs: queued runs now start instead of staying pending forever, a run whose model call fails (for example, a retired model) is marked failed with the error, and after downtime only the latest missed occurrence of a schedule runs instead of every one back to back Rule files that are symlinks now load Skills in .claude/skills are now discovered The editor tool no longer receives null in place of the text to replace from some models Refreshed the model catalog. Adds the AI/ML API, LowRouter, and Prime Inference providers. The v0 provider now offers only its default model, v0-1.5-md , and OpenCode Go uses its new https://opencode.ai/inference/go/v1 endpoint. The Cline free list adds Step 5 Preview. Default models change for 302.AI, CrossModel, Cortecs, DigitalOcean, NEAR AI Cloud, and Ofox (Claude Haiku 5.5), DevPass (LLM Gateway), LLM Gateway, and Meta (Muse Wonder 1.0), Aixy (GPT-6.1 Sol), CloudFerro Sherlock and Moark (GLM 5.3), Ambient, NanoGPT, Neuralwatt, and Novita AI Full Changelog : cli-v3.0.70...cli-v3.0.71

content: Plugins load in-process through one registry per process instead of a node/bun subprocess, so the compiled CLI and its hub no longer need a runtime on PATH, and plugins can use the Bun global under the Bun-built hub. CLINE_PLUGIN_MODE=sandbox keeps the subprocess sandbox. The registry wraps import, setup, hooks, tools and commands with timeouts and error capture, and tracks each plugin's state (loading/ready/degraded/failed/disabled) with its last error. A failing plugin no longer silently drops its tools: session.create accepts a plugins policy and returns pluginIssues , later failures reach affected sessions as status notices, the hub answers plugins.list / plugins.status / plugins.reload and broadcasts plugin.status_changed , and the daemon marks a plugin failed instead of shutting down when an uncaught error comes from it. Each session gets its own copy of every plugin module, so plugins that keep per-session state at module level keep working Turning reasoning off now works on every provider, not just a fixed list. Models whose catalog entry has no off option are sent nothing and keep their default, and models without a reasoning capability are skipped. Gemini and Vertex send exact thinkingBudget values only to models that advertise a budget; level-only Gemini models get a thinking level instead (they rejected thinkingBudget ). A request never carries both the portable reasoning option and a native provider control ( effort , thinking , thinkingConfig , …); the native one wins The cline provider's default model is the first entry of the Cline recommended-models list, falling back to anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5 . CLINE_DEFAULT_MODEL_ID moves from Claude Sonnet 5 to Claude Sonnet 5.5, and the openrouter provider default is now anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5 too estimateRequestInputTokens and createTokenEstimator no longer bill base64 image payloads at the text rate. A ~90 KB screenshot counted as ~30k tokens, so a few images triggered auto compaction long before the transcript was near budget. Each image now adds a flat ESTIMATED_TOKENS_PER_IMAGE (1600). New createImageAwareReplacer export in @cline/shared Auto compaction uses the resolved model's context window. When the discovered catalog entry had no limit but the selected-model override did, compaction was handed the bare catalog entry and ran against the wrong budget Scheduled runs: queued runs are claimed correctly under bun:sqlite , which bound the store's named parameters as NULL so the desktop hub never claimed a queued run and it stayed pending with no error. Runs whose agent turn ends with a provider error (such as a retired model id) are now recorded as failed with the error message instead of succeeding silently, and the run report keeps usage and tool calls. Queued cron occurrences superseded by a newer occurrence of the same schedule are cancelled, so a backlog no longer replays every missed slot back to back Rule files that are symlinks are now loaded from config directories instead of skipped. Edits to a link's target are picked up on the next refresh or new session resolveSkillsConfigSearchPaths scans .claude/skills , so skills authored for Claude Code are visible to Cline The editor tool advertises old_text as a plain string. When the schema allowed null, some models sent null instead of the replacement text. Null is still accepted at runtime and treated as omitted Composio connectors: signed-in sessions register Composio's meta tools (search, manage connections, wait for connections, multi-execute), so the agent can find connector tools across toolkits, hand the user a Connect Link for an app that is not connected yet, and run what it found. Connector tools are discovered through meta search; saved desktop connection state no longer supplies model tools. Hosts can supply their own authentication through the new connectorsRequest option ( ConnectorsRequest exported from @cline/core ), which is also forwarded to scheduled sessions. resolveComposioToolsStatePath is renamed to resolveComposioConnectionStatePath The Cline cloud sign-in helpers in @cline/core accept an AbortSignal , so hosts can cancel a pending sign-in while it is polling Cloud session refreshes update open sessions with titles renamed on the web, and keep renames made locally while a refresh is in flight Refreshed the model catalog (6,572 → 6,862 models). Adds the AI/ML API, LowRouter, and Prime Inference providers. models.dev no longer lists v0, so the v0 provider ships with only its default model, v0-1.5-md . OpenCode Go's base URL moves from https://opencode.ai/zen/go/v1 to https://opencode.ai/inference/go/v1 . The Cline free list adds Step 5 Preview. Default models change for 302.AI, CrossModel, Cortecs, DigitalOcean, NEAR AI Cloud, and Ofox (Claude Haiku 5.5), DevPass (LLM Gateway), LLM Gateway, and Meta (Muse Wonder 1.0), Aixy (GPT-6.1 Sol), CloudFerro Sherlock and Moark (GLM 5.3), Ambient, NanoGPT, Neuralwatt, and Novita AI Full Changelog : sdk/sdk/v0.0.92...sdk/sdk/v0.0.93

title: NVIDIA Announces New Investments in France’s Startups
summary: Companies in France are deploying agentic computing across industries spanning space, financial services, the public sector and scientific research, demonstrating how the country’s ecosystem has moved from ambition to application. France’s progress sits on deliberate groundwork. The AI Action Summit in February 2025 and Choose France Summits in 2025 and 2026 anchored major compute commitments […]
content: Companies in France are deploying agentic computing across industries spanning space, financial services, the public sector and scientific research, demonstrating how the country’s ecosystem has moved from ambition to application. France’s progress sits on deliberate groundwork. The AI Action Summit in February 2025 and Choose France Summits in 2025 and 2026 anchored major compute commitments on French soil. What the ecosystem has built since then spans the full stack. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements   NVIDIA’s Investments in France NVIDIA has been investing in France’s startup ecosystem, having previously invested in leading technology companies including Alice&Bob, Gradium and Scintil Photonics . Across all of Europe, NVIDIA has committed nearly $10 billion to the technology ecosystem. Today, NVIDIA announced new planned investments in Doctolib, Entalpic , Genesis AI and Pigment . These startups are innovating to solve challenges across healthcare, materials discovery, physical AI and business planning. Doctolib , a European healthcare technology company, builds agents that free up healthcare professionals to deliver better care, while providing patients with a digital health companion that improves access to care and supports more preventive, continuous medicine. Entalpic , a Paris-based startup, accelerates the engineering of advanced materials at the atomic scale, with particular expertise in surfaces and interfaces for semiconductor manufacturing and next-generation electronics. Genesis AI is a global robotics company developing general-purpose robots with frontier intelligence and capabilities through its foundation models, data collection systems, simulation infrastructure and robot hardware. Pigment , a Paris-based enterprise software company, builds a planning platform that helps businesses forecast performance, model scenarios and make decisions across finance, sales, workforce and operations. Sovereign AI Infrastructure France-based companies are expanding agentic infrastructure on NVIDIA technology. Bull is extending its European AI server production to NVIDIA Vera Rubin Ultra NVL72 systems, planned for 2028, with trays produced in Europe and rack integration at its Angers factory — inaugurated Friday, Oct. 2. Altair-1, the first satellite in a $1 billion, 50-satellite constellation with on-board autonomous capabilities, launched this month and has successfully reached orbit. Integrated by Loft Orbital and built in Abu Dhabi by Orbitworks , a joint venture between Loft Orbital and Marlan Space , the satellite is flying NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin edge modules, running Mistral’s models, for real-time Earth observation and autonomous operations in orbit. Open Models NVIDIA Nemotron open models are in production across French organizations that require sovereign, trustworthy data. LINAGORA and Docaposte have secured the CANUT framework agreement , making Twake.ai, built on NVIDIA Nemotron, the sole referenced sovereign digital workplace for more than 2,500 French public organizations. In financial services, SBS is launching a sovereign platform enabling banks to deploy governed generative and agentic services within their own environments, in collaboration with NVIDIA. Dassault Systèmes is using NVIDIA Nemotron open models and accelerated computing to advance its sovereign Industrial AI architecture, accelerating the training of its own Industry World Models and the development of its agentic Virtual Companions platform, grounded in science, physics and engineering for trusted industrial applications. Last week, Mistral introduced under private preview Mistral Large 4 open model, with state-of-the-art, open weight performance in cyber defense, manufacturing, finance and multimodal tasks, and a solid foundation for customizing models across key industries. Fondation Inria , with NVIDIA’s support, is launching a working group on open source advanced modeling and tool adoption, with findings to come in the spring of next year. Agents at Work Across Industries Across retail, public services, telecommunications and science, the pattern is consistent: open models and NVIDIA infrastructure are driving results in France. L’Oréal is integrating NVIDIA ALCHEMI into its research workflows so scientists can explore formulation possibilities in silico and better help guide laboratory research. Combining computational predictions with hands-on experimentation can make the discovery process up to 100x faster than traditional methods and maximize the potential of the group’s proprietary active ingredients. Mirakl has onboarded more than 70 million products with fine-tuned and open models running on NVIDIA GPUs and inference software, cutting seller catalog onboarding to under two hours. Photoroom and Vestiaire Collective a re demonstrating the measurable business impact of advanced visual modeling on marketplace performance. Omi helps brands bring accurate products into AI-generated marketing visuals at scale, combining its approved 3D digital twins with open models optimized on NVIDIA for 4x faster inference. In Côte-d’Or, ThinkDeep and Akila built a digital-twin agent — powered by NVIDIA Cosmos open world models, Nemotron and Omniverse libraries — managing nearly 5,800 kilometers of roads and buildings, cutting total operating costs by 10% and targeting 30% as deployment progresses. Port Sud de France runs goods processing and port security on ThinkDeep’s DeepBrain platform powered by Nemotron and Cosmos. Enchanted Tools, a robotics company headquartered in Paris, is deploying social robots to support patients in healthcare settings including pediatric cancer care. In telecom, Bouygues Telecom and Prisme.ai have launched AI Studio V2, powered by NVIDIA full-stack infrastructure, to offer all of its employees the ability to build their own agents, securely and in a controlled environment In quantum, Alice & Bob has integrated the NVIDIA NVQLink platform for its superconducting cat qubits, showing how GPUs can make quantum error correction more efficient, including for faster qubit modalities. Quandela has also been using NVQLink to build an integration between a DGX Spark system and its photonic qubits — advancing QPU-GPU supercomputing and exploring hybrid quantum-classical applications. Tune in to NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang’s GTC Berlin keynote on Wednesday, Oct. 21, at 11 a.m. CEST.   Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements
