title: Accessing OpenAI GPT models on Amazon Bedrock with global cross-Region inference in Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, and Taiwan
summary: Learn how to run OpenAI GPT-6 Sol, Luna, and Astra on Amazon Bedrock through global cross-Region inference from Singapore, Jakarta, Thailand, Malaysia, and Taipei. This post covers the Converse and OpenAI-compatible APIs, IAM and SCP permissions, quota sizing, and monitoring inference from your source Region.
content: Single-Region inference can throttle when demand exceeds local capacity. Teams in Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, and Taiwan need access to the newest OpenAI models beyond that capacity. Amazon Bedrock offers OpenAI GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna through global cross-Region inference from all five AWS Regions, and GPT-6 Astra from Asia Pacific (Singapore). This post shows you how to configure the call, set permissions, and monitor inference from your source Region. GPT-6 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, and GPT-6 Astra are all available through global cross-Region inference from the preceding Regions, on the bedrock-runtime endpoint. See Cross-Region inference in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. For the full list of source and destination Regions in each profile, see Supported Regions and models for inference profiles . In this post, we introduce the global cross-Region inference profiles and invoke them from Asia Pacific (Singapore) using the Converse API, the OpenAI-compatible APIs, and coding clients. We then cover the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and service control policy (SCP) configuration, quota management, and monitoring. Global cross-Region inference profiles for OpenAI GPT-6 The GPT-6 family offers three models, each available through global cross-Region inference. GPT-6 Sol brings strong reasoning and coding capabilities to complex tasks performed throughout the week. GPT-6 Luna makes focused, repeatable tasks practical at high volume. GPT-6 Astra handles complex reasoning, coding, and long-document work. All three accept text and image input, client-side tool use, and prompt caching. They differ on reasoning effort. GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna accept none, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max. GPT-6 Astra accepts the same levels except none. For GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna, see Bring more intelligence to everyday work with GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna on Amazon Bedrock . For GPT-6 Astra, see Take on your most ambitious work with GPT-6 Astra on Amazon Bedrock . Global cross-Region inference routes requests across supported commercial AWS Regions where the model is deployed, giving you broad access to Amazon Bedrock capacity. You invoke it by passing a global cross-Region inference profile ID in place of a model ID. Your source Region is where you make the API call. Amazon Bedrock selects the destination Region for processing. Billing, quota tracking, AWS CloudTrail, and Amazon CloudWatch all stay in your source Region. The following table lists the global cross-Region inference profile IDs and the source Regions covered in this post. Global cross-Region inference profiles Source Regions Destination Regions global.openai.gpt-6-sol global.openai.gpt-6-luna Asia Pacific (Singapore) ap-southeast-1 Asia Pacific (Jakarta) ap-southeast-3 Asia Pacific (Malaysia) ap-southeast-5 Asia Pacific (Thailand) ap-southeast-7 Asia Pacific (Taipei) ap-east-2 Supported commercial AWS Regions where the model is deployed global.openai.gpt-6-astra Asia Pacific (Singapore) ap-southeast-1 Supported commercial AWS Regions where the model is deployed Inference profile availability and Region support change as AWS adds Regions and profiles, so confirm both on the model card before you build: GPT-6 Sol , GPT-6 Luna , and GPT-6 Astra . For per-token rates, see Amazon Bedrock pricing . Getting started with OpenAI models on Amazon Bedrock Start with the prerequisites, then invoke any of the three profiles through the Converse API, the OpenAI-compatible APIs, or your existing coding client. Prerequisites An IAM identity with permission to invoke the profile. The IAM policy in the Security and permissions section grants only what these examples need. Your source Region activated. Only the Region you call from needs activating. You do not activate destination Regions, which run on Amazon Bedrock managed capacity. Singapore ( ap-southeast-1 ) is a Region that is enabled by default. Jakarta ( ap-southeast-3 ), Malaysia ( ap-southeast-5 ), Thailand ( ap-southeast-7 ), and Taipei ( ap-east-2 ) are opt-in Regions you must activate first. For more information, see Enable or disable AWS Regions in your account . A current AWS SDK or CLI. The OpenAI-compatible examples also require the OpenAI SDK and the Amazon Bedrock token generator. Install them with pip install boto3 openai aws-bedrock-token-generator . The Amazon Bedrock console lists all three global cross-Region inference profiles under system-defined inference profiles. See Figure 1. Figure 1: The three global OpenAI GPT-6 inference profiles among the system-defined profiles in the Amazon Bedrock console Invoke GPT-6 models through Amazon Bedrock Runtime Each model supports three access paths on this endpoint: the Amazon Bedrock Converse API, the OpenAI Responses API, and the OpenAI Chat Completions API. The OpenAI-compatible APIs are called on the /openai/v1 paths rather than through the AWS SDKs, and the endpoint accepts either Signature Version 4 (SigV4) or an Amazon Bedrock API key. Pass the global cross-Region inference profile ID as the model in every case. Converse API. This example calls GPT-6 Sol from Asia Pacific (Singapore) and logs the response. Set BEDROCK_PROFILE_ID to global.openai.gpt-6-luna or global.openai.gpt-6-astra to switch models, or call converse_stream for streaming. import logging import os import boto3 # AWS_REGION overrides this default, so set it to your source Region or unset it. REGION = os.environ.get("AWS_REGION", "ap-southeast-1") PROFILE_ID = os.environ.get("BEDROCK_PROFILE_ID", "global.openai.gpt-6-sol") PROMPT = ( "In three bullet points, explain when a workload should use " "cross-Region inference instead of calling a model in a single Region." ) logging.basicConfig(format="%(levelname)s %(message)s") log = logging.getLogger("bedrock-cris") log.setLevel(logging.INFO) client = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name=REGION) # AccessDeniedException points at the IAM policy. ValidationException usually # means the model ID is not a global cross-Region inference profile. response = client.converse( modelId=PROFILE_ID, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": PROMPT}]}], inferenceConfig={"maxTokens": 1024}, # GPT-6 Sol and Luna accept none through max. GPT-6 Astra rejects none. additionalModelRequestFields={"reasoning": {"effort": "low"}}, ) # Any effort above none can prepend a reasoningContent block, so pick the text # block by key rather than by position. text = "".join(b["text"] for b in response["output"]["message"]["content"] if "text" in b) log.info("Called %s from %s", PROFILE_ID, REGION) log.info("Stop reason: %s", response["stopReason"]) log.info("Response:\n%s", text) OpenAI Chat Completions API. Point the OpenAI SDK at the Regional endpoint and pass the same profile ID. import logging import os from aws_bedrock_token_generator import provide_token from openai import OpenAI REGION = os.environ.get("AWS_REGION", "ap-southeast-1") PROFILE_ID = os.environ.get("BEDROCK_PROFILE_ID", "global.openai.gpt-6-sol") PROMPT = "List three uses for a message queue." logging.basicConfig(format="%(levelname)s %(message)s") log = logging.getLogger("bedrock-cris") log.setLevel(logging.INFO) # provide_token mints a short-term key from your AWS credentials, valid up to 12 hours. client = OpenAI( base_url=f"https://bedrock-runtime.{REGION}.amazonaws.com/openai/v1", api_key=provide_token(region=REGION), ) response = client.chat.completions.create( model=PROFILE_ID, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": PROMPT}], max_completion_tokens=256, ) log.info("Called %s from %s", PROFILE_ID, REGION) log.info("Response:\n%s", response.choices[0].message.content) When migrating an existing OpenAI client: Set the model parameter on every request, including those referencing a previous response. Use supported tool types: function , mcp , custom , namespace , and tool_search . Configure the inference profile ID directly in your client rather than querying the models endpoint. Set up the ChatGPT desktop app and Codex CLI The ChatGPT desktop app and the Codex CLI share ~/.codex/config.toml , so one change covers both. Of the two built-in Amazon Bedrock providers, only amazon-bedrock-runtime accepts an inference profile. model = "global.openai.gpt-6-astra" model_provider = "amazon-bedrock-runtime" [model_providers.amazon-bedrock-runtime.aws] region = "ap-southeast-1" SigV4 signing means there is no key to rotate. Add profile = " " for a non-default profile, and set region explicitly, because the client otherwise falls back to AWS_REGION . Substitute another profile ID for model to change models. Codex reports a 272,000-token window for these profiles, which is its own bundled figure rather than a service limit. Raise it with model_context_window . This configuration needs Codex CLI 0.148 or later. Figure 2 shows the result in the app. Figure 2: The ChatGPT desktop app running GPT-6 Astra on Amazon Bedrock Security and permissions Amazon Bedrock offers a range of controls over inference. Two of them matter here. AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies control which roles can invoke which profiles, and service control policies (SCPs) apply organization-wide controls, including Region scope. This section covers both, and where request data lands. IAM permissions for global cross-Region inference To call any of these models through a global cross-Region inference profile, your IAM policy needs four statements: Access to the inference profile and the project/default resource in your source Region. Access to the foundation model in your source Region, scoped to the inference profile. The Region-agnostic Amazon Resource Name (ARN) for the foundation model, arn:aws:bedrock:::foundation-model/openai.gpt-6-sol , with aws:RequestedRegion set to unspecified to permit cross-Region routing. bedrock:CallWithBearerToken for API-key authentication. This IAM policy grants permission to invoke GPT-6 Sol through global cross-Region inference from ap-southeast-1 . Replace with your AWS account ID and ap-southeast-1 with your source Region. { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "GrantGlobalCrisProfileAndProjectAccess", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["bedrock:InvokeModel"], "Resource": [ "arn:aws:bedrock:ap-southeast-1: :inference-profile/global.openai.gpt-6-sol", "arn:aws:bedrock:ap-southeast-1: :project/default" ], "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:RequestedRegion": "ap-southeast-1" } } }, { "Sid": "GrantGlobalCrisInRegionModelAccess", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["bedrock:InvokeModel"], "Resource": ["arn:aws:bedrock:ap-southeast-1::foundation-model/openai.gpt-6-sol"], "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:RequestedRegion": "ap-southeast-1", "bedrock:InferenceProfileArn": "arn:aws:bedrock:ap-southeast-1: :inference-profile/global.openai.gpt-6-sol" } } }, { "Sid": "GrantGlobalCrisGlobalModelAccess", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["bedrock:InvokeModel"], "Resource": ["arn:aws:bedrock:::foundation-model/openai.gpt-6-sol"], "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:RequestedRegion": "unspecified", "bedrock:InferenceProfileArn": "arn:aws:bedrock:ap-southeast-1: :inference-profile/global.openai.gpt-6-sol" } } }, { "Sid": "AllowBearerTokenAuth", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["bedrock:CallWithBearerToken"], "Resource": "*" } ] } If you use streaming ( converse_stream or stream=True ), add bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream to the Action in the first three statements. Converse authorizes as bedrock:InvokeModel . If you only call Converse with SigV4 credentials, drop the fourth statement. To switch models, replace openai.gpt-6-sol with openai.gpt-6-luna or openai.gpt-6-astra throughout. For the complete reference, see IAM policy requirements for global cross-Region inference . Service control policy considerations for global cross-Region inference A global cross-Region inference request carries no Region name. Amazon Bedrock sets aws:RequestedRegion to unspecified , so a Region allowlist in an SCP denies the call, and the error names only the policy type, not which policy. That is a common reason a first call fails in an enterprise account. Rather than widening the allowlist, scope the exception. Amazon Bedrock populates the bedrock:InferenceProfileArn condition key during authorization, so an SCP can allow these profiles while keeping Region controls for everything else. The following SCP does that. { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "DenyOutsideApprovedRegionsExceptBedrockInvoke", "Effect": "Deny", "NotAction": [ "iam:*", "sts:*", "organizations:*", "account:*", "route53:*", "cloudfront:*", "waf:*", "wafv2:*", "shield:*", "support:*", "trustedadvisor:*", "health:*", "budgets:*", "ce:*", "cur:*", "tax:*", "billing:*", "bedrock:Invoke*" ], "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringNotEquals": { "aws:RequestedRegion": ["ap-southeast-1"] } } }, { "Sid": "DenyBedrockInferenceOutsideApprovedRegionsUnlessCris", "Effect": "Deny", "Action": ["bedrock:Invoke*"], "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringNotEquals": { "aws:RequestedRegion": ["ap-southeast-1"] }, "ArnNotLike": { "bedrock:InferenceProfileArn": [ "arn:aws:bedrock:*:*:inference-profile/global.*" ] } } } ] } The first statement enforces your Region allowlist for every service except Amazon Bedrock inference. The second denies that inference outside those Regions unless it routes through a global cross-Region inference profile. For geographic profiles, add their prefix (for example inference-profile/us.* ) to the ArnNotLike list, because geographic requests carry a real Region name. Keep your source Region in the allowlist, and add the global services your organization uses to NotAction . A blunter alternative is to add unspecified to your existing allowlist, which works but opens the same exception to every other service. For a ready-to-use policy file, see the aws-samples service-control-policy-examples repository . Data retention and abuse detection For automated offline abuse detection, classifier-flagged traffic is retained by AWS for up to 30 days and processed programmatically. Under cross-Region inference that retention happens in the destination Region, which for a global profile is any supported commercial AWS Region where the model is deployed. Eligible customers might request full zero data retention through their AWS account team. For more information, see Amazon Bedrock abuse detection and Data retention . If your organization has data residency requirements, take this to your risk and compliance team early. See the AWS Financial Services Compliance Center country pages for these five countries. We recommend you obtain your own advice on compliance with the requirements relevant to your business. Quota management GPT-6 quotas on bedrock-runtime are measured in tokens per minute (TPM), tracked against the source Region you call from. Input and cache-write tokens count 1:1, and each output token consumes 10 tokens of quota. For example, a request with 2,000 input tokens and 1,000 output tokens depletes 12,000 tokens from your quota. Amazon Bedrock reserves the full max_tokens up front, so set it close to the completions you expect. One quota covers InvokeModel , Converse, Responses, and Chat Completions. Review and raise it on the Service Quotas console from your source Region. Before production, request increases early and alarm on EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage in the AWS/Bedrock namespace at 70–80 percent of your allocation. See How tokens are counted in Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock endpoints and quotas for current values. Monitoring and logging Your operational surface stays in your source Region. Amazon CloudWatch metrics, AWS CloudTrail events, model invocation logs, quota accounting, and billing all remain in the Region you called from. You pay that Region’s rates, not the processing Region’s. CloudTrail records where each request was processed. AWS documents a global cross-Region inference profile’s destinations as its commercial Regions rather than enumerating them. GetInferenceProfile returns the Region-agnostic and source-Region model ARNs rather than a destination list. Your per-request record is additionalEventData.inferenceRegion in CloudTrail in your source Region. Inference on this endpoint is a management event, logged by default at no extra cost. CloudTrail Event History retains 90 days, so longer horizons need a trail or model invocation logging. Retrieve the CloudTrail events with this command. aws cloudtrail lookup-events \ --region ap-southeast-1 \ --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventSource,AttributeValue=bedrock.amazonaws.com \ --start-time \ --end-time \ --max-results 1 \ --query 'Events[0].CloudTrailEvent' --output text | python3 -m json.tool Set the window around a call you just made, because CloudTrail delivery lags by a few minutes. If the most recent event was a failed call, it carries an errorCode and no inferenceRegion . Raise --max-results and pick an event without errorCode . { "eventName": "Converse", "eventSource": "bedrock.amazonaws.com", "awsRegion": "ap-southeast-1", "managementEvent": true, "requestParameters": { "modelId": "global.openai.gpt-6-sol", "inferenceConfig": { "maxTokens": 1024 } }, "additionalEventData": { "inferenceRegion": "us-east-1" } } Metrics and coding-agent usage stay in CloudWatch. Where developers reach GPT-6 through a coding agent, CloudWatch Coding Agent Insights adds ready-made dashboards under GenAI Observability that break token use down by user, team, and cost center. The agents emit OpenTelemetry metrics natively. For Codex, see Set up OpenTelemetry for OpenAI Codex . Clean up This post adds an IAM policy and optionally an SCP statement and a logging destination. Detach or delete the IAM policy you attached, and revert the SCP entry if you added one. Delete the model invocation logging destination in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) or Amazon CloudWatch Logs if you created one, to avoid storage charges. The global cross-Region inference profiles are system-defined, so there is nothing to delete. Conclusion This post showed how to invoke GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna from five Asia Pacific source Regions, and GPT-6 Astra from Asia Pacific (Singapore), through global cross-Region inference on bedrock-runtime . Pass a global cross-Region inference profile ID as the model parameter, and configure the IAM policy and SCP exception from this post. The same endpoint serves the OpenAI-compatible APIs, so an existing OpenAI integration moves across by changing a base URL and a key. To get started, attach the IAM policy from this post, and send a first request through global.openai.gpt-6-sol . Size your tokens-per-minute quota at the 10x burndown rate, and confirm in CloudTrail that additionalEventData.inferenceRegion appears on your calls. For more information, see the Amazon Bedrock User Guide , Route model inference requests across AWS Regions with cross-Region inference , and Amazon Bedrock pricing .   About the authors Traci Lim Traci is a Senior AI/ML Specialist Technical Account Manager at AWS based in Singapore. A machine learning engineer by trade, he works with startups and enterprises to operationalize and scale AI/ML applications in production, with a focus on GenAIOps, Agentic Ops, operational excellence, and cost and performance optimization. Prior to AWS, Traci led engineering teams in the tech and financial industries, scaling distributed AI systems across AWS, Azure, GCP, and SAP. He is a builder at heart, always looking for ways to create meaningful impact through technology. Karan Jhaveri Karan is a Senior Technical Account Manager at AWS based in Singapore. He works with public sector and enterprise customers to take generative AI from experimentation to production at scale. He likes to stay hands-on, getting into the details and building out solutions that solve real operational problems. Melanie Li Melanie, PhD, is a Senior Generative AI Specialist Solutions Architect at AWS based in Sydney, Australia, where her focus is on working with customers to build solutions using state-of-the-art AI/ML tools. She has been actively involved in multiple generative AI initiatives across APJ, harnessing the power of LLMs. Prior to joining AWS, Dr. Li held data science roles in the financial and retail industries. Zohreh Norouzi Zohreh is a Senior Security Solutions Architect at Amazon Web Services (AWS). She helps customers make good security choices and accelerate their journey to the AWS Cloud. She has been actively involved in AI security initiatives, using her expertise to help customers build secure AI solutions at scale. Saurabh Trikande Saurabh is a Senior Product Manager for Amazon Bedrock and Amazon SageMaker Inference. He is passionate about working with customers and partners, motivated by the goal of democratizing AI. He focuses on core challenges related to deploying complex AI applications, inference with multi-tenant models, cost optimizations, and making the deployment of generative AI models more accessible. In his spare time, Saurabh enjoys hiking, learning about innovative technologies, following TechCrunch, and spending time with his family. Chris Dickens Chris is a Member of Product Staff at OpenAI focused on the OpenAI APIs. His work includes collaboration with AWS on Amazon Bedrock to make OpenAI’s frontier models widely accessible to developers.

title: Can we change an AI model’s architecture without retraining it from scratch?
summary: “Priming” reuses pretrained Transformer weights to build models with more efficient architectures at less than 1% of the original training cost and with throughputs up to twice as high.
content: AI agents are rapidly scaling: longer sessions, deeper reasoning chains, more autonomy. But the Transformer architecture underneath them still pays a memory tax that grows with the number of tokens it processes. As agents become more capable, that cost scales with them. Now, there’s a proliferation of hybrid architectures that use some combination of methods to achieve a better balance of memory, speed, and quality. Those methods include sparse attention, which selects a subset of past tokens to consider when selecting the next token; sliding-window attention, which preserves only the most recent tokens; and state space models, which compress information from the full history into a fixed-size state. These hybrid architectures can be understood as points in a sequence-model design space: to differing degrees, they mix information while traversing a sequence and passing through different states. What distinguishes them from each other is how they retain and use the past. Until now, exploring this design space has required training every new architecture from scratch, using trillions of tokens and hundreds of thousands of GPU-hours. This has made controlled comparisons of hybrid architectures extremely expensive. In a new paper, “Priming: Hybrid state space models from pre-trained Transformers,” our team at Amazon Web Services addresses this problem. We introduce priming, a method that leverages pretrained Transformer weights as a starting point to reduce the pretraining cost of hybrid architectures by more than 99%. With priming, model developers can ask questions that were previously too expensive to answer at scale: Which attention layers can be replaced by more-efficient layers? How many attention layers can be replaced without sacrificing quality? Which state space layer works best? And what does the trade-off between speed and accuracy look like? In our paper, we compare hybrid models that use three different types of state space models (Gated KalmaNet, Gated DeltaNet, and Mamba-2). Some of our findings: Not all state space models are equal. Under controlled conditions, Gated KalmaNet (GKA) performs best, followed by Gated DeltaNet (GDN) and then Mamba-2. GKA uniquely offers variable-length inference computation without retraining and gives the user direct control over its position on the speed-accuracy frontier. A good lossy summary of everything beats a perfect recording of the most recent past. State space models consistently outperform sliding-window attention (SWA), even when SWA gets twice the memory budget. Same quality, twice the throughput. A 32-billion-parameter GKA-based hybrid model matches its source Transformer on reasoning benchmarks while decoding up to twice as quickly with 128,000 tokens of context and reaching correct answers in as little as two-thirds of the wall-clock time. To foster further research on hybrid architectures, we have released a zoo of primed hybrid models at the eight-billion-parameter and 32-billion-parameter scales for long-context reasoning and instruction following, together with training code, optimized kernels, and a vLLM-serving plugin under the Apache 2.0 License. The attention mechanism A Transformer’s attention mechanism — which determines how relevant previously seen tokens are to the token currently being processed — relies on three different vectors, which take their names from database design: the query, the key, and the value. For each token, the query captures what that token is “looking for,” the key captures what it “offers,” and the value carries the actual information it will pass along. Relevance is computed by comparing the current token’s query against every other token’s key; the closer the match, the more that token’s value contributes to the output of attention. Each of these vectors is produced by multiplying the token by a learned weight projection matrix. The Transformer outputs one token at a time, and each output token becomes a new input, so the context grows one token at a time as well. To save computation, the Transformer thus stores the key and value projections of each new input in a “KV cache”. Two kinds of memory layers: Eidetic versus fading The attention mechanism gives Transformers what we call eidetic memory: verbatim recall of every past token. The possibility of recalling over an LLM’s entire context window is what made in-context learning, long-document reasoning, and retrieval-augmented generation possible. But it comes at a cost that scales with the number of input tokens. However, not all attention layers do the same job. Some perform long-range retrieval across tens of thousands of tokens. Others operate more locally, tracking the current clause, copying nearby tokens, and the like. The local ones don't need a growing cache: a compact, fixed-size summary of the past — what we call fading memory — suffices. Hybrid models mix both: attention layers (eidetic, growing cache) for the layers that need global recall and state space layers (fading, fixed size) for the rest. The result is a model with a reduced memory footprint that still has access to verbatim recall where it matters. Priming: Knowledge isn't locked to the architecture Exploring hybrids’ design space has been impractical because each hybrid configuration would normally require pretraining from scratch. Priming sidesteps this by reusing the stored knowledge in a pretrained Transformer's weights. Priming is possible because a Transformer is itself a special case of a state space realization. The outputs of both attention and SSM layers can be expressed as the result of multiplying the value sequence by a “mixing” matrix that decides how much each past token contributes to each current token. Attention computes the mixing matrix by multiplying the query and key matrices; an SSM produces a similar output through a recurrent state of fixed dimension that all past information must pass through. Priming takes advantage of this structural similarity: if an SSM with a fixed-dimensional state can produce a mixing matrix close enough to the attention layer's, the query, key, and value projections from the source Transformer can be reused as the SSM's own input projections, with only the SSM-specific parameters needing to be learned. Whether the approximation holds depends on whether the attention layer performs complex, long-range retrievals or simple, local operations. We distinguish between the two using a cheap empirical proxy: replace each layer with an SWA — which preserves only a fraction of the context — and measure the degradation. Layers that tolerate this substitution are natural candidates for SSM conversion: their mixing matrices don’t need to capture long-range relationships, so the state of an SSM can faithfully represent what they do. This proxy connects to a formal quantity from dynamical-systems theory, the Hankel rank of the layer's mixing matrix, which measures how much information must pass through the state bottleneck and therefore the minimum SSM state dimension required to realize the layer exactly. Priming proceeds in three stages: Layer selection: identify which layers can be faithfully compressed into a fixed-size state while retaining the rest as attention; Weight transfer and alignment: initialize SSM layers from the corresponding attention weights, then run a short distillation process aligning each SSM to the behavior of the layer it replaces; End-to-end adaptation: fine-tune the full hybrid model on next-token prediction, letting all layers coadapt. The entire pipeline consumes less than 0.5% of the source model's pretraining token budget, and it works across Transformer families (Qwen, Llama, Mistral), model classes (dense or MoE), and scales (eight billion to 32 billion and more). With priming we can now explore the design space, the layer type, the hybrid ratio, and layer placement cheaply and systematically, because every variant starts from the same strong initialization and requires minimal training, compared to pretraining. A controlled comparison of fading-memory layers For instance, consider this question: given the same data, the same training budget, and the same ratio of eidetic to fading layers, which SSM layer works best in a hybrid model? In our paper, we evaluate three families of state space models, each representing a different approach to using a fixed-size state: Mamba-2 applies a uniform scalar decay to the entire state at each step, a running average that forgets everything at the same rate. When a new token arrives, it is written into the state, while all previous entries are uniformly attenuated. Mamba-2 is simple and efficient but indiscriminate. Gated DeltaNet (GDN) adds targeted updates on top of uniform decay. Rather than decaying everything uniformly, it can selectively erase the value previously associated with a specific key before writing the new one (the delta rule). This makes it more expressive than Mamba-2: it can revise a specific association without uniformly decaying the rest. Gated KalmaNet (GKA) goes further. Its erase direction depends not only on the current key but on statistics of all past keys, a history-aware update that accounts for the cumulative structure of everything the model has seen. The theoretical expressiveness hierarchy predicts the empirical one: GKA > GDN > Mamba-2. The gap widens on long-context reasoning, where compression quality matters most, and narrows on short-context tasks. Furthermore, at the 32-billion-parameter (32B) scale, hybrid GKA is within 1% of its source Transformer trained on the same data, despite requiring half the KV cache at inference. Fading memory beats verbatim windowed memory An interesting finding in our study comes from a direct comparison of hybrid models using SSM layers and those using sliding-window attention (SWA), which retain a fixed window of recent tokens verbatim rather than compressing the past into a state. One might expect that verbatim recall, even over a limited window, would outperform lossy compression. After all, no information is lost within the sliding window’s range. And stacking multiple SWA layers increases the “receptive field” of the end-to-end model. Instead, every SSM-based hybrid we tested outperformed the corresponding SWA hybrid on long-context benchmarks, even when the window gets two to four times as much memory as the state. A runtime knob for speed versus accuracy: Variable computation at inference time GKA has a property that neither Mamba-2 nor GDN offers: variable test-time computation. Mamba-2 and GDN have the same computation budget for every input token, regardless of its content. GKA, by contrast, solves a regression problem iteratively, and the iteration count is adjustable at serving time without retraining. In practice, serving GKA at 10 iterations instead of its usual 30 sacrifices roughly 1% of its accuracy on AIME 2025 while delivering 10% faster decoding. A single trained model can serve multiple points on the speed-accuracy frontier, so model providers can offer different latency tiers without maintaining separate model variants. This connects to a principle we have discussed in earlier work: intelligence is the ability to allocate effort commensurate with difficulty. GKA's variable-computation mechanism is an architectural embodiment of this principle: a deployment that demands speed can run fewer iterations, while one that demands accuracy can run more. Faster reasoning, not just faster tokens Raw per-token throughput tells only part of the story. A model that is cheaper per token can still be slower end to end if its reasoning is weaker and it needs more tokens to compensate. The deployment-relevant question is how much more rapidly, in wall clock terms, the hybrid reaches a target accuracy. We measured this on AIME 2025, a challenging math competition benchmark, comparing our GKA-Primed-HQwen3-32B-Reasoner against the source Qwen3-32B trained on the same reasoning recipe. Both models generate similar-length thinking traces (a median of about 14,000 tokens on the full set, 28,000 on the hardest problems) — that is, they produce equally in-depth responses — but the hybrid has a much higher throughput. At realistic concurrency levels, where the Transformer's KV cache saturates GPU memory, the hybrid reaches target accuracy thresholds 1.2 to 1.4 times as quickly on the full benchmark and up to 1.6 times as quickly on the hardest problems. This is a consequence of the SSM layers' fixed-size state, which roughly halves the per-sequence memory footprint, enabling more concurrent operations on the same hardware. The throughput advantage grows with context length: 1.50× at 16K tokens, scaling to 2.06× at 128K for the 32B model (GKA at 10 iterations). With the 8B parameter models, the gains are even greater: 1.94× at 16K to 2.29× at 128K. At long context, KV cache reads dominate the forward pass through the Transformer, and halving the cache roughly doubles the effective batch size at memory saturation. This has implications beyond inference serving. In reinforcement learning (RL) post-training pipelines, throughput gates how rapidly the policy generates correct trajectories. The hybrid's advantage translates directly to a 20% to 100% increase in RL training data rate at a fixed GPU budget. Beyond the training window: Context extension with state composition Our primed hybrids natively support 128,000 tokens. But agent sessions, codebases, and long legal documents routinely exceed that. Extending context further would normally require another round of continued pretraining on curated data. Can the hybrid architecture itself generalize to longer contexts without additional training? Existing training-free methods for expanding the context window fall into two classes: those for pure Transformers (positional-embedding rescaling schemes like YaRN) and those for pure SSMs, such as our PICASO, which we presented last year at the International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR). Neither addresses the hybrid setting, where KV caches and recurrent states must be reconciled jointly. In our new arXiv paper, we describe a method of extending hybrid models’ context beyond their native limits without training. The procedure is simple: partition a long input into chunks shorter than the native context length and prepend a shared prefix to each chunk; process all chunks independently in parallel; concatenate the KV caches across chunks while merging the SSM states via the weighted-averaging scheme we introduced in our PICASO paper. This approach enables us to extend the context length of our primed hybrid models from 128K to 256K tokens while preserving substantial accuracy on both retrieval (RULER NIAH) and reasoning (BABILong) tasks at lengths the model was never trained on. In our experiments we show that hybrid state composition preserves the SSM expressivity hierarchy (GKA > GDN > Mamba-2). The hybrid design space is now open All artifacts discussed in this blog are released under the Apache 2.0 License in our Hybrid Model Factory on GitHub and our model zoo on HuggingFace: A collection of primed hybrids for long-context reasoning and instruction following (8B and 32B); The priming training code; Point-to-point sequence parallelism algorithms for SSM layers (up to 2.3 times as fast as all-to-all-based alternatives at multinode scale); Universal sequence parallelism for prototyping novel layers on long sequences without custom kernels or distributed-training expertise; Optimized Triton kernels for GKA decoding and training; A vLLM serving plugin supporting primed hybrid architectures with continuous batching, chunked prefill, and tensor parallelism for inference deployment at scale. If you serve long-context workloads, the 32B GKA reasoning model with the vLLM plugin gives you higher throughput with no quality loss on long context reasoning tasks. If you're scaling RL post-training, the hybrid's throughput advantage means more correct rollouts per unit time at a fixed GPU budget, for faster policy iteration without changing your training recipe. If you're researching new architectures, priming lets you evaluate any layer type under controlled conditions at a fraction of the pretraining cost while starting from a strong initialization. The universal SP module means you don't need custom distributed kernels to train at long context. Priming is not tied to a specific Transformer family or model class. Extending it to Llama, Mistral, or MoE models requires no algorithmic changes. We hope these tools enable the community to explore architectures beyond what we've tested and to develop new algorithms and training recipes for building scalable next-generation architectures for AI agents. For full details, see our paper, "Priming: Hybrid state space models from pre-trained Transformers". Code, models, and serving plugin are available on GitHub, and the models are also on Hugging Face.

title: Deploy decision models with llama.cpp on Amazon SageMaker AI
summary: Learn how to deploy decision models with llama.cpp on Amazon SageMaker AI. This technical how-to serves OpenAI-compatible chat completions with the AWS Deep Learning Container for llama.cpp, then extends the runtime with SemIf to return probabilities over declared options on CPU or GPU.
content: Applications that route requests, select agent actions, or assign policy outcomes often need scores over a fixed set of choices instead of free-form text. Deploying these decision models with llama.cpp on Amazon SageMaker AI gives you a managed path for serving quantized models on CPU or GPU infrastructure. This post continues a series on specialized AWS Deep Learning Containers (DLCs) for generative AI inference. Previous posts cover WhisperX , vLLM-Omni – Part 1 , and vLLM-Omni – Part 2 . In this post, you first use the AWS DLC for llama.cpp to serve OpenAI-compatible chat completions through SageMaker AI InvokeEndpoint . You then extend the same runtime with SemIf , formerly OpenJev, which returns probabilities over declared options without decoding an answer token. The accompanying code sample includes CPU and GPU deployment options. Solution overview Figure 1 shows two deployment paths from the same packaged model. The text-generation path uses the AWS DLC for llama.cpp and returns generated responses through the OpenAI-compatible API. The structured-decision path builds a child image that replaces the default server with a SemIf adapter and returns probabilities for declared options. Figure 1: Run the AWS DLC for llama.cpp or the SemIf child image on CPU or GPU, depending on the API and latency requirements of your workload For the standard path, package the model as model.tar.gz in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and reference the published DLC image directly. The container finds the first .gguf file under /opt/ml/model , maps POST /invocations to llama-server at /v1/chat/completions , and passes SM_LLAMA_CPP_* environment variables to llama.cpp arguments. The llama-server HTTP API doesn’t expose the final-position logits and state operations that SemIf uses. The structured-decision path therefore uses AWS CodeBuild to build a child image and store it in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) . The child image keeps the DLC’s compiled CPU or CUDA libraries while replacing its entry point with a SageMaker-compatible adapter. Understand the input and output schemas The AWS DLC for llama.cpp accepts the OpenAI Chat Completions schema. Send a messages array with role and content , plus generation controls such as max_tokens and stream : { "messages": [ { "role": "user", "content": "A customer cannot receive a password reset email. Reply with the best support queue." } ], "max_tokens": 64, "stream": false } The response uses the OpenAI-compatible choices array. Read generated text from choices[0].message.content . SemIf uses a constrained decision schema instead of chat messages. The request contains a caller-defined ID, unstructured state, a question, and an ordered list of allowed options: { "decision": { "id": "support-route", "state": "The customer cannot receive a password reset email.", "question": "Which queue should handle this request?", "options": [ {"id": "account_access", "description": "Account access support."}, {"id": "billing", "description": "Billing support."} ] } } The response returns option_ids , probabilities , and raw option_logits in the same order, along with prompt, timing, and pinned model metadata. With stable option IDs, your application can apply thresholds, fallbacks, and policy checks without parsing generated prose. SemIf belongs to a broader class of decision models that score application-defined outcomes from unstructured state. Other implementations include Jev , TypeSafe’s decision model and /v1/systemone API; Kev , a model server designed for TypeSafe API compatibility; and Strands Decider 2B , a purpose-built model for agent workflows with calibrated outputs. Choose the right decision workflows Use this pattern when your application defines the allowed choices at request time and needs a model to interpret unstructured context. Examples include routing a case to a queue, extracting one value from a known set, assigning an incident priority, checking a policy outcome, or selecting an agent action. Keep authorization and deterministic business rules outside the model, and validate model probabilities before treating them as operational confidence. Use the standard SageMaker AI text-generation path when you need OpenAI-compatible chat completions through InvokeEndpoint . The SageMaker AI image maps POST /invocations to the llama-server /v1/chat/completions endpoint. Build a child image only when your application needs behavior that this interface doesn’t provide, such as SemIf’s direct logits and state access. Removing answer-token generation doesn’t remove model inference. The model still processes the complete state, question, and option descriptions before SemIf reads the final logits. Keep prompts focused, and evaluate the selected model with labeled decisions from your application before production use. Tune for your latency and quality targets The following benchmark applies to the SemIf extension, not the text-generation endpoint. Model size, quantization, prompt length, runtime, and CPU thread count affect each decision. To quantify these trade-offs, we sent the same 231 public JevBench tasks serially to one CPU endpoint and one GPU endpoint. Configuration AWS DLC for llama.cpp Valid responses Accuracy Client p50 Client p95 Qwen3.5-4B Q4_K_M , ml.c6i.8xlarge , 32 threads llama-cpp:server-sagemaker-cpu-v1 231/231 179/231 (77.5%) 1.715 seconds 19.291 seconds Qwen3.5-4B Q4_K_M , ml.g6e.xlarge , full GPU offload llama-cpp:server-sagemaker-cuda-v1 231/231 180/231 (77.9%) 0.352 seconds 0.599 seconds Compared with the CPU configuration, the GPU endpoint was 4.9 times faster at p50 and 32.2 times faster at p95. The sample uses the SageMaker AI instance pools feature to list compatible GPU instance types in priority order, so SageMaker can select an alternative when the first preference isn’t available. The pool ordered g6e , g6 , g5 , then g4dn . SageMaker selected ml.g6e.xlarge , and startup logs confirmed that llama.cpp offloaded all 34 model layers to an NVIDIA L40S. The CPU and GPU images used different llama.cpp builds and produced different predictions on six hard tasks. Treat the one-answer accuracy difference as runtime variation, not evidence that GPU offload improves model quality. Smaller models reduced median latency, but the 2B and 0.8B candidates achieved 66.7 percent and 58.4 percent accuracy. The sample therefore keeps the 4B Q4_K_M model as its quality-first default. These measurements include network latency and aren’t service guarantees. Benchmark the complete model and infrastructure configuration against your own decisions. Use CPU for background, offline, or low-throughput workloads that aren’t latency-sensitive and can tolerate seconds of response time. Use GPU for interactive decisions, long prompts, or workloads with tight tail-latency targets. Keep state and option descriptions concise, group decisions that share the same state into one request, and scale endpoint instances for concurrency. Shared-state scoring reuses the common prompt prefix, while the adapter returns retryable HTTP 503 responses instead of allowing an unbounded queue around its stateful llama.cpp context. Prerequisites You need: An AWS account and an S3 bucket in your deployment AWS Region. Python 3.10 or later, Git, and the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI). A purpose-specific CodeBuild service role for the optional SemIf extension. An AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role that SageMaker AI can assume. Permissions for SageMaker AI, Amazon ECR, Amazon S3, CodeBuild, IAM pass-role actions, and Amazon CloudWatch Logs . Quota for a compatible x86 CPU or NVIDIA GPU SageMaker real-time endpoint. The text-generation example uses the CPU DLC and a fixed CPU instance. The SemIf extension keeps CPU as the default for workloads that aren’t latency-sensitive and offers an optional CUDA image with ordered instance pools. Review SageMaker AI pricing before creating an endpoint. Deploy a decision model and extend it with SemIf Use the following procedure to deploy the standard text-generation endpoint, then build the optional SemIf extension for structured decisions on CPU or GPU. Clone the code sample and install its dependencies. git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/sagemaker-genai-hosting-examples.git cd sagemaker-genai-hosting-examples/03-features/semif-decision-model python3 -m venv .venv . .venv/bin/activate python3 -m pip install -r deploy/requirements.txt Set the deployment values for your account. export AWS_REGION=" " export ARTIFACT_BUCKET=amzn-s3-demo-semif-artifacts export CODEBUILD_ROLE_ARN=arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/semif-codebuild-role export SAGEMAKER_ROLE_ARN=arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/semif-sagemaker-role export STANDARD_ENDPOINT_NAME=llamacpp-gguf export SEMIF_ENDPOINT_NAME=semif-decision-workflows Package the pinned GGUF model and tokenizer with CodeBuild. python deploy/prepare_model_build.py \ --region "$AWS_REGION" \ --bucket "$ARTIFACT_BUCKET" \ --codebuild-role-arn "$CODEBUILD_ROLE_ARN" \ --model-s3-uri "s3://$ARTIFACT_BUCKET/semif-llamacpp/model.tar.gz" Wait for the returned build ID to reach SUCCEEDED . The build records the source revisions and checksums in model-manifest.json and stops if the GGUF checksum differs from the validated value. Deploy the GGUF model with the AWS DLC for llama.cpp. Resolve a digest-pinned server-sagemaker-cpu-v1 image from the AWS DLC for llama.cpp documentation , then create the SageMaker AI model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint: export STANDARD_IMAGE_URI=" @sha256: " python deploy/deploy_standard_endpoint.py \ --region "$AWS_REGION" \ --image-uri "$STANDARD_IMAGE_URI" \ --model-data-url "s3://$ARTIFACT_BUCKET/semif-llamacpp/model.tar.gz" \ --role-arn "$SAGEMAKER_ROLE_ARN" \ --instance-type ml.c6i.2xlarge \ --name "$STANDARD_ENDPOINT_NAME" Select a server-sagemaker-cpu-v1 or server-sagemaker-cuda-v1 image rather than the corresponding EC2 image. The SageMaker AI images implement the /ping and /invocations container contract and map invocation payloads to chat completions. This walkthrough supplies the GGUF model through the SageMaker AI model artifact in Amazon S3. As an alternative, you can configure SM_LLAMA_CPP_HF_REPO and SM_LLAMA_CPP_HF_FILE to download a GGUF file from Hugging Face when the endpoint has network egress. You don’t need a Dockerfile or an ECR repository for this path. Wait for the endpoint to enter InService , then send an OpenAI-compatible chat request: python deploy/invoke_standard_endpoint.py \ --region "$AWS_REGION" \ --endpoint-name "$STANDARD_ENDPOINT_NAME" Build the optional SemIf child image and resolve its immutable digest. For CPU: python deploy/prepare_build.py \ --region "$AWS_REGION" \ --bucket "$ARTIFACT_BUCKET" \ --codebuild-role-arn "$CODEBUILD_ROLE_ARN" For GPU, build the CUDA child image instead: python deploy/prepare_build.py \ --region "$AWS_REGION" \ --bucket "$ARTIFACT_BUCKET" \ --codebuild-role-arn "$CODEBUILD_ROLE_ARN" \ --dockerfile Dockerfile.gpu \ --image-tag "gpu-$(date +%Y%m%d%H%M%S)" After the build succeeds, construct the immutable image URI: ECR_REPOSITORY_URI=$(aws ecr describe-repositories \ --region "$AWS_REGION" \ --repository-names semif-llamacpp-dlc \ --query 'repositories[0].repositoryUri' \ --output text) IMAGE_DIGEST=$(aws ecr describe-images \ --region "$AWS_REGION" \ --repository-name semif-llamacpp-dlc \ --query 'sort_by(imageDetails,&imagePushedAt)[-1].imageDigest' \ --output text) export IMAGE_URI="${ECR_REPOSITORY_URI}@${IMAGE_DIGEST}" The deployment script rejects mutable image tags. Deploy the SemIf endpoint. The CPU configuration uses a fixed instance type: python deploy/deploy_endpoint.py \ --region "$AWS_REGION" \ --image-uri "$IMAGE_URI" \ --model-data-url "s3://$ARTIFACT_BUCKET/semif-llamacpp/model.tar.gz" \ --role-arn "$SAGEMAKER_ROLE_ARN" \ --instance-type ml.c6i.8xlarge \ --threads 32 \ --name "$SEMIF_ENDPOINT_NAME" Wait for the returned endpoint name to enter InService . This path sets n_gpu_layers=0 . The adapter serializes scoring around one stateful llama.cpp context, so scale out with endpoint instances after measuring your workload rather than assuming parallel scoring inside one container. For the GPU image, provide ordered instance pools and request full model offload: python deploy/deploy_endpoint.py \ --region "$AWS_REGION" \ --image-uri "$IMAGE_URI" \ --model-data-url "s3://$ARTIFACT_BUCKET/semif-llamacpp/model.tar.gz" \ --role-arn "$SAGEMAKER_ROLE_ARN" \ --instance-pool ml.g6e.xlarge \ --instance-pool ml.g6.2xlarge \ --instance-pool ml.g5.2xlarge \ --instance-pool ml.g4dn.2xlarge \ --gpu-layers=-1 \ --provision-timeout 1200 \ --name "$SEMIF_ENDPOINT_NAME" Instance pools are ordered placement fallbacks, not inference load balancing. SageMaker selects one available type for the variant. Endpoint creation can take longer while SageMaker AI works through the pool. Check the startup logs for the selected GPU and a message confirming that all model layers were offloaded. Invoke the SemIf endpoint with the example decision. The request declares stable IDs for each allowed option: { "decision": { "id": "support-route", "state": "Customer asks to reset a forgotten password and says the reset email never arrived.", "question": "Which queue should handle this request?", "options": [ {"id": "account_access", "description": "Account access and authentication support."}, {"id": "billing", "description": "Billing and payment support."}, {"id": "sales", "description": "Sales and product evaluation."} ] } } python deploy/invoke_endpoint.py \ --region "$AWS_REGION" \ --endpoint-name "$SEMIF_ENDPOINT_NAME" The response preserves the option order and includes conditional probabilities, raw logits, token and prompt metadata, and the pinned model identity: { "result": { "id": "support-route", "option_ids": ["account_access", "billing", "sales"], "probabilities": [0.99996, 0.00003, 0.00001], "option_logits": [28.47, 17.92, 17.04], "prompt_sha256": "016267542103ab91422c425d2234ec7e1b9aef77f9d3e481b96db2de7cca470a", "readout": "quantized last-position logits restricted to declared answer slots; no generated tokens" } } Apply application-level thresholds and fallbacks. Don’t use a model decision as a substitute for authorization. Clean up Delete the SageMaker AI endpoint, endpoint configuration, and model: python deploy/cleanup_endpoint.py \ --region "$AWS_REGION" \ --name "$STANDARD_ENDPOINT_NAME" python deploy/cleanup_endpoint.py \ --region "$AWS_REGION" \ --name "$SEMIF_ENDPOINT_NAME" The script deletes only those explicitly named SageMaker AI resources. Delete the CodeBuild projects, ECR repository, model and source objects in Amazon S3, logs, and purpose-specific IAM roles when you no longer need them. Conclusion The AWS DLC for llama.cpp gives you a managed foundation for serving decision models on SageMaker AI across CPU and GPU instances. It can load GGUF models from SageMaker AI model artifacts or a configured Hugging Face repository, then serve OpenAI-compatible chat completions through InvokeEndpoint without requiring a custom container. When your application needs direct logits and model state operations, you can extend the DLC with a SemIf adapter. Choose CPU for workloads that aren’t latency-sensitive, and choose GPU when prompt prefill and tail latency affect the application experience. Review the code sample , AWS DLC for llama.cpp documentation , and SageMaker AI custom inference container contract to adapt the deployment for your workload.   About the authors Jyothirmai Kottu Jyothirmai is a Software Development Engineer on the AWS Deep Learning Containers team. She builds AI and machine learning infrastructure with a focus on container performance, reliability, and developer usability. Outside of work, she enjoys coffee, yoga, and exploring new places with family and friends. Daniel Wirjo Daniel is a Solutions Architect at AWS, focused on frontier AI startups. As a former startup CTO, he enjoys collaborating with founders and engineering leaders to drive growth and innovation on AWS. Outside of work, Daniel enjoys taking walks with a coffee in hand, appreciating nature, and learning new ideas. Daniel Quang Daniel is a Solutions Architect on the Frontier AI Startups team at AWS, where he helps the world’s largest and most strategic generative AI startups scale their infrastructure on the cloud. He holds a PhD in Computer Science from the University of California, Irvine, with a research focus on machine learning and bioinformatics. Dmitry Soldatkin Dmitry is the Worldwide Leader for Specialist Solutions Architecture, SageMaker Inference at AWS. He helps customers design, build, and optimize generative AI and machine learning solutions, with interests in deep learning and deploying machine learning at scale. He has a passion for continuous innovation and using data to drive business outcomes.

title: Run multi-node inference workloads using Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers
summary: Learn how to deploy one large language model across two GPU nodes on Amazon EKS using the multi-node Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers, with separate prefill and decode nodes behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint. The pre-built container ships the full inference stack, so you configure the deployment instead of assembling it.
content: This post shows how to deploy one large language model (LLM) across two GPU nodes on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) with the multi-node Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers . It uses separate prefill and decode nodes behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint. This kind of multi-node setup is common for tensor, pipeline, and data parallelism, as well as prefill/decode disaggregation inference workloads. In a previous post , we introduced the Ray Serve DLC and used it to stand up a small model behind an HTTP endpoint on a single GPU node. You had a working inference endpoint, and the container keeps the GPU stack compatible, including CUDA libraries, so you did not need to write boilerplate code. Ray is a distributed compute framework, so Ray Serve deployments can span multiple nodes. Customers use multi-node Ray Serve for several reasons. Some want to run foundation or open-weight models that are too large for a single GPU. Others need more throughput than one replica can deliver. Still others want to separate the two phases of inference to improve performance. In each case, customers must build the dependency chain themselves: choosing compatible libraries for the GPU stack and debugging issues when a component drifts out of alignment. This is undifferentiated work that takes time and effort away from delivering models. AWS Deep Learning Containers (DLCs) have long solved this kind of problem for training and inferencing workloads. DLCs are pre-built, performance-optimized Docker images that bundle a framework, its dependencies, and the GPU stack into a tested, patched combination you can pull and use immediately. With the launch of the Ray LLM DLC for multi-node deployments, that same approach now extends to multi-node inference. You get a container purpose-built for serving models behind an HTTP endpoint, maintained and tested by AWS, with the full inference stack already assembled. This post walks through implementing multi-node disaggregated inference using multi-node Ray LLM DLC: deploying a single large language model across two GPU-powered nodes on Amazon EKS cooperating behind a single endpoint. While one of the GPU nodes handles the prefill phase, the other GPU node handles the decode phase. Separating the phases prevents compute-heavy long prompts from stalling token generation for requests already in progress. This approach is well suited for workloads such as Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), document summarization, and agentic applications. We use the multi-node Ray LLM DLC, which ships Ray Serve LLM , NVIDIA Inference Transfer Library (NIXL) , and the Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) stack, and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with no application code. The complete code is available in the accompanying repository . Why prefill/decode (PD) disaggregation LLM inference has two distinct phases. Prefill processes the entire input prompt in parallel and builds the key-value (KV) cache. Decode then generates the response one token at a time, reading and extending that cache. Prefill is compute bound, and Decode is bound by memory bandwidth. When both phases share one GPU, they contend for the same resources, and the bursty, compute-heavy prefill work interferes with the steady, latency-sensitive decode work. Separating the prefill phase from the decode phase means you can select the hardware and serving properties for each phase, improving overall performance at scale. PD disaggregation places the two phases on separate nodes, so each phase runs without interfering with the other and can be scaled independently. The trade-off is that the KV cache built during prefill must be handed to the decode node, and that transfer should be fast enough not to erase the benefit. That is exactly why the interconnect between the nodes matters. What the Ray LLM DLC provides AWS DLCs are pre-built, performance-optimized Docker images that bundle a framework, its dependencies, and the GPU stack into a tested, patched combination you can pull and use immediately. All components are validated together before each release, so there is no version drift between the CUDA runtime, the framework, and the serving layer. Security patches are applied at build time. The Ray LLM DLC extends this to distributed LLM serving. It ships vLLM as the inference engine, Ray Serve’s HTTP as the serving layer, NIXL for KV-cache transfer between nodes, and the EFA stack ( libfabric and aws-ofi-nccl ) for high-bandwidth node-to-node communication. Because the Ray Serve LLM library includes a built-in application builder, the entire serving application is a block of YAML. There’s no handler class, no model archiver, and no custom image to build. A single helper, build_pd_openai_app , takes a prefill configuration and a decode configuration and wires the KV-cache transfer between them behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Architecture The following diagram shows how the deployment is laid out on Amazon EKS. A user request reaches the Ray head on the CPU system node, and the two GPU worker nodes run the prefill and decode phases of the model. Figure 1: Multi-node inference architecture on Amazon EKS, with the Ray head on a CPU system node and the prefill and decode phases on two GPU worker nodes The deployment is an EKS cluster inside a virtual private cloud (VPC). Nodes run in private subnets with outbound access through a NAT Gateway. A CPU system node (m7i.xlarge) hosts system workloads, the KubeRay operator, and the Ray head pod, which is CPU-only. Two GPU worker nodes (g6.8xlarge) run the Ray workers: one serving the prefill phase, and the other serving the decode phase. Both nodes pull the Ray LLM DLC from Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) . KubeRay watches the RayService you apply and wires the head-to-worker join automatically. Ray Serve places the prefill and decode deployments on the two GPU workers. The KV cache flows from the prefill worker to the decode worker over NIXL, using EFA through NIXL’s libfabric backend. The GPU node group is pinned to a single Availability Zone (AZ) because EFA cannot cross AZs. Prerequisites To follow along with this post, you need: An AWS account with billing enabled. Sufficient service quota for running two g6.8xlarge instances (at least 64 vCPU) in your target Region. AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) with credentials configured. kubectl CLI for communicating with a Kubernetes cluster’s control plane. eksctl CLI for creating and managing clusters on EKS. helm (package manager for Kubernetes) to install KubeRay operator. envsubst utility (part of the GNU gettext) to render the manifest. Verify that your AWS credentials are active with the following command: aws sts get-caller-identity Use the pre-built application to serve inference The application is the serveConfigV2 block in manifest/rayservice.yaml . It uses build_pd_openai_app , which takes a prefill_config and a decode_config and connects the KV-cache transfer between them: applications: - name: qwen import_path: ray.serve.llm:build_pd_openai_app # OpenAI-compatible PD app, built in route_prefix: / args: prefill_config: model_loading_config: { model_id: qwen3.5-9b, model_source: Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B } engine_kwargs: max_model_len: 4096 dtype: bfloat16 gpu_memory_utilization: 0.90 enforce_eager: true # Skip CUDA graph capture to reduce peak GPU memory kv_transfer_config: kv_connector: NixlConnector kv_role: kv_both engine_id: prefill kv_connector_extra_config: { backends: ["LIBFABRIC"] } deployment_config: { num_replicas: 1 } decode_config: model_loading_config: { model_id: qwen3.5-9b, model_source: Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B } engine_kwargs: max_model_len: 4096 dtype: bfloat16 gpu_memory_utilization: 0.90 enforce_eager: true kv_transfer_config: kv_connector: NixlConnector kv_role: kv_both engine_id: decode kv_connector_extra_config: { backends: ["LIBFABRIC"] } deployment_config: { num_replicas: 1 } A few settings carry most of the weight. max_model_len: 4096 sizes the context to fit the measured KV cache on the GPU. dtype: bfloat16 and gpu_memory_utilization: 0.90 set precision and how much VRAM vLLM can claim. enforce_eager: true skips CUDA graph capture to reduce peak GPU memory (model- and input-dependent). The kv_transfer_config setting is what makes disaggregation work: both phases use NixlConnector with kv_role: kv_both and a distinct engine_id (prefill on one, decode on the other). The critical setting is kv_connector_extra_config: { backends: ["LIBFABRIC"] } . Without that line, NIXL defaults to UCX, which runs at TCP speed even on EFA. The rest of the manifest, in rayClusterConfig , describes the pods. The head pod is CPU-only ( num-gpus: "0" ) and pinned to the system node group. Each worker pod requests one GPU and one EFA interface ( nvidia.com/gpu: "1", vpc.amazonaws.com/efa: "1" ) and targets the GPU nodes through nodeSelector: { role: gpu-worker } . It runs privileged: true because NIXL registers CUDA VRAM with the EFA NIC. The IPC_LOCK capability alone isn’t enough. The workers set FI_PROVIDER=efa , read VLLM_HOST_IP from the pod IP, and mount a shared-memory volume. Memory limits sit well above the roughly 18 GiB checkpoint so the OS page cache can hold it. For Qwen3.5-9B model loading on g6.8xlarge with the preceding cache configuration, the model weights loading drops from around 145 seconds to about 2 seconds on restart. Deploy on Amazon EKS All scripts share a single configuration file, scripts/env.sh . The script contains defaults for CLUSTER_NAME , REGION , K8S_VERSION , and NAMESPACE . Other defaults cover the system and GPU node groups, the KubeRay version, and the model. Override any variable by exporting it before running a script. From the project root, set a base directory, then load the variables: CURRENT_DIR=$(pwd) cd $CURRENT_DIR/ray-serve-multi-node/scripts source ./env.sh Step 1: Create the EKS cluster ./deploy_cluster.sh This provisions the EKS cluster (VPC, OIDC provider, core add-ons) and a CPU system node group that runs system workloads, the KubeRay operator, and the Ray head. Nodes run in private subnets with egress through a NAT Gateway, and cluster subnets are placed in the AZs that offer the GPU instance type. The script is idempotent and takes 15–20 minutes on a fresh run. Step 2: Add GPU worker nodes ./deploy_node_group.sh This creates the GPU node group: two g6.8xlarge instances with EFA enabled, pinned to a single AZ and labeled role=gpu-worker so the Ray workers target them. Enabling EFA also installs the EFA device plugin, which advertises vpc.amazonaws.com/efa on each node. This step takes about 5-20 minutes, usually longer on a first run. Step 3: Install the KubeRay operator ./install_kuberay.sh This installs the KubeRay operator using Helm, pinned to the system node group to keep the GPU nodes available for inference. KubeRay watches the RayService you apply next and wires the head-to-worker join automatically. This step takes about 1–2 minutes. Step 4: Deploy the RayService ./deploy_ray_service.sh This renders manifest/rayservice.yaml with your image, model, and naming variables using envsubst and applies it. KubeRay creates the head and two worker pods, and Ray Serve LLM brings up the prefill and decode deployments. The script waits for the head to be Ready, both workers to be Running, and finally for the Serve app to report RUNNING. Because each node loads the model, expect this step to take several minutes. Check status at any time, including which node each pod landed on and the GPU capacity available: ./deploy_ray_service.sh status Invoke the model After the Serve app is healthy, KubeRay creates a stable -serve-svc Service. Port-forward to it: kubectl port-forward -n inference svc/ray-llm-serve-svc 8000:8000 Because the DLC exposes an OpenAI-compatible API, you can list models and send a standard chat-completion request with no custom schema: curl --silent http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/models curl --fail --silent --show-error \ --request POST "http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/chat/completions" \ --header "Content-Type: application/json" \ --data '{ "model": "qwen3.5-9b", "messages": [ {"role": "user", "content": "Explain the benefits of prefill/decode disaggregation."} ], "max_tokens": 200, "temperature": 0.7 }' Verify EFA is being used NIXL falls back to a TCP-speed transport if it cannot use libfabric, and it does so without raising an error, so it’s worth confirming the backend it picked. Grep the worker logs: for POD in $(kubectl get pods -n inference -l ray.io/node-type=worker \ -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}'); do kubectl exec -n inference "$POD" -c ray-worker -- \ grep -rhoE "Backend (LIBFABRIC|UCX) was instantiated" /tmp/ray/session_latest/logs/ 2>/dev/null done | sort | uniq -c deploy_node_group.sh already prints the vpc.amazonaws.com/efa count per node when it creates the group. For a cross-node bandwidth number, the DLC ships a prebuilt NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) benchmark at /usr/local/bin/all_reduce_perf . Clean up To avoid ongoing charges, tear down the resources in reverse order: ./delete_ray_service.sh # Remove the RayService ./install_kuberay.sh cleanup # Uninstall the KubeRay operator ./delete_node_group.sh # Remove the GPU node group ./delete_cluster.sh # Delete the EKS cluster Conclusion and next steps You served a single model across two GPU nodes with prefill/decode disaggregation, and the entire application was a block of YAML, with no handler code, no model archiver, and no hand-assembled GPU and EFA stack. The multi-node Ray LLM DLC supplied the tested inference stack, KubeRay orchestrated the Ray cluster, and NIXL over EFA carried the KV cache between nodes. Your job was to configure it, not to build it. Common patterns for running multi-node inference include tensor and pipeline parallelism (sharding a model too big for one instance), data parallelism (replicating a model for throughput), and prefill/decode disaggregation (separating the two phases of inference onto different nodes). From here you can scale the decode replicas for more throughput, move to larger models with tensor or pipeline parallelism on larger GPU instances, or layer extra libraries onto the same tested base for models that need them. For the full code, the current list of image tags, and the underlying mechanics, see the accompanying repository , the Ray LLM DLC available images page , the Ray Serve LLM prefill/decode documentation , and the EFA documentation .   About the authors Ananth Raghavendra Ananth is a Senior AI Solutions Architect at AWS. He specializes in architecting distributed Gen AI applications running on NVIDIA GPUs, AWS Trainium and AWS Inferentia using platforms and orchestrators such as Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, Amazon EKS, Ray, SageMaker Serverless Inference, Amazon Nova Forge, and Slurm. Jinyan Li Jinyan is a Software Development Engineer at AWS on the Deep Learning Containers team, where she builds and maintains the ML container images that ship PyTorch, vLLM, Ray, and other frameworks to customers running workloads on Amazon SageMaker, Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2), and Amazon EKS, including the Ray LLM DLC used in this post. Felipe Lopez Felipe is a Principal AI/ML Specialist Solutions Architect at AWS. Prior to joining AWS, Felipe worked with GE Digital and SLB, where he focused on modeling and optimization products for industrial applications.
