title: OCP Global Summit: Amid Ecosystem Adoption, NVIDIA Opens Vera Rubin Architecture to Help Scale AI Factories Worldwide
summary: As AI factories grow from megawatts to gigawatts, building them takes more than advanced computing. Open standards are helping the industry scale AI infrastructure faster, more efficiently and more reliably. At the Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit, taking place in the San Jose McEnery Convention Center, NVIDIA announced new partnerships and contributions aimed at […]
content: As AI factories grow from megawatts to gigawatts, building them takes more than advanced computing. Open standards are helping the industry scale AI infrastructure faster, more efficiently and more reliably. At the Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit, taking place in the San Jose McEnery Convention Center, NVIDIA announced new partnerships and contributions aimed at creating a common foundation for next-generation AI infrastructure. NVIDIA contributed key NVIDIA Vera Rubin rack and compute tray designs to OCP through the open NVIDIA MGX architecture, giving system builders a common foundation for developing next-generation AI factory infrastructure. Together, these efforts span the AI factory itself, the utility grid that powers it and the rack-scale architecture at the heart of modern accelerated computing. NVIDIA and Partners Announce Open Architecture Advances At the OCP event, NVIDIA and partners made a handful of announcements: NVIDIA and hyperscalers published open standards for next-generation AI factories, including AI factory design standards and grid resilience. NVIDIA launched new open source software components for NVIDIA DSX AI Factory. Meta and NVIDIA advanced open AI networking with NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet SuperNIC and Spectrum-6 innovations. Visionbay introduced an 800V DC AI factory design for the Vera Rubin era. NVIDIA and Cisco announced the Ultra-Dense Small Form Factor Pluggable (USFP) standard, the industry’s first module ​for 400Gb/s-based networking fabrics. NVIDIA and Google announced Falcon Transport support on future NVIDIA ConnectX-10 SuperNICs and BlueField DPUs. Before a packed audience, Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA, discussed how open infrastructure is becoming a critical ingredient for scaling AI factories worldwide. The news at OCP spotlights how NVIDIA’s extreme codesign combined with open standards is accelerating deployment, improving power efficiency and driving tokens-per-watt performance.   Vera Rubin AI Factories Advance With MGX Rack Contributions at OCP NVIDIA joined industry leaders in contributing to the third-generation MGX AI data center reference design through OCP’s Open DC Initiative. Combined with open liquid-cooling technologies such as MQD and MQDB, the effort helps turn proven AI factory designs into industry standards that others can adopt, manufacture and scale. For NVIDIA Vera Rubin AI factories, the updated MGX 1.2 specification extends the open architecture for AI factories with rack-scale blind-mate liquid cooling, interoperable rack-scale interconnect infrastructure and a liquid-cooled 5,000A busbar designed for higher-power AI systems. It also adds native 19-inch equipment support and higher-density rack designs. MGX 1.2 further expands modularity with configurable I/O bays, fanless liquid-cooled compute trays, standardized power and cooling interfaces, and a common infrastructure that helps ecosystem partners build interoperable accelerated computing platforms. It improves assembly, test and service times to streamline manufacturing and field service to enable faster and more efficient infrastructure buildout. The architecture supports rack deployments up to 250kW while simplifying serviceability, deployment and infrastructure reuse. The Vera CPU rack design specification extends the NVIDIA MGX open architecture beyond accelerated computing, providing a purpose-built platform for the growing agentic AI era. While Vera Rubin NVL72 serves as the foundation for large-scale training and inference, the NVIDIA Vera CPU rack is designed to support tool calling, orchestration and sandboxed execution, helping AI agents interact with applications, data and services in real time. Built on the third-generation NVIDIA MGX rack architecture, the Vera CPU rack shares the same rack-scale design principles that unite compute, networking, power and cooling into a common modular platform. This approach enables partners to deploy specialized infrastructure while benefiting from a shared ecosystem, simplified integration and a consistent foundation for next-generation AI factories.   NVIDIA Launches New Open Source Software Components for DSX AI Factory NVIDIA DSX AI factory platform applies extreme codesign to unify computing, networking, power, cooling, facilities and software, helping AI factories operate as a single optimized system, maximizing AI output within available infrastructure constraints. At the center of this unified system is DSX OS, the open operating layer that turns the DSX architecture into coordinated, repeatable operations at scale. At OCP, NVIDIA expanded DSX OS with open source components for configuring networks, validating clusters, managing racks and provisioning bare metal: NVIDIA Config Manager : Automates switch configurations at scale, allowing customers to deploy, validate and maintain consistent AI factory network fabrics with minimal to zero manual intervention. NVIDIA Cluster Readiness Engine : Helps eliminate costly job crashes by stress-testing GPU clusters with real workload simulations to guarantee hardware health before training begins. NVIDIA Rack Management Service : Offers a rack hardware abstraction and operations solutions that treats racks as first-class units for improved AI factory scale firmware management. Cluster API Provider for NVIDIA Infrastructure Controller : Accelerates bare-metal deployment and tenant onboarding, turning raw AI hardware into production-ready clusters in hours instead of days. Developed from NVIDIA’s experience running NVIDIA DGX Cloud, these open source components enable cloud providers and software partners to integrate AI factory capabilities directly into their multi-tenant platforms. Developers can visit the DSX AI Factory Github page to explore and contribute to both the new and existing open source software components from NVIDIA DSX AI Factory platform.   NVIDIA and Hyperscalers Publish Open Standards for Next-Generation AI Factories For AI infrastructure to scale globally, it needs more than advanced hardware — it needs a common foundation that the entire industry can build on. At OCP, NVIDIA joined AMD, Google and Meta t o publish a new open specification that establishes that foundation. The Open Data Center Specification v0.7 defines a unified blueprint for next-generation AI factory facility design — from power architecture to cooling infrastructure to physical layout. The OCP Grid Resilience Specification , published by Google , Meta, Microsoft and NVIDIA, establishes how large-scale AI infrastructure should behave during utility grid disturbances: staying connected, responding automatically and restoring to near-full load within less than two seconds. With these standards now open, manufacturers around the world have a common target to build for. Equipment makers, colocation providers and data center operators can begin designing, fabricating and delivering the infrastructure layer that powers AI factories under construction globally — without waiting for proprietary specifications from individual customers. Being NVIDIA DSX reference design -compatible, these specifications provide a validated, deployable implementation of both specs, from facility layout and power architecture to the software that monitors and responds to grid signals in real time. For operators building Vera Rubin AI factories, there’s now a straight line from open community standard to a running system.   Visionbay.ai Designs 800VDC AI Factory for the Vera Rubin Era As AI factories grow larger and more powerful, one challenge looms over them all: delivering enough power to the accelerated computing systems driving the next generation of AI. At OCP, Visionbay unveiled plans for K-1, a next-generation AI factory platform designed around an 800 VDC architecture and built with future NVIDIA Vera Rubin deployments in mind. The project combines NVIDIA’s 800 VDC reference architecture with power and thermal technologies from Vertiv to create a scalable foundation for high-density AI infrastructure. The design addresses a growing industry challenge. As AI training, inference and reasoning workloads expand, rack power densities continue to rise. Traditional low-voltage power distribution becomes increasingly difficult to scale, requiring more copper, more cabling and more power-conversion equipment. By adopting NVIDIA’s 800 VDC architecture, K-1 creates a path toward higher-density AI infrastructure while preserving flexibility for existing deployments. Rather than requiring a complete transition on day one, the platform is designed to phase in 800 VDC distribution where it delivers the greatest benefit, helping operators prepare for future generations of accelerated computing without extensive facility redesign. The architecture is designed around cluster-level power centers that centralize AC-to-DC conversion and distribute 800 VDC closer to compute resources. The approach simplifies downstream power delivery, supports modular expansion and creates repeatable building blocks for future AI factory growth. K-1 also reflects the system-level design philosophy behind NVIDIA AI factories, where power, cooling and computing are engineered together. With support for liquid-cooled infrastructure, scalable power distribution and future Vera Rubin-class deployments, the project demonstrates how ecosystem partners are translating NVIDIA’s AI factory architecture into deployable infrastructure designed for the next era of accelerated computing.   Meta and NVIDIA Advance AI Networking With Spectrum-6 and Multiplane Technology At the event, Meta and NVIDIA announced that Meta is adopting NVIDIA Spectrum-6 102.4Tb/s Ethernet switches to build larger, higher-performance NVIDIA Vera Rubin AI factories on open networking. Spectrum-6 delivers twice the switching capacity and per-lane bandwidth of Spectrum-4, and provides a lossless Ethernet AI fabric at 200G per lane, with high effective bandwidth and performance isolation that keeps one job’s traffic from slowing another’s. Meta’s Spectrum-6-based switch, N-IceCube, slots into IcePack, Meta’s 100T, liquid-cooled rack. N-IceCube runs the Facebook Open Switching System (FBOSS), Meta’s open source network operating system that contributed to OCP to support efficient networking at hyperscale. FBOSS is built on the Switch Abstraction Interface, an OCP standard NVIDIA helped develop, providing a vendor-independent way of controlling switch hardware. Together, these technologies support agentic AI factories of more than 100,000 GPUs that train and serve massive mixture-of-experts models. The announcement marks the next step in a collaboration that combines Meta’s experience operating AI infrastructure at hyperscale with NVIDIA’s networking technology. At the heart of this collaboration is Spectrum-X Multiplane technology, enabled by Spectrum-6 switches and ConnectX-9 SuperNICs. Multiplane distributes GPU traffic in hardware across up to eight independent network planes, enabling AI factories to scale beyond 100,000 GPUs with fewer switch tiers and lower infrastructure costs. Multiple paths between GPUs improve network utilization and resilience: when a component fails, traffic shifts to the remaining planes, keeping GPUs productive and AI applications running, even at reduced bandwidth. Meta and NVIDIA worked together to strengthen that resilience through deployment experience and rapid engineering iteration. The teams validated improvements across on-premises and cloud environments. “We are excited about our close partnership with NVIDIA in making multiplane fabrics operationally scalable and performant, a critical requirement both for our own infrastructure builds and for our joint cloud partners,” said Omar Baldonado, senior director of data center and AI networking at Meta. “Extending FBOSS to Spectrum ASICs means we can run that same software stack across our fabrics, and Meta’s new Spectrum-based switch, N-IceCube, brings that into Icepack – our liquid-cooled 102.4T network rack for scale-out that connects upcoming generations of accelerators in our fleet.” Together, Meta and NVIDIA are developing an architecture and operational playbook that other AI infrastructure operators can adopt, turning lessons from demanding production workloads into more scalable, resilient and efficient AI factories.   With USFP, NVIDIA and Cisco Reinvent Pluggable Optics for AI Factory Scale As AI factories scale to support larger models and surging inference demand, every component of the infrastructure stack must deliver more performance, efficiency and simplicity — right down to the network connection itself. At OCP, NVIDIA and Cisco announced plans for USFP, a new optical pluggable transceiver module form factor designed to help AI factory builders scale next-generation AI fabrics while improving bandwidth density and power efficiency. With approximately the same footprint as the widely adopted 200Gb/s-per-lane OSFP form factor, USFP will provide a path to 400Gb/s-per-lane networking and will extend a transceiver-based deployment model already proven across generations of data center networks. Packing 16 full-duplex lanes with plans to scale up to 32 lanes, USFP will deliver four times the bandwidth density of traditional 200Gb/s-per-lane pluggable optics. The result is the ability to connect more compute resources without adding network tiers that can increase latency, power consumption and complexity. The new form factor is designed for the scale and efficiency demands of next generation AI factories, supporting higher-bandwidth fabrics while preserving the flexibility and serviceability that have made pluggable optics a mainstay of modern data centers. It also will deliver roughly 1.3x greater power efficiency, helping operators move more data with less energy. To help drive an open ecosystem, NVIDIA and Cisco are collaborating with TE Connectivity and Amphenol on cages, connectors and modules, with plans to advance USFP through a community-led, multi-source effort. Together, the companies are laying the foundation for more scalable, efficient and interoperable AI factory networking.   Google Falcon Transport Supports NVIDIA ConnectX-10 for Interoperable AI Networking NVIDIA and Google also announced Falcon Transport support on future NVIDIA ConnectX-10 SuperNICs and BlueField DPUs, helping improve network efficiency for large-scale AI infrastructure. Falcon is a transport protocol designed to deliver data reliably over Ethernet networks, which can otherwise drop packets under congestion. It supports AI and storage workloads through multipath load balancing, programmable congestion control, hardware loss recovery and per-connection security. This collaboration combines NVIDIA hardware acceleration with DOCA software to implement Falcon and extend NVIDIA networking to Google’s data center transport. NVIDIA and Google NICs can communicate over a common transport while applications retain standard RDMA programming interfaces. By distributing traffic across paths, adapting to congestion, recovering dropped packets and protecting connections, Falcon helps workloads make better use of available bandwidth and maintain predictable performance as Ethernet fabrics scale. Learn more by joining NVIDIA at OCP .

content: 2026.10.5-beta.2 Highlights Updates finish and recover: openclaw update settles stale handoff leases, completed receipts, and legacy 2026.9.8 recovery records instead of stopping on update-recovery-pending , keeps the service heap limit and webhook listeners, handles Windows short-name paths, and no longer reports accepted handoffs or successful updates as failures. ( #169038 , #169027 , #168388 , #168889 , #169035 , #169292 , #168927 , #168993 , #169037 , #169454 , #168905 ) Thanks @mkdelta221 , @waynegault , @chedong , @k94118 , @bluet , @sirius1024 , @RomneyDa , @sayitfast , and @hannesrudolph . Doctor keeps your plugins and data: Doctor preserves installed plugins' configuration when path safety checks block them, leaves malformed UTF-8 root memory files untouched, and recovery copies capture Canvas and Memory Core files before migrations move them, including on installs with no configured agents. ( #168111 , #169029 , #169436 , #169516 ) Thanks @obviyus , @wangmiao0668000666 , and @RomneyDa . Approved tool calls stay as approved: hooks can no longer change tool arguments after a trusted inline approval; plugins that transform arguments must request approval for their final arguments. ( #142700 ) Thanks @giodl73-repo and @giodl73 . Subagent message provenance: inter-session messages keep their [Inter-session message] safety envelope from the first request and through replay, so parent-sent instructions are never presented to a child as direct user instructions. ( #169130 , #169238 ) Thanks @RomneyDa . Control UI turns keep running: chat turns from paired devices survive ordinary pairing activity such as node heartbeats, other devices' updates, and tab reconnects; real revocations still stop them. ( #169457 , #169134 ) Thanks @Oldrich333 . Changes Tool approval hooks: ordinary hooks can no longer rewrite trusted-inline-approved tool arguments without another approval, and transforming plugins must request separate approval for their final arguments or the call is blocked; see docs/plugins/hooks/tool-policy.md for migration. ( #142700 ) Thanks @giodl73-repo and @giodl73 . Codex runtime compatibility: plugin admission rejects official Codex runtimes below 2026.9.7 with update and repair guidance, and incompatible plugins stay inspectable without being imported. ( #168930 , #168748 , #168749 , #168977 ) Thanks @ezimerman . Session notices: creating many sessions gives the main session one summary of new sessions instead of separate notices that crowd out reminders and wakes. ( #168239 ) Update performance: updates stop rehashing unchanged runtime files while retaining the running updater and publishing the candidate, reducing update I/O. ( #168958 ) Fixes Tool Search provenance: network results reached through Tool Search and Code Mode now taint the turn the same way direct network tool calls do. ( #169560 , #169332 ) Thanks @RomneyDa and @farisoftfry . Subagent provenance: child sessions keep the inter-session safety envelope on every replayed turn, and inter-session turns keep a stable provider prompt prefix across later turns and Gateway restarts. ( #169130 , #169238 ) Thanks @RomneyDa . Node commands and approvals: approved node commands replay when their prepared plan omitted session identity, Windows node shell commands keep quoted arguments, safe-bin commands accept trailing whitespace, and the Linux node service keeps its PATH when the login shell resets it. ( #161980 , #151622 , #158160 , #142847 , #168120 , #136677 , #134354 ) Thanks @Program-123 , @gaojian125 , @Dimitri-lcht , @igs-rogenlo , @yetval , @harjothkhara , and @abacha . Private reasoning: unfinished model reasoning stays private when a reply hits a token limit or content filter after a tool call. ( #168294 ) Doctor data safety: Doctor keeps blocked plugins' authored entries, enablement, policy, and slots; refuses to merge malformed UTF-8 root memory; captures Canvas and Memory Core files in new recovery copies (and works on installs with no configured agents); skips redundant cron backups for unchanged one-shot jobs; and honors Windows permissions for SQLite recovery snapshots. ( #168111 , #168066 , #169029 , #168567 , #169436 , #169516 , #168938 , #168838 , #169397 ) Thanks @obviyus , @wangmiao0668000666 , @RomneyDa , @harshitgupta31415 , and @WG-Mojo . Memory: daily-note flushes reject copied saved content instead of repeating blocks, and correcting an embedding provider's endpoint or credential refreshes cached index managers without a Gateway restart. ( #168123 , #151263 , #151055 ) Thanks @ruel225 and @Mirksen . Restart recovery: main sessions that were mid-turn during a Gateway restart resume on the next boot, interrupted completion replies are delivered instead of lost, and new replies wait for their agent to finish starting instead of failing with prepared reply dispatch runtime owner was not published . ( #168651 , #167814 , #167766 , #168826 , #157814 ) Thanks @goutamadwant , @marknilsn , and @xiaozishan . Reply routing: WebChat task completions stay in WebChat, mirrored external sends no longer change a transcript's reply destination, and Reef carries GitHub commit links without flagging their revision IDs as credentials. ( #168248 ) Prompt caching: conversations whose first message ends in whitespace keep a byte-stable prompt prefix, and OpenAI-compatible and local endpoints keep runtime context in a user-role message. ( #168725 , #168546 , #164791 ) Thanks @flanker-stack . Compaction: sessions skip a redundant host compaction after native-only compaction, safeguard compaction keeps configured AGENTS.md sections, and memory-flush runs keep provider-native compaction off. ( #168051 , #168015 , #168446 , #168131 , #168164 ) Thanks @ruel225 , @xydigitLybnnnn , @robertoronderosjr , @jakeaadams , and @obviyus . Control UI: chat turns survive unrelated pairing activity, typed /stop also cancels queued turns for the session, and open chats recover after a Gateway update or recovery reload instead of sticking on Server updated → Retry now , keeping their place. ( #169457 , #169134 , #167860 , #167859 , #168941 , #169194 ) Thanks @Oldrich333 and @masatohoshino . Telegram: polling connects again when the ingress worker runs from a source checkout or packaged plugin build, and tables next to quotes or lists keep their boundaries and values. ( #154286 , #154180 , #168383 , #168366 ) Thanks @xydt-juyaohui , @markfietje , @dhruv1220 , and @barry-ssb . Channels and voice: channels start again after a stopped-Tailscale failure, the Matrix probe stops its client after checking identity, and openclaw voicecall steer keeps stdout machine-readable JSON. content: Hermes Agent v0.21.7 Release Date: October 11, 2026 Patch release. This tag rolls up the ~204 PRs merged since v0.21.6 into a stable release for the desktop app (macOS Apple silicon, Windows), the Microsoft Store and MSIX, the installer, Docker and Hermes Cloud. Full curated notes for this window ship with v0.22.0. What this patch ships for source installs ( hermes update and the desktop app's updater on a git checkout): Updates now follow tagged releases. A source install of the official repository updates to the latest published vX.Y.Z release instead of every commit on main . An install already newer than the latest release stays where it is and waits for the next one; nothing is moved back. To keep following every commit: hermes update --set-channel main . Forks and mirrors keep following main . Store, MSIX and bundled desktop installs are unchanged. Choose the channel in the desktop app. Settings ▸ About ▸ Updates has an Update channel switch (Stable releases / Every commit) for source installs, and the update dialog now shows which channel you are on. Reasoning survives resume. Signed thinking replays after hermes chat --resume and on the next gateway turn, and Bedrock Converse reasoning models no longer get rejected on resumed sessions. Updates no longer fail behind some firewalls. Installs on main no longer fetch a release record that regional firewalls could answer with 403. The stable check uses your GitHub token when one is set ( GITHUB_TOKEN or gh auth login ) and reports a GitHub rate limit as a rate limit. About this release Measured at commit 1fd18277267152893a8a24792b79213e7ca3f899 , the window since v0.21.6 contains 740 non-merge commits across 4,156 changed files (+86,775 / −26,980), 204 merged PRs and 69 closed issues . Also in the window, undocumented here on purpose: plugins running built-in Desktop app actions ( ctx.runAction ) and a plugin SDK pet bubble ( ctx.pet.say ); core-made Codex requests so plugins never hold the token; skills installed mid-session reaching the model without a prompt rebuild; Krea 2 Medium Turbo as the default image lane for new paid subscribers, with a FAL fallback when managed Krea refuses a request; faster desktop updates (the React Compiler pass cached by content, the compiled renderer reused when only the install stamp changed, unchanged native inputs left in place); pinned installs that check out only the pin; compaction marks emitted to Relay; and new community plugins including memory-shield, command-ledger, Memoria, Model Router, wyoming-voice-bridge, codex-account-switch and redline. content: What Problem This Solves Fixes the saved cloud-startup toast recovery E2E failure after a private-draft discard reload, which blocks otherwise unrelated UI pull requests. User Impact No user-visible change. The test continues to check that recovery preserves the separate private draft, replays the saved first turn exactly once, and retains the later draft and queued message. Why This Change Was Made Introduced by 4606ea5 ( #168506 ), which intentionally made the automation readiness observer lazy. After the dialog-triggered reload, observing sessions.send proves the Gateway replay started, not that the renderer readiness hook has loaded. The next synchronous navigation helper read starts that lazy import but receives undefined and throws Control UI readiness hook is unavailable . Await the existing initial-roster/readiness helper before navigating in the toast branch. This preserves lazy production loading and all existing assertions and timeouts; it adds no alternate recovery or navigation path. No overlap with Pash/Sarah changes. Evidence The unchanged test fails on main with two passing cases and the toast case reporting Control UI readiness hook is unavailable . The same failure is visible in the inherited UI shard , and another PR's UI shard . Existing main reproduction evidence was reused rather than rerun. Candidate production-bundle Chromium run: 3/3 passed , including toast recovery (31.949 s). Command: node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.ui-e2e.config.ts ui/src/e2e/new-session-page.cloud-startup.runtime-load.e2e.test.ts --maxWorkers=1 . Full duration: 155.67 s. Targeted oxfmt --check passed. The first local attempt could not build because the copied installation lacked @solidjs/vite-plugin ; a frozen dependency install restored the worktree and the full scenario then passed. Merge danger: two-way door; reverting restores only the test synchronization defect. Blast radius is this production-bundle recovery E2E scenario; no product code, persisted state, or public contract changes. Co-authored-by: Ayaan Zaidi hi@obviy.us

title: v2.1.296
summary: What's changed Added a code key to the Claude apps gateway's managed.policies[] : the same settings as cli , also applied in Claude Desktop's Code tab; beside desktop , it turns on Claude Desktop's gateway mode Added autoCompactWindow to subagent frontmatter and --agents definitions, so a subagent can auto-compact earlier than the main conversation's window Added CLAUDE_CODE_WORKFLOW_SUBAGENT_MODEL to run every workflow agent on one model while other subagents keep theirs Added...
content: What's changed Added a code key to the Claude apps gateway's managed.policies[] : the same settings as cli , also applied in Claude Desktop's Code tab; beside desktop , it turns on Claude Desktop's gateway mode Added autoCompactWindow to subagent frontmatter and --agents definitions, so a subagent can auto-compact earlier than the main conversation's window Added CLAUDE_CODE_WORKFLOW_SUBAGENT_MODEL to run every workflow agent on one model while other subagents keep theirs Added CLAUDE_CODE_OVERLOADED_RETRY_MAX_DELAY_MS environment variable to set a longer maximum delay for the backoff when retrying an overloaded (529) request Added a note in /plugin on a plugin whose hooks are left out because another enabled plugin has the same name Added an allow_large option to the Read tool so Claude can read a text file past the usual size limits in one call when it needs the whole file and the context has room Fixed managed-settings PreToolUse hooks that deny a tool call with "continue": false , and managed prompt hooks that block one, refusing the call but not ending the turn Fixed PostToolUse hooks in managed settings not applying updatedMCPToolOutput in some sessions Fixed headless sessions starting a folder's .mcp.json or plugin MCP server that was switched off for that folder, after changing directory or reloading plugins Fixed a Claude apps gateway that serves allowedProviders with "gateway" locking out laptops that name that gateway in user settings Fixed a saved Claude apps gateway sign-in being ignored on machines whose managed settings set forceLoginMethod to gateway with no forceLoginGatewayUrl (regression in 2.1.295) Fixed --teleport opening an empty conversation when the session's history could not be read Fixed token counts for Haiku 5.5 and other models that take only adaptive thinking, which failed behind some gateways and were counted with budget thinking elsewhere Fixed resumed subagents being told that the user rejected a tool call that a session shutdown had interrupted Fixed hook output being altered when it contained text resembling a plugin hint tag Fixed secret redaction in shared transcripts and debug logs missing some values that follow a key with no value, including in JSON written inside a shell string Fixed a stray 52;c;… escape sequence printed on screen after copying in older VTE-based terminals such as MATE Terminal Fixed toasts and notifications waiting unseen for as long as the /diff panel or dialog was open Fixed Esc or an interrupt during a UserPromptSubmit hook or a mod's prompt.submit hook ending headless sessions, clearing the typed prompt, or letting the unchecked prompt through Fixed SessionStart hooks of a plugin loaded after a headless session starts being skipped when a different plugin with the same name, or another spelling of it, had already run Fixed claude self-hosted-runner printing misleading errors when registration is refused: it now names the org admin setting, or says a restarted on-demand runner needs a fresh work order Fixed a self-hosted runner session's git fetch, pull and push failing while another session of the same repository starts on a runner with --capacity above 1 Fixed workflow scripts silently truncating results, agent options and other values nested deeper than about 20,000 levels, and deeply nested results writing huge task output files Fixed a plugin's served $ methods running in the main session's working directory instead of the calling agent's, and ignoring the turn their calling hook holds Fixed $.agent.register succeeding from a mod's hook that was still running after the mod was reloaded or removed; the call is now refused Fixed $.http.fetch in mods refusing a HEAD request when the response declares a Content-Length over the 4 MiB body limit Fixed claude plugin marketplace add , marketplace update and plugin install failing with an internal error for a marketplace named like constructor ; add now refuses such names clearly Fixed a plugin secret named constructor or prototype being deleted by the next save of that plugin's options Fixed cloud sessions skipping auto mode's checks on Claude in Chrome actions that a saved permission allows when their feature flags had not loaded Fixed CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_INTERRUPTED_TURN re-running a finished turn after a restart when an MCP tool result had ended that turn Fixed Bash permission checks auto-approving some commands that assign the BASH_ARGV0 shell variable and then use it; these now prompt for approval Fixed Edit and NotebookEdit replacing every non-ASCII character in files that are not valid UTF-8 (Windows-1252, Shift-JIS, GBK); such edits are now refused Fixed a prompt sent just after ← being run twice, once unseen in the foreground, when the background service was slow to answer Fixed a prompt sent while SessionStart hooks were still running vanishing when ← moved the session to the background; it is still not sent, but ↑ now brings it back Fixed a late-loading plugin's SessionStart hook output reaching the new conversation after /clear in headless sessions Fixed PowerShell commands not seeing variables that hooks write to CLAUDE_ENV_FILE (when the file holds only plain assignments) Fixed Claude calling cloud sessions non-interactive and suggesting /mcp or claude mcp when an MCP server needs authentication Fixed /code-review ending on a raw JSON array in cloud sessions, the Agent SDK and IDE integrations; the findings now print as a numbered list Fixed auto mode occasionally refusing one update to your own artifact, saying its sharing had changed when it had not Fixed skills synced from claude.ai never finishing their install, and being downloaded again at every sync, when several sessions share a config directory Fixed a plugin synced from claude.ai being disabled when the marketplace dependency it declares was also synced from claude.ai Fixed a startup hang on macOS when plugin paths copied from a Linux machine pointed under /home Fixed the Workflow tool refusing script files with CRLF line endings, such as files checked out on Windows Fixed OpenTelemetry tool_result events missing git_commit_id after git commit -q or git -C commit Fixed CLAUDE_CODE_TRANSCRIPT_LOCAL_GC dropping a message from the saved transcript when its text held a Unicode line or paragraph separator (U+2028, U+2029) Fixed claude purge leaving a prompt in the history file when its text held a Unicode line or paragraph separator (U+2028, U+2029) Windows: Fixed PowerShell commands longer than about 1 KB always asking for permission, so allow rules and read-only detection now apply up to 32 KB Windows: Fixed stdio MCP servers being force-killed at shutdown; stdin now closes first and the process tree is killed only if the server is still running after 300 ms Windows: Fixed claude plugin install failing for GitHub owner/repo plugin sources on machines with no GitHub SSH key; the clone is now retried over HTTPS Windows: Fixed rm -rf /c/Users/ in Git Bash not asking in bypass permissions mode Improved fullscreen mode: the link under the mouse pointer is now underlined to show it can be opened Improved transcript toggle (ctrl+o) responsiveness in code-heavy conversations by caching syntax-highlighted code blocks Improved Claude Desktop's Code tab behind a Claude apps gateway: when a session can't start, including on a machine not set up for the gateway's code settings, the reason shows as a reply Improved the errors for a refused cloud session: they now say why your organization's policy couldn't be loaded, and name an API key or auth token that overrides your claude.ai login Improved --debug output to name unrecognized frontmatter fields in custom agent files, with a hint for likely typos Improved auto mode: a tool call that wasn't run because auto mode's check had no usable answer now shows as a dim "Not run" row instead of a red error Improved --debug output for hooks: command hooks on tool calls, prompts, SessionStart and Stop now log their command, plugin, outcome and duration when they finish, so a slow hook is identifiable Improved CLAUDE_CODE_TRANSCRIPT_LOCAL_GC : a large transcript file is no longer rewritten when that would free under 10% of it Updated /cost , the status line, --max-budget-usd and the SDK's cost figures to price Sonnet 5.5 cache reads at $0.10 per million tokens (was $0.20) Updated the bundled dataviz skill: lighter violet for the seventh series in light mode, softer primary text in dark mode, and compact y-axis labels like 1K Changed the default limit on MCP tool descriptions sent up front and on MCP server instructions from 2,048 to 4,096 characters Changed ← : a turn or ! command started while the session moves to the background is now stopped instead of finishing out of sight [VSCode] Fixed claudeCode.spinnerVerbs missing from the extension's settings, so settings.json now title: Investigating unintended model actions in our evaluations and internal use
ICYMI: What landed for AI builders in September 2026
summary: A monthly recap of the latest Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Strands updates from September 2026: broader model choice, faster serverless agents with built-in evaluation, and automated knowledge base syncing with native enterprise connectors.
content: A recap of the latest Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Strands updates from September 2026 At AWS, we believe the fastest path to enterprise AI is giving builders real choice at every layer: model, runtime, and tooling. That belief shapes how we invest across Amazon Bedrock, AgentCore, and Strands. Amazon Bedrock continues expanding access to leading frontier models so you can build and scale AI applications securely. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides the managed infrastructure to build, connect, and deploy enterprise agents using any framework or model. Strands  gives you an open source toolkit to build agents and run anywhere. As AI models become more capable and model choice expands, the industry conversations are shifting. Model performance is no longer the only question. Customers now weigh cost against benefit for their specific use case, and those decisions matter when delegating work to agents in production. AI agents are already moving into workflows that require them to reason over enterprise knowledge, operate across long-horizon tasks, and act in systems where security, accuracy, and governance matter. The focus is now shifting beyond the model itself to the broader system around it, including the context agents can access, the actions they can take, and how enterprise data is governed and protected. In September, updates across Amazon Bedrock, AgentCore, and Strands strengthened those foundations. New capabilities expanded model choice, made agent operations more efficient and measurable, and created more direct ways to connect AI applications with current business information. Run faster agents and evaluate what matters Build agents optimized for OpenAI models. Amazon Bedrock Managed Agents , powered by OpenAI, is now available in public preview, helping you build production-ready AI agents without sacrificing enterprise security. You can now use OpenAI models while keeping data within AWS, reuse existing AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions, and maintain full auditability through AWS CloudTrail. Durable sessions and built-in human approval workflows help reduce development overhead and mitigate risk. Agents now start faster with less infrastructure overhead. The latest AgentCore runtime , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, has more efficient memory management and lower cold start latency for serverless agents, so you pay for actual usage rather than the peak memory. You can run agents faster at lower cost with pay-as-you-go pricing and no need to pre-provision capacity. Sessions scale to zero when idle and run in hardware-isolated environments. Lower your token cost with frontier performance. Strands harness is a new open source agent harness that matches popular harnesses on accuracy while using 28 percent fewer tokens. You can spin up a production-ready agent in a single line of Python or TypeScript, with built-in context management, prompt caching, and memory, then deploy it anywhere. Let your models make big decisions safely, locally. Strands Decider 2B is a small, open source, 2B-parameter decision model that picks between predefined options (instead of generating text), delivering answers in ~115ms locally. It’s optimized for agentic AI tasks like tool selection, routing, and guardrails, with all code, data, and weights available on GitHub and Hugging Face. Find the right model for each workload Choose from a broader set of OpenAI models for your everyday work. OpenAI’s Astra, Sol, and Luna models are now generally available on Amazon Bedrock, with options for demanding projects, recurring complex work, and high-volume tasks. GPT-6 Astra is the flagship model for your most ambitious work, bringing deeper reasoning to complex decisions, document analysis, and software development with up to 1 million input tokens. It brings stronger reasoning and more precise judgment to complex business decisions, operates across software and files, and delivers professional-quality output aligned with organizational voice, templates, and standards. GPT-6 Astra Ultrafast adds a premium speed tier for GPT-6 Astra, built for workloads where speed matters most. It delivers up to 6x faster inference in the API, with up to 300 tokens per second. Sol brings near-Astra intelligence to coding, computer use, and professional workloads that run frequently. Both GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Sol are available on Amazon Bedrock. GPT 6.1 Luna is designed for high-volume tasks such as extraction, summarization, classification, and routing. Together, they help you balance intelligence, latency, and cost across workloads. Take on long-running coding and research with Claude . Model choices for Claude now include the latest versions to advance your coding and scientific work. Claude Fable 5.1 expands options for coding, scientific research, and enterprise workflows. Claude Opus 5.5 is built for agentic coding, knowledge work, and long-running tasks. It uses adaptive thinking to gauge how much reasoning a task needs and an effort parameter to set an upper bound on reasoning depth. Claude Sonnet 5.5 is a smarter, more efficient Sonnet suited to focused coding and knowledge work, delivering 30 percent lower cost per task at 30 percent faster speed than Claude Sonnet 5. Reason through complexity with a broader model portfolio. Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 is now available on Amazon Bedrock. According to Moonshot AI, Kimi K3 is its most capable model and the first open model to reach 2.8 trillion parameters. With a 1-million-token context window, native vision, and built-in prompt caching, it helps you build smarter apps 2.5x faster at lower cost than previous versions. xAI’s frontier models Grok 4.6 and Grok 4.7 offer a 500K token context window and support configurable reasoning effort and self-verification for more reliable long-running tasks. Together, these additions give you more flexibility when matching models to your requirements such as context length, latency, throughput, and cost. Get more control over your enterprise AI agents Keep agent knowledge current. With new automatic sync scheduling in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base, you can now configure daily, weekly, and monthly refresh options for all native data-source connectors. As a result, your enterprise AI agents retrieve the latest information. The user-managed setup for SharePoint, OneDrive, and Confluence reduces reliance on admin-managed service accounts when you already have the access you need. Connect more enterprise sources without maintaining custom ingestion pipelines. Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base now supports ServiceNow , Confluence Data Center , Salesforce, and Zendesk as native connectors to handle data crawling, metadata extraction, and incremental sync automatically. These connectors reduce the amount of custom ingestion code you need to build and maintain support content, internal documentation, and operational knowledge. Get started Explore Amazon Bedrock , deploy agents with the AgentCore CLI , or build your first agent with the Strands Harness SDK . Interested in learning how Amazon Bedrock can support your team? Connect with us to start the conversation. About the author Prachi Mishra Prachi is a Senior Product Marketing Manager for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore at Amazon Web Services (AWS), where she helps bring the power of production-ready AI agents to developers and enterprises worldwide.

title: How Postman runs Agent Mode for 40 million developers on Amazon Bedrock
summary: Building an AI agent that works in a demo is a different problem from running one for 40 million developers. Postman and AWS share the architectural patterns behind Agent Mode: controlling tool sprawl, exposing schema-based reads, and treating context as the real bottleneck, plus how it runs on Amazon Bedrock at scale.
content: Building an AI agent for a demo and operating one for 40 million developers are different engineering problems. Postman set out to build Agent Mode , an AI-native way to work across API testing , documentation , discovery, and implementation. The team expected model quality and prompt design to be the hardest problems. The deeper challenges came from integrating an agent into a mature product with years of interface-driven assumptions, a wide surface area, and specialized concepts. In this post, Postman and AWS describe the architectural patterns that emerged while making a mature product legible to an AI agent. These patterns include controlling tool sprawl, exposing schema-based reads, and treating context rather than capability as the primary bottleneck. We also explain how Agent Mode uses Amazon Bedrock for model flexibility, geographically scoped cross-Region inference, model-dependent zero data retention, and multi-tier prompt caching. Together, these lessons can help teams move production agents beyond prototypes. Why Postman built Agent Mode Agent Mode is Postman’s portal for working with the product in an AI-native way across testing, documentation, discovery, and implementation. Postman has evolved over 11 years, and developers and users learned to locate information through the interface by expanding sidebars, checking tabs, and opening requests. Re-engineering that awareness for an agent surfaced structural assumptions in the product’s APIs, user experience, and distribution of product knowledge. An agent reasons over data rather than navigating a screen. Figure 1 illustrates how Agent Mode works directly against the application. Figure 1: Agent Mode works directly against the Postman application. In this example, it opens a pull request and proposes next steps without requiring the user to navigate through the interface Agent Mode runs on Amazon Bedrock , which provides managed access to foundation models behind the agent. Supporting Postman’s global developer community creates variable, latency-sensitive demand with sharp traffic bursts. With Amazon Bedrock, Postman can scale this production workload without operating its own model-serving infrastructure while retaining flexibility in model selection and control over throughput, geographic processing, and cost. Figure 2 provides a high-level view of the production architecture before the following sections examine its components. Figure 2: Postman Agent Mode combines client-side tools, agent orchestration, purpose-built context, and Amazon Bedrock model inference. Tools are scoped for each task, and user approval remains part of actions that modify application state Human oversight is part of the production design. Agent Mode requires user approval before actions that modify application state. Postman also scopes available tools to the task, selects purpose-built context, and applies model-dependent data-retention settings. These controls reduce unintended actions and unnecessary data exposure, while production testing and monitoring remain necessary. As a responsible AI control, Postman uses Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to redact personally identifiable information before it reaches the underlying large language model (LLM). Enterprise admins can turn this on in Agent Mode’s guardrail settings. Handling tool sprawl In Agent Mode, tools define how the agent acts inside Postman. Early on, the team leaned toward highly atomic tools: small, precise actions such as opening a request, updating one field, or fetching a specific piece of metadata. That approach supported correctness and control in early iterations, but it also revealed several problems. Many real-world workflows require long sequences of tool calls. Even when each step was fast, the overall experience felt slow, because every action had to return to the model before the next one could begin. Users watched the agent step through actions they had mentally grouped as a single operation. In Postman’s testing, tool-selection errors increased once the visible toolset exceeded approximately 40 tools. The agent could call nonexistent tools, pass incorrect arguments despite valid schemas, or select tools that seemed semantically reasonable but were wrong in context. Larger or newer models reduced this behavior but didn’t remove it. Past a certain toolset size, exposing more tools can reduce agent effectiveness. The current architecture selects tools based on need and context and isolates individual execution threads. The model sees only the tools relevant to the current task. Figure 3 illustrates this dynamic selection process. Figure 3: The root agent queries a vector database of tool embeddings and narrows more than 170 tools to approximately 15 relevant to the request. It then hands those tools to a context-isolated sub-agent, so the model sees only the tools needed for the task A subtler problem was that many client APIs were implicitly coupled to interface state. Tools that modified requests needed certain elements to be open, while other tools opened new tabs as side effects. The agent had to open a request tab to read it, mimicking interface interactions instead of reasoning about data. Postman is actively decoupling tools from tabs, and its Native Git feature makes extensive use of this approach. For example, Agent Mode can now send requests in the background without an open tab, although user approval is still required. Builder takeaway: Treat your tool catalog as part of the context budget. Dynamically scope the tools exposed to the model per task, and decouple “what the agent can do” from “what the UI happens to have open.” Exposing schema-based reads For products such as the API Catalog, Postman consolidated multiple narrow views into a single query tool. These products expose structured data such as service uptime, test results, and endpoint response times across many services. Given the schemas of the underlying ClickHouse tables, the agent can generate complex queries with joins and WHERE clauses. This substantially reduces the number of distinct tools needed to answer an analysis question: SELECT toString(service_id) AS service_id, countMerge(total_events_state) AS total_requests, countMerge(error_events_state) AS total_errors, round(countMerge(error_events_state) * 100.0 / countMerge(total_events_state), 4) AS error_rate_pct, avgMerge(avg_latency_state) AS avg_latency_ms, quantileMerge(0.95)(p95_latency_state) AS p95_latency_ms FROM http_events_summary_1d WHERE service_id IN ('...list of service IDs') AND bucket_1d >= today() - 7 GROUP BY service_id HAVING p95_latency_ms 0 ORDER BY error_rate_pct DESC; With this approach, the engineering job shifts from building a tool per question to modeling the data well once . The agent can then generate a far wider variety of queries than the team could ever have enumerated as individual tools. Builder takeaway: Where you have well-structured data, give the agent schema-aware read access to a query engine instead of a proliferation of single-purpose read tools. You trade tool count for data modeling, which produces a better scaling curve. Context was the real bottleneck Postman initially assumed missing tools would be the biggest blocker. In practice, missing or incomplete context caused more failures than missing capabilities. Context is the agent’s understanding of where the user is in Postman, which entities are active, and what state has already been established. When that context was wrong or absent, even correct tools became ineffective. Figure 4 distinguishes the two forms of context supplied to the agent. Figure 4: Two kinds of context feed the agent. Broad, shallow background context is gathered automatically and minified for the prompt. Deep, focused selected context is chosen by the user and routed through a dedicated handler for each entity type. Each handler distills the entity into the information the agent needs The challenge was structural. Over 11 years, developers and users learned to find information through the interface. Re-engineering that awareness for an agent required multiple iterations to determine what mattered for each workflow and what was noise. Serializing the existing interface data model did not produce useful context because those objects were shaped for rendering and data transfer, not reasoning. Postman therefore built dedicated context handlers that distilled each entity into what the agent needed to know. As more objects gained handlers, truncation became the next problem. Many fields contain open-ended user-generated data, including request descriptions, OpenAPI specifications, and request payloads. This data can crowd the context window. Managing the context budget carefully is essential at scale and supports the filesystem-backed approach the team is exploring, where each handler does not need custom truncation and expansion logic. Builder takeaway: Don’t feed the model your rendering data model. Build purpose-shaped context handlers and treat the context window as a scarce, actively managed budget. Noise crowds out signal long before the model reaches its limit. Putting it all together As Agent Mode evolved, it became clear the system had to aggregate three distinct components, each solving a different problem. Client-side tools live in the Postman application and represent the final actions the agent can take, such as opening requests, modifying settings, running collections, and inspecting authentication. Agent Mode also uses server-side tools for functions such as web search and agent-loop management, but most tools operate on the Postman application. Generic agent instructions define system-level behavior, including how proactive Agent Mode should be, how it communicates uncertainty, and what baseline product knowledge it carries. A knowledge base uses a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) approach. Postman has a large product surface that includes multiple request protocols, mock servers, monitors, documentation, the API Network, workspace governance, variables, helpers, code generation, request settings, and collection runs. Encoding all of this in static prompts was not feasible, and most of it is irrelevant to a given query. For initial seeding, the team used Postman’s Learning Center to generate concise feature-specific articles. At runtime, Agent Mode selects knowledge articles based on the incoming query and available context. For example, when a user selects a mock server, Agent Mode injects the related article automatically. This keeps the agent lightweight by default while providing depth when needed. The knowledge base evolves with the application, so teams can ship Agent Mode documentation with new features. Running Agent Mode on Amazon Bedrock The three components previously described resolve to the same runtime action: an inference call to a foundation model (FM). At Postman’s scale, traffic is bursty and developer-driven. Routing, caching, and geographic processing controls help Postman accommodate traffic bursts, manage inference cost, and address workload-specific processing requirements. Amazon Bedrock provides four capabilities that matter most here. Model flexibility across the Claude family Agent Mode isn’t tied to one model. Through Amazon Bedrock model inference APIs , Postman can access supported Anthropic Claude models and route each workload to an appropriate model. A faster model can serve high-volume, latency-sensitive interactions, while a larger model can handle complex reasoning where quality matters more than cost. Moving between supported Claude models is primarily a configuration change rather than a new integration. This flexibility directly supports the tool-sprawl and context challenges described earlier. In Postman’s testing, newer and larger models reduced tool hallucinations, and Postman can adopt supported models without rebuilding the integration. See supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock . Cross-Region inference for high throughput Developer traffic is spiky, and provisioning for peak demand in one AWS Region can be costly. Agent Mode uses Amazon Bedrock cross-Region inference to automatically route requests among the destination Regions defined by an inference profile. At runtime, the application passes the selected inference profile ID or Amazon Resource Name (ARN) as the modelId in Converse or InvokeModel. The profile, applicable AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and service control policies, and quotas must permit every destination Region that Bedrock might select. Geographic inference profiles route requests only among supported Regions within a defined geography, such as the United States or European Union. This option combines increased throughput with a configured geographic processing boundary. Global inference profiles can route requests among supported destination Regions worldwide to provide additional throughput during traffic bursts. They are appropriate only when the workload does not require a geographically constrained processing boundary. Postman can select the inference profile per workload: a global profile for maximum available throughput or a geographic profile when processing must remain within the profile’s defined geography. This choice is explicit in the modelId used for each Bedrock inference request. # Schematic Converse request response = bedrock_runtime.converse( modelId=" ", messages=messages, system=system_blocks, ) Data residency and enterprise controls For enterprise customers, permitted processing geography can be as important as throughput. Geographic inference profiles constrain Bedrock routing to the profile’s supported destination Regions within the selected geography. This does not mean that inference runs inside Postman’s own AWS environment. Amazon Bedrock processes requests in the eligible AWS Regions for that profile, with data encrypted in transit and at rest. AWS states that Bedrock doesn’t use prompts and completions to train AWS models or distribute them to third parties. Postman has configured zero data retention with data_retention_mode set to none for supported Agent Mode models. Availability and behavior are model-dependent, so each production model must be checked against the current Amazon Bedrock data-protection and retention documentation . Prompt caching to keep costs in check A production agent resends substantial stable context on each turn, including system instructions, generic agent behavior, a core tool set, selected knowledge, and conversation context. Reprocessing the unchanged prefix on every request adds avoidable latency and cost. Agent Mode uses Amazon Bedrock prompt caching to reuse stable prompt prefixes. The near-immutable core, including the system prompt, agent instructions, and core tool definitions, uses a one-hour cache checkpoint. More variable context uses a five-minute checkpoint that refreshes on a cache hit. Bedrock requires the longer-lived checkpoint to appear before the shorter-lived checkpoint. The shorter tier suits interactive sessions because idle context expires, while the one-hour tier can amortize its higher cache-write price across many reads. Cache benefits and supported TTLs depend on the selected model. Teams can verify behavior through the cacheReadInputTokens and cacheWriteInputTokens usage fields and measure time to first token for their own workloads. # Schematic cache checkpoints in Converse content blocks {"cachePoint": {"type": "default", "ttl": "1h"}} # stable core {"cachePoint": {"type": "default", "ttl": "5m"}} # variable layer Builder takeaway: Treat inference as a routing-and-caching problem, not only a model-selection decision. Select the Claude model per workload, choose the appropriate cross-Region inference profile, and cache the stable prompt prefix with TTLs that match how frequently each layer changes. Best practices for scaling agents in production Distilled from Postman’s journey, for builders working on Amazon Bedrock: Budget tools as carefully as tokens. Dynamically select the tools exposed per task. In Postman’s testing, tool-selection errors increased as the visible toolset became large. Prefer schema-aware reads over tool proliferation. Model your data well and let the agent query it. Decouple agent actions from interface state. If a tool requires an open tab, the agent is navigating the interface rather than reasoning directly over data. Engineer context deliberately. Purpose-built context handlers beat serializing your rendering model every time. Manage the context window as a scarce resource. Truncation and expansion strategy is a first-class design problem, not an afterthought. Ship docs with features. A RAG knowledge base only stays useful if it evolves in lockstep with the product. Route and cache on Bedrock. Match each workload to the appropriate Claude model, choose cross-Region inference based on throughput and geographic requirements, and apply tiered caching to stable prompt prefixes. Conclusion Building Agent Mode required Postman to confront the gap between large language model capabilities and the structure of mature products: interface assumptions, coupled clients, sprawling tool catalogs, and knowledge distributed across documentation and teams. Dynamic tool selection, schema-based reads, and deliberate context engineering emerged as repeatable patterns at the scale of Postman’s developer community . Amazon Bedrock provides the managed model access, cross-Region inference , model-dependent retention controls , and prompt caching that support the production architecture. Whether you’re building your first agent or scaling an existing one, these patterns can help teams avoid common agent-integration and scaling challenges. To learn more, see the Amazon Bedrock documentation , including guidance for cross-Region inference , prompt caching , and data protection and retention . For related implementation guidance, read Effectively use prompt caching on Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock announces global cross-Region inference for increased throughput on the AWS Machine Learning Blog. To explore the product, see the Postman Agent Mode documentation . Postman’s production implementation is proprietary and isn’t available as a public sample repository.   About the authors Srinivas Kini Srinivas is a Senior Engineer on Postman’s AI team, building enterprise agents at the intersection of distributed systems and AI infrastructure. His focus is core agent architecture that keeps agents reliable and accurate at scale. Shubham Gupta Shubham is a Solutions Architect at AWS based in Bengaluru, India, supporting independent software vendors (ISVs). He works with engineering and leadership teams to design, build, and run their products on AWS, from first architecture to production, with a deep focus on generative AI and resilience at scale. Outside of work, Shubham is an avid hiker who brings the same preparation and persistence from the trail to building systems that last.

title: Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations With Frontier AI Agents
summary: Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs. Developers direct AI agents through […]
content: Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs. Developers direct AI agents through natural-language instructions, review results and guide changes. Omniverse libraries provide GPU-accelerated physics, rendering and sensor simulation capabilities. Explore the projects below to see frontier AI models such as GPT-6 Astra at work, and check back for new examples from NVIDIA teams and developers across the ecosystem.   Create an Editable Building Model From Site Scans https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/relay-video-v14-1080p.mp4   Planning warehouse automation requires a model of the building itself, but shelving and machinery can obscure its structure in site scans. Omniverse brings together real-to-sim tools and agent skills to help developers turn real-world captures into editable starting environments for physical AI simulation. David Wehr, from NVIDIA’s simulation technology team, built on that work using Astra to develop a workflow for digitally reconstructing a building without its contents. The goal is an editable, simulation-ready building model where developers can add or reposition shelving and machinery to evaluate warehouse layouts and automation plans before making physical changes. Wehr guided Astra to interpret panoramic photos, create building geometry and align it with point-cloud measurements. OpenUSD stores the models, while Omniverse’s ovrtx library renders results for inspection. Explore NVIDIA Omniverse agent skills to help agents build with Omniverse libraries.   Test Gas-Turbine Operating Scenarios With a Digital Twin https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Turbine-Lab-RTX-and-What-If-under-10MB-1.mp4   Before changing how industrial equipment operates, engineers need a way to explore the consequences. Pradeep Kaushik, a member of the NVIDIA Omniverse developer relations team, directed Astra to build a what-if analysis application around a simulated gas turbine and generator. The application lets users adjust conditions such as load, ambient temperature and fuel composition, then compare power, efficiency, fuel consumption and equipment response. Six test procedures explore scenarios including load changes, a stuck fuel valve and an exhaust-sensor error. The prototype gives engineers an interactive way to investigate how operating changes and faults could affect equipment behavior, supporting decisions about which scenarios warrant further testing. Astra used tools like Cantera for thermochemistry and SciPy for equipment dynamics. The application maps solver results to rotor animation and color-coded temperature, pressure and flow-velocity indicators in a 3D turbine. NVIDIA Omniverse libraries update the scene ( ovstage ), render it with RTX (ovrtx) and stream the view to the browser (ovstream). Engineers can rotate and zoom the cutaway, switch between indicators, and pause or scrub through a simulated response alongside charts and virtual instruments.   Build Simulation Scenes With Open Source SimReady Assets https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/kitchen_final_blog_with_music.mp4   With SimReady Central Library, announced at GTC Berlin , developers can access more than 2,000 simulation-ready USD assets from equipment manufacturers and asset providers for robotics simulations and AI factory digital twins workflows. Paul Kind, a member of NVIDIA’s Omniverse documentation team, pointed an AI agent to the library and guided scene assembly through conversation. His kitchen scene included 180 placements drawn from 63 unique library assets, alongside 18 custom geometry pieces. Kind reviewed renders produced with Isaac Sim and guided further adjustments. For robotics and factory workflows, developers can select SimReady assets with the simulation properties embedded to fit their required task then test in an assembled environment. Find assets in SimReady Central Library , and learn how to contribute .   Stress-Test a Warehouse Simulation at Scale https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infra-scale-demo-20260914_144614-Meeting-Recording.mp4   A warehouse simulation needs to keep running smoothly as more robot arms, conveyors and boxes fill the scene. When it slows down, developers need to identify what’s holding it back. Bhavik Sanganee, principal engineer at NVIDIA, used Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to build a warehouse simulation, increase its complexity and investigate slowdowns. Performance first fell below the target when the scene doubled in size. Running physics calculations, image rendering and video preparation concurrently restored performance and enabled further scaling. With 80 conveyors, 40 arms and 800 boxes, the simulation sustained 30 frames per second at full HD resolution during a two-minute test. The arms completed 640 successful box placements. Doubling the scene again reduced performance. Testing traced the slowdown to the physics and robot-control pipeline, giving Sanganee a specific area to improve. Start building with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries .   Test Robot Control for Flexible Cable Routing https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/scurve_rl_vs_astra_side_by_side.mp4   In electronics assembly, a robot may need to position a flexible cable around components before plugging it into a port. The cable bends as the robot moves it, and the connector must line up precisely to fit. Oyindamola Omotuyi, robotics technical marketing manager at NVIDIA, directed Astra to build a robot simulation using NVIDIA Isaac Lab , Newton physics and Omniverse rendering with a Robotiq gripper handling the cable. Astra also developed a reinforcement learning system that combined learned cable-routing movements with position-and-orientation feedback and corrective adjustments for USB-C insertion. The simulation gave Omotuyi a way to test cable handling and connector alignment before moving to physical-robot experiments. The controller used information supplied directly by the simulation. Next steps include testing a friction-held grasp and using information a physical robot could obtain from cameras and sensors. Get started with robot learning in NVIDIA Isaac Lab .   Turn Robot Computer-Aided Design Into a SimReady Asset Before testing whether a robot can pick up and move a box, developers need a simulation model with joints that move correctly and with grippers that can hold the object. A computer-aided design (CAD) model provides the robot’s shape, but it still needs physics properties to perform the task. Using an ABB Robotics YuMi robot, developers directed Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse content libraries to convert CAD files into OpenUSD, match the robot’s appearance to reference images, and configure joints and collision geometry. They checked the asset against SimReady Foundation requirements before testing it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. Both arms and grippers completed four cube pick-and-place cycles, using simulated finger contact and friction. These tests demonstrated behavior under the simulated conditions — estimated physical properties were not calibrated against the real robot. Follow the five-step SimReady tutorial .   Build a Humanoid Simulator for a Warehouse Environment https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Humanoid-Warehouse.mp4 Explore a gamified, physics-based control of a humanoid robot in first- and third-person view. Before automating warehouse tasks, developers need an interactive simulation environment to explore task behavior and evaluate how the work gets done. Frank DeLise, Omniverse product manager at NVIDIA, used Astra to turn a SimReady warehouse and humanoid robot into an interactive simulator with first- and third-person views. DeLise directed Astra to connect NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for physics ( ovphysx ), scene updates ( ovstage ), rendering ( ovrtx ) and the user interface ( ovui ). He also used Astra with SimReady ( simready-foundation ) to create the physical scene in simulation. Astra then generated animation and application code to bring those capabilities together. Learn how to prepare and validate SimReady robot assets with frontier AI models and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries.   Connect an Autonomous-Driving Testing Workflow https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/zero-to-alpamayo-under-10MB.mp4   Changing a scene, sensor or driving model can significantly affect autonomous-vehicle simulations. Doyub Kim, a manager on the simulation technology team at NVIDIA, asked Astra to build Zero to Alpamayo — a reusable simulation environment based on San Francisco’s Market Street. Kim directed Astra to map out the workflow, then connect asset creation, traffic, Omniverse RTX sensor simulation and Alpamayo driving in stages, checking each integration. The resulting prototype was a testing ground for comparing models and tracing how scene or sensor changes affect downstream driving behavior. A separate Cosmos3-Nano experiment varied weather and lighting in recorded simulation videos, allowing Kim to compare the driving model’s responses to the same scenario under different conditions.   Use Sensor Differences to Create and Improve Digital Twins https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/0_00-0_004-hubble_rivermark_Real_Sim_no_loop.mp4 Comparing recorded and simulated camera and lidar outputs gives developers key performance indicator-based feedback for refining a scene. To test robots and autonomous vehicles, developers need to know how closely simulated sensors match real ones. Ashley Reid, who works on RTX sensor validation at NVIDIA, directed Astra and Claude Fable 5 agents to compare ovrtx camera and raw LiDAR outputs with recorded data. The agents created two digital twins from scratch and improved two existing ones. Over about three days, Reid guided an iterative workflow in which agents measured differences, created or modified OpenUSD scenes, and checked the results. Changes addressed missing objects, geometry and materials, with acceptance depending on camera and LiDAR metrics. This gives developers a way to use measured discrepancies to guide scene creation and improvement. Start by rendering an OpenUSD scene with the ovrtx minimal Python example , then define a sensor measure to compare with recorded data.   Robo Olympics: Test Robot Skills With Simulation Teaching robots new movements means checking whether those actions work under physical constraints. Tae Kim, who leads NVIDIA Omniverse engineering and product, used sports videos and natural-language instructions to guide Astra in building Robo Olympics, an experimental project that tests simulated Unitree G1 humanoids performing sports movements. Under Kim’s direction, Astra built controllers and refined them through physics trials. Newton Physics Engine simulated behavior, the open source NVIDIA Warp framework accelerated calculations and ovrtx rendered scenes and virtual-camera images. In one experiment, the robot cleared a single hurdle in 64 of 100 simulation trials. The trials gave Kim feedback for improving the robot’s timing and control. Watch Kim explore building simulations with Astra and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries.   Test Robotic Disassembly With Computer-Aided Design and Simulation Before a robot can disassemble a product, developers need to know whether its tools can reach and remove the parts. Jens Jebens, a senior product manager for OpenUSD at NVIDIA, directed Astra to model a car suspension in PTC Onshape and configure it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim . With Astra, Jebens explored computer-aided design and tooling revisions for robots informed by simulation. The agent measured the available space and designed a wrench the robot could use to reach the suspension’s bolts. Jebens reported successful removal of a suspension component in simulation. This connects design and tooling decisions to disassembly results, offering a starting point for robot policy training. Explore the Onshape importer guide .   Bring the International Space Station Into the Browser Turning 3D models into an application requires connecting assets, live data and an interface. Nic Johns, an engineering director at NVIDIA, prompted Astra to assemble NASA assets into an OpenUSD International Space Station model with telemetry. Johns built the application with a single prompt, then used a follow-up prompt to shift the scene to Earth’s daytime side so the planet was visible. The workflow used Blender for asset preparation and Omniverse libraries for rendering ( ovrtx ), scene runtime (ovstage) and streaming (ovstream). The application brings 3D models and operational data into the browser, with Johns guiding its development through prompts and corrections. Try the Omniverse Real-Time Viewer skill .   Turn Captured Rooms Into Testing Environments A digitally reconstructed room needs editable objects and accurate physical behavior before developers can test interactions. Chirag Majithia, from the Isaac engineering applications team at NVIDIA, directed Astra to turn stereo camera captures into an editable OpenUSD studio. The workflow combined PyCuSFM, FoundationStereo and nvblox for reconstruction, with user review guiding object selection and placement. Astra assembled generated and Blender-authored assets and used USD Content Agents to configure how objects move and interact in simulation. Isaac Sim tests guided collision and contact revisions for doors and drawers. The studio connects captured geometry to interaction testing, making gaps and object behavior easier to inspect. Explore USD Content Agents. Have a simulation idea? Explore NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to start building with an AI agent.
